papers.abstract: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.
bullets: A rule-based reader answers only a fraction of questions correctly from the graph, revealing substantial memory loss and reading errors.
Four targeted graph repairs improve answerability from 27.2% to 37.4% and retrained QA accuracy from 71.4% to 75.9%.
Better object F1 does not necessarily improve answerability, showing that standard graph metrics can misrepresent QA utility.
A question-type prior outperforms the reader on every predicted graph, and graph memory reduces accuracy in one real-video test.
Findings are exploratory and based mainly on simulated multi-room scenes, with limited real-video validation.

papers.title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
papers.tldr: Vision-language scene graphs retain useful but unreliable memory for embodied QA, so evaluation should measure answerability—not accuracy alone.

papers.abstract: Language agents trained from self-generated experience must allocate a limited rollout budget across heterogeneous capabilities. A common strategy is to prioritize capabilities with strong current learning signals, but in on-policy learning these signals are endogenous: past allocation changes the policy and therefore the evidence available for future allocation. This can create a feedback loop in which under-trained capabilities receive increasingly fewer opportunities to improve. We formalize this effect through the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL), which shows that allocation history can change learning efficiency even under matched capability-specific exposure. Motivated by this, we introduce FEAST, a task-free adaptive sampling framework that separates opportunity allocation from compute allocation. FEAST dynamically discovers capability clusters while preserving their learning histories, maintains continued sampling opportunities across clusters, and reserves a rollout budget for each selected cluster. Within each budget, it progressively concentrates computation on prompts with informative reward variation. Across GURU-18K and SMC, FEAST improves average performance over competitive adaptive sampling baselines under matched rollout budgets, while better preserving learning progress on weaker capabilities. Ablation studies further support the complementary roles of cross-cluster opportunity protection and within-cluster selective allocation. Code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: On-policy allocation signals are endogenous, creating feedback loops that can starve under-trained capabilities.
The Quota-Efficiency Law formalizes how allocation history affects learning efficiency even with matched capability exposure.
FEAST separates opportunity allocation from compute allocation, dynamically clusters capabilities, and preserves their learning histories.
It reserves rollout budgets across selected clusters, then prioritizes prompts with informative reward variation within each budget.

Across GURU-18K and SMC, FEAST improves average performance over adaptive-sampling baselines under matched rollout budgets and better preserves weaker capabilities; ablations support both allocation mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Reliable language-guided perception is essential for embodied agents, where questions about objects, events, and their locations must be answered from long observation histories. Unlike conventional visual question answering, realistic robotic settings require reasoning over extended temporal horizons and persistent scene memory. We build upon the view-based memory paradigm and propose an efficient framework for long-horizon spatio-temporal question answering. While existing view-based systems typically store either text captions or visual embeddings, we extend the ReMEmbR-style memory with image paths that link each stored description to its original visual content. To make the stored annotations more informative, we replace uniform sampling during memory construction with an optical-flow-based frame selection strategy (PSFR) and store an object-centric descriptive scene representation instead of plain captions. We further equip a VLM-based agent with an adaptive retrieval tool that returns the image associated with the most relevant caption, allowing the agent to decide when visual inspection is needed. On the OC-NaVQA benchmark, LVMem outperforms ReMEmbR on binary and positional metrics with both backbones and matches or exceeds a 4D scene graph DAAAM baseline on binary accuracy, while operating on a lightweight view-based memory that requires no explicit graph construction.
bullets: Targets spatio-temporal reasoning over extended observation histories in embodied-agent question answering.
Extends view-based memory with image paths connecting stored descriptions to their original visual content.
Uses optical-flow-based frame selection (PSFR) and object-centric scene descriptions instead of uniform sampling and plain captions.
Adds an adaptive VLM retrieval tool that decides when to inspect the associated image.
On OC-NaVQA, outperforms ReMEmbR on binary and positional metrics and matches or exceeds DAAAM on binary accuracy without explicit graph construction.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed pipeline. Each temporal segment is processed by PSFR, which selects the most informative frames; the first selected frame is stored as an image path alongside the resulting object-centric scene description. At query time, the VLM agent invokes a visual retrieval tool that returns the image paired with the most relevant description, enabling joint reasoning over textual and visual evidence to reason jointly over both modalities.

Fig. 3. A question asking for the color of a horse sculpture. Text-based baselines describe the sculpture as “metal” and “reflective” and cannot determine its color. LVMem retrieves the corresponding frame and answers correctly based on the visible brown tone.

Fig. 1. Proposed LVMem approach. A long video sequence is divided into fixed-length segments, from which PSFR selects the most informative frames. An object-centric textual scene representation generator produces one scene description per segment from its selected frames, which is stored in memory alongside the segment’s timestamp, pose, and image path. For a given query, the VLM agent calls the image retrieval tool to obtain the image linked to the most relevant description, enabling joint reasoning over visual and textual evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robots to reason about semantic and spatio-temporal context, verify task-relevant objects, and guide sensing and navigation. Persistent memory can reduce redundant search for field robots, but when should a memory continue to guide behavior? Repeated misses may suggest that a memory is stale. Our experiments show why this evidence can remain ambiguous under VLM-based perception. Using a Boston Dynamics Spot with four fixed cameras and a persistent spatio-temporal visual memory, we measure negative-verification behavior across targets, viewpoints, language queries, and repeated revisits. False-negative rates vary substantially across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same detector outcome, and some matched target-present and target-removed experiments yield identical miss histories. This ambiguity persists under changed observation geometry, identity-preserving query reformulation, and conditioning on a previously verified target image. These findings raise two questions: is the object still there, and is this memory still useful for navigation? We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible memory-update mechanism that avoids double-counting correlated misses and stops using unsupported memories as direct navigation goals without claiming that the object is absent. Later positive evidence can restore a memory's use for navigation. One resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification, semantic frontier reasoning, and in-motion perception. In three matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local baseline selected a stale memory as its navigation objective in every case, whereas our method selected semantic frontiers in all three. A complementary trial re-verified the target during motion and promoted fresh memory. These results support revising memory actionability rather than interpreting failed detection as object absence.
authors: Sumukh Shrote, Shenbagaraj Kannapiran, Eric Eaton, Camillo Jose Taylor
bullets: VLM-based negative detections are ambiguous: false-negative rates vary, repeated nearby views can reproduce misses, and target-present and target-removed scenes may look identical.
The proposed dependence-aware, reversible updates avoid double-counting correlated misses and stop unsupported memories from serving as direct navigation goals.
Semantic frontiers become alternatives when memory confidence is insufficient; later positive evidence can restore navigation use.
On a Spot robot in three matched decision contexts, the baseline chose a stale memory every time, while the proposed method chose semantic frontiers in all three.
A motion-time recheck demonstrated that fresh positive evidence can promote memory again.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Persistent semantic-navigation system architecture. The robot combines four fixed cameras, persistent CLIP/FAISS visual memory, semantic frontier exploration, and a shared resident VLM. Historical observations are retrieved and strictly reverified before they can influence navigation. Negative evidence updates memory actionability from VERIFIED ACTIVE to SUSPECT and eventually DORMANT UNTRUSTED, while later strict positive evidence can restore navigation authority. When no trusted memory remains, the system selects a semantic frontier instead. A single resident Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct instance is shared across target verification, memory verification, frontier reasoning, and asynchronous perception during motion.

Fig. 1. Memory is not ground truth. A previously verified object can fail current VLM verification either because the environment has changed or because perception has failed. An episode-local policy forgets earlier failed verification and can repeatedly revisit the same remembered location. Our method instead revises the memory’s navigation authority without asserting that the object is absent, redirects search toward a semantically selected frontier, and preserves the memory for future positive evidence. The inset in (c) shows frontier candidates in the deployed 2-D navigation representation.

Fig. 3. Repeated VLM misses are redundant and can be ambiguous with respect to physical object state. In E2, Spot repeatedly leaves and returns to human-visible target viewpoints; nearby revisits frequently preserve the previous verifier outcome, with 90.0% of adjacent observations producing the same result. In E3, the corresponding objects are physically removed and the same anchor regions are revisited. For the three blue-chair anchors C1-C3, both target-present and target-removed conditions produce the identical six-observation history MMMMMM. Thus, the deployed detector observations alone cannot distinguish the two physical states.

papers.selection_reason: Persistent spatio-temporal memory for semantic navigation with VLM-based verification, fitting embodied memory and vision-language navigation.
papers.title: Memory Is Not Ground Truth: Revising Navigation Authority under Unreliable VLM Evidence for Persistent Semantic Navigation
papers.tldr: Robots should reduce a memory’s navigation authority after correlated detection failures without assuming the remembered object is absent.

papers.abstract: Dexterity is, at its core, finger-level control, yet existing dexterous manipulation and human-object interaction (HOI) generation methods rarely let one specify how an interaction is performed: five-fingered hands are often reduced to grippers, or finger usage is copied from individual human demonstrations. We present FineDex, a framework that makes finger-level intent both expressible and executable. FineDex learns coordinated human body, hand, and object motions that follow fine-grained instructions on hand selection, individual fingers, and contacts with articulated objects. To bridge generation and execution, FineDex leverages generated interactions as actionable priors for an agent that discovers physically feasible contact strategies through practice in a physics-based digital twin. By adapting at test time without per-instance retraining, FineDex generalizes across fine-grained instructions and object configurations. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art HOI generation quality and fine-grained controllability, substantial improvements in dexterous manipulation success, and successful deployment on a real dexterous humanoid robot.
authors: Yujia Zeng, Yuxin Chen, Yuzhen Song, Runhan Huang, Chensheng Peng, Yiyang Shao, Koushil Sreenath, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit control over hand choice, individual fingers, and contacts in existing HOI generation and manipulation methods.
Jointly generates coordinated human body, hand, and articulated-object motions conditioned on fine-grained interaction instructions.
Uses generated interactions as actionable priors for physics-based practice to discover feasible contact strategies.
Adapts at test time across instructions and object configurations without per-instance retraining.
Reports state-of-the-art HOI generation and controllability, improved manipulation success, and real humanoid-robot deployment.

papers.abstract: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.
authors: Jiacheng Zhang, Qixing Zhou, Haiyang Wang, Qipeng Gu, Shuzhe Wu, Feiyang Pan, Lue Fan, Dandan Tu, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses unstable mixed-task learning, inefficient rollout allocation, and continual domain expansion without separate specialists or distillation.
Uses a quota-based asynchronous rollout scheduler to balance gradient contributions and reduce off-policy effects across task domains.
Introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling to prioritize samples by mastery, encouraging frontier exploration while preserving learned capabilities.
Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5-27B improves from 43.6 to 54.2 and then 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier of Qwen3.8-27B.
Outperforms single-task RL while using less compute for policy updates, supporting MixRL as a compute-efficient post-training approach.

papers.abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting, the drastic loss of previously acquired capabilities when learning new ones, is a central challenge in language model fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely believed to be prone to such forgetting. Recent works have attributed this to the off-policy nature of SFT, arguing that on-policy learning is key to continual learning. In this paper, we challenge this premise. We show that while maximizing new-task performance can induce catastrophic forgetting, alternative hyperparameter choices (lower learning rate and batch size) can yield similar gains with little to no forgetting. With hyperparameters selected jointly for gain and retention, vanilla SFT retains prior capabilities far better than previously suggested and can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), an on-policy approach designed to mitigate forgetting. While SDFT can be more robust to hyperparameter choices, it also requires a retention-aware criterion to identify hyperparameter configurations that avoid catastrophic forgetting. Our results challenge the view that on-policy training is what enables learning with retention and raise broader questions about what drives catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.
authors: Nirmit Joshi, Nathan Srebro, Eran Malach
bullets: SFT can forget substantially when hyperparameters are chosen solely to maximize new-task performance.
Lower learning rates and batch sizes can achieve similar gains while greatly reducing forgetting.
Jointly tuning for gain and retention makes vanilla SFT more retention-friendly than previously believed.
SFT can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning, though SDFT is more robust to hyperparameter choices.
Both approaches require retention-aware evaluation to avoid configurations that cause catastrophic forgetting.

papers.selection_reason: Challenges catastrophic forgetting assumptions in SFT, relevant to continual learning and retention.
papers.title: Tune for Retention, Not Just Gain: SFT Forgets Far Less than You Think
papers.tldr: Catastrophic forgetting in SFT is often a hyperparameter problem: tuning for both task gains and retention can preserve prior capabilities with little forgetting, sometimes matching on-policy SDFT.

papers.abstract: Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4. In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection. On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
authors: Praveen Kumar Bodigutla, Yizhi Zhang, Sai Vivek Kanaparthy, Arup De
bullets: OKF-indexed memory organizes interactions by lineage to retrieve temporally and project-relevant episodes.
Procedure Memory learns reusable hiring decision procedures through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning.
OKF retrieval reaches 0.93–0.95 low-priority preference F1 and uses 69% fewer context tokens than full-history context.
Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39%; on PersonaMem-v2, the combined approach reaches 50.2% accuracy with 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history.
Smaller Jev-class models improve efficiency but more often miss temporally relevant evidence, emphasizing evidence selection.

papers.abstract: Effective robotic manipulation calls for multimodal memory and rapid adaptation to shifts in contact dynamics. However, many existing policies, which retain either visual or wrench history, may miss key cues from the other modality. Moreover, even with wrench memory, fixed policies can struggle when contact conditions shift at deployment. To this end, we introduce M$^{2}$AdaptVLA, a vision-language-action model that integrates visual and wrench memories with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, the model uses test-time training (TTT) to encode observation history in fast weights. Each entry in the bounded TTT bank combines the corresponding frame's features with a readout from these weights, preserving cues that predate the oldest retained frame. For wrench memory, a context gate controls how much the action expert draws on wrench history as it jointly denoises future actions and wrenches. For predictive test-time adaptation, the auxiliary wrench prediction loss also provides online self-supervision. Using measured wrenches as targets, we update low-rank policy adapters by backpropagating only through the final denoising step. Real-world experiments show that the TTT bank outperforms visual memory baselines on progress tracking, scene recall, and demonstration following. On contact-sensitive tasks, the context gate yields higher success rates than direct injection or gated cross-attention. Predictive test-time adaptation improves robustness to shifts in contact dynamics. On eight tasks requiring visual and wrench memory, M$^{2}$AdaptVLA achieves a mean success rate of 82.71%, a 31.46% absolute gain over the strongest baseline. The project page is available at https://tlf-tlf.github.io/M2AdaptVLAPage/.

Achieves an 82.71% mean success rate across eight visual-and-wrench-memory tasks, a 31.46-point gain over the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.
authors: Qishuai Wen, Rui Chen, Haiwen Li, Zhiyuan Huang, Qiwen Gu, Bingjie Gao, Geng Li, Jing Tang, Xiangxiang Chu, Chun-Guang Li
bullets: Addresses the high rollout costs and sparse rewards of agentic reinforcement learning at test time.
Creates a closed loop where a supervisor provides natural-language feedback and a hypernetwork converts it into parameter updates.
Combines dense verbal supervision with in-parameter adaptation rather than relying only on in-context learning.
On ALFWorld and WebShop, Qwen3-4B vSFT achieves higher success rates than GRPO and Reflexion.
The approach is evaluated for self-improving agents, with scope limited to the reported benchmark tasks and comparisons.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of our proposed vSFT. Given a task, the hypernetwork first internalizes the system prompt and few-shot examples into an initial LoRA adapter, and then progressively incorporates the supervisor’s feedback through subsequent trial-and-error iterations, thereby adapting the agent over time.

Figure 3 Hypernetwork meta-training pipeline. The curated dataset (right panel) is essentially an SFT dataset, but consists of condition-query-response triplets rather than query-response pairs. This design trains the hypernetwork to convert verbal feedback into LoRA adapters that effectively steer the agent’s behavior (left panel).

Figure 9 Illustration of hypernetwork-based parameter adaptation. The textual content to be internalized is first processed by the base model in a single forward pass to collect its key-value states in attention layers. The hypernetwork then uses these states to generate LoRA adapters, which are applied to the down-projection weight matrices of the FFN layers.

Figure 6 Comparisons on JSONSchemaBench. Figure 8 Training loss and success rates across epochs. We train the hypernetwork on ALFWorld’s training split (left panel) and evaluate on the two validation splits (right panel).

Figure 7 Task-agnostic and persistent improvement. Unlike our default setting, where each failed task has a separate LoRA adapter, we adapt the agent using a single LoRA adapter obtained by merging task-specific adapters collected from one of four splits: ALFWorld’s seen and unseen splits and WebShop’s evaluation and test splits. The adapted agent is evaluated either on the same split used for merging (in-split) or on the other split of the same benchmark (held-out). papers.title: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
papers.tldr: vSFT lets agents improve at test time by turning verbal feedback on failed trajectories into low-rank weight updates.

papers.abstract: Robots executing tasks in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty while operating with incomplete skills. Inspired by human curiosity, we investigate how robots can formulate task-relevant hypotheses, seek evidence, and acquire missing skills during task execution. We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, which operationalizes curiosity as selecting investigations that resolve task uncertainty and expand executable capabilities. Four modules connect dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. The planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition/execution cost. Missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission during acquisition; separate checks verify physical effects and acquired evidence. Newly admitted skills expand the executable investigation set, closing the loop between resolving uncertainty and acquiring capabilities. Simulation and real-robot experiments evaluate investigation, skill acquisition, and task execution. CHASE achieves 50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps, with 70-90% evidence resolution.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Wei Zhang, Chenlei Zhu, Naiyu Chen, Xihua Wang, Jie Chen
bullets: Targets task execution when robots face both incomplete information and missing capabilities.
Combines scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, skill acquisition, and verified execution.
Selects investigations by balancing information value, skill reuse, and acquisition or execution cost.
Uses bounded exploration, verified learning segments, and checks for physical effects and evidence validity.
Simulation and real-robot experiments report 50–80% task success and 70–90% evidence resolution under combined gaps.

papers.selection_reason: Curiosity-driven skill acquisition for robots, directly relevant to embodied learning.
papers.title: CHASE: Curiosity-Guided Skill Acquisition for Embodied Task Execution
papers.tldr: CHASE enables robots to resolve uncertainty and acquire missing skills on demand while executing tasks in partially observed environments.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.
authors: Wei Chen, Xiaodong Lu, Weihao Shen, Gongxun Li, Xingyu Guo, Qihang Sun, Fuwei Zhang, Zhao Zhang, Yikun Ban, Shuang Li, Deqing Wang, Fuzhen Zhuang
bullets: Targets limitations of streaming benchmarks with short or mostly independent task sequences.
Covers office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows with persistent workspaces and task dependencies.
Separates language-expressible knowledge acquisition (L1) from task-level capability development through execution and feedback (L2).
Analyzes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and reuse of experience in later tasks.
Findings show inconsistent framework performance, limited retry recovery, and that persistence or improvement on one task does not reliably transfer to others.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces EvoLink-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams, a critical area for research in continual and online learning.
papers.title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
papers.tldr: EvoLink-Bench evaluates whether LLM agents can learn and reuse experience across long-horizon task streams where later tasks depend on earlier outcomes.

papers.abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.
authors: Yan Lin, Zhongliang Guo, Jingyu Sun, Qiyan Zhao, Ruihong Zeng, Ying Chen, Zhengtao Yao, Yan Wen, Kunyu Peng, Yuxia Wang
bullets: One-call composition is poor: mean accuracy is at most 7.6%, versus 88.2%–100% when using two calls with an explicit intermediate output.
Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but does not eliminate interference, which is not explained by block length or per-token norm alone.
Skills with the same operation are not interchangeable: replacing learned partner blocks sharply reduces composition accuracy despite strong standalone performance.
Repair can harm the original skill, while rehearsal improves retention but provides limited transfer on Qwen2.5-0.5B.
The findings support evaluating compatibility, retention, and transfer—not acquisition alone—when building reusable skill libraries.

papers.selection_reason: Studies skill composition and retention in language models, relevant to continual learning and adaptation.
papers.title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models
papers.tldr: Independently learned soft-prompt skills often fail to compose or transfer reliably, even when each skill works well alone.

papers.abstract: A detector scores candidate detections, but the recall and false alarms at a given confidence threshold depend on the input distribution. We introduce Detector Operating Behavior Inference (DOBI), a second-level inference task: estimating a fixed detector's threshold-dependent, distribution-level operating response from the internal evidence of a single unlabeled image. DOBI treats the detector's threshold response, i.e. recall, false positives, and precision across thresholds, as a latent behavioral state under the current data condition. Controlled data-space sampling probes this state space offline, and a lightweight monitor learns the inverse map from one image to this state, whose single functional output supports multiple operating policies. In a controlled proof of concept with a fixed YOLOv10-Nano person detector and COCO-derived degradations, predicted PR behavior reduces mean absolute deviation from 0.128 for an image-independent mean-behavior prior to 0.054, and predicted functional distances track empirical regime distances (Spearman 0.96). From one unlabeled image, the inferred behavior selects operating points as well as a non-deployable lookup that knows the true regime (macro-regime $F_1$ 0.6604 for both, versus 0.6407 under pristine calibration; oracle 0.6620). On this discrete benchmark, regime-supervised curve lookups are strong controls. Pre-specified continuous and compositional probing shows where functional inference matters: on unseen combinations, the functional decoder has a lower mean curve error than a template lookup, increasingly with distance from the training conditions, whereas the lookup is more accurate for interpolation. These results establish the feasibility of single-image inference of distribution-level detector behavior over the probed conditions. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/dobi
authors: Stefan Becker, Simon Weiss, Wolfgang H\"ubner
bullets: Motivation: detector performance at a confidence threshold varies with the input distribution, but the current distribution is often unlabeled.
Method: offline controlled data-space sampling probes detector behavior, while a lightweight monitor maps one image to the corresponding behavioral response curve.
Contribution: a single inferred functional output supports multiple threshold-selection and operating policies.

In a YOLOv10-Nano proof of concept with COCO-derived degradations, DOBI reduced mean curve deviation from 0.128 to 0.054 and achieved Spearman 0.96 agreement between predicted and empirical regime distances.
Scope: functional inference helped most on unseen combinations and extrapolation, while template lookups were more accurate for interpolation on the discrete benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method (DOBI) to infer detector operating behavior (recall, precision) from a single unlabeled image. This is a form of test-time adaptation, fitting the Adaptation and Memory taxonomy.
papers.title: Detector Operating Behavior Inference via Data-Space Sampling
papers.tldr: DOBI infers a detector’s threshold-dependent recall, false positives, and precision from a single unlabeled image, enabling data-aware operating-point selection under changing conditions.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. Project Page: https://marslab-navigent.github.io/navigent.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/MarsLab-Navigent/Navigent
authors: Xinyu Zhou, Weiren Cai, Yitong Chen, Shenghai Yuan, Zihang Mu, Boyu Ma, Jiahua Dong, Yanshuo Lu, Jiaqi Bai, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Addresses unreliable long-horizon navigation, including mismatches between commanded and actual motion and missed landmarks or entrances.
Uses a frozen multimodal large language model with a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC).
GEC checks action-to-motion consistency and motion-to-landmark consistency using visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates.
Detected discrepancies trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery; historical visual memory tracks progress.
Reports 84.0%/86.0% success rate and 72.9%/69.1% SPL on R2R-CE/RxR-CE validation-unseen splits, respectively.

papers.abstract: Cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval suffers from substantial performance degradation on new subjects due to subject shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this shift by adapting pretrained models with unlabeled target-subject EEG. However, most existing TTA methods struggle to match supervision granularity to each query's prediction confidence, leaving many queries without reliable pseudo-labels. To address this, we propose a novel framework named Hierarchical Selective Test-Time Adaptation (HSTTA). HSTTA builds a hierarchy over gallery image embeddings, uses hierarchical selective prediction to assign each EEG query a supervision granularity matching its current prediction confidence, and constructs adaptation objectives accordingly. We further propose Cross-Session Consistency Calibration (CSCC), an unsupervised method that calibrates the global confidence threshold to target a predefined accuracy level for hierarchical predictions. Moreover, we introduce Reciprocal Hierarchical Backoff (RHB), which moves queries lacking reverse-matching support to coarser nodes to mitigate error reinforcement. Experiments on two public benchmarks and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of HSTTA and its key components. On THINGS-EEG2, HSTTA outperforms the strongest EEG-specific TTA baseline by 17.9 (13.4) and 8.9 (3.7) percentage points in Top-1/Top-5 accuracy, respectively, under cosine (CSLS) ranking. Further analyses show that HSTTA yields more accurate pseudo-labels during adaptation, supporting more reliable model updates.
authors: Hongzhou Chen, Yuhao Wei, Lianghua He, Yihang Liu, Zengqiang Wang
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by subject shift in new-subject EEG retrieval.
Builds a hierarchy over gallery images and selects prediction granularity according to each query’s confidence.
Uses Cross-Session Consistency Calibration to set confidence thresholds without labels.
Uses Reciprocal Hierarchical Backoff to move unsupported queries to coarser categories and reduce error reinforcement.
Validated on two public benchmarks; on THINGS-EEG2, it improves over the strongest EEG-specific TTA baseline by up to 17.9 percentage points in Top-1 accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet adapting them to sequential tasks requires Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). Existing replay-free methods expand prompts or routed LoRA experts across multi-layer decoders, incurring heavy parameter and routing overhead while shifting internal feature distributions. Instead, we identify the final linear layer of the vision-language projector as a high-capacity, coordinate-stationary bridge, where sequential updates easily induce interface drift by displacing historical visual tokens. While low-rank subspace adaptation offers a compact remedy, selecting directions solely from historical statistics or task gradients sacrifices plasticity or stability, and unconstrained multi-step updates still accumulate large drift. To resolve both issues, we propose Projector Refinement through Optimized Update Directions (PROUD), a continual subspace optimization framework for the terminal projector layer. At task onset, PROUD combines retained input statistics with initial gradients to analytically extract a metric-orthonormal subspace maximizing first-order task gain under a drift budget. During training, it regularizes updates within this fixed subspace via an exact Frobenius penalty before losslessly merging them with zero inference or routing overhead. Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones show that PROUD outperforms recent replay-free baselines in continual accuracy while curbing forgetting with a fraction of trainable parameters.
authors: Hao Yu, Quan Cheng, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Targets interface drift in the projector’s final linear layer, where sequential updates can displace historical visual-token representations.
Analytically selects a metric-orthonormal subspace using retained input statistics and initial task gradients under a drift budget.
Constrains training updates to this fixed subspace with an exact Frobenius penalty, then merges them without inference or routing overhead.
Experiments on UCIT and CoIN across MLLM backbones report higher continual accuracy and less forgetting than replay-free baselines, using fewer trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation transfers pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to new domains using a small set of labeled images. Most methods fit prompts, representations, or classifiers within an adaptation procedure specified in advance. Yet the visual distinctions needed for recognition can differ substantially across domains, motivating the question: Can an LLM agent use few-shot examples and model observations to design the adaptation procedure itself? We propose Agentic Model Editing (AME), an agentic framework that jointly designs input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting as an executable, domain-customized adaptation program. The agent inspects images, class semantics, model parameters, intermediate representations, and activations to formulate hypotheses about the target task. It implements and tests candidate programs on the support set, with aggregate validation accuracy guiding refinement and selection. Each program fits a complete domain model that is fixed before testing. The agent and its tools are shared across domains, while each domain receives its own adaptation program. Across eleven datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16, AME achieves the highest average accuracies of 81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with back-propagation among the compared methods. Further experiments demonstrate applicability across VLM backbones and LLM agents.
authors: Yusheng Zhao, Xiao Luo, Zhiping Xiao, Ming Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed adaptation procedures when visual distinctions vary across domains.
The agent inspects images, class semantics, model internals, representations, and activations to form adaptation hypotheses.
It jointly designs input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting, then iteratively tests programs on support data.
Each selected program is fixed before testing, while the agent and tools are shared across domains.
Across 11 datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16, AME reports average accuracies of 81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with it, and also works across backbones and LLM agents.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions. Procedures that determine actions from the current scene address this, but when they meet conditions that earlier attempts did not cover, revising them requires the measured effects of earlier actions. We therefore propose SEEK, an agentic framework that retains both, enabling robots to improve across attempts while keeping the underlying model fixed. To adapt retained knowledge to the current scene, SEEK adopts a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) that encodes manipulation as executable procedures and determines each action from current observations. As the robot executes these procedures, SEEK records the measured effects of its actions, including those from failed attempts, in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB). Where a retained procedure applies, it acts without a model request; where it meets a condition it does not cover, this evidence guides its revision. On RoboDojo, knowledge retained over ten attempts raises SEEK's average task score from 27.0 to 54.4 and its success rate from 19.7% to 48.0% across all 42 tasks. On 34 of these tasks with GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the same model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. https://zeyangguan.github.io/SEEK-Agentic-Robot-Manipulation/
authors: Zeyang Guan, Qihao Zhao, Rui Gong, Zhang Haitian, Yalun Dai, Yangyu Huang, Lingao Xiao, Haozhe Du, Xuehui Yu, Ye Lu, Jianjun Gao, Ruoyu Wang, Haowen Bai, Hao Li, Scarlett Li, Kim-Hui Yap
bullets: Addresses the problem of robots repeating mistakes because execution knowledge is lost when a task ends.
Uses a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy to choose actions from current scene observations.
Stores measured effects—including failures—in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank to revise procedures when needed.
Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, ten retained attempts increased average score from 27.0 to 54.4 and success rate from 19.7% to 48.0%.
With GPT-6.2 Astra on 34 tasks, SEEK reached 80.1 after five attempts versus 49.6 for direct acting, while using 77.6% fewer model requests.

papers.abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.
authors: Xiaoyang Lv, Peixin Wang, Jianhao Bai, Bai Xue, Min Zhang, Luke Ong
bullets: Addresses deployment-time safety failures caused by previously unseen obstacles or changed constraints.

Across four benchmarks and five new obstacles, repair succeeded in all cases within tens of seconds on average, while retraining from scratch usually failed.
When retraining succeeded, the proposed method was 17.3× faster on average, with 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical context, yet retaining extensive visual histories incurs growing storage and retrieval costs, while aggressive compression risks losing fine-grained information needed for subsequent decisions. Moreover, executed action histories capture intermediate behaviors that sparse visual observations may miss. Preserving this complementary context efficiently calls for modality-specific memory mechanisms that balance recent detail with long-term retention. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM, a world-action model equipped with hierarchical visual and interaction memories. $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM preserves recent visual observations in dense short-term memory while consolidating entries evicted from this window into fixed-size associative long-term memory through gated delta updates. Within the same short- and long-term hierarchy, interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations, complementing visual observations with behavioral context. These complementary memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise retrieval, enabling memory-augmented action generation with a bounded online memory footprint independent of episode length. On the memory-dependent simulation benchmarks MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves +53.2% and +61.2% absolute improvements in average success rates over Fast-WAM, respectively. These gains extend to real-world manipulation, where $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves a +29.3% absolute improvement over LingBot-VA in average success across three tasks. These results suggest that $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM offers a promising approach to efficient memory-augmented world-action modeling.
authors: Xiaopeng Zhang, Weiqi Yuan, Xin Zhu, Jiaxi Huang, Yueqi Hu, Yin Zhang, Jian Yao, Yanjie Li
bullets: Addresses the storage, retrieval, and information-loss challenges of retaining long visual histories, while capturing behavioral context missing from sparse observations.
Uses dense short-term visual memory and fixed-size associative long-term memory updated through gated delta consolidation.
Encodes executed action prefixes in a matching short-/long-term interaction-memory hierarchy.
Integrates visual and interaction memories through layer-wise retrieval for memory-augmented action generation with episode-length-independent online memory.
Reports absolute average-success improvements of 53.2% and 61.2% over Fast-WAM on MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, and 29.3% over LingBot-VA across three real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence. We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification. The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.
authors: Chao Chen, Fuqi Lin, Ze Chen, Ziyan Liu, Chen Li, Haishu Jiang, Bo Xu, Zihan Jiang, Yue Wu, Zheng Wang, Kun Wang, Zhihang Fu, Jieping Ye

Evolves models through coverage expansion, error-targeted synthesis, trajectory distillation, filtering, supervised fine-tuning, and post-RL refinement.
Evolves prompts and skills from recurring failures, with audits, replay, regression tests, and performance safeguards.
In a live product, it improved factual correctness by 10.5 points, answer length by 158.1%, and reduced latency by 41.3%; 30 rounds increased aggregate score by 10.8 points.

papers.abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.
authors: Bingqing Liu, Wei Liu, Zhiying Deng, Jun Wang, Yuhua Li, Ruixuan Li
bullets: Sequential model editing often causes catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only hundreds of edits.
Batch editing remains effective across tens of thousands of edits while preserving general capabilities.
The paper analyzes accumulated weight perturbations to explain degradation in existing sequential methods.
Existing methods show linear or logarithmic perturbation growth, while the proposed approach maintains time-invariant growth.
This behavior provides a theoretical guarantee of long-term stability and preservation of pretrained knowledge during large-scale editing.

papers.abstract: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 {\deg}C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.
bullets: Targets one untuned HVAC policy that operates unseen office buildings using metadata and sensor streams only.
Initializes first-order grey-box zone models from floor-plan coefficients and updates them online with recursive least squares.

Ablations show that either floor-plan information or online identification recovers most of the benefit of using both.
Results do not fully transfer to BOPTEST: online identification makes the priors comparable, while the floor-plan-only controller is least stable.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
authors: Tianmai M. Zhang, Hoda Shajari, Amr Hendy, Xiaohu Liu, Piyush Behre, Omar Zia Khan, Ankur Gupta
bullets: Studies how success- and failure-derived procedural memories support continual adaptation across heterogeneous, multi-domain tool-use tasks.
Introduces a retrieval-free workflow with customizable reflection, memory generation from both outcome types, and periodic consolidation under fixed capacity.
Online evaluation finds failure memory broadens coverage, success memory improves execution efficiency, and combining both captures both benefits.
Shows cross-domain memory generalization and continual adaptation over long task streams.
External evaluation on EvoMemBench supports DualPM’s portability as a general long-term procedural memory method.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.
authors: Keyan Guo, Rupam Patir, Haipeng Cai, Hongxin Hu
bullets: Coding agents often fix vulnerabilities when shown a failing security test but frequently reintroduce the same flaw in later sessions.
Persistent repair records and generic secure-coding principles do not reliably transfer lessons to new code.
PRECEPT evolves an agent-specific library of security principles by revising them against the agent’s own failures.
Revisions are retained only when fresh executions improve security while keeping functional success within a small tolerance.
On unseen task families, the weakest PRECEPT agent achieved 97.1% secure working code, versus 81.9% for the strongest unaided agent and 87.7% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Freezing older adapters does not ensure that a continual learner will select and use them properly at inference time. When multiple adapters exist, routing among them and identifying the adapter whose representation space matches the query's answer can be difficult. We propose CONTLORA, which replaces stored examples with compact class statistics for adapter selection and classification. Gaussian class models in a frozen representation select LoRA adapters, while accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features. Trained without retaining images or feature vectors, CONTLORA reaches 88.55% accuracy on 20-task CIFAR-100 and 86.99% on CUB-200. Across three benchmarks in the matched component study, its mean final accuracy differs from an independently trained stored-feature counterpart by at most 0.07 percentage points. Ablations show that improved task coverage need not improve classification and adapter composition also matters. On held-out classes, competitor-centered likelihood scores improve novelty AUROC over raw likelihood without altering routing ranks. These results support statistical memory as an alternative to example-retention approaches in the evaluated settings, while identifying task ambiguity as an ongoing limitation.
authors: Alireza Heidari, Thomas Veasey, Mariano Tepper
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of selecting the appropriate adapter when multiple frozen adapters are available.
Models classes with Gaussian statistics in a frozen representation for adapter routing.
Accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features.
Achieves 88.55% on 20-task CIFAR-100 and 86.99% on CUB-200; it closely matches stored-feature performance across three benchmarks.
Improves novelty detection with competitor-centered likelihood scores, while task ambiguity remains a limitation.

papers.abstract: Concept drift detection is a fundamental component of data stream learning, yet its empirical evaluation remains based on loosely defined protocols, ambiguous alarm semantics, and inconsistent metrics. We propose a principled benchmark grounded in an explicit formulation of drift observability and alarm semantics. Our framework introduces finite detection windows and repeated alarms, enabling a clear separation between detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, and employs a reproducible observer to provide a controlled and interpretable performance signal. Building on this formulation, we define normalized evaluation metrics and a composite score addressing limitations of existing measures. We validate the framework through a large-scale stress-testing evaluation of 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.
authors: Lorenzo Iovine, Giacomo Ziffer, Emanuele Della Valle
bullets: Addresses ambiguous alarm semantics, loosely defined protocols, and inconsistent metrics in drift-detector evaluation.
Defines drift observability and alarm semantics using finite detection windows and repeated alarms.
Separates detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, with a reproducible observer for controlled evaluation.
Introduces normalized metrics and a composite score to address limitations of existing measures.
Stress-tests 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.

papers.abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of choosing one model for tasks containing both easy and difficult subtasks.
Uses past runs to estimate recurring subtask quality and cost for each model, producing delegation guidance controlled by δ.
The lead model decides during execution which subtasks to delegate; neither model requires training.
On ViBench, performance increased from 70.2 to 78.5 with 19% lower cost; on Terminal-Bench, pass rate rose from 54% to 61% at similar cost.
Scope: evaluated on held-out ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks, with little implementation overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces partial routing for agentic workflows, delegating subtasks based on past performance, a form of test-time optimization and online adaptation.
papers.title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
papers.tldr: Partial routing lets a capable lead agent delegate selected subtasks to a cheaper model, improving performance while reducing cost without additional training.

papers.abstract: The goal of continual learning (CL) is to adapt to new data (plasticity) while retaining the knowledge acquired from old data (stability). Existing methods are explicitly designed to focus on balancing stability and plasticity to mitigate the challenge of catastrophic forgetting while promoting learning. However, the impact of order and nature of samples from the new data that the network is trained on remains an under explored factor. We argue that a CL algorithm should have the ability to rank incoming samples in terms of their relationship with prior data and their effect on the learning process. In this work, we investigate if scoring and prioritizing incoming data based on their semantic relationships with the model's current knowledge can benefit CL. We propose SACK, short for Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge, a plug and play technique for continual learning methods. SACK dissects categorical knowledge of the model into fine-grained concepts, computes the relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts in each experience, and uses this relationship knowledge for prioritizing new samples. Experiments across several types of CL methods (regularization, replay, and prompt based) in class incremental and task incremental settings demonstrate that integration of SACK not only improves accuracy and reduces forgetting but also handles long tail distribution, helps focus on semantically interpretable regions, and yields better calibrated and robust models compared to prior approaches.
authors: Shivanand Kundargi, Kowshik Thopalli, Tejas Gokhale
bullets: Addresses the underexplored impact of new-sample order and content on stability and plasticity.
Decomposes categorical knowledge into fine-grained concepts and relates old concepts to concepts in each new experience.
Uses these relationships to rank and prioritize samples as a plug-and-play addition to existing CL methods.
Across regularization-, replay-, and prompt-based methods, SACK improves accuracy, reduces forgetting, and supports long-tail data.
It also promotes semantically interpretable focus and produces better-calibrated, more robust models, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 11: Order-permutation robustness across four continual learning baselines (DER & DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020), CoDA-Prompt (Smith et al., 2023), and LwF (Li & Hoiem, 2017)) on CIFAR-100 under the CIL setting. Each method is evaluated with three independent class-order permutations, with shaded regions indicating variability across permutations. In all cases, SACK consistently improves both mean accuracy and stability across experiences, demonstrating that the order-robustness observed with iCaRL in the main paper generalizes across diverse CL frameworks.

Figure 1: Overview of SACK: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge. Given a model after experience t, we extract human-interpretable visual concepts from its internal representations and compare them with the concepts describing the incoming classes. SACK computes class-wise semantic relevance scores that prioritize examples whose concepts align closely with previously learned knowledge. These concept-aligned sampling weights guide the training of experience t+1, forming a lightweight curriculum that improves accuracy, stability, and interpretability across continual learning streams.

Figure 10: Effect of varying the concept-selection threshold τ on SACK with different continual learning baselines (LwF (Li & Hoiem, 2017), CODA-Prompt (Smith et al., 2023), DER and DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020)). For each method, we report mean CIL accuracy using SACK with τ ∈ 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, along with the original baseline performance shown as a dashed red line. Across all τ values, SACK remains consistently above the baseline, indicating that our method is not sensitive to the exact choice of concept threshold.

Figure 5: Analysis of robustness of SACK across diverse and challenging scenarios in the CIL setting with CIFAR100. (A) demonstrates that SACK is robust to the choice of the threshold τ which determines the number of concepts selected after performing CLIP-Dissect; (B) Performance of SACK under noisy concepts, which we simulate by corrupting a subset of concepts after each experience, demonstrates that SACK is resilient to concept noise. (C) Effect of perturbed class orderings across experiences. Even with shuffled class orders, SACK consistently outperforms the baseline, demonstrating robustness to task ordering. We observe similar trend on other methods. Please refer to Appendix, for additional analysis on other models and datasets in both CIL and TIL settings.
