papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.
authors: Luiz G. A. Alves, Aaron Vermeersch
bullets: LLMs can give incorrect answers with high confidence, making reliable confidence estimates important for high-stakes automation.
The approach trains a linear confidence head on the frozen backbone’s final-layer hidden state; text-only metamodels support closed models.
On graded answers drawn mostly from SQuAD and partly from TruthfulQA, the confidence head outperforms evaluated baselines and metamodels for high-accuracy gating.
Prompted confidence scores may appear calibrated but lack sufficient resolution for thresholding.
Transfer to unseen datasets is modest, though the confidence head is the most robust approach in the study.

figures.caption: Figure 2: LLM architecture and new confidence score head. The confidence score head reads the final-layer hidden state h ∈ R2304 at the last token of the concatenated prompt and generated answer and maps it to a probability by standardizing it coordinate-wise to z, then applying a linear layer and a sigmoid. The LLM backbone (gemma-2-2b-it, 26 layers, 4-bit) is frozen during training, and only the parameters of the confidence score head are updated. The answer is generated autoregressively under the output schema and appended to the sequence before the confidence score head reads it. The last position attends over the whole sequence so that a single vector can depend on the answer, the question, and the context together.

Figure 4: Automation performance of the confidence score estimation approaches. a) Accuracy of the automated answers as a function of the acceptance threshold. b) Coverage, i.e., the fraction of answers that are automated, as a function of the acceptance threshold. The star in both panels marks a shared operating point. At threshold 0.53, the confidence score head’s automated answers are 95% accurate and cover 62% of the workload.

Figure 3: ROC curves comparing the classification performance of the confidence score estimation approaches. Values in parentheses indicate each model’s ROC-AUC. The confidence score head is shown in red, the three metamodels in blue, the typed-decision model in green, and the remaining baselines in different shades of gray.

Figure 1: AI agent decision-making. The same agent in both panels retrieves, reasons, and produces an answer. a) All answers are acted on, and every wrong answer reaches the action unchecked. Alternatively, every answer can be routed to a reviewer in a human-in-the-loop approach. In this case, throughput is capped by the reviewers, and no answer is acted on without review. b) A confidence score for each answer gates the action. Answers above a threshold are acted on without review, while those below are routed for human review. The threshold value shown is illustrative.

Table 1: Calibration performance of the confidence score estimation approaches. ECE = expected calibration error. ECE, Brier score, and Reliability are better when lower, whereas Resolution, which measures discrimination, is better when higher. Brackets are 95% bootstrap intervals. The self-score (schema) is computed on its own generation pass (Methods).

Brackets are 95% bootstrap intervals, drawn on a shared resample so that differences between models are paired. The in-domain column repeats the ROC-AUC of Fig. 3, with intervals from Supplementary Table S2.

Table 2: Automation performance at different accuracy targets. Each cell is the coverage, i.e., the percentage of answers accepted at the threshold that reaches the given accuracy target. Accepting every answer gives 81% accuracy at 100% coverage.

papers.abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.
bullets: Targets cases where models identify the correct video moment but express its timestamp incorrectly.
LLM sessions inspect weights and activations to localize the source of errors, such as an MLP layer or separator token.
Edits improve grounding across TimeLens-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B, including larger gains on long videos.
Improving edits outperform same-sized random edits, and edited models run at the original speed.
Scope is limited to the reported timestamp-error cases and evaluated model/session settings.

papers.selection_reason: Repairs video grounding models via LLM-based weight editing, relevant to video understanding and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Temporal Weight Surgery: Repairing Video Grounding with LLM Editors

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive data streams, making edge computing essential for low-latency applications and 5G networks. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable adaptation through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but evolving streams challenge context relevance and computational efficiency. This work introduces SAIL, a framework for sparse adaptation of TFMs that reuses the model's key--value cache between adaptation events. SAIL reconstructs its support set only when drifts in stream structure indicate potential context inadequacy, while the structural representation itself is updated by changes in predictive performance. SAIL combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. Upon adaptation, a context budget is allocated proportionally to class mass, and the most recently updated micro-clusters provide representative observations for refitting. This limits context redundancy and computational cost while preserving recent structural information.
authors: Jo\~ao Neves, Afonso Louren\c{c}o, Lizy K. John, Eric P. Xing, Jo\~ao Gama
bullets: Targets context staleness and computational overhead in streaming IoT and edge-computing settings.
Reuses the model’s key–value cache between adaptation events instead of continuously rebuilding context.
Combines prequential error monitoring with class-specific online micro-clustering to detect structural changes.
Allocates context by class mass and selects recent micro-clusters as representative support examples.
Designed to reduce redundant context and computation while retaining recent stream structure.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SAIL. During routine prediction, the TFM reuses its key–value (KV) cache across successive batches. SAIL combines (i) identifies potential context inadequacy by monitoring changes in class-specific micro-cluster mass and feature-space coverage; (ii) reconstructs contexts, allocating the support-set budget proportionally to class mass and selects the most recently updated micro-clusters; (iii) monitors prequential prediction error and uses backtracking to identify reliable instances for updating the micro-clustering representation. Either drift signal triggers TFM adaptation, with a KV cache rebuilt.

papers.abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.
authors: Yilin Luo, Jin Hwa Lee, Andrew M. Saxe, Antonio Sclocchi
bullets: The study examines whether fine-tuning removes latent representations or merely suppresses their observable behavior.
Using transformers pretrained on a controlled hierarchical grammar and fine-tuned on restricted rules, it identifies two forgetting timescales.
Generation of excluded rules changes rapidly, with the rate linked to token–latent correlation, while their representations initially remain intact.
Representational forgetting occurs much more slowly as network parameters gradually drift.
Similar dynamics appear in a natural-language setting, suggesting the phenomenon may generalize beyond the controlled model.

papers.selection_reason: Studies forgetting timescale separation in LLM fine-tuning, relevant to continual learning and language model behavior.
papers.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning suppresses previously learned behavior quickly, while the underlying representations persist and are forgotten only through much slower parameter drift.

papers.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.
authors: Catarina Botelho, Ant\'onio Farinhas, John Mendon\c{c}a, Areti Vassilopoulos, In\^es Gon\c{c}alves, Maya D'Eon, Hugo Pitorro, Laura Cabello, Carrie Spadine, Nuno M. Guerreiro, Ricardo Rei
bullets: Frames harm by what occurs, who is involved, and when it occurs, separating harm assessment from intervention policy.
Uses clinician validation and LLM judges to support scalable annotation, and finds public benchmarks underrepresent harm directed at the user.
Trains MindGuard2 with supervised short reasoning traces and reinforcement learning that penalizes excessive reasoning length.
Matches the balanced accuracy of a substantially larger model at roughly 10× lower median latency across public benchmarks and real conversations.
Reports low false-positive rates at high recall; releases the guard model, synthetic conversations, and taxonomy-based annotations.

papers.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning

papers.abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.
bullets: AI configuration tuning must balance performance gains against limited search budgets and decision costs.
The study evaluates Jev as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider across eight AI tuning tasks, comparing it with conventional methods and an LLM.
Conventional optimizers rank first in six of eight comparisons, while established predictors outperform Jev in seven.
As a region guider, Jev identifies configurations with lower perplexity than the native tuner.

papers.abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.
bullets: Many failures stem from missing, distorted, or poorly selected context rather than weak inference.
It distinguishes three budgets: training, decision-time computation, and context infrastructure.
The model–infrastructure pair is the key unit of analysis, with context failures categorized by availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization.
A five-operation context lifecycle and utility–cost curves are proposed for evaluating context investments.
The agenda emphasizes grounded reporting, interaction-data and infrastructure costs, and safety for persistent adaptive systems.

papers.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
papers.tldr: Context scaling treats the infrastructure that acquires, represents, selects, and persists deployment state as a distinct frontier for improving AI systems.

papers.abstract: Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Mid-execution instruction changes expose trajectory hijacking: policies remain influenced by non-target task trajectories after a switch.
Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS) queries the same policy with interfering alternative instructions and uses target–counterfactual action differences to redirect behavior.
CAS is training-free, model-agnostic, and evaluated across five VLA/WAM policies, two benchmarks, and real-robot settings.
On CALVIN-Custom-Switch for switching times 15–21, CAS raises π₀.₅ from 5.8% to 54.6%.
CAS-guided successful rollouts provide stronger self-training supervision and improve generalization to unseen later switches.

figures.caption: Figure 5 provides an overview of our approach. CAS is a training-free, model-agnostic inferencetime method for mitigating trajectory hijacking during mid-execution instruction switching. Beyond inference, successful CAS-guided rollouts can be used for self-training, providing de-hijacking supervision and enabling iterative improvement of the underlying policy.

Figure 4: Visualization of trajectory hijacking and instruction-conditioned action contrast. Colors denote four tasks: put the wine bottle on top of the cabinet, put the bowl on top of the cabinet, put the cream cheese in the bowl, and turn on the stove. Colored curves show demonstration trajectories, and same-colored arrows show the corresponding 3D end-effector translational actions projected onto the 2D camera plane. Panels (a,b) show two forms of trajectory hijacking in bowl-tostove switching rollouts, with the first frame at ts and subsequent frames after the switch. In (a), the policy completes the non-target bowl task; in (b), it partially drifts toward the bowl trajectory. Panels (c,d) show instruction-conditioned actions predicted from the same observation under the four task instructions: they nearly overlap in (c) but remain clearly distinguishable in (d).

Figure 1: Illustration of trajectory hijacking and the intuition behind CAS. The robot is first instructed to pick up the red block and starts moving toward it. The instruction is then changed to pick up the blue block. Without CAS, the policy may fail to redirect sufficiently toward the blue block; instead, its post-switch behavior can remain drawn toward the red-block trajectory, a failure mode we refer to as trajectory hijacking. In (c), the dashed red arrow denotes the action predicted under the red-block instruction, and the dashed blue arrow denotes the action predicted under the blue-block instruction. CAS contrasts these two actions, and their difference provides a corrective direction, producing the green corrected action that steers the robot away from the interfering trajectory prior and toward the switched target.
Figure 2: Success rates of OpenVLA-OFT, π0, π0.5, Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA at different switching steps. Performance generally degrades with later switches.

Figure 6: Real-world comparison of mid-execution instruction switching. The instruction switches from picking up the red block to picking up the blue block. Without CAS, insufficient redirection leads to an empty grasp; with CAS, the robot successfully picks up the blue block.

Figure 3: Visualization of attention persistence after instruction switching. We visualize actionto-vision attention in OpenVLA-OFT at the last language-backbone layer (layer 31), averaged over attention heads and action-token positions. At an intermediate execution state, we switch only the instruction while keeping the visual observation unchanged. In both examples, attention remains concentrated on the gripper and the previous target object (red), rather than shifting toward the new target (green), suggesting that visual attention can remain biased toward previously relevant objects despite instruction changes.

Figure 5: Overview of CAS. (a) Under mid-execution instruction switching, strong visual priors can cause the policy to remain drawn toward a non-target trajectory, resulting in trajectory hijacking. (b) Inference-time CAS identifies interfering non-target tasks, uses target–counterfactual action differences to determine where to steer, and trajectory proximity to determine how much to steer. In the red-to-blue block example, the hijacking task happens to coincide with the source task, but this need not hold in general. For clarity, the arrows show a single action from the predicted action chunk. (c) Successful CAS-guided rollouts can be used for self-training (CAS-ST), and this process can be applied iteratively. The blue-boxed comparison illustrates the effect of CAS-ST: given the same observation, the policy produces more task-distinct actions after self-training.

Figure 10: Representative rollout sequences for π0.5. Under instruction intervention, the first grasp attempt is slightly misaligned, but the policy still approaches and interacts with the correct target. Under vision intervention, the policy instead exhibits erratic motion without a clear taskdirected manipulation pattern.

Figure 8: Representative rollout sequences for OpenVLA-OFT. Under instruction intervention, the policy behaves similarly to clean inference and successfully grasps the correct object, whereas under vision intervention the gripper repeatedly translates toward the right without exhibiting a recognizable manipulation behavior.

Figure 9: Representative rollout sequences for π0. Under instruction intervention, the policy still reaches and grasps the correct object, although it does not complete the lift. Under vision intervention, the gripper moves slowly toward the right with substantially reduced motion magnitude.

Figure 12: Representative rollout sequences for LingBot-VA. Under instruction intervention, the policy still executes a coherent manipulation behavior but grasps an object corresponding to a different task. Under vision intervention, the gripper instead drifts toward the right and slightly downward without exhibiting comparable task-like structure.

Figure 11: Representative rollout sequences for Fast-WAM. Under instruction intervention, the first grasp attempt is misaligned, but the policy continues to approach the correct target. Under vision intervention, the robot repeatedly moves toward the basket while rotating, substantially degrading the recognizable task-like manipulation behavior.

Figure 13: Representative mid-execution stop failure after explicit training on the “remain still” instruction. The source instruction is “put the bowl on the plate.” At the switching state, the instruction is changed to “remain still” (left). Despite the updated instruction, the robot continues to move substantially over the following 100 environment steps (right), resulting in a cumulative end-effector path length of 30.74 cm and a final displacement of 23.81 cm from the switching state.

Figure 21: Successful rollouts for a switch from put the bowl on the stove to push the plate to the front of the stove. Both rollouts ultimately complete the target task. Without CAS, the policy remains more affected by the source-task trajectory prior and approaches the plate from a less suitable interaction position. As a result, one side of the plate lifts during the push, making the manipulation less smooth. With CAS, the gripper redirects toward a more suitable position for interacting with the plate and pushes it more smoothly toward the target location. Thus, although both rollouts succeed, CAS yields a cleaner post-switch manipulation trajectory.

Figure 22: Successful rollouts for a switch from push the plate to the front of the stove to put the cream cheese in the bowl. Both rollouts eventually complete the target task. Without CAS, the initial post-switch redirection toward the cream cheese is insufficient, causing the first grasp attempt to miss. The policy must then re-approach the object and perform additional corrective motions before succeeding. With CAS, the gripper redirects more effectively toward the cream cheese and succeeds on the first grasp attempt, yielding a cleaner trajectory with fewer unnecessary intermediate actions.

Figure 23: Successful rollouts for a switch from push the plate to the front of the stove to put the bowl on the stove. Both rollouts ultimately succeed. Without CAS, the policy does not redirect sufficiently toward a favorable grasp configuration and awkwardly catches the front edge of the bowl before lifting it. With CAS, the gripper is redirected toward a more suitable grasp pose and stably grasps the side of the bowl, resulting in more direct progress toward the updated task. Despite identical binary success outcomes, the two rollouts therefore exhibit clearly different post-switch manipulation quality.

Figure 14: What the policy sees when robot-state cues are preserved or altered. Each panel pairs third-person and wrist inputs at rollout start. A uses current views; B freezes both views to the initial images; C hides the robot in the current third-person view and freezes the wrist input; D retains only the robot and bowl. A–D share a physical starting state. E5/E10 instead raise the default initial pose by 5/10 cm and use normal images. Views are re-rendered from recorded starts (configuration 10), upright and before policy preprocessing.

Figure 26: Another example of instruction-conditioned action predictions at the same robot state. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. The base checkpoint predicts very similar actions across all four instructions, whereas the two-round CAS-ST checkpoint produces clearly separated, task-dependent action directions.

Figure 28: Instruction-conditioned actions in a state where the base checkpoint confuses a subset of task instructions. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. In the base checkpoint, the wine-bottle and stove actions are biased toward the bowl region. After two rounds of CAS-ST, these actions shift toward directions more consistent with their respective tasks.

Figure 25: Instruction-conditioned actions for the same robot state before and after two rounds of CAS-guided self-training. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. Under the base checkpoint, the four actions nearly overlap and point toward the wine-bottle region. After self-training, the actions become clearly separated and point broadly toward their corresponding task-relevant regions.

Figure 27: Instruction-conditioned actions in a state where the base checkpoint already exhibits partial task-dependent separation. Colors correspond to wine bottle, bowl, cream cheese, and stove tasks. While some base actions are task-consistent, others remain misaligned. After two rounds of CAS-ST, all four actions become more clearly separated and better aligned with their corresponding task directions.

Figure 7: Action-level illustration of Counterfactual Action Steering. The robot switches from the source task put the bowl on top of the cabinet to the target task turn on the stove. Since the current end-effector position pt is close to the demonstration trajectory distributions of the bowlrelated tasks, CAS selects put the bowl on top of the cabinet (green) and put the cream cheese in the bowl (yellow) as hijacking tasks based on their small KNN distances, while excluding put the wine bottle on top of the cabinet (blue) due to its larger KNN distance. CAS contrasts the targetconditioned action atgt with the selected counterfactual actions ahj and aggregates the weighted directions atgt − ahj to produce afinal (red), which steers the robot away from interfering trajectory priors and toward the stove knob. For clarity, the arrows visualize the translational components of a single action from each predicted action chunk, taken at the same horizon index.

Figure 15: Task differences persist in the language backbone but are weaker in the action expert near the source object. We compare early (t = 10) and late (t = 25) states on the same wine-source trajectory. (a) Task separation persists across the language backbone: solid lines show object-token averages and dashed lines the shared final text token. (b) At the first flow update, all instructions start from identical action noise. Task separation grows through the expert in both states, but much less strongly in the late state. Axes show relative separation D (Eq. 6) with different scales. Curves precede final normalization; Table 13 reports module outputs after normalization.

Figure 18: Steering-weight sweep for CAS variants. We vary the fixed steering weight w ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8} for Source-only CAS and All non-target Fixed. Every tested setting of both variants outperforms the base policy. Source-only CAS achieves its best Switch SR of 35.4% at w = 0.6, while All non-target Fixed peaks at 23.3% at w = 0.4. Dashed horizontal lines show the base policy and full CAS for reference.

Figure 19: Hyperparameter ablations of CAS on CALVIN-Custom-Switch for ts ∈ [15, 21]. Starting from the default setting K = 30, δ = 0.1, and λ = 0.03, we vary one hyperparameter at a time while keeping the other two fixed: (a) steering strength λ, (b) number of nearest neighbors K, and (c) KNN distance threshold δ. The dashed line denotes the base policy without CAS.

Figure 17: Scene appearance variants used for evaluating robustness to visual train–test mismatch. The task semantics, object layout, and scene geometry remain unchanged across variants.

Figure 16: Visualization of task trajectory distributions under different object-pose regimes in CALVIN-Custom-Switch. The random regime instead samples object positions over a broader workspace region without fixed nominal centers, resulting in a qualitatively different trajectory structure.

papers.title: DeRail: Escaping Trajectory Priors via Counterfactual Action Steering for Mid-Execution Instruction Switching
papers.tldr: CAS helps robots switch tasks mid-execution by steering actions away from trajectories associated with outdated instructions, substantially improving switching success without retraining.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and stale points caused by append-only mapping in dynamic scenes.
Updates each point’s confidence using multi-view temporal evidence from segmentation, depth, and visibility consistency.
Combines point refinement with object tracking and re-identification to maintain identities through motion and relocation.
Improves mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet.
Supports downstream object navigation and embodied question-answering, with reported success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed dynamic semantic mapping framework. Given posed RGB-D observations, openvocabulary detections are generated and associated with object instances in the 3D semantic map. For each association, we perform a visibility-based point confidence update. Points supported by current detections, such as the green points on the table, receive higher confidence. In contrast, inconsistent outlier points, such as red points mistakenly fused into a bed instance due to previous segmentation errors, are down-weighted when later observations identify them as pillows. Points belonging to removed objects are identified through visibility reasoning, assigned lower confidence, and eventually pruned. Unobserved points in the current frame, shown in gray, remain unchanged until more evidence is collected in later frames. The semantic map is updated online in this frame-by-frame manner, while periodic instance-fragment merging reduces duplicate instances and re-identification preserves object identities when objects are relocated and re-observed at new locations.

Fig. 6: Example of handling under-segmentation. A pillow is initially fused into the chair instance due to undersegmentation. Once the pillow is correctly segmented in later frames, our method adds it as a separate instance and gradually removes the corresponding points from the chair instance through confidence updates.
Fig. 7: Example of in-view object tracking. Our method tracks the moving bowl in images and updates its location in the semantic map while preserving the same instance ID.

Fig. 5: Example of object fragment merging. A table is initially reconstructed as two separate instances due to temporally disconnected partial observations at 1s and 10s. As more observations become available at 12s, our method merges the fragments into a complete object instance.

Fig. 1: Dynamic open-vocabulary semantic mapping. Our method maintains a refinable object-centric 3D semantic map through point-level probabilistic updates. It handles dynamic objects that newly appear, move within the robot’s view, or are relocated out of view and later re-identified.

Fig. 9: Examples of object navigation and EQA tasks executed on the Spot robot. Our semantic map serves as an online memory that helps the LLM localize target objects, plan embodied skills, and answer questions.

Fig. 4: Example of handling incorrect detections. A plastic bag is mistakenly detected as a pillow, creating a false instance in the map. Our confidence update mechanism accumulates positive evidence for consistently detected objects and negative evidence for unsupported instances, eventually removing the false pillow while preserving the true one.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate sequences by progressively unmasking tokens, but errors introduced during decoding are typically irreversible. Recent work has shown that iterative correction can improve sample quality, yet existing theory fails to explain this given a learned, imperfect denoiser model. We re-formulate MDM inference as a Markov chain on the clean sequence space, defined by a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-introduces masks and then denoises. This helps us analyze the actual denoising trajectory towards the data distribution. The analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R$^2$D) inference, a purely test-time, finetuning-free, reward-free procedure. To further improve performance, we propose Trajectory Correction Training (TCT), a denoiser-training procedure that exposes the model to its own errors along the generation trajectory. On logical tasks, our approach exhibits a striking near-log-linear test-time scaling, achieving over 97% accuracy on hard Sudoku puzzles and over 99% accuracy on 3-SAT. Our approach also applies to pretrained models on actual language tasks, beating iterative correction baselines and the official Q-mode accuracy of LLaDA2.1-mini on HumanEval+.
bullets: Masked diffusion decoding errors are usually irreversible, limiting generation quality.
The paper models inference as a Markov chain using a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-masks tokens before denoising.
This analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R²D), a finetuning-free, reward-free, test-time method.
Trajectory Correction Training (TCT) trains denoisers on errors encountered during their own generation trajectories.
On logical tasks, the approach achieves over 97% Sudoku accuracy and over 99% 3-SAT accuracy, and improves pretrained-model results on language tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Inference scaling on Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT. R2D and ReMDM are run on standard training checkpoints, both using the standard variant; ProSeCo has its own training method. R2D scales near-log-linearly on both tasks and stays above ReMDM at every budget, whereas ProSeCo plateaus after a handful of correction steps.

Figure 2: HumanEval+ accuracy with the off-theshelf LLaDA2.1-mini (16B). The three colored bars are inference methods we run ourselves, and the two grey bars are the model’s own published Q-mode and S-mode results. R2D achieves the top accuracy, surpassing the official Q-mode performance.

Figure 4: Inference scaling on Sudoku-Hard (top) and 3-SAT (bottom), under standard training (left) and TCT training (right). The y-axis reports task accuracy and the x-axis the per-token correction budget M on a logarithmic scale; error bars are one standard deviation across three training seeds. The horizontal dashed line marks each panel’s own no-correction baseline. R2D scales near-log-linearly in all four panels and stays above ReMDM at every budget. Protocol details are in Section E.

Figure 3: Averaged number of function evaluations (NFE) per sample at the budget of Table 1 (lower is better), with accuracy in parentheses (TCT checkpoint for R2D and ReMDM). R2D exits early, whereas ReMDM and ProSeCo spend their full budget.

Table 1: Accuracy (in %) on Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT, organized by training method and inference method. ReMDM, R2D and ProSeCo use the same compute budget (256 steps per token for SudokuHard, 32 steps per token for 3-SAT). R2D is the primary driver for inference-time scaling, and TCT cooperates well with R2D to further raise performance.

Table 2: Compute-normalized comparison on Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT. Each inference method is reported with its accuracy (in %), averaged NFE, and per-sample wall time at batch size 1 on a single NVIDIA GH200 GPU. R2D is the only method that exits early: on Sudoku-Hard it reaches 97.5 in 49.4 s/sample where ReMDM reaches 92.3 in 187.9 s/sample — 5.2 points better at 3.8× less wall time. Measurement protocol in Section E.
Table 8: Denoiser architecture for Sudoku-Hard and 3-SAT. The two share a Qwen2-style backbone and differ only in vocabulary size and maximum position, which are dictated by the input encoding.

Table 3: HumanEval+ accuracy, averaged NFE and averaged wall time (in minute per sample) for the three iterative correction methods of Figure 2, all evaluated with the off-the-shelf LLaDA2.1-mini. R2D reaches the top accuracy while spending roughly half of ReMDM’s compute.

Table 5: Token preservation of the TCT-trained denoiser: The fraction of correct revealed tokens that survive a single forward pass without carry-over, averaged over three training seeds. On Sudoku-Hard the correct grid is an exact fixed point of the denoiser at every masking ratio; On 3-SAT it is not, and preservation is weakest precisely when the sequence is nearly complete, which is why carry-over is essential there and not on Sudoku-Hard.

Table 4: ReMDM implementation variants on the TCT checkpoint, comparing carry-over denoising against the sampling operator, at M = 256 on Sudoku-Hard and M = 32 on 3-SAT. Accuracy is in %, mean ± standard deviation over three training seeds × three inference seeds. The sampling operator dominates: argmax is the operator TCT trains under. Carry-over is close to free on Sudoku-Hard but decisive on 3-SAT. The standard checkpoint is not ablated; there we run the official carry-over + stochastic configuration.

Table 6: R2D (correction) inference design on Sudoku-Hard under TCT training. Each row changes one design element of Algorithm 1 relative to Default. Each cell reports accuracy (in %, mean ± standard deviation over three training seeds) with averaged NFE in parentheses. Low-confidence remasking almost removes the scaling effect; Removing early exit preserves scaling but at markedly higher NFE; Stochastic sampling in place of argmax costs accuracy at every budget while spending more NFE.

Table 7: Reveal rule in TCT training (Algorithm 2) on Sudoku-Hard, replacing the argmax reveal of Line 9 and the top-k confidence reveal of Line 11. Position selection is the load-bearing choice, while argmax reveal is a minor lever; Both approximations help rather than hurt.

papers.abstract: A planner using a learned world model can improve its predicted outcome while choosing a worse action. We study when expected free energy (EFE) can help decide how much computation to spend on a plan. An EFE-inspired objective combines goal distance with disagreement among stochastic predictions. We test candidate scoring, stopping, and online predictor updates separately. Stopping when elite cost stalls reduces refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. At the larger tested weights, rewarding disagreement lowers success with a frozen model. Penalizing it helps at some task and weight settings but harms others. When training data omit a region needed to reach the goal, online updates recover part of the resulting loss. The tested cost-stall rule can fail when further optimization exploits model errors, because predicted cost keeps falling after task success peaks. Cost progress can guide computation on a plateau, but protecting performance after a peak requires information about the consequences of the chosen actions.
bullets: Problem: A learned world model may predict improving outcomes while selecting worse actions, making test-time compute allocation difficult.
Method: Separately evaluate EFE-inspired candidate scoring, cost-stall stopping, and online predictor updates during latent world-model planning.
Stopping on stalled elite cost reduces unnecessary refinement on plateauing tasks, with mean success near fixed-depth references.
Rewarding stochastic-prediction disagreement lowers success with a frozen model; penalizing disagreement is task- and weight-dependent.
Online updates recover part of the loss caused by missing training data in regions needed to reach the goal, but cost-stall stopping can fail after success peaks.

papers.selection_reason: Expected free energy as a test-time compute controller for latent world-model planning with online updates.
papers.title: Knowing When to Stop Thinking: A Dissection of Expected Free Energy as a Test-Time Compute Controller for Latent World-Model Planning
papers.tldr: Expected free energy can help allocate planning compute when progress plateaus, but disagreement-based scoring is unreliable and cost-stall stopping can miss model-exploitation failures.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-scene interaction requires coordinated spatial reasoning, physical feasibility, and the ability to recover from compounding execution errors. Text-driven motion models are largely scene-agnostic and lack closed-loop correction, while geometry-conditioned approaches depend on paired scene-motion training or explicit 3D preprocessing that limits generalization to novel layouts and open-vocabulary goals. We present InteractAgent, an agentic multimodal LLM system for long-horizon human-scene interaction that plans, executes, observes, and reflects in a closed loop, using a single MLLM as both planner and evaluator and a frozen MotionLLM as the executor. InteractAgent integrates Online Observation for step-wise recovery decisions (continue/redo/replan) and Memory-Augmented Reflection for multi-round plan refinement with adaptive stopping. On UniHSI, InteractAgent improves task success and reduces penetration compared with training-free baselines. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/InteractAgent.
bullets: Addresses scene-agnostic text-driven motion generation and error accumulation in long-horizon interactions.
Uses one multimodal LLM as planner and evaluator, with a frozen MotionLLM executing motions.
Performs step-wise recovery via continue, redo, or replan decisions.
Refines plans across multiple rounds with memory-augmented reflection and adaptive stopping.
On UniHSI, improves task success and reduces penetration versus training-free baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of InteractAgent. Our framework couples a single multimodal LLM with a frozen MotionLLM executor. Two key components enable training-free, long-horizon interaction generation: (1) Online Observation provides step-wise visual feedback during execution, allowing the MLLM to correct local deviations; (2) Memory-Augmented Reflection aggregates planning–execution histories across rounds and refines future plans at the trajectory level. Together, these mechanisms form a dual-layer reflective loop that progressively improves motion quality and scene consistency.
Figure B.2: Online Observation example (steps 3–4 and final plan).
Figure 3. Trajectory visualization image used as a compact reflection signal for the MLLM.

Table 2. Comparison of SR and PC (Y/N decided by human) across different LLM types.
Table 3. Comparison of SR and penetration between Motion Executors.

papers.tldr: InteractAgent enables long-horizon human–scene interaction through closed-loop planning, execution, observation, and memory-based reflection.

papers.abstract: Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that the ability to learn a new language may depend on how easily previously acquired first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. This exploratory computational study extends a neural language-model approach to critical period effects by examining internal representations rather than behavior. A small two-layer GPT-2 model was trained on English and then on German (a relatively related L2) or Finnish (a relatively distant L2) through either Sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which limits change in parameters important for English. Mean-pooled hidden states for 20 held-out probe sentences per language were compared with those of the English-only model using cosine similarity at the embedding layer and two transformer layers after one and two L2 epochs. English similarity remained high in the transformer layers but became negative in the embedding layer. L2 similarity increased in the transformer layers, and German and Finnish differed more in the second transformer layer than in the first. EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001. With one training run per condition, these findings are preliminary.
authors: Uriel Benymon, Tristan Whipps, Armita Ghobadi
bullets: Motivation: L2 learning may depend on how readily established L1 representations can be modified.
Method: Train an English model, then German or Finnish using sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), and compare hidden-state cosine similarities.
L2 representations became more similar to the bilingual model’s states in transformer layers, while English similarity stayed high there but turned negative at the embedding layer.
German and Finnish diverged more in the second transformer layer than the first, suggesting language-related differences emerge deeper in the network.
EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001; results are preliminary because each condition had one training run.

papers.selection_reason: Sequential L2 training with EWC explores continual learning and catastrophic forgetting in LLMs.
papers.title: Modelling Billingual Learning Through LLM Training: A Critical-Period Exploration
papers.tldr: A small GPT-2 study probes critical-period effects by tracking how sequential versus stability-constrained bilingual training changes internal representations for related and distant second languages.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on new facts often erodes its general abilities. We find that standard fine-tuning lowers instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks by 35 points on average, and that these losses track a collapse in answer length: fine-tuned models at least halve their responses, and the further a response drifts from the initial model's length, the more often it fails. We propose InstructReplay: the initial model answers a set of general instructions once, and during fine-tuning the model is kept close to the initial model on these answers. Across three model families and two domains, InstructReplay reduces the average decline on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points and keeps answer length close to the initial model's, while learning the new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. It balances learning and retention better than seven adaptation methods in all six settings. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to replaying the model's own answers to general instructions rather than to the form of the loss.
authors: Xiaofeng Shi, Qian Kou, Hua Zhou
bullets: Standard factual fine-tuning causes major general-ability degradation, linked to sharply shorter answers.
The method first records the initial model’s answers to general instructions, then keeps the fine-tuned model close to them.
Across three model families and two domains, benchmark decline falls from 28.1 to 2.4 points on average.
It maintains answer lengths near the initial model’s while learning new facts as well as standard fine-tuning.
It outperforms seven adaptation methods across all six settings; controlled comparisons identify self-answer replay as the key factor.

papers.abstract: The ability to learn and generalize from limited experience, or sample efficiency, is a cornerstone of intelligence. How can we build language models that turn a few user interactions, a few snippets of unfamiliar code, or a handful of experimental results provided in context into knowledge that generalizes? Prior work has found that sleep, a process where the model performs $N$ recurrent forward passes to refine its representations of a chunk of context, can improve long-context reasoning (specifically, within SSM-attention hybrid models). We study whether this method also improves in-context adaptation on general, non-synthetic tasks for transformer language models. To this end, we pre-train language models up to 1.2B-parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Notably, longer sleep (i.e., using a larger number of recurrent forward passes $N$) enables the model to learn faster in-context on multiple few-shot algorithmic, question-answering tasks, while also achieving lower next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with $N=2$ and $N=4$ match the no-sleep baseline's loss using $2.10\times$ and $2.39\times$ fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.
authors: Sangyun Lee, Zhang Enyan, Michael Xu, Hao Tang, Zinan Lin, Weijia Xu, Chris Quirk, Jianfeng Gao, Giulia Fanti, Xiaodong Liu
bullets: Studies whether recurrent “sleep” passes improve in-context adaptation beyond prior long-context reasoning settings.
Pre-trains transformers up to 1.2B parameters with varying numbers of recurrent forward passes over context.
Longer sleep improves few-shot algorithmic and question-answering adaptation and lowers out-of-distribution next-token loss.
On held-out code, 2 and 4 sleep passes match the no-sleep baseline with 2.10× and 2.39× fewer in-context tokens.
The approach targets a better tradeoff between adaptation efficiency and decoding latency.

papers.abstract: Sparse world models for 4D semantic occupancy forecasting represent scenes with a small set of evolving queries to efficiently predict future geometry and semantics for autonomous driving. However, existing sparse world models face a bottleneck in using historical temporal evidence for long-horizon forecasting. They rely on scene states to carry historical information implicitly, allowing errors to propagate and accumulate across successive forecasting steps and causing geometric and semantic deviations. To address this limitation, we present MemAnchorWorld, a sparse occupancy world model that explicitly retrieves relevant historical geometric and semantic evidence for 4D semantic occupancy forecasting. Inspired by the von Restorff effect, we introduce a forecast-time-conditioned hierarchical dual-path memory-anchor retrieval mechanism. Guided by the effective age and semantic compatibility of historical information, it combines query-level candidate selection with point-level memory-anchor retrieval to provide historical evidence for sparse points at different forecast times. To better use memory anchors and existing features, a point-level residual adapter jointly gated by the task and forecast time separately controls residual corrections to semantics, occupancy confidence, and spatial positions. On Occ3D-nuScenes, MemAnchorWorld achieves an average mIoU of 13.55% and an average IoU of 22.84% across the 1-3 s forecasting horizons, attaining state-of-the-art performance on both metrics.Project page: https://memanchorworld.github.io/
authors: Xinyang Jia, Yuqi Zhang, Jiakai Wang, Yahu Yang, Guandong Pan, Chao Tong, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation in sparse world models that store temporal information only implicitly in scene states.
Uses forecast-conditioned hierarchical dual-path memory-anchor retrieval based on information age and semantic compatibility.
Combines query-level candidate selection with point-level retrieval for sparse points at different forecast horizons.
Applies a task- and forecast-time-gated point-level residual adapter to refine semantics, occupancy confidence, and spatial positions.
On Occ3D-nuScenes, reports 13.55% average mIoU and 22.84% average IoU over 1–3 s horizons, with state-of-the-art performance on both metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MemAnchorWorld. First, multi-frame images generate queries and positions. Next, dual-path retrieval selects candidate queries; point-level memory-anchor retrieval selects associated points and aggregates evidence. A point-level residual adapter corrects semantic logits, occupancy confidence, and positions. Finally, decoding heads generate semantic occupancy and the ego trajectory.

Figure 3. Qualitative 4D semantic occupancy forecasting on Occ3D-nuScenes. Columns show the current frame and forecasts at 1, 2, and 3 s. From top to bottom, rows show ground truth, SparseWorld, and MemAnchorWorld. Red boxes highlight local regions where MemAnchorWorld better predicts semantic occupancy and its spatial support over time.

Figure 4. Vehicle-occlusion forecasts at 1 s in two scenes. Columns show the future camera view, ground truth, SparseWorld, and MemAnchorWorld. Green and orange outlines mark the target and foreground vehicles, respectively.

Figure 1. Comparison of recurrent sparse occupancy forecasting and MemAnchorWorld. Recurrent forecasting updates scene queries through successive steps. MemAnchorWorld retrieves memory anchors from a separate historical memory and uses taskspecific gates to refine the outputs at each forecast horizon.

papers.title: MemAnchorWorld: A Sparse World Model with Horizon-Conditioned Memory Retrieval for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: MemAnchorWorld improves long-horizon 4D semantic occupancy forecasting by explicitly retrieving forecast-time-relevant historical geometric and semantic evidence.

papers.abstract: Neural networks in continual learning often lose plasticity: some neurons become inactive, while others fire almost constantly. This limits adaptation to shifting data and wastes capacity. Prior work mitigates this by periodically reinitializing low-utility units, but such resets can destroy previously learned features and do not proactively prevent low utility. We study a simple diagnostic measure: the firing rate of ReLU units, defined as the fraction of positive pre-activations. Low rates identify dead units, while very high rates indicate linearized, always-on units. Based on this view, we introduce a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range. Across continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, firing-rate distributions explain differences in plasticity across a range of approaches, including well-known techniques such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks. The same mechanism carries over to reinforcement learning, improving Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.
authors: Jan Robine, Marc H\"oftmann, Stefan Harmeling
bullets: Problem: Continual learning can produce dead or always-on neurons, reducing adaptability and wasting capacity.
Method: Adjust per-neuron activation thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range.
Finding: Firing-rate distributions serve as a diagnostic of plasticity across multiple continual-learning approaches.
Results: Load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, and improves Rainbow DQN on Atari over LayerNorm.
Scope: Demonstrated in supervised continual learning and reinforcement learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Continual ImageNet: Evolution of firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy with error bands (right), averaged over 10 runs. Standard training collapses neuron activity toward 0%, while BatchNorm, L2 regularization and CBP keep firing more balanced. The temporal alignment between balanced firing rates and rising accuracy is what connects the two; per-method findings are in the main text.

Figure 2: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy with error bands (right), averaged over 15 runs. Accuracy is relative to the from-scratch Resets baseline, which is the zero line. Continual training drives neurons gradually inactive, while resets and CBP keep firing patterns from collapsing, and accuracy follows those trends; per-method findings are in the main text.

Figure 13: Continual ImageNet: Effects of non-affine normalization on firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right). Non-affine BatchNorm + L2 clusters firing rate near 50%, while non-affine LayerNorm + L2 broadens the distribution across layers. Both configurations improve accuracy, with non-affine LayerNorm achieving the highest performance of all methods. Enforcing 50% via load balancing on top of non-affine LayerNorm tightens rates but lowers accuracy.

Figure 9: Continual ImageNet: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions over tasks. Rows correspond to methods, columns correspond to successive layers. Early layers stay active while later layers collapse in the baseline; CBP shows heterogeneous behavior; non-affine BN + L2 maintains near-balanced firing rates across layers.

Figure 7: Rainbow DQN: Human-normalized scores (0 = random, 1 = human) on 6 Atari games for four variants: the original baseline, a baseline with LayerNorm (LN), and load balancing at a 50% target and CBP instantiated on that LayerNorm agent (LB 50% @ LN and CBP @ LN). Curves show the mean over 5 random seeds and are smoothed with a time-weighted exponential moving average.

Figure 8: Rainbow DQN: Firing-rate distributions, one row per game and one column per agent, in the same order as Figure 7. The baseline collapses to very low rates in both games; LN lifts them part of the way; load balancing holds the hidden layers near the 50% target, with the residual mass at 0% and 100% coming from the value head, which is excluded by design. The contrast between the two games explains the accuracy result: LayerNorm alone already raises firing in BattleZone, leaving load balancing little to add, while in DemonAttack it does not.

Figure 4: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) for different load-balancing ranges, averaged over 15 runs with ±1 standard error bands; accuracy is relative to Resets. Loose bounds (5–95%) reproduce reset-like behavior with improved accuracy, while control near 50% yields further gains, surpassing resets and prior methods. The LB 50% panel concentrates nearly every neuron in a single bin, so it is dark apart from the line at 50%.

Figure 10: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions over tasks. Continual training and CBP exhibit linearization in Block 2. Load balancing with a 95% upper limit prevents it, at the cost of some saturation at the limit in the early layers.

Figure 11: Continual ImageNet: From left to right: fraction of dormant neurons (threshold τd = 0.01), weight magnitudes, overall maximum spectral norm across layers, and effective rank (Lewandowski et al., 2025), over tasks. Dashed lines indicate variants built on a BatchNorm backbone (BN + L2, except L2 init + BN, which adds no further L2). Averaged over 5 runs with ±1 standard error bands.
Figure 19: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions for all approaches.
Figure 15: Continual ImageNet: Test accuracy of additional baselines. Dashed lines indicate variants built on a BatchNorm backbone (BN + L2, except L2 init + BN, which adds no further L2).

Figure 12: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: From left to right: fraction of dormant neurons (threshold τd = 0.01), weight magnitudes, overall maximum spectral norm across layers, and effective rank (Lewandowski et al., 2025), over tasks. Averaged over 5 runs with ±1 standard error bands.

Figure 5: Entropy: Continual ImageNet (left) and class-incremental CIFAR-100 (right), with H(s), ∑ i H(si), and TC(s) computed on the test set, averaged over 3 random seeds. On continual ImageNet the three configurations are the Baseline, BN + L2, and BN + L2 with load balancing at 50% (“+ LB 50%”); on class-incremental CIFAR-100 they are the Baseline and load balancing at 5–95% and 50%.

Figure 6: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) for ReLU, LeakyReLU, and GELU, all based on the BN + L2 setup. In the right plot the dashed lines show the results for load balancing 50%.

Figure 3: Continual ImageNet: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) under BN + L2 with and without load balancing, averaged over 10 runs with ±1 standard error bands. Constraining neurons to intermediate regimes (40–60% or 50%) improves accuracy over both the unconstrained baseline and CBP.
Figure 18: Continual ImageNet: Layer-wise firing-rate distributions for all approaches.

Figure 14: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) under non-affine normalization and normalized skip connections; accuracy is relative to Resets, as in Figure 4. Both modifications steer firing rates toward balanced regimes and improve accuracy beyond resets and CBP.

Figure 17: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Firing-rate distributions of the first and second ReLU within all ResNet blocks. Left: Non-affine BatchNorm baseline; the second ReLU distribution is skewed. Right: Non-affine BatchNorm on the skip path before addition re-centers the second ReLU pre-activation, yielding a more symmetric distribution around 50%.

Figure 16: Continual ImageNet: Firing-rate distributions (left) and test accuracy (right) for ReLU, LeakyReLU, and GELU, all based on the BN + L2 setup. In the right plot the dashed lines show the results for load balancing at 50%.

Table 4: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Final test accuracies averaged over tasks 15–20, with the standard error of the mean over 15 runs. The class order is drawn from the run’s seed and all methods use the same 15 seeds, so the last column reports the paired per-run difference against Resets — the from-scratch reference the accuracy panels are also plotted against. The gain from pairing is smaller here than on continual ImageNet (1.2–1.8× against 2–5×): that window is 100 nearly independent tasks, this one is 5 consecutive tasks whose difficulties are strongly correlated. Rows are ordered by accuracy, which is also the order of the paired difference. ∗ p < 0.05, ∗∗ p < 0.001, two-sided paired t-test, df = 14.

Table 3: Continual ImageNet: Final test accuracies averaged over tasks 1900–2000, with the standard error of the mean over 10 runs. All methods are evaluated on the same 10 task sequences, so the last column reports the paired per-run difference against the tuned BN + L2 reference. Task-sampling variance is shared and cancels there, which resolves a comparison 2–5× more precisely than either mean for methods built on that reference. The gain is smallest for the least stable methods — for the Baseline the two standard errors are the same, because its run-to-run spread is driven by its own instability rather than by which classes it was given. Rows are ordered by accuracy, which is also the order of the paired difference. ∗ p < 0.05, ∗∗ p < 0.001, two-sided paired t-test, df = 9.
Table 1: Continual ImageNet: Hyperparameters and sweep ranges. Set-valued entries are the values considered in our sweeps.
Table 2: Class-incremental CIFAR-100: Hyperparameters and sweep ranges. Set-valued entries are the values considered in our sweeps.

Table 5: Rainbow DQN: Final human-normalized scores (± standard error of the mean over 5 seeds) using a time-weighted exponential moving average. LN is Rainbow DQN with LayerNorm in the hidden layers, and the last two columns are load balancing and CBP instantiated on it. Bold marks the unique best mean in each row; rows with no bold entry have a tie for the best mean.

papers.selection_reason: Firing-rate load balancing sustains plasticity in continual learning, directly matching continual/online learning.
papers.title: Load Balancing Neurons: Firing-Rate Control Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Controlling ReLU neuron firing rates helps preserve plasticity and improves continual-learning performance without destructive neuron resets.

papers.abstract: Virtual staining synthesizes special-stain images from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), extending the information available from an existing digital slide. However, a fixed inference rule can leave available real target-stain references unused, limiting query-specific correction of stain appearance at deployment. Test-time adaptation (TTA) provides a mechanism for this reference-guided, query-specific refinement without retraining the generator. We therefore propose FewRef-5, a reference-assisted TTA method for virtual staining built on StainPromptInversion. We extract tissue-masked optical-density means and standard deviations from five real Masson's trichrome (MAS) training patches and average them into a fixed stain target. A scheduled statistic-matching loss introduces this target into per-query visual-prompt optimization alongside our edge/Gram consistency penalties and the inherited reconstruction objectives. The target remains unchanged across queries, avoiding recursive dependence on earlier generated outputs while the pretrained generator stays fixed. On recorded H&E-to-MAS outputs for 1,989 queries, FewRef-5 reduces target-set FID from 183.201 to 166.904 and increases source-referenced SSIM from 0.92787 to 0.94996 relative to our Edge+Gram variant. Source PSNR and MS-SSIM decrease, showing an endpoint trade-off rather than uniformly better reconstruction.
authors: Wenxuan Wang, Liwen Wang, Mingmin Wu, Xingbo Dong, Zhe Jin
bullets: Addresses unused real target-stain references and limited query-specific correction in fixed-rule virtual staining.
Applies fixed-reference test-time adaptation on StainPromptInversion with tissue-masked optical-density statistics averaged from five MAS patches.
Optimizes per-query visual prompts using scheduled statistic matching plus edge/Gram consistency and inherited reconstruction objectives; the generator remains fixed.
Across 1,989 H&E-to-MAS queries, target-set FID improves from 183.201 to 166.904 and source-referenced SSIM from 0.92787 to 0.94996 versus Edge+Gram.
PSNR and MS-SSIM decrease, indicating a trade-off rather than uniformly improved reconstruction.

The recorded checkpoint has a nominal 1,000,000-trainingstep label (previously “1M”); inference uses 50 DDIM steps. No query-paired real MAS is available.

Figure 1. Our adaptation built on StainPromptInversion: added edge/Gram consistency and the FewRef-5 constraint. Source and style inversions supply reconstruction targets. The prompt is fitted with fixed pretrained weights. Its optional OD term uses the frozen realreference target in FewRef-5; the schematic symbol M corresponds to mR. Intermediate states and curves are schematic. The MAS thumbnails are archived outputs for one shared input.

Figure 3. Analytical coefficient illustration. For five EMA writes with β = 0.9, the initialization retains weight β5 and recent writes receive larger coefficients. The fixed reference average gives its five patches equal weight. These are formula-derived coefficients.

Figure 2. Tissue masking and OD-statistic extraction illustrated on an archived FewRef-5 output. The binary mask and channel distributions are computed from that image. The reference target averages the same six statistics over five real training patches.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a fixed-reference test-time adaptation method for virtual staining, providing a specific technique for test-time adaptation that could be transferable to domain adaptation in embodied systems.
papers.title: FewRef-5: Fixed-Reference Test-Time Adaptation for Virtual Staining
papers.tldr: FewRef-5 uses five fixed real MAS references to adapt virtual staining at test time, improving stain-target similarity and SSIM while reducing PSNR and MS-SSIM.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.
authors: Jialong Peng, Shihao Zhou, Feng Yan, Wen Xiao, Haozheng Wang, Wenqi Ren, Wenyuan Sheng, Jian Qiao, Jiaxu Miao, Lin Ma, Chao Yang
bullets: Addresses the data and annotation costs that limit existing robotic in-context learning methods.
Encodes demonstrated and completed interaction action–effect sequences into reusable visual-action memories.
Predicts the upcoming execution intent to retrieve relevant experience from memory.
Conditions a vision-language-action model with retrieved experience tokens and gated cross-attention.
Reports gains over a baseline across RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-robot experiments, including stronger improvements on unseen tasks.

Backbone outputs support action generation and next-step intent prediction. The intention decoder and intention predictor use residual MLPs. papers.abstract: Learned driving planners keep being updated after deployment as new logs arrive, yet continual learning evaluations rarely ask whether an update improves on the deployed model, and their verdicts rest on unstated evaluation choices. We present ContinualDrive, a deployment-anchored benchmark for post-deployment continual learning of driving planners. It updates a deployed planner on real-world nuPlan logs one scenario-type group at a time, evaluates the same checkpoints in open and closed loop, makes four measurement axes explicit (evaluation loop, reference checkpoint, temporal aggregation and stream protocol), and anchors a three-valued release verdict to the deployed checkpoint. We study two planners (PlanTF and Diffusion Planner) under full fine-tuning and adapter or LoRA updates, with and without replay or gradient projection, in three task orders. Verdicts can reverse or vanish when one axis changes: open-loop ADE ranks the final PlanTF model above the deployed one in half of its core-suite runs, whereas every closed-loop score ranks it below; backward transfer misses this loss, which on average is already present when each group has just been learned; and regime rankings vary far less across training seeds than across task orders. In the core suite of full and adapter updates, no regime measurably improved on the deployed planner in closed loop; on a panel more than ten times larger every evaluated final checkpoint trails it, and joint training on all groups recovers much of the loss without exceeding its nuPlan closed-loop score. We distill these findings into a reporting contract and will release the code and all checkpoints.
authors: Zirui Li, Zhiqi Mao, Yangang Ren, Heye Huang, Haohan Yang, Qihang Huang, Zhan Chen, Chen Lv
bullets: Benchmarks continual updates on real-world nuPlan logs, processing scenario-type groups sequentially.
Makes evaluation choices explicit across loop type, reference checkpoint, temporal aggregation, and stream protocol.
Evaluates PlanTF and Diffusion Planner with full fine-tuning, adapters/LoRA, replay, gradient projection, and multiple task orders.
Open-loop and closed-loop verdicts can disagree; backward transfer may miss degradation that appears immediately after learning each group.
No tested update regime improved on the deployed planner in closed loop; task order affected rankings more than training seed.
