papers.abstract: Visual-inertial-leg (VIL) state estimation offers cost-effective localization for legged robots, adding only a camera to the onboard IMU and joint encoders. However, learning-based leg odometry is limited by its supervision: networks trained in simulation suffer from the sim-to-real gap, while real-world labels require costly sensors or inherit the errors of visual estimates. To address this, we present AirLeg, a self-supervised VIL SLAM system in which vision and leg proprioception improve each other from training to deployment. We pre-train the leg odometry network in simulation and adapt it to the robot without ground truth through imperative learning, where multi-sensor bundle adjustment uses the leg odometry to refine the visual map, which in turn supervises the network. During deployment, the fused estimates adapt the network online. To improve both localization and this supervision, a dual-window estimator fuses vision, IMU, and leg odometry, relates loaded feet to the visually reconstructed terrain through a deformation-aware constraint, and weights the constraints by variance component estimation. AirLeg completes all 17 GrandTour sequences with the lowest average error (0.19 m) among 19 methods. On a low-cost quadruped, it achieves the lowest drift (0.6%) with only 0.5 h of unlabeled data, in real time on an embedded computer.
authors: Kuan Xu, Tianxin Hu, Ruofei Bai, Ruimeng Liu, Yuefan Hao, Zeyu Jiang, Zitong Zhan, Shenghai Yuan, Chen Wang, Lihua Xie
bullets: Addresses simulation-to-reality transfer and costly or inaccurate real-world supervision for learned leg odometry.
Uses imperative learning: multi-sensor bundle adjustment refines the visual map with leg odometry, which then supervises the network.
A dual-window estimator fuses vision, IMU, and leg odometry with deformation-aware terrain constraints and variance-based weighting.
Completes all 17 GrandTour sequences with the lowest average error among 19 methods (0.19 m).
On a low-cost quadruped, reaches 0.6% drift using 0.5 hours of unlabeled data and runs in real time on embedded hardware.

The gyro-correction head additionally receives the raw gyroscope measurement.

papers.abstract: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments. We evaluate the robustness of representative examples of three important classes of RL algorithm in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment. These are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is a model-free on-policy algorithm, Soft-Actor-Critic (SAC), which is a model-free off-policy algorithm, and Drama, which is a model-based algorithm. The agents must learn to successfully park in four different scenarios, which are presented successively, with parking spaces oriented at varying angles. We find off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay, while model-based algorithms do not appear to offer any direct advantage over model-free algorithms. These experiments also highlight the additional challenges of finding robust abstractions of the environment, and oversensitivity to hyperparameters.
authors: Kim N. Nolle, Ivana Dusparic, Rhodri Cusack, Vinny Cahill
bullets: Studies continual learning in non-stationary cyber-physical environments, focusing on retention of previously learned behaviors.

Finds replay may improve robustness to forgetting in off-policy methods.
Highlights challenges in learning robust environment abstractions and sensitivity to hyperparameters.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.
authors: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
bullets: Addresses the mutation or disappearance of moving objects after they leave and re-enter the camera view.
Couples perspective video generation with low-frame-rate panoramic evolution without auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs.
Uses Geometric Anchoring for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation for temporal aggregation.
Supports both latent-level and attention-level camera conditioning architectures.
Experiments on a new dynamic benchmark show gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the OmniPersist framework. Tokens from the dense perspective stream and the temporally sparse panoramic stream are jointly processed by a shared, frozen Diffusion Transformer (DiT) block adapted via LoRA. The two streams coordinate across space and time via dedicated learned feature projections to exchange complementary context. GeoAnch transfers spatially aligned features at synchronized timestamps, while TemComp aggregates features across neighboring timestamps for intermediate observations. For illustration, we depict a temporal sampling interval of s = 4 in image-space indices.

Figure 3. Generation results on I2V across camera revisits. papers.abstract: Pansharpening aims to fuse a single observed image pair, comprising a low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image and a panchromatic (PAN) image, to obtain a high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) image. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance due to their strong capability of extracting nonlinear features. However, distribution shifts between training data and test images can degrade the performance of pretrained pansharpening networks, limiting their generalization in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework that uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair to select and update only a subset of the pretrained network's parameters. Specifically, the framework uses cross-scoring to identify parameter groups whose updates improve reconstruction across image patches. It then updates the selected groups by minimizing a loss that combines a spectral consistency term with a newly designed spatial consistency term. Experiments show that the adapted networks perform better than their pretrained counterparts and outperform representative state-of-the-art pansharpening methods on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView series datasets.
authors: Jin-Liang Xiao, Liang-Jian Deng, Yu-Xuan Zhang, Hua Meng, Zhengchun Zhou
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by distribution shifts between training and real-world test images.
Uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair and cross-scoring across patches to identify parameter groups worth updating.
Optimizes selected parameters with spectral and newly designed spatial consistency losses.
Experiments on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView datasets show improvements over pretrained networks and representative state-of-the-art methods.

This observation motivates the selective adaptation of the most beneficial parameters rather than indiscriminately updating the entire network.

papers.abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).
authors: Joonghyuk Shin, Alex Trevithick, Katar\'ina T\'othov\'a, Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Jaesik Park, Shalini De Mello, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Riccardo de Lutio, Haithem Turki
bullets: Video world models often lose long-term visual consistency, while explicit 3D worlds lack photorealistic appearance.
M2R stores rendered features on mesh surfaces in each object’s coordinate frame and retrieves them by rasterizing visible surfaces.
This makes appearance move with objects, persist across revisits, and remain shared among observing agents, with memory tied to surfaces rather than frames.
Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and coding-agent-authored worlds.
It more than doubles object permanence, nearly doubles cross-agent consistency, and renders 720p video at 40 FPS.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. M2R renders each agent’s view from the initial frame and renderings of a shared scene mesh. As agent A explores, it stores generated keys and values in a surface memory, indexed by the mesh surfaces they depict. When agent B encounters the same surfaces, it retrieves and renders them as agent A saw them (a). We train our renderer on rollouts that revisit earlier views. With a one-chunk window, it must render each revisit from the memory it wrote, supervised by a frozen teacher that sees the full past (b).

Figure 8. Multiple agents. We show a rollout in MutableWorlds in which two agents look from the same viewpoint (A) and meet twice (B). AgentGarten and Code World Model show agent 2 a different building (A2) and fail to preserve agent 2 across meetings (B). M2R is the only method to share appearance between agents.

Figure A14. MutableWorlds. We show a bakery drawer that is reopened after 39 s (top) and a room that is revisited from two views (bottom). Code World Model moves from a quay into a room and changes the furniture, and AgentGarten changes the drawer, its contents, and the view through the window, while M2R preserves all of them.

Figure A13. HSSD. We show a drawer that is reopened after 41 s (top) and a vase that is moved from a counter (A) into a fridge (B) while the camera looks away (bottom), in the layout of Fig. 6. Code World Model and AgentGarten change the contents of the drawer and keep the vase on the counter or draw a darker one, while M2R preserves both. The frame at the bottom left is the reference render at the first visit.

Figure A16. Multiple agents with a dynamic object. In a harbor workshop, we show cross-agent consistency for a place (A) and for a tool drawer that agent 1 opens and agent 2 reopens 38 s later (B), and agent persistence from both cameras at two meetings 34 s apart (C, D). AgentGarten and Code World Model show agent 2 another place, draw the drawer without its tools, and change or lose the other agent in at least one view, while M2R keeps the place, the tools, and both agents. The left column shows both input views, the agents’ paths, and the given geometry at the first meeting, in which the agents are boxes.

Figure A15. Multiple agents. We show two rollouts in the layout of Fig. 8, in a woodland campsite (top) and on a street (bottom), with an input view (the box marks the other agent) and both agents’ paths (agent 2’s dashed). AgentGarten and Code World Model show each agent a different place, and AgentGarten also draws another person or a signpost at the first meeting. Figure 3. Surface memory. We assign each pixel p to the cell c that contains its surface point x(p) in the object’s coordinate frame (top). After each chunk, we record the token that best covers each visible cell, keeping only the first and latest (bottom left). When we revisit the lantern after it has moved, each new token i reads the past tokens that most of its pixels point to (bottom right).

papers.tldr: M2R gives video world models persistent, object-centered visual memory so appearances remain consistent across movement, revisits, and multiple agents in real time.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models can continuously acquire useful experience through test-time interaction, reflection, and prompt optimization, yet turning such experience into model itself to ensure self improvement remains challenging. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides a natural mechanism for internalizing test-time information into model parameters, yet it largely assumes that the gener- ated experience is worth learning. We show that this assumption does not always hold: experiences that improve test-time performance may provide limited or even harmful training signals. To better characterize which experience should be inter- nalized, we systematically analyze diverse mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models, and find that gradient-based alignment is a more reli- able indicator of downstream distillation gains than immediate test-time improve- ment. Based on this finding, we propose E2L, a self-evolution framework that iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their esti- mated training utility. E2L closes the loop between experience generation and parameter learning, enabling agents to autonomously produce experience suitable for self-improvement.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Gangyi Zhang, Dong Wang, Yang Liu, Daoxuan Liu, Jiancan Wu, Shiu-hong Kao, Wu Liu, Yicong Li, Yongdong Zhang
bullets: Problem: Test-time experiences that improve performance may still provide weak or harmful signals for parameter learning.

Contribution: A closed-loop framework for producing experiences specifically suited to model self-improvement.

papers.abstract: Resolving local atomic structures such as defects and interfaces from electron microscopy contrast relies heavily on researcher judgement, leading to low efficiency and subjective standards. Here we present PhyEvo-Mic-RSI, a physics-guided and expert-informed recursive self-improvement framework that turns one-off human corrections into reusable, verifiable capabilities by updating executable operators, parameters and routing rules with versioned inheritance. Given researcher-defined tasks, the system selects analysis paths from image features without expert labels, while testing and inheriting code updates under fixed budgets. Combining physical priors with expert feedback improves atomic point-defect detection over larger models and raises cross-material interface coverage from 5.13% to 72.11% within a 10% area budget. Adapting the framework to micrographs from unseen studies further separates touching nanoparticles by aligning optimization with particle-level measurements. This work moves computational microscopy beyond standalone models and static scripts towards self-evolving platforms that accumulate human scientific expertise

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation. The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions. To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time-Training. RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations. Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory. During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory. To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states. The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent. RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks. Real-world videos, code and hf-weights are available in our project website.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented large language model (LLM) driving agents can reuse past experience, yet previously learned corrections often fail to transfer when traffic conditions change. A key limitation is that existing memories mainly record observed outcomes, providing little evidence about alternative actions. We introduce XMind, a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving to "Think Twice" through cross-memory reasoning. XMind integrates working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The agent first makes an initial decision from the current context and then cross-checks it against retrieved historical experience. If a conflict arises, it makes a second decision guided by the retrieved evidence. To construct reliable episodic memory, XMind evaluates alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and stores the verified outcomes as structured risk capsules. These capsules are retrieved by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics. Across closed-loop highway simulations, XMind achieves success rates of 83.3-93.3%, exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average. Evaluation on K-Risk further demonstrates lower decision risk on unseen real-world high-risk interactions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. Code is available at https://github.com/xiangxiangliuwo/XMind

The resulting evidence is stored as risk capsules in episodic memory for reuse across episodes. The LLM parameters remain frozen throughout the whole process.

papers.abstract: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.
authors: Ruijie Ma, Haoyue Liu, Mingda Zhang, Dongxu Yue, Xiaoying Tang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining sufficient visual evidence from growing, variable-quality observation histories with limited computation and memory.
Constructs memories by selecting informative full frames that satisfy object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements.
Incrementally updates memories by locally reselection affected frames as new observations arrive, preserving coverage efficiently.

papers.abstract: AI-generated music has become common on music streaming platforms, and listeners often cannot distinguish it from music made by humans. AI-music detection is therefore needed, but detectors trained on a fixed set of generators often fail on unseen generators. As new generators emerge frequently, updating a universal detector, a single model for all generators, typically requires substantial training data and computation, while risking performance degradation on previously learned generators. We therefore introduce IncrementDET, a detector that learns each new generator by a process called enrollment. For each generator, IncrementDET trains one linear classifier, which we call a needle, to separate samples of that generator from a fixed set of human reference tracks. Enrolling a new generator adds one needle while the previously constructed needles remain unchanged. A Sidak correction keeps the overall false-positive rate at its target as needles are added. To compare detectors under these conditions, we define the task of continual AI-generated music detection and introduce a benchmark in which generators arrive one at a time. The benchmark measures the accuracy of a detector before and after each update and the cost of each update. For this benchmark, we also construct EvoMusicFake-17K, a dataset of instrumental music from six recent generators and four human music platforms. Compared with SpecTTTra, a state-of-the-art universal detector, IncrementDET learns a new generator more accurately from only a few samples, generalizes better to unseen generators and better preserves detection performance on previously learned generators, at a substantially lower update cost. The structure of IncrementDET can also be applied to the detection of generated images and video, where new generators are released just as frequently.
authors: Runbao Du, Wei Li, Qile He
bullets: Addresses the failure of fixed-generator detectors and the high cost and degradation risks of updating universal detectors.
Enrolls each generator with a linear “needle” classifier trained against fixed human reference tracks; existing needles remain unchanged.
Uses Sidak correction to maintain the target overall false-positive rate as more needles are added.
Introduces continual AI-generated music detection and the EvoMusicFake-17K benchmark covering six generators and four human platforms.
Reports better few-shot learning, unseen-generator generalization, retention of prior detection performance, and lower update cost than SpecTTTra under the benchmark setting.

papers.abstract: Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. We present RoboHarness-RL, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models. To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop LiteHarness, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance. With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%). Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to $4\times$, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/RoboHarness-RL/
authors: Liyang Li, Mingyu Liu, Xiaoman Li, Zhiyue Zhao, Jin-Chuan Shi, Canyu Zhao, Haokai Zhang, Jinyuan Tian, Linhao Zhong, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen

Introduces LiteHarness, a hierarchical-memory system that keeps multi-turn contexts compact while preserving task performance.
With Qwen3.5-9B, RL improves success on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Pro, and randomized unseen RoboTwin scenes.
RL reduces repetitive tool calls, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback.

papers.abstract: Even when multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer incorrectly, their internal cues often point to the relevant region. A widely used remedy re-presents the cue-selected region as an enlarged crop to supply finer detail. However, we find that much of its gain requires no new detail: it largely survives when the crop comes from the already-seen low-resolution input, and partly even when the region's cached tokens are merely copied. Part of re-presentation's gain thus comes from drawing attention to evidence the model already holds. We propose InCue, a test-time framework that makes better use of this evidence without additional visual input. InCue treats visual attention and predictive-entropy gradients as Internal Cues, couples them into a spatial target, and optimizes only an offset on the existing visual tokens to steer attention toward it. Under matched visual-token budgets, InCue achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming recent test-time methods and improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V$^*$ and 23.4% on its hard samples. Its gains carry over to eight general benchmarks. Code will be available at https://github.com/paul-swu/InCue.
authors: Shuwei Wu, Siyue Yu, Longin Jan Latecki
bullets: Re-presenting cropped regions helps partly by highlighting evidence the model has already seen, not only by supplying finer detail.
InCue combines visual-attention and predictive-entropy gradients to identify a spatial target.
It optimizes an offset over existing visual tokens, avoiding additional visual input while preserving matched token budgets.
The method reportedly achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving four MLLMs by up to 8.9% on V* and 23.4% on hard samples, with gains across eight general benchmarks.
Scope: InCue is a test-time framework and relies on internal cues available from the MLLM.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of InCue. The MLLM stays frozen, and the only free variable is an additive offset ∆U on the cached visual tokens U0. RCR amplifies J inside the best-scoring window W ⋆ to form the spatial target T . Test-time optimization then updates ∆U to increase the overlap between the current attention A(k) and T (k). The cues and the target are refreshed at every step k, and the answer is read out after K steps (Output): here it changes from (C) pink to the correct (D) black.

papers.abstract: Hybrid physics-neural simulators embed neural networks in partial differential equation (PDE) solvers to model unresolved subgrid dynamics while preserving resolved physics and conservation laws. Because closure outputs feed back across time steps, single-step offline regression does not directly minimize multi-step rollout error, motivating online trajectory optimization. Solver backpropagation through time (BPTT) is the standard online solution when solver derivatives are available, yet many operational Fortran and C/C++ simulators expose only non-differentiable, forward-only interfaces. We introduce FORGE (Forward-Only Response and Gauss-Newton Estimation), an online framework that trains embedded networks from forward runs alone by decoupling exact network derivatives from black-box simulator dynamics. Stage I warms up the rollout via a low-dimensional Gauss-Newton step along output-orthonormal weight directions, canceling multi-layer feature drift via a final-layer correction. Stage II perturbs spatial output fields to fit a gain-bounded causal linear response operator across rollout steps, solves for regularized target outputs, and updates all weights via network backpropagation. Across five 2D and 3D benchmarks spanning phase separation, reaction-diffusion, fluid and MHD turbulence, and ocean circulation, FORGE outperforms gradient-free, reinforcement-learning, and emulator-based baselines, cutting coarse-solver test mean squared error (MSE) by 50%-96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, outperforming the strongest forward-only baseline by 16%-69%, and recovering 88%-98% of Solver BPTT's gains. Code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/FORGE.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Tianrun Gao, Haomin Wen, Xiaomeng Huang
bullets: Addresses multi-step rollout optimization when operational Fortran/C/C++ simulators expose only forward, non-differentiable interfaces.
Uses a two-stage approach: low-dimensional Gauss–Newton warm-up with final-layer correction, followed by response-operator fitting and network backpropagation.
Evaluated on five 2D/3D benchmarks covering phase separation, reaction-diffusion, turbulence, and ocean circulation.
Reduces coarse-solver test MSE by 50–96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, recovering 88–98% of BPTT’s gains.
Scope: targets embedded neural closures in PDE-based hybrid simulators with forward-only access.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models need to continually acquire new manipulation skills while retaining the ability to follow previously learned instructions. Experience replay (ER) can mitigate catastrophic forgetting, but retaining only a small number of historical expert frames per task leaves many old-instruction responses without direct supervision. Under limited replay, we observe a structured failure mode in which an earlier instruction can trigger a subsequently learned, competing goal. To address this gap, we propose Cross-Instruction Anchoring (XIA), which supplements expert replay with instruction-conditioned response preservation. At each task boundary, XIA freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions paired with current observations. This extends supervision beyond stored historical examples without requiring additional expert replay data. Experiments across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites demonstrate improved success rates and reduced forgetting compared with ER under identical historical expert-data budgets. Additional RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support the effectiveness of XIA.
authors: Ziyang Chen, Dehua Chen, Shaoguang Wang, Xu Yan, Hao Huang, Tao Chen
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when continual VLA learning uses only small historical expert-data budgets.
Identifies a failure mode where old instructions trigger newly learned, competing goals.
Freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions under current observations.
Improves success rates and reduces forgetting versus experience replay across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites.
RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support its effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.
authors: Shanmuga Venkatachalam, Quinn Jacobson, John Paul Shen
bullets: Uses temporal coding with at most one spike per input line and multi-segment dendritic neurons.
Learns all 4-bit integer weights through local reward-modulated STDP, avoiding backpropagation through time; inference uses comparisons and additions.
Achieves 78.6% on CREMA-D with 2.34M synapses and 98.82% on UrbanSound8K-AV with 1.38M synapses.
Reports 23–106× lower weight memory and two- to three-orders-of-magnitude lower measured synaptic energy than spiking baselines.
Supports single-pass learning on CREMA-D and rapid continual adaptation to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

papers.tldr: NeuTNN-AV enables highly efficient low-precision multimodal audio-visual spiking classification with competitive accuracy, compact synapses, and rapid online learning.

papers.abstract: Old and new document embeddings coexist during incremental gallery re-encoding. RELAY trains a new query encoder with a learned projection against the original gallery, then freezes both to train the new document encoder. The same query vector scores both document versions throughout a single re-encoding pass. After backfill, optional query refinement drops the projection and reuses the stored document vectors. Across three text-to-image retrieval upgrades on COCO and Flickr30K, RELAY improves Recall@1 on untouched galleries by 8.66-10.23 percentage points over the original systems. For direct re-encoding, RELAY ranks first in both Qwen-to-Qwen upgrades and second in CLIP-to-Qwen by area under the Recall@1 curve, under both native scoring and matched calibration. With embeddings held fixed, calibrating scores separately for each document version can reduce drops in Recall@1 during backfill and change which method achieves the highest backfill AUC. After query refinement, final Recall@1 is within 0.97 percentage points of conventional joint training in all three upgrades.
authors: Yu Wang, Chuan Qin, Qiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses compatibility between old and new document embeddings during gallery backfill.
Trains a projected query encoder against the original gallery, then freezes it to train the new document encoder.
A single query representation scores both document versions during one re-encoding pass; optional refinement later removes the projection.
Across three COCO and Flickr30K text-to-image upgrades, it improves untouched-gallery Recall@1 by 8.66–10.23 points over the original systems.
Final Recall@1 after refinement is within 0.97 points of conventional joint training; calibration can affect backfill performance and rankings.

papers.abstract: Pretrained antipodal grasping networks generalize well to canonical shapes but frequently fail zero-shot on novel objects with irregular mass distributions, thin rims, or unfamiliar handles. While episodic experience memory adapts a frozen base policy without retraining, naive retrieval suffers from visual appearance bias, negative transfer from overriding working base grasps, and degenerate closed-loop acquisition. We present VG-GP, a plug-and-play Visuo-Geometric Gaussian Process memory framework for closed-loop $SE(2)$ residual grasp transfer. First, we fuse color-invariant surface-normal DINOv2 features, canonical $SE(2)$ gripper-aligned 3D local heightmaps, and contact-geometry descriptors under a product kernel with Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) lengthscales learned strictly on source objects. Second, we model the joint posterior over the base grasp and candidate $SE(2)$ alternatives, overriding the base policy only when the joint-covariance Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) clears a risk-sensitive threshold. Third, an online counterfactual curation gate using single-record necessity and sufficiency interventions quarantines source experiences causing negative transfer. Fourth, we close the acquisition loop via Bayesian Expected Improvement (EI) over equal-budget $SE(2)$ probes. Across 42 disjoint YCB objects in ManiSkill3 (20 source, 12 development, 10 held-out test), VG-GP wraps a pretrained GR-ConvNet base policy and raises physical lift rate across all 22 unseen objects from 38.6% (34/88) to 53.4% (47/88) with zero regressions (+13 rescues, 0 losses; object-clustered 95% CI [+6.8%, +22.7%], exact McNemar $p = 0.00024$). On the 10 held-out objects, EI active acquisition reaches 45.0% (18/40 vs. 32.5% base, 5/7 of oracle headroom), achieves 55.0% probe divergence over passive fallback, and monotonically reduces epistemic uncertainty.
bullets: Addresses failures caused by irregular mass distributions, thin rims, unfamiliar handles, visual bias, and negative transfer.
Uses a Gaussian Process over appearance-, geometry-, and contact-based features to predict $SE(2)$ grasp adaptations.
Overrides the base grasp only when a joint-covariance risk criterion is satisfied, while quarantining harmful source experiences.
Uses Bayesian Expected Improvement to select equal-budget closed-loop probes and reduce epistemic uncertainty.
Across 22 unseen objects, lift rate increased from 38.6% to 53.4% with zero regressions; on 10 held-out objects, active acquisition reached 45.0% versus 32.5% for the base policy.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an episodic visuo-geometric memory framework for closed-loop grasp adaptation, directly relevant to robot manipulation and embodied memory.
papers.title: VG-GP: Uncertainty-Gated Visuo-Geometric Memory for Negative-Transfer-Resistant Grasp Adaptation
papers.tldr: VG-GP improves zero-shot grasp adaptation on unfamiliar objects by combining visuo-geometric memory, risk-gated transfer, and active probe selection without retraining the base policy.

papers.abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.
bullets: Introduces a representation-level Fisher-like matrix to rank hidden directions by their influence on downstream computation.
Across pretrained vision networks, a small task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance and is often more compact than geometry-based alternatives.
The compressed subspace is more robust to adversarial attacks targeting the full network.
Functionally distinct directions, such as shape- and texture-sensitive subspaces, can be separated and selectively ablated.
These subspaces support continual learning and expose task-dependent inter-model alignment that full-space comparisons miss.

papers.tldr: Deep networks often rely on a low-dimensional, task-sensitive “functional spine” that preserves behavior, improves robustness, and reveals distinct computational roles.

papers.abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.
authors: Yaswanth Chittepu, Raghavendra Addanki, Anup Rao, Branislav Kveton, Scott Niekum
bullets: Full interaction histories often retain irrelevant observations and actions, creating unnecessary input overhead.
The paper defines a sufficient state abstraction by preserving task performance of a fixed reference agent, rather than exactly matching its behavior.
Deterministic recursive programs are searched using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm.
On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, abstractions maintain near-reference success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively.
The learned programs explicitly show what information is retained, updated, and discarded.

papers.abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.
bullets: Targets recognizable, recurring stuck states in robot foundation models rather than random failures.
A language-model agent reads and writes the policy’s parameters, repurposing near-silent action-expert neurons as failure-triggered corrective switches.
Applied to the simulated pi0.5 policy, edits to roughly 0.0002% of parameters improved success on recurring failures, including after task fine-tuning.
Reversed and random edits support that improvements came from the intended corrective behavior.
Works best when failures are internally recognizable and a simple correction can resolve them.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.
authors: Javier Movellan, Manjot Bilkhu, Young-mok Jung, Sirajul Salekin, Henry Tran, Zhao Huang
bullets: Models each chunk’s answered queries with a mixture of von Mises–Fisher components anchored at its embedding, plus a time-varying latent utility.
Provides a closed-form online filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates from curator feedback.
Unifies several existing retrieval-feedback methods as special cases under fixed or simplified assumptions.
Matches prior methods on unchanged-query settings but outperforms them when new chunks make old ones obsolete.
On a nine-month personal-agent memory, improves Recall@5 from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little effect on never-queried chunks.

papers.title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: BRAG is a Bayesian online retrieval model that adapts to changing chunk utility and improves long-term memory retrieval, especially when newer information supersedes older content.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit near-zero forgetting in specific continual learning settings with experience replay. However, robustness to domain shift of learned tasks remains unexplored. In this work, we study the robustness of Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under out-of-distribution (OOD) data using the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. While the in-domain (ID) setup achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting, OOD performance on previous tasks quickly collapses. Specifically, we show that during the continual learning process, the OOD capabilities of the model degrade, following a shared representational pattern across domain shifts, which is also visible behaviorally in the two simpler suites. Representational analysis shows that drift concentrates in the multimodal and action features. Linear probes indicate that OOD features still retain task-relevant information, but appear unreadable, consistent with representation misalignment. These findings suggest that even when ID stability remains intact, severe OOD forgetting can still occur, accompanied by representational drift during continual learning.
authors: Adri\`a Ruiz, Bart{\l}omiej Twardowski, Tinne Tuytelaars, Sergi Masip
bullets: Studies Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under continual learning on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus.
Finds that OOD performance on previously learned tasks rapidly collapses despite stable in-domain performance.
Identifies shared representational drift across domain shifts, concentrated in multimodal and action features.
Linear probes show OOD features retain task-relevant information but become difficult to read, suggesting representation misalignment.
Shows that ID stability alone is insufficient for assessing continual-learning robustness.

papers.title: Near-Zero Forgetting Is Not Enough: Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Continual Learning of Pretrained VLAs

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li, Zhixiang Lu, Haolin Yang, Jianxu Chen, Yifan Lu, Di Fan, Yutong Xie
bullets: Addresses repeated orchestration errors when agents choose and sequence spatial tools.
Stores condition–action Experiences and procedures with activation and termination conditions as Skills.
Uses contrastive rollouts to estimate an Experience’s utility and consolidates consistently useful ones into Skills.
Combines Experiences and Skills through three designs, including skill-activated experiences.
Achieves the best accuracy across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, covering 20 settings.

papers.abstract: Continual echocardiographic segmentation remains challenging due to catastrophic forgetting, domain shifts, and heterogeneous anatomical supervision. Existing continual-learning methods often struggle to preserve previously acquired knowledge while adapting to new imaging distributions, particularly under limited replay memory and incomplete anatomical annotations. To address these challenges, we propose the Reliability-Aware Replay Network (RAR-Net), a continual segmentation framework integrating multi-factor exemplar prioritization, protected task-aware memory, forgetting-conditioned adaptive replay, and structure-aware supervision. RAR-Net combines class, boundary, image, anatomical, and temporal reliability criteria to prioritize informative historical examples, while adaptive replay regulates their contribution during sequential training. Structure-aware supervision further reinforces previously learned anatomical knowledge when subsequent datasets provide incomplete annotations. Extensive experiments performed on CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic demonstrate that our RAR-Net achieves the highest final average accuracy among the evaluated continual-learning methods, with competitive historical knowledge retention and segmentation performance approaching the offline joint-training reference. These findings indicate that coordinating reliability-guided memory management, forgetting-conditioned replay, and anatomy-specific supervision can support knowledge retention and adaptation under the evaluated sequence of heterogeneous echocardiographic datasets.
authors: Zahid Ullah, Sieun Choi, Jihie Kim
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting, domain shifts, limited replay memory, and incomplete anatomical annotations.
Prioritizes historical exemplars using class, boundary, image, anatomical, and temporal reliability criteria.
Uses task-aware memory protection and forgetting-conditioned replay to regulate past-example contributions during sequential training.
Adds structure-aware supervision to preserve anatomical knowledge when new datasets have incomplete labels.

Across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic, achieves the highest final average accuracy among evaluated continual-learning methods, with retention and performance approaching offline joint training.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overview of the RAR-Net framework for continual echocardiographic segmentation. The model sequentially learns CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic using a shared segmentation network and protected replay memory. Training combines current-task, replay, and structure-aware losses, while an exponential moving average (EMA) of previous-task forgetting adaptively controls the replay weight λ (e) r . Historical samples are prioritized using class, boundary, image, anatomical, and temporal reliability factors. Memory allocation follows predefined task weights normalized over the observed tasks.

Fig. 6 Qualitative LV segmentation comparison on EchoNet-Dynamic. Each row corresponds to the CL method indicated in the figure. From left to right, the columns show the input echocardiogram, GT LV segmentation, predicted LV segmentation, and pixel-wise disagreement map. White regions indicate disagreement between the prediction and GT. The predominantly contour-like errors indicate that the remaining disagreement is concentrated mainly near the LV boundary.

Fig. 3 Reliability-aware protected memory mechanism of RAR-Net. Candidate samples are evaluated using complementary class, boundary, image, anatomical, and temporal reliability factors, which are combined into a unified priority score. Samples are subsequently maintained within taskspecific protected memory partitions to limit domination by newly observed domains. The illustrated 450/900/450 partition represents the protected-memory configuration after all three tasks have been observed; at earlier stages, the predefined relative task-allocation weights are renormalized over the tasks observed up to that point to determine the corresponding memory quotas. Priority-aware sampling retrieves representative previous-task examples for subsequent replay learning.

Fig. 4 CL evaluation protocol of RAR-Net across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic. The first two datasets provide LV, MYO, and LA annotations, whereas EchoNet-Dynamic provides LV-only supervision. From the second task onward, training incorporates protected replay memory with reliability-aware sample selection and stage-wise normalized task-allocation weights. After each task, the model is evaluated on all previously observed domains to assess segmentation performance, knowledge retention, forgetting, and transfer.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.
bullets: Addresses redundant re-encoding, short usable history, and coarse episode-level reward signals in MLLM-based navigation.
Uses recurrent Gated DeltaNet state plus a short recent-frame window and keyframes selected by their impact on the recurrent state.
Maintains constant-size memory, enabling fixed computation per step and whole-episode training with inference-level memory use.
Introduces Counterfactual Rewind, which revisits a rollout near its closest goal approach, applies expert corrections, and credits actions by outcome change.
Reports 71.9% success on R2R-CE and 73.6% on RxR-CE val-unseen; runs at 104 ms per step and improves prior single-RGB performance by 9.1 points on R2R-CE.

papers.abstract: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. In five-task sequences with slow forgetting, the stored bracket outperforms the EWC penalty on MNIST and CIFAR-10 features (by 0.16-0.17) and ties it on Fashion-MNIST; it fades as summaries age on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, where a Taylor estimate from the same summary holds up better. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition, provided the summary is kept fresh.
bullets: Learning order differences closely track forgetting, supporting a link between non-commuting task gradients and catastrophic forgetting.
Using only the old task’s stored gradient and top 20 Hessian eigenpairs, the bracket ranks slow forgetting during new-task training.
For well-learned tasks with slow forgetting, it outperforms or matches Elastic Weight Consolidation and sometimes matches access to old data.
It fails for rapidly forgetting domain shifts and partially learned tasks, where residual gradients and stale summaries dominate.
In longer task sequences, its advantage diminishes as summaries age; a Taylor estimate can remain more robust.

papers.title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
papers.tldr: A stored Lie-bracket summary can predict slow catastrophic forgetting without old data, but becomes unreliable when forgetting is fast, the old task is poorly learned, or summaries become stale.

papers.abstract: Recent studies of embodied agents based on frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) develop harness engineering around the MLLM, such as harnesses with post-trained policies and recursive self-improvement loops. Yet whether these additions exceed the native capability of the MLLM remains unexplored. We introduce SimplEvo to explore how far an MLLM can improve under direct control when it retains its execution experience in self-written text memories. It requires no weight updates, post-trained policies, or privileged information. The MLLM writes a coordinate-free task memory once from a single demonstration. Under a strict train-test protocol, it then creates a bounded working memory on training episodes only and refines it after each episode with lessons on procedure, completion, and recovery. Both memories stay fixed at test time. On EBench, SimplEvo lifts the success rate (SR) of GPT-6-Astra under direct control from 46.7% to 81.7%, and tops the RoboDojo leaderboard with 69.63% SR and a score of 75.32. Compared with memories that also store past visual frames, SimplEvo reaches a similar SR with text memory alone while using fewer tokens. With its memories fixed, SimplEvo also generalizes to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations. Moreover, the working memory transfers across models: written by GPT-6-Astra, it can be reused as is by weaker MLLMs and improve their performance without any adaptation of their own.
bullets: Addresses whether harness engineering can surpass an MLLM’s native capability through direct, experience-based memory evolution.
Creates a coordinate-free task memory from one demonstration and refines bounded working memory after training episodes with procedural, completion, and recovery lessons.
Keeps both memories fixed at test time, while generalizing to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations.
Raises GPT-6-Astra’s EBench success rate from 46.7% to 81.7% and achieves 69.63% success on RoboDojo.
Text-only memory matches visual-frame memory success with fewer tokens and can transfer across models without adaptation.

papers.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.
bullets: Addresses distributed knowledge and privacy barriers that limit centralized GraphRAG.
Uses lightweight knowledge indices for federated routing to relevant clients without exposing graph structures.
Constructs controlled-disclosure evidence abstracts from retrieved subgraphs for server-side reconstruction.
Experiments show consistent improvements over existing baselines in retrieval and downstream generation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The architecture of FedGRAG. This process consists of a pre-process and a query phase. During the pre-process phase, the client and server perform collaborative training to extract lowdimensional graph embeddings; the client then uploads prototypes to the server to construct a prototype graph. In the query phase, the server routes the query to the appropriate semantic cluster on the client. Subsequently, an evidence subgraph is constructed within the cluster, and the server aggregates these reconstructed evidence facts to generate retrieval results.

papers.abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.
bullets: Evaluated four open-weight models on 15,200 math attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors and testing 27,568 counterfactual continuations.
Verbalized confidence did not distinguish erroneous from correct reasoning, with near-chance error detection and confidence often remaining very high after mistakes.
Externally injected low-confidence tokens improved downstream correction across all models, especially with active rethinking instructions.
Injecting doubt into correct reasoning could harm performance, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points.
Self-correction is therefore limited primarily by in-situ error detection, not by the ability to repair errors once uncertainty is supplied.

papers.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li, Xinlin Zhuang, Zhixiang Lu, Haolin Yang, Jianxu Chen, Yifan Lu, Zhiran Zhang, Yutong Xie
bullets: Introduces 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, starting from a single view.

Uses 3D-verified questions, masked-evidence abstention tests, and human verification of over 95% of sampled questions.
Across 23 VLMs, the strongest models seek evidence purposefully but lose useful information through limited memory.
Weaker and specialized models perform near random exploration or fail to reason from gathered evidence.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces ActSpace-Bench, a novel benchmark for evaluating active exploration and spatial reasoning capabilities of VLMs in 3D indoor scenes, directly addressing the gap in 'active spatial intelligence' and highlighting memory limitations during exploration.
papers.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: ActSpace-Bench evaluates whether vision-language models can purposefully navigate real indoor spaces to gather evidence for spatial questions, revealing strong evidence-seeking but major memory and reasoning limitations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3\% and 90.6\% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2\% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3\% vs. 93.7\% success).

Uses structured memory and parameterized recovery primitives, with mandatory post-repair verification.
Achieves 91.3% and 90.6% average success on RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, while reducing VLM calls by 74.2% versus chunkwise monitoring.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Qinglong Zheng, Changyi Yang, Tong Wei, Andy Mao, Zetian Li, Chaoran Cheng, Hui Ren, Ruihan Guo, Xianrui Zhong, Xizheng Yu, Jingyuan Li, Xi Zhu, Kaiqu Liang, Chang Xu, Zun Qian, Zidi Xiong, Yuezhu Zhao, Xu Huang, Ge Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that fixed model weights cannot adapt lifelong without costly or temporary methods such as reflection, memory, search, or prompting.
The agent analyzes its own task records, identifies an inefficient hidden-state behavior, and rewrites a single weight tensor overnight.
It evaluates each edit against the unchanged agent on practice tasks and retains only changes that do not degrade performance.
Across thousands of held-out episodes, the retained edit improves task completion while reducing steps, wasted actions, and token use at the same per-step cost.
Improvement remains stable over multiple rounds; among four model sizes, only the 27B agent exhibits this behavior, within the described household setting.
