papers.selection_reason: Embodied agent self-improves by editing its own weights between tasks, enabling continual lifelong learning.
papers.title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: A 27B embodied language agent continually improves itself by safely editing its own weights between tasks, without training, gradients, auxiliary models, or inference-time overhead.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.
authors: Yicheng Xu (Zhejiang University), Wencan Jiang (Zhejiang University), Zihao Zhu (Stanford University, AGIBOT Innovation), Keru Zhou (Tsinghua University), Chang Zhou (AGIBOT Innovation), Li Liu (AGIBOT Innovation), Maoqing Yao (AGIBOT Innovation), Yong Liu (Zhejiang University), Jiangning Zhang (Zhejiang University)

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.
authors: Jianyu Wu, Yizhou Wang, Encheng Su, Jinouwen Zhang, Pengze Li, Lintao Wang, Chen Tang, Aoran Wang, Wanli Ouyang, Shixiang Tang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of self-consistency, which discards earlier reasoning and can reinforce incorrect majority answers.
In-Context RSI re-solves questions using previous solutions as references, allowing inference to build on earlier attempts.
In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority.
Experiments report +13.89% average accuracy over the base model and +4.79% over the strongest self-consistency method at the same test-time budget.

papers.abstract: Active 3D reconstruction aims to allocate a sparse view budget to recover complete geometry and high-fidelity renderings. However, existing methods degrade sharply in multi-room homes: myopic next-best-view scoring gives transit no credit for distant rooms and over-polishes irreducible nearby residuals, whereas dense mappers reach far rooms only by streaming thousands of frames. We propose ROAM-GS, a training-free active multi-room reconstruction framework that couples persistent goals with selective views: each decision selects a goal and a variable-horizon prefix toward it, capturing only at its endpoint. A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores poses by projecting post-update defects and viewing directions. Persistent goals credit transit with their remaining value and are released once arrivals stop measurably improving them. Without per-scene tuning, ROAM-GS achieves state-of-the-art multi-room reconstruction while preserving single-room Replica fidelity, raising mean coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and from 47% to 96% (+11.7 dB PSNR) on HM3D, and matching 90-minute dense mapping using $173\times$ fewer views.
authors: Jiawei Jiang, Haonan Zhou, Wendi Hu, Jiabei Hu, Yina Xiang, Kaiyue Zhou, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Addresses myopic view selection, which neglects distant rooms and over-focuses on nearby irreducible errors.
Uses a training-free planner that selects a goal and a variable-length transit path, capturing only at the endpoint.
A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores candidate poses using projected post-update defects and viewing directions.
Persistent goals assign value to transit and are released when further arrivals stop improving reconstruction.
Raises coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and 47% to 96% on HM3D, while matching dense mapping with 173× fewer views.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ROAM-GS. Selective views (bottom) truncate the path to the goal view at variable horizons: only the prefix endpoint (orange) is captured, while query poses (hollow) are credited from memory. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts, that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance degradation upon deployment. We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics model. This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations, including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated low-friction surface.
authors: Rui Dai, Shunpeng Yang, Zhen Fu, Maolin Lei, Jiaqi Song, Hua Chen, Nikos Tsagarakis
bullets: Static domain randomization can fail under unseen payload and friction changes.
The method adapts a learned dynamics model to deployed target conditions.
A concurrent teacher–student scheme updates both the policy and dynamics model.
The adapted dynamics model is integrated into on-policy reinforcement learning.
Bipedal experiments show adaptability under payloads up to 80% of self-weight and oil-lubricated low-friction surfaces.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved significant milestones, yet its reliance on the i.i.d. assumption renders it vulnerable to real-world distribution shifts. While Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm for on-the-fly enhancement, its application to driving is hindered by two barriers: (i) multi-task adaptation dependency, where updates to upstream perception also affect downstream planning, while perception confidence alone does not directly assess these downstream effects; and (ii) continuous adaptation instability, where recursive online updates over long horizons cause compounding parameter drift. To address these challenges, we propose P2-TTA, a plug-and-play TTA framework for the continual adaptation of end-to-end driving models. P2-TTA coordinates adaptation through a joint objective combining perception entropy minimization with a retrospective temporal planning consistency objective derived from observed ego motion. To stabilize online updates, we use an EMA teacher as a moving parameter reference and reject candidate updates that increase historical planning loss. Extensive experiments across multiple models demonstrate that, by updating an average of 0.11 per mille of parameters with an average adaptation time of 19.9 ms on different backbones, P2-TTA achieves average recovery rates of 36.4%, 30.0%, and 9.3% for L2, collision rate, and PDMS, respectively, under severe distribution shifts. Under a shared perception-planning objective, P2-TTA achieves the highest L2 and collision recovery among the compared TTA baselines on UniAD.
authors: Shiyu Fang, Yiming Cui, Qihang Huang, Zhan Chen, Collister Chua, Wenhui Huang, Peng Hang, Chen Lv, Jian Sun

Combines perception entropy minimization with a temporal planning-consistency objective based on observed ego motion.
Uses an EMA teacher and rejects updates that worsen historical planning loss to limit parameter drift.
Across multiple backbones, updates only a very small parameter subset with low adaptation latency and recovers performance under severe distribution shifts.
Reports the strongest L2 and collision recovery among compared TTA baselines on UniAD under a shared perception–planning objective.

papers.abstract: General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub- network in a Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration.
authors: Nilay Kushawaha, Abdalla Swikir, Fares Abu-Dakka
bullets: Represents each skill as a dedicated expert in a Progressive Neural Network, preserving previously learned skills.

Real-robot experiments demonstrate compositional manipulation and expert orchestration.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (\textit{CPT}) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (\textit{MCQA}) accuracy alone, offering only a narrow view of how adaptation unfolds. We jointly track factual knowledge via \textit{MCQA} and open-ended behavior via pairwise preference rankings across $18$ checkpoints for each of eight instruction-tuned \textit{Qwen} models ($0.5B$ to $8B$), adapted to German medicine with \textit{CPT} and \textit{SLERP} merging. The two axes converge at consistently different rates, with preference rankings reaching $90\%$ of their total gain after a median of $1.7B$ tokens versus $3.5B$ for \textit{MCQA}. A judge-free token-distribution measure reaches this threshold at $1.9B$ tokens. Per-aspect scores indicate that these early preference gains largely reflect surface alignment, meaning models can sound domain-appropriate before their factual knowledge catches up. Larger adapted models close more of the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, whereas preference gain per FLOP falls by about an order of magnitude across our size range. We therefore argue that judge-based preference scores, which can plateau while \textit{MCQA} knowledge is still improving, should not be used alone to infer adaptation convergence or domain readiness.

Per-aspect analysis suggests early preference gains mainly reflect surface alignment rather than fully acquired medical knowledge.
Larger models reduce the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, but preference improvement per FLOP declines sharply with model size.
Preference scores may plateau while factual knowledge continues improving, limiting their use as a standalone convergence signal.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models have made substantial progress, yet reliable closed-loop driving in complex traffic remains challenging. Beyond improving individual models, system-level orchestration offers a complementary approach by coordinating driving capabilities and computation. We introduce ROSE-Drive (Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution), a model-agnostic framework that jointly orchestrates driving execution and computation. It coordinates frozen driving models with driving skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers. A distilled vision-language model (VLM) proposes driving tasks and scene relations. Shared physical state and persistent tasks support capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels, maintains task responsibility through handover, and uses execution feedback to select controllers, reuse valid motion references, and schedule model inference. Offline revisions use execution records to refine skills and their coordination through a stable task interface. Successive system stages inherit these revisions while model, perception, and VLM weights remain fixed. Evaluations with four driving models on Bench2Drive v0.0.3, Bench2Drive v0.0.4, and Fail2Drive show accumulated capability and transfer before target-benchmark revision. On held-out Longest6, driving score (DS) rises from 25 to 52 for AutoMoT and from 22 to 47 for SimLingo across system stages, while both systems skip new model inference on over 71% of control steps.
authors: Qihang Huang, Zhidong Wang, Zirui Li, YuJie Yan, Jingsong Liang, Shiyu Fang, Collister Chua, Zhan Chen, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reliable driving in complex traffic through system-level orchestration rather than model retraining.
Uses a model-agnostic orchestrator with a distilled VLM, shared physical state, persistent tasks, adaptive scheduling, and controller handovers.
Refines skills and their coordination from execution records while keeping driving, perception, and VLM weights fixed.
Across multiple benchmarks and four driving models, held-out Longest6 driving scores improved substantially across system stages.
More than 71% of control steps skipped new model inference for both reported systems, reducing runtime computation demand.

figures.caption: Figure 2. ROSE-Drive system architecture. Capability composition selects and combines outputs. Task continuity maintains responsibility through execution and handover. Adaptive scheduling determines when to run the driving model and reuse motion references. The VLM proposes driving tasks and scene relations every five control steps, while the orchestrator updates task state at every step. papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.

Uses hints for within-task decisions and completed-task outcomes to update cumulative reward estimates.
Proves regret bounds that improve with hint accuracy, plus a matching lower bound tied to prediction error and policy count.
Experiments on realistic coding benchmarks outperform static steering and naive online adaptive baselines.

papers.abstract: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Shuaicheng Niu, Baian Chen, Weirui Ye, Jihun Hamm, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses hidden deployment shifts such as altered object weight, weakened joints, and controller lag.
Uses observed robot motion and an inverse-dynamics model to infer the commands the original robot would have needed.
Weights competing robot-response hypotheses, including no-change, by how well they predict inferred command labels.
Requires no reward, gradient updates, or data collected from the changed robot.
Across 11 physical shifts, improves average success from 27.8% to 62.9% and preserves performance when physics is unchanged.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step. To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability--- we propose \textbf{\oursfull (\ours)}, a framework that calibrates WAMs' confidence--- adaptively triggering System~2 only when necessary, and distilling System~2's knowledge to form an evolving System~1. First, \ours equips a frozen WAM with \textbf{calibrated self-assessment}: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video--action features is trained via our proposed \textbf{cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning} using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a \textbf{calibrated success probability} at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions. Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk---invoking System~2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System~2 reliability. Third, as System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM's capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System~1 can operate standalone without System~2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.
authors: Wenhao Li, Yu Han, Xiu Su, Dehao Wu, Keke Huang, Shan You, Fei Wang, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses WAM failures in challenging scenes and the high latency and cost of invoking System 2 at every step.
Trains a lightweight judgment token with cross-fitted temporal-difference learning from binary rollout success/failure signals.
Uses calibrated success probabilities to switch between WAM control and System 2 assistance chunk by chunk.
Distills System 2 takeover trajectories into the WAM to repair capability gaps and support later standalone operation.
Mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating aim to preserve existing capabilities during self-evolution.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Judgment-in-the-Loop (JiL) framework. (2) Adaptive System 1 & 2 Takeover (Sec. 3.3): At each decision step, qθ schedules control chunk by chunk; the WAM hands control to a GPT-6-Astra-based agent when qθ < τ and reclaims execution once confidence recovers above τback. (3) Capability-Gap Consolidation (Sec. 3.4): Keeping πbase frozen, successful agent takeovers (Dhelp) are combined with mastered-skill anchor data—the WAM’s own confident successes (Down) and pre-training replay (Dreplay)—into Dmix to train a separate repaired action expert πrep, distilling System 2’s recovery skills into System 1. (4) Erosion-Free Confidence-Gated Deployment (Sec. 3.5): During standalone deployment, πbase dynamically switches to πrep when base confidence qbase drops below τ and reclaims control once confidence recovers, repairing hard states without degrading mastered skills or invoking System 2 (scores shown: Fast-WAM on RoboTwin 2.0, 1 round).

papers.abstract: Model routing assigns each query to a suitable foundation model, but tasks and available models keep changing, and existing routers are either untrained for the pool at hand or fit once and forget earlier tasks when updated. We present AdaptRouter, an adaptive router trained by policy learning: a compact multimodal decision model reads each question with cards describing the current experts and learns from native task feedback, without routing labels, to select one frozen expert. Open-weight and API experts share the router, its inputs, and the quality-cost trade-off but use different losses: cheap open-weight experts are explored with RL, whereas paid API experts are queried once and their cached feedback is reused as soft labels. New tasks are learned without replay, new experts enter as cards, and an open-weight quality-first advantage provably keeps cost from overriding quality. Across four task stages, AdaptRouter loses at most 0.4 points on earlier tasks, whereas feedback-trained routers lose up to 7.0, and as its pool grows from three to ten experts, its accuracy rises from 67.2% to 72.1%. On five API models, it exceeds GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra (low) by over 22 points at under a third of their cost.
authors: Jingpu Yang, Fengxian Ji, Tianhao Li, Juanfan Wu, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang

Across four task stages, earlier-task performance drops by at most 0.4 points; accuracy increases from 67.2% to 72.1% as the pool grows from 3 to 10 experts, while outperforming two cited API models by over 22 points at less than one-third their cost.

papers.abstract: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.
authors: Keuntae Kim, Beomseok Lee, Hyunwoo Kim, Yong Suk Choi
bullets: Backward and forward transfer are interface-dependent, not single model-level properties.
A trained head often shows severe forgetting, while a new probe reveals near-complete recoverability; backbone diagnostics fall between these extremes.
Across encoder and decoder backbones, stability and plasticity show a consistent negative relationship, supported by multiple clustering-free and clustering-based diagnostics.
Just LM-Head Tuning recovers most of the joint-training gap for replay- and distillation-based methods, but less for plain sequential fine-tuning.
The study recommends reporting the evaluation interface alongside forgetting and transfer measurements.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).
authors: Yiheng Du, Jingqi Tian, Xu Jiang, Jiexuan Zhang, Shuyu Wang, Zecheng Tang, Jian Zhang
bullets: Maintains task state and subgoals across visual updates so remembered object identities and progress guide current actions.
At each update, infers an event, revises the task state, grounds a subgoal in the current scene, and generates an action.
Jointly trains one VLA to reason and act without an external reasoning model.
Uses exact likelihoods of memory text tokens for GRPO refinement from rollout rewards while keeping action generation deterministic.
Reports 66.46% on RoboMME, 79.83% on its Reference category, and 90.08% on LIBERO-Mem; it doubles RoboMME success versus an otherwise identical non-recurrent model.

papers.abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. We propose AutoSECO, an automated skill evolution method that learns reusable solver-development guidance from experience. The challenge is that external evaluation measures the completed solver, while the skill guides decisions during development. AutoSECO connects this feedback to guidance deficiencies by tracing performance shortfalls through solver code and recorded development decisions. Revisions are expressed as general instructions and retained only if a fresh solver developed under the revised skill achieves a lower mean evaluation gap. Evolved solely on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP), the skill guides fresh agents in developing solvers for capacitated vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and three-dimensional bin packing without further skill evolution. On TSP, the final mean benchmark gap is 0.52\%, compared with 0.98\% for the skill-evolution baseline SkillOpt. Across all four problems, the evolved skill achieves better aggregate results than no skill guidance, the initial skill, and SkillOpt. The same frozen skill also supports solver development under alternative model--harness configurations. These findings suggest that solver-development experience can be retained as reusable expertise for general-purpose LLM agents.
authors: Zirui Zhu, Cong Zhang, Ni Zhang, Kuan Xu, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Addresses the limited reuse of problem-specific workflows for LLM-generated combinatorial optimization solvers.
Traces solver performance shortfalls through code and development decisions to identify deficiencies in reusable skill guidance.
Retains revised guidance only when a freshly developed solver achieves a lower mean evaluation gap.
A skill evolved only on TSP transfers to vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and 3D bin packing, including under alternative model–harness configurations.
On TSP, AutoSECO reaches a 0.52% mean benchmark gap versus 0.98% for SkillOpt; it also achieves better aggregate results than the listed comparison settings across all four problems.

papers.abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) should continually adapt to users' evolving preferences. Yet extracting preference changes from noisy interaction histories while supporting inexpensive updates remains challenging. We introduce WASP (Weight Adaptation for Streaming Personalization), a recurrent framework that captures fine-grained preferences directly from raw user interactions and generates personalized LoRA adapters without expensive per-user optimization. Specifically, WASP achieves this by training a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation and outputs adapter weights in a single forward pass. As new interactions arrive, WASP updates this representation without reprocessing full interaction history, enabling continual adaptation with per-update costs independent of history length. Experiments on personalization benchmarks and chronological interaction streams show that WASP sustains high-quality personalization over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets. Together, these results support efficient streaming personalization and facilitate privacy-preserving on-device deployment.
authors: Linxi Xie, Chonghua Liao, Mengxuan Wu, Guandao Yang, Zhangyang Wang, Kai Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting to changing user preferences from noisy interaction histories at low cost.
Uses a recurrent framework with a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation.
Produces personalized LoRA adapter weights directly, avoiding expensive per-user optimization.
Updates user representations incrementally, with per-update cost independent of interaction-history length.
Experiments show sustained personalization quality over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets, supporting on-device deployment.

papers.abstract: An artificial neuron computes and learns, but it does not live: the units of a network are fixed when it is designed, and every one of them is kept and paid for whether it is used or not. We give each neuron a second pathway. Beside its Task Path, the usual computation and gradient learning, a dual-pathway neuron has a Growth Path: a nutrient flows from the outputs back through the network, every layer receives the same fixed budget, and each unit is fed in proportion to how much the units above it use it. A well-fed unit divides and a starving unit dies. This allocation is not a separate analysis or pruning step: it runs throughout training and reads only activations and weights. The task is still learned from labels with the ordinary loss, and the training procedure gains no phase, no schedule and no target size. Because the budget is conserved, the competition is zero-sum and a single number sets the size of the network. Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. With Adam the network ends 1.0 to 1.2 points more accurate on the domain than the same network trained ordinarily, at 24% to 60% of its compute, and at 12% of the compute it is still ahead; a random choice of the same number of units gives no gain. Letting starving pretrained units sleep instead of die keeps 1.2 to 4.6 points more of the rarely used content. Over 800 changing tasks a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy while ordinary networks decline. With plain SGD the gains are smaller: at deployment the method trades compute against rarely used content, and on one of the two continual-learning streams it only ties networks of equal size. The experiments are small (three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data); what they show is that a conserved, loss-free second pathway can decide by itself which units a network needs.
bullets: Adds a second, label-free pathway alongside ordinary task learning: nutrient flows backward from outputs and is allocated according to unit use.
Well-fed units divide while starving units die or sleep; a fixed budget controls network size without a separate pruning phase, schedule, or target size.
On narrower deployment domains with Adam, networks retained higher accuracy while using 24–60% of the compute, with gains still reported at 12%.
Sleeping rather than deleting unused pretrained units preserved more rarely used knowledge; across 800 changing tasks, accuracy remained stable while ordinary networks declined.
Results were smaller with SGD and are limited to small three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data.

papers.abstract: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Yuyou Zhang, Janet Wang, Ming Liu, Yijiang Li, Yikai Wang, Weirui Ye, Ding Zhao, Jihun Hamm
bullets: Introduces a benchmark that compares robot memory with the environment paused versus continuously changing.
Covers 29 task families across realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes and controlled ManiSkill tasks, including distractor changes and no-change cases.
Across 34,176 episodes and 16 models, realistic changed-object success drops from 97% when paused to 50% when the world runs.
Slower reasoning does not solve the problem; models often perceive changes but act using stale pre-change camera frames.
Looking again before acting largely closes the realistic gap, but repeated swaps of identical objects still expose memory failures.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.
authors: Jiarui Guo, Jinkai Zhang, Yuanhong Yu, Yongchen Zai, Futang Zhu, Ruizhen Hu, Sida Peng, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Addresses the overhead of dense scene graphs and the non-executable nature of image–text scene records.
Builds an area-segmented occupancy map with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes.
Uses the map to explore unvisited areas and generate executable routes to known locations.
Introduces agent-guided relocalization to match current observations against stored memory and localize within prior maps.
Outperforms baselines across several navigation settings, with especially strong path-efficiency gains, and transfers to a real quadruped robot.

papers.abstract: A frozen language model can give a wrong answer because a fact is unavailable, a reliable passage is ignored, or an unsupported claim survives generation. We review 116 works on inference-time hallucination intervention and its foundations. We trace the development from retrieval and controllable generation to methods that act on input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer. For each family we compare its source of evidence, model access, preparation cost, and the task on which a correction can be established. For activation steering, we distinguish estimating a subspace from applying a state-dependent edit and separate interventions on the prompt from those on the generated prefix. Published comparisons show why faithfulness to a source, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage must be measured separately. Applications in time-sensitive question answering, document synthesis, and visual grounding identify when source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation limits a reported gain.
bullets: Hallucinations can arise from missing facts, ignored reliable evidence, or unsupported claims that persist through generation.
Interventions target input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer.
The review compares methods by evidence source, required model access, preparation cost, and task-specific correction evidence.
For activation steering, it distinguishes subspace estimation from state-dependent editing, and prompt interventions from generated-prefix interventions.

Evaluation should separately measure source faithfulness, factual correctness, informativeness, and answer coverage; gains may be limited by source authority, evidence availability, or capability preservation.

papers.abstract: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.
authors: Fr\'ed\'eric Li Combeau, Nicolas Michel, Toshihiko Yamasaki
bullets: CL-P trains across shifting domains, then adapts online to a future preview domain before evaluating on all seen domains.
Naively combining CL and TTA can damage the recently trained domain and increase forgetting, largely due to shared BatchNorm statistics.
DOSE infers domain membership online and applies adaptation to each image in proportion to its likelihood of belonging to the preview domain.
Across 24 evaluated settings with ResNet and ViT backbones, DOSE matches or improves on CL alone in every setting and on the naive combination in all but one.

papers.selection_reason: Combines continual learning and test-time adaptation under domain shift; proposes adaptive domain inference for seamless CL+TTA integration.
papers.title: Bridging the Gap between Continual Learning and Test-Time Adaptation with Domain Preview
papers.tldr: The paper introduces CL-P, a setting combining continual learning and test-time adaptation under train- and test-time domain shifts, and proposes DOSE to reduce adaptation-induced forgetting.

papers.abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.
bullets: The study examines simulated homes where a resident becomes sick, recovers, and later becomes sick again.
It compares a room-history rule, language-model summaries, and language models with access to raw sighting histories.
The room-history rule outperforms summary-only memories; adding sighting history closes the gap.
Summarizing on top of the history provides no measurable benefit, while history-based methods improve when illness recurs.
Deleting the first illness removes the rule’s advantage and part of the history-based methods’ gains.

papers.abstract: AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.
authors: Teng Cao, Yu Deng, Kristian Kersting
bullets: Across five domains and up to seven author models, agents developed high-scoring task programs.
When environments changed, agent-written runtime checks missed at least half of the resulting failures in four domains.
A monitor trained from normal-run records detected most missed failures in three domains.
Agents generally repaired detected failures, but unrevealed failures remained unrepaired.
Self-improvement evaluations should measure failure detection—not just task scores.

papers.selection_reason: Self-improving agents that detect and repair their own failures during deployment; test-time adaptation of agent code.
papers.title: Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents
papers.tldr: Self-improving agents can achieve high task performance yet fail to detect many environment-induced errors, revealing a critical gap between fixing failures and noticing them.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving systems must not only interpret the current scene but also anticipate perceptual challenges such as occlusions, sparse observations, and recurring failure patterns. However, most existing LiDAR semantic segmentation methods operate in a frame-centric manner, processing each scan independently and discarding past contextual experience, which limits robustness under dynamic scene changes. We propose DREAM, a Dual-memory REAsoning framework for continual LiDAR seMantic segmentation that reframes perception as an experience-driven and anticipatory process. DREAM maintains two complementary memory banks in a strictly online setting: a latent memory that stores compact semantic abstractions of previously observed scenes, and an error memory that records representations associated with uncertain predictions. At each timestep, relevant memory entries are retrieved via cosine similarity and integrated into the feature space through a lightweight modulation mechanism, enabling the model to reinforce consistent semantic patterns while suppressing recurring failure modes. The backbone remains frozen and no past scans are replayed, ensuring computational efficiency and bounded memory growth. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks demonstrate that DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with consistent improvements on dynamic and small-scale objects, highlighting the effectiveness of persistent and error-aware memory for robust long-horizon perception.
bullets: Targets frame-by-frame LiDAR segmentation methods that discard contextual experience and struggle with dynamic changes, occlusions, and sparse observations.
Maintains a latent memory of compact semantic scene abstractions and an error memory of uncertain-prediction representations.
Retrieves relevant memories via cosine similarity and applies lightweight feature modulation to reinforce consistent patterns and reduce recurring failures.
Operates online with a frozen backbone, no past-scan replay, and bounded memory growth.
Experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, especially for dynamic and small-scale objects.

papers.tldr: DREAM improves continual LiDAR semantic segmentation by using dual online memories to recall useful scene patterns and suppress recurring errors without replaying past scans.

papers.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.
authors: Panagiotis Kasnesis, Lazaros Toumanidis, Amalia Contiero Syropoulou, Christos Chatzigeorgiou
bullets: Targets persistent agents in physical environments rather than short-lived task crews.
A planner generates Python actors at runtime, while supervisors restart crashed actors with state intact.
MQTT enables topic-based coordination, external event access, and live migration between edge nodes.
A recorded demo creates a camera-to-lamp workflow, repairs a deliberate division-by-zero, and migrates the agent to a Raspberry Pi.
The extended system includes topic-graph visualization, hand-written-agent support, model management, security details, and limitations.

papers.abstract: Steering one neuron of a small language model can impose a topic or a quirk without training, yet replications show that many published single-neuron recipes are fragile or nonspecific. This paper asks whether an interpersonal stance can be controlled in this manner. The stance studied is a distant crush, a chatbot character that is guarded, intermittently warm and inconsistent. In Qwen3.5, 4B, contrasting activations on hand-written guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 of layer 9 as a candidate for controlling this stance. Increasing this neuron activation made the characters replies more distant. Three language models rated this change as stronger than the effects of changing randomly selected neurons, and a blind human comparison supported the finding. Changing the interventions direction between messages also shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles. This suggests that a language model conversational stance can be personalized without finetuning.
bullets: The paper tests whether one-neuron steering can control an interpersonal stance rather than only topics or quirks.
Contrasting guarded and eager replies identified neuron 7515 in layer 9 of Qwen3.5 4B as a candidate.
Increasing its activation produced more distant replies, while reversing intervention direction shifted replies between warmer and more distant styles.
Three language models and a blind human comparison judged the targeted change stronger than changes from randomly selected neurons.
The findings suggest a possible route to personalized conversational character control without fine-tuning, but also highlight concerns about fragile or nonspecific single-neuron recipes.

papers.title: Single-Coordinate Activation Steering for Controllable Social Stance in Language Models
papers.tldr: A single activation coordinate can steer a language model toward a more distant or warmer conversational stance without fine-tuning, though the approach is model- and stance-specific.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.
authors: Daojun Liang, Xiao Hong, Pei Zhang, Yinglong Wang, Shuo Li, Jing Chen, Ying Guo, Hu Zhang
bullets: Addresses vulnerability to distribution shifts and non-stationarity caused by single-pass forecasting.
Uses an architecture-agnostic generator–synthesizer framework with augmentation, retrieval, or adapters for candidate generation.
Combines or ranks candidates through aggregation, classification, or scoring methods.
Scaling the number of candidates increases test-time compute and also supports uncertainty and interval forecasting.
Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones report consistent gains in predictive accuracy and calibration.

papers.abstract: Cross-subject brain-to-image retrieval aims to identify viewed images from unseen subjects' brain signals. However, inter-subject variability hinders alignment of brain-image representations, while independent query ranking tends to concentrate predictions on a few candidates, making accurate retrieval difficult without target labels. We propose STAGE (Structured Test-Time Adaptation with Global Entropic Soft-coupling), a structured test-time adaptation framework for recovering cross-subject alignment from uncertain brain-image correspondences. Moment calibration reduces statistical discrepancies between features, while coupling-weighted initialization establishes initial alignment. Coupling-guided adaptation further refines residual feature mismatches, and soft-coupling ranking coordinates candidate competition across queries to prevent overly concentrated matching assignments. Using only unlabeled target batches, STAGE maintains consistent matching from feature calibration to image retrieval while keeping both encoders frozen. Experiments on three public datasets validate STAGE's retrieval performance. On THINGS-EEG2, STAGE achieves 68.25% Top-1 and 90.47% Top-5, improving Top-1 by 18.52 percentage points over SCORE recovery and CSLS on identical frozen NICE features. Calibrated on 200 queries and a 200-image gallery covering their identities, STAGE retains 42.05% Top-1 when ranking 1,854 images with the transform frozen.
authors: Yihang Zou, Ruixi Liang, Chunmei Qing, Junpeng Tan, Haichuan Wei, Wanxiang Luo, Gao Wu, Haodong Li, Xiangmin Xu, Yefeng Zheng
bullets: Addresses inter-subject brain-signal variability and prediction concentration in image retrieval without target labels.
Uses moment calibration, coupling-weighted initialization, and coupling-guided adaptation to refine brain-image alignment.
Applies global entropic soft-coupling to coordinate candidate competition across queries.
Validated on three public datasets; on THINGS-EEG2, it achieves 68.25% Top-1 and 90.47% Top-5 retrieval.
With a frozen transform, it retains 42.05% Top-1 when ranking 1,854 images after calibration on 200 queries and 200 images.

papers.abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
authors: Honghao Feng, Shanhan Qu, Kai Tong, Shuquan Man, Huiping Zhuang
bullets: P-TAP gradually shapes a session’s lightweight adapter with escalating adversarial queries, then uses the accumulated state to answer a final harmful request.
Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, updates increased attack success by 13.00 percentage points with greedy decoding and 22.25 points with best-of-10 sampling.
The attack’s effect largely disappears when adaptation uses unrelated or benign same-topic text instead of adversarial queries.
Incoming-query screening caught every attack stream, whereas a perplexity-based unsafe-adaptation detector missed all successful attacks.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.
bullets: The model analyzes its reasoning, weights, and activations in a persistent Python session to design self-edits.
Edits use white-box primitives such as singular directions, activation contrasts, rank-one projections, and tensor computations.
Each candidate is evaluated on a hidden gate set, and only strictly improving edits are merged before the next generation.
On Qwen3.8-27B math problems, five generations improved gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45%.
Held-out performance also improved, indicating that the self-edits generalized beyond the loop’s gate set.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The gradient writes the weights, or the model does. Top: in existing self-improvement the model writes data or chooses hyper-parameters, and SGD computes the weight change. Bottom: in SELFWRITE the model reads its own wrong and right answers, contrasts its activations on them, and writes a program that projects the contrast direction out of one of its layers (code simplified). The rank-one edit is merged only if it improves the model on a hidden gate set, and the edited model Mg+1 writes the next edit. No gradient tool is used and no training step is taken.

Figure 2: One generation of SELFWRITE. (1) Observe: the current model Mg answers 500 freshly drawn problems four times, and the editor reads its own answers, reasoning included (Section 3.2). (2) Write: eight independent sessions of the editor Mg, each with up to 30 tool rounds over a white-box toolkit for its own weights, each return a program that builds one LoRA ∆Wk (Section 3.3). (3) Select: every candidate is graded once on the hidden gate, paired problem by problem with Mg; the largest strictly positive gain is merged, and Mg+1 becomes the next editor (Section 3.4); gate statistics reach the sessions of later generations. Bars are schematic. The test split is never shown to the editor.

Figure 3: An illustrative SELFWRITE program (real tool names and signatures; layers and constants are examples): contrast the model’s activations on its own wrong and right answers, and project the contrast direction out of the layers’ output matrices.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
authors: Shuaicheng Niu, Guohao Chen, Kevin Z. Shen, Yunbei Zhang, Peilin Zhao, Yinan Zhang, Cyril Leung
bullets: Problem: Distribution-shifted prediction errors can mislead latent-world-model planners, and it is unclear which corrections should persist across episodes.
Method: Decompose prediction error into an action-shared offset and an action-dependent component.
Key finding: The shared offset shifts the planner’s goal; tracking it alone recovers 91% of AdaJEPA’s planning gain, while episode-specific corrections should not persist.
Contribution: sft-JEPA combines a fast, episode-resetting learner for transient offsets with a slow LoRA learner for recurring and action-dependent errors.
Results: It leads benchmark averages across PushObj, PointMaze, RoboCasa, and OGBench, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of sft-JEPA: One world model, two learners on two timescales. The pretrained θ0 (gray) stay frozen. The fast learner (blue) adapts the predictor’s last block and final LayerNorm after every executed chunk and is reset when the episode ends. The slow learner (green), LoRA on every block, is updated after every episode on windows from past episodes and is kept. The curves are schematic.

Figure 1: Two kinds of test-time prediction error. (a) Illustration with four action chunks from the current latent zt. Each prediction (dot) differs from the true outcome (ring) by an offset b shared across actions (blue) and an action-dependent part (green). (b) Composition of the frozen model θ0’s error energy on PushObj. (c) Offset and action-dependent energies of each method relative to θ0 on PushObj (shape I), along with planning success rates. AdaJEPA and our fast learner alone (Fast only) mainly reduce the offset. Reusing the previous episode’s shift (Shift-Prev) enlarges the offset. Compared with AdaJEPA, Slow@100 (trained on 100 earlier episodes) further reduces the action-dependent error but only slightly reduces the offset. Our sft-JEPA@100 further reduces both parts and achieves a higher success rate.

Figure 2: What each method fixes. Each dot is a probe state visited on the unseen PushObj shape I. Left/Down means a smaller offset/action-dependent error. Light gray dots show the frozen model θ0, the others show the method, and the arrow joins their means. Numbers give planning success and both error energies relative to θ0 (rC and rA). Shift-Ada/Prev shift all predictions by one vector, fitted in the current or previous episode. In-episode adaptation moves the states mainly left. Moving them down needs training on many episodes.

Figure 7: Runtime per episode. Mean wall-clock time per episode on PushObj (dark) and PointMaze (light). Each run covers 50 episodes on an RTX 3090 GPU. Episodes end at success, so methods that succeed earlier take less time.

Corrections fitted within the episode and Slow@100 lower it, whereas those carried over from the previous episode raise it or barely change it. A never-reset fast learner lowers it less than Fast only. (b) Success of a never-reset fast learner relative to Fast only, in each 50-episode stage. With 30 replans (allowing more updates), the drop grows with every stage. (c) Action-dependent error relative to the θ0 for a LoRA trained on m episodes. T (light), I (dark).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time training in latent world models and proposes a slow-fast approach for planning under distribution shift.
papers.title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
papers.tldr: A slow-fast test-time training method separates transient from recurring world-model errors, improving planning across diverse benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.
bullets: Clinical-trial outcome predictions by frontier LLMs are unreliable and only modestly above chance in the reported tasks.
A frozen SAE on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is used to identify clinical concepts, while sparse probes estimate each concept’s association with trial outcomes.
For each new protocol, the system provides concept evidence with outcome direction and strength, which the audited LLM uses to revise its prediction.
The method improves balanced accuracy by 9.6–12.0 points for deepseek-v4-flash across five tasks and by 8.0 points for GPT-5.6-terra on trial completion.
The probe module also produces auditable natural-language explanations directly from verified concept contributions, without an additional inference-time LLM.

papers.abstract: Prompt learning provides a parameter-efficient way to adapt pretrained vision--language models through text and visual prompts, but noisy labels prevalent in real-world data inevitably bias prompt updates and thereby undermine adaptation effectiveness. Prior work on robust prompt learning focuses on suppressing unreliable updates under noisy supervision. We uncover a pivotal yet overlooked aspect--prompt allocation: shifting the parameter budget between text and visual prompts can substantially enhance robustness while keeping the training objective and total budget fixed. However, suitable prompt allocations vary across tasks and are unknown a priori, rendering brute-force candidate training computationally prohibitive. We propose GPrompt, a training-free method that derives allocation between text and visual prompts using only loss gradients at initialization before prompt optimization. Using a small sample of images and generated pseudo-labels as shared supervision, GPrompt performs an initialization probe to extract paired text and visual loss gradients, and characterizes the geometry of their trace-normalized Gram matrices through both concentration within each modality and overlap between modalities. GPrompt then derives a closed-form allocation, and projects it onto feasible prompt counts under the exact parameter budget, enabling task-specific selection without training candidate configurations. Experiments across eleven datasets show that GPrompt outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 7.75% while selecting configurations close to the best allocation identified through exhaustive training. The average runtime of gradient probe across datasets is 99.9% lower than that of exhaustive candidate training.
authors: Jiazhe Zhang, Zibin Geng, Qiang Ma, Xuefeng Jiang, Yijun Lin, Jingyi Wang, Yu Yan, Xingzhou Zhang, Min Liu, Yuwei Wang, Sheng Sun
bullets: Prompt allocation between text and visual prompts strongly affects robustness under noisy labels, but the best split is task-dependent.
GPrompt performs a training-free initialization probe using a small image sample and generated pseudo-labels.
It analyzes trace-normalized Gram-matrix geometry to derive a closed-form allocation, then projects it onto feasible prompt counts.
Across 11 datasets, GPrompt improves over the strongest baseline by up to 7.75% and selects allocations near the exhaustively identified best.
Its gradient probe reduces average runtime by 99.9% versus exhaustive candidate training.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve by retaining feedback as reusable memories or skills, but every mistaken approval can shape many future behaviors. Two updates can provide exactly the same evidence to a verifier yet produce opposite safety outcomes, so the verifier cannot distinguish them from that evidence alone. We introduce DoppelVet, a verification framework that checks proposed updates before they enter an agent's persistent state. Without access to safety labels, DoppelVet constructs an alternative that matches every signal used by the existing verifier. It replays both updates from the same state and directly compares their behaviors in both presentation orders before deciding whether to retain the candidate. We evaluate DoppelVet on DoppelVet-Grid and DoppelVet-Tool, covering executable programs and natural-language memories. Across nine open-weight and proprietary verifiers, DoppelVet raises mean harmful-update detection AUC from 0.762 to 0.940 on DoppelVet-Grid and from 0.681 to 0.826 on DoppelVet-Tool, outperforming VaG and AgentDoG 1.5. On DoppelVet-Grid, it reduces trajectories experiencing degradation from 30.39% to 0.43% over a ten-generation self-update loop and leaves no final degradation.
authors: Yifan Duan, Du Yin, Siyuan Zheng, Chao Xue, Lihuan Li, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Targets the risk that mistaken updates propagate into many future behaviors.
Builds an alternative indistinguishable to the existing verifier without using safety labels.
Replays both updates from the same state in both presentation orders and compares their behavior.
Improves harmful-update detection AUC across executable-program and natural-language-memory settings.
Substantially reduces degradation during a ten-generation self-update loop on DoppelVet-Grid.
