Introduces retrieval skills that adapt search targets, memory operations, temporal ranges, and stopping decisions based on the current evidence state.
Evolves skills through reward-guided policy improvement, accepting useful policy patches without updating model parameters.
Across four benchmarks, achieves 60.1% average accuracy and an 8.6-point average gain over prior best methods.

papers.abstract: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl.
authors: Keryan Chelouche (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France, Fondation L\'eonie Chaptal, Sarcelles, France), Petr Dobias (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France), Nistor Grozavu (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France), Olivier Romain (ETIS UMR 8051, CY Cergy Paris Universit\'e, ENSEA, CNRS, Cergy, France)

DINOv3-PiSSA is presented as the first use of a self-supervised image foundation backbone for radar micro-Doppler HAR.
Its Small variant matches prior Base-size PEFT in-distribution accuracy with 4.5× fewer total parameters and only 3% trainable.
It ranks first among evaluated PEFT methods, with transfer gains of 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points as shift severity increases.

papers.abstract: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.
authors: Yue Che, Jingze Wang, Chen Guoyi, Yujie Wu, Xuming Ran, Mingkun Xu
bullets: Addresses growing storage costs and declining retrieval quality as lifelong edits accumulate.
Retrieves relevant edits in an external semantic space while injecting knowledge into the LLM’s internal representation space.
Uses sparse, storage-efficient updates while leaving base model parameters untouched.
Reduces per-entry storage to about 10.2% of the original and remains resilient through up to 16K edits.
Improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods on a challenging benchmark.

papers.abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.

papers.tldr: EgoWitness reveals that current VLMs struggle with instance-level spatial memory in egocentric video, while the EgoClue agent substantially improves reasoning through retrieval, verification, and temporal-spatial tools.

papers.abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10{\deg} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.
authors: Wai Ka Sun, Waiyiu Pong, Bowen Wang
bullets: A collision-free route can still fail when the robot approaches a stair or ledge with the wrong position or heading.
A 27-minute teaching session records one successful crossing for each terrain transition as reusable route events.
Before each transition, an entry gate triggers turning or backing up when the robot is more than 10 cm or 10° from the taught approach.
Under localization noise, compliant crossings increased from 24.1% to 88.6%; simulation and real-robot tests also showed improved recovery and reliable completion.
The method was demonstrated over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain, with six autonomous successful runs in competition.

For each crossing, E = max(|d|/(0.10m), |∆ψ|/(10◦)); E ≤ 1 means that both configured limits are met. White boxes mark zero-offset controls. Bottom: cumulative distributions of the absolute crossing errors over all records. The kinematic model delays the commands and feeds back a synthetic gait.

Figure 3: Passage-conditioned navigation: what is stored, what is observed, and what each decision does. (a) Teaching, the map, and configured rules compile once into the stored route L; a body sweep and a full kinematic run check it before use. (b) At every control step, the stored route, the local observations, and the candidate motions share one route frame; the robot compares the stored entry with its live pose and adapts its speed along the passage. (c) The decisions of one step, with excerpts of the robot’s log and simulation results.

Figure 5: The robot’s own log: earlier versions stop at the first ledge; the final version is refused there, backs up, crosses, and finishes. (a) The stored route: gait intervals, steep ground, and three ledges. An earlier version stored the ledges as waypoints; both of its full-speed runs stall at the first. The final version stores each ledge as an event with an entry gate and reaches all 29 waypoints in 387 s without a hold (Table 11). (b) The logged offset and forward command at the first ledge.

Figure 4: One run on the robot across successive terrain transitions. Eight frames in route order, each with its time in the run. The strip plots the elevation of the stored route, coloured by stored gait, and marks where each frame was taken. Bystanders’ faces are pixelated.

Figure 21: Matched replays of two discordant trial pairs. The frames and full XY traces come from saved states of matched pose-noise trials: terrace seed 3007 and stairs seed 3012. For each task, we selected the lower-median successful completion time among the discordant pairs of the further 30-seed cohort (two terrace candidates and six stair candidates). The selected cases show discordant outcomes. On stairs, the live-sensing run ends with software completion but misses the ordered-goal criterion, so it is scored as a failure. The terrace frames use the matched failure time of 48.76 s; the live-sensing run completes later, at 61.50 s. The stair frames show their own labelled terminal times. The replays load the recorded qpos/qvel and compute forward kinematics at each saved state. Both methods use the same camera orientation and distance, centred on their recorded robot positions.

Figure 20: Completion under vertical scaling of the scene. Each point combines four tasks and ten paired pose-noise seeds (40 trials per method and scale). Error bars are 95% percentile seed-block bootstrap intervals from 20,000 draws, which keep all four tasks together within each seed. The markers are offset horizontally only for visibility; all four methods use exactly the scale shown. Lines connect the measured settings; intermediate scales were not evaluated. Vertical scaling changes one scene, and robot parameters stay fixed. The descent task includes an approach waypoint and differs from the earlier multi-terrain descent subroute.

Figure 7: From recorded passes to the stored route. (a) The three complete teaching traces and the compiled route with its 29 waypoint entries. (b) A recorded local correction near a ledge, with the compiled crossing, approach direction, and gait intervals. The curve and the fields are the compiler’s stored output.

Figure 15: A displaced robot rejoins the reference and continues toward the next transition. The four replay frames, the XY trajectory, and the event markers come from one earlier nominal run with rejoining on and entry conditioning on. The distance curves compare all four matched settings (A: entry conditioning; R: rejoining) and project the raw XY onto the frozen original centerline. Curves that overlap are drawn without offsets. The strips of requested and confirmed gait zoom into 26–30 s of the run shown; the last replay frame comes before the acknowledgement. The replays render stored simulator states at fixed simulation times, with a robot-centred camera at a shared view direction and distance.

Figure 8: Field scenes and their passage geometry. (a) Stone stairs, (b) a soil-to-path transition, and (c) a gabion ledge, each shown with a sketch of the passage geometry that matters there. Amber marks visible terrain boundaries. Teal arrows show approach directions on schematic diagrams that are not to scale. Bystanders’ faces are pixelated.

Figure 9: Terrain transitions and their passage conditions. Each pair shows a field scene above and its geometry below: height and entry direction, local surface variation, route curvature, and slope transitions. The schematics are not to scale. Bystanders’ faces are pixelated.
Figure 10: Ledge approach and repositioning. Video frames of the robot show the approach, the repositioning, the second approach and ascent, and the traversal that follows.

Figure 17: A full-route run in contact simulation with our two learned policies. One recorded run of the archived stack: 30 of 30 waypoints over 260.5 m in 618 s of simulated time. The stairs policy drives the green intervals in 15 of the 16 stairs zones, and the walking policy drives the rest, including the descent through the remaining zone (brown). Every stairs zone is preceded by an approach (orange) or alignment (pink) phase.

The upper plane shows the archived simulation-reference XY, the waypoints, and the flat and stairs segment labels. Terrain names come from stored annotations. The axonometric sketch combines these XY task fields with map elevations and exaggerates height for readability.

Figure 18: Asymmetric actor–critic in the archived controller-training branch. The critic receives privileged training information. The actor uses its configured proprioceptive, command, previous-action, and phase inputs. The numbers give the hidden widths; the drawn neurons are schematic. Solid arrows show data flow, and dashed arrows show parameter updates. The actor and critic use matching observation terms with different scaling and noise settings. The diagram describes the archived controller-training setup.

Figure 13: Rejoining the stored reference on six route segments. Left: final distance to the original reference in 32 matched rejoining-off/on pairs. Lines connect runs with the same route, seed, and entry setting. Right: the same runs by segment, with median bars. WP05–08 has one qualifying seed, and the other segments have three. The mean distance falls from 1.142 m to 0.113 m. A pair enters the analysis only if all four factor combinations received the displacement.

Figure 19: Live sensing raises aggregate completion on the fixed task suite. (a) Task-balanced completion over 700 trials per configuration. Each task has weight 1/7, and each of the two conditions weight 1/2. (b) Paired differences against both graph alternatives, by task and pooled. The 95% intervals come from 20,000 percentile seed-block bootstrap draws, which keep both conditions and all task strata together within each seed. They describe seed variability on one reconstructed scene. Appendix P gives the task protocol, the corrected rock-area start, and the full completion and fall counts.

The grey line and band show the undisplaced runs of the same sets and their 95% seed-block interval; the bars show the interval of the rejoining rate. (b) Rejoining runs that returned inside the corridor, among those that left it. The first dotted line marks the widest corridor half-width on the route; beyond the second, at 1.5 m, the robot is more than 1.5 m from the line and holds by rule.

Figure 2: The field route, and the robot at every waypoint. (a) The stored route on the field map, coloured by stored gait, with its 29 waypoints and three ledge events. (b) The robot at each waypoint on site, numbered in route order; each number takes the colour of the route at that waypoint.

Figure 11: Terrain along the route and local elevation profiles. A–D mark four sections of the reference route on a grey map, in the same colours as their profiles. The 0.1 m import surface takes the per-cell minimum of the archived point cloud, over cells with at least two returns. Each section samples the frozen reference XY every 0.1 m and uses only known cells. The sections have 254, 133, 223, and 140 stations; missing map samples are left as gaps. Panel scales differ. Left: the share of handoffs that pass and the share that end in a fall, against the true heading error at the handoff; bars are 95% intervals. Right: all 604 handoffs, split by the gate’s entry bound.

Table 6: What a reference costs to prepare. Durations are measured from the recorded pose trails, for the recordings that the reference uses. The one-time map recording took 25 minutes.

Table 15: Displacement-size sweep, 23 seeds. Ordered completion (%) on the route–seed sets in which all four cells received the displacement, with a hold, with rejoining, and for the undisplaced rejoining-on runs of the same sets (two runs per set and arm). Intervals resample complete seeds 20,000 times. The last column gives, among the rejoining runs that left the corridor, how many returned inside it. The 1.2 m row is the comparison of Table 13. The lower panel counts, on the same sets, the runs that reach the next goal of the segment after the displacement (the window analysis at the end of this appendix). The corridor half-width differs between segments (0.25 to 0.8 m), so some runs leave the corridor at the smallest displacements.

Table 17: The recovery results under the two scoring rules. Left: the benchmark’s rule, used in Tables 13 to 16. Right: the competition’s waypoint rule, used in Section 5.3 and Figure 1. Intervals resample complete seeds 20,000 times.

Table 22: Full raw counts for the final route comparison. C: ordered completion; F: recorded fall. Each task has 100 trials per configuration (50 seeds times two conditions), and each configuration has 700 trials in total. Falls and goal completion are scored separately.

Table 18: Pass rate of the learned stairs policy against the true entry error (contact simulation, 378 runs, 604 handoffs). Left: runs with a heading bias. Right: runs with a lateral bias. Bottom: all handoffs, split by the gate’s entry bound of 10◦ and 0.10 m. A handoff passes when the stairs zone is completed and control returns to the walking policy.

Table 13: Recovery factorial with the seed extension. Intervals resample complete seeds 20,000 times. With rejoining enabled, the robot keeps going and can fall later. With rejoining disabled, it holds.
Table 3: Share of ledge crossings inside both entry limits. 147 records per cell, 735 with noise.

Table 5: Gate exceptions. Each cell gives the share of the 147 ledge records inside both limits and the number of the 49 rollouts that end in a hold. “Outside” counts crossings outside the limits. It is zero in every cell with R ≥ 1.

Table 7: Effect of removing each component in the development batch. Entries are percentage-point changes from the current core on matched cells, with equal weights for the three routes and the three conditions. A positive completion change means more completed tasks; a positive event change means more recorded events. The batch has 135 attempts. Contacts and falls are sampled at 50Hz and are not mutually exclusive. The full counts are in component outcome counts.csv.

Table 23: Full ordered-completion counts for the geometry cohort. Each cell has ten attempts, all under pose noise. Tasks and paired starts are fixed within each scale. The 1.0 setting is the unscaled control on the same host.

Table 14: Three ways to respond to a displacement. Completed runs per segment, over the cells in which all three arms received the 1.2 m displacement. Intervals in the text resample complete seeds 20,000 times.

Table 20: The alignment before each stairs zone switched on and off (contact simulation, learned stairs policy, 288 runs, twelve seeds). The robot is displaced sideways by 0.2 to 0.6 m when it is 0.76 m before each of five zones. Without alignment the stairs policy takes over at the scheduled arc length whatever the pose. In the zone reached at about 50◦ the difference has Fisher exact p = 0.002.

Table 21: The learned ledge policy at the competition’s gabion ledge (contact simulation, 2,925 entries). Entries start 0.55 to 1.2 m from the lip at 0.1 to 0.3 m/s, with lateral offsets of up to 0.3 m. A climb counts when all four wheels are on the deck and the robot stays upright for 1 s. A run that neither climbs nor falls within 20 s counts as a stall.

Table 8: Completion per batch and paired differences between configurations. The three batches contain 324 attempts in total. Within each batch, three route segments and three conditions have equal weight, with three seeds per cell and four configurations. Each difference subtracts the priorenabled reference of the same batch. We keep the batches separate because their execution environments and seed sets differ.

Table 9: The effect of entry timing depends on the observation source. Each effect subtracts the no-lead setting on matched cells. The nominal and pose-noise conditions, and deceleration off and on, have equal weights. The design has 48 executions, 18 of them reused records. The effects are for this fixed-segment diagnostic. All sixteen condition-level counts are in entry factor counts.csv.

Table 12: Ordered completion (%) for the full expanded factorial. Each entry has 24 attempts: eight route segments times three seeds. The intended-displacement column divides by all 24 attempts with an intended displacement, including those where the ground check failed or the trigger point was not reached.

Table 16: Inserted box on open stretches, 23 seeds. Ordered completion, runs that touch the box, and runs that end in a hold, with rejoining off and on: 184 runs per arm and offset (four segments, two entry settings). The offset is the lateral distance of the box centre from the route. The corridor half-width is 0.8 m, and the body is 0.6 m wide. Intervals resample complete seeds 20,000 times. The no-box row gives the undisplaced runs of the same segments from the factorial.

Table 19: Climbs by the learned stairs policy in 60 archived end-to-end contact-simulation runs. A handoff passes when the stairs zone is completed and control returns to the walking policy. “Recover” means that a waypoint inside the zone was missed and the recovery behaviour was triggered.

papers.selection_reason: Passage-conditioned navigation with taught crossing memory for wheeled-legged robots; fits embodied robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
papers.tldr: Passage-conditioned navigation helps wheeled-legged robots reliably enter stairs and ledges by remembering and enforcing successful crossing directions, without a robot model or additional training.

papers.abstract: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.
bullets: Targets the cost and risk of revising every answer, which can damage already-correct facts.
Routes uncertain answers to an editor that performs bounded exact-text replacements with valid source coordinates and legal edit operations.
On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, it improves over a verified revision chain by 0.82 F1 and 1.24 Judge points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls.
Direct editing improves native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, with gains of 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 F1 points, respectively.
Results support selective editing as an efficient quality–cost tradeoff, but show a completeness gap on an external PerLTQA subset and unresolved source-obligation effects.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MemMend framework. A selective gate routes candidate answers to source-linked local edits. Original memories remain available to the editor and deterministic source-coordinate and edit-legality checks; other paths preserve the candidate. Preparation supplies either the main conversational pipeline’s answer, a memory backend’s native answer, or a fresh Reader answer over fixed trajectory evidence. The highlighted patch is schematic.

Figure 1: A recorded LoCoMo repair. Both revision paths propose the same source-linked replacement, “Nature” to “Sunsets.” The verified chain vetoes the edit and retains the broad answer; MemMend accepts it. Answers are verbatim and memory excerpts are shortened. Call counts cover revision.

Table 2: Complete-system LoCoMo scores on 1,986 questions. F1 and Judge mean are percentages; protocols are described in Section 4.3. MemMend has the highest displayed F1 and Judge mean, exceeding PropMem by 5.04 and 7.64 points, respectively.

Table 1: Matched conversational revision on 1,986 LoCoMo questions. Judge accuracy, relevance, and completeness (Acc., Rel., Comp.) and their mean are percentages. Extra calls count revision work after the shared upstream pipeline. Bold marks the best displayed quality scores.

Table 15: All external-system answer paths on 1,986 LoCoMo questions. Source Reader regenerates answers from expanded original sources; the two subsequent paths apply selective MemMend or ungated local review to that Reader. MemMend increases F1 and Judge over Source Reader for all three systems. PropMem retains a higher native F1.

Table 17: Gate sensitivity: all nine policies compared with the primary gate and with restoration only. Differences and paired 95% intervals are points. The threshold is the strict whitespace-word cutoff for the length branch. Four decimals retain the small effects near zero.

Table 3: Editing the original answers of three memory systems on all 1,986 LoCoMo questions. SP: MemMend selective patching; UP: ungated patching; SR: selective rewriting. Bold marks the highest F1 within each row. Calls are incremental logical editor invocations for each variant. SP improves every native baseline and exceeds SR while using fewer calls than UP.

Table 16: Gate sensitivity with fixed LoCoMo answers. The primary threshold remains 20 whitespace-separated words; the length branch fires strictly above the threshold. Extra calls include restoration and editing. Among branch deletions, removing abstention has the largest effect; lowering the threshold increases calls for a small quality gain. Bold marks the highest displayed quality scores.
Table 4: Fresh LoCoMo source/locality factorial. Source denotes the EDIT citation obligation; all policies retain the same original evidence. Local edits have higher F1 than whole-answer rewrites.
Table 7: Routing over fixed LoCoMo answers. Random rows average all twenty seed-specific mixtures; their budgets are matched in expectation.

Table 9: Blinded model audit of 250 questions from the fresh LoCoMo factorial. Changed counts are unweighted; percentage rates use inclusion weights and all sampled questions. Repairs/harms are changed answers crossing the audit adequacy boundary.
Table 13: Separate 150-question LoCoMo development calibration of coverage planning. The candidate and all deletions underperform the freshly generated MemMend comparator.

Table 5: LongMemEval-V2 Small transfer on the same 451 fixed evidence packets. Tokens per question include the fresh Reader and revision. Selective patching uses far fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar observed accuracy.
Table 6: LoCoMo component deletions from the same generated cohort as Table 1. Differences are MemMend minus the row, with paired 95% intervals in percentage points.

Table 8: All source/locality factorial contrasts. Differences and paired 95% intervals are percentage points. Positive source effects favor required citations; positive locality effects favor local edits.
Table 10: Paired trajectory comparisons: selective patching minus each comparator. Wins/losses count questions correct only for selective patching/only for the comparator.

Table 11: Trajectory controls matched to selective patching in expected cost. A mixture revises with probability p and otherwise retains the Reader answer. Differences are selective patching minus the mixture.

Table 12: External PerLTQA dialogue subset: 200 questions from 31 characters. Differences are MemMend minus each comparator, with paired 95% source-group intervals. Iterative revision scores higher than MemMend on both F1 and Judge.

Table 14: All fifteen native-answer editing contrasts, in F1 points with paired 95% intervals. SP: selective patching; UP: ungated patching; SR: selective rewriting. Each cell uses all 1,986 questions. SP improves over Native and SR on every backend, while UP attains higher F1 than SP.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MemMend, a selective revision framework for memory QA that reduces inference cost by only revising potentially incomplete answers.
papers.title: MemMend: A Selective Revision Framework for Memory Question Answering
papers.tldr: MemMend selectively revises only potentially incomplete memory-based answers, improving quality while substantially reducing editing calls.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.
authors: Kai Shi, Shiqi Zhao, Zimo Li, Hairong Qu, Hongyu Ma, Yongsong Yang, Jiahao Ai, Ziran Yin, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the gap between local latent reachability and persistent, task-level execution.
Uses a frozen LeWorldModel with a proposer for intermediate targets and CompassFlow to search trajectory-prior actions under limited evaluation budgets.
Adds patch-token spatial feedback and observation-based memory for phase transitions and bounded recovery.
State-indexed targets enable cross-episode context-goal composition.
Achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach on 1,000 TEST Cube trials; predictive ranking improves matched PushT success from 4.7% to 44.9% and TwoRoom from 33.8% to 77.7%.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Observation-grounded Cube execution and bounded recovery. (a,b) Nominal execution and forced-opening recovery in different official TEST episodes; frames are shown at nonuniform steps. (c) Forced opening at t = 43–45 leads to rollback at t = 46, discarding three unexecuted actions. (d) Matched full-panel T3 semantic completion (1,000 episodes): 5.8% OFF versus 80.4% ON; whiskers show 95% Wilson intervals.

Figure 2: LeCompass planning and execution interfaces. (a) History, final goal, and span κ condition the proposer; its latest inverse-normalized prediction supplies the scoring reference. (b) CompassFlow decodes 25-action candidates with eight Euler steps. Source-CEM evaluates three 64-source rounds, using frozen LeWM to score predicted outcomes. The reference enters scoring, not the trajectory prior. (c) Cube acquisition reads current patch tokens; placement also uses cached final-goal tokens to estimate displacement and block height. (d) Observation-based memory confirms phases and permits bounded recovery from contact loss in CARRY. The placement controller assigns action channels, after which grip-floor and release actuators may override the gripper command. Environment observations update the encoded history and patch tokens.

Figure 1: Three interfaces from local prediction to task-level execution. (a) Observed history and the final goal yield a local latent reference. (b) Target-independent CompassFlow generates action candidates; frozen LeWM scores them against the reference, and Source-CEM refines sources over three 64-sample rounds. (c) Cube uses patch-token readouts and observation-based memory for action realization, phase transitions, and bounded recovery.

Figure 7: Checkpoint-normalized distances. All A, G, and E distances are divided by the checkpointspecific q0.95(G). This sets the 95th-percentile global-pair reference to one for cross-checkpoint scale comparison without changing within-checkpoint distance ordering.

Figure 8: Successful execution on PushT and TwoRoom. (a) A pusher moves a T-shaped block to the target pose while also matching the target pusher position. (b) A disk-shaped agent crosses the doorway and reaches a specified position in the other room under collision-aware dynamics; the dashed blue circle marks the 16-pixel target region. Both sequences use CompassFlow Source-CEM with proposed latent targets, trajectory-field checkpoint 0, and 192 predictive evaluations per plan; replanning occurs every five actions on PushT and every 25 on TwoRoom. The five execution frames are evenly spaced between initialization and the first successful post-action observation; t counts executed actions, and the rightmost column shows the goal reference. These are illustrative reruns: PushT uses a non-TEST case and TwoRoom a strict TEST case; neither contributes to the reported rates.

Figure 4: Predictive selection and spatial readout evidence. (a) Proposed-target IID best-of192 selection versus matched unranked execution on official TEST PushT, strict TEST TwoRoom, and Cube. Points represent three field checkpoints for PushT/TwoRoom or three source seeds for Cube; whiskers are within-repeat paired 95% intervals, and labels give mean ± sample SD. (b) Scoring-target contrasts in the same Cube IID suite, separate from the headline run; the net proposed-minus-unranked effect remains unresolved. (c) Initial (open amber) and adapted (filled teal) median XY readout errors on identical controller-induced frames: 5,338 for acquisition and 5,580 for placement. Separate closed-loop validation improves confirmed picks from 47/113 to 93/113 and, with acquisition fixed, placement native reach from 11/93 to 92/93 on the same 93 confirmed-pick episodes.

Figure 5: Projected-CLS planning-latent XY probes. MLP R2 on the same 14,656 validation frames as Table 17. The probes assess XY readout, not height or action-conditioned ranking; poor decoding does not establish that the latent lacks the information.

Figure 6: Frozen-latent distance distributions. Empirical CDFs of one-latent-step distance A, global-pair distance G, and proposer error E (labeled A, G, and E) for independently trained domain checkpoints. Distances are unsquared L2 in unnormalized 192-D projected CLS space. Dotted lines mark A = median(A), G = q0.95(G), and E = median(E).
Table 10: Proposer training configuration. The architecture and optimization settings are shared across PushT, TwoRoom, and Cube.

Table 2: Finite-budget local inference. Success (%) at 192 predictive evaluations per plan on official TEST PushT (500 episodes) and strict TEST TwoRoom (500 windows). h is the nominal maximum execution prefix in raw actions. Flow-based methods report mean ± sample SD over three field checkpoints; action-space CEM uses single fixed runs. Final-goal rows retain the existing target-attribution runs.

Table 3: Full-episode Cube execution and bounded recovery. (a) T1 native 4-cm reach, semantic completion, and predictive budget on 1,000 official TEST episodes. Native reach includes frame zero; completion requires completed release and post-third-opening containment. B/h is nominal predictive evaluations per environment step; – denotes not evaluated. (b) Matched T3 Recovery ON/OFF under the same perturbation, readouts, and monitoring; only bounded recovery changes. Further diagnostics are in Appendix G.

Table 1: State-indexed target composition. Success (%) on official TEST panels with 9,000 predictive evaluations per plan. (a) Cross-episode T2 without an episode-specific waypoint schedule. papers.abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
authors: Jiayi Chen, Lizhe Chen, Yujia Chen, Shihan Dou, Ming Zhang, Chendi Ge, Shiguang Ni, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang, Maxm Pan

Uses controlled retention ratios with an iterative adjustment procedure for fair comparison across compactors.
Covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks.

papers.abstract: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. This paper presents a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN that connects a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent. Physical measurements are organized as evidence for both model adaptation and subsequent experiment planning. We examine an implementation of the physical-feedback pathway using ping-pong handover as a case study. The system completes 12 physical executions organized into six baseline--candidate pairs, updates the student from measured outcomes, and evaluates the revised model on reserved physical configurations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.

The case study highlights parameter-dependent generalization and the operational behavior of the physical-feedback loop.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon world modeling in partially observable environments requires compact memories that preserve spatial structure despite accumulated localization drift. Inspired by hippocampal episodic and spatial memory and the multi-periodic coding of entorhinal grid cells, we propose HiSTFormer, a hierarchical spatiotemporal world model, which adopts a layer-wise organization of local temporal RoPE and multi-periodic spatial RoPE, together with content-conditioned address offsets, to capture recent temporal context and long-range spatial structure. A fixed-capacity memory keeps KV storage and per-step attention cost bounded as the sequence grows. On MemoryMaze and HM3D, HiSTFormer outperforms strong world-model baselines within the training sequence length and generalizes substantially better to prediction horizons far beyond those seen during training, while using a compact model. The hierarchical spatiotemporal design remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, with consistent gains as depth increases. These results show that hierarchical spatiotemporal organization and content-adaptive spatial addressing provide effective inductive biases for efficient long-horizon world modeling.
authors: Tiantian Li, Junfeng Lu, Yifei Wang, Zhaoyang Zhang, Lei Wang, Tianyi Qian
bullets: Targets spatial-structure loss caused by localization drift in partially observable, long-horizon environments.
Combines layer-wise local temporal RoPE, multi-periodic spatial RoPE, and content-conditioned address offsets.
Maintains fixed-capacity KV memory, keeping storage and per-step attention cost bounded as sequences grow.
Outperforms strong baselines on MemoryMaze and HM3D, with stronger generalization to horizons beyond training.
The approach remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

Cuts model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with corresponding success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points.
In physical tasks, achieves 18 versus 14 successes, while reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.

papers.abstract: States with identical protected observations can admit different future interventions. Each transition specifies its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. Composing these records in execution order distinguishes protocols with equal net consumption and different initial reserve requirements. At a fixed state, a weighted Gram operator determines the linear response ellipsoid and a quotient identifies directions attainable only through cooperation between blocks. Nonlinear systems with identical complete affine data can have incomparable finite-budget response sets. In regular charts, the first correction to quadratic minimum cost is a covariant cubic form involving the third derivative of cost and the Hessians of protection and response. At singular gates, sequential feasibility depends on the peak reserve along the path. A history-weighted operator detects responses outside the old channel's range closure. Controlled congruence characterizes exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics, and a two-cut value identity separates the effect of paid verification from that of subsequent action selection. On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of $2\times10^{-5}$. Over 200 arrivals they recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections. Each yielded over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of historical-channel-only AdamW. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation and neutral renewal began on the same protected logit fiber in distinct structural strata. Both admitted all 200 subsequent writes. Fixed continuation yielded 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost. Renewal had a smaller KL excess on the first candidate tested at every arrival and used fewer full verification scans.
bullets: Equal protected observations may conceal different intervention futures, initial reserve requirements, and sequential feasibility constraints.
Weighted Gram and history-weighted operators characterize attainable response directions, including cooperative and previously inaccessible channels.
The theory covers nonlinear cubic cost corrections, singular-gate reserve peaks, deterministic reductions, and a two-cut decomposition of verification and action-selection value.
On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens and recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections over 200 arrivals.

Under the expanded contract, both policies admitted all 200 writes; fixed continuation achieved 1.74× greater loss reduction per squared write cost, while renewal had lower first-candidate KL excess and fewer full scans.

papers.abstract: Smoothed online learning has recently been studied as a way to bypass hardness results for the fully adversarial setting, which can be overly pessimistic. In this framework, the adversary is constrained to generate contexts from distributions having a bounded density with respect to some fixed base measure $\mu$. Prior work makes the strong assumption that $\mu$ is known to the learner, with notable exceptions including Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). In this paper, we study sequential probability assignment (a.k.a., online learning with log loss) with smooth, well-specified data in the more general setting where $\mu$ is \emph{unknown}, without the Lipschitz condition imposed in the work of Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). We prove regret upper bounds against both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries: the adaptive bound is controlled by empirical $\ell_\infty$ Hellinger entropy, while the oblivious bound improves this dependence to empirical $\ell_2$ Hellinger entropy, the notion that has been shown to characterize the complexity of learning with i.i.d. data (Bilodeau et al., 2023). Both bounds are obtained through algorithms based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers. We complement these results with a general lower bound, showing that our upper bounds are essentially tight for some natural classes, which implies a separation in the difficulty of smoothed online learning between regimes where $\mu$ is known and where it is unknown.
bullets: Studies smooth, well-specified online learning with log loss without assuming the learner knows the base measure or that model classes are Lipschitz.
Provides regret bounds for both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries.
The adaptive bound depends on empirical ℓ∞ Hellinger entropy, while the oblivious bound uses the less stringent empirical ℓ2 Hellinger entropy.
Both algorithms are based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers.
A general lower bound shows the guarantees are essentially tight for some classes and reveals a difficulty gap between unknown- and known-measure settings.

papers.title: Sequential Probability Assignment against Smoothed Adversaries with Unknown Base Measure
papers.tldr: This paper develops near-tight regret guarantees for sequential probability assignment against smoothed adversaries when the underlying base measure is unknown.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained models provide transferable representations for class-incremental learning (CIL). However, sequentially adapting these representations introduces optimization costs and may disrupt old-class feature structure. This motivates us to explore whether the discriminative potential of these representations can be further exploited by continually accumulating class information while keeping the encoders frozen. To this end, we propose TAP, a new and novel framework for tapping the discriminative potential of frozen representations in class-incremental learning. It accumulates visual and semantic class information in the frozen CLIP embedding space with only lightweight optimization. TAP comprises three modules: class-conditional visual distribution modeling, class-adaptive semantic calibration, and visual-semantic posterior fusion. The first module retains class means and within-class scatters, combining class-specific and shared covariances to stabilize distribution estimation. The second module learns class-specific weights over text templates from current-task images, adapting text representations to downstream classes. The third module combines the visual and semantic posteriors through a weighted product of experts for prediction over all seen classes without retaining images from previous tasks. Across nine datasets under two incremental protocols, TAP achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining the highest average incremental and final-stage accuracies among the compared methods. The code is provided as an ancillary file.
authors: Zihao Wang (Shandong University), Yu-Wei Zhan (Zhejiang University of Technology), Xiao-Qian Liu (Shandong University), Zhen-Duo Chen (Shandong University), Weitong Liu (Shandong University), Xin Luo (Shandong University), Xin-Shun Xu (Shandong University)
bullets: Addresses the optimization cost and feature disruption caused by continually adapting encoders in class-incremental learning.
Models class-conditional visual distributions using class means and within-class scatters with shared and class-specific covariances.
Calibrates class-specific text-template weights from current-task images to adapt semantic representations.
Fuses visual and semantic posteriors with a weighted product-of-experts for prediction across all seen classes.
Achieves the highest average incremental and final-stage accuracies among compared methods across nine datasets and two protocols.

papers.abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
authors: Linfeng Dong, Jianwei Niu, Jiuyi Zhao, Ruibing Feng, Xinghao Wu, Wu Yang, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu, Mu Li
bullets: Addresses memory-augmented VLA models that either retrieve past observations without reasoning or let long histories interfere with current perception.
Uses a vision-language backbone to infer the current subtask from timestamped history and preserve this reasoning as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought.
A flow-matching action expert uses the latent memory while Perception Attention directly grounds actions in the current view.
Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions to reduce inference cost for long histories.
Achieves strong simulated and real-world performance, including 68.8% average success on real-world memory tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ActMem. (b) Inside the backbone, the subtask tokens that form Memory CoT follow the history and the current view in the sequence, so under the causal mask they read both, and their hidden states become Ct; the action expert receives only Ct, not the history tokens. (c) Efficient Memory CoT Inference. Consecutive decisions usually share the same subtask, so the previous subtask is reused as a draft and verified against the updated context in a single parallel pass. papers.abstract: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.
bullets: Defines composability through an interference functional combining cross-task curvature overlap with signed task-vector alignment.
In the quadratic setting, the functional exactly equals merged-model excess loss and uses angles measured in the curvature metric rather than Euclidean space.
A curvature-guided regularizer bounds displacement in the base curvature metric during non-convex training and yields an inverse penalty relationship for the curvature component of interference.
The regularizer does not similarly reduce the first-order term caused by solutions being nonstationary for the task loss.
Experiments confirm the predicted budget and ceiling; the functional tracks merging degradation, but is no more rank-correlated than Euclidean displacement in a transformer study.

papers.selection_reason: Provides theoretical analysis and regularization for merging fine-tuned models, addressing interference in continual learning and LLM adaptation.
papers.title: Interference Bounds and Merge-Aware Training Dynamics for Composable Fine-Tuned Models
papers.tldr: The paper develops curvature-aware bounds and regularization for predicting and controlling performance loss when merging fine-tuned models, while showing that first-order effects can remain dominant.

papers.abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.
authors: Boyin Tan, Jiadong Zhang, Xiaosong Ma, Chun Jason Xue, Xiaowei Huang, Youcheng Sun
bullets: Addresses a limitation of outcome-level self-evolution, which cannot distinguish incorrect instructions from instructions the agent failed to follow.
Uses coverage labels—follow, not-follow, or not covered—to guide targeted skill revision.
A persistent root-cause analysis agent validates revisions on subsequent runs, while a maintainer builds a shared strategy library across tasks.
Across three benchmarks and executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7%–70.5% of tasks, outperforming initial skills and the strongest baseline.
Removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

papers.title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
papers.tldr: SkillPlumber improves agent skills by using instruction-level coverage to identify and revise the specific instructions that cause failures or are not followed.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Dongheon Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: At least 96% of observed failures are stalls: the object remains stationary while the model predicts progress.
Stalls arise both with and without distribution shift, challenging the attribution of failures solely to model error.
Unstick combines on-policy fine-tuning with a fixed-weight loop breaker: prediction-error memory or random re-initialization at each replan.
Residual memory recovers most adaptation gains on pushing tasks; re-initialization works well for shape shifts but less for visual shifts.
The findings identify planning-loop fixed points as a major limitation of warm-started gradient-descent planners.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and remedies planning-loop failures in JEPA world-model planners for robotic pushing, relevant to world models and embodied planning.
papers.title: Stuck in Place: Stall Diagnosis and Remedies for JEPA Planners
papers.tldr: JEPA planners on pushing tasks often fail because gradient-descent planning gets stuck in fixed-point idle plans, and Unstick mitigates this by breaking the loop with residual memory or re-initialization.

papers.abstract: Despite learning transferable features, fake image detectors may struggle on unseen domains due to mismatched decision boundaries. Our analysis shows that features extracted by the frozen forensic encoder remain discriminative, but the source-trained decision boundary does not fully exploit this information. However, correcting this boundary without source data or target labels remains challenging, as unreliable source predictions may lead to incorrect adaptation. To address this issue, we propose Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation (GraRA), which refines the source decision boundary using only unlabeled target data. To determine which classifier directions to update, GraRA constructs a compact residual subspace from uncertainty-weighted target features and keeps it orthogonal to the source classification direction. To guide these updates, it uses source-score anchors to generate soft labels through target-graph diffusion, while neighborhood consistency regularizes residual learning within the constrained subspace. The learned correction is merged into the source classifier, requiring only 32 optimized coefficients and no additional inference branches. On diverse unseen OpenMMSec domains, GraRA achieves 84.36\% accuracy and 91.34\% AUC, improving over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, respectively. Further analysis shows that reliable source predictions and locally consistent neighborhoods help guide residual learning, allowing GraRA to correct ranking errors that a simple threshold shift cannot address. \textcolor{cvprblue}{Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Shichuang Xie, Qishuai Ding, Tong Qiao, Liquan Shen, Guorui Feng
bullets: Frozen forensic features remain discriminative across domains, but the source-trained decision boundary can misclassify target images.
GraRA learns a compact residual correction in an uncertainty-weighted target-feature subspace orthogonal to the source classification direction.
Source-score anchors, target-graph diffusion, and neighborhood consistency provide soft supervision without source data or target labels.
Using only 32 optimized coefficients and no extra inference branch, GraRA reaches 84.36% accuracy and 91.34% AUC on diverse unseen OpenMMSec domains.
It improves over the source detector by 4.33 and 3.50 percentage points, correcting ranking errors beyond what threshold shifting can fix.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of GraRA. Given unlabeled target images, a frozen source detector extracts target features and source logits. GraRA then adapts the source classifier in three stages. (a) An Uncertainty-Aware Residual Subspace is constructed from uncertainty-weighted target features and kept orthogonal to the source classification direction to constrain classifier updates. (b) Source-Guided Target Graph Diffusion uses real and fake anchors to guide semantic diffusion on a target k-NN graph, generating graph-refined soft targets. (c) GraphConsistent Residual Optimization combines semantic consistency and graph smoothness losses to optimize residual coefficients within the constrained subspace. The learned residual is merged into the source head for target inference.

Figure 5. Understanding boundary adaptation in GraRA. (a, b) Decision boundaries of the source classifier, shifted source classifier, and GraRA on two representative targets. (c) Relationship between 5-NN label purity and final AUC gain on unseen target domains.

Figure 1. Motivation for GraRA. (a) The source classifier separates real and fake samples in the source domain. (b) Domain shifts can cause decision boundary mismatch even when frozen features remain discriminative. (c) Unconstrained adaptation may amplify errors from unreliable source predictions. (d) GraRA combines graph-refined supervision with constrained residual learning to correct the source decision boundary.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation (GraRA) for cross-domain fake image detection using unlabeled target data.
papers.title: Decision Boundaries Matter: Graph-Regularized Residual Adaptation for Cross-Domain Fake Image Detection
papers.tldr: GraRA adapts a fake-image detector to unseen domains by correcting its decision boundary using only unlabeled target data, improving both accuracy and AUC.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
authors: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu, Wei Mo, Maomao Li, Jiayan Xu, Jiayuan Wu, Yihao Xiao, Linhua Ye, Zhonghua Peng, Ruize Han, Jialong Sun
bullets: Targets VLA adaptation under deployment distribution shifts without source-domain retraining.
Addresses zeroth-order estimation noise, which can cause long-horizon adaptation to stall or degrade.
Uses a lightweight online historical error predictor fused with instantaneous zeroth-order estimates, without backpropagation or extra forward passes.
Theory links estimation variance to convergence limits in high-dimensional, small-population settings.
Experiments on LIBERO and real robots report higher success rates, improved closed-loop stability, and better post-disturbance recovery under low memory.

papers.selection_reason: VLA test-time adaptation with low-memory zeroth-order optimizer; directly relevant to embodied AI and test-time learning.
papers.title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: Dune stabilizes low-memory zeroth-order test-time adaptation for VLA models by combining current perturbation estimates with time-conditioned historical error predictions.

papers.abstract: Continual SAR interpretation requires multimodal large language models to learn incoming sources while retaining earlier task abilities. This is difficult when acquisition and geographic shifts alter visual evidence, regionally concentrated categories bias answers, and historical images are scarce. We address this problem with Historical On-Policy Distillation (HOPD), which reuses source-acquisition LoRA states as persistent teachers for one evolving student. Archiving each state before consolidation preserves a stable source reference. The teachers supervise student-generated prefixes, transferring historical behavior to the student's changing generation contexts. To enrich sparse replay, original-view teachers guide augmented historical student views while preserving spatial coordinates. This knowledge is consolidated into a single deployed adapter that requires no source identity. On SARVQA-CL, our source-incremental evaluation protocol, HOPD achieves the highest final mean score of 54.51 among the compared methods, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.96 points. It also improves the final source-macro score in every evaluated task over shared-memory Replay-SFT, with gains across source orders. These results support source-acquisition history as supervision for retaining earlier task performance during continual SAR adaptation. Code and data: https://github.com/zcablii/HOPD.
authors: Yuxuan Li, Derrick Goh Xin Deik, Zheng-Peng Duan, Qianru Sun, Weijie Li
bullets: Addresses forgetting under acquisition and geographic shifts, biased categories, and scarce historical imagery.
Archives each source-specific LoRA state before consolidation and uses it for on-policy distillation from student-generated prefixes.
Augmented historical views are supervised by original-view teachers while preserving spatial coordinates.
Consolidates knowledge into one deployed adapter without requiring source-identity information.
On SARVQA-CL, HOPD reaches a final mean score of 54.51, 2.96 points above the strongest baseline, and outperforms Replay-SFT on final source-macro scores across tasks and source orders.

papers.tldr: HOPD preserves earlier SAR interpretation abilities during continual learning by using archived acquisition-specific LoRA models as teachers for an evolving student.

papers.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.
bullets: Uses a frozen encoder with a control ladder: factory decoder, Bayesian head, affine map, and full fine-tuning only as an escape hatch.
A conjugate Normal-Inverse-Wishart Bayesian head updates from labelled trials without gradient optimization.
Clean-referenced gating reduced adaptation entry from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the factory decoder retained for about 87% of clean cells.
Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matched or exceeded frozen-trunk accuracy across five encoder architectures at roughly 23× lower fit time than full fine-tuning.
Natural-drift checks showed no reliable head accuracy gain, emphasizing cost efficiency and clean-data safety; adaptation severity varied across datasets.

This is why we report a boundary map, not a universal policy.
