papers.selection_reason: Resource-priced adaptation gating for deployed BCI decoders; directly relevant to test-time and online adaptation.
papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
papers.tldr: A gated, resource-priced adaptation ladder safely limits EEG decoder updates while preserving efficiency under distribution shift.

papers.abstract: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $\Omega((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.
bullets: Studies retaining actions while updating beliefs, balancing predictive loss against costs for changing actions.
Provides an attainability criterion based on prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, with an equivalent decreasing-weight dual.
Shows adaptive timing and private randomization do not expand the attainable region.
For excess O((log T)^r), 0<r<1, proves every policy requires Ω((log T)^(2−r)) expected revisions, while a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound.
Verifies the framework for logistic decision models, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors, under stated regularity assumptions.

figures.caption: Table 1: Feasibility for logarithmic charges cα. Equality is infeasible at every strict threshold.

papers.selection_reason: The theoretical framework for a Bayesian learner updating posterior beliefs and deciding when to change actions under adjustment costs is relevant to test-time adaptation and deployment-time learning.
papers.title: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when a Bayesian learner can jointly achieve low cumulative predictive excess and finite lifetime adjustment costs, and gives matching revision-rate bounds.

papers.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.

papers.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
papers.tldr: Keel uses a frontier multimodal model to diagnose and edit a VLM’s weights, removing image-reasoning loops without retraining or increasing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of continual-learning-style memory systems that retain information indefinitely.
Uses a fixed-capacity LoRA substrate with k-hot rank combinations to reduce interference and independently control temporal decay.

Achieves 86% of oracle performance, balancing recall and abstention better than continual-learning and RAG baselines.

papers.title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters

papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
bullets: Addresses OOD failures caused by scarce, multimodal robotics data and policy overfitting to small distribution shifts.
Combines LVM/VLM semantic reasoning with object-relational distance pairs along meaningful geometric axes to form task-specific guidance.
Transfers motion patterns from successful in-distribution rollouts without retraining the policy.
Works in simulation for pose and task-goal shifts and on a real robot for cable placement and unseen-object steering.
In reported experiments, it more than doubled success one grid step outside training positions and nearly eliminated object confusion when steering toward unseen objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our visual-geometric policy steering framework. Offline analysis (at task initialization, once per episode): (1) we retrieve the most relevant successful in-distribution rollout τ∗ by weighted image (DINOv2) and text (CLIP) similarity; (2) a VLM selects the task-relevant object-relational distance pairs per motion phase (e.g., gripper–cube distance d1, cube–table distance d2, gripper orientation θ), evaluated per timestep into the reference trends Φ; (3) a VLM with SAM2 matches the demonstration objects to the live OOD scene (e.g., the cylinder takes the cube’s role), re-targeting each pair. Online steering (every action chunk): (4) perception projects the live scene into the same distance space and aligns each pair to Φ within a window, giving the reference d∗. At every denoising step, a differentiable dynamics model F forecasts the features d(A) of a candidate chunk A, and a line-searched gradient step on the trajectory loss corrects the frozen policy’s velocity field, yielding the steered chunk A′.

Fig. 5. Positional generalization. Every rollout is plotted at the Mahalanobis distance of its measured cable position (dots near 100 are successes, near 0 failures), with per-zone success rates and 95% Wilson intervals (squares) and a per-method logistic fit, crossing 50% at 2.8σ (base) and 3.4σ (VG-Steer).

Fig. 9. Visual-geometric guidance via VLM-selected distance pairs. Offline (a–c): the demonstration is segmented (Gemini 3 Flash + SAM2) and split into sub-trajectory phases (STRAP); the VLM selects each phase’s entity pairs, projections, and sub-goal constraints. Online (d–e): the live scene is matched to the demonstration, and the guidance steers the frozen policy so the selected projected distances track the reference.

Fig. 4. Positional sweep on cable bagging, in the camera view. (a) Training distribution of the 110 cable grasps in the demonstrations. (b) The single reference rollout, with its end-effector path split into sub-trajectories. (c, d) Per-cell outcomes: dots mark the measured cable position of every trial, filled green for success, red rings for failure.

Fig. 2. Differentiable guidance injection. At each denoising step, the candidate chunk is rolled out by forward kinematics, and the guidance loss (position, orientation, gripper) is differentiated; a golden-section line search sets the step size, and the correction is applied to the policy’s velocity field, steering the trajectory without modifying weights.
Fig. 8. Real-world outcome breakdown (share of rollouts, counts on bars). Residual failures concentrate in grasp and transport, which the guidance does not address.

Fig. 7. Task variation on cable bagging. Left: the single reference rollout above the new setting in which cable, banana and spoon share the workspace. Center, right: confusion matrices (instructed object in rows, reached object in columns) for the base and the guided policy.
Fig. 6. Disambiguating the target object in a cluttered scene. In red and blue, the distance pairs used per sub-trajectory (ST0 approach, ST1 transport).

Fig. 3. Per-action-chunk inference overhead on π0.5 (mean over the four suites, CUDA-synchronized). With VG-Steer a chunk takes ∼73 ms in total (1.2× the base’s ∼61 ms), comparable to gradient-only VLS (∼70 ms total); full VLS costs ∼20× more, scaling with its particle count (20 here).

papers.title: VG-Steer: Visual-Geometric Policy Steering from In-Context Aligned Abstractions
papers.tldr: VG-Steer adapts frozen robot policies to shifted tasks and poses by using vision-language-guided geometric cues from successful demonstrations to steer nuanced manipulation motions at test time.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.
authors: Arjun Choudhry, Aditya Narayanan, Raghav Mallampalli, Po-han Li, Sai Shankar Narasimhan, Raimi Shah, B. Aditya Prakash, Shubhankar Agarwal
bullets: Time-series forecasters cannot use future information to verify candidate forecasts, unlike language models.
BGAA uses rolling-origin backtests on the series history to evaluate structured context transformations.
It discards views that underperform the original context and averages the survivors’ predictive distributions.
Across tested benchmarks, BGAA reduces MASE by 0.5–5.9%; a 313M model with TTC outperforms larger models in its family.
The remaining gap to oracle view selection highlights window-level view selection as a key challenge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: BGAA system overview. (1) The observed context is the only input available at test time. (2) A fixed pool of transformed views is generated, and (3) each is forecast with the same frozen TSFM. (4) Forecasts are mapped back to the original observation space. (5) A leak-free rolling-origin backtest scores the views against the base and admits the best candidates. (6) The admitted forecasts are aggregated with the base forecast to produce (7) the final predictive fan.

Figure 2: Test-time compute improves MASE under estimated inference-FLOPs scaling. On GIFT-Eval (97 configurations), lines connect four test-time compute budgets for each frozen model; stars denote published models at 1× compute. Each rung uses the model’s measured benchmark PFLOPs scaled by its measured forward-pass ratio (base + gate + apply)/base. The CRPS ladders also improve over their corresponding bases.

Figure 3: Pareto curves for accuracy vs computational cost. (fev-bench, 100 tasks). Lines are our test-time compute ladders over a frozen model, cheapest rung first; stars are published models on fev-bench. A rung sits at its model’s measured 1× benchmark PFLOPs times the measured forward-pass ratio (base+gate+apply)/base. As in Section C.1, charging each extra pass at the base-pass cost is a conservative accounting convention for models with variable-length computation, since some views shorten the context.

Figure 9: Views move the same contexts toward different regions of each model’s rollout distribution. We use ancestral rollouts from each model’s quantile head as a proxy for its learned forecasting behavior and visualize the resulting 20-dimensional shape-feature space with joint t-SNE. Colored points are rollout samples, grouped by kmeans mode; black points are real GIFT-Eval contexts; arrows show the mean displacement induced by each view. We use the same contexts and views for both models, but diff moves toward different rollout modes: for CHRONOS-2, a low-iqr over std, high-step max mode with mass 0.07; for TIREX-2, a high-kurtosis, high-skew mode with mass 0.02. This provides the geometric counterpart to the fingerprint result. t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods, but distances should not be interpreted metrically.

Figure 7: Qualitative examples for BGAA improvements. Selected forecast windows for which BGAA improves over the frozen base model. Each subfigure shows the admitted views, their candidate forecasts, and the resulting BGAA prediction relative to the realized horizon.

Figure 10: Summary of the mechanism analyses in Section 6. (a) Admitted families vary across domains. (b) Individual views induce consistent displacement directions. (c) These displacements can align with different modes of each model’s rollout distribution. Figure 9 visualizes the same effect in a rollout-based proxy for each model’s learned forecasting behavior.

Figure 6: Agreement between backtest and hindsight view rankings for CHRONOS-2 on GIFT-Eval. (a) Fraction of configs whose realized best view lies in the backtest’s top-k. Ranked per config, the backtest’s top-1 contains the best view for 19–20% of configs and its top-3 for 31–33%, well above both the most-selected-view heuristic (10% at k=1) and random selection (1.3% at k=1). The top-1 hit rate is therefore about 15× chance. Ranked per window, the top-1 hit rate falls to about 11%. (b) Share of the hindsight MASE gain recovered by the top-k: the per-config top-1 recovers 32–33%, while the per-window top-1 recovers about 27%. Because the per-window target depends on the realized outcome, we use it only as a diagnostic rather than as an achievable target for a verifier that observes only x.

Figure 5: Backtest rankings are strong per configuration but much weaker per forecast window. For CHRONOS2 on 93 GIFT-Eval configurations, median Spearman ρ between leak-free backtest and realized view rankings falls from 0.63 per configuration to 0.25 per window. Results use 8,313 sampled windows and MASE.
Figure 8: Qualitative examples for BGAA improvements. Additional successful forecast windows under the deployed policy.

(b) CDFs of per-config MASE changes for the policies in Table 3. (c) MASE improvement as a function of the number of available backtest windows N and forecast horizon H . papers.selection_reason: Proposes a test-time compute algorithm (BGAA) that spends inference compute to verify and select candidate forecasts, fitting test-time learning/optimization.
papers.title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.tldr: BGAA enables causal test-time compute for time-series foundation models by backtesting and averaging only the most useful context views.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Long-horizon planning suffers from compounding prediction errors and weak guidance from distant goal similarity.
GEMS generates structured intermediate subgoals and selects relevant states from Latent Experience Memory (LEM).
A distance gate chooses whether to evaluate predicted outcomes against the generated subgoal or a retrieved memory state.
Across manipulation, navigation, and reaching tasks, GEMS achieves success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World.
The method outperforms evaluated world-model planning baselines, while relying on a frozen world model.

papers.title: GEMS: Generation and Experience Memory for Subgoal-Guided Long-Horizon World Model Planning

papers.abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Mark Hamilton, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Vincent Sitzmann, Yilun Du, Ayush Tewari
bullets: Targets the poor out-of-distribution generalization of fast, feedforward 3D reconstruction networks.
Uses inverse generative modeling to recover latent variables that best explain a monocular image.
Combines a generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network to avoid degenerate flat reconstructions.
Reports stronger OOD reconstruction accuracy than feedforward networks across controlled synthetic and real-world tasks.
Introduces adaptive test-time inference that allocates more computation to ambiguous inputs.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model. At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps. Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.
bullets: Model-merging interference can be estimated before fully evaluating candidate merges, reducing expensive coefficient search.
Derivatives must be measured at the receiver model: they predict per-task and per-example changes, while backbone-based derivatives are weakly predictive.
Full multi-task merges require two evaluations along the merge path rather than one.
LR-Merge freezes receiver-local responses to form an affine surrogate and optimizes coefficients via convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes.
The method improves tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified mergers; its surrogate supports new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

papers.abstract: The rise of powerful, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust natural language inference (NLI) systems. These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. However, this continual, multi-tasking approach can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned tasks are lost, especially in domains lacking specific labels. Rehearsing past examples with labels can further exacerbate this issue by causing overfitting, hindering the system's ability to classify new categories. To tackle these challenges, this research proposes ICARE, a novel framework with two key components: an instance selection module and a knowledge distillation method. The former is based on representation learning, which meticulously selects training examples to present to the NLI system. The latter, knowledge distillation with feature and logit-level transfer, facilitates knowledge transfer between tasks. This leverages pruning techniques and optimized objective functions to transfer both essential feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while adapting to new patterns. Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets have demonstrated ICARE's effectiveness. The framework achieves a significant improvement in target accuracy and reduction in the ``forgetting metric''. These results solidify ICARE's ability to preserve and leverage learned knowledge across diverse tasks, ultimately enhancing the adaptability and performance of NLI systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/CongSon01/ICARE_NLP.git
authors: Son Duong, Truong X. Tran, Hai-Anh Tran
bullets: Addresses continual multi-task NLI settings where adapting to new domains can erase previously learned task knowledge.
Uses representation-based instance selection to choose training examples for new tasks.
Applies knowledge distillation at both feature and logit levels, with pruning and optimized objectives, to transfer prior knowledge.
Evaluations on benchmark text-classification datasets report improved target accuracy and reduced forgetting.
The abstract does not specify particular datasets, numerical gains, or limitations.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame
bullets: Agents must learn unfamiliar games from limited attempts while gameplay continues during reasoning.
The study compares model-as-policy, using real-time action chunking, with code-as-policy, where a model writes, tests, and revises a program between runs.
Across 170 GameWorld tasks and at most eight one-minute executions, code-as-policy achieved 47.80% mean progress versus 30.90% for the trained controller.
Code-as-policy led across all five game categories; improving controller weights on one game produced only modest gains.

papers.abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.
bullets: Fixed steering may not fit the diverse knowledge and reasoning needs of individual queries.
Q-NeuS identifies a compact, subject-guided candidate neuron space and generates query-specific neuron modulation coefficients with a lightweight gate.
Neu-GRPO trains the gate using relative performance across multiple neuron-intervention configurations.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks report consistent improvements, broad model-scale applicability, and cross-benchmark transfer.
The abstract does not specify particular datasets, numerical gains, or limitations beyond its evaluated scope.

papers.tldr: Q-NeuS adaptively steers query-relevant neurons at inference time to improve LLM performance without changing the base model or requiring inference-time labels.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Qu\'ebec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Qu\'ebec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.
authors: Eeham Khan, Richard Khoury, Leila Kosseim
bullets: Studies CPT across nine LLMs using a budget-matched 30M-token protocol.
CPT benefits models with weaker existing competence in Quebec French, but is not uniformly useful.
Literary text drives most gains, while corpus register determines which regional expressions are learned.
Improvements mainly affect expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence.
CPT can reduce reading comprehension, effects that aggregate scores may hide.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of continual pre-training for dialectal adaptation, directly relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Qu\'ebec French
papers.tldr: Continual pre-training helps Quebec French adaptation selectively, with benefits shaped more by the model’s initial competence and corpus composition than by additional data volume.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.
authors: Zeguan Xiao, Zhuocheng Liang, Yun Chen, Yong Wang, Guanhua Chen, Pinyan Lu
bullets: Addresses the degradation of general capabilities caused by model adaptation.
Uses local preservation-loss geometry to define a nearly invariant, low-curvature update space.
Scales the approach with K-FAC curvature approximations and a factorized projection; CurvLoRA provides a more efficient low-rank variant.
Across math reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning, achieves competitive task performance while better balancing acquisition and retention than baselines.
On TOFU and MUSE, improves the trade-off between targeted forgetting and retained knowledge, approaching from-scratch retraining retention.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.
authors: Guilherme Guedes, Marco Apolinario Lainez, Charlotte Frenkel
bullets: Addresses online, one-sample-at-a-time adaptation and limited edge-device resources.
Uses a dual-phase wake/sleep design inspired by brain learning cycles.
Wake phase: RISC-V MCU performs efficient inference and gradient-free prototype updates.
Sleep phase: a smart charger uses available energy and memory for rehearsal-based gradient updates.
On CORe50 NICv2-391, it reports 78.6%–81.6% accuracy, 7.79–10.54 s latency per sample, and lower learning cost than quantized latent replay.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a dual-phase platform for efficient Continual Learning at the edge, utilizing a wake-sleep cycle to balance adaptation and consolidation with resource constraints.
papers.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge

papers.abstract: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.
authors: Rong Zou, Haiqing Hao, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses feature staleness when visual content changes between image observations.
Uses events to incrementally transport and correct multi-layer DINOv3 features from an anchor image.
Trains a lightweight updater end-to-end on synthetic data without downstream-task supervision and transfers to real event streams without adaptation.
Across three real-world datasets and five task settings, it outperforms evaluated event-based methods for detection, segmentation, and depth estimation.
On DSEC with a 200 ms-old anchor, it improves anchor predictions by 30.9 mAP, 11.6 mIoU, and 15.9% AbsRel, while reducing FLOPs by 82.4% and latency 2.5× versus image re-encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ALIVE. (a) Training uses synthetic RGB–event sequences. A frozen DINOv3 encodes every RGB frame: F0 initializes the feature state (with memory h0 = 0), and later frames provide teacher features Ft. For each event packet E(t−,t], the ALIVE updater Uθ predicts a displacement dt that transports both the features and the memory, a residual correction ∆t that yields Ut, and a signed, zero-sum 3× 3 kernel kt per token that refines Ut into F̂t. The ConvGRU memory ht conditions the residual and the refinement. All modules are trained jointly with feature-level losses only, without task labels or task heads. (b) The trained updater is applied without adaptation to real event streams. Moment matching aligns the per-channel statistics of F̂t with the anchor moments to produce the updated features F̄t, and frozen task heads trained on DINOv3 features of real RGB images read F̄t directly. Predictions are shown 200 ms after the anchor on DSEC, and detections are drawn on the RGB frame at that time for visualization only (C: car, P: person).

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on test samples. Each column shows one sample at its target time, and each view is followed by a zoom of the framed region. The top four rows show the anchor frame, the events between the anchor and the target time (red: positive, blue: negative), the target frame, and the ground truth. The other rows show the predictions of the frozen heads from the features of each method. Detection: predictions in orange and ground truth dashed in green. Depth: red (near) to blue (far), with one range per sample. Apart from Current RGB, no method receives the target frame, and the ground truth is shown for reference only.

Figure 3. Accuracy versus update cost (top) and versus anchor age (bottom). Each column is one task–dataset setting, evaluated with a frozen task head shared by all methods. Top: accuracy pooled over all anchor ages against the time per feature update. The dashed line marks the stale anchor features, the dotted line marks the 5 ms limit for updates at 200 Hz, and the star marks the goal of reaching the accuracy of Current RGB within this limit. Current RGB encodes the target frame itself, which is unavailable between frames. Bottom: accuracy at each anchor age. The blue line connects the best baseline at each age, and its markers identify the method as in the top row. Arrows give the gain of ALIVE over the stale features at the longest age (for AbsRel, the relative decrease).

The ∆ row gives the absolute gain for detection and segmentation and the relative change for depth. The cost of one feature update is measured on one NVIDIA GH200 (FP32, batch size 1, 640 × 640 inputs). GFLOPs count convolutions, matrix multiplications, and attention. papers.title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
papers.tldr: ALIVE efficiently keeps frozen visual foundation-model features current between image frames by using event streams, improving downstream vision tasks while avoiding repeated image encoding.

papers.abstract: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning (EFCIL) requires models to learn new classes sequentially without retaining training samples from previous tasks. Continual concept bottleneck models (CBMs) make their predictions interpretable by identifying visual concepts in an image and using them to score each class. However, these methods typically focus on preserving learned concepts or approximating past classes with generated features, which can leave new concepts underused in old-class predictions. We propose RetroCBM, which retains a small set of vocabulary-independent statistics relating frozen visual features to the embedding space of a pretrained vision-language model. Even after earlier training images have been discarded, we can use these statistics to supervise new concepts. To do so, we develop a retroactive regression rule that yields the same predictor for each new concept as class-balanced ridge regression on all images seen so far. We then reproject the stored statistics to recover the full-history squared classification loss and thus learn how much each new concept should contribute to old-class predictions. Since the classifier may use systematic concept errors to distinguish nearby classes, we further introduce a graph-weighted penalty on the margin shifts caused by those errors. Across six datasets, RetroCBM outperforms state-of-the-art interpretable methods in all class-incremental settings, with an 18.1\% relative gain in mean average incremental accuracy over the strongest exemplar-free baseline.
authors: Yang Ji, Ying Sun, Yuanxin Zhuang, Yuting Zhang
bullets: Addresses EFCIL, where models must learn sequentially without retaining past training images.
Stores vocabulary-independent statistics linking frozen visual features to a pretrained vision-language embedding space.
Uses retroactive regression to reproduce the new-concept predictor from class-balanced ridge regression over all previously seen data.
Reconstructs historical classification loss and applies a graph-weighted penalty to control margin shifts from systematic concept errors.
Across six datasets, it achieves an 18.1% relative mean average incremental accuracy gain over the strongest exemplar-free baseline among interpretable methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Model architecture. At inference (bottom), the sparse classifier scores all seen classes from the concept responses predicted for each image. During training (top), retroactive regression updates all current concept predictors using stored statistics from all seen classes. We then reproject these statistics to update the classifier and penalize error-induced margin shifts between neighboring classes.

papers.selection_reason: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning with concept bottlenecks, directly relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: Retroactive Concept Bottleneck Models for Exemplar-Free Class-Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: RetroCBM enables interpretable exemplar-free class-incremental learning by using stored feature statistics to retroactively train and calibrate new concepts for both old and new classes.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.
authors: Siqi Xiang, Zhipeng Xu, Shengrui Liu, Zulong Chen, Chunyan Miao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets inefficient perception of long interaction histories in LLM-based agents.
Renders past interactions as images and allocates resolution according to relevance to the next decision.
Uses a lightweight, teacher-guided relevance estimator optimized to preserve decision consistency.
Works across multiple tasks and backbones and can complement existing memory management methods.
Scope: focuses on adaptive perceptual granularity rather than deciding what memories to retain or retrieve.

papers.abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.

papers.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.
authors: Wenhao Yuan, Longhui Yuan, Zexi Jia, Ningzhe Shi, Jingwei Li, Shipeng Cen, Pengcheng Luo, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Targets lifelong learning beyond fixed tasks, curricula, and objectives.

papers.abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.
authors: Haotian Xu, Yue Hu, Zhengqiu Zhu, Tuo Feng, Wenguan Wang, Quanjun Yin

On Test Unseen, it improves navigation error, success rate, and success-weighted path length, with efficient 0.68-second inference and 8.6 GB peak memory on one A100.

papers.abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.
authors: Philippe Forest, Giulia Lioi, Mai Pham Quyen, Alix Lamouroux, Javen Shi, Adrien Merlini
bullets: Addresses the gap between strong within-subject decoding and poor generalization to unseen individuals without collecting labeled calibration data.
Introduces incremental transductive calibration: each EEG query is decoded first, then accumulated unlabeled data and the known candidate gallery are used for calibration.
GALA aligns EEG embeddings with the gallery using shrinkage whitening, hubness correction, and Sinkhorn–Procrustes alignment with continually estimated query frequencies.
On THINGS-EEG-2 with 200 candidate images, accuracy for a new subject improves from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes.
Across 60 settings, GALA is the most accurate label-free method, averaging 6.6 percentage points above the strongest competitor at stream end.

papers.abstract: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.
authors: Mohammad Ali Vahedifar, Behzad Bozorgtabar, Qi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the conflict between preserving existing knowledge and deleting selected knowledge.
Scores each weight for retention and deletion, dividing the network into four update zones.
Freezes retention-only weights, clears deletion-only weights, and orthogonally removes contested knowledge.
Uses remaining capacity with teacher-guided self-distillation to learn incoming tasks.
Matches or outperforms strong baselines across CL and MU settings, including image generation and dangerous-content removal; practicality is demonstrated on a PAI dataset.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon visual agents must do more than inspect images: they must turn observations into evidence that remains usable as a task unfolds. Existing active-perception methods teach agents where and how to look, while a final-answer reward gives little structure for deciding which observations satisfy dependent subgoals or should be retained for later use. We present ViStep-RL (Visual Stepwise Reinforcement Learning), which models execution as a dependency-linked graph of evidence-bearing subgoals. A verifier tracks which subgoals are supported by valid evidence, and changes in graph potential provide a net-progress learning signal; an active memory protocol preserves evidence across turns and links retrieval to downstream use. On ViInteract, ViStep-RL reaches 60.0% strict completion with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, compared with 10.0% for the base model and 46.5% after supervised fine-tuning. Controlled studies show that incremental task-state rewards outperform cumulative rewards by 3.2 points, while active evidence writing improves strict completion by 7.75 points over automatic writing. Under a common interaction framework, the task-trained ViStep-RL policy achieves 59.5% answer accuracy, 24.0 points above the strongest of six general-purpose reference models. Held-out episodes confirm the gain at both Qwen scales, and gains extend to three external visual reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Junyang Chen, Yao Qin, Xiao Li, Ningchao Wang, Yiguo Qiao, Wenbin Li, Xin Geng
bullets: Represents execution as a dependency-linked graph of evidence-bearing subgoals.
Uses a verifier and graph-potential changes to provide incremental progress rewards.
Employs active memory to write, retain, and retrieve evidence for downstream subgoals.
Achieves 60.0% strict completion with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on ViInteract, versus 10.0% for the base model and 46.5% after supervised fine-tuning.
Improvements also transfer to held-out episodes and three external visual reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Training-free open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) has made strong progress by adapting CLIP-like representations to dense prediction, but its remaining errors are often local, structured, and tied to the active label space. A successful correction must be visually plausible, legal under the target vocabulary, and executable in the segmentation score field. We propose SEER, a training-free test-time repair layer for Semantic Evidence and Executable Region propagation. SEER casts post-prediction OVSS repair as evidence-conditioned label propagation. The OVSS score space proposes compact candidate labels, a frozen VLM verifies closed-set regional evidence, and an execution gate certifies whether the evidence is legally and semantically actionable. The accepted label is then propagated by an OVSS-side policy: coherent high-confidence regions allow broad propagation, while object- or boundary-risk cases use conservative score-grounded propagation. Across eight standard OVSS benchmarks, SEER reaches 58.0 average mIoU without updating OVSS weights. Matched-input controls isolate the repair mechanism, while resource measurements report the cost of the complete frozen system.
authors: Junyang Chen, Xiao Li, Yiguo Qiao, Wenbin Li
bullets: Targets local, structured OVSS errors that depend on the active label vocabulary.
Uses OVSS scores to propose candidate labels and a frozen vision-language model to verify regional semantic evidence.
An execution gate accepts only evidence that is both vocabulary-legal and actionable in the segmentation score field.
Applies broad propagation to coherent high-confidence regions and conservative score-grounded propagation near objects or boundaries.
Achieves 58.0 average mIoU across eight standard OVSS benchmarks without updating OVSS weights; controls and resource measurements assess the repair mechanism and full-system cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SEER. SEER converts regional VLM evidence into executable OVSS label propagation. papers.title: SEER: Semantic Evidence for Executable Region Propagation in Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation

papers.abstract: Replay-free domain-incremental learning trains a model on the same classes in successive domains without keeping earlier images. Per-domain learners freeze a pre-trained ViT and train an additional expert for each new domain: the small set of parameters and the classification head learned on that domain. Test images carry no domain label, so a router selects one expert for each image. Recent work trains this router. However, a training-free Mahalanobis router costs the analyzed learners under 2.7 points of final accuracy relative to always selecting each image's own-domain expert. The experts, not this router, limit accuracy. Our learner, Lamarck, therefore uses this router and strengthens the experts. Its adapters, small trainable layers that correct every image token after each deep ViT block, add 4.4 points of final accuracy on the deepfake benchmark CDDB-Hard. In addition, each expert is initialized from its predecessor at no extra cost: the domains share their classes, so an image misrouted to a later expert loses less. Against twelve frozen-backbone baselines under one protocol, Lamarck is first on CDDB-Hard by 5.2 points, second on DomainNet and OfficeHome, and highest in mean accuracy.
authors: Gyutae Oh, Hyunmin Kong, Jitae Shin
bullets: Problem: Test images lack domain labels, so routing among domain-specific experts is difficult, while the experts themselves also limit accuracy.
Method: Add trainable adapters after each deep ViT block and use a training-free Mahalanobis router.
Method: Initialize each new domain expert from the previous expert, exploiting shared classes and reducing harm from later-expert misrouting.
Results: Adapters add 4.4 final-accuracy points on CDDB-Hard; Lamarck ranks first on CDDB-Hard, second on DomainNet and OfficeHome, and highest in mean accuracy.
Scope: Evaluated against twelve frozen-backbone baselines under one protocol.

papers.selection_reason: Replay-free domain-incremental learning with inherited adapter experts and a training-free router; directly relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: Inherited Adapter Experts for Replay-Free Domain-Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: Lamarck improves replay-free domain-incremental learning by strengthening per-domain adapters and inheriting each expert from its predecessor, achieving top or near-top results across benchmarks without storing past images.

papers.abstract: Biological learning systems acquire knowledge incrementally through broad, reusable representations established early and kept largely stable, while integrating new experience with minimal interference with previously learned knowledge. Replay-based methods approximate this by storing samples or features from previous tasks and mixing them into the current task. However, memory buffers grow with the number of tasks and may retain task-specific noise that reduces generalization. To address these limitations, we propose PatchAdaNet (Patch Adapter Network), an unsupervised class-incremental learning method for image classification that continually updates feature representations using autoencoders. Since images share structural features such as edges, corners, and shapes, we first divide each image into patches and train independent autoencoders on external data to reconstruct each patch. The layers of all patch encoders are aggregated into global frozen layers that generalize across tasks and remain fixed throughout learning. Learnable adapters then build global image representations from these features to reconstruct the entire image. To prevent feature drift without storing data, we introduce the Global Feature Centroid (GFC), a fixed-size running average of adapter outputs updated after each task to penalizes representation drift. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is applied to the learnable layers to preserve previously learned features by constraining important weights. Finally, a linear classifier is trained on the frozen latent representation and GFC for class-incremental evaluation. We evaluate PatchAdaNet in both CNN and Vision Transformer settings on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, miniImageNet and 5-Datasets, providing a comparative study of the two architectures under identical class-incremental settings. Code is available.
authors: Kamel Aouaidjia, Yanchao Duan, Zihui Zhen, Xin Li, Yongfei Lv, Chongsheng Zhang
bullets: Targets replay-based class-incremental learning, which can require growing memory and retain task-specific noise.
Trains independent patch autoencoders on external data, aggregates their encoders into frozen global layers, and uses learnable adapters to reconstruct full images.
Maintains a Global Feature Centroid (GFC) to penalize representation drift without storing prior data.
Uses Elastic Weight Consolidation on learnable layers and trains a linear classifier on frozen latent features plus the GFC.
Evaluated with CNNs and Vision Transformers on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, miniImageNet, and 5-Datasets under matched class-incremental settings.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes PatchAdaNet for unsupervised class-incremental learning using patch autoencoders and global adapters to prevent feature drift.
papers.title: PatchAdaNet: Unsupervised class incremental learning using local patches and global adapters
papers.tldr: PatchAdaNet enables unsupervised class-incremental image learning by combining reusable patch features, task-adaptive adapters, and fixed-size drift protection without replay buffers.

papers.abstract: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.
authors: Kamel Aouaidjia, Yanchao Duan, Zihui Zhen, Xin Li, Yongfei Lv, Chongsheng Zhang
bullets: Targets knowledge loss in regularization-based continual learning as task sequences grow.
Uses independent autoencoders to decompose inputs into complementary, independently learned representations.
Applies weight regularization within representations, localizing updates and reducing interference across tasks.
Evaluates representations with a linear classifier on several sequential image-classification benchmarks.
Reports competitive performance against supervised and replay-based continual-learning methods.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.
authors: Sachith Abeywickrama, Peiliang Gong, Emadeldeen Eldele, Min Wu, Chau Yuen

papers.abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Weiming Yang, Kaidi Yang
bullets: Fixed latent horizons can hurt performance because later reasoning may reorganize candidates and weaken support for the correct answer.
Latent CoT progresses through stages: early steps form frontier reasoning states, while later steps may provide diminishing or negative benefits.

A lightweight estimator adaptively adjusts the inference horizon without retraining the language model.
Across multiple arithmetic benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points and reduces latent computation by up to 29.0%.

papers.abstract: In precision manipulation, small errors in alignment or force can cause jamming or deformation, making contact feedback essential for adapting pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models to these tasks. A single tactile observation leaves the response to recent actions ambiguous. Direct tactile fusion during post-training can also disperse the action expert's visual attention and reduce the share it allocates to contact regions. To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA augments pretrained VLAs with lightweight tactile modules. A queryable action-response memory retrieves recent contact responses so that the action expert can combine them with immediate tactile feedback. Contact-guided gaze supervision concentrates the visual attention of the tactile semantic token on image regions corresponding to fingertip contact. CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33% mean success across three MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50% for direct tactile fusion with the same sensor inputs. It also achieves 67% success on an optical-tactile task from the public UniVTAC benchmark and 66.7% mean success across three real-robot tasks. These results show that tactile post-training helps pretrained VLAs adjust to changing contact.
