papers.abstract: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.
bullets: The study tests whether continuing to learn state labels helps an agent adapt when interaction cues change their meaning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

papers.abstract: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.
authors: Jianhuan Mao, Mengxiao Zhu, Yue Pei, Lei Li, Haogang Zhu
bullets: Evaluates reconstruction-based time-series anomaly detection under controlled test-time adaptation.
Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five seeds, normal-only updates do not reliably improve detection.
Among 180 settings, 63 recover a clear detection gain, while 90 show no clear gain.
Reduced reconstruction objectives do not consistently translate into better anomaly ranking.
The observed failure patterns persist across practical adaptation variants and modest label perturbations.

papers.abstract: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.
authors: Gaoxiang Linghu, Haonan Zhou, Xuanhe Liu, Weili Xu, Kaiyue Zhou, Jun Xiao, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when updating 3D Gaussian fields with new observations.

Uses per-Gaussian learning weights to balance current evidence with cross-state reliability.
The weights control both parameter updates and optimizer-memory refresh, renewing reliability over time.
Improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline across CL-Splats, WAT, and CL-3D; performs best on changed and unchanged views in CL-3D.

This weight governs both parameter adaptation and optimizer-memory refresh. Cross-state reliability is updated at state boundaries using resolved pressure and final support. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating continual learners.

Figure 2. Comparison of 3D Gaussian continual learning paradigms. (a) Existing methods treat Gaussians as update targets. Replay and regularization may retain obsolete content or hinder adaptation, while selective local optimization can propagate 2D detection errors into 3D updates. papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
authors: Xuji Zhang, Qilin Zhong, Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Jian Di, Kun Li, Yang Cao, Wenjun Lv
bullets: Addresses unreliable decisions when policies must retrieve relevant information from long, redundant observation histories.
Uses Recall-Relocalization to connect episodic memories to the current view through a small number of recall slots.
Converts recall slots into Gaussian source components via Recall Anchors, guiding flow-policy generation toward intended actions.
The transport network completes actions from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy.
Reports 80.4% average success on MIKASA-Robo, with gains of 20.3 and 18.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline on simulated and real-robot task suites, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RecallFlow. The present observation is encoded into tokens Zt. Recall–Relocalization lets Zt read the episodic memory bank and decodes K recall slots, each attending to the current view through a heatmap Hk. Recall Anchors turns each slot into a Gaussian anchor in action space; with a standard Gaussian, the anchors form the source p0. A transport network conditioned only on Zt carries x0 ∼ p0 to the action chunk, so memory reaches the action solely through the source.

Figure 3. Evaluation tasks in simulation. (a) RecallSuite consists of five memory-dependent tasks: the cue is seen only earlier in the episode, and the candidates look identical when the robot must decide. (b), (c) Tasks from MIKASA-Robo and RoboMimic.

(c) RecallFlow achieves the highest success rate on all four tasks. (d) The three behaviors observed on No Repeat: repeating one cup, touching one cup twice, and touching each cup once.

(a) At a decision of a NOREPEAT episode, all thirty samples of RecallFlow head to the untouched container from the source on, whereas long-history DP starts from noise and commits only in its last generation steps. (b) Over 15 decisions, the source samples of RecallFlow are already at the target. (c) RecallFlow therefore keeps its success rate with a single generation step.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.
authors: Zecheng Hao, Zihan Huang, Shenghao Xie, Jiyuan Zhang, Zhaofei Yu, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from fixed, uniform firing patterns in spiking vision transformers.
Uses attention-guided AdaE-IF routing to assign fine-grained firing to salient regions and coarse firing elsewhere.
Adds S-GSA and S-LGU for selective spike emission at token and channel granularity.
Trains routing and firing precision with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum.
On ImageNet-1k, reports 1.02–2.45 mJ per image and a 32×–72× accuracy-per-energy ratio.

Bottom: data flow of S-GSA, S-LGU and the parameterized S-FFN variants (I)(II) with convolution kernel size k and expansion ratio r.

Figure 4. Fine-grained energy breakdown of AdaS-ViT Large on ImageNet-1k. Module-level (a)–(c) and Operator-level (d)–(f) statistics of SOPs and average spike firing rates. For each block, Bar hues identify the module family, the total height of a bar denotes the theoretical SOPs Upper-bound while its dark lower segment denotes the actually incurred SOPs, the curve on the right axis reports the average firing rate.

Figure 1. AdaS-ViT establishes a compelling accuracy-energy frontier for spiking vision transformers. (a) Qualitative comparison of training paradigms over six axes covering training cost and inference behavior: prior paradigms trade these objectives against one another, whereas our test-time adaptive routing maintains a uniformly strong profile across all of them. (b) Quantitative comparison with prior SNN-based works on ImageNet-1k. The horizontal axis denotes top-1 accuracy and the vertical axis reports Ratio AE, i.e., the accuracy delivered per millijoule of inference energy. AdaS-ViT occupies the top-right region alone with the smallest bubble area, indicating markedly higher energy efficiency at a fraction of the parameters of prior art.

Figure 2. AdaE-IF: from uniform to adaptive and efficient spike firing. Top-left: the firing-rate curve of a vanilla IF/LIF neuron is ideally a uniform staircase, yet diverse input current patterns {Ilt} yield divergent firing rates F̃l 1:T for identical average input current Ĩl1:T , which accumulate across layers into conversion error and spatio-temporal gradient inconsistency. Bottom: AdaE-IF maps each spike firing pattern to its bit-granular equivalent, aligning training gradients and enabling precise regulation of Synaptic Operations (SOPs); guided by the attention score of the spiking feature map (Middle), it routes each token to a coarse-grained pattern that preserves energy efficiency, or a fine-grained pattern that enhances representation at only marginal extra cost; jointly scheduled under an ultra-low energy budget (Top-right), the two modes realize test-time adaptive firing precision.

Here T denotes the inference time-steps, Energy is the estimated inference energy per image, computed following the convention of [54]. Ratio AE quantifies the accuracy delivered per unit of energy cost, where a higher value indicates better energy efficiency.
Table 2. Generalization across data scales and modalities: comparison with prior SNN learning methods on static (CIFAR-10, CIFAR100) and neuromorphic (CIFAR10-DVS) benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.
authors: Mengran Li, Xichen Yan, Bo Li, Chengyang Zhang, Jinfeng Xu, Zheng Lin, Zelin Zang, Zhen Lei, Jiebo Luo, Victor C. M. Leung, Stan Z. Li

papers.abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.
bullets: Studies Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B models with nightly LoRA updates across long-running WebShop and τ²-bench tasks.

A discernment-based judge stayed near oracle performance for two weeks in most tested lives, then declined to self-judging levels by day 60.
Across 97 lives, the fraction of failed lessons strongly predicted outcomes (Spearman ρ = −0.81); user learning struggled when users could not see results.

papers.title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
papers.tldr: User-feedback learning can help small language models, but it often decays unless the feedback judge reliably filters out failed attempts and users can observe the true outcome.

papers.abstract: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
authors: Siqing Li, Luming Yang, Yijia Jiao, Junze Deng, Alper Yilmaz
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen planners to notice when executed actions differ from commands.
Runs the world model in reverse to score hypothesized actuation shifts against actual observations.
The shift-specific score separates actuator shifts from the model’s intrinsic prediction error and supports locally optimal detection, estimation, and source identification.
Self-correction improves success on PushT and Cube tasks and reduces real-robot reach error from 36 mm to 3–5 mm.
Scope: evaluation covers simulated manipulation tasks and a real robotic arm with sealed or unknown action shifts.

papers.selection_reason: Frozen latent world model used for action-conditioned planning and self-correction; directly addresses test-time adaptation of embodied planners.
papers.title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
papers.tldr: A frozen visual world model can detect, estimate, and correct action-execution errors by comparing observed outcomes with shift-conditioned predictions.

papers.abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires learning from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of model training speed. When training cannot keep pace, computationally expensive gradient-based methods update less frequently, limiting adaptation. Analytic methods reduce this overhead, but their frozen backbones cannot adapt representations to changing distributions. We propose DuoCL, a dual-path OCL framework whose fast analytic path accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch while its slow path periodically adapts the backbone. The slow path adjusts its sample count to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning. Feature alignment compensates for drift in the accumulated classifier statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline in each setting. DuoCL consistently outperforms analytic learning under distribution shifts, with gains of up to 4.00 percentage points on CIFAR-C, and achieves higher accuracy than prior methods across disjoint class-incremental, domain-incremental, and Si-Blurry settings.
authors: Jebacyril Arockiaraj, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between incoming data rates and gradient-based training speed in online continual learning.
Accumulates feature statistics from every minibatch through a fast analytic path while a slow path periodically updates the backbone.
Adapts slow-path sample counts to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning.
Uses feature alignment to compensate for drift in accumulated classifier statistics.

Improves online accuracy by 9.67 percentage points on average over the strongest gradient-based baselines across four datasets and three budgets, with gains up to 4.00 points over analytic learning on CIFAR-C.

papers.abstract: Unlabeled test data can improve the zero-shot classifier of a vision-language model, yet transductive and test-time adaptation methods often fall below the zero-shot baseline when only a few vocabulary classes are present in a batch or when streams are correlated. We trace this failure to a shared design: every class owns independent parameters estimated from its own samples, so absent or rare classes are left at biased text anchors or fitted to foreign samples. We propose Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (GRAFT), which models the adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field that is partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, together with an explicit class-presence model. Inference is closed-form and gradient-free on cached features. Anchor-only shrinkage and a single global shift are the two extreme settings of the prior; absent classes are provably harmonic extensions of the present ones, and the pooling strength can be chosen by empirical Bayes. Under the realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, GRAFT improves over the zero-shot model in every setting and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.
bullets: Addresses failures of transductive adaptation caused by independently estimating each class from sparse or absent samples.
Represents adapted prototypes as text anchors plus graph-pooled displacement fields with a Gaussian Markov random field prior.
Uses an explicit class-presence model and closed-form, gradient-free inference on cached features.
Absent-class prototypes become harmonic extensions of present classes; pooling strength is selected via empirical Bayes.
Improves over zero-shot models across eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, and outperforms anchor-based transduction when few classes are present.

papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.
authors: Minghe Zhang, Xuetao Kang, Yifei Ming, Yanfei Chen, Han Yu, Yufan Zhuang, Chen-Yu Lee
bullets: Targets regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat in editable AI-agent harnesses without weight updates or external graders.
Decomposes tasks into pre-execution self-checks and uses directional regret to distinguish new failures from unresolved problems.
Selects candidate edits with group-relative fitness and applies a Soft-HURT gate that accepts gains only when they outweigh regressions.
Scopes specialized fixes and protects gated behaviors from regression; deployment uses one frozen harness in a single pass.
Across memory, skill-evolution, continual-task, and domain-reasoning benchmarks, it improves performance while reducing forgetting, memory pollution, and deployment token usage.

papers.abstract: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $\rho$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.
authors: Nischal Subedi, Cencheng Shen, Peng Zhao
bullets: The study refines the view that spectral initializers help only through update magnitude.
Theory and first-step analysis explain how finite-sample subspace stability and task alignment affect adaptation; alignment is summarized by coefficient ρ.
PivotLoRA uses activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions plus an early output-preserving orthogonal pivot.
It ranks best on average across 13 methods in few-shot BERT-base classification and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, despite a smaller initial input-factor norm.
Benefits shrink with more labeled data; extensions also report gains on 7B/8B Llama classification and GSM8K and StrategyQA.

papers.abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.
authors: Jinjun Peng, Wailiang Zhao, Baishakhi Ray, Zhou Yu, Jufeng Yang
bullets: Studies plasticity and stability at the module level across declarative memorization and procedural learning tasks.
QK and VO projections are most plastic for procedural tasks, while MLPs are most plastic for declarative memorization.
Stability does not mirror plasticity: updating QK preserves more stored declarative knowledge than updating MLPs or VO.
Reset-and-recovery experiments suggest plasticity reflects a module’s primary computation or storage role, whereas stability depends on all capabilities relying on that module.
Similar asymmetric dynamics appear in experiments with a realistic model and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a module-level analysis of plasticity and stability in Transformers for continual learning, offering insights relevant to lifelong learning in agents.
papers.title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
papers.tldr: In transformers, the modules that learn most readily are not necessarily those that best preserve prior knowledge, with the relationship depending on task and functional role.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
bullets: Studies whether agents need explicit instructions for how to self-improve.
Agents receive basic tools, resources, a goal, and a compute budget, but no prescribed learning loop or real-world data.
In gameplay, agents construct their own context-based self-learning algorithms and update text artifacts from collected experience.
Their strategies resemble self-regulated learning and self-generated curricula from prior cognitive and machine-learning research.
Learned artifacts improve performance across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Do capable models specify their own self-improvement? We give a frozen LLM (here, Claude Opus-5) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset {Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay}, and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure. At the start (t = 0) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later (t = 60), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update.

Figure 7: Self-improving agents use learnability-seeking task selection. (left) Across models, most generated games are easy. (right) Newer model generations spend the most effort (# replays) on games with low to medium win rates. Observed win rates are computed over the first k plays for each game (k ∈ [2, 6]). This can lead to an inverted-U resembling learnability objectives in asymmetric self-play and UED.

Figure 6: Self-improving models display human-recognizable learning strategies. Alignment scores to 13 subprocesses of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning cycle, annotated by an LLM judge and averaged over 3 teacher sessions per model. Models that self-improve score higher across most subprocesses. Average over seeds; individual seeds in Appendix D.2.

In the first example (task-strategies) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second (learning goal orientation) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions.

(Right) We ablate the teacher’s toolset and Gameplay constraints; performance initially improves on both PuzzleScript-t20 and PuzzleScript-t30 with richer toolsets, however declines on PuzzleScript-t30 after adding t20-specific token and turn budgets. Error bars show ±1 SD over three independent teacher seeds.

Figure 5: Algorithmically measured behaviors. (Right: Updates) For GPT and GLM, newer generations exhibit more updates that improve the observed win rate on at least one self-generated game. For Opus and GLM, newer models prefer smaller context updates.

Figure 9: Improvements from self-organized learning transfer across benchmarks. Player performance is evaluated at intermediate context updates along the self-learning trajectory on PuzzleScript-t20, PuzzleScript-t30, ARCAGI-L1 and MazeBench. papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?

papers.abstract: Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.
authors: Zhouhan Qian, Sicheng Chen, Chad Wong, Tianyi Zhang, Enhui Chai, Zeyu Liu, Fei Xia
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when MIL models learn new WSI tumor subtypes without full historical data or task identifiers.
Uses multiple learnable queries per class to aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations.
Employs a shared prediction module to limit parameter growth across incremental stages.
Freezes old class queries and combines experience replay with knowledge distillation to preserve prior knowledge.
Experiments across eight TCGA tumor subtypes show improved performance and reduced forgetting in most learning settings versus competing methods.

papers.title: EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification
papers.tldr: EviSlide-MIL enables class-incremental whole-slide image classification by adding new tumor classes while preserving knowledge of previously learned ones.

papers.abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.
authors: Dewu Zheng, Yang Ye, Hongyu Zhang, Jun Yu, Yanlin Wang
bullets: Introduces a dataset of 350 complete training-experiment trajectories spanning seven task categories.
Annotates individual experimental decisions for quality and masks supervision on low-quality behavior.
Evaluated with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench for autonomous post-training.
Training on RSI-Prime produces a 31.95% relative improvement over the original GLM-5.3.
The work focuses on developing model-training capability as a foundation for future RSI systems.

papers.tldr: RSI-Prime trains LLMs to make better model-training decisions, improving autonomous post-training performance and supporting recursive self-improvement.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.
authors: Rose N. Kwon, Samy Mammeri, Sabyasachi Sahoo, Christian Gagn\'e, Thomas Jiralerspong
bullets: Narrow harmful-task fine-tuning can produce harmful behavior beyond the training distribution.
Inoculation prompting reduces this emergent misalignment but may leave the behavior conditionally accessible.
Textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete trigger predictor.
Prompts that induce activation states resembling the inoculation context are more likely to restore suppressed behavior.
Activation-space analysis may help detect residual vulnerability during evaluation.

Red bars show the mean EM rate across five inoculated dataset-specific models.

Figure 5. Prompt-level EM and caps0.8 rate versus text-similarity baselines for the inoculated models. Each point is an eval-time trigger prompt, colored by evaluation domain. The x-axes show lexical or string-based similarity between the trigger prompt and the inoculation prompt: token Jaccard similarity, SequenceMatcher ratio, and TF-IDF cosine similarity. The y-axis shows prompt-level EM and caps0.8 rate. These text-only baselines are positively correlated with re-elicitation, but only moderately, suggesting that lexical and surface-form similarity to the inoculation prompt do not fully explain trigger strength.

Panels (a,c,e,g) plot behavior against Train Ref., the cosine similarity to the mean pre-response hidden state of inoculated training examples; panels (b,d,f,h) plot behavior against BGE prompt-text similarity to the inoculation prompt. Panels show EM and capitalization correlations across layers; selected analysis layers are marked in each model.

Figure 1. Prompt-level correlations between predictors and re-elicited behavior. The hidden-state predictors are evaluated at the selected TRAIN REF. layers: L16 and L27 for EM and capitalization, respectively, in Qwen 7B, and L32 and L47 in Qwen 14B. papers.tldr: Activation-state similarity, rather than text similarity alone, predicts when evaluation prompts can re-elicit behavior suppressed by inoculation prompting.

papers.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
authors: Yuanhao Zeng, Shaocheng Lan, Ao Lu, Kuang Yan, Heng Lin, Xinang Xu, Yuan Luo, Yueting Wang, Yexin Li, Ruo Shan, Kan Ren
bullets: The Resolution Hypothesis attributes evolution failures and inconsistent results to unreliable improvement identification.
At the candidate level, useful artifacts exist, but selection is roughly no better than random at distinguishing them from harmful artifacts.
Selection errors accumulate across evolution rounds, preventing reliable bootstrapping on some tasks.
At the method level, typical performance gaps are smaller than run-to-run variation, making rankings unstable.
The findings motivate evaluation systems that make genuine improvements detectable and accumulable.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the bottleneck of evaluation noise in self-improving agents. This is highly relevant to LLM agent evolution and test-time evaluation, offering insights into improving agent self-improvement loops.
papers.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
papers.tldr: Agent evolution is often limited less by generating improvements than by noisy evaluation that cannot reliably recognize and preserve them.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.
authors: Jason Liang, Dylan Waldner, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: The study tests four Schwartz value types across diverse coding tasks and repeated self-improvement iterations.
Openness-to-change values improve held-out performance, while conservation values can underperform having no value guidance.
Values alter the algorithms agents build, including their size, complexity, and overall approach.
Allowing agents to revise their own values reduces behavioral differences; values distilled from AI literature show no detectable benefit over none.
The findings support values as a way to shape agent behavior, with effects depending on task and value design.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of value statements on self-improving coding agents, relevant to LLM behavior and test-time adaptation. The findings on how values shape agent output are transferable to agent design and alignment.
papers.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
papers.tldr: Value statements in persistent instructions can steer self-improving coding agents toward different solution strategies and performance levels, but designing those values still requires human oversight.

papers.abstract: Analytic continual learning replaces iterative gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pre-trained representations, summarizing all past sessions in two running sufficient statistics: the feature autocorrelation matrix $\Sigma_t$ and the class cross-correlation matrix $\Gamma_t$. Lifting backbone features into a wide random code of dimension $M \gg D$ substantially improves linear separability across tasks, but forces $\Sigma_t$ to grow quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Under a fixed persistent memory envelope $\Bcal$, a learner faces a fundamental structural trade-off: store exact pairwise co-activations inside a narrower feature code, or expand to a wide code while compressing cross-coordinate interactions. We observe that the coordinate self-variances $v_t = \diag(\Sigma_t)$ and class statistics $\Gamma_t$ grow only linearly with $M$, whereas off-diagonal interactions dominate memory. We introduce \method (\textbf{Co}ordinate-\textbf{Re}stored \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning), which retains $(v_t, \Gamma_t)$ exactly, maintains off-diagonal co-activations through a streaming rank-$q$ factor $F_t$, restores exact diagonal variances via $\Sighat_t = F_t^\top F_t + \Diag(v_t - \diag(F_t^\top F_t))$, and solves the full $M\times C$ normal equations via the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, \method matches dense full-covariance readouts within $0.09$ points while cutting persistent state by $90.7\%$ ($35.9$ vs.\ $385.3$ MiB). Under equal memory envelopes of $16$--$80$ MiB, prioritizing expansion width $M$ over covariance rank $q$ outperforms exact narrow readouts in $17$ of $18$ configurations by up to $+2.19$ points.
authors: Elena Voss, Pixel Nomand, Marcus Hale, Sofia Reyes
bullets: Analytic continual learning stores feature and class sufficient statistics, but wide random codes make covariance storage quadratic in feature width.
CoReACL retains feature variances and class statistics exactly while approximating off-diagonal covariance with a streaming rank-q factor.
A diagonal correction restores exact variances, and Woodbury identities solve the resulting full-width readout efficiently.
Across five benchmarks, it matches dense covariance readouts within 0.09 points while reducing persistent memory by 90.7%.
With equal 16–80 MiB budgets, wider feature codes beat exact narrower readouts in 17 of 18 configurations, by up to 2.19 points.

papers.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
authors: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
bullets: ExploitBench agents frequently stop with execution budget remaining, leaving their ultimate exploitation capability unclear.
Continuing after the first stop yields additional verified gains, but progress diminishes over longer runs.
Less productive continuation is linked to repeated stop responses and summaries that preserve unproven impossibility judgments.
SCoRe compacts context during stop bursts and marks such judgments as unproven, improving verified capability over evaluated continuation baselines.
With SCoRe, MiMo reaches 67.0% capability coverage at 2,000 turns, versus 32.4% under the original stopping policy and 58.6% for GPT-5.5’s 300-turn reference results.

papers.abstract: Counting distinct objects in a video is hard when the camera returns to places it has seen. A vision-language model that reads the whole video answers with a few small numbers, and one that reads it in parts counts an object again in every part that shows it. Object trackers need the category before the video is read, or a fixed vocabulary. We observe that a memory for counting does not need to know what it is looking for, only where it has been: objects rarely leave a room between visits, so parts of a video grouped by place share almost no objects, and a place can be recognised before any question is asked. Building on this, we introduce PlaceTally, a question-blind test-time memory model that constructs a place graph for each video. Each video fragment joins the place of its best earlier match or opens a new place, because a strong match is rarely wrong while a true return often matches weakly. A frozen vision-language model counts each place once from at most 128 of its frames, so every read has a bounded input and the memory grows with the number of places; the graph is built 15 times faster than real time. On RevisitCount, our benchmark of real room re-recordings, it scores 62.5% mean relative accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms, against 51.2% and 44.3% for the same model reading the whole video. It stays level as rooms return more or less often, while a fixed correction of summed visits moves from 38.5% to 61.4%.
bullets: Motivation: Whole-video vision-language models struggle with long videos, while chunk-wise counting repeats objects and trackers require predefined categories.
Method: Group video fragments by their best visual match to earlier fragments or create a new place, then count each place once with a frozen vision-language model.
Design: Each place is read from at most 128 frames, bounding input size while memory scales with the number of places.
Results: On RevisitCount, it achieves 62.5% accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms, versus 51.2% and 44.3% for whole-video reading.
Scope: The approach is designed for videos involving revisits to physical places and assumes objects generally remain within rooms between visits.

papers.abstract: Existing agentic manipulation systems treat pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies as opaque, language-only primitives: when a policy call fails under unfamiliar instructions or scene perturbations, the agent cannot steer its behavior and is forced into futile retries or costly manual takeover. We present InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable and inspectable tools through a bidirectional geometric interface with vision-language agents. In the forward direction, test-time geometric guidance translates an agent-specified end-effector target into input gradients through the action expert via a differentiable command-to-pose mapping, while soft-time target alignment treats arrival time as a latent execution index to match the target pose without distorting the policy's approach motion. In the reverse direction, action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks and calibrated camera reprojections back to the agent, allowing it to diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise targets for subsequent VLA calls, or locally adjust motion segments on top of the guided trajectory. Making the VLA controllable not only boosts online agentic tool use, but also unlocks effective recursive self-improvement (RSI), achieving state-of-the-art performance of 99.4\% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62\% on RoboDojo, and 89.4\% on RoboCasa365. Project page: https://lingwupro.github.io/InteractVLA/.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Shifeng Bao, Yihan Lin, Haitao Shen, Yining Luo, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of treating VLAs as opaque, language-only tools under unfamiliar instructions or scene changes.
Uses bidirectional geometric interaction: agents guide VLA actions toward target poses and inspect action chunks with camera reprojections.
Soft-time target alignment matches target poses while preserving the policy’s natural approach motion.
Supports agentic diagnosis, target revision, local trajectory adjustment, and recursive self-improvement.
Reports 99.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62% on RoboDojo, and 89.4% on RoboCasa365.

(c) This interactive interface improves online tool-use success on both LIBERO-Plus and RoboDojo.

Each row presents successive stages of task execution from left to right, demonstrating coordinated grasping, reorientation, and placement under agent guidance. For Move Cube, we show the robot’s overhead camera view to highlight the tight clearance between the cube and the cup, illustrating the precision required for placement. Full video demonstrations are available at https://lingwupro.github.io/InteractVLA/.

The agent then specifies geometric targets to explore alternative motions and discover new solutions through InteractVLA. As experience accumulates, the agent shifts toward consolidating existing strategies for task completion, slowing the growth of both execution steps and token consumption and increasing success rate substantially.

papers.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.
authors: Yoonho Choi, Taehyeon Han, Seonghyeon Lee
bullets: Problem: Agents often over-explore repositories and continue calling tools after sufficient evidence has been gathered; standard SFT can reproduce this behavior.
Method: Truncate training trajectories at the earliest sufficient-answer step, add a rationale explaining why stopping is appropriate, and emphasize that rationale during fine-tuning.
Results: JET reduces tool calls by 11–33% on self-generated trajectories and 18–28% versus SFT on expert trajectories.
Across two repository-QA benchmarks and two open-weight 8B models, JET largely preserves performance and lowers inference cost.

papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.
authors: \"Omer Faruk Akg\"ul, Shuli Jiang, Yuting Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiaohan Fei, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Previously useful skills may lower task performance by over 10 percentage points or raise execution cost by nearly 40% after changes.
The impact depends on which environment details become outdated and whether current observations let the agent compensate.
Selective maintenance replays checks from successful executions to detect conflicts, repair affected state, validate updates, or rebuild when needed.
Across four task settings and two models, maintenance improves accuracy by up to 67 percentage points and reduces execution steps by up to 37% versus stale-state reuse.
Scope: results cover the evaluated task settings, models, and environment changes; no change description is provided to the agent.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.
authors: Yican Zhao, Bolin Yang, Ruizhe Wang, Haiyang Guo, Fuji Yang, Bingo Wing-Kuen Ling, Zelin Zang
bullets: Latent distance-to-goal objectives can create local minima, especially near walls, corners, and dead ends.
EKR penalizes candidate plans near a novelty-gated memory of visited latents using a top-k Gaussian kernel.
Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR improves reported average success while using the same planning budget.
It reduces stuck episodes and revisits, often steering plans away from visited states even at higher base cost.
The method transfers without tuning to DINO-WM with CEM and improves performance on Wall, PointMaze, and Push-T tasks.

papers.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.
authors: Siqi Lai, Haitao Li, Hao Liu
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational cost of repeatedly invoking LLM-based System-2 reasoning.
Builds a modular harness containing procedures, state memory, and world models for richer decision context.
Uses utility-driven retrieval and environmental feedback to select and recursively revise harness modules.
Experiments on three datasets show improved decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings while preserving low-latency execution.
As the harness improves, fewer System-2 interventions are needed, amortizing reasoning costs over time.

papers.abstract: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://towzeur.github.io/RCR/.
bullets: Neural-collapse classifiers can separate samples within their task while routing them to the wrong task block globally, causing high Task-IL but low Class-IL accuracy.

Reported gains reach up to +6.75 FAA over the reference and preserve Task-IL performance, with larger improvements in difficult routing regimes.

papers.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.

papers.abstract: Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze $13\times13$, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on $9\times9$ and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.
authors: Xianyao Li, Ruitong Tian, Rui Min, Fang Xu, Jing Du

papers.abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.
authors: Peng Yu, Xiaoyu Wen, Zhida He, Ziyuan Zhou, Han Qi, Shao Zhang, Qiaosheng Zhang, Ying Wen, Chaochao Lu

papers.abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.
authors: Guochen Zhou, Yijun Yang, Qiqi Duan, Qing Su, Weiming Ou, Li Shen, Shihao Ji, Yuhui Shi, Zhisong Zhang
bullets: Offline-to-online distribution shifts make it difficult to choose a fixed optimism–pessimism balance.
Optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, while pessimistic policies perform better on familiar online tasks.
The method formulates the trade-off as a bi-objective problem and constructs a Pareto policy pool with MOSAIC.
A hierarchical contextual bandit selects the most suitable policy during online fine-tuning.
HiP3 achieves the strongest aggregate performance across same and novel tasks, including under stronger distribution shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3). In the offline stage (gray box), our MOSAIC algorithm generates a diverse pool of Pareto policies exhibiting varying optimism-pessimism trade-offs via multi-objective optimization with reference vectors and neighborhood search. In the online stage (blue box), a contextual bandit (LinUCB [33]) selects a candidate policy conditioned on the current state from the top-K subset; the selected policy is then fine-tuned via a Dyna-style method [15].

Figure 1: (a) Pareto policy pool discovered by HiP3, containing policies with different optimism-pessimism trade-offs. P1 maximizes model-predicted return (most optimistic), P4 minimizes uncertainty (most pessimistic), while P2 and P3 represent balanced trade-offs. (b) On the novel online task (details in Appendix C.1), optimistic P1 achieves the highest return. (c) On the same online task, pessimistic P4 achieves the highest return. Together, these results motivate preserving multiple trade-off policies offline and deferring the choice among them to online adaptation, rather than committing to a single trade-off in advance.
