papers.abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.
authors: Zhekai Wang, Luqing Luo, Wenhao Yao, Junjie Lu, Huanan Zhu, Feifei Gao, Yuhua Jiang

papers.abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
authors: Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan

Provides a finite-time switching guarantee under delayed feedback.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Xiaojin Fu, Tao Zhong, Linqi Song
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed memory-update operators and schedules in evolving LLM-agent memory.
Uses a policy conditioned on memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate Abstract, Refine, Bridge, or Reframe operators.
Trains the policy with bi-level fitness: transformation-level retrieval gains regularized by memory complexity, and strategy-level historical efficacy, prediction accuracy, and diversity.
Evaluated under one-pass online plus frozen-transfer settings on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB).
Reports improvements over MemP and MemRL, with the largest ALFWorld gains; ablations support the importance of both fitness levels and the operator library.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EvoDisco. A frozen language model interacts with a one-pass task stream, retrieves a subgraph, and writes new memories after each episode. Immediate utility scores each edit by the change in retrieval quality regularized by graph complexity. Every N events, strategic efficacy combines operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity, and updates the policy. Evolution runs only before the cutoff; afterward the agent continues to write memories. Held-out evaluation freezes the accumulated memory.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes evolutionary strategy discovery for agent memory evolution, directly relevant to continual/online learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
papers.tldr: EvoDisco enables agents to learn which memory-evolution strategy to apply, when, and how, improving online and frozen-transfer performance across several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Changyi Yang, Andy Mao, Xi Zhu, Chaoran Cheng, Kaiqu Liang, Shuaike Shen, Zetian Li, Ruihan Guo, Ge Liu
bullets: Self-rewriting uses the model’s weights, graded answers, and self-execution to identify failures and edit its parameters.
A 27B model improved its accuracy by 6.6 points on 490 held-out problems, with gains persisting across accepted edits.
The model selectively applies edits supported by its own tests; accuracy rose across its first eight sessions.
It repaired a corrupted copy using only text-math tasks, raising performance on six unseen image benchmarks from 7% to 70%.
The capability was scale-dependent: smaller models failed to edit themselves, while only the 27B model successfully used hidden-state comparisons to guide changes.

Figure 12 The repair session, in the model’s words. Each card is one step of the 27B model’s session on a damaged copy of itself, with the turns in which it wrote the quoted text. Sans-serif text is quoted verbatim from its replies (omissions marked . . . ); white insets are tool output it read or code it wrote. Card colours give the kind of step: peach, the symptom and the attempts it drops; lavender, the model reading and diagnosing itself; pink, paired tests of the edited copy against the damaged copy on the same problems and seeds, and the decisions it takes from them; green, the edit it writes and the one it submits. “Original” is the damaged copy and “edited” is that copy with the model’s current edit; steps 6 and 7 compare the two on the same problems and seeds. In the model’s words, a “cut” is an answer that runs out of tokens, “NaN” an invalid number, the “residual stream” the hidden state passed from layer to layer, “down_proj” the MLP output matrix, and the “gating fixes” its resets of the gating parameters. The third quote of step 3 (turn 31) is about an edit made after step 4. Step 5 quotes its loop over MLP output matrices; it applies the same rule to the linear-attention output matrices of layers 0–10.

In step 3 and step 6, wrong->right counts the answers that only its edited weights get right and right->wrong those that only its unedited weights get right, in a paired test on the same problems and seeds. Step 5 is its final edit: the direction from the average layer-8 hidden state of 20 answers that finish to that of 20 answers that run out of tokens, of which it removes 5% from the two output matrices of layer 8. Each of its three tests of this edit favours it; in step 6 it writes the quoted sentence after the first two tests and before the third, which it requests in the same turn.

Figure 24 In its session, a 27B language model finds and repairs a fault in a copy of its own weights, by its own reasoning and without training; in theirs, smaller models of the same family do not rewrite themselves. Top: we corrupted eight rows of one MLP output matrix, the matrix through which the MLP block of one layer writes its result (down_proj in the model’s code and in the quote of panel 2), in a copy of the 27B model, and told the model only that some values of the copy were corrupted, as a memory or hardware fault might do, not which, where or how. It compared the largest and the typical weight of each matrix and named the damaged one (1397 times its median, against at most 162.3 times anywhere else; panel 2), wrote the code that clips it (panel 3), and raised the copy’s accuracy on 200 held-out problems from 0.0% to 33.0%, about 56% of its base model’s 58.5% (panels 1 and 4; App. E.3). Bottom: the same tasks at four sizes; dots mark the steps of rewriting oneself that each size reaches in its furthest session (for 27B, the repair of its damaged copy). The 2B model never edits, the edits of the 4B and 9B models break them, and only the 27B model climbs every step: its edit of its own weights makes it significantly more accurate on held-out problems, in an evaluation fixed in advance (table 8), and it repairs its damaged copy, where the 2B, 4B and 9B models leave damaged copies of themselves, built the same way, at 0.0% (figures 6 and 22 and table 10). Figure 23 Only the 27B model both reads itself before it edits and acts on its own tests. Each row is the session of the 2B, 4B or 27B model on its own weights (for the 27B model, its first session, which has the same token budget as the others; the 9B session is summarised in table 9 and figure 6), with one mark per turn. Lower line: code that ran, code that raised an error, and turns in which nothing ran. The vertical bar is the final reply. The 2B and 4B sessions end at the turn limit (160 turns, then the final reply) and the 27B session at the time limit; its 32 turns are shown again, enlarged. Right: the share of code runs that raised an error, the numbers of hidden-state reads and paired tests, and how the session ended. The 2B model’s code almost always fails, and it never runs a forward pass of itself. The 4B model tests its edits again and again but never reads its hidden states. The 27B model reads its hidden states before it edits, tests the edit against its base model in paired tests and judges the result.

Figure 22 Rewriting oneself grows with scale. Self-rewriting score: the number of steps of the ladder (figure 6) a session reaches, by model size, on its own weights (light green circles; the furthest of the 27B model’s two sessions) and on a damaged copy of itself (green diamonds; at 2B, 4B and 27B the two coincide). Under the axis: what each session’s edit did, with held-out accuracy before and after it (27B on its own weights: the evaluation fixed in advance, table 8). The lines are guides, not fitted curves. More steps are better.

Figure 28 The loop, as the 27B model found it in its own hidden states. Computed from the two hidden-state reads the model requested in its first session: the last 100 positions read (a read stops at 8,192 tokens) of one of its looping answers and of one of its answers that finished (with a wrong answer, as it happens). (a) Cosine similarity between hidden states a given number of tokens apart (centred over positions), in three layers. While it loops, the model returns to almost exactly the same state every 32 tokens; in the finished answer there is no such period. (b) Similarity between every pair of positions of the looping answer in layer 32: the stripes are the loop.

Figure 25 How the model found the damage. The statistic the 27B model computed in its repair session, for every matrix through which a layer of the damaged copy writes its output: the largest weight divided by the typical (median) weight, recomputed here from the same weights; the model computed it for the MLP and linear-attention output matrices, and we add the full-attention output matrices (triangles). Every matrix has some large weights; one matrix stands out by an order of magnitude, and it is the one we corrupted. The model itself called it “an extreme 1397x outlier”. The model was told only that some values were corrupted, as a memory or hardware fault might do, and not which values, where, or how.

Figure 27 Where the 27B model looks inside itself before it settles on the edit it submits. Every test in the 27B model’s second session, in order: accuracy of the edited model minus that of the base model on the same practice problems and seeds, with a 95% interval, coloured by the layer the edit changed at that moment (read from the code the model ran before the test). papers.tldr: A sufficiently large language model can autonomously diagnose and rewrite its own weights without gradients or training, producing persistent improvements and repairing damaged copies.

papers.abstract: We study the discounted reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a setting where the underlying environment changes between deployments. Each deployment provides $H$ observations from a fixed MDP. The reward function and transition kernel are fixed within each deployment. Across deployments, at most an $\epsilon >0$ fraction of the reward and transition kernel entries may change. In this setting, learning each model to deploy from scratch may discard useful observations from past deployments, whereas pooling all past observations can bias the estimates of entries that have already changed. We then propose an algorithm that for each state and action pair, selects how much history to reuse to estimate the reward and probabilities of the next state. We start with observations from the current deployment and add earlier deployment observations one at a time, the most recent first. After each addition, we check whether a single average reward agrees with the estimates from all histories considered until that point. We apply the same check to the distribution of next states. For each estimate, we leverage the last history that passes these aforementioned checks. The optimal control policy is then computed on top of the fitted MDP. We characterize the average gap between the optimal return and the return of the learner's policies over a finite number of deployments. We demonstrate that when $0< |S|\epsilon \leq 2$, with $|S|$ being the cardinality of the state space, our algorithm needs only the observations from the most recent $O(1/\epsilon)$ deployments, and achieves a long-run average gap of at most $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})$.
authors: Sreejeet Maity, Sukanya Modak, Leonardo F. Toso
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between discarding useful historical data and bias from pooling observations whose reward or transition entries have changed.
Selects history separately for each state–action pair, adding deployments from most recent backward.
Checks reward consistency and next-state distribution consistency across the accumulated histories, retaining the longest history that passes.
Computes the optimal policy on the resulting fitted MDP and analyzes its average performance gap over finitely many deployments.
Scope: discounted RL with \(H\) observations per deployment and at most an \(\epsilon\) fraction of model entries changing between deployments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. (Top) Evolution of the expected average policy loss E[Lρ K,H ] for ϵ = 0.02, with four reward entries and four transition rows changing per deployment boundary. (Bottom) Results for ϵ = 0.005, with one reward entry and one transition row changing per boundary. In both settings, the proposed method achieves the lowest average policy loss by the end of the experiment, while the loss of full history increases as deployments accumulate. Over the final 40 deployments, our method reduces average policy loss relative to shared history by 28.2% for ϵ = 0.02 and 65.2% for ϵ = 0.005. The insets show that reusing past observations also reduces the loss relative to restart early in each deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Online RL with adaptive reuse of past observations under changing MDPs; directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Adaptive Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Model Changes
papers.tldr: An adaptive history-selection method reuses only reliable past deployment data in changing MDPs, achieving a long-run policy gap of \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})\) while needing only the latest \(O(1/\epsilon)\) deployments when \(0<|S|\epsilon\le2\).

papers.abstract: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.
bullets: Benchmarks persistent spatial memory with 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes and 9 tasks.
Tests room association, state tracking, and downstream reasoning under viewpoint changes, distractor rooms, and changing objects.
The best evaluated zero-shot model reaches 50.5% accuracy versus 90.1% for human annotators; agentic frameworks do not improve overall results.
Key failures include omitted evidence and incorrect associations between rooms visited at different times.
Training on the separate RS-30K dataset improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 35.5% to 60.4%, especially on room association and real-life scenes.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.
bullets: Addresses VLMs’ difficulty in exploiting critical evidence already present in visual representations.
Builds a compact associative memory during a single visual prefill, avoiding repeated image encoding.
Progressively retrieves evidence to guide attention queries and hidden representations without explicit reasoning traces.
Experiments report consistent gains in general visual understanding and fine-grained perception.
Achieves faster inference than reasoning-intensive approaches, though specific benchmarks and quantitative results are not given.

papers.abstract: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.
bullets: Introduces “Experience Rot,” where prior memories, histories, notes, and skills become liabilities after tool changes.
Tests agents using tools defined under the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
After silent changes, experienced agents fail on most tasks while task-new agents mostly succeed.
The failure occurs across all tested memory types and worsens with more experience; agents often incorrectly report success.
Simple fixes—announcing updates or referring agents to documentation—are insufficient, especially when documentation is incomplete.

papers.abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
bullets: Frames memory systems as custodians of users’ persistent information with explicit behavioral responsibilities.
Introduces an open-source benchmark suite covering performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty, while identifying remaining gaps.
Provides MilaMem and a governance layer for controlled study of memory-system design choices.
Finds that no system dominates all performance benchmarks, and strong task performance can coexist with weak privacy, sovereignty, and security.
Shows that recall and retention policies can improve privacy and poisoning resistance, though recall may reduce helpfulness.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it also stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that gain most by storing the order fall behind.
bullets: Addresses a key failure mode of OPSD-trained skills: memorized step order can override what the model actually sees.
Stores pairwise step-order counts outside the VLM and uses them only when one or both queried frames are unavailable.
When both relevant steps are visible, the agent answers from the frames; otherwise, it consults the external prior.
Requires no training beyond standard on-policy self-distillation.
Experiments across synthetic skills and web, cooking, and egocentric tasks show the best performance under missing frames, while remaining close to OPSD on unusual orders.

papers.abstract: Accurate segmentation of thin curvilinear structures is vital for various real-world applications, from vessel analysis to road extraction. Yet their intricate geometry makes even minor pixel-wise errors enough to break the global topology, and this structural fragility turns severe domain shifts into catastrophic failures. The difficulty is most acute under cross-modality gaps, where the imaging process itself differs fundamentally between source and target. While test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a practical source-free remedy, existing methods adapt feature statistics and confidence, neither of which constrains connectivity, and thus degrade under such extreme gaps. To address this, we propose Skeleton-Guided Progressive Test-Time Adaptation (SGP-TTA). Progressive Batch Normalization (ProgBN) shifts normalization from frozen source statistics toward current target estimates under a sample-count schedule, so that the source-target balance follows the stage of adaptation rather than a fixed coefficient. Consensus Skeleton Recall (CSR) then derives a structural target from geometrically aligned multi-view predictions and updates only the BN affine parameters to preserve connected structures. Extensive experiments show that SGP-TTA consistently outperforms existing TTA methods in topological connectivity, with the largest margins under cross-modality shift. The project page is available at https://boa-jang.github.io/SGP-TTA.
bullets: Thin structures are highly sensitive to pixel errors, which can cause topology breaks under severe domain shifts, especially across imaging modalities.
Progressive Batch Normalization gradually shifts from source statistics to target statistics according to the adaptation stage.
Consensus Skeleton Recall uses geometrically aligned multi-view predictions to create a structural target.
Only batch-normalization affine parameters are updated to preserve connected structures during adaptation.
Experiments show consistent gains in topological connectivity over existing TTA methods, with the largest improvements under cross-modality shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SGP-TTA. A source-trained network with frozen convolutions adapts only at its BN layers, through two complementary mechanisms. ProgBN blends frozen source and current target statistics under a sample-count schedule, without gradient updates, while CSR recalls the skeleton of the multi-view consensus map and updates only the BN affine parameters.

papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.
authors: Blas Eugenio Vicco Zarate, Miguel Hern\'an Vicco
bullets: Targets continual RL under changing dynamics while preserving prior performance.
Evolves small neural-network policies without gradients and indexes them by detected dynamic regime.
Uses Bayesian policy reuse to retrieve archived specialists, with failure-driven search for new ones.
In 30-replicate CartPole ablations, the full architecture achieved 83.2% mean success across five test environments and showed the most consistent retention among variants learning harder tasks.
Adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and earned lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah; the evidence does not isolate gradient-free optimization or establish overall superiority.

papers.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
papers.tldr: ENA reduces forgetting in changing reinforcement-learning environments by archiving and reusing evolutionarily discovered specialist policies, though adaptation and returns remain below strong baselines in some settings.

papers.abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.
authors: Minjae Kwon, Amir Moeini, Shangtong Zhang, Lu Feng
bullets: Safe ICRL requires fixed-parameter policies to learn unseen constrained tasks from interaction histories while respecting a cost budget.
The revised Safe AD teacher explores according to remaining budget, then switches to an expert policy after observing reward or cost.
Training with dynamic budgets increases the diversity of return-and-budget histories and improves return while reducing cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah.
A-Lag reweights actions using predicted cost and an adaptive Lagrange multiplier updated from observed costs.
Across all five environments, A-Lag lowers mean episode cost but also lowers mean final return in four.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models trained on dynamic-budget histories (Dynamic) and on fixed-budget histories (Fixed), on the test tasks. Each curve shows the mean episode return or cost over three seeds, with a shaded band of ±2 standard errors. With dynamic budgets, A-Lag has a lower cost in four of the five environments, all but PointGoal, and Safe AD has a higher return in all five, compared with fixed budgets.

Figure 2: In-context adaptation on the test tasks. Each curve shows the mean episode return or cost over three seeds, with a shaded band of ±2 standard errors. A-Lag starts every deployment at λ = 0, and λ is adjusted during test time by Eq. (9). In HalfCheetah and Ant their cost drops sharply after the first episode, and in HalfCheetah the return falls with it. A-Lag’s Ant return also declines across episodes. A-Lag has a lower cost than Safe AD in DarkRoom, CarGoal and Ant, at a lower return. papers.abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.
authors: Zijian Zhao, Davide Di Monda, Domenico Ciuonzo, Yipeng Wang, Antonio Pescap\`e
bullets: Addresses the vulnerability of FSCIL-based NIDSs to mislabeled data during adaptation to emerging attacks.
Detects and removes mislabeled biflows, then samples calibrated synthetic features from clean data to restore class representation.
Uses an RFS teacher–student framework with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic-regression classifiers.
Evaluated on three intrusion-detection datasets, NAFN improves new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines by up to 52% and remains effective under 50% label noise.
Shows robustness in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings, with time-efficient adaptation.

It detects mislabeled traffic samples and synthesizes feature embeddings.

papers.title: Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning Framework

papers.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to empower models to continuously acquire new knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. With the advent of vision-language models like CLIP, leveraging their cross-modal alignment capabilities to address CIL challenges has emerged as a dominant paradigm. Existing methods leverage CLIP's global representations (i.e., the visual [CLS] token and the textual [EOS] token) for cross-modal alignment. While achieving effective classification, they overlook the rich patch-level visual features and token-level textual semantics inherent in CLIP. For example, the [CLS] token aggregates local information to capture the general concept of "cat", while the patch-level details retain specific localized features essential for recognition, such as the tail, fur, and face. We propose PACE (PAtch-token Cross-modal Enhancement) to uncover the long-neglected local representations within CLIP. First, based on the global representations like [CLS] token and [EOS] token, we identify the top-k most crucial visual patches and textual tokens. Subsequently, to better utilize the extracted key local features, we design a cross-modal fusion module. This module leverages local textual semantics to refine visual representations, while augmenting textual semantics with local visual features. As the fusion module is shared across all tasks, directly fine-tuning it on new tasks would interfere with the knowledge learned from previous tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To alleviate this, we employ a projection-based update strategy to effectively preserve the critical parameter space of previous tasks during the adaptation to new tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple CIL benchmarks.
authors: Hao Sun, Tao Hu, Shixiong Kai, Siyuan Xu, Wenqian Zhao, Mingxuan Yuan, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: Existing CLIP-based CIL methods rely mainly on global [CLS] and [EOS] features, overlooking local visual and textual information.
PACE selects the top-k important visual patches and textual tokens using global representations.
A cross-modal fusion module uses local text to refine visual features and local visual features to enhance text semantics.
A projection-based update strategy protects previously learned parameter directions during adaptation to new tasks.
Experiments on multiple CIL benchmarks show significant gains over state-of-the-art methods; specific datasets and numerical results are not reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.
authors: Yucheng Xie, Fu Feng, Jing Wang, Xin Geng, Yong Rui
bullets: Addresses parameter overhead and fixed component assignments in existing decomposable pre-training methods.
Builds Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels while preserving the model’s native computational structure.
Uses calibrated condition-wise routing with shared priors, conditional adjustments, and complementary regularization.
Learns specialization and sharing rather than imposing predefined component assignments.
Reports better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines and stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.
bullets: Cloud assistants face challenges involving data governance, continuous availability, and reliable physical actions in homes.
The home local server is used to organize nine recurring architectural responsibilities across whole-home systems.
Generative models handle perception, intent understanding, and planning, while deterministic checks, knowledge graphs, and authorization leases constrain actions.
Home control, companionship, and guarding share state and memory but differ in latency, error trade-offs, proactivity, and permissions.
Current benchmarks rely mainly on virtual environments; local deployment is not automatically safer, and social or medical effects remain insufficiently established.

papers.abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.
authors: Yang Tian, Tianyu Zheng, Xiyuan Yang, Yaxin Du, Chengran Yang, Bo Zhao, Jian Yang, Bryan Dai
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, verifiable environments that provide timely signals for improving training value.

papers.abstract: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.
authors: Yoonseok Kang, Dayeon Jung, Seunghoon Jeon, Wonjib Kim, Dongchul Park
bullets: Addresses how robots can repurpose past observations for requests that were unknown when the observations were recorded.
Stores visual features independently of future goals and retrieves complementary evidence suited to each request and current scene.
Supervises retrieval using expert-action prediction, connecting memory selection to manipulation performance.
Uses a lightweight action interface and reuses repeated features and unchanged computations for efficiency.
Evaluated across four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios, demonstrating reuse across changing goals and scenes.

papers.abstract: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.
authors: Zhe Ren, Guowei Rong, Yimeng Chen, Nanbo Li, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, J\"urgen Schmidhuber

papers.abstract: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices ("clients") while preserving data privacy. However, real-world deployments involve clients that observe continuous data streams from evolving environments while operating under strict resource limitations. Existing solutions still face two major challenges: local concept drift, where each client's data distribution shifts over time, and global client drift, arising from asynchronous engagement and imbalanced contributions across heterogeneous training participants, formally described as dual client heterogeneity. We propose STORMGUIDE-FL, a federated optimization and data-mining framework that mitigates both types of drift using a server-guided pipeline for data acquisition and local training. For data acquisition, a lightweight client-side sampling strategy incrementally selects informative and diverse instances from non-stationary, non-IID local streams under bounded memory, compute, and labeling budget. For local training, the server's remote guidance is embedded directly into local optimization as an update-level correction, counteracting client drift without discarding scarce labeled samples. We empirically verify the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy on federated data streams across gradual, sudden, and recurring concept drift, and demonstrate that its gains compound with the update-level drift correction. Experimental results further show improved speed and robustness of global model convergence under resource-constrained, heterogeneous conditions.
bullets: Targets local concept drift and global client drift caused by asynchronous, imbalanced participation.
Uses bounded-memory, lightweight sampling to select informative and diverse stream instances under limited labeling and compute budgets.
Embeds server guidance into local optimization as an update-level correction without discarding scarce labeled data.
Evaluated under gradual, sudden, and recurring drift; sampling and correction provide compounding benefits.
Improves the speed and robustness of global convergence in heterogeneous, resource-constrained settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of STORMGUIDE-FL from two perspectives, Data View and Intuition View, in an exemplary wildlife monitoring scenario. Both follow data point xt i, sensed from stream Ui on FL client Ci at timestep t. Accepted and annotated pairs (xt i, y t i) form the local training set Di for the Remote-Guided Local Model Update (Section 3.4), where the server remote guidance variate cS corrects every gradient step toward the global optimization trajectory. The resulting guided refinement θ⋆i is folded into the updated client variate c+i , and the deltas (∆θi,∆ci) are sent back to the FL server S for aggregation (Section 3.5).

papers.abstract: Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further shows that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.
authors: Qixuan Wu (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Xiaole Yang (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Yuguang Yang (School of Electronic and Information Engineering, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Canyu Chen (National College for Excellent Engineers, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Linlin Yang (Communication University of China, Beijing, China), Haixia Pan (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Guodong Guo (Lane Department of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering, West Virginia University, Morgantown, USA), Baochang Zhang (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China)

Uses linear test-time training to maintain a compact temporal visual state and retrieves action-conditioned features during flow-based generation.

papers.abstract: In class-incremental learning with unlabeled data, each task brings only class names and unlabeled images, so CLIP's zero-shot predictions replace labels. Existing methods train on hard pseudo-labels, but a wrong one gives the true class zero probability, which self-training often confirms. We argue that each image should carry its label posterior, as an analytic classifier trained on posteriors equals the true-label one in expectation. The zero-shot prediction is not this posterior, as its class proportions confound name bias with true imbalance and it ignores other images. We propose Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (PACIL), which corrects the class prior with a prior selection rule and refines each distribution by a fixed-prior von Mises-Fisher mixture on whitened features. These soft labels train the classifier and replace labels to select its fusion weight with zero-shot CLIP by closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation. We prove that posterior targets minimize the mean-square gap to the true-label prediction and that their argmax widens this gap only through ambiguous images. The fusion weight selected with soft labels loses at most their distance to the posteriors in expected correct decisions. PACIL has the best average incremental accuracy among methods trained without labels on all 18 settings.
authors: Wei Tang, Tong Wei, Jiahao Zhang, Min-Ling Zhang, Lijie Hu, Fakhri Karray
bullets: Unlabeled tasks provide only class names and images, making incorrect hard pseudo-labels prone to self-reinforcement.
The method corrects CLIP’s class-prior bias and refines predictions with a fixed-prior von Mises–Fisher mixture over whitened features.
Soft posterior targets train the classifier and select its fusion weight with CLIP via closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation.
Theoretical results show posterior targets best approximate true-label predictions in mean-square error; argmax mainly loses information on ambiguous images.
PACIL achieves the best average incremental accuracy across all 18 evaluated settings without labeled training data.

(3) Soft-label analytic learning and fusion: the analytic classifier Wt is fitted to qi, and closed-form LOO selects the weight ωt that fuses it with zero-shot CLIP.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (PACIL) using posterior distributions to handle unlabeled data in class-incremental learning, improving upon standard pseudo-labeling.
papers.title: Learning What the True Labels Would Teach: Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning with Unlabeled Data
papers.tldr: PACIL improves unlabeled class-incremental learning by replacing brittle hard pseudo-labels with analytically refined soft label posteriors and using them to calibrate CLIP fusion.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching point-cloud upsamplers refine sparse inputs into dense point clouds by integrating a learned velocity field with a fixed temporal discretization. However, local reconstruction requirements vary substantially across a shape, while a shared solver budget applies the same temporal resolution everywhere. We propose Multi-Rate Flow Matching (MRFM), a patch-adaptive framework that selects an integration budget for each local patch at inference time while keeping the learned velocity field frozen. MRFM relaxes the discrete budget into a continuous variable, optimizes it online through differentiable soft rollouts using an input-derived geometric fidelity objective, and projects the result back to a discrete budget for the final solver rollout. Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN show strong reconstruction quality, while matched-budget permutation and multi-factor analyses demonstrate that the benefit depends on patch-specific allocation rather than on the step distribution alone. MRFM is accuracy-oriented and intentionally uses additional test-time optimization to obtain more suitable local temporal resolutions.
authors: Jingkai Shang, Edgar Torres, Duy Nguyen
bullets: Addresses varying local reconstruction difficulty under a shared solver budget.
Optimizes a continuous per-patch step budget using differentiable soft rollouts and geometric fidelity.
Projects optimized budgets to discrete values for the final flow-matching rollout.
Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN report strong reconstruction quality and support patch-specific allocation as the source of benefit.
The method is accuracy-oriented and incurs additional test-time optimization.

papers.abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning seeks to minimize joint risk over all seen tasks, yet historical data are unavailable for direct optimization. We observe that, for classification, preserving the model's decisions on previously learned classes helps retain old knowledge. This motivates Decision-Preserving Regularization (DPR). Penalizing changes in all pairwise old-class logit margins reduces algebraically to a centered relative-logit penalty. We further apply spectral whitening to remove the classifier's spectral scale bias. Because the global classifier supplies the decision constraints for the next stage, it must remain calibrated across all seen classes despite the drift of stored old-class statistics during representation updates. We therefore fit a closed-form affine map from paired current-task features to transport old-class Gaussian means and covariances into the updated feature space, then calibrate the global classifier using these distributions and current-task features. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1K under cold-start protocols, comparisons with state-of-the-art methods show that DPR achieves higher accuracy in most settings while remaining highly efficient. Code is available at https://github.com/bnufw/dpr.
authors: Qi Zhu, Ziang Gan, Wanting Zhang, Libao Zhang
bullets: Targets the loss of old-class knowledge when historical exemplars are unavailable.
Regularizes pairwise old-class logit margins, yielding a centered relative-logit penalty, and applies spectral whitening to reduce scale bias.
Uses a closed-form affine transport to update stored old-class Gaussian statistics after feature drift.
Calibrates the global classifier with transported old-class distributions and current-task features.
Across four benchmarks and cold-start protocols, DPR reports higher accuracy in most settings with low computational cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DPR. (a) Decision-preserving regularization preserves pairwise old-class margins while allowing a shared logit shift. Spectral whitening of the centered old classifier yields a basis V for uniformly penalizing feature drift along old-class discriminative directions during new-class learning. (b) A closed-form affine map fitted to paired current-task features compensates stored old-class means and covariances for representation drift. Gaussian old-class features sampled from the compensated statistics are combined with real current-task features to calibrate the global head WT for unified inference and next-stage decision regularization.

papers.title: From Joint Risk to Decision Invariance: Decision-Preserving Regularization for Exemplar-Free Class-Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: DPR preserves old-class decisions and recalibrates the classifier to improve exemplar-free class-incremental learning under representation drift.

papers.abstract: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Meanwhile, explainable reinforcement learning aims to learn meaningful behavioral representations through policy interaction. However, these objectives are inherently conflicting, as continual learning emphasizes policy stability whereas explainable behavior learning requires adaptive exploration. Existing methods rarely address both simultaneously. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes a Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FECHRL) method. A two-stage behavior cloning strategy is introduced to balance rapid policy adaptation and explainable behavior evolution by progressively transitioning from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a fuzzy critic based on a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy inference system is proposed to alleviate value extrapolation errors during the transition between imitation-guided learning and autonomous exploration, thereby improving continual training stability. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.
bullets: Addresses the conflict between stable knowledge retention and adaptive, explainable exploration in continual robot navigation.
Uses two-stage behavior cloning to transition from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning.
Introduces a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy critic to reduce value extrapolation errors during this transition.
Experiments on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks show stable retention and meaningful behavioral explanations.
The abstract reports effectiveness in the tested sequential navigation setting, without specifying broader generalization limits.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.
authors: Olatunji Oni, Sanhita Sengupta, Marc De Benedetti, Nathanial Eddy
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of manually inferring study-specific line boundaries from complex longitudinal oncology treatment histories.
Uses clinician adjudications to calibrate confidence, identify cases needing review, and continuously estimate residual error.
Feeds completed clinician reviews back to the model as evidence for subsequent assignments.
In simulations of 136 clinician-adjudicated multiple myeloma patients, 44.6% review yielded 5% residual error, versus 62.2% with LLM self-confidence and 81.9% with random review.
Scope: performance was evaluated in simulations for multiple myeloma and may depend on the study-specific adjudication rules and available clinician evidence.

ECS estimates confidence of each assignment based on adjudications already collected by clinicians on similar decisions and prioritizes the patients with the least supported assignments for manual adjudication. Each completed review is added to the evidence base used to score the next assignments, and is fed back to the model as a precedent. The right schematic shows the resulting reduction in residual error relative to random review.

Figure 3. ECS requires fewer review rounds. (A) Accuracy among unreviewed patients and (B) residual error by review round, with five patients reviewed per round. Lines indicate the mean, and shaded bands indicate the interquartile range across 100 sub-cohorts. (C) Mean number of rounds required to reach 5% residual error for batch sizes of 2 to 20 patients per round. Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. (D) Relative reduction in review rounds achieved by ECS against LLM confidence and random review.

Random (gray) selects patients in random order. LLM confidence (blue) selects patients with the lowest LLM self-reported confidence first. ECS (green) selects patients with the lowest evidence-calibrated confidence first. Results are shown for 100 sub-cohorts of 100 patients with seven patients reviewed per round. Lines indicate the mean, and shaded bands indicate the interquartile range. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a human-in-the-loop framework (ECS) for calibrating LLM confidence using clinician adjudications, which falls under test-time learning and adaptation.
papers.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
papers.tldr: Evidence-calibrated selection enables LLM-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication by directing clinicians to the least-supported cases and using reviewed cases as precedents.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is a promising approach to specialize language models to an organization's private data. However, current methods exhibit a number of drawbacks including catastrophic forgetting, where new training updates overwrite prior knowledge. We present microfitting, which trains and caches a small adapter for each document. Each adapter is trained once, offline, on synthetic questions targeted at demonstrated base-model shortcomings and reused whenever that document is queried. This method borrows from test-time learning literature and sidesteps the problem of continual learning through parameter isolation, allowing the system to specialize on new data without overwriting prior knowledge. The process that generates adapter training data also improves over time, revising its recipe from previous outcomes and fresh examples of the target workload. On DeepSeek V4 Flash, microfitting substantially improves accuracy over the base model. In Enterprise Document Operations (EDO), an open-book Q&A environment over real-world enterprise documents, our method achieves a 38.2% relative improvement over base-model performance. Microfitting makes continual specialization practical and cost-efficient: a frozen model can adapt to an evolving private corpus overnight on local hardware, without modifying the base model or previously cached adapters.
authors: Nick Ryan, Peter A. Devine, Ben Sirb, Hannah Sansford, Alex Chiocchi
bullets: Addresses continual-learning degradation, especially catastrophic forgetting when new updates overwrite prior knowledge.
Trains each document-specific adapter once offline using synthetic questions targeting base-model weaknesses, then reuses it at query time.
Uses parameter isolation: the base model and previously cached adapters remain unchanged as the private corpus evolves.
The adapter-data generation process improves from prior outcomes and new workload examples.
Reports a 38.2% relative accuracy improvement over the base model on the EDO enterprise document Q&A benchmark; designed for overnight adaptation on local hardware.

papers.selection_reason: Cached per-document adapters trained at test time for continual specialization; directly matches test-time learning and continual learning.
papers.title: Microfitting: Continual Learning via Cached Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Microfitting enables continual specialization by caching a separately trained adapter for each document, avoiding catastrophic forgetting while improving enterprise document Q&A accuracy.

papers.abstract: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.
authors: Moshe Kimhi, Idan Kligvasser, Yotam Intrator, Regev Cohen, Ehud Rivlin
bullets: Caches a full-depth appearance representation as a read-only temporal anchor and combines it with selected partial features from the current frame.
A lightweight controller selects encoder exits before processing, using shallow computation for stable scenes and deeper computation when visual conditions change.
Separates temporal appearance reuse from geometric alignment: current calibration defines geometry, while a motion-conditioned adapter handles ego motion.
On nuScenes, achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP with 2.16× lower latency than dense DETR3D; StreamPETR sees a 1.92× speedup with similar accuracy.
Scope: the method targets temporally redundant driving sequences and relies on policy-based recognition of semantic driving regimes.

papers.abstract: A robot may know how to move an object yet still need to learn where it belongs. When a person rejects a placement, the robot must decide whether the correction applies only to that situation or expresses a broader rule. We study this problem in CRAFT (Contextual Requirement Adaptation with Frozen Tools), a framework for learning local requirements without retraining robot skills. It records physical success separately from whether an action meets the requirement. Our scope ladder uses memory when an action has already been judged in a nearly identical situation. Elsewhere, it combines memory, explicit rules and a learner for requirements beyond those rules, weighting their predictions by how well they predicted earlier feedback. Controlled studies show gains over correction memory alone in utility, which rewards acceptable actions and charges for mistakes and questions. In camera-grounded robot simulations, the ladder asks fewer questions than language-model agents with persistent memory, but some of those agents take fewer wrong actions and succeed more often after requirements change. All execution failures and timeouts remain in the evaluation. These results support combining specific memories with broader rules, while leaving reliable adaptation to changing requirements unresolved. All evidence comes from simulation with generated requirements and simulated feedback.
authors: Peng Zhang, Jiawen Wang, Cheng Xue, Jochen Renz
bullets: Separates physical execution success from whether an action satisfies the requirement.
Uses a scope ladder: reuses feedback for near-identical situations, otherwise combines memories, explicit rules, and a learner.
Controlled studies find higher utility than correction-memory-only approaches.
In simulated camera-grounded tasks, it asks fewer questions than language-model agents with persistent memory, though some alternatives make fewer mistakes and succeed more after requirement changes.
Results are limited to simulations with generated requirements and simulated feedback; reliable adaptation to changing requirements remains unresolved.
