papers.abstract: Agentic navigation must maintain goals and adapt actions from incomplete evidence despite execution failures and delayed inference. We present AgenticJevNav, which links goal-directed planning, evidence memory, event-triggered verification, and bounded execution. The Agent plans from RGB, odometry, memory, and feedback, retaining goal ownership while authorizing a bounded action set. Jev reviews structured evidence after blocked/failed execution or two consecutive low-progress segments. Version, freshness, and once-only checks govern decision application. A single executor and independent RGB reflex constrain motion. Goal revisions revoke obsolete requests and actions before replanning. Across six simulated task families, AgenticJevNav achieves 73.33% SR over 60 trials, 21.67 percentage points above the next-best Agent-only aggregate control under differing historical protocols. A real-world GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment achieves 70.0% success over 30 trials, including bounded search reporting. Together, the simulation and physical-robot results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture, while remaining failures highlight opportunities to improve grounding, approach planning, and runtime.
authors: Shuning Zhang, Shuli Zhang, Yunheng Wang, Wei Lu, Jiaxi Zhang, Yihang Kang, Tao Wang, Xiangyu Chen, Yixiao Feng, Kai Sheng, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses navigation under incomplete evidence, execution failures, and delayed inference.
Integrates evidence memory, event-triggered Jev reviews, version/freshness checks, and bounded action authorization.
Uses a single executor, an independent RGB reflex, and goal-revision mechanisms to prevent obsolete actions.
Achieves 73.33% success across six simulated task families and 70.0% success on a real GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment.
Remaining failures point to grounding, approach planning, and runtime limitations.

papers.abstract: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
authors: Chenhao Ding, Jizhou Han, Lixin Xiu, Muyao Wang, Songlin Dong, Hideki Nakayama
bullets: Addresses the underuse of feedback from previous navigation episodes in online VLN.
Success-Failure Memory retrieves task-relevant successful and failed experiences using incoming instructions.
Prior-Anchored Adaptation reinforces successful trajectories, suppresses failed ones, and limits drift from a frozen pretrained policy.
Evaluated on REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE with five navigation backbones, showing consistent gains.
On REVERIE unseen validation, DUET’s SR rises from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of R2A. (a) The agent navigates using the adapted policy and obtains queried feedback or a self-predicted outcome. (b) Success–Failure Memory: Before navigation, the incoming instruction triggers the retrieval of the most similar experience from the entire memory based on instruction similarity, together with a randomly sampled experience. (c) Prior-Anchored Adaptation: The preceding episode and recalled experiences jointly update the policy through reference-relative outcome learning and pretrained-policy regularization.

Figure 5. Qualitative examples of task-cued recall on REVERIE val-unseen. (a) Failure memory: recalling a previously failed navigation experience helps the agent avoid stopping at an incorrect sink. (b) Success memory: recalling a successful experience guides the agent toward the target phone. In both cases, Task-Cued Recall reaches the intended destination, while uniform replay fails.

Figure 1. Learning from past successes and failures for navigation. (a) People recall successful experiences and mistakes to guide navigation. (b) Similar visual cues may cause an agent to confuse a kitchen with a laundry room; replaying a past failure helps correct this mistake. Inspired by episodic memory, R2A reuses successful and failed experiences with outcome feedback for adaptation.

papers.abstract: Whether a sidewalk is passable depends on who is trying to pass: people who use the same mobility aid disagree about the same image, so one label per scene, or per aid, is wrong for many of them. We introduce few-shot personal accessibility perception: from K answers of a person never seen before, predict their judgment of sidewalk scenes never seen before. PassCal separates a shared description of the scene from the person's interpretation of it. The description comes from the internal state of a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and from barrier type, severity and context properties predicted by a detector trained on 14.9k public audits; the interpretation, a calibration of the person's response style and a weighting of the properties, is fit from their answers. On 8,883 judgments in which each of 135 verified mobility-aid users rated the same 50 sidewalk scenes, with people and scenes both held out, eight answers lower the Brier score from 0.550 to 0.479. The same VLM prompted with those answers reaches 0.562, and the same calibration without the scene 0.521. Conformal risk control turns predictions into passable, blocked or "depends on you" statements with a bounded expected rate of wrong statements over people; at 5%, eight answers raise the share of decisive scenes from 27% to 42%. Audit-supervised properties improve all sixteen vision and VLM encoders we test and outperform attributes from a sidewalk navigation VLM.
authors: Wesley Maia, Angel Martinez-Sanchez, Maitrayee Keskar, Ross Greer
bullets: Sidewalk accessibility is person-dependent, so one label per scene or mobility aid can misrepresent individual users.
PassCal separates shared scene description from personal interpretation using frozen VLM features, detected barrier properties, and user-specific calibration.
With eight answers, Brier score improves from 0.550 to 0.479 on held-out users and scenes; direct VLM prompting reaches 0.562.
Conformal risk control produces passable, blocked, or “depends on you” statements with bounded expected error; decisive-scene coverage rises from 27% to 42% at 5% risk.
Audit-supervised barrier properties improve all tested vision and VLM encoders and outperform attributes from a sidewalk-navigation VLM.

papers.abstract: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) recognizes unseen attribute--object pairs by recombining primitives from seen compositions. Existing methods stop sharing evidence at deployment: fixed prototypes cannot exploit unlabeled test streams, while composition-wise refinement cannot propagate corrections across pairs sharing a primitive. We introduce PRISM, an online CZSL framework that extends primitive sharing to test-time adaptation. Its Hierarchical Knowledge Accumulation Module (HiKAM) factorizes prototype migration into composition-, attribute-, and object-level residual banks. A Priority Visual Memory Queue (PVMQ), initialized by Prototype Queue Initialization (PQI), grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence. The same adaptive core supports exhaustive Full PRISM and recall-calibrated Adaptive PRISM-Lite, which selects candidate budgets from held-out ranks. Comprehensive closed- and open-world experiments on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA demonstrate the state of the art, with Full PRISM achieving the best open-world AUC and harmonic mean on all three benchmarks and the best closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA. Fine-grained long-tail and non-stationary primitive-block evaluations reveal gains on under-supported concepts and stable adaptation under prolonged skew. Adaptive PRISM-Lite further delivers substantial efficiency gains in the full open-world space with only a small accuracy cost. PRISM thus combines primitive-shared online adaptation, multimodal grounding, and candidate-aware inference.
authors: Jianhua Wang, Zhihang Zheng, Yang Liu, Jiale Du
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed prototypes and pair-specific updates that cannot use unlabeled test streams or share corrections across related attributes and objects.
Uses HiKAM to update composition-, attribute-, and object-level prototype residuals, extending primitive sharing to test-time adaptation.
Grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence through a Priority Visual Memory Queue initialized by PQI.
Full PRISM achieves the best reported open-world AUC and harmonic mean on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA, with strongest closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA.
PRISM-Lite reduces open-world inference cost with only a small accuracy decrease; evaluations also show gains for long-tail concepts and stability under prolonged distribution skew.

papers.abstract: Conventional experience replay typically applies fixed preservation constraints to historical exemplars, overlooking variations in how learned representations, predictions, and anatomical structures change during sequential training. To address this limitation, we propose Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay Loss (DCSRL), an exemplar-adaptive supervision mechanism that regulates anatomical preservation according to source-referenced knowledge drift. DCSRL operates within a reliability-guided replay framework that selects informative historical exemplars using anatomical content and boundary characteristics while adaptively regulating replay during training. For each retained exemplar, DCSRL constructs a frozen source-task reference signature and subsequently measures changes in feature representations, class probabilities, boundary responses, and predicted anatomical structures. These complementary drift measurements are aggregated and normalized to generate bounded, exemplar-specific coefficients that dynamically adjust boundary and structural replay losses without modifying the underlying memory-selection policy. We evaluate DCSRL under sequential learning across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic, comparing its performance with regularization-, distillation-, and replay-based continual-learning approaches. Experimental findings indicate that DCSRL improves overall final segmentation performance and anatomical boundary preservation, particularly under heterogeneous imaging conditions, although trade-offs remain in knowledge transfer across tasks. These findings suggest that source-referenced multidimensional drift conditioning offers a promising direction for adaptive anatomical knowledge preservation in continual cardiac ultrasound segmentation.
authors: Zahid Ullah, Jaeyoon Seo, Jihie Kim
bullets: Fixed replay constraints may fail to reflect changes in representations, predictions, boundaries, and anatomical structures during sequential learning.
DCSRL builds frozen source-task reference signatures and combines multidimensional drift measurements into bounded, exemplar-specific replay coefficients.
A reliability-guided replay framework selects historical exemplars using anatomical content and boundary characteristics.
The method improves final segmentation and anatomical boundary preservation across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic, especially under heterogeneous imaging conditions.
Knowledge-transfer trade-offs remain across tasks.

(B) For each retained exemplar, a source-task reference signature is constructed from its normalized bottleneck representation, spatially averaged class probabilities, boundary-response statistics, and predicted segmentation mask. The stored reference remains frozen during subsequent continual-learning tasks.

papers.abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.
authors: Braghadeesh Lakshminarayanan, Ojas Phadake, Qi Chen, Dominik Baumann
bullets: Pretrained diffusion controllers may generate unsafe trajectories when deployment constraints change, such as added or repositioned obstacles.
The method treats the pretrained diffusion model as a prior over finite-horizon state-input sequences.
It uses exponential tilting with a constraint-violation penalty to adapt the sampling distribution.
Online tilt adjustment depends on the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification.
Metropolis-adjusted Langevin sampling in the model’s Gaussian noise space approximates the adapted distribution.

papers.abstract: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.
authors: Kejia Fan, Yajiang Huang, Jianheng Tang, Jinfeng Xu, Huiping Zhuang, Anfeng Liu, Houbing Herbert Song, Yunhuai Liu
bullets: Addresses continual service construction where evolving, heterogeneous data can cause catastrophic forgetting.
Uses gradient-free residual blocks with closed-form solutions to overcome the underfitting of single-layer analytic methods.
Employs a cross-recursive least-squares strategy for distributed continual training.
Theoretical and experimental analyses support improved heterogeneity invariance and deep representation.
With 20 residual layers, accuracy improves by 8.85%–9.83% over a single-layer analytic baseline, while computational costs fall by over 94% versus gradient-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Task configurations in factories, warehouses, and everyday physical environments change over time. Physical AI systems therefore need to incorporate new facts into scene memory while preserving valid information about equipment, objects, and operating constraints. We study updates to this parametric semantic-memory layer and present a joint evaluation of correction and preservation under finite update budgets. At fixed current fact count and memory parameter count, the protocol combines independent single-fact updates, budget trajectories, old-to-new answer diagnostics, and first stable success. Using a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA, we evaluate seven preparation conditions and six update budgets on four-field synthetic semantic configurations. In two exposure-matched history conditions, increasing the budget from eight to 32 updates raises joint success from 6.25% to 94.79% and 91.15%, respectively, while exact obsolete-value outputs fall from 174/192 and 166/192 to zero. Constant32, which matches preparation steps but repeatedly trains on unchanged content during the first 32 events, achieves higher early joint success at eight steps (53.65%); at 32 steps, it reaches 85.42%, below both changing-history conditions. These results distinguish rapid correction under a small budget from simultaneous correctness of the new fact and the other three facts after further training. For both changing histories, most cases remain jointly correct at all subsequent measured points from step 16 onward. Output analysis shows that short-budget failures primarily retain the old value; repeated training on the new fact together with the other current facts progressively replaces these obsolete answers.
bullets: Studies correction and preservation of semantic scene memory under finite update budgets.
Uses a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA across seven preparation conditions, six budgets, and synthetic four-field configurations.

Repeated training on unchanged content improves early correction but underperforms changing-history training at 32 updates.
Short-budget errors mainly retain obsolete values; longer updates progressively replace them, with most cases remaining jointly correct after step 16.

papers.abstract: Recent pre-trained vision-language models often encounter a Multi-Domain Task-Incremental Learning (MTIL) scenario in practice, where a set of classes of multi-modal tasks arrive incrementally. Due to privacy concerns and memory constraints, MTIL with pre-trained models encounters forgetting of knowledge from old tasks, degradation of zero-shot transfer capability, and underfitting of new-task knowledge. To overcome these challenges, previous MTIL methods attempt to learn a discriminative cross-task identification (CTI) module and an effective new-task adaptation (NTA) module. However, current CTI modules suffer from severe task confusion between seen and unseen tasks, and NTA modules cannot adaptively balance the performance and parameter cost while incorporating task-specific knowledge. To alleviate the above dilemmas, we propose an effective and efficient TSP-DLoRA method for MTIL, which consists of Task Subspace Projection (TSP) and Dynamic Low Rank Adapter (DLoRA) modules. Specifically, our TSP module includes a task identifier classifier based on task-specific subspaces and a feature projection strategy that can determine the identifier associated with samples from both seen and unseen tasks. Our DLoRA improves the knowledge adaptation from new tasks by dynamically assigning Low Rank Adapter (LoRA) across transformer layers based on the task distributions. Experimental evaluations across 11 datasets, using three performance metrics, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/FerdinandZJU/TSP-DLoRA.
authors: Hao Fu, Qian Feng, Hanbin Zhao, Jiahua Dong, Xu Tan, Lina Wei, Chao Zhang, Hui Qian
bullets: Addresses forgetting of old-task knowledge, reduced zero-shot transfer, and underfitting of new tasks under privacy and memory constraints.
Uses Task Subspace Projection to identify seen and unseen tasks through task-specific subspaces and feature projection.
Uses Dynamic LoRA to allocate low-rank adapters across transformer layers according to task distributions.
Evaluated on 11 datasets with three metrics, showing the method’s effectiveness.
The abstract does not report specific numerical results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The training process of the DLoRA module in our method. The DLoRA module integrates LoRA into the first Lt transformer layers of both the image and text encoders. The gating mechanism before the LoRA modules in the image encoder determines whether to activate the LoRA based on the feature F ′ v(x) derived from the original CLIP. Only the LoRA and the gating mechanisms are trained, while the remaining parts are kept frozen.

Figure 1: (a) Comparison with existing methods. Unlike ZSCL, our method eliminates the need for additional storage and improves parameter efficiency. Compared to MoE-Adapter, our approach incurs significantly lower computational overhead with fewer trainable parameters. In contrast to DIKI, ours not only achieves higher accuracy but also precisely distinguishes whether samples belong to previously seen tasks (Precise Task ID). (b) Mechanism comparison. Existing training-free CTI applies the same NTA operation to both seen and unseen tasks, restricted by a weight “W ”. Conversely, our TSP module explicitly identifies the boundary between tasks, directing unseen samples to the original CLIP while processing seen samples with DLoRA. (c) Performance trade-off. Our method achieves a superior trade-off between average accuracy (both seen and unseen tasks) and parameter efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 3: The workflow of the TSP module of our method in training and inference processes. During training phase, for image dataset of every task, the TSP module decomposes the image features via SVD and selects top r singular vectors from the right singular vector matrix to be the corresponding task subspace. During inference phase, for every test sample, the TSP module computes the cosine similarity between the raw feature extracted from original CLIP and the subspaces associated with each seen task. The result is compared against a threshold, denoted as “thres.”. The sample is classified using the corresponding DLoRA module if the cosine similarity exceeds the “thres.”. Otherwise, the original CLIP model is utilized to classify the sample.

Figure 6: Visualization of six task-specific distributions generated by the TSP module. We randomly selected 1,000 samples from each dataset. The majority of samples are correctly classified, as shown by their corresponding colors. A small number of samples are misclassified as unseen tasks, while an even smaller number are incorrectly assigned to other seen tasks. Overall, the TSP module achieves an accuracy exceeding 90% for each task.

Figure 4: The distribution of similarity scores for the TSP module across different tasks. The red line denotes a threshold set at 0.96. papers.abstract: We study relationship-specific continual reply prediction for one-to-many private communication: a system predicts an author's reply to a recurring contact and updates its personalization state when the actual reply becomes available. We propose TRACE (Temporal Relationship-Aware Communication Evolution), which uses author-level lexical habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen language model, with a feedback-driven policy controlling revision. On 216 test emails from eight Enron users, all four main TRACE configurations achieve higher mean BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore and lower mean Reply Style MSE than Base LLM and Base RAG. Component ablations show mixed effects and do not establish statistically reliable improvements in Reply Style MSE after multiple-comparison correction. More accurate state forecasts and larger revision budgets do not consistently improve reply-level metrics. These exploratory findings expose the challenge of turning evolving relationship-specific expression estimates into useful generation guidance.
bullets: Targets one-to-many private communication where reply style varies by relationship and evolves over time.
Uses author-level language habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen language model.
A feedback-driven policy revises personalization state when the true reply becomes available.
Across 216 test emails from eight Enron users, four TRACE configurations improved average BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore while lowering Reply Style MSE versus Base LLM and Base RAG.
Ablations found mixed effects; corrected analyses did not establish reliable Reply Style MSE improvements, and better state forecasts or larger revision budgets were inconsistent.

papers.abstract: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.
authors: Yiting Chen, Kelin Yu, Sarthak Kaingade, Bryan Trinh, Kaiyu Hang, Roberto Martin-martin, Nima Fazeli, X. Alice Wu
bullets: Addresses forceful multi-finger manipulation under uncertain contact and interaction dynamics, beyond geometry-based interaction.
Uses tactile-observable interaction representations with cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contacts.
Adapts motor behavior from tactile history while coordinating an upper-body manipulation policy with a pretrained locomotion controller.
Trained entirely in simulation and transferred zero-shot to a Unitree G1 with multi-fingered hands.

Both modules are then frozen, and the adaptation encoder is trained through latent regression to estimate the interaction latent from a 2s history of deployable observations. (d) During real-world deployment, the adaptation encoder updates the interaction latent online from tactile interaction history and conditions the frozen tactile-centric policy to generate manipulation motor commands.

papers.abstract: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).

In coding continuations, SIM improved final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation across ten source runs.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.
authors: Lei Zhou, Youwen zhu, Rongke Liu
bullets: Output-level verifiers may infer unlearning from provider-controlled predictions without confirming removal of training-data influence.

Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV) compares intermediate representations between original and unlearned models.
RUV analyzes activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support, using retained controls and joint permutation calibration.
Across tested settings, ODR deception was highly effective, while RUV achieved high verification accuracy and rejected most deceptive submissions.

papers.abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.
bullets: Studies knowledge transfer in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules.
Compares one agent retaining eight lives of history with eight one-life agents linked by 300-character notes.

Writing each note from the full prior record recovers 70–82% of the loss, while evidence prompts, note revision, and structured ledgers do not help.

papers.abstract: In continual learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to acquire new capabilities through lightweight adapters such as LoRA, yet the reuse of pretrained adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone. This limits the transfer of learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models. We propose GRAFT (Generalist Reuse of Adapters via Feature-space Transfer), a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse. GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces. We evaluate GRAFT on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks, transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL, and five multimodal tasks, where Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs are directly reused. Compared with randomly initialized LoRA adapters, GRAFT improves performance on most evaluated tasks. These results show that GRAFT provides a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across language and multimodal models in continual learning.

papers.abstract: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.

papers.abstract: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing often faces a domain-incremental learning problem: as new product configurations enter production, prediction models must learn from newly available data while preserving performance on earlier configurations that remain in operation. In this paper, we empirically study the operational value of continual machine learning methods for addressing this challenge in predictive maintenance, using real-world maintenance data from Bosch. The setting at Bosch covers 25 product configurations over five years, which creates a practical challenge for predictive maintenance models, as such models must be updated with data from newly introduced configurations without reducing performance on configurations learned earlier, a phenomenon known as "forgetting". At the same time, retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining models is often infeasible in high-volume manufacturing since industrial machines generate too large data volumes. To address this challenge, we combine continual machine learning with robust optimization to support predictive maintenance. We then compare continual machine learning with a broad set of baselines, including fine-tuning, domain-adaptation methods, online learning methods, and configuration-specific models. Across experiments, continual machine learning methods achieve stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than the baselines, with a reduction of cost-related indicators of more than 40 % relative to the baselines. Our results demonstrate the operational value of continual machine learning for decision support in maintenance when product portfolios grow over time and historical manufacturing data cannot be fully retained.

papers.tldr: Continual machine learning combined with robust optimization helps predictive-maintenance models adapt to new product configurations while reducing forgetting, improving predictive performance, and lowering maintenance costs.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can improve long- horizon interactive decision-making through test-time evolu- tion, yet existing methods face three information bottlenecks: memory retrieval overemphasizes textual similarity, candi- date harnesses are often behaviorally redundant, and whole- harness rewriting may overwrite useful evidence or introduce cross-component inconsistency. We introduce Trident, which improves experience utilization, behavioral exploration, and harness evolution through boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion- based updating, respectively. We evaluate Trident on five benchmarks spanning text games, web interaction, and cod- ing tasks. Across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt- oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and consistently outperforms non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and automated prompt optimization base- lines. Compared with the strongest baseline, APEX, Trident yields relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3% on the three backbones, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity stud- ies further show that the three designs provide complementary gains and remain robust to parameter variations.
authors: Kaijie Chen, Liang Yan, Yilan Wei, Jiachen Luo, Zhihao Dou, Jiashu Qu, Haoran Liu, Junli Wang
bullets: Addresses three bottlenecks: similarity-biased memory retrieval, redundant candidate harnesses, and risky whole-harness rewriting.
Uses boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion-based updates.
Evaluated across five text-game, web-interaction, and coding benchmarks with three LLM backbones.
Achieves the best average performance and outperforms several non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and prompt-optimization baselines.
Ablations show the components provide complementary gains and are robust to parameter variations.

papers.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio-visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention-based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task-stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature- and logit-level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio-visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM-CIL.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored challenge of audio-visual class-incremental learning, where models learn new classes without forgetting old ones.
Uses dense audio and visual representations from frozen multimodal foundational models.
Introduces attention-based contextual guidance, with audio representations guiding visual class recognition across incremental tasks.
Applies feature- and logit-level distillation to improve stability and mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
Reports consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods across multiple audio-visual CIL benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Audio-visual class-incremental learning with frozen multimodal foundation models directly fits continual learning and multimodal foundation model topics.
papers.title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: A framework adapts frozen multimodal foundational models for audio-visual class-incremental learning by using audio as stable contextual guidance for visual representations and distillation to reduce forgetting.

papers.abstract: Class-incremental learning must recognize all classes seen so far without task labels. Logit replay methods such as DER and DER++ mitigate forgetting by matching the model's past predictions on stored examples. Deleting this matching reveals its benefit, but the resulting accuracy cost cannot show whether the stored scores themselves are needed, or whether the cost survives correction of the classifier's bias toward recent classes. We propose a diagnostic framework that treats a cached prediction as temporally heterogeneous supervision: it separates classes known when an example was stored from classes learned afterward, edits each group, and evaluates every model before and after a task-level offset that leaves within-task predictions unchanged. On CIFAR-100 with DER++, suitable fixed constants replace the unrefreshed stored scores of later-learned classes within an equivalence margin of 1 percentage point, and the offset reduces the cost of deleting their matching from 14.9 to 1.8 points. Reassigning the non-gold scores of classes known at storage, which preserves their values and each task's target probability, costs 4.3 points before and 4.0 after the offset, and a parallel cost persists in image distillation. In the tested fixed-head setting, the large cost of deleting later-class matching is thus mostly correctable by this offset, whereas the smaller cost of disrupting class correspondence persists. Code and data are available at anonymous.4open.science/r/replay-preserve-E22B.
bullets: Logit replay stores past predictions, but its accuracy benefit may reflect either useful supervision or correction of bias toward recent classes.
The proposed diagnostic separates scores for classes known at storage from those learned later, then applies a task-level offset that preserves within-task predictions.
On CIFAR-100 with DER++, replacing unrefreshed later-class scores causes only a 1-point-equivalent change, and offset correction reduces the deletion cost from 14.9 to 1.8 points.
Disrupting non-gold scores for classes known at storage retains a 4.3-point cost before correction and 4.0-point cost after it; a similar effect appears in image distillation.
In the tested fixed-head setting, later-class matching is largely correctable, whereas class correspondence is not.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies what replay must preserve in class-incremental learning, a core continual/online learning problem.
papers.title: What Must Replay Preserve? Separating Correctable Bias from Class Correspondence
papers.tldr: In class-incremental replay, much of the benefit of matching past predictions compensates for recent-class bias, while preserving class correspondence remains genuinely important.

papers.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
authors: Sandip Nandi, Aishwarya Bose, Apurba Bose, Soovadeep Bakshi
bullets: Evaluates detection, prevention, and execution costs in a replayable limit-order-book simulator across 1,680 LLM-agent sessions.
All observed conduct alerts involved self-matches; gates prevented these alerts but aggregate gating reduced Sonnet’s two-sided fills by about 15%.
A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet’s alerts but harmed Haiku’s fills without a detectable alert benefit.
Search-based probes found split-order schedules that evaded the implemented rules; a learned baseline caught all 2,400 searched episodes but falsely flagged 15% of a large maker’s sessions.
Results varied with market assumptions, and the study does not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'TradeGauntlet', a simulator for evaluating compliance controls in autonomous trading agents, relevant to testing LLM agents in complex environments.
papers.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
papers.tldr: TradeGauntlet provides reproducible simulations for testing whether autonomous trading controls prevent misconduct without excessively impairing legitimate trading, revealing that zero alerts can hide important weaknesses.

papers.abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.
authors: Disha Sheshanarayana, Sai Linisha Reddy Goli
bullets: Introduces Verification Transport, which measures judgment stability across native, abstracted, and restored views of identical executions.
Evaluates four benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four protocols, and three abstraction boundaries while holding task, trajectory, outcome, ground truth, criterion, and verifier fixed.
Finds transport failures of about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation.
Direct verification more often gives incorrect verdicts, while evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols more often abstain when observability is limited.
Restoring execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, but recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Verification Transport' to measure the reliability of LLM verifiers when execution evidence is abstracted or compressed, relevant to agent evaluation at inference time.
papers.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
papers.tldr: LLM verifier judgments can change substantially when the same agent execution is viewed through abstraction boundaries, so native-view accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating reliability.

papers.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
authors: Wang Ma, Debarun Bhattacharjya, Junkyu Lee, Nhan H Pham, Harsha Kokel, Qiang Ji
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing black-box uncertainty methods to distinguish aleatoric uncertainty (prompt ambiguity) from epistemic uncertainty (knowledge gaps).
Uses stochastic decoding as an inner ensemble and meaning-preserving prompt perturbations as an outer ensemble, measuring variability in embedding space.
Applies the law of total covariance to decompose uncertainty, with a bias-corrected epistemic estimator for finite nested samples.
Provides theoretical guarantees covering estimator bias, links to Bayesian uncertainty targets, and failure modes missed by consistency-only methods.

Across five QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs, matches leading black-box error ranking at matched generation budgets while also decomposing uncertainty; a pilot extends the approach to claim-level factuality without retraining.

papers.abstract: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.
authors: Tao Hu, Ling-Xiang Zhang, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting and linear parameter growth in task-specific MoE expansion.
Consolidates functionally overlapping experts into a fixed-capacity generic pool.
Factorizes remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact private cores.
Uses frozen historical retrieval keys and orthogonally regularized new keys to stabilize routing.
Dynamically routes inputs across shared and private pools without requiring task labels at inference; experiments report superior performance with substantially lower parameter overhead.

papers.abstract: Handwritten text recognition (HTR), particularly when applied to historical documents, remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated data and the substantial domain shifts caused by variations in handwriting styles, document degradation, acquisition conditions, and linguistic characteristics. While large amounts of unlabeled target-domain data are often available, effectively exploiting them requires adaptation strategies tailored to the specific requirements of HTR. We propose DRA-HTR, an unsupervised generative domain adaptation pipeline specifically designed for HTR and built upon the DRANet framework. The proposed approach combines source-domain pretraining, unsupervised adaptation to the visual characteristics of the target domain, relying on the generation of target-style source samples for task-specific training. We further investigate the integration of post-HTR correction to complement visual adaptation with language adaptation, relying on large language models, which we introduce as DRAL-HTR. The proposed framework is evaluated across seven HTR datasets spanning four languages, using a single set of hyperparameters for all source-target combinations. The recognition model achieves state-of-the-art performance on four datasets and competitive results on the remaining three. In addition, the proposed DRA-HTR establishes a new state-of-the-art for domain adaptation across all seven datasets and substantially improves overall robustness and training stability compared to the original DRANet framework: it reduces the Character Error Rate (CER) in average by 13.52 percentage points, and the average standard deviation decreases from 7.23 to 1.11 percentage points. Finally, post-HTR correction further reduces the CER by 2.16 percentage points.
authors: Gayan H. Pathirage, Florent Imbert, Denis Coquenet, Elisa H. Barney Smith

Evaluated on seven datasets across four languages with one hyperparameter setting for all source–target pairs.
Achieves state-of-the-art domain adaptation on all seven datasets, reducing average CER by 13.52 percentage points and improving stability; post-correction gives a further 2.16-point CER reduction.

The generated images are constrained using adversarial, reconstruction, latent-consistency, and perceptual objectives. papers.abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.

papers.abstract: Agent-based image restoration has achieved promising performance by coordinating restoration tools to handle heterogeneous and coupled degradations. However, existing agents often improve their decisions through accumulated successful and failed executions, without explicitly identifying the conditions under which learned restoration strategies remain effective. Consequently, changes in degradation severity, spatial coverage, or interactions may invalidate previous decisions, while providing limited guidance on how these decisions should be revised. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RecurIR}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables restoration agents to learn when and how to revise their decision rules. Specifically, we introduce a policy-hypothesis discovery mechanism to identify testable, condition-dependent rules through matched tool executions. We then design a rule-falsification-driven task evolution mechanism to generate targeted degradation variations, examine the validity of learned rules, and identify their applicability boundaries. Based on the resulting evidence, we develop a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism that learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions. We further incorporate independent verification to retain effective revisions and use the resulting feedback to guide subsequent hypothesis discovery and task evolution. Through this recursive process, RecurIR progressively refines its restoration policies as degradation conditions change. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

papers.abstract: For imbalanced data streams with delayed labels, is it worth adding a streaming oversampler, or does continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions already recover the cost of the delay? We address this through an extensive experimental comparison of streaming oversampling and continuous re-evaluation under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay. Streaming oversamplers are typically evaluated under the test-then-train assumption of immediate labels; their behaviour under these conditions, assessed through re-evaluation, has not been systematically studied. We close this gap with a decision framework that predicts when oversampling adds value over re-evaluation, organised around three axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window, and operationalised as a competition between a recovery channel (re-evaluation) and a minority-coverage channel (oversampling). Evaluating $15$ classifiers on $6$ synthetic and $6$ real streams, we find: re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but is silent on stationary ones; oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration; and cost--performance Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, where fronts partition by drift regime. Method selection should therefore be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves, not inherited from synthetic benchmarks.
bullets: Studies imbalanced data streams with delayed labels and concept drift, comparing streaming oversampling with continuous re-evaluation.

Across 15 classifiers, 6 synthetic streams, and 6 real streams, re-evaluation recovers delay-related losses on drift-active streams but has little effect on stationary streams.
Oversampling showed statistically detectable additional benefit in only one real-data configuration; synthetic cost–performance recommendations did not transfer reliably to real streams.

papers.title: When Does Oversampling Help? A Decision Framework for Imbalanced Data Streams Under Label Delay and Concept Drift
papers.tldr: A decision framework shows that oversampling rarely adds value beyond continuous re-evaluation, so method choice should adapt to drift, minority learnability, and label-delay conditions.

papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is typically evaluated on large client cohorts, where subsampling and cross-client averaging amplify privacy and smooth injected noise. Personal biosignal applications such as wearable EEG instead involve small federations of a handful of subjects, a regime whose interaction with formal client-level DP is largely uncharacterized. We study differentially private federated class-incremental learning in this small-cohort regime, combining a public EEG dataset with a custom four-channel MUSE 2 recording set into a K=5-client federation, and give a masked per-class training protocol that avoids degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision under class-incremental streaming. We propose FedEEG, combining Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive FedProx term, and show it reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to FedAvg, FedProx, and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay reduces mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A class-scoping diagnosis yields $50.5\%\pm3.6\%$ accuracy with 6 seeds and 2.02 times chance. We also introduce head-scoped client-level DP, which protects the classification head and alone reduces the achievable $\varepsilon$ by 200 times at a matched round budget; combined with fewer communication rounds it reaches $\varepsilon\!\approx\!10.4$ with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.
authors: Baran Can G\"ul, Ali G\"ul\"umser, Nasser Jazdi, Michael Weyrich
bullets: Addresses the underexplored interaction between client-level differential privacy and small federations of wearable-EEG subjects.
Uses masked per-class training to prevent degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision during class-incremental learning.
Combines Synaptic Intelligence with a lagged adaptive FedProx term; balanced-batch replay further reduces mean forgetting by 56.7%.
Head-scoped client-level DP reduces the achievable privacy budget by 200× at a matched round budget and reaches ε≈10.4 with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.
A class-scoping diagnosis achieves 50.5% ± 3.6% accuracy across six seeds, or 2.02× chance.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. (a) The achievable ε reduction decomposed into two isolated factors, each measured while holding the other fixed: head-scoping alone (at the original 9-round budget) already gives 200×; a further, independent 48× comes from reducing communication rounds. The larger share of the total 9,615× reduction is attributable to head-scoping itself and not to training for fewer rounds. (b) Utility (FM) of the DP-protected 3-round run against its properly matched non-DP counterpart at the identical round budget (paired t-test, p=0.20), and against the original 9-round non-private protocol for context only.

Fig. 1. (a) Each aggregation scheme shown at its own evaluated rounds, not on a shared round axis: sample-count-weighted FedAvg degrades from round 1 to round 8 under this federation’s extreme client-size imbalance, uniform weighting improves from round 1 to round 15 but dilutes the two client-unique classes (Sec. V-A), and √ n-weighting is the adopted operating point at its own near-peak (round 7). (b) Per-class accuracy under √ n-weighted joint training at round 7: every class substantially exceeds chance except “alerted,” motivating the class-scoping diagnosis in Table II.
