papers.title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
papers.tldr: TTB bakes cross-view attention into lightweight MLPs at test time, enabling up to 23× faster novel-view rendering while maintaining state-of-the-art quality.

papers.abstract: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.
authors: Abigail L. Tenenbaum, R. Thomas McCoy
bullets: Meta-learning enables rapid adaptation to related functions, but the underlying mechanism is unclear.
The study represents each rapidly learned function by concatenating its adapted network parameters into a single vector.
Additive and subtractive relationships among these vectors mirror symbolic relationships among the corresponding functions.
Recombined parameter vectors produce networks that implement the predicted functions without direct training.
The findings suggest that meta-learning creates systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through parameter space.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Model and analogy performance across architectures and function domains. Each panel shows F-scores across ten independent MAML-tuned initializations for one (architecture, domain) pair. “Adaptation” shows the performance of networks directly adapted to implement novel functions in the domain. “Analogy: single type” shows how well networks constructed using analogies over the initially specified component pair implement the intended novel functions, as measured by the mean F-score, while “Analogy: mean-max” reports, for each initialization, the highest mean F-score obtained across analogy types corresponding to alternative syntactic representations (see Section 3.4). Colored bars show means across initializations, black points show individual initializations, and black error bars show ±1 standard deviation. For ABgeom, only one analogy type is available, so the two analogy measures are identical.

Figure 5: Analogy performance across initialization and training conditions. Each panel shows mean-max F-scores across ten independent initializations for one (architecture, domain) pair. “Random, converge” and “Pre-train, converge” show analogy performance for parameter vectors trained to convergence from random and conventionally pre-trained initializations, respectively. “MAML, converge” shows analogy performance for parameter vectors trained to convergence from MAML-tuned initializations, while “MAML, rapid adapt” shows analogy performance for parameter vectors rapidly adapted from MAML-tuned initializations, as in the main experiment. Colored bars show means across initializations, black points show individual initializations, and black error bars show ±1 standard deviation.

Figure 1: Outline of the full analogy pipeline. A concrete example illustrates how meta-learning a parameter initialization θ for rapid adaptation within a structured domain of functions [a, b] induces corresponding geometric structure in the space of parameter vectors θ[a,b] adapted from θ to implement specific functions. (A) We specify a domain of sequence-generating functions [a, b], characterized by the sequence distributions D([a, b]) they generate. (B) The network meta-learns θ by iteratively adapting it to implement specific [a, b] functions ([5, 42] in the step shown), then updating θ based on how well the resulting parameter vectors (θ[5,42] in this step) implement the intended functions. (C) After meta-learning, we rapidly adapt θ to several functions (adaptation shown with thin arrows), verifying for each that the resulting network generates a distribution of sequences that matches the distribution generated by the corresponding function — that is, that the adapted parameter vector successfully implements the intended function. (D) We construct a new parameter vector via analogy over these adapted parameter vectors (W = θ[1,5] + θ[2,6] - θ[2,5]) and show that it implements the function predicted by the corresponding symbolic analogy ([1, 6] = [1, 5] + [2, 6] - [2, 5]) without any direct adaptation to that function.

Figure 4: Examples of the different ABlength analogy types used in our experiments. Each row shows an analogy drawn from one of our experimental analogy sets, with functions specified in terms of all three equivalent syntactic components, L.A, L.B, and L.total. Checkmarks indicate the syntactic representation under which the analogy is well-formed; crosses indicate alternative representations under which the same analogy is not well-formed. Thus, each analogy type tests a particular hypothesis about which pair of syntactic components might be reflected in the geometry of accessible parameter space.

Figure 6: Schematic making explicit the compositionality of adaptation updates. We recast the Figure 1D analogy over adaptation endpoints (labeled there with θ’s) as an analogy over the corresponding adaptation updates (thin arrows, labeled here with v’s). The single-step update vector vf is computed from the shared initialization based on 100 example sequences generated by the target function f . These analogies are equivalent in our experiments because each adaptation endpoint can be decomposed into the shared initialization plus its single-step update vector, θf = θ+ vf , causing the shared initialization terms to cancel in the original endpoint analogy.

Figure 2: Examples of randomly generated analogies used in our experiments. The intended function is shown on the right-hand side of the equation. As written, each analogy varies B while holding A fixed, but swapping the first two terms yields an equivalent analogy that can be interpreted as varying A while holding B fixed.

Figure 7: Schematic of one outer-loop step of MAML. A random function f is drawn from the domain and the network rapidly adapts from θ to task-specific parameters θf using one training step and limited data. The performance of θf on unseen data is then used to compute the metaupdate from θ to θ′. The process repeats from θ′ with a new function.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes compositional structure in meta-learned parameter spaces that enables rapid adaptation, relevant to adaptation and memory research.
papers.title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
papers.tldr: Meta-learned neural networks organize function representations in parameter space so that vector arithmetic can compose new functions without direct training.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free R\'enyi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $\lambda=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most $0.02$ in all but one model-rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning-forgetting frontier. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomohiro-sawada/lora-capacity-utilization
bullets: Standard LoRA updates often have effective rank well below the configured rank, especially at higher ranks.
The proposed method adds a stable, differentiable, SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling objective.
Across mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, a penalty of λ=0.01 reduced mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 versus unpenalized LoRA.
Training perplexity generally improved or changed by at most 0.02, with one model–rank exception.
The balance between learning and retention remains configuration-dependent; effective rank is proposed as a trainable objective, not only a diagnostic.

papers.abstract: Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a facial morph. We investigate whether labelled validation data can improve a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator through prompt selection rather than model fine-tuning. Version~1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked instruction using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide classification errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures, and decision inconsistency. Version~2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback. On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2, and PIPE, the selected Version~1 prompt achieves a (19.17\%) morph attack classification error rate (MACER), with (0.00\%) observed bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER), compared with (70.00\%) MACER for a controlled manual prompt. The paired (50.83) percentage-point difference has a (95\%) subject-bootstrap interval of ([43.33,58.33]). Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation~0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains (31.67\%) test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version~1 are landmark-based (LMA) morphs. Overall, the results show that prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM-based D-MAD performance, while also highlighting the challenge of recursive prompt refinement under a compact 10-subject validation setting.
bullets: The approach selects or revises prompts using labelled validation feedback and a security-oriented loss emphasizing missed morph attacks.
The best Version 1 prompt achieved 19.17% MACER and 0.00% BSCER on a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs.
It outperformed a controlled manual prompt by 50.83 percentage points in MACER, with a 95% subject-bootstrap interval of [43.33%, 58.33%].
Recursive prompt revision did not improve over the best initial-generation prompt and yielded 31.67% test MACER.
All 23 attacks missed by Version 1 were landmark-based morphs; validation was limited to 10 subjects.

The selected prompt is fixed before test evaluation. Test responses are subsequently combined by deterministic decision and score fusion.

papers.abstract: Layer-local self-supervised objectives remove the backward pass between layers, but almost all still compute their loss over a batch of samples and are therefore local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), a spatially and temporally local learning rule for self-supervised representation learning from sequential input streams. The key idea is to instantiate a VICReg-style objective with temporally adjacent positives and non-differentiated running population statistics, yielding a per-neuron online loss with bounded state. The objective is a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis, and its gradient is a Hebbian update of the feedforward weights and an anti-Hebbian update of one lateral matrix per layer. The aim of the experiments is to show that the rule works in a small network, not to compete with backpropagation. On a class-chunked MNIST stream, a two-layer fully connected network trained with batch size one outperforms random features (96.48% versus 95.09% linear-probe accuracy) and classical SFA, and a variant that relaxes both locality constraints is comparable to supervised backpropagation. Because training and inference use the same computation, the network can keep learning from unlabeled data during inference without loss of accuracy.
bullets: Uses temporally adjacent positives and running population statistics in a VICReg-style objective.
Produces per-neuron online updates with bounded state: Hebbian feedforward and anti-Hebbian lateral updates.
In a small two-layer network on class-chunked MNIST, batch-one training achieved 96.48% linear-probe accuracy versus 95.09% for random features.
The method outperformed classical SFA, while a less-local variant was comparable to supervised backpropagation.
Training and inference share the same computation, enabling continued unlabeled learning during inference without accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.
authors: You Wu, Guhong Zhang, Hongwei Li, Xinyue Hong, Yuan Jia
bullets: Benchmarks 16 memory subchallenges across 9 spacecraft-operation tasks, using 140 templates and 2,240 instances.

Memory systems and RAG improve same-session performance over native Pi Agent, while no memory system clearly beats RAG overall.
After session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points; gains are stronger for instruction retention and result reuse than for state tracking or energy reservation.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. authors: Zhuo Han, Yeqiang Wang, Xinran Wang, Hongwei Han, Yi Xiong, Zunian Wan, Jianbo Mao, Huan Peng, Yongcheng Liu, Wei Shan, Maoqing Yao
bullets: Addresses VLA policies that overlook spatial structure and task history when making action decisions.
Adds features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model to temporal memory alongside visual representations.

Achieves the highest average success rate among compared methods across LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent's state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments requiring coordinated use of heterogeneous memory contents. In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds compared with MemRL, while preserving compatible KV states as task progress updates the memory context.
authors: Saehun Chun, Wonje Choi, Jinwoo Jang, Taeyoon Kwack, Honguk Woo

papers.abstract: In long-horizon manipulation, a robot may need to take different actions under identical observations, depending on task progress and the outcomes of earlier attempts. We refer to this ambiguity as decision aliasing. Resolving it requires the policy to maintain memory of its execution history. To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact event memories using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues. However, these criteria may miss events that matter for task success. We instead propose an outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success. Following this principle, we introduce CGEM, a critic-gated event memory that uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability. Positive and negative changes are encoded as progress and failure records, respectively. Failure records are discarded once the corresponding subtask is completed. In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment with exactly computed success probabilities, CGEM achieves 88.0% success, compared with 0.0% for both a 36-step observation window and a kinematic event memory. Removing failure records reduces success to 1.7%.
authors: Xuanzhuo Liu, Chuankang Li, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Addresses decision aliasing, where identical observations require different actions based on task history.
Uses a critic to gate event memory by estimated changes in success probability.
Stores positive changes as progress records and negative changes as failure records, deleting failures after the related subtask is completed.
In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment, CGEM reaches 88.0% success versus 0.0% for a 36-step observation window and kinematic event memory.
Removing failure records drops success to 1.7%, highlighting their importance.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.
bullets: Separates adaptive candidate generation from confirmatory evaluation and bounded canary deployment.
Tests frozen candidates on fresh paired audits against a prespecified primary objective.
Protects declared capabilities using reference-relative non-inferiority tests and governance constraints.
Provides simultaneous lower bounds for countably many adaptively generated candidates, with evaluator calibration and reference-replacement bridge tests.
Monte Carlo experiments illustrate calibration under evaluator optimism; guarantees are conditional and do not cover universal safety or arbitrary distribution shift.

papers.abstract: AI-generated image detectors face significant challenges when deployed in real-world environments, particularly when test samples are produced by unseen generators that deviate from the source training distribution. Existing detectors often rely on a single type of evidence, such as semantic representations or low-level generation traces, making them vulnerable when the corresponding cue becomes unreliable. Moreover, adapting detectors to newly emerging generators usually requires target labels or retraining, which is costly and impractical. To address these challenges, we propose Dual-Evidence Disagreement-Constrained Adaptation (DEDCA), a test-time adaptation framework for generalized AI-generated image detection. DEDCA constructs a dual-evidence detector by combining CLIP-based semantic evidence with trace evidence extracted from shuffled entropy and residual statistics, and introduces a reliability-aware gate to perform sample-specific adaptive fusion. Our key idea is to exploit the disagreement between the two evidence streams as an unlabeled adaptation signal, enabling the detector to adjust to target-domain shifts without relying on target labels or blindly trusting a single prediction stream. Experiments show that DEDCA achieves superior performance on the GenImage benchmark by outperforming state-of-the-art AI-generated image detectors and test-time adaptation methods with 92.0\% average accuracy.
authors: Hao Tan, Qimin Zhang, Lihuang Fang, Kebing Jin, Jinghui Qin
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts caused by unseen image generators in real-world deployment.
Combines CLIP-based semantic features with generation-trace evidence from shuffled entropy and residual statistics.
Uses a reliability-aware gate for sample-specific fusion of the two evidence streams.
Exploits disagreement between evidence streams as an unlabeled adaptation signal, avoiding target labels or retraining.
Reports 92.0% average accuracy on the GenImage benchmark and outperforms prior detectors and test-time adaptation methods.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.
authors: Sahit Chintalapudi, Xiaoyan Wang, Aryan Zoroufi, Aditya Agarwal, Nancy Kanwisher, Tom\'as Lozano-P\'erez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling
bullets: Addresses long-horizon manipulation with occlusion and uncertainty.
Interleaves sensing actions into task-and-motion plan skeletons designed for full observability.
Uses persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map.
Evaluated on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks with heavy occlusion and partial visibility.
Outperforms baselines lacking active perception or persistent memory.

papers.abstract: Motion imitation enables humanoid robots to acquire whole-body skills such as walking and dancing. However, fine-tuning an entire policy for a new skill can affect existing behaviors, while training a separate policy for each skill increases training and maintenance costs. We present PERA, a method for learning new skills by reusing existing motion capabilities. PERA freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an additional task expert and its routing score using task rewards or teacher-action supervision. In Unitree G1 simulation, each added task module contains approximately 1.03% of the parameters of the base actor. Built on our pretrained policy, PERA successfully completes all ten new tasks. Disabling the expert restores the original computation path of the base policy, which still fully executes all 126 original motions. Enabling the expert also improves the execution of some dance motions not used to train that expert, indicating that its benefits extend beyond its training motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further demonstrate the applicability of PERA to different base policies.
authors: Shangchao Hu, Yadan Sun, Xibo Yu, Wei Huang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between catastrophic interference from fine-tuning and the cost of maintaining separate policies.
Freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an added task expert with its routing score using rewards or teacher actions.

papers.abstract: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).
bullets: EWC can underweight well-fitted samples because its empirical Fisher scales importance by loss-gradient magnitude.
CLOC shows that EWC is the first-order form of preserving each old sample’s loss.
IEWC removes this unintended weighting by penalizing output changes along each sample’s loss-level set.
The approach also prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix.

Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC matches or improves EWC and outperforms EWC-DR; on ImageNet-R, uniform IEWC gains 2.00 percentage points over matched EWC (95% CI: 0.93–3.07).

papers.abstract: Autonomous optical networks require monitoring systems capable of adapting to evolving disturbances without repeated retraining or service interruption. We propose a continual event recognition framework for state-of-polarization (SOP)-based optical monitoring based on prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration. The framework supports recognition of known disturbances, detection and integration of novel events, and investigates whether overlapping disturbances can be inferred through compositional reasoning from existing prototypes. Experimental validation on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed demonstrates 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy, successful adaptation to novel disturbances without encoder retraining, and reveals that overlapping optical disturbances exhibit varying degrees of latent compositionality. While some overlaps can be recognized in a zero-shot manner through prototype composition, others require explicit few-shot registration. These results establish continual event recognition as a promising paradigm for future autonomous optical network monitoring systems.

Combines prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration.
Achieves 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed.

papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.
authors: Lujia Zhong, Yihao Xia, Jianwei Zhang, Shuo Huang, Xinyu Nie, Mingyang Xia, Zhiwei Deng, Jiaxin Yue, Xinkai Wang, Junhan Zhao, Yonggang Shi
bullets: Covers 56 execution and workflow-reconstruction tasks across seven tool ecosystems and multiple neuroimaging modalities.
Tests skill evolution through distillation of execution trajectories on familiar, unseen, and cross-model tasks.
Assesses scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer’s disease studies and raw cohort data.
Agents perform nearly perfectly with supplied protocols, but performance gaps widen without procedural guidance.
Distilled skills improve acquisition tasks and transfer across models, while unseen-task gains are inconsistent; reproducible outputs can still conflict with expert conclusions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.
authors: Miao Pan, Kaixiang Yao, Xiaohe Zhou, Xu Wang, Qinfeng Li, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Targets three missing abilities: causal failure localization, capability-aware adaptation, and experience-driven decision revision.
Builds recovery data by perturbing successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and retaining observable, recoverable failures.
Uses Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision with evaluation-first SFT to structure failure diagnosis before recovery planning.
Applies OPD to reduce errors from self-generated planning prefixes without adding a deployment-time branch.
Improves composite task success by 6.1 points with a frozen VLA and manipulation/navigation success by 13.9 points with fixed GPT-5.5 execution.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding aims to continuously process incoming visual observations, making the retention and retrieval of relevant information increasingly important as the video history grows. Although existing benchmarks include memory-related questions, question-answering accuracy alone does not reliably measure memory capabilities. Incorrect predictions may arise from failures in visual understanding rather than forgetting, whereas correct predictions may rely on linguistic priors or recent observations without requiring historical memory. To address these ambiguities, we introduce MemInStream, a benchmark dedicated to evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding. We develop an evidence-controlled validation protocol that associates each question with temporally localized evidence intervals. The protocol validates evidence solvability and memory necessity by retaining questions that models can answer from the annotated evidence but cannot resolve using recent observations, post-evidence observations, or textual input alone. This helps disentangle memory limitations from understanding failures while reducing memory-independent shortcuts. MemInStream provides a systematic evaluation of memory capabilities through four major categories, covering Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking \& Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory across diverse video scenarios. Overall, \textsc{MemInStream} provides a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for systematically evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.
authors: Zhenqi He, Dunyuan Xu, Yang Bo, Kien T. Pham, Yanghao Wang, Shuhan Li, Xintong Guo, Yuyang He, Fang Liu, Huankang Guan, Jingyan Chen, Rui Liu, Long Chen
bullets: Existing question-answering accuracy can conflate memory failures with visual understanding errors or linguistic and recency-based shortcuts.
Each question is paired with temporally localized evidence intervals in an evidence-controlled validation protocol.
The benchmark keeps questions that are solvable from the evidence but not from recent observations, post-evidence content, or text alone.
It evaluates four capabilities: Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking & Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory.
The benchmark targets diverse streaming-video scenarios and aims to disentangle memory limitations from other sources of failure.

papers.abstract: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the child. We construct this upbringing in a finite world and study whether care survives the mother's departure, new situations and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto. A finite role certificate supports transfer within a declared world family. When the hidden representation changes, an update is accepted only if a care readout recovers the required judgements with a prescribed margin and bounded weights. With a correct successor model, fixed exact role encoding and protected updates, the certified measure preserves the care boundary under arbitrary own reward. An explicit quotient condition transfers the finite certificate across the declared family, while two-request and finite-stock counterexamples identify when the role code ceases to suffice. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for readout feasibility and prove preservation under repeated accepted updates. In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks complete all 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. Execution uses the learned gate without a world-model check at each action. A matched comparison reproduces a future-aware shield's decisions, whereas removing future lookahead permits avoidable lapses. Reward and source-contamination thresholds, together with witness-falsification trials, identify the conditions on which the construction depends. The construction shows how learned care can survive further learning in a finite world under explicit conditions on representation, supervision and execution.
bullets: Care is modeled using a harm vocabulary, a learned measure of future acceptability, and an execution veto.
A finite role certificate supports transfer across a declared family of worlds, while protected representation updates preserve care judgments with a required margin and bounded weights.
Theoretical results give necessary and sufficient readout feasibility conditions and prove preservation under repeated accepted updates.
In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks completed 270 speech episodes without harmful words and avoided unnecessary harm across 486 episodes.
Two-request and finite-stock counterexamples expose when the role encoding is insufficient; removing future lookahead allows avoidable lapses.

papers.title: An Approach to Hinton's Mother-Child Proposal: Neural Networks Learning and Preserving Care in a Finite World

papers.abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

bullets: Addresses the need to update agent expertise as Earth-observation tools, tasks, and workflows change.
Externalizes tool-call knowledge into reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files.
Refines skills through real tool-chain execution, dual-judge feedback, and observation-grounded component-level routing.
Improves tool selection, argument correctness, execution order, and task completion across multiple frontier and open-source LLMs.
Supports cross-model skill transfer without parameter updates or retraining.

papers.abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $\tau^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.

A 2×2 ablation suggests external rules provide new knowledge, while trained weights make already-solved tasks more reliable.
The study closes most of the gap to three frontier models under the same evaluation protocol.

papers.title: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent

papers.abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.
authors: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets world-model failures when robot dynamics change unexpectedly, such as after grasping an unknown payload.
Uses a fast correction for prompt adaptation and a slow correction for retained dynamics, with prediction errors driving both.
Dynamically reweights pretrained experts without modifying their parameters.
Evaluated on five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, achieving lower multi-step mean error than ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task.
Reported gains cover early adaptation, transient disturbances, and long-horizon retention; code and datasets are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.
bullets: Addresses conditional generative modeling when target data are scarce and source and target response spaces may differ.
TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head while keeping the source representation fixed; TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a regularized representation correction.
Derives conditional squared Wasserstein risk bounds covering source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration.
Shows adaptation can achieve faster risk rates than generators limited to frozen context information when the source representation has a smooth correction.

A target-validation and switching procedure has an oracle guarantee and can avoid increasing conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator; simulations and real-data applications demonstrate practical gains.

papers.tldr: A theory-backed transfer-learning framework for conditional flow matching uses either a frozen source representation or an adapted one to improve generation with limited target data while guarding against negative transfer.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object tracking faces modality-induced appearance discrepancies and abrupt target-position shifts that can arise from modality switching, UAV motion, and inter-sensor offsets. Although existing methods model modality and spatial variations, they primarily rely on offline representation learning and offer limited localization-oriented adaptation during testing. To address these challenges, we propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), which derives spatial and temporal adaptation signals from unlabeled test sequences for online optimization. Specifically, we design a controllable token shift auxiliary task, which imposes explicit spatial correspondence between predefined token translations and resultant localization offsets, generating stable annotation-free spatial adaptation signals. Furthermore, we introduce a temporal backward prediction auxiliary task to exploit frame-wise temporal dependencies, effectively mitigating cumulative localization errors in continuous tracking. To suppress interference from unreliable tracking samples, we develop a reliability-aware update gating strategy to screen valid adaptation signals and stabilize online parameter updates. Experiments on CM-UOT demonstrate that TSAT achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing test-time adaptation methods, exhibiting superior robustness under frequent modality switching and severe spatial displacement. Experiments across tracking frameworks and datasets further validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of TSAT.
authors: Yun Xiao, Hailong Ye, Zhicheng Zhao, Lei Liu, Amir Hussain
bullets: Addresses appearance discrepancies and abrupt target shifts caused by modality switching, UAV motion, and sensor offsets.
Uses a controllable token-shift auxiliary task to generate annotation-free spatial localization signals.
Adds temporal backward prediction to exploit frame dependencies and reduce cumulative localization errors.
Applies reliability-aware update gating to exclude unreliable samples during online adaptation.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on CM-UOT and effectiveness across tracking frameworks and datasets, especially under frequent switching and severe displacement.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes online test-time adaptation for cross-modal UAV tracking with auxiliary token-shift and temporal tasks.
papers.title: Test-Time Selective Adaptation for Cross-Modal UAV Object Tracking with Token Shift

papers.abstract: Federated learning often assumes that data is fixed in advance, which is unrealistic in many real-world scenarios where new data continuously arrives, causing catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose FCLPF (Federated Class Incremental Learning with Pseudo Features), a method that uses pseudo features generated from prototypes to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Our approach reduces communication costs and improves efficiency by eliminating the need for past data and avoiding computationally heavy models like GANs. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 show that FCLPF achieves an average accuracy of 51.87% and an average forgetting of 9.62%, significantly outperforming existing baselines with an average accuracy of 47.72% and forgetting of 20.46%. On TinyImageNet, FCLPF achieves 37.56% accuracy and 3.14% forgetting, compared to the baselines' 27.69% accuracy and 24.46% forgetting, demonstrating the superior performance of FCLPF.
authors: Min Kyoon Yoo, Yu Rang Park
bullets: Addresses continual arrival of new classes in federated learning, where fixed-data assumptions cause catastrophic forgetting.
Generates pseudo features from class prototypes to retain knowledge without past data.
Avoids exemplar storage and computationally heavy GAN-based approaches, reducing communication and computational demands.
On CIFAR-100, achieves 51.87% average accuracy and 9.62% forgetting, versus baselines’ 47.72% and 20.46%.
On TinyImageNet, achieves 37.56% accuracy and 3.14% forgetting, compared with 27.69% and 24.46% for baselines.

papers.abstract: The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene's relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale. The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot's Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at https://emvit-mde.github.io.
authors: Dimitrios Chatziparaschis, Georgios Georgakis, Adnan I. Ansar, Shehryar Khattak, Konstantinos Karydis
bullets: Addresses uncertain generalization of affine-invariant monocular depth models in novel, unstructured environments.
Refines dense disparity to recover relative scene structure and predicts a baseline scalar for metric scale.
Trains a lightweight Vision Transformer online using sparse LiDAR, with optional ego-motion and gradient matching to preserve fine details.
Evaluated on public sequences including KITTI, showing faster and more accurate adaptation than existing foundation MDE models.
Code and supplementary materials are planned for public release.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Self-supervised virtual stereo system for online metric adaptation in MDE. Based on an affine-invariant inverse depth input da and camera’s focal length f , our Ego Motion (EM)-ViT framework decodes depth reconstruction into dense disparity refinement d̂ and an effective baseline prediction B̂, achieving scale-to-structure disentanglement. The integrated disparity refinement module (e.g., dRefNet) uses a single image It, with optionally previously captured frames Iref and their corresponding poses p, to metrically fine-tune generated depth D̂t, while pose corrections can be provided in real-time via the odometry refinement module (e.g., odomNet). Our lightweight EM-ViT framework is self-supervised by sparse LiDAR annotations, photometric reconstruction, and gradient matching loss, to provide real-time, accurate, and fine-grained monocular depth estimation.

Fig. 6: Moments during online training. We demonstrate our model’s online MDE adaptation in the unexplored garage environment, by presenting the total training loss (top left), the δ1 score (top right), and depth prediction instances on unseen images (bottom).

Fig. 12: Qualitative evaluation of depth prediction of our method in different Martian scenes. By using a single image our method is able to generate depth maps of the observed area without being affected by ambient conditions. Specifically, in cases of low solar phase angle and poor area texture, the applied Flight Stereo [11] method shows depth discontinuities, in contrast to the EM-ViT. We showcase our method’s generated point clouds for each Martian scene in different view points.

Fig. 7: Ground-truth density and depth map fidelity. Our method preserves high-fidelity structural detail during disparity reconstruction via the proposed gradient matching supervision scheme LGM(d̂, da) with local corrections, even in cases with less LiDAR annotations (i.e. Garage and CitrusFarm).

papers.title: Adapting Monocular Depth Estimation in Novel Scenes through Disparity Refinement and Robot Ego-Motion
papers.tldr: EM-ViT adapts foundation-model monocular depth predictions to metric depth in new robotic scenes using sparse LiDAR and optionally robot ego-motion.

papers.abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.
authors: Binghang Lu, Lang Cao, Changhong Mou, Yige Sun, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Zheyuan Deng, Tian Yuan, Bing Hu, Runyu Zhang, Na Lu, Guang Lin
bullets: Benchmarks 1,001 cases across 42 classical and fractional PDE templates.
Tests noise-free data, substantial Gaussian noise, and hard out-of-distribution settings.
RSI-PDE shortlists equations by residual loss, refines coefficients and solvers using relative L² feedback, and gates policy or memory updates with validation.
Across four frontier models, RSI-PDE raises average pass rates over single-run baselines and native harnesses while using fewer recorded model calls.
The benchmark targets workflows requiring equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration.

Figure 4 | The residual-guided RSI-PDE workflow. (1) The agent starts without the equation: the family 𝑘 and the coefficients 𝜃 are unknown, and it receives 256 samples, the known forcing, initial and boundary data, and the class library. (2) A frozen LLM, steered by its self-written policy 𝜋 and memory 𝑀, writes the program 𝑃, whose router identifies the case and dispatches it to a class solver. (3) In the sandbox, residual ranking by min𝜃 Lres (𝑘, 𝜃; 𝑢𝑎) ranks candidate families and keeps the five best; forward solves and public relative 𝐿2 checks then refine the equation choice and its coefficients. (4) Public relative 𝐿2 errors, the self-test and the validation gate decide what is kept. Accepted (𝑃, 𝜋, 𝑀) carry into the next round, so the policy and memory evolve with the solver; a rejection returns its 𝐿2 errors and reasons. The bottom row follows a toy viscous Burgers case (𝜈★ = 0.01): the residual fit on a smoothed field gives 𝜈 = 0.0171, and gated 𝐿2 feedback refines it to 𝜈 = 0.0101, below 𝜏. papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.
authors: Songshi Liang, Ting-En Lin, Zixuan Huang, Yuchuan Wu, Yongbin Li, Zihe Wang, Rui Yan
bullets: Identifies inter-domain null-space misalignment as the cause of multi-task editing collapse.
Introduces a Conflict Index to quantify geometric interference between editing tasks.
Uses conflict-aware task ordering to reduce cumulative interference.
Applies dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the available null space when needed.
Experiments across five domains and three backbones show improved multi-task editing while preserving general capabilities and handling incremental task arrival.

papers.abstract: Embodied continual learning requires controllers to infer changing situations, retain prior behavior and reuse motor skills without task labels or known boundaries. The challenge is deciding when to recover earlier behavior and which skills can support new learning. We introduce Situation-guided Primitive Integration for Recurrent Embodiment (SPIRE), a recurrent-spiking system that infers latent contexts from action-outcome evidence and learns context-specific motor actors online. Mature actors become protected sources that combine with a target-context residual to drive recurrent-spiking motor populations. Across coordinate, three-joint and hidden-force control, SPIRE maintained control, autonomously inferred situations, retained prior behavior and accelerated acquisition of an unseen source composition, reducing mean interactions to criterion by approximately 40% relative to matched fresh controllers. Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early acquisition in every matched intervention, demonstrating causal reuse. Against seven recurrent continual-learning and modular-control comparators, SPIRE achieved 2.4 times the mean prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible task-free alternative selected for each paired stream. These results demonstrate autonomous recovery and causal reuse of motor skills for new learning in continuous embodied control.
authors: Yiyang Jia, Mingyang Lyu, Gongce Cao, Feifei Zhao, Yinqian Sun, Yi Zeng
bullets: Addresses continual control without task labels or known task boundaries.
Infers latent contexts from action–outcome evidence using a recurrent-spiking system.
Learns online context-specific motor actors and combines protected source actors with target-context residuals.
Across three control settings, it retained prior behavior and reduced interactions to criterion by approximately 40% versus matched fresh controllers.
Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early learning, supporting causal motor-skill reuse; SPIRE also outperformed task-free comparators on prior-learning advantage.

papers.abstract: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.
authors: Jaiaid Mobin, Avinash Maurya, M. Mustafa Rafique, Bogdan Nicolae
bullets: Targets evolving sensor distributions in deadline-constrained surrogate workflows, where concurrent serving and fine-tuning cause GPU contention and latency variability.
Fuses inference and training samples into one forward pass, applying backpropagation only to training samples.
Uses a polynomial-time offline scheduler that exploits nonlinear batch-size latency and repetitive workloads.
Evaluated on real-world Ptychographic reconstruction with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.
Improves reconstruction MSE by up to 30%, inference MSE by up to 50%, and reduces deadline misses by 13%–22% versus a multi-context baseline.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP can classify images into categories they were never explicitly trained to recognize, but accuracy degrades when test images differ in style or source from their training data. A common remedy generates randomly cropped and flipped copies of each test image, called views, and combines their predictions. Since some views miss the object, methods must identify which views to trust. The dominant approach uses prediction entropy to measure confidence and retains the most certain views. Other methods use signals such as embedding typicality. Despite repeated refinements of these scoring functions, the information they rely on, the model's own response to each view, remains largely unexamined. We investigate this choice while holding other pipeline stages fixed. First, we show that view selection, rather than the gradient update, accounts for almost all accuracy gains. We then examine whether entropy identifies useful views when predictions are wrong, despite at least one view predicting the correct class. In these cases, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones no better than chance, recovering only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views. This finding holds across two image encoders and under a control ruling out an obvious statistical artifact. An exact analysis explains this limitation: entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors. We identify an unused signal already available in the augmentation pipeline: the fraction of the original image retained by each crop. Ranking views by this quantity improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested. A pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.
bullets: View selection, not the gradient update, accounts for nearly all reported accuracy gains in the evaluated pipeline.
When at least one augmented view is correct, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones about as well as chance.
Entropy recovers only about one-twentieth of the accuracy achievable by an oracle selecting among the same views.
Ranking views by the fraction of the original image they retain improves accuracy over entropy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets.
A pre-method measurement predicts which datasets benefit from this alternative signal.

papers.abstract: Classification of lung adenocarcinoma into poorly differentiated (PD) and well-to-moderately differentiated (WMD) subtypes plays an important role in patient survival; however, consistent classification is difficult due to inter-observer variability among pathologists. Collecting data from multiple hospitals is also challenging due to patient privacy concerns. This study proposes a web-based federated learning system that shares only locally trained model weights without sharing patient data between institutions. The UNI2 foundation model and CLAM-SB were used to classify pathological whole slide images. A four-client federated learning system was constructed, and the NLST cohort was reserved exclusively for external validation. In centralized evaluation, joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperformed single-institution training on external validation, confirming the necessity of multi-institutional data integration. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedNova were compared as federated learning algorithms under identical experimental conditions. Test AUC ranked as FedBN, FedProx, FedNova, and FedAvg. FedNova showed the most balanced classification performance between PD and WMD. L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity was applied to reduce model transmission size. FedAvg, FedProx, and FedBN showed a tendency of decreasing Test AUC under pruning, while FedNova achieved improved Test AUC across all sparsity levels. A web-based application was developed supporting slide upload, local training, AI classification, and attention heatmap-based visualization. The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning was confirmed as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification performance while protecting patient privacy.

papers.abstract: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = \rho / (\mu_i + \rho)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $\Delta_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $\Psi(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $\omega^* = (4\nu^2 \Sigma / c')^{1/3}$, $c' = \sigma^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)$, and the plug-in strength $\rho^* = \sigma^2 / (n\delta^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}} = \rho (e^{\zeta q} - 1) / (\zeta q)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.
bullets: The method analyzes how periodic anchor refreshes affect forgetting, lag, and estimation variance in each spectral direction.
It derives an optimal refresh rate, plug-in prior strength, and a finite-dimensional random-matrix correction for the anchor.
The online SPAR procedure calibrates window length and prior strength from residuals.
Across a 27-configuration grid, the calibrated window responds to drift without divergence; defaults also transfer to hourly electricity and BCI IV 2b streams.
The algebra, refresh dynamics, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4; reported approximation error is within 5% at fixed operating points and 13% at the method’s own operating points.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of automating end-to-end OpenFOAM workflows for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). However, current progress is bottlenecked by two critical limitations. First, existing evaluations are dominated by tutorial-level cases and execution-oriented metrics, masking a substantial executability--acceptability gap: successfully executed simulations often fail to satisfy prescribed numerical or quantity-of-interest (QoI) criteria. Second, domain expertise in existing systems is tightly coupled with bespoke agent architectures, limiting its reuse and continual refinement across agent implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce ExtFoamBench, a challenging benchmark for OpenFOAM agents that spans five axes of workflow variation, and separately assesses execution completion, numerical soundness, and QoI satisfaction. Complementing this, we propose EasyFoam, an agent framework that decouples CFD expertise into modular, externalized skills driven by a dual-loop mechanism. An execution loop constructs workflows from explicit task requirements and uses structured simulation evidence to diagnose failures and guide targeted repairs. Meanwhile, an evolution loop distills task experience into reusable skill updates selected through paired evaluation. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that EasyFoam achieves substantially higher task acceptance rates than baseline agents, establishing this work as a starting point for future research toward self-improving CFD agents.

bullets: ExtFoamBench evaluates agents across five workflow-variation axes, separating execution completion, numerical soundness, and QoI satisfaction.
