papers.abstract: Adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models to deployment-time distribution shifts is important for reliable robotic operation, but conventional first-order adaptation can exceed the memory budget of inference-oriented deployment platforms. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a forward-only alternative with inference-level memory, but accurate gradient estimation requires many perturbation queries, making naive ZO prohibitively slow for large VLA models. We present VLA-ZO, a framework for fast ZO adaptation that exploits the structure of VLA computation. By confining adaptation to the action side, VLA-ZO keeps the expensive vision-language prefix frozen and reuses its conditioning states across perturbation queries and optimizer steps, while schedule-aware prefetching hides state-transfer overhead. On LIBERO camera-viewpoint shifts, VLA-ZO reduces end-to-end adaptation time by 25.59$\times$ at $q=16$ and 32.54$\times$ at $q=64$ relative to baseline ZO, while improving average task success from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% and 63.58%, respectively. These results show that making ZO faster can make larger query budgets practical, providing a promising path toward resource-efficient VLA adaptation on deployment platforms.
bullets: Targets deployment-time adaptation to camera-viewpoint distribution shifts without the memory cost of first-order optimization.
Adapts only the action component while freezing and reusing the expensive vision-language prefix across queries and optimizer steps.
Uses schedule-aware prefetching to hide conditioning-state transfer overhead.
On LIBERO, achieves 25.59× and 32.54× faster adaptation than baseline ZO at query budgets of 16 and 64, respectively.
Average task success improves from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% at q=16 and 63.58% at q=64.

papers.tldr: VLA-ZO makes zeroth-order adaptation of vision-language-action models practical on memory-limited robotic deployment platforms by reusing frozen vision-language computations and accelerating perturbation queries.

papers.abstract: Wearable and bedside electrocardiogram (ECG) monitors must adapt to patient-specific morphology to maintain arrhythmia detection accuracy across users, yet personalization is typically performed offline and cannot account for individual physiology, electrode placement, or recording drift. On-device adaptation by backpropagation is expensive for microcontroller-class medical devices because it requires an optimizer state, repeated backward passes through convolutional layers, and labeled arrhythmic beats that may not be available at deployment time. This letter proposes prototype-only head adaptation as a compact personalization primitive for TinyML ECG systems. A one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1-D CNN; 1,314 parameters and 72.6k multiply-accumulate operations per beat) is trained offline on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database under an inter-patient protocol, frozen as a feature extractor, and exported to a PSoC 6 microcontroller. Patient-specific adaptation then reduces to computing closed-form class means in a 32-dimensional embedding space, requiring no convolutional backward pass, no iterative optimization, and only one forward pass per support beat. Prototype adaptation improves inter-patient macro-F1 from 0.635/0.639/0.646 to 0.731/0.771/0.797 at 1/5/10-shot, outperforming linear stochastic-gradient-descent (SGD) head fine-tuning at every shot count for the target tiny backbone. On-device replay over 18 one-shot episodes on a PSoC 6 Cortex-M4F matches the host macro-F1 for the prototype head (0.798), with 11.39 ms per beat, 5.2 KB flash, and 22.2 KB SRAM. A restricted variant that updates only the normal-class prototype from passively buffered sinus beats yields a consistent +0.05 macro-F1 gain, reducing the annotation burden during initial
bullets: A frozen 1-D CNN extracts 32-dimensional ECG embeddings on a microcontroller.
Personalization computes closed-form class prototypes from 1, 5, or 10 support beats, requiring one forward pass per beat.
Inter-patient macro-F1 improves from 0.635–0.646 without adaptation to 0.731–0.797 with prototype adaptation.
On PSoC 6, replayed one-shot episodes match host performance at 11.39 ms per beat, 5.2 KB flash, and 22.2 KB SRAM.
Updating only the normal-class prototype from passively buffered sinus beats provides a consistent +0.05 macro-F1 gain.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to improve an agent using its own task experience. Its practical value depends on whether performance gains justify the full cost of self-improvement and task execution. We evaluate this trade-off on continual task streams, scoring each task before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. We define the \emph{RSI Tax} as the token cost of the self-improvement process and include it alongside task-execution costs in end-to-end evaluation. Across six methods and two language models, a bounded-note baseline matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI, with mean total-token savings of 65.6-71.0\%. We decompose the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs, and track subsequent use of the associated state or artifact. For these three RSI methods, verification accounts for 74.8--93.6% of the aggregate RSI Tax. A substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated with states or artifacts that are not used later in the evaluated streams. These results expose a practical limitation of costly RSI procedures: improvements in the deployed agent need not justify the expense of the improvement process. They motivate RSI objectives that jointly optimize the RSI Tax and expected task-execution cost while ensuring continued growth in agent capabilities across the task stream.
bullets: Evaluates self-improvement on continual task streams, charging both task execution and the full RSI process.
Introduces the “RSI Tax,” covering verification, exploration, and writing costs.
Across six methods and two language models, bounded notes achieve comparable or better observed accuracy with 65.6–71.0% lower mean total-token cost than three RSI methods.
Verification dominates the RSI Tax, accounting for 74.8–93.6% of its aggregate cost.
Many costly states or artifacts are not subsequently used, motivating objectives that jointly optimize capability growth and total cost.

papers.selection_reason: Cost analysis of recursive self-improvement on continual task streams informs online learning and adaptation decisions.
papers.title: The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost
papers.tldr: Costly recursive self-improvement may not pay off: a simple bounded-note baseline matches or outperforms several RSI methods while using far fewer total tokens.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation assigns each sample a domain teacher but typically updates shared student parameters. We introduce Domain-Routed Delta Optimization (DRD-MOPD), which specifies which parameter components each domain's samples update. The student is the sum of a frozen base and trainable components initialized from expert-minus-base weights. All components participate in every forward pass; four update modes define the correspondence between sample domains and components, each with independent optimizer states. We analyze these update rules and measure retention of the original expert geometry through angles, projection coefficients, and energy. Prior work such as Open-MOPD distills directly from the base model; 97.02% of its released final checkpoint's increment energy lies outside the span of the original expert directions. In comparison, our Own checkpoint after 20 updates retains coefficients near one along each component's original direction and pairwise angles ranging from 88.04 to 92.41 degrees; its exported BF16 student's increment has 4.90% outside energy, versus 10.52% for the sum of saved FP32 components. The same checkpoint achieves a 32.72% macro score across six benchmarks, compared with 32.44% for its initial task-arithmetic merge. These measurements describe geometry and capability at the evaluated training stages and settings.
bullets: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation usually updates shared student parameters, risking loss of the original experts’ structure.
The student combines a frozen base with trainable expert-minus-base components; all components are used during inference, but domain-specific routing controls which are updated.
Four update modes assign domain samples to components, each with independent optimizer states.

After 20 updates, the Own checkpoint retained near-unit original-direction coefficients and showed 4.90% outside energy in the exported BF16 student increment, versus 97.02% for Open-MOPD’s released checkpoint.
The Own checkpoint scored 32.72% macro across six benchmarks, compared with 32.44% for its initial task-arithmetic merge; results are limited to the evaluated stages and settings.

papers.abstract: Intermediate-fusion cooperative perception lets a vehicle detect objects beyond its own field of view by fusing features shared by nearby agents. When only a collaborator's cameras are degraded by fog, motion blur or exposure errors, the features it shares drift away from the training distribution while the ego input stays clean, and cooperation can become worse than not cooperating at all. Test-time batch-normalization adaptation, the standard training-free remedy, estimates statistics over the pooled batch of all agents and therefore normalizes both the clean ego and the corrupted collaborator with a mixture of two distributions. We show that this mixing harms even the clean ego: when the ego shares BN statistics with a corrupted collaborator, its detection from its own features drops by 3.58 to 6.68 AP@0.5 points although its cameras are untouched. We propose AgentNorm, an agent-wise test-time normalization that i) estimates the normalization statistics of every collaborator from its own current observation and ii) anchors the ego to its source statistics, so that the ego path remains exactly the original model. AgentNorm has no learnable parameters, needs no gradients or labels, is independent of the order of test frames, and runs locally on each agent without changing the transmitted features. On camera-based OPV2V with four fusion checkpoints and collaborator-only corruptions, AgentNorm raises AP@0.5 under severity-5 fog from 29.42-37.25 to 43.32-58.86 and outperforms pooled normalization by 5.53-12.94 points under fog and motion blur, at an extra latency of 2.3 ms per frame. On the real-world DAIR-V2X-C dataset, it outperforms pooled normalization in all ten infrastructure-corruption settings. We also report the cases it does not fix: occlusion, which removes image content rather than shifting feature statistics, and the case in which all agents share the same shift.
bullets: Problem: Pooled batch-normalization statistics mix clean ego features with corrupted collaborator features, degrading even the untouched ego path.
Method: Estimate each collaborator’s normalization statistics from its current observation while anchoring the ego to its original source statistics.
Contribution: A training-free, gradient-free, label-free, order-independent method that runs locally without altering transmitted features or adding parameters.

Results: Under collaborator-only fog and motion blur, AgentNorm substantially outperforms pooled normalization; on OPV2V, severity-5 fog AP@0.5 reaches 43.32–58.86 versus 29.42–37.25, with 2.3 ms extra latency.
Scope: It does not address occlusion or scenarios where all agents experience the same distribution shift.

papers.selection_reason: Agent-wise test-time normalization extends test-time batch-norm adaptation to corrupted collaborative perception.
papers.title: Agent-Wise Test-Time Normalization for Camera-Based Cooperative Perception with Corrupted Collaborators
papers.tldr: AgentNorm prevents corrupted collaborators from harming clean ego perception by applying separate test-time normalization per agent.

papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly supplies transcripts for educational NLP, but aggregate word error rate (WER) can conceal errors concentrated in learner speech, multilingual turns, and speaker attribution. We compare platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted, and commercial ASR configurations on held-out sessions of online L2 Spanish interaction between L1 English learners and their instructors and tutors. Because English is the learner's shared first language, the interactions contain Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns. Evaluation combines overall WER and character error rate (CER), WER disaggregated by speaker role and language context, and diarization error rate (DER). We also adapt Whisper large-v3 and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize with LoRA using human-corrected in-domain classroom data. MOSS adaptation produced consistent improvements across speaker roles and language contexts, whereas Whisper showed smaller gains. Domain match proved more important than data volume: Larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora did not outperform the smaller classroom corpus, where learner speech and code-switching are embedded in instructor--learner interaction. The open-weight MOSS adapter was competitive with commercial Muse Voice Transcribe on WER and CER and achieved lower system-provided DER on the recordings eligible for each system. Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech. The findings demonstrate the value of condition-aware evaluation and interactionally matched data for bilingual educational ASR.
bullets: Aggregate WER can hide errors tied to speaker role, language context, and diarization.
The study evaluates multiple ASR configurations on online L2 Spanish classrooms, including Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns.
LoRA adaptation improved MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize consistently; Whisper gains were smaller.
Domain match mattered more than corpus size: a smaller classroom corpus outperformed larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner datasets.
Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on in-domain adaptation of ASR models (Whisper, MOSS) for educational settings, specifically addressing code-switching and learner speech.
papers.title: Beyond Aggregate WER: In-domain Adaptation, Learner Speech, Code-Switching, and Speaker Attribution in Online Spanish Learning Classrooms
papers.tldr: Condition-aware evaluation and interaction-matched adaptation reveal that classroom-specific data improves bilingual educational ASR, especially for learner and code-switched speech.

papers.abstract: We introduce Reduced-rank Mahalanobis Distance (ReMaD), a novel prototypical distance-based refinement to classification and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection using pretrained models without finetuning. We use embeddings of the target dataset to fit closed-form distribution statistics in the model's latent space which can classify in-distribution samples and detect OOD samples, all without training or prior knowledge of the OOD data. Building on prototype classification and OOD detection, we analyze the distribution properties of large pretrained models when processing new datasets; based on this analysis, we formulate a simple modification to Mahalanobis Distance to adapt models' latent space distributions to new domains by removing unused features, without the finetuning or hyperparameter searches required by other adaptation procedures. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method to adapt existing large pretrained image embedding models to new classification domains outside their trained capabilities by testing across four target datasets, with competitive performance in both classification and OOD detection.
bullets: Fits closed-form distribution statistics from target-dataset embeddings in the model’s latent space.
Modifies Mahalanobis Distance by removing unused latent features, yielding a reduced-rank classifier and OOD detector.
Requires no model training, finetuning, or prior knowledge of OOD data.
Evaluated across four target datasets with competitive classification and OOD-detection performance.
Scope: performance depends on the pretrained representation and target-domain embeddings.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
bullets: Builds a domain-agnostic stream from all three ARC-AGI editions, with tasks recurring after gaps and fresh tasks continuously introduced.
Uses a shared feedback budget to compare memory-based and weight-based learners, including agent actions, demonstrations, and retries.
Evaluates post-stream memorization on encountered tasks and generalization on unseen tasks.
Persistence rarely improves memorization without explicit expert guidance, and harness methods underperform simple demonstration caching.
Weight-based learning improves performance on unseen tasks, unlike the tested harness-based methods.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.
bullets: On RoboMME counting tasks, brief pauses or wrist fidgets trigger phantom progress and sharply reduce success.
The failure comes from a temporal shortcut: steady-paced demonstrations make timestamps predictive of progress.
Changing timestamps alone induces early stopping with fast clocks and repetition with slow clocks.
Removing time encodings is insufficient because null-event frames still occupy sampled memory slots.
Event-based memory indexing restores at least half the lost performance without retraining; pause-injection training fails to fix the issue and harms counting.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with $\ell_2$-regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. Building on this characterization, we derive two key consequences. First, we obtain closed-form expressions for the margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, revealing a precise margin trade-off: the regularization parameter controls the balance between retention and adaptation. Second, we analyze adapter merging, proving that merged models achieve positive margin on each task and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that balance margins across tasks and maximize the margin over their union. These results lead to a simple, training-free merging rule, which we term \textit{margin-based LoRA merging} (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of vision and language classification tasks.
authors: Ziqing Xu, Hancheng Min, Lachlan Ewen MacDonald, Salma Tarmoun, Enrique Mallada, Weijie Su, Rene Vidal
bullets: Analyzes LoRA for multiclass linear classification under near-orthogonal tasks and ℓ2 regularization.
Shows that, in an intermediate regularization regime, the optimal adapter aligns with the fine-tuning max-margin solution.
Derives a margin trade-off between retaining pre-training knowledge and adapting to new tasks.
Proves that merged adapters can maintain positive margins across tasks and derives optimal mixing coefficients.
Experiments on vision and language classification tasks validate the theory, with MaLoRA matching or outperforming several baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.
bullets: Formalizes self-evolving multimodal agents using four criteria plus self-reference.
Analyzes a three-stage loop: experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation.
Compares self-evolving and fixed loops to separate scenario-specific limits from design-inherent limits.
Frames mechanism transfer as trade-offs dependent on resources such as output equivalence and checkable outcomes.
Classifies mechanisms as portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant, and proposes matched-budget tests for unresolved judgments.

papers.abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.

papers.abstract: Unipolar neurons are the predominant type of nerve cell in the octopus and in most other invertebrates. A single neurite (a fiber extending from the cell body) branches into a tree that carries both input and output synapses. The branches send graded local outputs to nearby cells, and one site on the main neurite sends a global output to distant targets. This paper proposes a network of such neurons and a learning rule for it. Each neuron is modeled as a tree of passive segments, whose activations are computed exactly as the steady state of a linear system. The network learns from reward alone, with a rule called recirculation. After each forward pass, a second pass sends requested changes of the outputs back through the same connections. Each synapse then adjusts its weight using only quantities available at its own location. Because the system of each neuron is symmetric, this update closely follows the gradient of the error in the predicted reward. Two mechanisms limit forgetting when tasks are learned in sequence: a task code inhibits a different subset of branches in each task, while consolidation lowers the learning rate of synapses that changed strongly in the recent past. The model is evaluated on a sequence of MNIST and Iris tasks. The network maintains high accuracy with low forgetting, whereas gradient-based training of the same network forgets earlier tasks almost completely.
bullets: Models each neuron as a branched tree of passive segments with activations computed from a linear steady-state system.
Uses two network passes: a forward pass and a feedback pass that locally adjusts synapses using only information available at each synapse.
Recirculation exploits neuron symmetry to approximate the gradient of prediction-error reward.
Task codes and consolidation reduce interference and forgetting across sequential tasks.
On sequences of MNIST and Iris tasks, the model maintains high accuracy and low forgetting, unlike gradient-based training of the same network.

papers.title: Unipolar Neuron Networks Trained by Recirculation for Reward-Based Continual Learning

papers.abstract: Personalizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as intelligent assistants has recently emerged as an active research topic, where an MLLM is expected to go beyond generic, one-size-fits-all replies, and instead generate responses grounded in user-specific objects, entities, and concepts encountered during interactions. Nevertheless, existing studies mainly focus on personalizing MLLMs on a static, predefined set of personalized concepts and require users to manually and frequently extend this set to accommodate newly emerging concepts, which is infeasible in dynamic-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we recast conventional MLLM personalization as an Open-Set problem, and propose TAME-O, the first long-context open-set personalized MLLM assistant. Specifically, TAME-O introduces a training-free, plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill (CR Skill). It enables the assistant to automatically unlock novel concepts during prolonged human-MLLM interactions while preventing confusion with previously unlocked ones, allowing the MLLM to continually grasp more and more concepts and progressively refine the modeling of known ones. Extensive experiments under the open-set personalization setting underscore the efficacy of our method.
authors: Rongpei Hong, Jian Lang, Ting Zhong, Fan Zhou
bullets: Existing personalization methods rely on a static concept set that users must manually update, limiting use in dynamic environments.
TAME-O is a long-context, open-set personalized MLLM assistant.
Its plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill automatically unlocks novel concepts during extended interactions.
The method helps distinguish new concepts from previously learned ones while progressively refining known concepts.
Experiments in open-set personalization support the effectiveness of the approach.

papers.abstract: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.
authors: Philip Matthias Winter, Maria Wimmer, Bernhard Sch\"{a}fl, David Major, Dimitrios Lenis, Astrid Berg, Theresa Neubauer, Ariharasudhan Muthusami, Johannes Novotny, Georg Zotti, Katja B\"{u}hler
bullets: Addresses the gap between open-world recognition and interactive medical segmentation.
Combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation.
Converts non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners.
Improves predictions on classes absent from training and transfers zero-shot across unfamiliar domains and imaging modalities.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments. In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed. Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don't capture maritime spatial organization needs. We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places. In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places. The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines. These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.
authors: Kim Alexander Christensen, Dina Zimmermann, Martin Steinert, Eleni Kelasidi
bullets: A representative outdoor 3D scene-graph method transfers reasonably to maritime environments for many geometry-supported objects, but produces substantial physical-entity fragmentation.
The method preserves the underlying mapper and post-processes accumulated evidence to consolidate fragments using metric-semantic cues and geometry-grounded multi-view VLM reasoning.
Consolidated entities are grouped into local places, while maritime macro regions are built from map priors and onboard water and structure observations.
The resulting representation reduces fragmentation, supports matching fixed local places across repeated traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on reviewed queries over tested baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the maritime scene-memory pipeline. It first accumulates persistent map fragments and their observation histories, followed by a conservative geometricsemantic consolidation. Selected geometrically grounded multi-view observations are then processed by a visionlanguage model (VLM) at two abstraction levels: physicalentity reconciliation decides which fragments belong to the same object, while place formation groups persistent entities and observations into meaningful local places. In parallel, coarse maritime regions are derived from geographic topology and onboard water/structure evidence. Local places are associated with these regions and corresponding places are related across repeated traversals, forming a persistent scene memory for contextual retrieval.
Fig. 3: Macro regions compared. The first is defined by [39] while P00 and P03 are from our method. The regions are largely consistent, with one small extra region in P03.

Fig. 4: Place persistence and retrieval at the Northern port quay. The same fixed setting is matched despite different vessel occupancy and reconstructed geometry. Place relations retrieve 6/6 reviewed vessel records across P00 and P03, compared with 3/6 for the 50m radius baseline centered at the P00 anchor location in both surveys.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.
authors: Ruize Zheng, Xuyang Liu, Siyu Ren, Xiaobing Tu, Yinggui Wang, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Standard next-token prediction has model-dependent effects: it helps Llama-3.2-3B but degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base on the same mathematical corpus.
OPMD replaces passive imitation with active, query-driven knowledge acquisition from states visited by the student.
At selected anchor positions, it samples student-policy trajectories and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher.
On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves Qwen over its base model and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline.
The method adds no inference-time overhead and is designed to integrate with continual pre-training pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the OPMD compared with standard NTP, along with training dynamics. (a) Standard NTP: Rigid token-by-token imitation on specialized domain corpora leads to severe policy collapse. (b) OPMD Pipeline: (1) Anchor Token Identification (ATI) & Alignment: A proxy model identifies informative trigger tokens via predictive entropy, followed by context deduplication and strict budget alignment. (2) On-Policy Rollout & Distillation: The student generates continuations from prefix prompts and receives dense teacher guidance through a student-weighted Top-16 log-ratio reward at each rollout step. (c) Performance Dynamics: OPMD completely eliminates NTP policy collapse and achieves substantial, stable reasoning gains across benchmarks.

Figure 4: Training dynamics of Anchor Token Identification (ATI) strategies. MATH-500 and Minerva pass@16 and avg@16 for the Qwen3-1.7B student across all three ATI strategies are plotted against raw training token volume (millions). In the evaluated setting, OPMD variants remain above the base model throughout training, whereas the NTP baseline degrades rapidly. Among these arms, OPMD-high attains the highest observed peak avg@16 on both benchmarks.

Figure 1: Empirical validation of NTP mid-training data sensitivity across base models with different capabilities. Under identical NTP CPT on a 1B-token subset streamed from MegaMathWeb-Pro, Llama-3.2-3B achieves accuracy gains, whereas Qwen3-1.7B-Base suffers substantial performance degradation on the MATH-500 and Minerva benchmarks.

Figure 3: Training dynamics of OPMD with different teacher scales versus standard NTP. Performance trajectories (pass@16 and avg@16) of the Qwen3-1.7B student on MATH-500 and Minerva are plotted against raw training token volume (in millions). NTP performance declines, whereas OPMD improves with either the Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-14B teacher. The two teacher settings show broadly comparable trajectories over the evaluated range.

papers.title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
papers.tldr: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD) makes continual pre-training model-aware by distilling a frozen teacher on trajectories sampled from the evolving student, improving mathematical adaptation where standard next-token training can hurt.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.
authors: Zhijian Li, Jiawei Song, Chao Ren, Yidan Zhang, Peijin Wang, Xian Sun, Kun Fu
bullets: Addresses the lack of verifiable evidence in report-level disaster assessment using vision-language models and agents.
Uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow over bitemporal optical imagery.
Builds a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph to organize disaster-related changes across space and time.
Extracts graph evidence and attaches inline citations, creating a link from each report statement to supporting imagery.
Outperforms compared baselines on DisasterM3 and RSCC, with reported gains of 13.5% and 15.34% on the respective metrics.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of DisasterAgent. The framework processes multimodal inputs through two primary stages. (1) Skill Routing: Driven by the VLM’s interpretation of the query, the system dynamically routes to appropriate skills within a pre-defined repository and seamlessly registers the required functional tools. (2) Skill-Guided Workflow: Guided by the registered skills, the framework sequentially executes a three-step pipeline comprising Perception, Evidence-based Augmentation, and Generation.

Fig. 4. Illustration of the SCE extraction pipeline. The VLM first reasons over the STPG to generate atomic factual claims. Each claim is then independently verified against the raw bitemporal images to obtain a confidence score. Finally, claims with scores above the threshold are filtered to form the robust SCE set.

Fig. 7. Detailed ablation results across individual evaluation metrics on the DisasterM3 benchmark. The figure illustrates the incremental performance improvements in (a) disaster captioning and (b) restoration advice when integrating the expert toolkit, STPG, and EA into the base model.

(c) Caption produced by DisasterAgent, which distinguishes inundated roads and farmland from buildings assessed as intact and retains uncertainty for some structures, with selected claims linked to numbered evidence references (scores: DAP 5, DDR 4, FC 5). (b) Caption produced by Qwen3.5-27B, which misclassifies the event as a mudslide or debris flow and introduces unsupported claims of sediment deposition, altered drainage channels, and restricted road access (scores: DAP 1, DDR 0, FC 1). Fig. 1. Comparison between standard VLM inference and the evidencegrounded reasoning of DisasterAgent. (a) A user query for a disaster impact caption from a bitemporal optical image pair. (b) An existing VLM generates an unverified report and misidentifies the disaster type. (c) DisasterAgent invokes perception tools and attaches inline citations to pixel-level visual evidence, mitigating hallucinations and producing more accurate captions.

Fig. 3. Illustration of the STPG. (a) The Spatial Perception Graph constructs the spatial relationships between diverse geographical targets (e.g., buildings, roads, forests, farmland, and water) within a single phase. (b) The Temporal Evolution Edges establish the cross-phase mappings, explicitly capturing state transitions such as “maintained”, “shrunk”, “expanded”, “transitioned to”, “disappeared”, and “appeared”, while integrating domain-specific damage level assessments (e.g., building damage, road damage).

Fig. 10. Design of the perception tools. (a) Disaster type recognition encodes the pre- and post-disaster images with a shared DINOv3 ViT-L/16, fuses their patch tokens, and predicts one of ten disaster categories together with a confidence score. (b) Building damage assessment segments building instances with SAM3, consolidates them across the two dates, and assigns an instance-level damage label by coverage-aware voting over the masks from ChangeOS or ChangeMamba.

(b) Caption produced by Qwen3.5-27B, which misclassifies the event as a landslide and introduces unsupported descriptions of slope-related soil and rock movement (scores: DAP 2, DDR 2, FC 1). (c) Caption produced by DisasterAgent, which identifies the tsunami and describes damage to buildings, roads, vegetation, and farmland, with selected claims linked to numbered evidence references (scores: DAP 5, DDR 4, FC 5). (d) Ground truth caption.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning enables language models to adapt using rewards derived from their own answers. However, majority voting can reinforce incorrect solutions even when correct alternatives are available. Our training audit shows that false positives (incorrect responses receiving positive rewards) dominate reward errors. We focus on a practical regime where ground-truth rewards are difficult to obtain at scale, while a limited labeled source set is available. We introduce TRUER, a framework that uses limited supervision to train a reward rectifier that distinguishes correctness from consensus. To achieve this goal, we train the rectifier with an emphasis on incorrect majorities and correct minorities, targeting cases where consensus and correctness disagree. After that, we freeze the rectifier and use it to correct rewards during subsequent test-time adaptation. By improving reward accuracy and thereby model performance, TRUER consistently outperforms naive TTRL in both metrics across all evaluated configurations.
authors: Mingxiang Shen, Jinhao Li, Jiaming Xu, Yibo Han, Guohao Dai, Yijia Zhang, Ningyi Xu
bullets: Targets false-positive rewards, especially incorrect answers supported by majority voting.
Uses a limited labeled source set to train a rectifier that separates correctness from consensus.
Emphasizes incorrect majorities and correct minorities, where consensus and correctness conflict.
Freezes the rectifier and applies it to reward correction during later test-time adaptation.
Consistently outperforms naive TTRL on reward accuracy and model performance across evaluated configurations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: TRUER overview and learning dynamics. Top: limited source labels train an erroraware rectifier, which is then frozen to correct rewards during test-time adaptation. Bottom: starting from the same sampled answer distribution, naive TTRL can reinforce a wrong majority, whereas TRUER can recover a correct minority and support policy learning.

Figure 3: Reward correction on MATH500. Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B with a Qwen3-4B rectifier. (a) FP/FN counts on identical responses; retention is relative to majority voting. (b) Reward accuracy over 15-update windows and endpoint Pass@1 on each method’s own trajectory.

Figure 8: All 30 AMC23 TRUER checkpoints. Solid curves are separately completed, matched evaluations of each checkpoint without rectifier-based selection. Dashed lines mark the final epoch 30 TTRL and Oracle scores; their intermediate sampled checkpoints were not retained. papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed. In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).
bullets: Focuses on attacks that manipulate agents’ semantic memory and alter their behavior.
Uses signed knowledge-base entries to prevent unauthorized or malicious knowledge manipulation.
Combines a local Prolog-like Horn-clause inference system with private access to an external knowledge base.
Describes Python implementations offering privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy via IT-PIR.
Scope is semantic memory; episodic and short-term memory attacks are not addressed.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.
authors: Zhiyuan Huang, Shengan Zheng, Chenghu Yang, Song Zhang, Lingyun Li, Chen Yu, Weiquan Huang, Linpeng Huang
bullets: Targets the inference cost and inefficiency of reusing experience in tool-based LLM agents.
Uses rules to shortlist advice and a fine-tuned 1.7B classifier to score candidate suggestions.
Employs micro-contracts for reusable interface checks and a Prompt Value Table to manage repetition, cooldowns, and token budgets.
In AppWorld and WebShop, it achieved 270 successes—29.8% more than Base—and replaced 4,987 diagnosis calls.
Reduced auxiliary control time versus Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0% across the two environments.

papers.abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.
authors: Jakub Suliga, Pankhuri Vanjani, Nisarga Nilavadi, Wolfram Burgard, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Addresses deployment failures caused by shifts in physical dynamics without retraining or identifying changed parameters.
Learns residual corrections from latent prediction errors and applies them both within the latent predictor and to its predicted latent state.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts.
With three adaptation episodes, real-robot success reached 90% for the center-of-mass shift and 100% for the friction shift.
Dual-site correction outperformed single-site adaptation; learned corrections captured both general prediction mismatch and shift-specific information.

papers.tldr: A frozen latent world model can rapidly adapt to changed robot dynamics using self-supervised residual corrections learned from just three interaction episodes.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.
bullets: Distribution shifts arise from geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual changes between training and deployment data.
The study evaluates Alibi-Detect, NannyML, and PyTorch-OOD using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts.
It examines both shift-detection behavior and processing latency.
Results show differences among tools and implementations, motivating lightweight, latency-aware monitoring for resource-constrained aerial platforms.

papers.abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
authors: Xu Luo, Jiaying Yang, Hao Wu, Junlin Xie, Zijin Hong, Ji Zhang, Lianli Gao, Jingkuan Song
bullets: Long action chunks create high-dimensional optimization problems for online RL, making real-world adaptation costly.
ExRL adds a lightweight adapter that predicts each chunk’s execution length.
The adapter is trained with off-policy RL in a low-dimensional space whose expressivity increases with chunk size.
Experiments in simulation and on real robotic tasks show sample-efficient adaptation across diverse long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific tuning.

papers.abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable, users must still recognize when and how to ask for help, leaving many opportunities for useful support unrealized. Proactive agents hold the promise to close this gap, but effective proactivity requires understanding users' real-time activities and personalizing intervention timing so that assistance is offered when it is likely to be helpful rather than disruptive. We introduce deep personalization, a closed-loop process that connects continuous context observation with continual agent adaptation: an agent observes user activity, selectively retains long-term context, and adapts intervention decisions from implicit feedback. We initiate deep personalization in Coco, a proactive desktop agent, by having a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity, maintains compact long-term user modeling context, and learns when assistance is desirable from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal, explicit requests, and repeated work patterns. We further develop efficient on-device strategies to enable the Observer Agent to run on local AI compute platforms without streaming raw activity data off-device. For evaluation at scale without collecting sensitive real-user activity, we introduce a data-synthesis pipeline that transforms existing computer-use trajectories into OSWorld-Persona, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. On OSWorld-Persona, deep personalization improves macro F1 across three model backbones from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48 after adaptation, a 2.4-3.0x relative gain. In a week-long user study, we observe that Coco improves its macro-averaged F1 score from 0.199 to 0.515. These results suggest that on-device deep personalization can make proactive agents more timely and increasingly aligned with each user's everyday work.
authors: Yijia Shao, Song Bian, Junxian Guo, Jindong Jiang, Zhen Dong, Huizi Mao, Diyi Yang, Song Han
bullets: Addresses the challenge of offering help proactively without requiring users to request it or causing disruptive interruptions.
Introduces a closed-loop approach combining continuous activity observation, compact long-term user modeling, and adaptation from implicit feedback.
Implements the approach in Coco using a separate on-device Observer Agent that avoids streaming raw activity data off-device.
Introduces OSWorld-Persona, a synthesized benchmark for evaluating persona-conditioned intervention decisions while avoiding collection of sensitive real-user activity.
Adaptation improves macro F1 from 0.12–0.19 to 0.35–0.48 across three model backbones; a week-long user study reports improvement from 0.199 to 0.515.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
authors: Saber Malekmohammadi, Kevin Kuo, Virginia Smith, Golnoosh Farnadi
bullets: Shows that frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ LoRA with Gaussian initialization approximates full fine-tuning through rank-dependent stochastic gradient perturbations.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art baselines with half the client overhead.

papers.abstract: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).
bullets: Targets spurious program selection and search-cost growth when reasoning from only 2–5 demonstrations.
Uses mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, virtual ATP gating, residual patch synthesis, and early rejection.
Adds 512D random-projection EFE exploration with dead-signature pruning for CPU-native search.
Achieved 57/400 ARC-AGI-1 tasks at pass@2 with 1.62 s/task, including 38/350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks.
Also reported 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting in a synthetic continual-learning stream and 15/15 levels in a 5-game interactive suite.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.
authors: Komal Thareja, Mats Rynge, Berent Aldikacti, Angelina Ju, Ian Lumsden, Anirban Mandal, Rajiv Mayani, Kin Wai Ng, Hamza Safri, Michael Stealey, Sai Swaminathan, Michela Taufer, Karan Vahi, Michael Zink, Ewa Deelman
bullets: Addresses the gap between AI-generated workflow code and safe, observable execution on shared scientific infrastructure.
Projects a curated knowledge base into multiple coding agents and introspects workflow interfaces and execution sites.
Grounds agent diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry for distributed-run awareness.
Constrains actions through federated identity, per-user environments and credentials, observability, and approval controls.
Case studies across scientific workflows, including EHT M87 reconstruction, show the mechanisms operating as designed, including recovery from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution.

The platform tier that spawns and authenticates it is either the JupyterHub gateway on a research cloud or an OOD app on a campus cluster. Model access goes through a provider-neutral gateway with a prompt guard, and usage telemetry flows to a collector inside the platform.

Each transition makes structured information from the workflow and execution systems available to Studio, including planner output, scheduler state, the JSONL event stream, and analyzer reports, together with the introspected argparse schema derived from the workflow generator. Proposed fixes return to the workflow as patches, closing the diagnose, fix, and resubmit lifecycle through replanning and resubmission rather than relying on terminal scraping.

Right: the workflow-debugger agent’s summary after rebuilding and verifying the four container images. Figure 3: The public gateway’s sign-in page. A user signs in through CILogon with their home institution’s credentials, and the workspace is created on first sign-in. The page summarizes the three-step lifecycle (describe, run, watch) and the parts of the workspace.

Figure 2: The Studio home page. The navigation rail on the left lists the views in the order a scientist works (home, analyses, data, examples, resources, notebooks), followed by the chat, terminal, website, feedback, and settings entries. The home page offers four starting actions and four example requests that each hand a prompt to the assistant, and a link that starts the guided tour.

Figure 4: The run panel of a workflow project in Studio, here for a streamflow workflow the assistant built from one chat prompt. The settings (gauge list, lookback window, retry policy, minimum number of gauges, and an optional site catalog) are derived from the generator’s argparse interface by abstract-syntax-tree introspection, without executing user code. Every field, default, and help string comes from the interface the agent wrote. Below the settings the user chooses where the workflow runs (Studio’s shared pool, or only nodes the user connects from their own cluster or allocation). One button prepares, plans, and submits the workflow.

Figure 6: Studio’s live graph view of a completed run, driven by the same event stream the agent reads, beside the chat in its workflow-debugger mode. The workflow (five stream gauges fetched, analyzed, and combined) was built from one chat prompt, and the chat transcript on the right is the agent explaining the fix that made this run succeed after an earlier failure. Node colors track live scheduler state (succeeded, running, pending, failed, held).

Figure 8: The help card. After a failed workflow has been re-run and the rerun has finished, Studio asks one question at the point where the answer is meaningful: did the assistant’s suggestion fix it? The four answers are one click each, and the card is rate-limited so that it does not become a survey users learn to dismiss. Here the EEG workflow of Section 8.5 succeeded on its fourth run after the assistant diagnosed the earlier failure. The chat is in its default mode, which routes each message to a specialist agent role.

papers.abstract: We studied domain shift in adult elbow fracture classification from radiographs when training on a large public dataset and deploying on a small, institution-specific dataset (UofL). We implemented a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) to align feature distributions across source (MURA) and target (UofL) domains while optimizing fracture classification. A pretrained convolutional backbone was adapted to grayscale inputs; the task head predicts fracture presence, and a gradient-reversal-based domain head encourages domain-invariant features via adversarial learning. We compared four settings: (1) Source-only, (2) Target-only (limited labels), (3) Naive merge (pooled training), and (4) DANN (MURA to UofL). Evaluation on UofL test data uses AUC-ROC, and accuracy. DANN outperformed Source-only and Naive merge baselines by reducing domain bias without overfitting to the small target set. Ablations showed that progressive adversarial weight, dataset-size-aware domain loss, and domain-balanced sampling improved stability and target performance. Results demonstrated that domain alignment is a practical path to robust clinical generalization from public to local data.

papers.abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.
authors: Ke Wang, Atakan Topcu, Hossein Momeni, Molin Zhang

papers.abstract: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is commonly trained on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, but storing and replaying those features becomes a practical bottleneck for long-form video, especially in incremental TAS where past-task data must remain available to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Recent TAS replay and condensation methods reduce this burden, but they rely on dense frame-wise annotations and allocate storage through fixed segment-level structures, limiting their flexibility for long procedural videos whose frame complexity varies substantially over time. We introduce Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (ARQ-VAE), a compact and label-free memory representation for TAS features that learns a discrete residual quantization of frame-level video features and then adaptively truncates the residual chain on a per-frame basis, retaining only the residual prefix that best reconstructs each frame feature. This yields a practical compact feature memory that does not depend on frame-wise labels and can therefore support multiple TAS settings with the same stored representation, while a lightweight fine-tuning stage further improves reconstruction quality for the truncated codes that are actually retained. Across standard TAS benchmarks, ARQ-VAE achieves a substantially improved storage-performance trade-off over prior replay and condensation baselines. On Breakfast, our final representation reduces training-set storage from 28 GB for the original I3D feature bank to 10 MB while retaining strong downstream segmentation performance; with ASFormer, it achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in the supervised setting. We further show that the same label-free memory remains effective for incremental and unsupervised TAS. We position ARQ-VAE as a practical memory representation for TAS and a promising direction for broader dataset condensation applications.
authors: Gerard Donahue, Guven Gergerli, Ayush Gupta, Reza Ghoddoosian, Enna Sachdeva, Faizan Siddiqui
bullets: Addresses the storage and replay bottleneck of large frame-feature banks, especially for incremental TAS and long procedural videos.
Uses discrete residual quantization with per-frame adaptive truncation, retaining only the code prefix needed to reconstruct each feature.
Requires no frame-wise labels, enabling one shared memory representation across multiple TAS settings.
A lightweight fine-tuning stage improves reconstruction of the truncated codes that are actually stored.
On Breakfast, storage drops from 28 GB to 10 MB while ASFormer achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in supervised TAS; the abstract reports improved storage-performance trade-offs over prior baselines.

papers.abstract: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.
authors: Delin Zhao, Zhengrong Yue, Junlin He, Yali Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed practice sources, which may fail to expose new weaknesses as capabilities change.
Alternates updates to a curriculum harness that proposes informative challenges and an execution harness that develops reusable revisions.
Uses admitted challenge snapshots to compare execution revisions while keeping the other component fixed.
Starting from compact LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting deployment outperformed evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels.

On LIBERO-PRO, it achieved 74.0% success, improving over the initial deployment and direct VLA-controller execution; case studies cover practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

papers.abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.
authors: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
bullets: Third Eye separates immediate utility from the utility of a subsequent native update.
