papers.tldr: Generalist AI models can directly control diverse robots with strong zero-shot reliability, outperforming specialist manipulation policies and improving further through persistent memory.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO)}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.
authors: Haoyu Wang, Ru Wang, Yuanyuan Wang, Jiaxian Guo, Mingming Gong
bullets: TTRL relies on self-generated majority-vote pseudo-labels, but their reliability is not fully understood.
Pseudo-label error consists of population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation; the former is generally unidentifiable without external supervision.
PC-Dr.DPO uses observed vote reliability for prompt-conditional robust reweighting, reducing the influence of sampling-sensitive prompts.
A cache-based mechanism is added to limit self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation.
Across 30 settings, it matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.

Uses a dynamically computed risk mask to protect stability-critical factual parameter regions.
Integrates edited knowledge at inference with prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion.
Experiments on two multimodal benchmarks show competitive performance across five metrics and stability over 1,000 sequential updates.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt--parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate's own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.
authors: Jungtaek Kim, Jaden Park, Jongwon Jeong, Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis, Kangwook Lee

Independent probing and deployment-only feedback introduce additional costs and assumptions.
Experiments show fewer switches can help or hurt; text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection but more failures because it excludes stronger configurations.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
authors: Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of surpassing human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning.
Learns a distinct world model for each episode by updating model parameters at test time, rather than relying only on contextual memory.

papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) has evolved from 2D image-based approaches to multi-modal methods that leverage the complementary nature of RGB images and 3D point clouds. Among these, memory bank-based methods, which identify anomalies by the discrepancy between each query patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, have proven particularly effective. However, two limitations remain: (i) employing frozen pretrained encoders yields insufficient discrimination between normal and anomalous features due to the domain gap, while existing contrastive learning-based adaptation struggles to capture the spatial relationships required for precise localization; and (ii) pixel-level anomaly maps interpolated from patch-level distance scores remain coarse, lacking fine-grained detail. To address these limitations, we propose EPAR (Embedding Predictive Adaptation and Refinement). We adapt encoders by predicting the embeddings of masked regions to capture spatial relationships, together with patch-level Variance-Invariance-Covariance (VIC) regularization, resolving the poor discriminability between normal and anomalous features caused by the domain gap. We further propose a Noise Suppression Network that refines coarse maps by learning the relational discrepancy between each patch feature and its nearest normal prototype, rather than the anomaly's appearance. This relational signal remains valid for unseen real defects, despite being learned from synthetic anomalies. EPAR demonstrates strong practical applicability, excelling in few-shot settings and improving AUPRO@1% on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies by +1.8% and +1.9%, respectively.

bullets: Addresses domain-gap-induced feature ambiguity and coarse patch-level anomaly localization in RGB–3D detection.
Uses masked-region embedding prediction with patch-level VIC regularization to adapt pretrained encoders and capture spatial relationships.
Introduces a Noise Suppression Network that refines anomaly maps using discrepancies between patches and nearest normal prototypes.
Learns refinement from synthetic anomalies while targeting relational signals that transfer to unseen real defects.
Improves AUPRO@1% by 1.8% on MVTec 3D-AD and 1.9% on Eyecandies, with strong few-shot applicability.

papers.abstract: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
authors: Tong Guan, Alexander Chemeris, Yiqing Guo, Warren Jin, Zhao Li, Shirui Pan, Ming Jin
bullets: Introduces Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), replacing offline one-shot processing with persistent stateful reasoning over open-ended streams.
Presents LiveTS-Suite: 18 tasks across six capabilities, covering over 5K streams, 2.2B timesteps, and 15K response events.
Combines hybrid temporal encoding, persistent memory for historical evidence and task states, and elastic inference synchronization to reduce lag.
Reports a score of 90.0 versus 79.3 for Opus 5, with 206× lower p95 latency than its backbone using a 4B-parameter model.
Demonstrates real-time continuous understanding on a Jetson edge device.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
authors: Ruiyi Yang, Zechen Li, Lihuan Li, Du Yin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim

Releases records only after reserved-probe verification meets relative and absolute criteria; failed skills remain retrievable.
Reduces the retrievable-memory footprint while staying close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate or random release.
Improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls across interactive and reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: While feed-forward segmentation networks perform well on large cohorts, they degrade in constrained clinical settings with few training samples and imaging artifacts. Human vision, by contrast, remains robust under these conditions, a property partly attributed to the recurrent and feedback connectivity of the visual cortex, which refines visual information over time. Inspired by this, we append lightweight recurrent refinement blocks to segmentation backbones, namely Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), modern Hopfield networks and convolutional GRUs, and study their behaviour as the number of iterations increases at test time (including beyond the training horizon). Evaluated on two open-source datasets, Kvasir- SEG and ARCADE, our recurrent blocks add less than 1.5% parameters and yield gains on clean data (up to 1.4 pp) and under noise (up to 17 pp) while reducing HD95. Code is available at https://github.com/joaodsmarques/recurrencehelpsegmentation .
authors: Joao D. S. Marques, David Calhas, Arlindo L. Oliveira
bullets: Feed-forward segmentation models can degrade in small-sample, artifact-heavy clinical settings.

On Kvasir-SEG and ARCADE, the blocks add under 1.5% parameters, improve clean-data performance by up to 1.4 percentage points, and improve noisy performance by up to 17 percentage points while reducing HD95.

papers.abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. papers.abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.
authors: Boran Zhao, Yanbin Hu, Jun Ye, Zhenxian Hu, Yuxin Zhai, Jin Cui, Pengju Ren
bullets: Addresses noisy, redundant episodic memories that obscure transferable manipulation principles in complex 3D scenes.
Consolidates detailed experiences into compact semantic memories capturing essential, generalizable knowledge.
Prunes episodic memories already represented by semantic memories to increase effective memory capacity.
Composes multiple episodic and semantic memories for more flexible cross-scenario task solving.
Evaluated on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus across VLA backbones; pi_0’s average success rate improves from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

papers.abstract: Data stream processing has become central to modern machine learning applications, with concept drifts and novel class appearances posing the primary challenges faced by recognition methods. Adapting to concept drifts while also being able to detect novel classes and distinguish groups of unknown observations can be seen as a step towards effective method employment in an open-world setting. This work proposes a classification method that can detect and learn the distributions of new, unknown classes, as well as adapt to concept drifts once the distribution of known classes shifts. The proposed method uses the autoencoders' reconstruction errors and the KDE that models their distribution. The autoencoders incrementally adapt to the changing distributions of known classes via weight fine-tuning, resulting in continuous adjustment to evolving concepts. Conducted experiments used a diverse set of synthetic data streams, embeddings of a real-world static CIFAR dataset arranged into a stream to simulate concept drifts and the emergence of unknowns, as well as real-world datasets where novelty is observed. The methodology was compared with state-of-the-art approaches with three-criterion recognition quality assessment and resource consumption evaluation. The results indicate that the proposed method is competitive with reference approaches in stationary environments and performs best when concept drifts occur.
bullets: Addresses open-world stream recognition with both shifting known classes and emerging unknown classes.
Uses autoencoders’ reconstruction errors modeled by kernel density estimation to identify and learn novel-class distributions.

Evaluated on synthetic streams, simulated CIFAR streams, and real-world novelty datasets using recognition and resource criteria.
Competitive in stationary settings and performs best among compared approaches under concept drift.

papers.abstract: Real-world robot deployment requires adapting learned policies to unseen obstacles without collecting new demonstrations or retraining. Existing policy-level guidance often applies obstacle corrections independently at individual horizon steps, which may address local obstacle violations but fail to coordinate the action sequence into a complete, task-directed detour. How obstacle responses should be propagated across the action horizon to coordinate complete, task-directed avoidance motion remains underexplored. We introduce an inferencetime obstacle-guidance framework for pretrained relative-action diffusion policies. It rolls out cumulative relative actions into a workspace trajectory, evaluates obstacle interactions along the trajectory with an SDF-based obstacle model, and propagates each obstacle response to all contributing action increments during denoising. Real-robot experiments across seven obstacleconstrained scenarios spanning four manipulation tasks show that our method achieves 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free task successes, compared with 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action pointwise guidance. Ablations show that the relative-action horizoncoupled formulation provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.

Ablations indicate that relative-action horizon coupling provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection (L3OD) is a fundamental 3D perception task, yet its performance is often compromised by domain shifts arising from diverse sensor configurations and environmental conditions. Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods primarily leverage self-supervision in the spatial domain, yet they frequently confound semantic content with domain style due to the sparse, non-Euclidean nature of point clouds. To overcome this limitation, we propose FIND (Frequency INvariance Disentanglement), a novel TTA framework that precisely disentangles domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference within the frequency domain. Our methodology utilizes B-Spline fitting to construct locally adaptive filters integrated into a dual-stream architecture: an Invariant Stream extracts robust features to guide pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency against domain perturbations. By combining invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization, our approach dynamically extracts robust domain-invariant features while suppressing domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and robust corruption benchmarks demonstrate that FIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/llldx03/FIND.
authors: Dongxiao Li, Zixuan Hu, Ling-Yu Duan
bullets: Addresses sensor- and environment-induced domain shifts in LiDAR-based 3D object detection.

Experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and corruption benchmarks report significant improvements over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.
authors: Chao Liang, Ke Chen, Fengxiaoxiao Li, Shibo Huang, Yufeng Sun, Zhaokai Yin, Jianhuan Lai, Haozhe Feng, Chenghuan Jia, Zhipeng Zhang

Reports strong benchmark and real-robot performance, including 45.40% success on 100 BEHAVIOR tasks, 95.05% on RoboTwin 2.0 with the full system, and 57.92% across 12 household tasks.
In a long-horizon coffee task, history-conditioned recovery substantially improves completion after filter-handling failures; the system also reports 427.1 samples/s training throughput.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/ACTOR.
authors: Jihwan Bang, Sumyeong Ahn, Hwanjun Song, Jae-Gil Lee
bullets: Addresses the gap between fully unsupervised TTA and directly supervised online adaptation.
Enforces a future-only constraint: queried labels cannot correct the current prediction, only later samples.
Routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label querying, and memory-based correction.
Uses consistency and reliability checks over previously queried labels to reuse sparse evidence conservatively.
Improves strong VLM-TTA baselines across ten cross-domain benchmarks and an ImageNet-based domain-transfer benchmark with negligible inference overhead.

ACTOR instantiates this idea in a training-free and plug-and-play manner.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $\pi_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses skill retention and phase-dependent skill composition in vision-language-action policies.
Finds that per-skill low-rank updates occupy a distinguishable low-dimensional parameter subspace.
Stores each skill as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter, augmented with trainable residuals.
Uses a VLM-conditioned per-chunk router supervised by an action-derived oracle to select primitives based on task progress.
On RoboCasa365, reports 56.43% atomic-skill and 20.00% composite success, versus 17.86% and 17.50% for a two-stage π₀.₅-LoRA baseline; also validates on a real AgileX PIPER robot.

papers.abstract: The limited supervision available for the few-shot adaptation of vision-language models makes gradient estimation particularly noisy. We find that the gradient magnitudes are severely miscalibrated, while the signs of a small top-magnitude subset remain informative. This motivates SignSparseSGD and DynSignSparseSGD, two state-free optimizers that use gradient magnitudes only to select where to update and fixed-magnitude signs to decide how to update. The static variant fixes the support after the first minibatch. The dynamic variant refreshes it at every step. Across 11 datasets, three CLIP backbones, and five shot levels, the proposed methods are competitive with or outperform parameter-efficient and optimization-based baselines on average, while exhibiting markedly lower sensitivity to long training schedules. They introduce no task-specific modules, maintain no first- or second-moment optimizer states, and use one shared configuration across datasets, backbones, and shot levels. Our code is included in the supplementary materials and will be released upon publication.
authors: Nairouz Mrabah, Ismail Ben Ayed, Mahdi S. Hosseini, Eric Granger
bullets: Few-shot supervision makes gradient estimates noisy, with magnitudes unreliable but signs informative among the largest-magnitude gradients.
The methods select update locations using gradient magnitudes and apply fixed-magnitude signed updates without optimizer state.
SignSparseSGD fixes the selected parameters after the first minibatch; DynSignSparseSGD refreshes them at every step.
Across 11 datasets, three CLIP backbones, and five shot levels, they are competitive with or outperform listed baselines on average.
They are less sensitive to long training schedules and use one shared configuration without task-specific modules.

papers.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.
authors: Chris von Csefalvay, Pranav Doma, Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Tam\'as F\"oldi
bullets: Evaluates large editor models modifying a smaller target model across ten text-editing objectives.
Constrains editors to four weight-access tools and fixed budgets for rollouts and tensor inspection.
Uses clean-environment validation to compare edited and unmodified target models.
Finds highly uneven capabilities across models and tasks, with Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol notably strong.
Alias acquisition and recoding were easiest, while structured responses resisted all attempts; success did not generalize well across task families.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.
authors: Hengwei Zhao, Qirui Wang, Zhuo Zheng, Xiaoyan Lu, Rusty Feagin, Wenzhe Jiao
bullets: Addresses the labeling bottleneck in rapid disaster-response mapping, where PEFT alone does not ensure label efficiency.

Experiments on global disaster benchmarks show effectiveness and robustness; a 2025 Los Angeles wildfire application demonstrates practical potential under limited supervision.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in long-lived systems, where task requirements may change after training. In such settings, part of the original output space may become obsolete: a class, prediction region, or learned behaviour may no longer be valid. Existing approaches either leave the obsolete behaviour intact or require fine-tuning, which can be expensive. We propose Deep Repurposing (DR), a post-hoc framework for adapting models under task obsolescence. DR estimates the latent geometry of obsolete and retained regions, removes obsolete-supporting components, and reallocates retained-compatible evidence through an analytic repair map without gradient updates. This yields repaired predictions and representations in which obsolete regions no longer act as valid outputs, while useful obsolete structure can support the retained task. Across multiple task settings, DR removes obsolete behaviour while preserving retained utility. More importantly, across classification benchmarks, DR matches or exceeds competing unlearning and editing baselines in retained accuracy, eliminates obsolete predictions, and adapts up to $60\times$ faster than competing unlearning methods.
bullets: Addresses task obsolescence in long-lived deployed models, where parts of the output space become invalid.

papers.abstract: Alignment does not eliminate behavioral errors in language models. Models may still refuse benign requests, call unnecessary tools, or yield to false user claims. Current methods mitigate such errors as a computation problem, and rarely explore if the desired behavior is already encoded in the model's representation. Motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information remains linearly decodable from the final hidden state even when the resulting logits produce the undesired behavior, we introduce HeadEdit, a gradient-free method that calibrates model behavior through the unembedding matrix. HeadEdit extracts a low-rank behavioral subspace from paired completions and uses each prompt's coordinates within it to generate a vocabulary-wide correction, thereby implementing implicitly adaptive steering without manually specified target tokens or parameter updates. HeadEdit improves all nine experimental settings across three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities. It also reveals a connection to gradient-based alignment. HeadEdit's low-dimensional representation partly predicts how preference tuning changes output logits on unseen prompts. The subspace learned from the model can also be reused after tuning, improving performance without re-extracting or retuning. These results show that HeadEdit provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable way to calibrate model behavior through the unembedding matrix.
bullets: Addresses residual behavioral errors such as unnecessary refusals, tool calls, and susceptibility to false user claims.
Uses paired completions to learn behavior-relevant directions, then steers outputs without gradients, parameter updates, or manually chosen target tokens.
Improves performance across nine settings spanning three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities.
The learned subspace partly predicts preference-tuning logit changes on unseen prompts and can be reused after tuning without re-extraction.
Provides a lightweight, interpretable link between representation-based steering and gradient-based alignment.

papers.abstract: We study an endogenous nonstationary stochastic bandit problem with latent linear dynamics, where actions affect both immediate rewards and the future evolution of an unobserved latent state. Rewards are bilinear in the current action and latent state, inducing history-dependent rewards and a nontrivial long-horizon planning problem. The existing explore-then-commit approach achieves $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret by uniformly exploring to estimate the latent dynamics and then committing to an optimized open-loop action sequence. We show that this rate can be improved via adaptive block-level optimism. Our key step is a cyclic approximation: under stable dynamics, the infinite-memory reward process can be truncated, and the open-loop benchmark can be approximated by optimizing a finite-memory block-level proxy. Building on this reduction, we propose a UCB-based block algorithm that maintains confidence sets for the truncated dynamics parameters and selects blocks optimistically. We prove a regret bound of order $\tilde{O}(\sqrt T)$, significantly improving over the previous $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ guarantee for the same model. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first $\tilde{O}(\sqrt T)$ regret guarantee for latent linear-dynamics bandits with bilinear reward observations and an open-loop action-sequence benchmark.
bullets: Actions influence both immediate bilinear rewards and an unobserved evolving state, creating history dependence and long-horizon planning challenges.
Stable dynamics enable truncating the infinite-memory reward process and approximating the open-loop benchmark with a finite-memory block proxy.
The proposed UCB-based method maintains confidence sets for truncated dynamics and selects action blocks optimistically.
The analysis establishes a \(\tilde O(\sqrt T)\) regret guarantee for the model and benchmark studied.

Figure 2: Cumulative reward on delayed latent linear-dynamics bandit instances with different levels of stability and delay.

papers.abstract: Long-term object search requires learning where objects usually appear from repeated but uneven observations of a changing environment. We formulate retrospective open-vocabulary memory as probabilistic inference from censored observations, where the key idea is to reason with evidence per opportunity: a detection or non-detection should influence belief only in proportion to the robot's opportunity to observe the corresponding location. We introduce ECROM, which uses this principle to estimate long-term prevalence for concepts specified only at query time and converts the resulting belief directly into an active-search prior. To evaluate this problem, we introduce a controlled long-term benchmark in ten HM3D homes that independently varies object placement and observation opportunity across repeated traversals. ECROM improves support-level AP on held-out queries by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric. The benchmark, dataset, and code will be open-sourced. Project page: https://jiaming.im/ecrom/
bullets: Addresses learning object-location prevalence from repeated, uneven observations.
Models detections and non-detections as censored evidence weighted by observation opportunity.
Supports concepts specified only at query time and converts beliefs into active-search priors.
Evaluated on a controlled benchmark spanning ten HM3D homes with varied placements and observation opportunities.
Improves support-level AP by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric.

papers.abstract: Token-level certainty is widely used as a proxy for correctness in LLM training and inference. However, the performance of certainty-based methods depends both on the information in certainty scores and on how those scores are used. We therefore directly assess certainty's predictive ability through controlled empirical evaluations across models and tasks. We distinguish two prediction targets: identifying questions a model is more likely to answer correctly and distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. In our experiments, certainty is generally better at identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly than at distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. Certainty also varies systematically across token types and positions within words, reflecting local properties of words and text form. Information about question difficulty appears early in generation, while the weaker information about answer correctness is more concentrated near the end. These findings show that the information certainty provides for decisions depends on the prediction target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions in the response are included in aggregation. We further demonstrate the practical value of these findings for test-time compute. We allocate the number of responses using certainty early in generation and weight answer votes using certainty near the end of each response. Compared with a fixed-sampling majority-voting baseline, this approach increases overall accuracy from 78.71\% to 79.54\% while reducing generated-token cost by 82.4\%.
bullets: Certainty better predicts which questions a model will answer correctly than which response to a given question is correct.
Certainty varies by token type and word position, so aggregation choices affect its usefulness.
Difficulty information appears early in generation, whereas weaker correctness signals concentrate near the response’s end.
Using early certainty to allocate samples and late certainty to weight votes raises accuracy from 78.71% to 79.54% while cutting generated-token cost by 82.4%.
The findings depend on the prediction target, model, certainty metric, and selected token positions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes token-level certainty in LLMs and proposes a test-time compute strategy using certainty for sampling and voting, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Certainty Is Not Just Correctness: Rethinking Token-Level Certainty in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Token-level certainty is more useful for judging question difficulty than answer correctness, but strategically using it at different generation stages improves accuracy while greatly reducing test-time compute.

papers.abstract: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-ν_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.
bullets: Nearest-neighbor preservation alone can miss large-scale structural errors: high local fidelity may still move many passages between themes.
The study evaluates local fidelity at 10 neighbors and global fidelity across 30–50% of the memory.
A bound links global fidelity to near–far rank violations, which closely track compression distance noise.
Locality-aware quantization (LAQ) adds a far-end hinge objective to OPQ codebooks while preserving bytes, rotation, and search.
LAQ improved global fidelity in all 52 held-out runs, led seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scaled to one million passages, and preserved evidence recall.

papers.abstract: Much of human culture is tacit and is typically learned through situated social interaction. As LLMs are deployed as interactive agents across diverse communities, assessing their cultural competence demands moving beyond existing question-answering approaches, shifting from what they know to how they adapt. In this work, we broaden the scope of cultural adaptation in NLP by investigating whether LLMs can adapt through repeated interactions via a sandbox environment. By reframing cultural adaptation as a continuous process of norm assimilation through social interaction, our work demonstrates that memory mechanisms foster longitudinal learning across repeated interactions, facilitate transfer to different social settings, and enable multilingual norm assimilation across five languages. Together, our findings lay the groundwork for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.
bullets: Frames cultural adaptation as continuous norm assimilation through situated interaction.
Uses a sandbox environment to study adaptation over repeated interactions.
Finds that memory mechanisms support longitudinal learning and transfer across social settings.

papers.abstract: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is observational theory learning: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.
bullets: Generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs.
Learners receive only observed transitions—without program labels, task identities, or support examples.
Controls program complexity, curriculum progression, recurring subprograms, and continual evaluation with level skipping.
Seven representative baselines plateau below ceiling, with larger gaps at higher curriculum levels.
Targets observational theory learning, beyond solving isolated few-shot visual reasoning puzzles.

Theory application combines them to explain new observations.

papers.abstract: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL
bullets: Targets privacy-preserving medical FL under long-tailed local and global data distributions.
Addresses the common assumption that test data follow a uniform, known distribution.
Uses adaptive re-sampling, expert-classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to reduce classifier and feature-space bias.
Ensembles retrained expert classifiers at inference to handle agnostic test distributions.
Experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets report better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: GTAFL framework workflow: (1) Clients receive global model and expert parameters, then perform local training with GI-GDS sampling and gradient computation. (2) Clients transmit class-wise gradients and model parameters to the server. (3) Server performs aggregation, expert retraining using optimized global federated features, and self-supervised refinement with unlabeled data. (4) The server sends the updated global model and expert classifiers parameters to clients. (5) Expert ensemble inference for test-agnostic prediction.

Fig. 5: Performance comparison of GTAFL and CReFF on varying CIFAR10 data fractions. GTAFL demonstrates greater robustness as the data size decreases. papers.abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.

papers.abstract: A child who learned to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace this to what learners read when deciding. A position, count or time takes new values as input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine solves five benchmark tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves, among them duplication and binary addition, and beyond the reach of its cycles it fails on the curve the theory predicts. Given larger cycles after training, a machine that saw no string longer than five symbols reverses a string of a million without error. Its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
bullets: Coordinate-like inputs such as positions and counts can exceed training experience, while coincidence-based relations remain size-invariant.
The proposed memory uses cycles whose state grows with input size but is read through finite, symmetry-based observations, linked conceptually to grid cells, place cells, and hippocampal indexing.
Its computational power is characterized as equivalent to Turing-machine computation synchronized with input.
Trained on strings of at most 40 symbols, it solves five benchmark tasks that the abstract reports LSTMs and Transformers do not solve, including duplication and binary addition.
With larger cycles after training, it reverses a million-symbol string despite seeing no training string longer than five; performance fails beyond cycle capacity as theoretically predicted.

papers.abstract: Lifelong object maps must estimate whether an object remains at its previously observed location after it leaves view. Existing persistence filters rely on class-based survival priors, making them difficult to apply reliably in open-vocabulary settings. We introduce HiPer, a hierarchical persistence filter that derives persistence beliefs directly from data rather than semantic categories. For a new object, HiPer retrieves visually and geometrically similar training instances and estimates an initial survival rate from their observed histories, without requiring class labels. This estimate initializes a conjugate Beta belief over the object's survival probability, which is updated in closed form using detections and missed observations under Rosen's persistence-filter framework. When an object is re-identified at a new location, its persistence belief is transferred with the object, enabling the map to learn object-specific mobility over time. Experiments on 120 held-out simulated sequences show that HiPer consistently achieves the best performance among competing methods. Retrieval-based priors outperform CLIP-derived label priors, and object-specific online learning provides further gains. Results on 47 held-out 3RScan environments demonstrate that the proposed retrieval-based prior also outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in real-world settings.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting whether out-of-view objects remain at their mapped locations in open-vocabulary settings.
Retrieves similar training instances to initialize a Beta belief over each object’s survival probability.
Updates persistence beliefs in closed form from detections and missed observations.
Transfers beliefs when objects are re-identified, enabling object-specific mobility learning over time.
Outperforms competing methods in simulated sequences and held-out 3RScan environments; retrieval priors beat CLIP-based label priors.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.
bullets: Addresses test-time scaling when a strong target-problem verifier is unavailable.
Uses asymmetric self-play to generate and improve solutions without verifier dependence.
On a difficulty-calibrated LiveCodeBench v6 subset, it outperforms evaluated baselines across verifier strengths.
In the no-verifier setting, it delivers a 35% absolute improvement in mean@8.
Performance gains largely disappear when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Test-Time Self-Play. The solver policy is rewarded for correctly solving the synthetic problems, while the proposer is rewarded for generating synthetic problems near the solver’s current learning frontier (both via GRPO; see the red arrows). The synthetic problem history provides context for the proposer and fills a replay buffer B. After a sufficient number of iterations, the test-time trained solver can then attempt the target problem.

papers.abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.
bullets: Addresses the stability–plasticity trade-off in continual reinforcement learning.
Separates slow, generalizable long-term learning from fast, situation-specific adaptation.
Introduces a novel non-parametric approximation for transient value estimation in complex tasks.
Enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic.
The approach is evaluated empirically and theoretically, with scope focused on the studied task settings.

papers.abstract: Scientific predictors guide costly experiments, yet returned measurements often reveal errors that matter for subsequent experimental choices. WeightLoop turns this feedback into persistent model updates through a reusable Weight-Space Programming (WSP) editor. We use GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek to construct update programs from the scientific objective, model computation and editable parameters. These programs use accumulated measurements to estimate parameter corrections, validate them on feedback and save accepted changes in the original model. With identical feedback and writable parameters, four pretrained scientific predictors obtain 5.10-18.56% lower primary error. For weather prediction, changing four output-bias parameters reduces root mean squared error by 13.28%. Functional ranking and sequential discovery further connect reusable editing programs to improved experimental choices.
bullets: Addresses the problem of scientific models failing to incorporate newly returned measurements into future choices.
Introduces reusable Weight-Space Programming editors that generate parameter-update programs from the objective, model, and editable weights.
Programs estimate and validate corrections from accumulated feedback, then save accepted updates in the original model.
Across four pretrained scientific predictors, the approach reduced primary error by 5.10–18.56% under identical feedback and writable parameters.
A weather-prediction edit to four output-bias parameters reduced RMSE by 13.28%; ranking and sequential discovery also benefited.

papers.abstract: We study a two-stage online optimization problem: at each round, a meta-learner first selects an agent-environment pair, then the chosen agent interacts with the environment, and receives a reward. We introduce Meta-Frieren, a general framework for maximizing cumulative reward in this setting. Our analysis yields a simple UCB-style criterion for meta-level selection and recovers prior guarantees as special cases while extending them to broader settings. We instantiate Meta-Frieren with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions. We also derive, to our knowledge, the first high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling, specialize it to finite and parametric function classes, and integrate it into Meta-Frieren. Experiments support our theoretical results and demonstrate that Meta-Frieren can be successfully applied to hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes.
bullets: Addresses two-stage online learning, where a meta-learner chooses an agent–environment pair before interaction.
Introduces a UCB-style meta-level selection criterion that recovers prior guarantees and extends them to broader settings.
Instantiates the framework with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions.
Derives a high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling and incorporates it into Meta-Frieren.
Experiments support the theory and demonstrate hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes.

papers.abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).
bullets: Addresses the limits of one-off benchmarks and holistic scores for deployed agents.
Evaluates span, trace, conversation, and engagement levels across Execution, Substance, Trajectory, and Results, with Conduct as a constraint.
Uses provenance, adjudication, versioned rules, and atomic evidence to handle biased raters and censored outcomes.
An inner loop audits evidence, rules, and metrics; an outer loop drives improvement through per-component regression checks.
Case studies suggest evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring, with reported ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81 and kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth, which limits context length, batch size, and decoding throughput.
Amortises values using lightweight per-head predictors, storing residuals only for poorly reconstructed tokens; this provides 4× near-lossless value compression.
Combines value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression in an asymmetric pipeline.
Reconstructs only selected KV pairs during decoding, achieving up to 5× higher peak decode throughput at 4× compression.
Composes with quantisation and eviction to reach 26.9× compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces LowRAM, a test-time KV cache compression method using value amortization and low-rank keys, directly addressing memory efficiency and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
papers.tldr: LowRAM compresses KV caches by separately exploiting low-rank keys and predictable values, enabling aggressive, composable memory savings with near-lossless decoding.

papers.abstract: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.
authors: Sihang Chen, Chen Ye, Wei Chen, Xiaohan Lei, Zhipeng Tang, Sha Zhang, Yuan Zhang, Zixuan Chen, Jiajun Deng, Houqiang Li, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Introduces nine tasks requiring interaction history at key decision points.
Covers environment memory—locations, attributes, and relationships—and process memory for task progress and scheduling.
Uses Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation to derive later constraints from the robot’s own earlier actions, reducing fixed-target shortcuts.
Provides 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training and an HMAP baseline with structured memory and subgoal-conditioned control.
Scope: evaluates memory-dependent behavior in mobile manipulation rather than general-purpose memory.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering information that is no longer visible, such as an object's location before occlusion or the order of a demonstrated action sequence. A large vision-language planner can read this history, but calling it before every action chunk is slow and costly. We present a three-tier system for the RoboMME benchmark. GPT-6 Astra (System 2) selects a grounded subtask from stored visual history, a $\pi_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy (System 1) executes it, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor (System 1.5) checks after each action chunk whether the subtask is finished. The instruction is kept until the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs, while the policy keeps acting on new observations. On RoboMME, the system succeeds in 79.13% of episodes with an average of 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode. This is 34.62 points above the best published non-oracle baseline and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which gives the low-level policy ground-truth subgoals.
authors: Bingao Chen, Haoquan Fang, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the need to remember occluded object locations and demonstrated action order without invoking a large planner before every action chunk.
Astra (System 2) selects grounded subtasks from visual history; π0.5 executes them; a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor detects subtask completion.
The system retains instructions until completion or a task-specific event, while the policy acts continuously on new observations.
It averages 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode, outperforming the best published non-oracle baseline by 34.62 points.
Performance remains 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which provides ground-truth subgoals.

papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of the daily evolution of sea ice concentration (SIC) is central to improving the credibility and operational forecasting capability of deep learning-based sea ice prediction. However, existing deep learning methods often couple the underlying sea ice evolution relationships and data errors within high-dimensional nonlinear mappings, making it difficult to construct a stable and verifiable evolution core and apply it reliably to practical forecasting. To address this issue, this study proposes a reanalysis-forecast dual-domain decoupled framework for learning sea ice evolution operators. The framework builds upon a lightweight physical baseline to generate daily evolution trajectories, employs a temporally constrained joint multi-lead compensation network to com?pensate for unresolved processes, and introduces an ice-mass?aware transport mechanism to suppress numerical dissipation. In the forecasting stage, the parameters of the base evolution core are fixed, while a lightweight variable-semantic adaptation mechanism calibrates inter-domain distributions and evolution responses, thereby separating forecast-domain errors from base evolution errors. Experiments show that the constructed base evolution core can accurately and stably simulate daily sea ice evolution at both short-term and annual scales under reanal?ysis forcing, and can be effectively transferred to the forecast domain through lightweight adaptation, achieving stable prac?tical forecasting capability while preserving the base evolution structure. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/zhangmaqun65535/SNM upon acceptance of this manuscript.
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of sea-ice dynamics and data errors in existing deep-learning forecasting methods.
Uses a lightweight physical baseline, a temporally constrained multi-lead compensation network, and ice-mass-aware transport to model unresolved processes and reduce numerical dissipation.
Freezes the base evolution core during forecasting and applies lightweight variable-semantic adaptation to correct domain shifts.
Experiments indicate stable evolution simulation from short-term to annual scales under reanalysis forcing and effective transfer to the forecast domain.
The approach is scoped to Arctic sea-ice concentration evolution and forecast-domain adaptation; specific quantitative results are not reported in the abstract.

During forecasting, the evolution core remains frozen. Variable-Specific Input Adaptation (VSIA) calibrates the observed initial condition and forecast forcings, while Response-Domain Semantic Correction (RDSC) further refines the output. The model thereby establishes a structured separation among physical propagation, multi-lead residual learning, and forecast-domain adaptation.
