papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP enable zero-shot classification from arbitrary class names, but under test-time corruptions, their visual encoder projects distorted features onto incorrect textual anchors with high confidence: a phenomenon we term modality bias. Standard entropy minimization reinforces these overconfident errors, which creates a confirmation-bias loop and collapses the predicted label distribution. We propose an online test-time adaptation (TTA) method that breaks this loop at three levels. At the representation level, a frozen self-supervised backbone (e.g., DINO v2) is combined with CLIP through a cross-covariance logit ensemble. CLIP text prototypes are projected into the feature space of this text-free backbone, so the self-supervised branch classifies native image features and is less affected by the text bias of CLIP. At the optimization level, a gated test-time information-maximization objective pairs per-sample sharpening with batch-level diversity, while an adaptive gate excludes unreliable samples from the gradient. At the prediction level, an online logit adjustment corrects the residual class-distribution skew. CDIM outperforms the compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, and remains competitive in continual and mixed-domain TTA. Extensive analyses and ablation studies verify the contribution of each of its components. Our code is available at https://github.com/B1ueC1oud/CDIM
authors: Taehoon Kim, Wonjun Hwang, Hyunsouk Cho
bullets: Targets CLIP’s tendency to confidently map corrupted images to incorrect text prototypes, causing modality bias and prediction collapse.
Uses a frozen DINOv2-style backbone with cross-covariance logit ensembling, projecting CLIP text prototypes into a text-free image-feature space.
Applies gated information maximization: sharpens reliable per-sample predictions, promotes batch diversity, and excludes unreliable samples from updates.
Performs online logit adjustment to correct residual class-distribution skew.
Outperforms compared CLIP-based online TTA baselines on ImageNet-C, CIFAR10-C, and CIFAR100-C, while remaining competitive in continual and mixed-domain settings.

papers.abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.
authors: Xuwei Tan, Jingchun Huang, Ming Cai, Shuangquan Lyu, Tiange Wang, Yinzhi Wang, Ronghua Shi, Jingwei Song, Yang Jingsong, Yinghui Xia, Hehua Fan, Yifan Zhou, Hanxin Chen, Jiwei Song, Tianyu Shi
bullets: Targets the cold-expert problem: published experts may receive requests despite limited creator evidence or availability.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
authors: Vimal William, Yuanzhe Li, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang
bullets: Long-context retrieval is concentrated in a small number of layers, while other recurrent states encode similar information via layer-specific transformations.
Anchor places recurrent TTT memory only at these anchor layers and uses a cross-layer state read by many layers.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, it achieves 2.3–3.1× higher recall and 6.7–8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs.
It uses a 10× smaller recurrent state, retains 91–95% of teacher MMLU accuracy, and reduces latency by up to 4.3× versus softmax attention.
The approach also generalizes to other hybrid-attention designs.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Anchor architecture and recurrent-state coverage. Left: Anchor-F maintains a private recurrent state in every layer, while Anchor keeps one shared state per anchor group and removes the interior states entirely, reducing recurrent state by 16× (201.0 → 12.6MB at 32k context). Each reader accesses the shared state through its own learned read map χ(·). Right: coverage over query (rows) and key (columns) positions. Green marks the local sliding window, red the span served by the recurrent state. Anchor-F requires one such state per layer; Anchor serves layers l1, . . . , L from a single shared state.

Figure 9. Cross-layer similarity generalizes across linearization methods. Debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity for every pair of layers, on the recurrent-state readouts of our TTT hybrid (Anchor-F), LoLCATs, and Liger on Mistral-7B over identical PG-19 and WikiText inputs. In all three models, layers share information while their cosine similarity remains small, indicating that this information is encoded in different bases.

Figure 7. Hybrid architecture of ANCHOR and full self-attention. ANCHOR and full self-attention layers are interleaved at a 3:1 ratio, so that softmax attention accounts for 25% of all layers. Within each group, the three ANCHOR layers retain their own sliding-window attention for local context but share a single recurrent state for long-range context: the leading layer writes the state, and each layer reads it through its own learned read map χℓ(·). The subsequent full self-attention layer attends over the entire sequence, providing exact retrieval at regular depth intervals, while the recurrent state per group remains constant in sequence length.

Figure 2. Layer-wise contribution of each branch to long-context retrieval. ∆CE (nats) on AR-32k when the TTT (top) or SWA (bottom) branch is removed at a single layer, broken down by the distance between a query and its target. Warm cells indicate degradation, that is, a larger increase in loss when the branch is removed. The TTT branch contributes almost nothing across the interior layers (ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) but dominates at the boundary layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}), whereas SWA contributes broadly at every depth. The color scale is symmetric-log with a linear region below 0.01, and both panels share one scale.

(a) Training on LMSE alone matches the teacher’s attention outputs closely, reducing the loss by over 25×, yet perplexity rises from 5.3K to 236K: the student reproduces each layer’s output while losing the ability to model language. (b) Adding next-token supervision LCE resolves this, lowering both losses together and reaching a perplexity of 34, which provides a stable initialization for the TTT parameters.

Figure 10. Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. Accuracy across context lengths (1K–8K) and needle depths for Llama-3.1-8B, a LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention), and the ANCHOR 3:1 hybrid. ANCHOR reaches a mean accuracy of 0.95 (baseline 1.00), whereas the LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention) (0.33) retrieves reliably only at 1K or when the needle lies near the end of the context.

Figure 6. Study on Performance–efficiency trade-off. ANCHOR evaluated on reasoning (MMLU) and recall (SWDE, FDA, SQuAD) benchmarks, together with end-to-end throughput and recurrent state size. (a) Reasoning accuracy of the ANCHOR series against LoLCATs; targeted placement of the cross-layer recurrent state improves reasoning. (b) Throughput (tokens/s) against reasoning accuracy; ANCHOR attains 4.3× higher throughput than the baseline at comparable accuracy. (c) Recall accuracy against recurrent state size; ANCHOR improves recall over LoLCATs by 2.3–3.1× while using a 10.2× smaller state.

Each point is one layer pair, plotted as debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity on cross-window targets, that is, those whose source lies beyond the local window. Interior pairs ( , ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) are drawn separately from anchor pairs (▲, ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}). papers.abstract: Aggregate scores for continual learning algorithms rest on a distribution over task orders that is rarely stated. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution, which separates training variation from order variation, and apply it to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs). Task order accounts for 65\% to 91\% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90\% to 99\% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task: the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders, the leading algorithm in current-task error and backward transfer is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. Backward transfer depends on the order mainly through its reference term, which weights the first task most heavily, so relative improvement and final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics tracks the position of the smallest task, and weighting orders by it leaves the algorithm ranking unchanged. These results call for benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores. The code and data are available \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/task-order-cl-4f7b/}{here}.
authors: Zirui Li, Yunlong Lin, Haohan Yang, Xiaocong Zhao, Chen Lv
bullets: Aggregate continual-learning scores should specify the distribution over task orders.
Across four tasks, all 24 orders, four algorithms, and three replicates, order caused 65–91% of variation in current-task error and backward transfer.
The starting task explained 90–99% of the order effect because the smallest task could not be learned from a cold start.
Beyond the first stage, order effects were comparable to training variability, and algorithm rankings were often not clearly separated.
Order-weighting via a transition-direction descriptor did not change rankings; the authors recommend order-, starting-task-, warm-start-, and final-error reporting.

papers.abstract: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.
authors: Keru Wang, Michael Xu, Ken Perlin, Nebojsa Jojic, Andrzej Banburski-Fahey
bullets: Addresses how socially distributed knowledge can be combined and surfaced within a co-located community.
Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM connects fragments, distills group knowledge, and responds in context.
Some memories function as instructions, allowing members to modify the system’s behavior.
A two-week deployment with 46 people and a follow-up workshop with 14 explored open-ended use.
Members used it to share daily life, query the collective memory, track routines, play games, and discover unfamiliar people and topics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: How SEAM handles one post, with an illustrative example rather than a case from the deployment. A post (A) enters both retrieval layers. They output reflections on the memory related to this moment, as well as context resolved regarding what actions to carry out and how to carry them out; The reply (D) is composed from both outputs with every claim grounded in the posts backing it, and the post, its follow-ups and the connections learnt are written back (E). Members can also read the knowledge wiki directly and leave a comment on any page, which the consolidation agent acts on at its next pass.

papers.abstract: High-resolution range profiles (HRRPs) provide compact radar target representations but exhibit strong aspect sensitivity, complicating class-incremental recognition when historical data are unavailable. Changes in viewing aspect shift scattering-peak locations and amplitudes, while reflector groups may produce responses resembling ships. Existing dynamic expansion methods can also incur substantial parameter and memory overhead. To address these challenges, we propose P-SER, a Physical Consistency-Constrained Scattering Expandable Representation framework for exemplar-free class-incremental HRRP recognition. P-SER reconstructs dominant scattering points from complex-valued sum- and azimuth-difference-channel HRRPs and observation geometry. The reconstructed spatial structure, target extent, and energy distribution are used to derive class-level scattering prototypes and sample-level saliency priors, providing physically grounded constraints for feature learning and old-class knowledge retention. A primitive scatterer dictionary further characterizes local strong-scattering mechanisms and calibrates uncertain ship--reflector predictions at inference. Meanwhile, lightweight residual adapters are incrementally introduced into a shared HRRP backbone to learn new classes with limited model growth. Experiments on simulated and measured HRRP datasets show that P-SER delivers competitive recognition performance without retaining old-class exemplars, while maintaining physical consistency, interference robustness, knowledge retention, and model scalability.
authors: Fangyi Wang, Peng Zhao, Haipeng Wang
bullets: Addresses HRRP aspect sensitivity, ship–reflector confusion, and the memory burden of retaining historical exemplars.
Reconstructs scattering points from complex sum/azimuth-difference HRRPs and observation geometry to derive class prototypes and sample saliency priors.
Uses a primitive scatterer dictionary to model local scattering mechanisms and calibrate uncertain ship–reflector predictions.
Adds lightweight residual adapters to a shared backbone for learning new classes with limited model growth.
Experiments on simulated and measured HRRP data indicate competitive recognition, physical consistency, interference robustness, knowledge retention, and scalability without old exemplars.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems that automate machine learning pipeline construction from minimal user input. However, existing agentic AutoML methods either depend on rigid templates that limit adaptability, target narrow task domains, or rely on free-form code generation that lacks reliability guarantees, leaving intermediate errors to propagate silently and degrade the final model. We present EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline synthesis built on expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs, executed through a validation-gated harness. The framework decomposes pipeline construction into four phases coordinated by three agents: an Orchestrator that enforces validation gates, advancing each phase only when its outputs pass structural, execution, and semantic checks, which precludes error propagation and keeps every artifact auditable; an Executor that runs expert-grounded skills, grounded in the nnU-Net workflow and pairing reusable templates with online adaptation; and a Curator that performs post-run evolution, consolidating the scripts and guidance recovered during a run into the skill library so it improves across datasets. We evaluate EvoML on eight datasets spanning six sophisticated, real-world ML task types, against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools. EvoML achieves full automation and the best final model quality on all eight, spanning segmentation (up to 0.94 Dice), classification (0.99 accuracy), reconstruction (0.95 SSIM), and denoising (0.79 normalized PSNR), while transferring to broader ML tasks.
authors: Zixiao Zhao, Jing Sun, Zhe Hou, Mengze Li, Qian Liu, Cheng-Hao Cai, Zijian Zhang, Xin Wang, Gillian Dobbie, Jin Song Dong
bullets: Targets unreliable and inflexible agentic AutoML approaches that lack safeguards for intermediate pipeline outputs.
Uses three agents—Orchestrator, Executor, and Curator—across four phases of pipeline construction.
Validation gates check structural, execution, and semantic correctness before each phase can proceed, keeping artifacts auditable.
Expert-grounded templates adapt online, while post-run curation expands the skill library across runs and datasets.

Evaluated on eight datasets across six real-world task types, EvoML achieved full automation and the best final model quality in the comparison; reported task metrics include up to 0.94 Dice, 0.99 accuracy, 0.95 SSIM, and 0.79 normalized PSNR.

papers.abstract: Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However, new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data or reliable supervisory signals for further training. We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store what it learns: domain-specific skills and instructions on when to apply them, along with memories of past task experiences and reflections on what to improve. Recursa bootstraps the repository from domain materials and then refines it through recursive self-improvement. It uses parallel learners to execute tasks and synthesize local improvements, then validates and merges the improvements into the knowledge repository. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash.
authors: Erkang Zhu, Yin Lin, Xiaorong Shi, Xuanrui Lin, Jingren Zhou
bullets: Addresses domain adaptation when expert-created data and reliable training signals are scarce.
Stores domain skills, usage instructions, task memories, and improvement reflections in a knowledge repository.
Bootstraps the repository from domain materials, then uses parallel learners to propose, validate, and merge improvements.
Improves held-out all-pass rates on Harvey LAB’s Firm Knowledge benchmark for both evaluated models.
Scope: evaluated on a single benchmark and two model settings described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pretrained backbones has become standard practice in multi-sensor computer vision---yet two questions remain open: which pretrained weights transfer best to multi-sensor setups, and can in-domain pretraining outperform off-the-shelf solutions? Frameworks like MultiMAE demonstrate the utility of masked autoencoding in a multi-modal context, but rely entirely on dense, model-derived modalities. It is unclear how robustly these methods translate to real-world applications that use physical sensors, where the aggregation of diverse public datasets for large-scale pretraining inherently introduces modality sparsity. To investigate this systematically, we curate a multi-sensor autonomous driving collection of $2.82M$ images from 16 publicly available datasets, incorporating both physical hardware modalities (RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event) and model-derived modalities (Stereo Depth, Segmentation). We use this collection for in-domain pretraining based on the MultiMAE approach. We adapt MultiMAE's loss formulation to accommodate sparse samples, and study the effect of an enforced encoder bottleneck for modality alignment and of additional losses specific to dense reconstruction (SSIM and FFT). We then systematically compare against common pretrained backbones (ViT, MAE, DINO and MultiMAE) across downstream sensor fusion tasks. We find that MultiMAE is a surprisingly strong out-of-the-box baseline, transferring effectively even to modalities it has never seen, while our targeted modifications yield incremental but consistent improvements on multi-sensor transfer and overall robustness.

bullets: Curates 2.82M images from 16 public autonomous-driving datasets spanning RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event, stereo depth, and segmentation.
Pretrains on this heterogeneous collection with a MultiMAE-based approach adapted for modality-sparse data.
Studies encoder bottlenecks for modality alignment and SSIM/FFT losses for dense reconstruction.
Compares ViT, MAE, DINO, and MultiMAE backbones across downstream sensor-fusion tasks.
Finds MultiMAE transfers effectively even to unseen modalities; targeted modifications improve transfer and robustness incrementally and consistently.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to support prediction and planning in embodied agents, but the knowledge is usually established before deployment and then carried into later encounters. Continual operation faces a different problem. A familiar environment may change, and the agent must use previous experience without allowing old expectations to override current physical evidence. This study asks what repeated physical experience must contribute for a spatial world model to become progressively more useful rather than simply more persistent. A physics-grounded dynamic maze separates recurring spatial change from the continuous consequences of action. Cross-episode Spatial Change Memory learns relations among environmental transformations, while state-action-outcome experience refines predictions of motion. Structured experience progressively reduces the need for future route correction and transfers to spatial transitions not encountered during learning. The advantage disappears when past changes contain no information about future ones. Continuous navigation further shows that predictive memory changes behavior when a previous decision becomes invalid but leaves behavior unchanged when the decision remains correct. Physical tests expose a complementary limit: correct topology does not guarantee correct action prediction, and accumulated physical experience reduces this mismatch within the modeled dynamics. The results characterize continual world knowledge as experience that improves future prediction and action beyond stored episodes while remaining revisable by the physical outcomes it is intended to predict.
bullets: Continual operation requires using past experience while remaining responsive to current physical evidence.
Cross-episode Spatial Change Memory captures recurring environmental transformations, while state-action-outcome experience improves motion prediction.
Structured experience reduces future route corrections and transfers to unseen spatial transitions when past changes predict future ones.
Navigation behavior changes when prior decisions become invalid but remains stable when they are still correct.
Physical experience reduces mismatches between correct environmental topology and inaccurate action predictions within the modeled dynamics.

papers.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
authors: Peizhi Niu, Ge Shi, Vaibhav Gorde, Sarthak Ghosh, Christos Faloutsos, Min Cheng, Kevin Chen
bullets: Addresses gaps in static agent harnesses, including proprietary policies, undocumented behavior, and state-dependent recovery paths.
Distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages containing reusable actions and recovery strategies.
Improves TheAgentCompany checkpoint pass rates by 4.6–6.1% over the strongest compared baseline across three models, while using 57–61% less storage.
Controlled studies find that human-defined schemas and explicit deduplication can hurt performance, whereas human diagnosis substantially improves failed-trace learning.
One round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0–10.9%, suggesting agents should organize memory while humans diagnose failures.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: The challenge requires training only on synthetic LiDAR while evaluating on unseen real roadside LiDAR and synthetic-cloud realism.
Recovering the correct coordinate frame increased the combined score from 0.3520 to 0.5147.
Per-class NMS prevented suppression of closely grouped pedestrians, raising detection mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295.
Modelling real-cloud null returns at (0, 0, 0), absent from synthetic data, improved distributional realism.
The final entry achieved a combined score of 0.7457, with detection mAP 0.4382 and realism score 0.9251.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on Sim2Real V2X LiDAR detection for autonomous driving, addressing specific sensor alignment and post-processing issues for real-world navigation.
papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A diagnostic-focused Sim2Real V2X LiDAR pipeline substantially improved detection and realism by fixing coordinate-frame errors, using class-specific NMS, and modelling null returns.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: Targets detection trained only on synthetic LiDAR and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, alongside synthetic-data realism scoring.
A parameter-free geometric refinement addressed small-object localization, yielding a reported 86% relative pedestrian AP gain.
Fixing a post-processing rule that removed valid predictions produced the largest detection improvement: 335% relative on the Van class.
Analytical examination of realism metrics identified one component as a closed-form function of nine summary statistics.

The proposed submission methodology combines independently controlled class-wise experiments, enabling pre-submission score prediction and transparent reporting of negative results and data provenance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Sim2Real LiDAR detection for roadside navigation, focusing on geometric refinement and distributional alignment for real-world deployment.
papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A PointPillars-based Sim2Real roadside LiDAR system improves challenge performance through geometric localization refinement, post-processing repair, and analytical realism optimization rather than a new detector architecture.

papers.abstract: Lifelong (continual) anomaly detection systems must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting how to recognize anomaly types seen earlier -- a property known as backward transfer. A common way to try to improve backward transfer is to reshape a model's internal representation around learnable concept centroids, typically coupled with a new way of scoring anomalies based on distance to those centroids. Because these two design choices are usually introduced together, it is unclear which one is actually responsible for any performance gain. In this paper, we unbundle the two mechanisms within a VAE-based lifelong anomaly detector and study them separately. We find that used purely as a training-time regularizer -- while leaving anomaly scoring unchanged -- latent cluster separation can improve detection quality and backward transfer, though whether it outperforms the alternative scoring approach depends on the dataset's underlying representation. Switching to distance-based scoring is instead where most of the instability commonly associated with this class of method actually originates; we identify and explain the underlying mechanism. This benefit depends on the dataset's underlying representation, and we report this as practical guidance for choosing between the two design choices, rather than as a list of caveats.
bullets: Lifelong anomaly detectors must retain recognition of previously learned anomaly types while learning new tasks.
The study disentangles latent cluster separation from distance-based anomaly scoring in a VAE-based detector.
Using cluster separation only during training can improve detection quality and backward transfer without changing scoring.
Distance-based scoring is identified as the main source of common instability in this method family.
Which design is preferable depends on the dataset’s underlying representation.

papers.abstract: The last decades have seen a revolution in autonomous robotics. Deep learning approaches and their hardware implementations have made it possible to endow robots with extraordinary perceptual capabilities. In addition, they can also benefit from advances in Automated Planning, allowing them to autonomously solve complex tasks. However, on many occasions, the robot still acts without internalising and understanding the reasons behind a perception or an action, beyond an immediate response to a current state of the context. This gap results in limitations that affect its performance, reliability and trustworthiness. Deep learning alone cannot bridge this gap, because the reasons behind behaviour, when it emanates from a model in which the world is a black-box, are not accessible. What is really needed is an underlying architecture based on deeper reasoning. Among other issues, this architecture should enable the robot to generate explanations, allowing people to know why the robot is performing, or has performed, a certain action, or the reasons that may have caused a certain plan failure or perceptual anomaly. Furthermore, when these explanations arise from a cognitive process and are shared, and thus validated, with people, the robot should be able to incorporate these explanations into its knowledge base, and thus use this understanding to improve future behaviour. Our article looks at recent advances in the development of self-aware, self-evolving robots. These robots are designed to provide the necessary explanations to their human counterparts, thereby enhancing their functional capabilities, in the quest to gain their trust.
bullets: Deep learning and planning enable capable autonomous robots but often do not expose the reasons behind perceptions, actions, failures, or anomalies.
Black-box models limit explainability, reliability, and human trust.
Causal, reasoning-based architectures are presented as a way to generate meaningful explanations.
Robots could incorporate explanations shared and validated with people into their knowledge base to improve future behavior.
The article reviews recent advances in self-aware, self-evolving robots, without reporting specific experimental results.

papers.abstract: Federated continual learning must integrate new tasks over time without losing earlier-task knowledge. Most existing methods attach an anti-forgetting mechanism to the client-trained, server-aggregated loop of federated learning, which holds back new learning to preserve earlier knowledge and burdens resource-constrained clients. We propose ReSCENE, which structurally mitigates catastrophic forgetting by having each client upload a small condensed surrogate of its local data while the server keeps the surrogates of past tasks and trains the global model on them together with the current task surrogates. For efficient server memory, we introduce temporal herding, which selects the more recent surrogates from the pool accumulated over a task into a compressed buffer. Our study provides a theoretical analysis showing that this buffer can represent the original task data more closely than full accumulation of all surrogates. Across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, ReSCENE achieves the strongest accuracy over seven baselines, by up to $31.1$ points of average accuracy, while requiring as little as $0.11\times$ of the client computation and up to $179\times$ less upload than the model-update baselines. ReSCENE further demonstrates its effectiveness when scaled to larger client populations and larger models while remaining efficient, which makes it a practical method for federated continual learning.
bullets: Clients upload small condensed data surrogates instead of relying solely on anti-forgetting mechanisms during local training.
The server jointly trains on current and historical surrogates to retain earlier-task knowledge.
Temporal herding compresses accumulated surrogates into an efficient buffer while theoretically preserving task information.
Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet report the strongest accuracy among seven baselines, with substantially lower client computation and upload costs.
The approach remains effective with larger client populations and models, though its scope is evaluated on the listed benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.
bullets: Isolation-based LoRA methods can suffer from “spectral starvation” when historical null spaces contain little incoming-task variance.
BISECT splits a fixed rank budget into an invariant block from joint historical/current spectral modes and a novelty block from whitened orthogonal complements.
A closed-form precision gate consolidates invariant atoms while retaining novelty atoms at full gain.
Across eight incremental settings spanning five benchmarks, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines without extra inference parameters or FLOPs.
The method remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of BISECT at session t. (I) Using the historical Gram state G<t and current-task Gram Gt, BISECT determines the layerwise rank split (kinv, knov) from the top-r spectral energy threshold η, extracts the invariant carrier Pinv from the joint Gram G1:t via randomized SVD, and synthesizes the orthogonal novelty complement Pnov via Cholesky-whitened generalized Rayleigh extraction. (II) Both basis blocks Pinv, Pnov remain locked while the up-maps Qinv, Qnov are optimized by SGD on Dt. (III) Each rank-1 invariant atom is folded into W (t−1) with its closed-form posterior precision weight ω⋆ j ∈ [0, 1], while novelty atoms fold at unit weight, yielding zero inference overhead.

papers.tldr: BISECT improves exemplar-free continual learning with LoRA by preserving shared knowledge while allocating capacity to genuinely novel task information.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.
bullets: Targets catastrophic forgetting without adding a new LoRA branch for each task.
Uses asymmetric read/write behavior: full-rank forward inference and sparse, input-aligned backward updates.
A cosine router selects the top-q unlocked atoms for gradients, while coherence regularization protects inactive directions.
Tracks activation history and spectral norms to attenuate updates and lock consolidated adapter atoms.
Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA methods with constant parameter count.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the RASP pipeline. Stage 1 (Left): Every input batch traverses all r rank-1 atoms in the forward pass without truncation; a cosine probe modulated by an image-level scene gate ϕ(x̄) and a usage-equalizing prior scores the unlocked pool Pt−1. Stage 2 (Middle): Only the top-q unlocked channels At receive backward gradients, while a Frobenius Gram coherence penalty Rdec pushes active synthesis columns orthogonal to non-updated and locked columns. Stage 3 (Right): Cumulative routing trace c̃j and rank-1 spectral norm σ̃j form the consolidation index ωj = √ c̃j σ̃j , driving continuous Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking.

Figure 4. Trajectories, resilience, and system cost. (a) On CIFAR100, RASP matches the top expansion method across all 10 sessions at constant size. (b) On CUB-200, shared forward reading yields a +8.48 pp final lead over branch-isolated SplitLoRA. (c) Silencing the top-m task-associated atoms after training collapses isolated branches (−23.84% at m = 10) but costs < 1% on RASP, confirming distributed encoding. (d) Training time and peak VRAM on CIFAR-100.

Figure 3. Mechanistic analysis of RASP. (a, b) Effect of plasticity ratio q/r on ∆FAA (relative to q = r) and Average Forgetting across four benchmarks; stars mark the operating configurations in Table 2. The optimal q/r shifts rightward as domain divergence from ImageNet-21K increases. Figure 1. Motivation for RASP. (a) Across all four benchmarks, decoupling full-rank forward reading from sparse backward writing consistently outperforms both unmasked shared updates (q = r) and symmetric top-q gating, with trace-spectral consolidation providing an additional boost. (b) On CIFAR-100, unmasked shared training suffers severe old-task logit drift; symmetric gating curbs drift at the expense of forward rank; RASP suppresses 84.0% of cumulative logit drift while preserving full forward capacity. (c) At T = 10 sessions under a unified ViT-B/16 protocol, RASP occupies the Pareto frontier of final accuracy versus total adapter parameters.

(b) Routing trace c̃j dominates in shallow blocks and spectral norm σ̃j dominates in deep blocks; their geometric mean ωj equalizes layer-wise consolidation pressure. papers.abstract: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.
bullets: Addresses continual training under shifting data without retraining on the full history.
Uses the model’s own next-token predictions to create gradient-matching targets from unlabeled data.
Maintains a rehearsal memory and re-distills it with each incoming batch for online updates.
Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, gains 10 accuracy points using as few as five examples.
A hybrid selection–distillation pipeline reduces runtime by 30% at similar accuracy and improves over selection-only methods by up to 12.6 points.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the components of OLGA. (a) Synthetic text is generated by matching its training gradient to that of real data, alternating with a step that maps it back to real tokens. (b) A frozen language model’s next-token predictions replace ground-truth labels, so gradient matching works on unlabeled data. (c) A running rehearsal memory extends offline distillation to an online data stream. Each new batch is distilled together with the memory, which the model then retrains on. (d) Our hybrid design first uses cheap selection to shrink each batch, then distills what remains into the few examples kept, which cuts runtime on large data.

papers.abstract: Semantic change detection in remote sensing aims to identify and characterize land-cover transitions observed in pairs of satellite or aerial images. Existing methods assume a fixed set of change categories, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios where changes of interest may vary, for example across geographies or over time. In this work, we tackle the problem of class-incremental semantic change detection, where a model progressively learns to detect new types of semantic change. To do so, we exploit the hierarchical structure of land-cover semantics, where newly introduced categories correspond to fine-grained refinements of existing ones, and represent said semantic categories in hyperbolic space, which is particularly well suited to represent such hierarchical relationships. To capture semantic changes, we introduce HyperFlow, a method relying on Busemann prototypes, modeling change as an anomaly in a learned semantic flow within the hyperbolic embedding space induced by segmentation. HyperFlow couples change detection to class-incremental semantic segmentation, enabling class-incremental semantic change detection. We also present HiChange, a new large-scale, high resolution remote sensing dataset with detailed, fine-grained hierarchical labels. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperFlow achieves both strong change detection and semantic segmentation performance across incremental steps. In particular, we show that progressively refining semantic categories, rather than considering them all directly, yields improved change detection, highlighting the benefits of incremental learning for semantic change detection.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed change categories in remote sensing, where new categories may emerge across regions or over time.
Represents hierarchical land-cover categories in hyperbolic space and uses Busemann prototypes to model semantic flow anomalies.
Couples change detection with class-incremental semantic segmentation to progressively learn new change types.
Introduces HiChange, a large-scale, high-resolution dataset with fine-grained hierarchical labels.
Experiments show strong detection and segmentation across incremental steps, with category refinement improving change detection.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CI-SCD via Hyperbolic Flow. (1) Land-cover semantics are naturally organized in hierarchies. (3) Hyperbolic semantic flow: a vector field transforming the embeddings of the first image into the embeddings of the second image is learned. The hyperbolic distance between the positions of the predicted embeddings and the observed positions indicates change. papers.abstract: Computer-use agents for scientific software require application-specific expertise. Much of this expertise is documented in human-authored software manuals and web pages. However, turning these resources into executable, reusable skills remains challenging due to mismatches between documented and deployed software versions and differences in scope between documentation coverage and task requirements. We introduce ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework combining resource-to-skill construction with execution-guided skill evolution. First, ScienceCUA identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories, and generalizes them into reusable Skills. Command catalogs, syntax constraints, and shortcuts are organized separately as References for on-demand lookup. Then, ScienceCUA uses execution feedback to drive skill self-evolution by contrasting successful and failed trajectories for the same task, identifying deficiencies, revising existing skills or adding new ones, and updating the skill library only after repeated validation in real environments. To enable reliable evaluation without benchmark noise or task leakage, we introduce two improved benchmarks. ScienceBoard-Verified provides an audited and corrected basis for measuring task performance, while ScienceBoard-VE separates skill evolution from final testing through disjoint evolution and test tasks and further supports native-agent evaluation. Experiments show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success rate by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, while skill self-evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. ScienceCUA turns software documentation into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, offering a practical way for general-purpose agents to use scientific software reliably and at scale.
bullets: Addresses the gap between human-authored documentation, deployed software versions, and real task requirements.
Constructs reusable Skills from documented tasks and trajectories, while organizing commands, syntax constraints, and shortcuts as queryable References.
Evolves skills by comparing successful and failed executions, revising or adding skills, and validating updates repeatedly in real environments.
Introduces ScienceBoard-Verified and ScienceBoard-VE to reduce benchmark noise, task leakage, and confounding between evolution and testing.
Initial resources improve average task success by up to 7.23 percentage points; self-evolution raises the total gain over baseline to up to 17.12 points.

papers.abstract: Multimodal test-time adaptation (TTA) enables pretrained multimodal models to accommodate distribution shifts during inference using only unlabeled test data, without recourse to the original training data. Compared with unimodal adaptation, multimodal adaptation is further complicated by the coexistence and interaction of multiple representation perspectives. This complexity is particularly pronounced under modality reliability shifts, which preserve modality availability but degrade information quality, and modality availability shifts, which render the corresponding modality entirely inaccessible. Category-conditional Gaussian modeling offers a natural starting point for handling such distributional variations, having proven effective in unimodal test-time adaptation for characterizing representation distributions, yet its extension to multimodal settings requires a more elaborate formulation. To this end, we propose Adaptive Probabilistic Gaussian Calibration (AdaPGC), which extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling across modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations for probabilistic calibration under multimodal distribution shifts. AdaPGC continuously updates category-conditional Gaussian models over modality-specific and fusion representations, using the resulting probabilistic predictions to calibrate source model predictions and guide reliability based rectification, while exploiting their joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations. Extensive experiments under diverse modality corruption and missingness conditions demonstrate that AdaPGC effectively improves robustness under both modality reliability and availability shifts. Our source code will be released at https://github.com/XuJinglinn/AdaPGC-plus.
bullets: Addresses multimodal distribution shifts caused by reduced modality reliability or complete modality unavailability.
Extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling to modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations.
Continuously updates Gaussian models during inference using unlabeled test data.
Uses probabilistic calibration for prediction correction and joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations.
Experiments across diverse corruption and missingness conditions show improved robustness to both shift types.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed multimodal test-time adaptation framework. The input consists of paired video and audio streams affected by reliability shifts (modality corruption) or availability shifts (missing video/audio). For complete instances, the pretrained source model feeds the fused representation zF into the shared classifier to obtain source logits s; for incomplete instances, it instead uses the representation of the available modality, zV or zA. The category-conditional Gaussian means and priors are initialized from the pretrained classifier, while the covariance and cross-covariance matrices are initialized as identity matrices. During adaptation, these parameters are updated using target-stream statistics to define the discriminants gV , gA, and gF and conditional estimators EV →F and EA→F . For incomplete instances, the available modality representation is used to estimate category-conditional fused representations, whose Gaussian predictions are combined with the unimodal predictions to obtain calibration logits r. For complete instances, the fused Gaussian discriminant produces the calibration logits r = gF (zF ), while discrepancies between unimodal and fused Gaussian predictions guide reliability-aware one-sided alignment.

Fig. 4. Sensitivity of AdaPGC to wc and wg on Kinetics50. Rows correspond to audio corruption (a–d), video corruption (e–h), and missing-modality settings (i–l). Fig. 1. Illustration of modality reliability and availability shifts in multimodal TTA. Under availability shifts, missing modalities make the corresponding modality-specific representations unavailable and prevent the fusion representation from being directly constructed, motivating its recovery from the remaining modality.

papers.abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) for outdoor 3D object detection remains largely underexplored. Existing outdoor studies are limited to single-benchmark evaluations, with SDCoT++ considering KITTI and CL2OD considering nuScenes under different incremental settings. This makes it difficult to assess whether observed continual-learning behavior generalizes across autonomous-driving benchmarks. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first unified cross-benchmark analysis of outdoor class-incremental 3D object detection across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks, covering both two-task and multi-stage settings. We investigate: (1) how severely existing 3D detectors forget previously learned classes, (2) how incremental training exposes the stability-plasticity dilemma between knowledge retention and new-class acquisition, and (3) which forms of supervision are most effective for balancing these objectives. We introduce CL3DOD, a class-incremental 3D detection framework that restores missing supervision for previous classes using predictions from the previous-stage detector, preserves old-class responses through query-wise knowledge distillation, and employs EMA-based temporal consistency regularization. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes reveal a consistent stability-plasticity dilemma across both benchmarks. CL3DOD generally achieves a more favorable stability-plasticity balance than controlled incremental baselines and improves upon published prior methods in the reported benchmark comparisons. This advantage persists across multiple incremental stages, demonstrating strong retention of previously learned knowledge while maintaining effective new-class acquisition. Our code, evaluation setup, and incremental task splits will be publicly released.
bullets: Provides the first unified cross-benchmark study covering two-task and multi-stage incremental settings.
Finds consistent forgetting and a stability–plasticity trade-off across both autonomous-driving benchmarks.
Restores previous-class supervision using prior-detector predictions, query-wise knowledge distillation, and EMA temporal consistency.
Reports a more favorable stability–plasticity balance than controlled baselines and improvements over published methods in the evaluated comparisons.
Scope is limited to the KITTI and nuScenes benchmarks and the incremental settings studied.

papers.abstract: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting remains an important open question. In this paper, we investigate this open question through a comprehensive empirical study of continual harness self-evolution. We organize three software engineering task datasets into six different evolution directions and apply two representative harness evolution methods to perform continual evolution along these directions. Our experimental results show that evolution on a subsequent dataset can substantially undermine the performance on previously seen datasets. For example, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Meta-Harness improves its performance on SWE-Bench to 94.0% after evolution. However, after further evolution on FeatureBench, its performance on SWE-Bench drops to 32.0% by the fifth round, corresponding to a 66% relative decrease. Finally, based on our experimental findings, we identify several insights, providing directions for the continual self-evolution of agent harnesses. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/continual-harness-evolution.
bullets: Prior harness self-evolution studies largely focus on single-task improvement, leaving continual multi-task evolution underexplored.
The study evaluates continual harness self-evolution across three software-engineering datasets, six evolution directions, and two representative methods.
Subsequent evolution can substantially degrade earlier capabilities: SWE-Bench performance fell from 94.0% to 32.0% after further FeatureBench evolution in one example.
The findings reveal challenges in sustaining continual evolution and provide insights for developing less forgetful agent harnesses.
Scope: an empirical study of harness evolution; it does not modify foundation-model parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of our study on continual harness self-evolution.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining high-quality work on complex productivity tasks with sustained monitoring and decision-making.
Separates task strategy from execution management: models choose actions, delegation, and acceptance while the runtime maintains state and feedback.
Supports direct or delegated execution, synchronous or asynchronous subagents, and shared editing of documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes.
Uses hierarchical workspaces, persistent semantic memory, and job logs to make work resumable across agents and sessions.
Across 12 benchmarks and six application categories, it was highly competitive with Codex and DeepSeek Harness; a five-round post-training case study improved average scores from 33.19 to 42.95.

papers.abstract: On July 1, 2025, Vietnam reduced its 63 provinces to 34, abolished its 696 districts, and replaced its 10,035 commune-level units (wards) with 3,321. ViAdminShift, a Vietnamese language resource about this event, consists of 7,995 benchmark items, 2,281 retrieval passages from pre- and post-reform Wikipedia revisions and dated templates, and old-to-new tables that a released script rebuilds from the official conversion table (not redistributed). Changed items store the pre-reform answer (except 121 address items), a $2\times2$ design uses untouched units as controls, and 400 addresses appear without diacritics. The tables agree with an independent lineage on 10,564 of 10,565 official pairs, disagreements were settled against the resolutions, and the probing-track scorer agrees with both authors' blind labels (Cohen's $κ=0.91$ and $0.89$). Data, outputs, code, and a datasheet are released. In the probing track, at least 20 of 67 models know the reform. Fourteen of them give the new province alone for at most 11% of plain questions about old addresses (old province only: 14-100%); a bare date recovers up to 100%. Post hoc (80 province-free addresses, single runs), with reasoning off, today's date in the system prompt leaves 68-100% old-province-only answers for 10 of 12 models; with reasoning, an "as of" prefix in the question leaves none for seven of eight. On the 1,262-item benchmark subset, with same-source old and new passages, small models unaware of the reform give 14-30% outdated answers and the five benchmark-track knowers (also differing in size or provider) 0-5%.
bullets: It covers 7,995 benchmark items, 2,281 dated retrieval passages, old-to-new administrative tables, and 400 undiacritized addresses.
A 2×2 design uses changed units and untouched controls; tables are reconstructed from the official conversion table and validated against an independent lineage.
At least 20 of 67 tested models show awareness of the reform, but plain questions about old addresses often produce outdated or incomplete answers.
Adding a date or explicit “as of” context substantially improves temporal disambiguation in the reported probes.
The dataset, outputs, code, scorer, and datasheet are released.
