papers.abstract: Knowledge is how understanding accumulates across people and generations: durable records that outlive their producers and that others can check, combine, teach, and correct. AI agents are now built and run by many independent users and organizations, and each agent is upgraded, replaced, or retired within months. Yet what an agent learns stays trapped in model parameters, a transient context window, or a system-specific memory store that is appended to and retrieved from rather than processed. We argue that the next generation of AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent. In this loop, agents discover knowledge from their environments and trajectories; the layer internalizes it by turning fragmented, heterogeneous records and experience into composable, revisable understanding; and agents across systems and generations use the result and return new outcomes for revision. While discovery and use have advanced rapidly with large language model agents, internalization remains the bottleneck. We argue that internalization should become a persistent object of training and maintenance-centered on condition-preserving conceptualization of events and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning across noisy, heterogeneous representations (text, tables, graphs, rules, and programs). To power this layer, we call for knowledge foundation models that provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation, and outline a research agenda showing how an explicit knowledge layer delivers reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.
bullets: Current agents keep learning trapped in parameters, context windows, or system-specific memories, limiting reuse and continuity.
The proposed loop separates knowledge discovery, internalization, and use, with internalization identified as the main bottleneck.
Internalization requires condition-preserving conceptualization and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning over heterogeneous, noisy representations.
The paper calls for knowledge foundation models to provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation.
An explicit knowledge layer could improve reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The knowledge-centric loop across agents and generations. Independent agent systems, built on different models and run by different organizations, discover knowledge and contribute it to an explicit knowledge layer. The layer is internalized by transformations and reasoning, and the results are used by other systems and by later generations, which inherit, revalidate, and revise them.

Figure 2: A knowledge foundation model inside the knowledge layer. It combines explicit knowledge, supporting observations and experience, and the implicit capacities of existing models, organizes shared computation across transformation and reasoning layers while delegating exact computation to symbolic components, and produces deductive, inductive, and abductive results whose status is recorded before they are written back. Implicit priors inform inference but do not become knowledge without evidence.
Table 1: Four types of knowledge [66] and their counterparts in AI systems.
Table 2: Qualitative comparison of explicit knowledge forms. Aggregation refers to counting, ranking, and comparing over many units. Ratings are our assessment.

Table 5: Routes to reasoning over knowledge and what each leaves open in the setting of §5.3, in our assessment. Each route is a candidate component of a knowledge foundation model rather than a competitor to it.
Table 3: Maturity of each stage of the knowledge-centric loop, in our assessment of the literature we examined.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes knowledge internalization and persistent knowledge layer for agents, relevant to continual learning and agent memory.
papers.title: Toward Knowledge-Centric AI: Discovering, Internalizing, and Using Explicit Knowledge Across Agents and Generations
papers.tldr: The paper argues that future AI should use a shared, explicit knowledge layer that agents continuously discover, internalize, revise, and reuse across systems and generations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.
bullets: Addresses hybrid federation where data are split across samples and feature modalities, with modality absence and site heterogeneity.
Combines availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation.
Establishes convexity and smoothness under fixed maps and propensities, plus curvature, optimization-rate, and risk-bound results.
Worst-site aggregation improves performance under heterogeneous and reversed or size-balanced site designs.
On two activity-recognition benchmarks, the selected correction is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site; regularization effects vary by dataset.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustrative sample and modality partitions in hybrid federated fusion. Sites group distinct patient records vertically; independently held modality blocks form the horizontal partition. Original device icons depict baseline records, ECG monitoring and wrist/ankle inertial sensors (IMUs). Check marks indicate observed blocks and crosses indicate record-level absence; the baseline remains observed. IDs, devices and availability patterns are schematic, not clinical study data. Computational row groups need not coincide with statistical sites. Raw feature blocks remain with their custodians. 2D-Fed denotes 2D-FedSMKL.

Figure 2: Availability-corrected additive fusion for one sample. Observed modalities are inverse-probability weighted, whereas an absent block contributes zero rather than an imputed signal. Under the stated missing-at-random assumption and with the true observation propensities, the correction recovers each full-data linear score contribution in expectation. Estimated propensities are clipped to limit instability, which can introduce bias.

Figure 4: Compact simulation trends for the three incomplete-sample fusion methods. The legend label 2D-Fed denotes the proposed 2D-FedSMKL method. Left: the robust objective separates from mean-risk alternatives as site heterogeneity increases. Right: the methods remain close at moderate modality absence, with only modest separation at severe absence. Error bars show standard deviations across matched replicates.

Figure 3: Smooth worst-site aggregation. Log-sum-exp provides a differentiable approximation to the largest site risk, and its gradient gives the adaptive weight qs. Decreasing ρ approaches worst-site training; increasing ρ approaches π-weighted mean-risk training.

Figure 5: Paired component effects in the secondary factorial study under controlled MAR block absence. Panels correspond to MHEALTH and UCI HAR at 35% and 65% target absence. Points are paired mean differences in worst-site macro-F1 and horizontal bars are unadjusted 95% paired t intervals over 20 matched masks. Positive values favor the first-listed component: robust minus mean aggregation, conditional on IPW or zero filling; and IPW minus zero filling, conditional on mean or robust aggregation. The vertical dashed line denotes no difference. The figure focuses on the absence levels for which paired inferential contrasts are tabulated.

Table 3: Availability correction under the primary protocol (35% target absence, ten masks, 1400 rounds). Worst-site macro-F1 and paired difference against IPW mean, with the 95% interval over ten masks. The last row is the configuration selected on validation data and is the model summarised in the abstract.

Table 2: Public-data results with fold-fitted preprocessing for source validation and final source-only representations, under 35% controlled MAR block absence. Entries are mean (sample SD) over ten matched masks. Zero-fill SMKL, and the zero-filled inference of complete-case CS, place an absent block at its observed training mean, which is mean imputation on standardized blocks. The oracle uses unmasked data and is fitted once, so its SD is zero across masks.

Table 1: Predictive performance in the primary simulation setting (35% target optionalmodality absence and heterogeneity h = 0.8). Entries are mean (standard deviation) over 20 replicates. The oracle uses fully observed modalities and is not feasible in practice.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses multimodal fusion under hybrid federated learning, which falls under continual and online learning paradigms.
papers.title: Hybrid Federated Learning for Multimodal Fusion under Missing Modalities and Site Heterogeneity
papers.tldr: 2D-FedSMKL enables multimodal federated learning with missing modalities and heterogeneous sites, offering theoretical guarantees and improved worst-site robustness in simulations and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.
bullets: Addresses identity drift in faces and garments when the target pose differs substantially from a single reference image.
Generates pseudo-ground-truth frames at key poses, filters them with a reference-only sampler, and trains a per-subject low-rank adapter on static clips.
Requires only one reference image—no subject video, ground-truth frames, or labels.
On TikTok and UBC Fashion, improves the base model on every reported metric and matches or surpasses adaptation using five real frames.
Synthetic static clips can supervise more effectively than real motion videos because they preserve appearance without disrupting temporal priors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. From one reference image xref and a driving pose sequence P , a pose-conditioned generator G synthesizes pose-targeted pseudo-ground-truth frames Dpseudo of the subject. (a) Reward-guided generation: for each key pose, G draws several candidates as an interacting particle system and resamples them in-loop toward a DINO body-similarity reward to xref , then selects the final frame by ArcFace face identity. Every reward is read from the reference alone (our reference-only reward-guided sampler). (b) Test-time personalization: a per-subject LoRA ∆θ adapts the frozen base animator Fθ on static clips of the selected frames. The adapted model Fθ+∆θ renders the personalized video V̂ . No subject video, no ground truth, and no human feedback are used.

Figure 3. Temporal stability. Top: the driving frames. For Base (middle) and Ours (bottom), the leftmost column is that method’s output frame and the remaining columns are consecutive framedifference maps over the same frames. The non-personalized base produces widespread inter-frame residual across the face and torso (temporal flicker), whereas our adapted model confines residual to true motion boundaries and stays stable, reducing mean interframe residual by 60% over the frames shown. Brighter indicates larger frame-to-frame change.

Figure 7. Human preference study. Distribution of 1–5 ratings for ours, Animate-X, the unadapted base, and Moore-AnimateAnyone, on four axes. Thirty-four respondents, 180 ratings per bar group. Ours places 93% of appearance-alignment ratings at 4–5, against 38% for the base model; the ordering is the same on all four axes. Protocol in Appendix B.2.

Figure 8. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Motions and Backgrounds. Examples illustrating variations in background, motion complexity, and clothing style. Our approach consistently preserves holistic appearance and pose alignment while producing sharper, more realistic details than competing methods.

Figure 9. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Appearance and Illumination. Examples covering variations in skin tone, lighting conditions, and clothing texture. Our approach maintains consistent subject appearance and realistic fine-grained details across all scenarios, clearly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 6. Pose-conditioned generator G. G is built on FLUX.1 Kontext [21] paired with a pose ControlNet [57]. The target pose is VAE-encoded and read by a frozen ControlNet (14 joint blocks, 38 unified blocks), whose pose-aware features condition the main DiT. The reference image and initial noise are encoded and denoised by the main DiT, into which we inject the trainable LoRA [13]; a text encoder supplies the prompt. The output latent is VAE-decoded to the subject rendered under the target pose. Backbone weights are frozen (snowflake); only the LoRA adapters are trained (flame).

Figure 5. Pseudo-frame count and supervision source. (a) FVD (orange) is lowest at K=5; FaceID (teal) dips at K=9 and peaks at K=21 at a similar FVD (values from Tab. 6). (b) Seven-metric comparison of supervision sources (outward = better, per-axis min–max over the rows of Tab. 5): Ours forms nearly the outer envelope, while self-distillation collapses on body similarity and temporal consistency.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on hard poses. For two subjects we show the reference and driving pose alongside the base, our adapted model, and ground truth. Insets crop the face. The base reconstructs identity and garment detail inconsistently as the pose departs from the reference, while our adaptation preserves both.

Figure 10. Cross-Domain Comparisons: Animated Characters. Examples from the Unseen100-Val evaluation set featuring 2D and 3D animated characters unseen during training. Our approach generalizes beyond photorealistic subjects, faithfully preserving stylized appearance details and character proportions while maintaining temporal coherence under complex motion.

Figure 11. Adaptation is bounded by pseudo-frame quality. Top (HQ): high-quality pseudo frames (Supervision) yield faithful adapted outputs (Output frames). Bottom (LQ): degraded pseudo frames for the same subject yield weaker outputs. This is why the reference-only sampler selects high-quality frames before adaptation.

Table 12. Sensitivity to the generator’s domain tuning. G’s LoRA receives from no tuning (off-the-shelf FLUX.1 Kontext with the pose ControlNet) to our default of 4,000 steps, with the rest of the pipeline fixed. Teacher is the fidelity of the selected pseudo-frame to the real frame at that pose, and downstream is the adapted model’s video quality (trim, 3 TikTok sequences).

Table 2. Quantitative comparison on cross-domain performance on the Unseen100-Val set after training on TikTok. Off the training distribution, our adaptation reaches the only FVD below 100 (92.5) and the lowest dtSSD, while every other method stays above 125.

Table 4. Component ablation. Each designed component is removed and compared against real-frame supervision (Real-5) and the unadapted base. FaceID and BodySIM are over the full video. Generator G is a per-frame reference with no temporal model, so it lacks FVD/dtSSD and is not ranked.

Table 17. Per-stage test-time cost, single H100 80 GB, 832×480, one TikTok subject, with 81-frame inference. Time is generation only for the inference rows and wall-clock elsewhere. Peak GPU is the maximum resident device memory during the stage, and Alloc. the torch allocator peak where the pipeline reports it (protocol in Appendix F.1).

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in production agents involves transforming accumulated experience into reliable model updates while adapting to evolving business policies. We present CARE (Customer-service Agent Retrospective and Evolve), a grounded RSI framework that operationalizes this process in customer service. Its goal is to replace a frontier proprietary incumbent with an in-house mid-sized model that continues learning after deployment. After a one-time cold start on governed production traces, the current model serves production traffic alongside the incumbent, and its own failures drive the next update. A 24/7 inspection process establishes failures through evidence-blinded, independently reviewed judgments. Attribution separates model errors from defects in Skills, tools, or the harness, routing component failures to repair. Model-attributable trajectories are truncated at the first erroneous decision and paired with verified repairs. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) then updates the model using the same model as teacher, with the diagnosis and repair supplied as privileged information unavailable to the student. To support continued evolution as business requirements change, training mixes failures from different Skill/SOP versions, each judged against the policy in force when it occurred. Candidates run an executable simulation test compiled from the latest SOP and then frozen, followed by offline inspection of the resulting traces. Promotion requires a combined simulation-and-inspection score at least at parity with the deployed version, confirmation through an online comparison with the incumbent, and human approval.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reliable recursive self-improvement under changing business policies.
Uses evidence-blinded, independent review to identify failures and attribute them to the model, Skills, tools, or harness.
Truncates model-error trajectories at the first wrong decision and trains with verified repairs via on-policy self-distillation using privileged diagnoses.
Mixes failures across Skill/SOP versions and evaluates candidates in frozen, executable simulations plus offline trace inspection.
Requires parity with the deployed version, online comparison with the incumbent, and human approval before promotion.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CARE. Phase I bootstraps an in-house policy πθ0 from governed production traces of the incumbent system. Phase II is the recursive loop. The current model πθk serves part of the production traffic; 24/7 online inspection turns its own conversations into reviewed failures; attribution separates model-attributable failures from component failures, which are repaired outside the model; model-attributable failures are cut at the first erroneous decision and repaired, and the model distills from itself on that decision, with the hindsight visible only to the teacher. The candidate is measured by the evaluation system, where it runs a simulation test compiled from the latest Skill/SOP and then frozen, and its simulation traces are inspected offline; it is promoted only if the combined score of the two is at least at parity with the deployed version and an online comparison with the incumbent confirms it. After cold start, training data come from the model’s own failures and the teacher is the model itself. Stages tagged in red are driven by an external frontier model rather than by the in-house model. The operating context is revised independently of the loop: a revision reaches the deployed model through its input and the evaluation system through a recompiled test (Section 3.3).

Figure 3: Online inspection and attribution. Production conversations of the in-house model are frozen into a case set Qt and pass an evidence-blinded inspection (Eq. 18) that separates ranking, capacity-aware admission from three strata (Eq. 20), analysis, and independent review with reconciliation, and ends in one of four terminal states (Eq. 21). Terminal states feed back to the screener (Eq. 23). Only confirmed failures reach attribution, which routes model-attributable cases, together with their diagnosis d, to incremental task construction, routes component failures to repair, and holds cases whose cause cannot be isolated.

Figure 2: The cold-start data engine. (a) Admission keeps complete, context-keyed conversations that pass language, structural, and evidence-anchored semantic checks; only no_problem conversations enter Ds, and rejected or unresolved records are never backfilled. (b) Allocation splits a fixed budget N over region groups, the scenarios of each group, and the regions of GCC4, applying the capacity-constrained equal split of Eq. 8 at every level, and then freezes the selected members S. (c) Refinement borrows tone from linked human conversations for eligible turns while preserving every protected field; a rejected rewrite keeps the original conversation, and only a failed final check removes it.

Figure 4: Retrospective repair construction. (a) A confirmed failure is cut at the first decision the model got wrong. Everything the model could see at that moment becomes the student input; the erroneous output, the rest of the conversation, the outcome, and the diagnosis become hindsight. (b) The proposer uses hindsight to write a minimal repair that remains justified by the decision-time input alone, an independent verifier accepts or rejects it, and each accepted tuple can be projected into SFT, DPO, or OPSD data. Every case ends in exactly one terminal state.

Figure 6: The executable simulation environment. Before the run, the frozen case is split into one view per module (Eq. 38): the user simulator receives the user’s goal, initial knowledge, and signal-gated reactions; the system simulator the initial state and event schedule; the agent only its operating context; and the assessment the branch and the oracle, which no participant sees (Eq. 37). During the run, the orchestrator mediates every exchange, only the system simulator changes business state, and each participant receives its own projection of that state. After the run, the trace and the state log are judged against the oracle, and each case ends in pass or fail (Eq. 41). The traces are also inspected offline (Section 7.2).

Figure 5: Attribution-guided on-policy self-distillation at the failing decision. The student samples a fresh decision ŷ from the decision-time input x. A frozen copy of the same model, additionally given the privileged information I (diagnosis, incident-time SOP, and verified repair), reads the same prefixes, so at every token position both models give a distribution over the vocabulary. The loss compares the two on the teacher’s top-K tokens, in the forward direction with a floor at zero in the deployed configuration, and is backpropagated directly. Gradients flow only into the student, and I stays on the teacher side of the privileged boundary. The direction of the KL divergence, K, and the floor are ablated in Section 8.7.

Figure 7: Recursive improvement of CARE-31B over six versions. (a) Online satisfaction of each version against the incumbent serving concurrently in the same period; the vertical scale is omitted. (b, c) Offline metrics of CARE-31B, with reference models as dashed lines; Gemma-4-31B-IT (zero-shot, 79.00%) and Qwen3.8-27B (77.08%) fall below the range of (b), and GPT-6-Luna (5.55%) and Qwen3.8-27B (9.17%) are omitted from (c) for legibility.

papers.abstract: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.
bullets: Evaluates five LLM-based agents and six agent harnesses on 59 papers spanning simulation, quantum algorithms, and quantum-property characterization.
Finds a fundamental mismatch between information communicated in scientific papers and what autonomous agents need for executable reproduction.
Shows that human intervention can identify missing information and repair failed reproduction workflows.
Introduces Residual Agents, a quantum-tailored self-improving system that reuses externally verified workflow repairs under fixed models and limited adaptation.
Builds an extensible model-context-protocol platform for incorporating verified research workflows and new papers.

figures.caption: FIG. 3. Performance of RA for computational quantum science. Reproduction success across 59 reproduction tasks is plotted against model-inference cost per task on a logarithmic scale. Marker shape denotes the agent system or harness type, marker color denotes the underlying model family or access mode, and marker size indicates wall-clock time per task; semitransparent markers denote earlier model generations. Labels identify the corresponding model or harness. RA, the proposed self-improving AI scientist, runs DSH as its executor and is drawn as the DSH marker inside a gear; the dashed line indicates the Pareto frontier between reproduction success and inference cost. A brown ring marks GPT models accessed through an application programming interface (API).

FIG. 2. AI-assisted reproduction reveals inconsistencies in the scientific record. a, Reproduction assessment across three directions of computational quantum science. Grey denotes studies with no identified problem, whereas increasingly dark red indicates Level I–III issues according to their severity and resolvability. b–d, Representative Level I–III cases. From top to bottom, each case shows the scientific problem, the identified reproduction issue—including the paper’s claim, the contradiction found by the AI scientist and expert feedback—and the reproduced results before and after expert correction, each compared with the original result. For the panel b, a machine-learning configuration discrepancy resolved using the released code. For the panel c, an ambiguous experimental procedure requiring expert resolution. For the panel d, a fundamental inconsistency between the reported quantity, released code and theoretical constraints that cannot be resolved from the available scientific record. Dashed black and solid red curves denote the reported and reproduced results, respectively.

FIG. 1. Paper-to-result reproduction in computational quantum science. a, Scientific papers from three research directions in computational quantum science are converted into reproduction tasks centred on a target figure within OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment. In OmniQ, a plan agent and an execute agent reproduce the source code and the target figure, and a judge agent compares the reproduced figure with the published one. b, The mechanism of the self-improving AI scientist RA for computational quantum science. The planner decomposes a research plan into sub-plans, each executed by an executor and evaluated by a critic. Failed steps are revised and re-executed, with the planner replanning when necessary. A judge evaluates the assembled result. Upon failure, expert feedback is processed by the residual agent to refine executor guidance, critic criteria and planner strategies.

papers.abstract: Personalizing large language model assistants requires adapting their responses to individual users, including the selection of content, reasoning approach, level of detail, and form of presentation. Such preferences are often latent, becoming visible only when users respond to an initial answer and request revisions. We investigate whether these feedback trajectories can be converted into a reusable personalization signal without explicit preference profiles or labels, prompt-time access to interaction histories, or model parameter updates. We introduce UPSHIFT (User Preference Steering from Human-AI Interaction Feedback Traces), a training-free method that compares the hidden representations of initial and feedback-conditioned responses within each session, averages the resulting trajectory displacements across a user's sessions, and injects the aggregated preference direction when answering a new query. The method is motivated by the implicit-preference hypothesis: although an individual conversational transition may reflect topic progression or task-specific correction, changes that recur across sessions retain a component that captures how the user wants responses to be adjusted. We validate the preference-representation capability of UPSHIFT on PrefEval. In evaluations with 40 simulated users, every tested configuration improves preference alignment over the unsteered baseline on held-out topics for both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B; the best configuration increases macro-averaged Elo from 1364.0 to 1605.2 and from 1341.9 to 1591.8, respectively. Matched-user and positive-versus-negative controls further demonstrate that these gains arise from the user-specific preference direction and its learned orientation. These results show that interaction histories can provide compact, reusable supervision for lightweight personalization.
bullets: Addresses latent user preferences revealed through requests to revise initial answers.
Compares hidden representations of initial and feedback-conditioned responses, then averages session-level changes across a user’s interactions.
Injects the aggregated, user-specific preference direction into responses to new queries using a training-free procedure.
On PrefEval with 40 simulated users, all tested configurations improved held-out preference alignment for both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B.
Controls indicate gains come from the user-specific preference direction and its learned orientation.

figures.caption: Table 1: PrefEval accuracy (%) by preference domain. The best result in each column within each evaluation mode is bold.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free method to steer LLM responses using feedback traces, a form of test-time adaptation.
papers.title: UPSHIFT: User Preference Steering from Human-AI Interaction Feedback Traces
papers.tldr: UPSHIFT extracts recurring user-preference directions from feedback-driven interaction traces to personalize LLM responses without profiles, prompts containing histories, or parameter updates.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.
bullets: Addresses failures of Markovian VLA models on tasks requiring working memory and persistent context.
Uses factorized event detection with event-triggered updates to maintain task-relevant language history.
Evaluated on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks with 56 variants, including five inter-episode tasks.
Improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and reaches 78% subtask success on compositional generalization.
Uses up to 4.5× less memory and runs 2.5× faster than a keyframe baseline at long horizons.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall Architecture of HeLM. The High Level Policy (HLP) integrates language memory with a pretrained VLM, which switches between a ‘detect mode’ that monitors events and an ‘update mode’ that updates these events into language memory. The Low Level Policy (LLP), a pretrained VLA, executes action commands generated by the HLP.

Figure 1: Example of non-Markovian task. Due to architectural limitation, a vanilla VLA loses track after pressing the red button and presses it again. HeLM successfully executes the task by storing progress in language memory, allowing the HLP to guide the LLP correctly.

Figure 4: The Real-World Evaluation Suite of HeLM. Our tasks are categorized into two types based on their temporal memory requirements. (Top) Intra-episode tasks (A1–A5) evaluate working memory within a single instruction. (Bottom) Inter-episode tasks (E1–E5) assess episodic context across task boundaries.

Figure 5: Intra-episode real-world evaluation results. HeLM achieves the highest average subtask success rate on five intra-episode tasks. In contrast, Keyframe-HLP fails to detect termination in A1, A4 (denoted by ⋆), while the baselines PCMB-π0 and Naı̈ve-π0 (denoted by ⋆⋆) fail both sequencing and termination across all trials. Under strict task success, HeLM retains 81.3%, while KeyframeHLP drops to 29.3% and both PCMB-π0 and Naı̈ve-π0 drop to 0%. papers.abstract: With the growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) across diverse domains, concerns regarding their safety have grown substantially. LLM unlearning has emerged as a pivotal approach to removing harmful or unlawful content while maintaining utility. Despite increasing interest, the challenges of continual unlearning, which is common in real-world scenarios, remain underexplored. Successive unlearning tasks often lead to intensified utility degradation. To effectively unlearn targeted knowledge while preserving LLM utility, it is essential to minimize changes in model parameters by selectively updating those linked to the target knowledge, thereby ensuring other knowledge remains unaffected. Building on the task vector framework, we propose a new method named ALKN (Adaptive Localization of Knowledge Negation), which uses dynamic masking to sparsify training gradients and adaptively adjusts unlearning intensity based on inter-task relationships. Comprehensive experiments across three well-established LLM unlearning datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms baseline methods in both unlearning effectiveness and utility retention under continual unlearning settings.
bullets: Addresses utility degradation caused by successive unlearning tasks.
Uses a task-vector framework with dynamic masking to sparsify training gradients.
Adaptively adjusts unlearning intensity according to relationships between tasks.
Evaluated on three established LLM unlearning datasets under continual unlearning settings.
Reports better unlearning effectiveness and utility retention than baseline methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The comparative experiments on the TOFU dataset using the baseline method to sequentially unlearn five disjoint subdatasets. (a) The unlearning of preceding tasks results in the partial forgetting of subsequent tasks, as reflected in the reduced conditional probabilities of task data predicted by the model. (b) Under comparable unlearning performance, continual unlearning exhibits significantly greater utility degradation than independent unlearning due to the effects of cascading degradation.

Figure 3. The diagram illustrating the training process of the intermediate model πθtft for the t-th unlearning task. The training loss LESL is computed using entropic soft labels (Section 3.1). Gradients Gu derived from the loss are masked using a binary mask with an underlying vector mt, dynamically updated based on Gu, Gr and M (Section 3.2). The masked gradients are then employed to update the model parameters θtft with an adaptive learning rate α̂t (Section 3.3).
Figure 4. Model utility (MU) and changes of F-Rouge of five unlearning tasks on TOFU dataset for the Llama2 model.
Figure 6. Max/Min Model Utility (MU) across five unlearning tasks on TOFU dataset for Llama2 model.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in open-world environments where safety risks cannot be fully predefined. However, most existing guardrail mechanisms remain static, relying on fixed rules, prompts, or classifiers that generalize poorly to emerging risks. Here we present EVOLVE, a tool-level self-evolving defense framework that formulates agent security as a process of cumulative security evolution. Inspired by how human societies transform experiences into transferable protective knowledge, EVOLVE externalizes security knowledge into executable guardrail tools that are continuously inherited, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction. Across multiple benchmarks, backbone models, and embodied environments, EVOLVE consistently outperforms existing defenses across diverse risk scenarios with +22\% average F1 score. We further validate the framework in real-world robotic and autonomous agent systems. Our results suggest that scalable agent safety may require continuously evolving defense systems rather than static guardrails.
bullets: Targets the limitations of static rules, prompts, and classifiers in open-world environments with unforeseen safety risks.
Models security as cumulative evolution, externalizing protective knowledge into reusable executable guardrail tools.
Tools are continuously inherited, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction.
Across benchmarks, backbone models, and embodied environments, EVOLVE reports a 22% average F1 improvement over existing defenses.
The framework is additionally validated in real-world robotic and autonomous-agent systems, though its scope centers on continuously evolving defenses.

papers.abstract: Online Active Learning (OAL) aims to extend deep learning from static inference after offline training to continuous adaptation during real-time interaction with a changing physical environment. This transition is essential for safety-critical applications, but it raises a central theoretical question: whether the online parameter update process remains stable when scaled to multilayer neural architectures. This paper develops a stability-focused OAL framework. The framework uses prediction error as a feedback signal to update a structured deep model, thereby linking online learning with Lyapunov-based energy minimization. We show that prediction error convergence alone is insufficient for global parameter convergence because multilayer networks may admit high-dimensional manifolds of equivalent output solutions. The analysis therefore separates output error regulation, internal zero dynamics, interlayer coupling, and parameter convergence. Persistency of excitation and active damping are then used to remove the residual null-space modes that remain after output error convergence. A cascaded Lyapunov analysis establishes asymptotic stability of the overall OAL learning process, while monotonic activation functions and diffeomorphic layer mappings provide the uniqueness condition for the target parameter trajectory. The resulting proof provides a theoretical basis for applying online adaptive learning to large-scale neural systems in nonstationary and safety-critical settings.
bullets: Addresses whether online parameter updates remain stable as neural systems adapt continuously in changing, safety-critical environments.
Uses prediction error as feedback and decomposes stability into output regulation, internal zero dynamics, interlayer coupling, and parameter convergence.
Shows that prediction-error convergence alone cannot ensure unique parameter convergence because multilayer networks may have equivalent-output solution manifolds.
Uses persistency of excitation and active damping to eliminate residual null-space modes.
A cascaded Lyapunov analysis proves asymptotic stability under monotonic activations and diffeomorphic layer mappings.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification requires the representation of contiguous spectral signatures and spatial context under limited labeled supervision. Vision test-time training (TTT) offers an alternative to fixed-weight token mixing by performing self-supervised inner-model updates on the input sequence, but its application to center-pixel HSI classification remains insufficiently characterized. We present ViTTT-HSI, a spectral-spatial adaptation of the vision test-time training (ViT3) architecture. A spectral-aware embedding stem extracts ordered-band information using spectral convolution and forms spatial tokens without reducing their spatial resolution. Two ViT3-based TTT encoder blocks perform patch-conditioned token mixing, followed by the fusion of center-pixel and neighborhood-average features for classification. We evaluate the framework on Indian Pines, Pavia University, Salinas, and Houston 2013 using ten random seeds and dataset-specific training fractions of 1% or 5%. The mean overall accuracies are 97.6390%, 98.8753%, 99.3292%, and 98.4283%, respectively. Ablations reveal a substantial contribution from the TTT inner update on Indian Pines and a smaller positive contribution on Pavia University, while the relative benefits of the spectral stem and feature fusion depend on the dataset. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using patch-conditioned vision TTT for spectral--spatial HSI classification and highlight the role of the inner adaptation mechanism.
bullets: Targets HSI classification with limited labeled supervision while preserving spectral signatures and spatial context.
Uses a spectral convolution stem, resolution-preserving spatial tokens, and two patch-conditioned ViT3-based TTT encoder blocks.
Fuses center-pixel and neighborhood-average features for final classification.
Evaluated on Indian Pines, Pavia University, Salinas, and Houston 2013, achieving mean overall accuracies of 97.6390%, 98.8753%, 99.3292%, and 98.4283%, respectively.
Ablations indicate that TTT inner updates are especially beneficial on Indian Pines, while other component benefits vary by dataset.

papers.abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $ρ= 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.
bullets: Frames drift response as a state machine with explicit triggers and costs for retraining, alerts, and rollbacks.
Gates retraining on detected drift, label availability, and measured degradation; promoted models must pass a two-stage canary.
Evaluated prospectively against six baselines across 13 real and semi-synthetic streams.
At higher retraining costs, RAR outperformed three alternatives on four streams within bounded cost windows, but results versus the cost-aware policy were heterogeneous.
RAR retrained before true drift less often than detector-triggered retraining, while removing the canary improved utility on 11 of 13 streams.

papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) follows the pretrain-finetune paradigm: an agent is first pretrained on historical data and then adapted through online interaction. We study offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay, where the agent must improve using only the pretrained model and newly collected experience. A key challenge is to avoid catastrophic failure, a sharp early performance collapse during online fine-tuning, while still achieving strong asymptotic performance. Through controlled experiments, we show that removing offline replay can induce catastrophic failure, while retaining strong conservative regularization from offline RL can suppress final online performance. We also find that common stabilization strategies do not reliably prevent early collapse, and that the critic-side mechanisms we test are insufficient on their own. Motivated by these findings, we propose ANCHOR, a simple adaptation method that anchors the actor to the offline-pretrained policy early in online fine-tuning, anneals this constraint over time, and retains only a small residual conservative critic regularizer. We provide a theoretical interpretation showing that KL anchoring helps preserve critic reliability across nearby occupancy distributions, with a two-phase regret bound explaining when anchoring should be maintained or relaxed. Across FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit tasks, ANCHOR substantially reduces catastrophic failure while maintaining strong asymptotic performance. Ablations show that KL annealing and the residual conservative weight are important for balancing early stability and online adaptation, while additional analysis shows that ANCHOR is most beneficial when the pretrained policy contains useful behavior to preserve. Code is available at https://github.com/Cho-Geonwoo/ANCHOR.
bullets: Offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay can cause catastrophic early performance collapse.
Strong conservative regularization may prevent collapse but limit eventual online improvement; critic-only stabilization is insufficient.
ANCHOR anchors the actor to the pretrained policy early, anneals the KL constraint, and keeps a small residual conservative critic regularizer.
Theory links KL anchoring to critic reliability under nearby occupancy distributions and gives conditions for maintaining or relaxing the anchor.
Experiments on FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit show reduced catastrophic failure with strong asymptotic performance; benefits are greatest when pretrained behavior is useful.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ANCHOR improves both early stability and final performance. From top to bottom, the plots correspond to: batch size, actor learning rate, critic learning rate, critic hidden dimension, actor hidden dimension, LayerNorm in the critic, LayerNorm in the actor, and the duration of the offline pretraining phase. Increasing αKL slows the critic shift, but does not reliably prevent early performance collapse.

Figure 3: KL annealing improves early stability while preserving final performance. ANCHOR is compared with the fixed-KL and no-KL variants. The fixed-KL variant improves early stability but can limit final improvement, while the no-KL variant adapts aggressively but causes early collapse.

Figure 8: Sensitivity to batch size and UTD ratio. We vary the batch size (top) and UTD ratio (bottom) across three tasks. ANCHOR is generally robust to these choices, although larger batch size and larger UTD can increase learning instability.

papers.abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires finalizing solutions from reasoning that is distributed across the individual attempts of many agents. However, useful intermediate reasoning can remain unexploited when collaboration is limited to voting on conclusions reached among individual agents, or aggregating long, noisy collections of reasoning trajectories in context. In this work, we propose TTT-Consolidate, a framework that uses multi-agent reasoning trajectories as adaptation data to improve a model's subsequent reasoning. TTT-Consolidate jointly consolidates trajectories into parametric representations through test-time training, then generates a new solution by conditioning on the consolidated information. We meta-learn how to consolidate using bi-level optimization at training time, where an inner loop encodes reasoning trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter, and an outer loop learns meta-parameters for the inner loop such that the consolidation is helpful for the model to synthesize a final solution. As no large-scale corpus of diverse reasoning trajectories exists for training aggregation methods, we construct the OpenParallelThinking corpus composed of 12,810 math problems paired with a mixture of trajectories from six LLMs. Evaluated on challenging math and STEM benchmarks, TTT-Consolidate outperforms the best aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points, even under matched compute and runtime settings, with the gap widening at larger model scales. TTT-Consolidate also recovers from unsuccessful individual trajectories more robustly, an ability that improves as the number of available (even incorrect) trajectories increases. Finally, we demonstrate that TTT-Consolidate benefits from both SFT and RL-based outer loop objectives. We will release TTT-Consolidate and OpenParallelThinking for use in future work on reasoning aggregation.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of voting and aggregating noisy reasoning traces in context.
Encodes multiple trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter during an inner-loop test-time training phase.
Uses bi-level meta-learning to optimize how trajectory information is consolidated for final-solution synthesis.
Introduces OpenParallelThinking, a corpus of 12,810 math problems with trajectories from six LLMs.

papers.abstract: Financial time-series forecasting is still difficult owing to the non-stationary nature of the market, regime changes, and catastrophic forgetting, which makes conventional deep learning models hard to adapt in the long term. To achieve uncertainty-aware robust financial forecasting in the face of changing market conditions, this study proposes a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network with Continual Learning (HQNN-CL). The proposed framework combines Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) based regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth parameterized quantum circuits, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), experience replay, and probabilistic forecasting in a single architecture. The framework was tested on four real-time stock datasets: Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata and Tata Consultancy Services, and compared with seven state-of-the-art forecasting models, including recurrent and Transformer-based models. The experimental results show that HQNN-CL has outperformed other methods on the Systems Limited (RMSE = 3.0149) and Teradata (RMSE = 0.8909) datasets and is within 0.32% and 0.40% of the best baseline method for Microsoft and Tata Consultancy Services, respectively. The proposed framework also generates well-calibrated probabilistic forecasts within the range of 89.5% to 96.5% empirical coverage rate, has zero catastrophic forgetting (BWT = 0.0000) for all sequential learning tasks, and consistently shows positive forward transfer. Ablation and statistical significance analyses also validate the performance of adaptive quantum feature learning and continual adaptation under heterogeneous market conditions, regime-wise.
bullets: Targets non-stationary markets, regime shifts, and catastrophic forgetting in long-term financial forecasting.
Combines Gaussian HMM regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth quantum circuits, EWC, experience replay, and probabilistic forecasting.
Evaluated on Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata, and Tata Consultancy Services stock datasets against seven forecasting models.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents that answer questions about their route need a memory of what they saw, and scene graphs are a natural form for it. A vision-language model (VLM) can receive such a graph as text or through a graph encoder, but accuracy alone cannot show whether the graph holds the episode's facts, reaches the model, or is actually relied on. In this diagnostic study, we introduce a graph-swap test for the last of these: each episode is given another episode's graph, and we count how many answers change. On an embodied question-answering benchmark with routes through two to seven rooms, we use it to compare ways of delivering scene-graph memory to a fine-tuned VLM. As text, the memory is used strongly, adding 30 points on route questions. As a graph, it is not, and we trace why: the encoder preserves the information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard it. Giving each node its own input token recovers part of it, a gain of 8.3 points on route questions that the swap test confirms comes from the graph. The test also exposes a shortcut that accuracy hides: when the same facts appear in the text, the model ignores its graph. The test thus offers a cheap check of whether a VLM uses its scene-graph memory, and our analysis points to how that memory should be delivered.
bullets: The study tests whether scene-graph memory is represented, reaches the VLM, and actually influences answers.
It swaps each episode’s graph with another episode’s graph and counts answer changes to measure graph reliance.
Text-based graph memory is strongly used, improving route-question performance by 30 points.
Graph encoders preserve information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard its usefulness.

Giving each graph node its own input token recovers part of the benefit, with an 8.3-point route-question gain confirmed by the swap test; duplicated text facts can cause the model to ignore the graph.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed model using only unlabeled target data, but standard entropy-based methods often rely on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift. We propose MIRA, Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation, a source-free online adaptation method that uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations to probe prediction reliability. For each target batch, MIRA reuses a single feature extraction pass and samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, forming an efficient local predictive distribution. Rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior, MIRA treats the perturbation scale as a local probing radius and selects a batch-specific scale using mutual information (MI) and prediction agreement. The resulting perturbation-sensitivity signal identifies predictions that are confident and locally stable under classifier perturbations, while suppressing brittle predictions with high stochastic disagreement. MIRA then performs adaptation with an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss, which down-weights perturbation-sensitive or low-confidence samples before they drive entropy minimization. This weighted loss reduces the influence of brittle predictions that can otherwise cause harmful adaptation under distribution shift. The method requires no source data, retraining, model ensembles, or offline posterior fitting, and can be applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood, suggesting that mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation yield more robust online TTA than deterministic confidence.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of entropy-based TTA to reinforce overconfident mistakes under distribution shift.
Uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations and one feature-extraction pass to estimate local prediction reliability.

papers.abstract: Networks that keep learning overwrite what they know. Prevailing remedies replay stored data, distil from old models or freeze the backbone. The brain suggests a different division of labour: the hippocampus indexes where experience lies in cortex while the cortex keeps learning. We show that this division lets a fully trainable network keep learning without cross-task replay, a teacher or inference-time memory. After each task, a training-only hippocampal memory indexes the input geometry of every group of synapses sharing an input, residual energy included, and limits each synapse's movement per direction before and after the optimizer. This class-free geometry carries most of the protection; with conflict detection on top, the method cuts absorption of established classes by near-duplicates several-fold against every compared method. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of one principle keeping whole networks learning across four architecture families and models up to 8 billion parameters. Methods that freeze the backbone hold up only as far as its representation already separates the classes; here the whole network keeps learning to tell near-duplicates apart, leading the frozen-backbone baseline by 17.5 points on TACRED. Without the memory, much old knowledge stays decodable but beyond the network's reach.
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting caused by continual learning overwriting established knowledge.
Indexes input geometry and residual energy for synapse groups, constraining synaptic movement before and after optimization; conflict detection adds further protection.
Works across four architecture families and models up to 8 billion parameters.
Reduces absorption of established classes by near-duplicates several-fold versus compared methods.
On TACRED, outperforms a frozen-backbone baseline by 17.5 points; without memory, old knowledge may remain decodable but inaccessible.￼

papers.abstract: The transition of information-centric artificial intelligence to safety-critical applications is impeded by the limitations of conventional offline-training paradigms in open-world environments. This paper presents Control AI, an architecture for Online Active Learning (OAL) inspired by the continuous Prediction-Evaluation-Correction process of biological intelligence. The framework combines the hierarchical representation capacity of deep neural networks with the real-time error-feedback adaptation of adaptive control. A prediction model maps sensory input into a latent manifold, an optional latent model represents transitions in that space, and a reconstruction model maps the latent state back to observable signals. Residuals between predictions and measurements provide the internal learning signal. Spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction architectures prevent OAL from collapsing to a trivial identity mapping, while coupled, dual, and localized variants shorten error-transmission paths. Localized predictive coding style OAL is implemented through guidance-backpropagation and target-backpropagation architectures, and hybrid and scaled variants support high-dimensional deployment. The paper focuses on the architectural rationale and the progression from a conceptual feedback loop to practical large-scale configurations.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of offline training when safety-critical systems encounter changing, unanticipated conditions.
Combines deep hierarchical representations with real-time adaptive-control feedback.
Uses prediction, optional latent transition modeling, reconstruction, and residual errors as the learning signal.
Introduces spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction plus localized, dual, coupled, hybrid, and scaled variants to avoid trivial identity mappings and support larger deployments.
The abstract emphasizes architectural rationale and configuration progression rather than reporting quantitative experimental results.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.
bullets: Addresses fixed experience-retrieval pipelines that do not adapt experience use to task context.
Uses a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller to choose among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL actions.
Jointly decides whether to invoke experience, which memory format to use, and when to consolidate guidance.
Updates both the experience memory and routing policy online from task feedback.
Across four benchmarks and four backbones, improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points and reduces token use by 5.7–62.5× versus ACE with GPT-5.2.

papers.abstract: AI agents often rely on persistent memory to retain user preferences and operational rules across sessions. However, this capability introduces a new safety risk: malicious instructions from messages, documents, or Web content can be retained in memory and influence future tasks even after the original attack content is removed. Existing attack success metrics, however, fail to capture who is affected and how attacks translate into downstream harm during otherwise normal task execution. We introduce MemHarmBench, a victim-centric benchmark for evaluating cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. MemHarmBench considers three categories of potential victims: users, workspace/project owners, and external stakeholders. Our evaluation first exposes an agent to malicious instructions and tests whether they are retained in memory. We then remove the attack content and initiate a new session with a legitimate task while preserving the agent's memory. We jointly evaluate whether the agent follows the attacker's intent, completes the legitimate task, and exhibits observable execution anomalies. Across multiple agent systems, we find that cross-session attacks can remain behaviorally stealthy: agents often complete tasks normally and exhibit no detectable anomalies while still making critical decisions aligned with the attacker's intent. By connecting malicious memory retention to downstream decisions and affected parties, MemHarmBench provides a systematic framework for exposing safety risks that conventional attack- and task-success metrics may overlook. We publicly release MemHarmBench at https://github.com/Kirito14IT/MemHarmBench.
bullets: Targets cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents.
Tests whether malicious instructions persist after the original content is removed and affect a subsequent legitimate task.
Jointly measures attacker-intent adherence, legitimate-task completion, and observable execution anomalies.
Finds that attacks can remain behaviorally stealthy: agents may complete tasks normally without anomalies while making attacker-aligned decisions.
Provides a publicly released benchmark for connecting memory retention to downstream decisions and affected parties.

papers.abstract: B2B outbound sales involves high transaction values and relationship-based trust, so closing a deal typically requires multiple rounds of outreach building on prior context. Existing LLM-based sales agents operate within single sessions and cannot carry forward context or refine strategies from experience. Methods that do learn from experience store lessons as unstructured text and treat all outcomes as equally informative, with no mechanism to distinguish a flawed strategy from an external factor. We propose SPAR, a self-evolving framework that models selling strategies as testable hypotheses and refines them without parameter updates. A double-loop architecture lets an inner loop adapt to individual merchants through episodic memory while an outer loop evolves a shared strategy playbook through causal attribution and hypothesis-driven evolution. In a live A/B test on the 1688 platform with over 200,000 merchants, SPAR achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth. Human evaluation by domain experts rates SPAR at 4.62 out of 5 on overall sales quality, the highest among all methods.
bullets: Targets the lack of cross-session memory and strategy refinement in existing LLM-based sales agents.
Models sales strategies as testable hypotheses rather than unstructured lessons.
Uses a double-loop design: episodic memory adapts to merchants, while causal attribution evolves a shared strategy playbook without parameter updates.
In a live 1688-platform A/B test involving over 200,000 merchants, SPAR increased conversion by 15.8% and high-intent merchant growth by 35.8%.
Domain experts rated its overall sales quality 4.62/5, highest among the evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is expected to adapt to evolving environments and recognize previously unseen categories, making generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation (GCD-TTA) an important problem. However, existing works treat GCD and TTA separately, while the limited semantic information in 3D point clouds makes GCD-TTA under domain shift more prone to feature collapse when combining GCD with TTA. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework for GCD-TTA in 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation. Specifically, in the first stage, we adaptively aggregate local 3D features according to geometric density variations and obtain reliable pseudo labels under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, we cast category discovery as an optimal transport assignment process for globally consistent grouping of novel categories. Meanwhile, semantic features from 2D vision foundation models are fused with 3D point cloud features to enrich 3D semantic information and promote a more separable feature space. Extensive experiments on Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI, and Synth4D to nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 out of 10 benchmark splits and improves the overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.
bullets: Addresses feature collapse when jointly performing category discovery and test-time adaptation under domain shift.
Aggregates local 3D features using geometric density variations and enforces global class-wise prototype consistency for reliable pseudo-labels.
Models novel-category discovery as an optimal-transport assignment problem for globally consistent grouping.
Fuses semantic features from 2D vision foundation models with 3D features to create a more separable representation.
On three cross-domain benchmarks, achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 of 10 splits and improves mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.

papers.abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $τ^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.
bullets: Long agent contexts make repeatedly scoring the full prefix expensive, while fixed cross-layer reuse schedules cannot react to new tool evidence.

papers.abstract: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.
bullets: Applies a rank-8 shift after every decoder block of a frozen backbone, using only 0.03–0.05% additional parameters.
Supports runtime control over injection strength, phase, and shift-space mixing, with no harness tokens at inference.
Recovers source-harness gains in 8/10 preregistered settings; transfers positively across 5/7 task pairs and composes without the interference seen in stacked text instructions.
Improves budget-matched harness search by 1.45× and matches or exceeds same-capacity LoRA performance with fewer parameters.
The method transfers across 1B–8B models, but effective gain locations depend on the model–task pair.

papers.abstract: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches $15.0\times$ the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches $1.065C$ while every control stays within $C$, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields $\varepsilon$ lower bounds ($3.25$ at $δ=10^{-5}$) below the advertised guarantee ($4.38$). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.
bullets: LLM.int8 uses batch-wide outlier routing, allowing one record to affect other records’ frozen-backbone computations.
The paper bounds sensitivity inflation and specifies a record-isolation contract for private fine-tuning.
Native-stack audits find a constructed witness reaching 15× the add/remove bound and a smaller native excess of 1.065C.
Record-owned precision dispatch preserves the same batched GEMMs, while direct contract checks reveal violations more efficiently than release-level audits.

Orange: the 10 candidates that exceed C by more than 0.1%. At the original screening radius C=1 most gradients are not clipped, the added record contributes less than C, and no candidate exceeds the bound. (b) Forty fresh native cases for the top candidate at C=0.25 and C=0.001: native batching exceeds the bound by 6.53% at both radii, while record isolation, threshold zero, BF16 and NF4 stay within it. At B=16, one pair in five computes at least one column in FP16 only because another record crossed the threshold. (b) Number of records, out of 16, whose own outlier set differs from the batch union in each layer; blank cells have no outlier columns. Figure 1. Frozen weights do not make records independent. LLM.int8 sends an activation column to an FP16 path if any row of the flattened batch reaches the threshold τ , and applies that batch-wide set to every row. (a) Adding or changing one record (x) therefore changes the arithmetic of unchanged records (r1, r2), although all weights are frozen and quantization scales are per row.
