papers.selection_reason: Addresses privacy and sensitivity in private quantized fine-tuning, offering a technical contribution to LLM memory and adaptation mechanisms.
papers.title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Cross-record precision routing in LLM.int8 can violate record-level sensitivity assumptions in private quantized fine-tuning, but record-owned dispatch restores isolation without extra GEMM computation.

papers.abstract: Learned reward models allow reinforcement-learning agents to use demonstrations, implicit feedback, safety constraints, social norms, or other sources that do not provide a complete hand-designed scalar reward. However, a learned reward model can assign high reward to unwanted behavior. A policy can exploit these errors during training. Later requirements can also identify additional regions where the deployed reward should change. We introduce \emph{flywheel-guided patching}, a mechanism for making such localized corrections without retraining the learned evaluator. An Alignment Flywheel identifies overgeneralized or constraint-violating regions and compiles verified findings into suppression patches. We instantiate the mechanism for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning using MoE-GUIDE, placing patches in the model's latent space and retrieving only a small local subset during online reward evaluation. In the main MuJoCo benchmark, we evaluate patching without expert-state reset warm starts. We also test whether operator-specified norms absent from the demonstrations can be compiled into the same reward interface and compare this with enforcing the corresponding rules online. The results show that localized corrective information can modify an existing learned reward without providing a complete replacement reward. Compilation can reuse judgments that are expensive or unavailable during control. Cheap deterministic rules may be simpler to check directly at each step. Code for MoE-GUIDE, Alignment Flywheel, and flywheel patching is at https://github.com/decide-ugent/Alignment-Flywheel.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model without labels by rewarding answers that agree with the majority, but it collapses the policy onto its majority answer and can remove the correct answer from the samples. Exploration can prevent this collapse, yet its strength is chosen by trial and error, and how the training algorithm changes the required strength is unclear. We model training on a single problem as a continuous flow of the logits of a softmax policy and analyze which policies are stable as the exploration coefficient varies. Only collapsed policies are stable below a lower boundary and only policies spread over many answers above an upper boundary, and we derive these boundaries in closed form for an agreement reward with smoothing toward the uniform policy, compute them for the majority reward of TTRL on policies with one leading answer and bound them with interval arithmetic for actions on ordered bins. We prove that under exact gradients, the learning rate and, in a mean-field model, the normalization of GRPO leave these boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through them together with the reward but shift them when exploration bypasses them. Exact sums on these policies then show that a bonus for rare answers needs a coefficient above $1/\log(G-1)$ for groups of $G$ samples before the normalization and about two to three times that after it. In free-form TTRL on MATH-500, a bonus placed before the normalization prevented collapse and kept more correct answers among the samples, although it lowered pass@1.
bullets: TTRL’s majority-agreement reward can collapse the policy onto one answer and eliminate correct alternatives from samples.
A continuous logit-flow analysis identifies three exploration regimes, with closed-form stability boundaries for agreement rewards with uniform-policy smoothing.
Learning rate and GRPO normalization affect the boundaries differently depending on whether exploration is applied before or after reward normalization.
For groups of G samples, rare-answer bonuses require coefficients above 1/log(G−1) before normalization and roughly two to three times larger after normalization.
On MATH-500, pre-normalization exploration prevented collapse and retained more correct answers among samples, but reduced pass@1.

papers.abstract: We study \textit{best-of-both-worlds} (BOBW) algorithms for linear bandits, which aim to simultaneously guarantee $\gO(\sqrt T)$ regret in the adversarial regime and $\gO(\log T)$ regret in the stochastic regime over $T$ rounds. For finite action sets, we introduce \emph{information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader} (\IAFTRL{}), the first BOBW algorithm based purely on the follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) framework that attains an $\gO(\cstar\log T)$-type regret in the stochastic regime, where $\cstar$ is the information-acquisition complexity that characterizes instance-dependent optimality in linear bandits, while retaining the $\gO(\sqrt{T})$ regret guarantee in the adversarial regime. This resolves the open problem posed in~\cite{LeeEtAl2021,KongZ023,ItoT23,ZhaoItoLi2025}.
bullets: Introduces information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader (IAFTRL), the first purely FTRL-based best-of-both-worlds algorithm for linear bandits with finite action sets.
Achieves O(c* log T)-type regret in the stochastic regime, where c* is the information-acquisition complexity characterizing instance-dependent optimality.
Retains O(sqrt T) regret in the adversarial regime.
Resolves an open problem posed in prior work on BOBW linear bandits.

papers.title: Best-of-Both-Worlds FTRL for Linear Bandits: The Interplay of Information Acquisition, Corruption, and Geometry
papers.tldr: A new FTRL-based algorithm, IAFTRL, achieves best-of-both-worlds regret for linear bandits with finite action sets: O(log T) instance-dependent stochastic regret and O(sqrt T) adversarial regret.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.
bullets: Evaluates expert, FFN, and layer pruning on mathematical and coding benchmarks using pass@k at matched sampling budgets.
Finds that some heavily pruned models can match or exceed original models in reasoning coverage and solve problems absent from original samples.
Shows that lower pass@1 can reflect reduced sampling efficiency rather than loss of solvable-problem coverage.
Severe pruning increases repetition and generation unreliability, potentially raising total token use despite shorter individual responses.
Argues that pruning should be assessed by both coverage and the sampling cost needed to reach it.

papers.tldr: Pruned LLMs may retain broad reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, but often require substantially more sampling to obtain correct solutions.

papers.abstract: Federated time-series forecasting is increasingly important in applications where temporal data are distributed across privacy-sensitive clients, such as environmental monitoring, smart cities, and industrial sensing. A central limitation of current continual-learning protocols is that they usually assume predefined task boundaries, whereas deployed forecasting systems receive an uninterrupted stream and must decide autonomously when adaptation is necessary. This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting under concept drift. We introduce a drift-aware continual-learning protocol in which each client monitors prediction-window RMSE, calibrates a robust median threshold from the offline base period, and triggers adaptation only after persistent degradation. To mitigate forgetting, we propose a TwoTierReplay mechanism that separates fixed offline representative memory from online memory. The offline tier preserves long-term knowledge learned during the base phase, while the online tier captures recent distributional changes after drift. Experiments on the Beijing Multi-Site Air- Quality dataset with 12 clients, three forecasting targets, and three horizons show that TwoTierReplay achieves the best stability-plasticity score in all nine target-horizon configurations. It improves over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%. These results suggest that explicit temporal structuring of replay memory is a practical and effective mechanism for task-free federated continual forecasting.
bullets: Addresses continual forecasting without predefined task boundaries in privacy-sensitive, distributed time-series settings.
Clients monitor prediction-window RMSE and adapt only after degradation persistently exceeds a robust threshold calibrated from the base period.
TwoTierReplay separates fixed representative offline memory from online memory that captures post-drift data.
On the Beijing Multi-Site Air-Quality dataset, it achieved the best stability–plasticity score across all nine target–horizon configurations.
It improved over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%; scope is limited to the evaluated dataset, clients, targets, and horizons.

A persistent drift alarm at any client triggers local adaptation at all K clients; the server aggregates only model parameters and rebroadcasts the updated global model.

papers.selection_reason: Task-free federated continual forecasting with two-tier replay under concept drift.
papers.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Task-Free Federated Continual Forecasting via Two-Tier Replay under Concept Drift
papers.tldr: TwoTierReplay reduces catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting by combining long-term offline memory with recent online replay triggered by persistent drift.

papers.abstract: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). Unlike conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, HAFL employs asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergences for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives, respectively, and formulate optimization problems to jointly determine optimal hyperparameters to minimize global training latency. Evaluations demonstrate that HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for benchmark DNNs and datasets, offering promising FL systems across remote areas with 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.
bullets: Targets decentralized, resource-limited terrestrial clients in space-air-ground integrated 6G networks.
Uses satellites as aggregators, broadcasters, additional training clients, and inter-satellite relays.
Replaces synchronous updates with asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates and provides convergence analyses for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives.
Jointly optimizes hyperparameters to reduce global training latency.
Experiments show faster initial convergence, comparable final performance, and fewer global rounds with lower communication cost for benchmark DNNs and datasets.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $π$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
bullets: Existing memory methods rely mainly on the initial request, potentially missing preferences and constraints that emerge during execution.
Pulse uses an independent lightweight memory agent to monitor task progress and identify personalization needs or preference conflicts.
The agent retrieves user and project memories and delivers targeted interventions during relevant stages.
Reinforcement learning optimizes the timing and content of interventions.
Pulse scores 71.9% on π-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, with the highest overall scores among compared methods and improved task efficiency.

papers.abstract: Virtual metrology (VM) aims to estimate costly or delayed metrology variables from heterogeneous sensor signals and in-line measurements, and it acts as a critical component of semiconductor manufacturing. While recent data-driven models have improved VM accuracy, most are trained in batch settings and assume stationary data distributions. In practice, however, production environments evolve continuously due to equipment degradation, process adjustments, and maintenance events, making conventional batch-trained VM models difficult to maintain under temporal distribution shifts. In this work, we propose GRAPE (Global Regression with Adaptive Prediction Enhancement), a practical online learning framework for VM in evolving wafer-processing environments. GRAPE integrates a stable global predictor based on interpretable representations with two lightweight streaming adapters that correct feature-level and environment-level shifts through online updates. Experiments on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets, including chronologically held-out blind-test streams, show that GRAPE improves robustness and generalization under real temporal drift compared with both conventional batch-learning methods and existing online learning baselines.
bullets: Addresses the failure of batch-trained VM models under temporal shifts caused by equipment degradation, process changes, and maintenance.
Combines a stable global predictor with lightweight online adapters for feature-level and environment-level drift correction.
Evaluated on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets with chronologically held-out blind-test streams.
Shows improved robustness and generalization under real temporal drift versus batch-learning and existing online-learning baselines.

papers.abstract: Lifelong Person Re-identification (LReID) aims to match the same person using sequentially collected data. In practical long-term deployments, however, the model must handle both domain shifts across cameras and scenes, and irregular clothing changes of the same identity. This gives rise to the Cloth-Hybrid Lifelong Person Re-identification (CH-LReID) task, which demands balancing cloth-relevant and cloth-irrelevant knowledge in streaming data. While existing LReID methods have explored replay-based or distillation-based anti-forgetting strategies, they typically fail to sufficiently model stage-aware domain distributions and cross-stage feature continuity under exemplar-free training. To address this problem, we propose a Distribution-Aware Adaptive Differentiated Knowledge Consolidation (DADKC) framework. The core idea is to enhance the existing Differentiated Knowledge Consolidation (DKC) paradigm with adaptive distribution modeling. To this end, three lightweight modules are designed: (1) an Anchor Pool Adapter (APA) to retrieve learnable anchor cues for refining identity features; (2) a Phase Path Mixer (PPM) to perform stage-aware expert routing for integrating domain-specific distribution paths; and (3) a Stage Bridge Alignment (SBA) module to regularize the continuity of base, anchor, and path representations between adjacent stages. Extensive experiments on the CH-LReID and LReID benchmarks show that DADKC gains 4.1%/4.5% mAP/R1 on Order-1 and 3.6%/3.4% mAP/R1 on Order-2 over the DKC baseline, and lowers weighted forgetting from 2.4%/1.7% to 1.8%/1.4%, while storing neither historical images nor per-image features. The code is available at https://github.com/fire667/DADKC.
bullets: Targets Cloth-Hybrid Lifelong Person Re-identification, where identities may change clothing across sequential domains.
Extends Differentiated Knowledge Consolidation with adaptive distribution modeling through three lightweight modules: APA, PPM, and SBA.
APA refines identity features using learnable anchor cues; PPM routes samples through stage-aware domain paths; SBA aligns representations across adjacent stages.
Compared with DKC, DADKC improves mAP/R1 by 4.1%/4.5% on Order-1 and 3.6%/3.4% on Order-2, while reducing weighted forgetting.
Operates without storing historical images or per-image features.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.
bullets: Problem: Using the newest capture timestamp as truth fails when an agent reverses an action and the current state is represented by an older frame.
Method: Retain all frames and re-date retrieved tokens using valid times inferred from the agent’s action log.
Theory: Newest-timestamp selection is correct only when all current views are newer than all outdated views; after a return, the action log may be essential.
Results: After undo, current-state coverage rises from 0.36 to 0.62 for FAR and from 0.003 to 0.19 for HY-WorldPlay.
Scope: Re-dating is especially beneficial when moved tokens receive little weight, and the paper introduces a calibrated metric for evaluating memory after undos.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires policies to act on information that is no longer visible. Modified objects may leave the field of view, while completed subtasks continue to constrain future actions. Existing approaches extend temporal context through recurrent state updates, test-time training, or storage and retrieval of past observations. As horizons grow, these mechanisms can still leave the policy to infer task state from long, redundant, and viewpoint-dependent visual experience. We argue that long-horizon agents benefit not merely from remembering more, but from remembering task-relevant state changes and progress. We propose Memory of Object States and Task Progress (MOST), a policy-internal memory framework that compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens. Historical and predictive future tokens are explicitly supervised with object states and subtask progress, structuring memory around what has changed in the world and what has already been accomplished. The resulting memory directly conditions action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage. We further introduce RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Across RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and real-world robot experiments, MOST consistently outperforms Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), the previous state-of-the-art model. It raises average success from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. MOST also outperforms a matched visual-history memory variant, showing that effective long-horizon memory depends not only on how much experience is retained, but on whether it preserves decision-relevant progress and world-state changes.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of acting on modified objects and completed subtasks that are no longer visible.
Compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens representing historical object states and predicted future task progress.
Uses these tokens to condition action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage.
Introduces RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark for multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation.
Reports gains over XR-1 and a matched visual-history memory variant across simulation and real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Memory Expert architecture. Historical multi-view observations are encoded into history tokens, and future queries are appended to form the memory sequence. The sequence is processed with block-causal self-attention and conditioned on the instruction through cross-attention. During training, each token predicts its subtask and the state of every relevant object. The output of each Memory Expert layer conditions the corresponding Action Expert layer.

Figure 2: MOST overview. MOST integrates a Vision Language Model, a Memory Expert, and an Action Expert within one end-to-end policy. The Vision Language Model encodes the current observation and instruction. The Memory Expert represents sampled history as object states and task progress, and the Action Expert uses both contexts to generate continuous actions. Task-state supervision is training-only.

papers.abstract: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.
bullets: Addresses the need to retain motion history and earlier visual evidence missing from current observations.
Trains memory with temporal supervision from predicted future visual features.
At execution, uses spatially normalized prediction discrepancies to selectively update the visual state.
Improves success from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO and 14.4% to 83.8% on RMBench M(1).
Also improves general manipulation and spatial-perturbation robustness, with 7.7 ms mean inference overhead on an NVIDIA H800.

Figure 2: PREM architecture. (A) PREM compares the cached prediction with observed visual features at each spatial location to compute prediction discrepancy. (B) The spatially normalized discrepancy regulates how much of the candidate visual-state update is incorporated. (C) An actionconditioned predictor predicts the next visual features from the incoming visual state, observed visual features, and latent action representation. The prediction objective supervises memory learning. The cached prediction provides a reference for subsequent visual-state updating.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.
bullets: Addresses routing interference, where similar new skills displace previously correct skills as libraries grow.
Rewrites only each incoming skill’s name and description to clarify capabilities, distinctions, and exclusions.
Requires no router training, labeled data, or per-skill feedback.
On a 731-skill, ten-session setting, it selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries versus 36.4% with original metadata.
Outperforms competing methods across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, with gains transferring to the Codex CLI agent harness.

figures.caption: Figure 3: This figure gives an overview of SKILL++, to show how it refines an incoming skill before the router reads it. SKILL++ first retrieves similar earlier skills from a record of their original names, descriptions, bodies and synthetic queries. Three components then refine the new skill independently. Description differentiation rewrites its description around what makes it unique, scope exclusions list related work that it does not cover, and name clarification makes an overlapping name more specific. The refined name and description enter the library that the router reads, and the original skill joins the record for future additions.

Figure 2: This figure compares three ways of handling a growing skill library, to position our problem. (a) Continuous router training follows arriving skills but retrains the router at every step, risking catastrophic forgetting of earlier skills. (b) One-shot skill optimization refines a fixed skill set once, so it ignores skills that arrive later. (c) SKILL++ keeps the router frozen and refines each new batch against similar earlier skills, so both earlier and new skills are selected for the queries that need them.

Figure 4: This figure shows FC@5 as the library grows (sizes in Tab. A2), to test whether routing stays accurate. (a) The main router, Claude Haiku 4.5 (Tab. A1). (b)–(e) Four other routers (Tab. A4). With every router, Vanilla declines while SKILL++ leads or ties at every checkpoint.

Figure 5: This figure breaks down the routing errors at S9 into two forms and seven types (defined in Appendix C.2), to show which errors SKILL++ removes. All panels draw on the eight combinations of Tab. A3. (a) The 200 Vanilla errors, by form (inner ring) and type (outer ring). (b) Errors per type under Vanilla and SKILL++, as a share of the Vanilla errors. (c) Errors per form when one component or all three are added to Vanilla, shown in the same way. SKILL++ removes most errors of both forms, and each component mainly reduces one form.

Figure 1: This figure presents an example of routing interference, to show why incoming metadata needs refinement. The router reads only skill names and descriptions. (a) For a query about an AI paper, it selects the AI paper-writing skill. (b) A biology paper-writing skill arrives with the same metadata, and the router selects it instead. (c) SKILL++ refines only the incoming skill against the earlier one, so the router selects the correct skill again.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty and expense of manually designing or offline-optimizing agent policies.
Combines ongoing task execution with optimization, allowing inspectable harness code changes and strategy revision.
Uses a protected mechanism layer to preserve execution history and control policy activation.
Reports lower model cost across open-world game, AppWorld, SREGym, and coding tasks, with comparable correctness or completion.
Scope: results cover long-running objectives and selected benchmark environments; the abstract does not establish broader generality.

papers.abstract: Performativity arises when prediction-informed decisions change the data-generating process, creating feedback between deployment and learning. This phenomenon occurs in policy-making and in self-evolving AI systems that shape their own future training data. Statistical inference is challenging because estimation errors in earlier predictors affect subsequent data distributions and propagate into later updates. We develop an end-to-end framework for statistical inference under performativity. For repeated risk minimization and repeated gradient descent, we establish central limit theorems at fixed deployment rounds and derive covariance recursions that capture both current-round sampling variation and uncertainty inherited from earlier deployments. We develop consistent covariance estimators using policy perturbations and score matching. These results can yield asymptotically valid confidence regions for population iterates and the performative stable point. We further extend prediction-powered inference to this dynamic setting, combining labeled observations with predictions on additional unlabeled data to improve statistical efficiency. We evaluate our framework in synthetic, semi-synthetic educational, and self-evolving large language model routing settings. Our experiments demonstrate that ignoring propagated uncertainty can lead to substantial undercoverage even after repeated retraining. Together, these results provide statistical tools for learning systems that help determine the distributions from which they learn. Our work establish a complete statistical inference under performativity, introducing new challenges and inference settings that we believe will provide substantial value to policy-making, statistics, and machine learning.
bullets: Performativity creates feedback: prediction-driven decisions alter the data distribution used for later learning.
For repeated risk minimization and gradient descent, the work derives central limit theorems and covariance recursions across deployment rounds.
It proposes consistent covariance estimation via policy perturbations and score matching, supporting asymptotically valid confidence regions.
Prediction-powered inference incorporates unlabeled data and model predictions to improve efficiency in dynamic settings.
Experiments across synthetic, educational, and language-model routing settings show that ignoring inherited uncertainty can cause substantial undercoverage.

papers.abstract: Before foraging, desert ants perform learning walks (LWs) to acquire visual memories around their nest. With experience, these walks expand, become straighter, and contain fewer visual scans. We previously proposed a model in which these behaviours emerge from the angular mismatch between path integration (PI) and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass (VC). Here, we test whether this mechanism can generate learning walks on a physical robot, despite the sensory and motor noise inherent to real-world conditions. We implement the model on a four-wheeled robot equipped with a panoramic camera, an IMU and wheel encoders providing compass and stride information for PI, and test it outdoors using a replicated desert-ant experimental setup. The PI--VC mismatch regulates walking speed, turning, pirouettes, and returns to the nest, while PI provides a teaching signal for visual learning. The robot autonomously decides when to acquire visual memories, while its behaviour gradually shifts from exploration towards foraging as visual learning progresses. The robot reproduces desert-ant LW features, including expanding and straightening trajectories, decreasing pirouette frequency, and improved visual homing. These results demonstrate that a simple error-driven mechanism can generate key features of learning walks under real-world conditions, supporting its plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants. More broadly, this work illustrates how physical robots can be used to test biological models.
bullets: Learning walks emerge from angular mismatch between path integration and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass.
The mechanism controls speed, turning, pirouettes, nest returns, and visual-memory acquisition.
Implemented on an outdoor four-wheeled robot with a panoramic camera, IMU, and wheel encoders despite real-world noise.
The robot reproduced expanding and straightening paths, fewer pirouettes, and improved visual homing as learning progressed.
Results support the mechanism’s plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants and demonstrate physical robots as tools for testing biological models.

Fig 15. Relationship between prediction variance and visual-compass accuracy on the robot. (A) Absolute angular error of the centroid of 10 consecutive raw visual-compass predictions (1 s of sampling), relative to the ground-truth nest direction derived from GNSS position. During these 1-s windows, the maximum angular spacing between headings was 54.31◦ ± 20.63◦ (mean ± SD), with a maximum of approximately 100◦, while the maximum linear spacing between sampled positions was 0.287± 0.212 m, with a maximum of approximately 0.8 m. Only LW3 and subsequent LWs were included, excluding LW1 and LW2. Mean centroid error increased monotonically with circular variance, from 20.42◦ in the lowest-variance bin (0–0.1) to 83.32◦ in the highest-variance bin (0.9–1.0). Prediction variance was positively correlated with centroid error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.358, p < 0.001), with a linear R2 = 0.167 and mutual information of 0.113 nats. Error bars show standard deviations, which increased with variance. The variability in all variance bin was quite high, hence the low correlation and low predictability despite a clear trend on average. (B) Frequency distribution across all the one-second prediction samples across circular-variance bins. Low-variance samples were more frequent. This could be used to weight visual-compass predictions against PI, or to distinguish familiar from unfamiliar locations. Unlike the visual familiarity or novelty signals commonly derived from MBON activation in visual-compass models [1, 34, 41, 48], this signal would reflect the consistency of successive directional predictions rather than the familiarity of the visual input itself.

papers.abstract: Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.
bullets: The study analyzes why candidate generation and aggregation fail to consistently close the pass@1–pass@N gap.
Ranking error follows a bias–variance decomposition: extra compute reduces variance, but bias only falls initially before plateauing.
Scorpio jointly scores randomly grouped candidates and improves verification, tree search, and aggregation across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks.
It improves verification accuracy by up to 7 percentage points, reduces inference cost by 17–42% at comparable peak accuracy, and improves tree-search accuracy by up to 10 points.
Aggregation scaling improves by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Test-time search using SCORPIO matches or outperforms prior methods without any training. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on AIME 2024 and LCBv6. We compare SCORPIO, which jointly scores partial solutions during search, with ThinkPRM-1.5B (Khalifa et al., 2025), which uses a trained process reward model, and DeepConf, which uses confidence scores derived from token probabilities. We vary the number of initial solutions: N ∈ {8, 32, 128} for SCORPIO and ThinkPRM, and N ∈ {16, 64, 256} for DeepConf to keep total costs comparable. Top-1 accuracy is plotted against total inference cost. Similar trends are observed for Qwen3.5-4B (see Fig. 20).

Figure 2: SCORPIO scales better with inference compute than prior verification methods across math (HMMT), puzzle (RG Games), and code benchmarks (LCBv6). We compare SCORPIO’s scoring with V1 (Singh et al., 2026), a recent test-time scaling algorithm that scores candidates through pairwise comparisons between similar candidates, and pointwise scoring, where LLMs evaluate candidates in isolation. SCORPIO jointly scores candidates in groups of four. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens, and is scaled by repeating candidate evaluations. Results are averaged over 20 seeds, with shaded regions indicating 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 1: Sampling more candidates improves the chance of a correct answer, but selecting it does not scale well with N . (a) The gap between pass@1 and pass@N exists even for frontier models on agentic tasks.1 (b) As N increases, the gap between pass@N and the selection accuracy of V1 (Singh et al., 2026), a recent self-verification method for scaling test-time compute, widens. (c) A similar trend holds for Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA) (Venkatraman et al., 2025). For (b) and (c), we run each method until accuracy plateaus; refer Sec. E.1 for further details.

Figure 10: A judge from a different model can reduce ranking bias. Candidates generated by Qwen3.5-4B are scored with SCORPIO (K = 4) either by Qwen3.5-4B itself (the self judge) or by one of four other judges, on HMMT Feb 2025 (top) and LCBv6 (bottom). We plot bias2, variance, ranking error, and top-1 accuracy as the number of scoring rounds M increases, averaged over 20 repetitions; shaded regions show 95% confidence intervals for top-1 accuracy. At M = 20, replacing the self judge with GPT-OSS-20B reduces the ranking error from 0.17 to 0.07 on HMMT and from 0.23 to 0.13 on LCBv6, and improves top-1 accuracy from 67.6% to 75.0% and from 57.0% to 71.6%, respectively.

Figure 11: Different models have different biases. For every pair of a correct and an incorrect candidate generated by Qwen3.5-4B, we record whether the self judge and another judge rank the correct candidate higher after M = 20 scoring rounds of SCORPIO (K = 4), on HMMT Feb 2025 (top) and LCBv6 (bottom). Fractions are averaged over questions and 20 repetitions.

Figure 7: Pruning candidates with SCORPIO allows RSA to scale with pool size N . Using GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6, we plot (a) accuracy across L = 1→ 10 aggregation rounds for different pool sizes N . Increasing N degrades RSA performance, whereas RSA + SCORPIO improves with larger pools. One failure mode contributing to this degradation is shown in (b): RSA amplifies rare incorrect responses over successive rounds on problem 120. LCBv6 requires a complete Python solution in a single turn and does not permit tool calls. However, RSA amplifies rare incorrect responses containing tool calls over successive rounds, with the effect becoming more severe as N increases (see Fig. 22). After each round, SCORPIO scores all N candidates, and only the top N/2 are used to construct aggregation sets for the next round, limiting this bad-mode amplification. Results are averaged over 8 seeds, with 95% CI.

Figure 20: Test-time search using SCORPIO matches or outperforms prior methods. Results for Qwen3.5-4B on AIME 2024 and LCBv6. Top-1 accuracy of test-time search versus total inference cost on AIME 2024 and LCBv6 for Qwen3.5-4B. We vary the number of solutions we start with: N ∈ {8, 32, 128} for SCORPIO and ThinkPRM, and N ∈ {16, 64, 256} for DeepConf to keep total costs comparable. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 9: Residual bias dominates ranking error as compute grows. Variance and squared bias of the ranking error of SCORPIO (K = 4) versus the number of scoring rounds M for Qwen3.5-4B (top) and GPT-OSS-20B (bottom). Black circles show the squared bias, which flattens as M grows, and teal squares the variance; curves show least-squares fits of a+ b/ √ M to the variance. The box gives the fitted a, b, and R2 for the variance, and the share of the ranking error due to squared bias at M = 20. Using the asymptotic variance a together with the squared bias at M = 20, we estimate that bias would account for 91% to 99% of the ranking error as M grows.

Figure 8: Increasing compute does not change the mean of the score distribution, but can reduce the bias in rankings. At low compute (solid curves), overlapping score distributions allow the incorrect candidate to receive a higher score than the correct one. Averaging more evaluations (dotted curves) concentrates the scores around their respective means. Since the correct candidate has a higher mean score in this example, this makes an incorrect ordering less likely, reducing the pair’s squared bias (E[Zij ]) 2.

Figure 4: Larger groups reduce variance faster but can increase bias. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on HMMT (math) and LCBv6 (code). Increasing the group size allows more evaluations within the same cost budget, reducing variance faster. However, these gains can come at the expense of increased bias: on LCBv6, K = 8 yields higher bias than smaller groups. Similar trends are observed for Qwen3.5-4B (see Fig. 18).

Figure 12: V1 (Singh et al., 2026) accuracy plateaus well below pass@N , and the gap widens as N increases. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6. (a) Increasing the candidate pool from N = 8 to N = 128 yields modest gains in selection accuracy, while the gap to pass@N grows from roughly 5 to 11 percentage points. Points show means over 20 seeds, with error bars indicating 95% confidence intervals. (b) Accuracy plateaus as inference compute increases for each pool size, remaining below the corresponding pass@N ceiling (dashed lines). Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 13: RSA’s (Venkatraman et al., 2025) final accuracy decreases as the candidate pool grows. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6. (a) Increasing N from 8 to 128 lowers final accuracy, widening the gap to pass@N from roughly 12 to 26 percentage points. Points show means over 8 seeds, with error bars indicating 95% confidence intervals. (b) Each curve tracks accuracy over successive aggregation rounds for a fixed N . Larger pools plateau at lower accuracy despite higher compute costs. Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 21: Repeated evaluation of partial solutions improves search accuracy. Top-1 accuracy of test-time search using SCORPIO versus total inference cost on AIME 2024, HMMT Feb 2025, and LCBv6. We fix the number of solutions we start with at N = 128 and vary the number of times the random grouping and scoring process is repeated, M ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Repeated evaluations improve accuracy over M = 1 across all three datasets. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 15: SCORPIO achieves higher accuracy on math and similar accuracy at lower cost on code compared with PPT (Kwok et al., 2026). Selection accuracy versus total inference cost for GPT-OSS-20B with N = 128 candidates. On HMMT Feb 2025, SCORPIO (K = 4) improves peak accuracy by 8 percentage points over PPT. On LCBv6, it reaches PPT’s accuracy at 1.5× lower total cost. PPT’s strategy proceeds in two phases: an initial ring phase ensures that every candidate is evaluated, followed by a tournament phase. Points labeled “ring” show accuracy after the first phase, while k = 1 and k = 2 indicate whether one or two evaluations are used per pair. Curves show mean accuracy, with shaded regions indicating 95% confidence intervals. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 14: V1 (Singh et al., 2026) also exhibits a widening selection gap on HMMT Feb 2025. Results for GPT-OSS20B. (a) Increasing N from 8 to 128 yields modest gains in selection accuracy, while the gap to pass@N grows from roughly 6 to 11 percentage points. (b) Selection accuracy plateaus as inference compute increases, remaining below the corresponding pass@N ceiling (dashed lines). Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 22: Larger pools amplify tool-call responses in RSA, while SCORPIO limits their amplification. Proportion of responses containing tool calls across aggregation rounds for a single LCBv6 problem using GPT-OSS-20B. This is a single-turn task that requires a solution in a Python code block. Some responses attempt tool calls to test their logic, which we identify using the pattern to=[A-Za-z_]. The harness does not support tool calls, and 95% of these responses receive zero reward. Tool-call responses remain uncommon with N = 8 but become increasingly common with N = 32 and N = 128 as aggregation rounds progress. In RSA + SCORPIO, candidates are scored using SCORPIO after each round, and only the top half of candidates are used to build aggregation sets for the next round. This selection reduces the proportion of tool-call responses to nearly zero across all three pool sizes.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the limits of test-time compute for self-evaluation and introduces Scorpio, a method for joint scoring of candidates, fitting the test-time learning subtopic.
papers.title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation
papers.tldr: More test-time compute does not reliably improve self-evaluation because ranking bias eventually plateaus; Scorpio addresses this by jointly scoring grouped candidates.

papers.abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.
bullets: Addresses ineffective self-generated summaries for long-context agents and the difficulty of learning note-taking with RL alone.
Bootstraps hindsight-annotated note-taking through fine-tuning, then applies RL with answer, note-quality, and confidence-calibration rewards.
Although trained for compaction, it generalizes at test time to context folding and confidence-based backtracking.
On four book-level QA benchmarks with books up to 2.5M tokens, accuracy improves from 36.9% to 67.8% while staying within a 20K-token window.
Achieves performance near the much larger GLM-5.3 agent at lower cost and exceeds the reported GPT-5.5 agent and full-book-context baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. (a) We inject note-taking actions into collected demonstrations. (b) SFT initializes the policy, and GRPO reinforces its actions across context resets with a shared trajectory advantage. (c) At inference, context folding retains notes and recent turns, and confidence guides retries and answer selection.

Figure 3: Validation answer accuracy over RL training for the models in Table 1. The gray dot marks a single outlier evaluation of the RL (Single Window) run, caused by reward hacking that led us to tighten the answer length limit. While SFT + RL and RL only variants start at similar validation accuracy, SFT + RL outperforms RL only by 15% at the end of training due to more effective compaction behavior instilled by the SFT.

Figure 1: Context management methods incorporated in this work. (a) Compaction starts a new window containing only the saved notes and discards all prior turns. (b) Context folding additionally retains the turns after the latest note. (c) Confidence-based backtracking resumes from an earlier note checkpoint after a low-confidence answer and generates an alternative continuation.

Figure 4: Mean context-window restarts per RL training rollout. Legend names follow Table 1; training uses compaction into fresh windows. Faint curves show perstep values; bold curves show five-step trailing means. SFT + RL checkpoints retain compaction ratio robustly during the RL training process, while compaction ratio in RL only checkpoints collapses.

Table 1: Test accuracy (%) on LiteraryQA (LitQA), NovelHopQA (NHopQA), NovelQA, and SagaScale (Saga); n is the number of test questions. Tokens are the mean per rollout, and cost is for the full test set. Bold marks the best result among ablation and proposed methods. MEMENTO is best on every dataset. In the same harness, it nearly matches GLM-5.3 (67.8 vs. 69.3 micro) at 1/9 the cost. It beats GPT-5.5 High in both settings, including full-book context (67.8 vs. 56.7), at ∼1/54 the cost. It is also within 6.5 points of full-context GLM-5.3 at ∼1/26 the cost. †Evaluated on up to 100 random questions per dataset; cost is extrapolated to the full test set.

Table 2: Ablation of our training and inference components. We report test-set accuracy (%) of the confidenceaware variant of each checkpoint. Rows add training stages (SFT on synthetic data, then RL), and columns add inference-time components cumulatively (context folding, then confidence-aware backtracking). Accuracy improves along both axes: each training stage helps under every inference setup, and each inference component helps for every checkpoint. The best accuracy is shown in bold.

Table 4: GRPO hyperparameters, shared by the four RL conditions. The policy and fixed KL reference start from the corresponding SFT checkpoint, or from Qwen38B for the RL-only baselines. The confidence reward weight is λ = 0.10 through step 160 and 0.25 thereafter, and variants without confidence use λ = 0. Reported RL results use step 222.

Table 3: SFT hyperparameters, shared by the variants with and without confidence. Sequences exceeding the limit are truncated from the left, and an assistant turn cut by truncation is excluded from the loss. We use the final checkpoint after two epochs.

Table 5: Inference and generation hyperparameters. Qwen sampling applies to GRPO, validation, and test runs. Response budgets include tool observations, except for per-turn generation caps; the folding segment budget is a soft limit. Tool outputs are truncated from the right; full-book inputs retain the beginning. In the retry schedule, n counts note calls accumulated at that retry. Notes and retries do not apply to the no-compaction baseline.

papers.selection_reason: RL-based context compaction for long-context agents, directly addressing LLM memory management and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
papers.tldr: MEMENTO trains a compact Qwen3-8B agent to manage long contexts effectively, substantially improving book-level QA while using at most 20K context tokens.

papers.abstract: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) is critical for medical image segmentation as it adapts a model to an unlabeled target domain without accessing source data, thereby preserving data privacy. However, its effectiveness is often limited by confirmation bias: self-training models tend to miss small polyps, hallucinate foreground, and produce imprecise contours. We propose MedRT-SFSeg, a real-time SFDA framework built on a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture. Mask-DHF fuses precision- and recall-oriented predictions into stable pseudo-instances, while DURR uses the sign of pixel-level dual-head disagreement as a directional cue to expand or shrink masks, and additionally recovers missed instances and suppresses hallucinations. Seg-MARD further regularizes feature representations through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling. Experiments on bidirectional adaptation between Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB show that MedRT-SFSeg achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice and 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, improving the non-adapted baseline by 7.7 and 9.8 Dice points while running at more than 62 FPS end-to-end. These results suggest that segmentation-aware dual-head supervision can improve pseudo-label quality without sacrificing real-time inference. Project page: https://danielnguyen-05.github.io/MedRT-SFSeg
bullets: Addresses confirmation bias in unlabeled target-domain adaptation, especially missed small polyps, false foreground, and inaccurate contours.
Uses a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture with Mask-DHF for stable pseudo-instances.
DURR expands or shrinks masks based on directional dual-head disagreement, while recovering missed instances and suppressing hallucinations.
Seg-MARD regularizes features through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling.
On bidirectional Kvasir-SEG/CVC-ClinicDB adaptation, it achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice, 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, and over 62 FPS end-to-end.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of MedRT-SFSeg. A source-trained dual-head segmentation model is first adapted to the target domain with AdaBN and Mean-Teacher self-training. Mask-DHF constructs reliable pseudo-instances from O2O/O2M predictions, while DURR performs reliability-aware signed routing and Seg-MARD regularizes multiscale features. Only the adapted O2O Student is used at inference.

Fig. 2. Boundary correction analysis on representative target-domain cases. From left to right: input image; ground truth; Student prediction; error decomposition (true positive, false positive, and false negative regions); overlay of ground-truth (green) and predicted (red) boundaries; and absolute mask error. Residual errors are primarily localized near polyp contours, illustrating the boundary-sensitive behavior targeted by signed routing.
Table 1. Comparison with prior source-free domain adaptation methods in both adaptation directions between Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB. Best in bold red, secondbest underlined blue.
Table 3. Deployment efficiency and adaptation cost of the final MedRT-SFSeg model in both adaptation directions.
Table 2. Ablation study across both adaptation directions. Dice and IoU are reported in %, ASD and HD95 in mm. Best in bold red, second-best underlined blue.

papers.selection_reason: Source-free domain adaptation for real-time segmentation, relevant to test-time adaptation methods.
papers.title: Directional Dual-Head Supervision for Real-Time Source-Free Polyp Segmentation
papers.tldr: MedRT-SFSeg improves real-time source-free polyp segmentation by using dual-head disagreement to refine pseudo-labels and correct missed or hallucinated regions.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints. We present No Frames, Just Frequencies, a bandwidth-efficient source-assisted adaptation framework that characterizes distribution shifts using compact frequency descriptors computed on-device. Rather than transmitting camera frames, the glasses compute and send frequency descriptors to a host device that contains a replica of the model. The host device maps the received frequency descriptor to a distribution shift operator that synthesizes out-of-distribution data and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol. We evaluate the framework on mixtures of ImageNet-C corruptions using convolution-based (ConvNeXtV2-Femto), self-attention-based (DeiT-Tiny), and hybrid (TinyViT-5M) vision models, on person classification (Visual Wake Words), and on object detection (MS-COCO). Our results reveal that adaptation driven solely by the transmitted descriptors recovers $93-95\%$ of the supervised oracle adaptation gain on all three architectures, $82\%$ on Visual Wake Words and $94$--$98\%$ on MS-COCO. Notably, adaptation quality degrades gracefully as the descriptor resolution decreases from $224 $ to $28$ pixels, consistently across architectures, enabling bandwidth reductions from $213\times$ to $784\times$ across the frequency descriptors.
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in on-device vision under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints.
The glasses compute frequency descriptors; a host maps them to shift operators, synthesizes out-of-distribution data, and adapts a model replica.
Evaluated across ImageNet-C, Visual Wake Words, and MS-COCO with convolutional, attention-based, and hybrid vision models.
Descriptor-only adaptation recovers 93–95% of supervised oracle gains across architectures, 82% on Visual Wake Words, and 94–98% on MS-COCO.
Reducing descriptor resolution from 224 to 28 pixels degrades performance gracefully while enabling 213×–784× bandwidth reductions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview of the proposed bandwidth-efficient TTA framework. An edge device (i.e., Smart Glasses) computes compact frequency descriptors (RAPSD, DCT, or DWT statistics) from incoming camera frames on-device. Only these descriptors are transmitted to the host device, keeping the per-frame uplink within a low-bandwidth budget instead of streaming raw frames. The host device maps the received descriptor to a synthetic corruption distribution through a sequential pipeline of training corruptions. The host device generates synthetic corrupted data batches from locally stored in-distribution images, and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol [19, 44]. Finally, the updated parameter subset is transmitted back to the edge device.

Figure 5: Descriptors ablation at 224 input resolution: the NFJF adaptation loop re-run with the frequency descriptor replaced by the model-based alternatives. ActStats denotes the first layer and block activation statistics and FeatFinal the pooled pre-logits embedding. Same layout as Fig. 2. ActStats attains the highest adaptation accuracy, improving on DCT by 0.67pp on average and approaching Oracle - CE within 0.71pp. This adaptation gain costs on average 2.3× the DCT payload (a fixed 708B versus architecture-dependent 768–3072B). Computing ActStats requires executing the deployed model’s first layer and block, ≈ 100× the number of DCT FLOPs (∼ 150-180 versus 1.6MFLOPs), whereas the frequency descriptors need no model execution.

Figure 2: Per-architecture accuracy across four input resolutions (28, 56, 112, 224), reported for each frequency descriptor (RAPSD, DCT and DWT). NFJF is compared against three resolution-independent references: No Adapt and Oracle - E baselines and the Oracle - CE empirical upper bound. Bars report the mean over the 63 test DAGs of ImageNet-C; error bars indicate ±𝜎 . Oracle - E accuracy markedly improves on NoAdapt only for ConvNeXtV2-Femto and destabilizes on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT-5M, confirming the fragility of unsupervised entropy-based adaptation under distribution shift. NFJF accuracy improves on No Adapt across all three architectures for resolutions > 28 and it surpasses Oracle - E at all resolutions on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT5M. For ConvNeXtV2-Femto, NFJF mostly surpasses Oracle - E at 112 and 224 input resolutions.

Figure 3: Descriptor visualizations under a sample DAG (brightness→ shot noise→ contrast, each at severity 2; Section 5.1), normalized with clean-data statistics. Brightness amplifies the DC component across all descriptors and resolutions; shot noise amplifies high frequencies, an effect that diminishes at lower resolutions since the reduced-scale JPEG decode acts as a low-pass filter. Contrast reduces the midfrequency bands left free by the other two corruptions.

Table 2: Framework generality across person classification and object detection. Entries report themean (boxmAP onMS-COCO; accuracy [%] on Visual Wake Words) per-DAG paired gain (±𝜎) over the 63 test DAGs. The No Adapt row reports the absolute performance under shift, the common reference of every adaptation gain. The best per-column adaptation gain is reported in bold. The trends observed in Fig. 2 persist: every adaptation gain is positive and approaches the supervised Oracle as the resolution increases, whereas Oracle - E (VWW) collapses below No Adapt.

Table 1: Four-stage ISP corruption DAG. Each DAG is restricted to one corruption per node drawn from the disjoint set C𝑠 , a subset of ImageNet-C [11] corruptions following [7]. Each sample composes one corruption from each stage in the high-order degradation sequence following [46].

papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time adaptation with highly bandwidth-efficient frequency descriptors; relevant to test-time learning and efficient deployment.
papers.title: No Frames, Just Frequencies: Bandwidth-Efficient Deployment-Time Adaptation for Smart Glasses
papers.tldr: A smart-glasses framework enables privacy-preserving, bandwidth-efficient model adaptation by transmitting compact frequency descriptors instead of camera frames.

papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of image manipulation techniques has raised growing public security concerns. Existing Image Forgery Localization (IFL) methods can accurately localize manipulated regions but are often unable to adapt to newly emerging forgeries. In real-world forensic scenarios, data typically arrive sequentially, yet continual model adaptation remains largely unexplored in IFL. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first continual learning framework for IFL and establish a comprehensive benchmark under two realistic data-evolution protocols: cross-dataset and cross-content continual learning. Evaluations of representative state-of-the-art IFL and continual learning methods reveal substantial performance degradation, highlighting two key challenges: (1) adaptively capturing intrinsic forensic traces from incoming data across unseen domains, and (2) preserving previously acquired forensic knowledge during sequential adaptation. To address these challenges, we propose a forensic-aware continual adaptation framework. First, a forensic trace mining module employs Spatial Mixture-of-Forensic-Experts (SMoFE) to dynamically route complementary forensic cues across spatial locations, together with Forensic Evidence-Guided Dense Prompting (FEGDP) to transform low-level forensic traces into structured localization evidence for SAM. Second, Fisher-weighted LoRA Gradient (FLAG) surgery identifies old-task-sensitive adaptation directions and suppresses conflicting updates, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while preserving plasticity for emerging forgery domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both pixel-level forgery localization and image-level forgery detection across diverse continual learning scenarios.
bullets: Introduces the first continual learning framework and benchmark for image forgery localization under cross-dataset and cross-content data evolution.
Finds that existing localization and continual learning methods degrade substantially when adapting across unseen domains.
Uses SMoFE to route complementary spatial forensic cues and FEGDP to convert low-level traces into structured evidence for SAM.
Applies FLAG surgery to suppress updates that conflict with old-task knowledge, reducing catastrophic forgetting while preserving adaptation.
Reports state-of-the-art pixel-level localization and image-level detection across diverse continual learning scenarios.

papers.title: Forensic-Aware Continual Adaptation for Image Forgery Localization
papers.tldr: A forensic-aware continual learning framework enables image forgery localization models to adapt to emerging manipulation types while retaining prior forensic knowledge.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
authors: Shengguang Wu, Suning Huang, Cherie Ho, Ria Doshi, Hao Zhu, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Addresses the costly, manual redesign of agent harnesses for new robots and benchmarks.
A coding model observes rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness over optimization episodes.
Evaluates evolved harnesses on held-out scenes and tasks, improving average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks.
Automatically discovers strategies such as clearing jammed arms, approaching obstacles horizontally, and reusing grasp-depth experience through persistent memory.
Benefits are strongest when the benchmark differs substantially from the policy’s training data; scope is demonstrated across multiple benchmarks and policies.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ROBOARCHITECT turns a frozen policy into a performant robotic agent without updating its weights: a coding model iteratively refines the harness from execution traces. Starting from a bare policy (VLA), ROBOARCHITECT evolves a robotic agent equipped with auxiliary tools and persistent memory. The right side illustrates experiment conditions (§4.1) that test how well the evolved harness generalizes.

Figure 8: Held-out episodes differ from the optimization episodes either in scene arrangement (unseen scenes) or in the task itself (unseen tasks) (§4.1). Left, unseen scenes: the same tasks with scene configurations dealt out alternately. Right, unseen tasks: different tasks that require similar underlying skills.

Figure 9: The unified harness is evolved only on a training pool of procedurally generated episodes and evaluated on the benchmarks’ own standard episodes (§4.1 and §4.2). Top, optimized on: procedurally generated scenes, objects, instructions & tasks form the training pool. Bottom, held out: the benchmarks’ own standard episodes, unseen during harness evolution.

Figure 1: Wrapping a frozen policy in an evolved harness raises its held-out success rate from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks, often past the same policy finetuned on the benchmark (§4.2). papers.abstract: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.
bullets: Addresses rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions that limit observation-only DRL routing.
Uses per-satellite episodic memory, local and neighboring state, recent routing history, and a Transformer-based decision network.
Trains with Approximate Information State (AIS)-based auxiliary objectives.
In experiments, RAMA reduced mean and tail latency versus DDQN and achieved further gains with online updates across tested constellations.
Scope: results are reported for 140-satellite Kepler and 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1 networks.

papers.tldr: RAMA improves decentralized LEO satellite routing by retrieving useful past experiences alongside current network information, substantially reducing latency and remaining stable under changing conditions.

papers.abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.
bullets: Forgetting is evaluated as degraded prediction of standard web text after instruction tuning or subject-specific further pretraining.
The study fits a fixed vocabulary bias, alone or with a temperature, to correct final-token logits across 14 model pairs ranging from 1B to 7B parameters.
On held-out correction data, bias-only recovery is under 10%, while bias plus temperature recovers up to 36%.
Math further-pretrained models show the greatest loss and recover almost none of it with these corrections.
A controlled random-damage simulation recovers 29% despite having no planted bias or temperature shift, suggesting the method can capture spurious improvements.
