papers.abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.
authors: Jun Liu, Dajie Sun, Zhenglun Kong, Zhenjiang Fan, Peiyan Dong, Fan Yang, Wenbin Zhangg, Geng Yuan, Xue Lin, Yanzhi Wang, Dong Huang
bullets: On clean Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa data, a learned value selector underperforms random selection, while a hindsight oracle offers only limited, statistically uncertain gains.
Most states (82%) have identical candidate outcomes, leaving little headroom for candidate selection.
Token pruning reduces per-forward FLOPs by up to 47%, but achieves at most 1.15× measured end-to-end speedup on the deployed path; adaptive allocation remains inconclusive.
A silent rendering corruption increases on compute-heavy planning paths without affecting the official direct-policy result.
The authors release a corruption detector, fix, and scripts, and recommend auditing decision signal, realized efficiency, and evaluation integrity separately.

figures.caption: Figure 2. A premise-first audit of test-time scaling in Cosmos Policy on RoboCasa. (1) Planning selection. Limited variation in candidate outcomes constrains the headroom for selection, and the deployable value selector underperforms random selection, while the hindsight oracle provides only modest evidence of improvement. (2) Adaptive allocati n. Substantial nominal FLOPs reductions translate into modest end-to-end latency gains, while the joint allocation effect remains unresolved at the available noise and statistical power. (3) Evaluation reliability. Rendering corruption becomes much more frequent in the compute-intensive planning path than under directpolicy or best-of-N evaluation, while the official direct-policy result remains essentially unaffected. All findings are scoped to the tested Cosmos Policy–RoboCasa configuration.

Figure 5. The premise-first methodology as a chain of gates. Each candidate test-time-scaling gain passes three checks in order before it is credited: verify that the decision signal exists (causal ablation and oracle ceiling); a statistical power gate that halts a run which cannot resolve the pre-registered outcome; and closed-loop measurement under framebuffer-sentinel render-integrity checking. A “no” at the first gate reports a negative result and at the second an inconclusive one, separating a genuine negative from an underpowered or invalid measurement.

Figure 3. Auditing best-of-N planning selection. (a) Success-rate difference against the random baseline for the deployable value selector and the hindsight oracle, under state-level and episode-level bootstrap, with 95% CIs. The value selector is below zero under both schemes; the oracle estimate crosses zero under episodelevel resampling and is an upper bound, not a deployable selector. (b) Only a minority of query states show any outcome variation across candidates and repeated executions, leaving little for a selector to recover in the rest; a stricter decomposition (Supplement Section 13) further separates stable between-candidate differences from variation that is not stable across repeats.

papers.abstract: How to reuse a pretrained locomotion policy for precise loco-manipulation is still an open problem. We propose an online method to learn the closed-loop dynamics under a frozen locomotion policy. The learned model predicts floating-base motion and improves loco-manipulation accuracy. However, unobserved latent conditions of the policy introduce heterogeneous responses, meaning that the same observed state will lead to different motions. Direct learning without accounting for this heterogeneity introduces bias and fluctuations into dynamics estimates, degrading floating-base prediction and end-effector tracking. To address this problem, a contaminated Gaussian model is proposed to approximate the effects of latent conditions. The model uses two Gaussian components to approximate predictable and unpredictable responses under the same observed state. Then, the contaminated Gaussian model is combined with a Gaussian process to construct an online learner using random Fourier features (RFFs). The learner estimates each response's probability of belonging to the predictable component and uses it to weight online updates, capturing predictable responses while reducing bias and fluctuations caused by heterogeneous observations. With consistent and unbiased dynamics estimates, model predictive control (MPC) predicts floating-base motion accurately and enables precise loco-manipulation. A finite-sample error bound is established to ensure uniform convergence in online learning. Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate consistent end-effector tracking across different manipulator configurations and tasks, with errors of 0.01 m.
authors: Tianlin Zhang, Weipeng Xia, Lingwei Zhang, Yiyang Shao, Zhongyu Li, Yun-Hui Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reusing pretrained locomotion policies for accurate loco-manipulation.
Uses a contaminated Gaussian model to separate predictable and unpredictable responses caused by unobserved policy conditions.
Combines this model with a Gaussian process and random Fourier features for online, probability-weighted dynamics updates.
Integrates the learned dynamics with model predictive control to improve floating-base and end-effector tracking.
Simulation and hardware experiments achieve consistent tracking across manipulator configurations and tasks, with 0.01 m errors; a finite-sample error bound supports uniform convergence.

papers.abstract: This paper presents an opinionated set of ten desiderata intended to inform the design and evaluation of reinforcement-learning agents that learn continually throughout a continuing lifetime. We use these desiderata to examine a representative selection of existing approaches. Progress on individual desiderata is valuable, but the longer-term aim should be to integrate all ten within a single agent. To our knowledge, no published evaluation has yet provided evidence for such an integration. Likewise, the representative benchmarks we review probe different parts of this target, but separate evaluations do not establish that the corresponding properties coexist within one agent throughout a continuing lifetime. As a secondary contribution, we therefore present a compact persistent-world scenario as a playable companion to the desiderata and outline a proposed benchmark that examines a broad range of associated behavioral capabilities together within one such lifetime.
authors: Nis Meinert, Jakob Gawlikowski, Edward Grant, Max Cyprys, Nathan Schurr, Neil Boston, Alfredo Ibias, Milind Tambe, Janusz Marecki
bullets: Proposes ten desiderata for designing and evaluating agents that learn continually throughout a continuing lifetime.
Reviews representative approaches and benchmarks, finding that they typically address only subsets of the desiderata.
Emphasizes that progress on individual properties does not show they coexist within a single agent over time.
Introduces a compact persistent-world scenario as a playable companion and outlines a broader integrated benchmark.
No published evaluation is identified as demonstrating all ten desiderata together in one agent.

figures.caption: TABLE 1 Coverage of the desiderata by representative benchmarks and by our proposed benchmark. Ratings refer to the protocols and readouts described in the cited studies and in our proposal. The last row gives the intended coverage of the benchmark proposed for our playable companion. For D1, the columns describe whether the task-free, non-episodic, and online conditions are instantiated: fully; partially; not instantiated. For the behavioral columns, indicates that a dedicated protocol or readout directly probes the property; indicates incomplete component coverage or indirect or confounded evidence; indicates that the property is not probed. The system-level desiderata D3–D5 are omitted.

TABLE 4 Mapping from six behavioral desiderata to situations that may arise during a continuing lifetime and to associated readouts. The core situations may all occur within the same task-free, non-episodic online interaction under D1, and whether or when they occur depends on the agent’s behavior. The mapping is not one-to-one: D6 and D7 overlap in the same lifetime situation, while the salty-bean situations couple retention and credit under D6, prediction under D8, and evaluation under D9. These proposed readouts provide the basis for the companion’s coverage ratings in Table 1.

papers.title: Continual Reinforcement Learning Is an Integration Problem
papers.tldr: Continual reinforcement learning should be evaluated as an integrated lifelong-agent problem rather than as a collection of isolated capabilities.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.
authors: Kathrin Korte, Christian Metzner, Akshay Bedhotiya, Viet Anh Khoa Tran, Eleni Nisioti, Sebastian Risi
bullets: Task similarity, data-change rate, and presentation order can refer to different levels of the learning setup.
Partitioning the same data trajectory at different granularities changes measured continual-learning outcomes.
Changing presentation order or the underlying data’s similarity structure also affects results.
A review of representative benchmarks finds that these properties are often not fully specified.
For models with undisclosed pretraining data, underlying-data properties are embedded in the model’s initial state.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A learner enters the setting. (a) A learner occupies one point in a stream at a time. Its lifetime scope is the breadth of experience the stream covers as a whole, of which only the past is available to it and the future is unobserved. (b) The same stream under a single partition. Similarity is defined for every pair of tasks and computable from the data once the boundaries are fixed. What a learner retains of each task is a separate quantity (Sec. 2.3). (c–e) A teacher–student stream in which the teacher’s weights follow a fixed trajectory, with the student trained on tasks sampled along it. Curves show mean squared test error on each task after the whole stream has been traversed, shaded by standard error over five initialisations, with task position on the horizontal axis. Full setup in Sec. B. (c) Partition granularity, N ∈ {5, 10, 50}, which alters similarity between tasks and change within them together. (d) Presentation order at N = 50. Reversing the stream reverses the profile of retained error across it, and shuffling removes its structure. (e) Distance traversed by the teacher across the stream at N = 50, which sets the overall similarity between its regions.

Figure 1: One stream, many partitions. (a) A stream is a realized, ordered sequence. Colour denotes content of experience; nearby colours indicate related experience. (b) A task cut produces a task sequence. Segment width = task scope. (c) Change within a task depends on scope. (d) Similarity between tasks depends on scope: coarse segments span heterogeneous stretches and overlap; fine segments are narrow and largely disjoint. S(KN , CN ) is the similarity of two tasks under a partition into N tasks. (e) The same segments in a different order are a different stream, since a stream is a realized order. None of (c)-(e) is a property of the stream alone; each is dependent on stream & cut. Everything here is learner independent. Fig. 2 shows what changes once a learner is present.

Figure 3: (a) Changing different parameters in the teacher has different effects on forgetting in the student. (b) Changing the stream scope (i.e., the intrinsic dimensionality of the teacher’s weight trajectory) affects forgetting in the learner.
Table 1: Properties of the realized stream, task discretization, and learner.

Table 2: Benchmark families against the properties of Sec. 2. Superscripts denote the status of the entry (✓ specified; ◦ not stated by the benchmark but our reading of its description, judged recoverable from the released data and not computed here; ? unspecified and not recoverable from the protocol, with a marker alone indicating that the protocol gives no value). For Similarity, ✓ marks that the benchmark states how tasks were constructed, which constrains the kind of relatedness without providing a magnitude. Two of the reviewed benchmarks provide more information. Ibrahim et al. [2024] grade their two shifts as weak or strong, and Wołczyk et al. [2021] report forward transfer between every pair of tasks for a reference agent, a learner-level quantity that they also use to set the task order. For Scope, a class count fixes how many labels fall in a task without stating the breadth of experience they cover, and is recorded as ?; only Liu et al. [2023] is marked with ✓, for declaring per suite which factors are held fixed and which vary. The Order/Exposure column records the presentation regime, while the realized ordering within it is typically drawn per run rather than fixed by the benchmark. The last two columns, Task identity at test time and Boundaries, are two facets of the learner’s access. Each entry is recorded at whichever level the benchmark specifies.

papers.tldr: Continual-learning measurements depend on whether assumptions concern the data, its task partition, or the learner, and these levels should be distinguished explicitly.

papers.abstract: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.
bullets: Pooled coverage can appear near nominal while individual-cell coverage is extremely poor, motivating fleet, batch, and cell-level reporting.
A residual-free weighting scheme uses frozen signature features, batch labels, and cycle indices to partially close this gap.
The 10th-percentile cell coverage improves from 0.750 to 0.830, while worst-cell coverage rises from 0.642 to 0.694, with no deferrals.
Weights can worsen performance under protocol drift, and limited battery diversity bounds repair capacity.
Within-domain behavior replicates, but intervals collapse on a cross-chemistry external set.

Target 20 saturates at achieved ESS ≈ 18 (cap flag, §8.3).

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.
authors: Siqi Li, Ziyi Bai, Xinrun Xu, Tinglei Huang, B\"orje F. Karlsson
bullets: Defines six requirements for embodied memory, including world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning.
Categorizes methods into eight architectural families, such as recurrent states, fast weights, visual/symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems.
Reviews benchmark practices for distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task-solving ability.
Highlights open challenges in retrieving relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs, and consolidating knowledge across episodes.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Representative works organized by embodied memory requirement. Six timelines group studies by the historical information an agent must preserve: hidden world state, action-induced state change, task state, delayed-relevance evidence, active belief maintenance, and cross-episode experience. Each row identifies the corresponding computational challenge and arranges works by year. Solid boxes denote methods or systems; dashed boxes marked B denote benchmarks. Works may appear in multiple rows when they address several requirements. Timelines are independently spaced for readability, with no ordering implied among works from the same year. Dates follow the cited bibliography, using the conference year where available and the preprint or report year otherwise.

Figure 1: Overview of the survey. The scene illustrates how observations and interaction outcomes become unavailable to current perception yet remain relevant to later decisions. Embodied memory preserves this evidence as world state, task state, and experience through repeated writing, updating, and retrieval.
Figure 2: Conceptual boundaries and implementations of embodied memory. The six requirements in Sec. 3 describe task demands; the architectural categories in Sec. 4 describe implementation choices.

Table 2: Capability envelopes of embodied-memory architectures. The requirement column is a diagnostic cross-reference to Sec. 3; A1–A7 are non-exclusive mechanism or organization families, while A8 denotes their composition. Episodic retrieval and skill consolidation are two modes within A7, not additional top-level categories.

Table 1: A computational taxonomy of non-Markovian embodied memory requirements. Each requirement is associated with a distinct latent state, computational challenge, memory operation, and characteristic failure mode.

Table 4: Coverage of the six memory requirements from Sec. 3 in memory-oriented benchmarks. EB (R1): Entity Binding; SS (R2): State Supersession; TS (R3): Task-State Tracking; FU (R4): Future-Utility Estimation; BC (R5): Belief Calibration; EA (R6): Experience Abstraction. These are the computational operations associated with the same six requirements, not six additional memory types. ✓denotes systematic task coverage, while △ indicates partial or indirect pressure without dedicated evaluation. The mapping is our interpretation of task protocols, not a claim of causal isolation; HuMeGo concerns pre-goal object history, with selection and state-change coverage treated as indirect; EMem-Bench’s EA mark concerns its controlled generalization family, while MemTransfer probes reuse under mismatch rather than learning an abstraction mechanism.

Table 3: Evaluation interfaces, outcomes, and memory implications of general embodied benchmarks. Entries summarize the named benchmark protocols rather than prescribing one universal sensor or action configuration. A score should be interpreted using its own completion rule and observation privileges.

papers.title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory

papers.abstract: Continual adaptation to new tasks is essential for robots deployed in the real world, but adapting pre-trained policies remains challenging due to parameter growth and the need for continual demonstration collection. Parameter-Efficient Continual Fine-Tuning (PECFT) isolates task-specific updates, but adapter-per-task designs require demonstrations and grow with the task set. We propose ResMerge, a two-stage framework that learns mergeable residual policies atop a frozen pre-trained policy: residual reinforcement learning (RL) acquires task-specific corrections without additional expert demonstrations during adaptation, and parameter-space merging consolidates compatible residuals to reduce stored parameters. We introduce Residual-Field Consistency (RFC), a simple, bounded, and interpretable metric that assesses compatibility in residual action-field space by comparing correction direction and magnitude. Experiments on LIBERO across two backbones and on a real-world Franka robot show improved continual learning performance over strong PECFT baselines, while selective merging reduces the residual-parameter footprint. Project website: https://resmerge.github.io/.
authors: Kefei Zhu, Lingyun Xu, Yue Xin, Xiaoqi Li, Caixin Guo, Xincheng Du, Yuanpei Chen, Yaodong Yang, Hao Dong
bullets: Addresses the need to adapt pre-trained robot policies without continually collecting expert demonstrations or storing one adapter per task.
Uses a frozen base policy with residual reinforcement learning to learn task-specific corrections.
Merges compatible residual policies in parameter space to reduce the stored residual footprint.
Introduces Residual-Field Consistency (RFC), a bounded and interpretable metric based on correction direction and magnitude.
Shows improved continual-learning performance on LIBERO and a real Franka robot, with selective merging reducing residual parameters.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. ResMerge framework. In the Learn stage, a LoRA-parameterized residual policy Rcand is trained on the new task via residual RL with πbase frozen. In the Merge stage, Rcand is merged into the most compatible existing expert when their Residual-Field Consistency (RFC) meets or exceeds a compatibility threshold; otherwise it is added as a new expert.

Fig. 4. Sequential RFC analysis on the real robot. Streamlines show the compared correction fields; background color indicates local directional agreement (green) or opposition (red). Statistics use full observations and actions; the plotted projection is only a visualization. (a) RFC accepts (R1, R2), producing RAB . (b) RFC rejects (RAB , R3) and retains R3. (c) RFC accepts (R3, R4), producing RCD . Two consolidated experts serve all four tasks.

Fig. 3. Overview of the experimental platforms and tasks. A Franka Panda with a Leap hand performs four sequential pinch- and power-grasp tasks; three frames illustrate each rollout. The bottom strip shows representative LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Object tasks used for simulation comparisons.

TABLE IV: Effect of residual architecture. LoRA and MLP residuals are compared before and after merging and refinement.

TABLE II: Real-world evaluation. We report continual learning metrics in (a) and average success with residual-expert counts in (b).

papers.selection_reason: Residual policy learning with parameter merging directly addresses continual adaptation of robot policies and fits both robot learning and continual learning.
papers.title: ResMerge: Residual Policy Learning and Merging for Continual Adaptation of Pre-trained Robot Policies
papers.tldr: ResMerge enables continual robot-policy adaptation by learning demonstration-free residual corrections and merging compatible task updates to limit parameter growth.

papers.abstract: This work introduces three lightweight enhancement modules for medical lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability, particularly under data-scarce and computationally constrained environments. Current mainstream methods struggle with the lack of high-quality annotations for rare pathologies, which often leads to severe morphological distortions during inference, despite achieving seemingly ideal DSC scores. Furthermore, the isolated development of individual segmentation tasks restricts cross-domain methodological innovation, underscoring the need for leveraging shared knowledge across different lesions within the same anatomical region. However, constrained access to historical data and annotations hinders efficient knowledge extraction and triggers catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new classes. To address these challenges, we first propose DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling to optimize differentiable topological structures and boundary continuity. Second, we introduce 3D Group Prompt, which extracts domain-universal knowledge via curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts together with text prompts built on SAT baseline. Finally, we replace conventional output layers with Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head equipped with synonym-resolved routing, which brings negligible computational cost and enables fast incremental learning for new categories without sacrificing performance on old tasks. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering both organ and lesion segmentation verify the efficacy of our modules.
bullets: Addresses rare-pathology annotation scarcity, morphological distortion, catastrophic forgetting, and siloed task development.
DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling improves differentiable topology and boundary continuity.
3D Group Prompt extracts shared domain knowledge from volumetric image-mask alignment and text prompts.
Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head supports fast addition of new categories with negligible computational cost while retaining prior-task performance.
Ablations on abdominal and extra-abdominal organ and lesion datasets support the effectiveness of the proposed modules.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of DT-MorphLoss. The overall pipeline proceeds as follows: 1) a Sigmoid activation and Otsu binarization convert the prediction map into a binary mask; 2) the mask is fed in parallel into two branches, where the morphological-loss branch applies erosion and dilation to compute Lmorph, while the distance-transform branch extracts an edge mask to produce a distance field for Ldt.; 3) the two terms are weighted and combined with the standard Dice loss (Ldice) and cross-entropy loss (Lce) to obtain the total loss.

Fig. 3. Overview of Many-to-one-CSH. Visual queries are encoded into multi-level features, while the text branch uses a Hash function to map various input texts into corresponding targets within a vocabulary registry and generate specific prompts. These prompts are transformed into distinctive text embeddings ωi, which are sequentially combined with the visual features and fed into a parameter generator composed of multiple specialized MLP heads. This module dynamically generates prompt-conditioned weight parameters θi that directly modulate the layers within the segment head, allowing the decoded query features to be processed into final masks.

Fig. 2. Overview of GroupPrompt3D. A 2D Swin encoder extracts features from both a support volume and a query volume. The support path processes features through a concept filter, while the query path extracts multi-scale representations via a decoder. Crucially, since the target labels in the support and query volumes do not perfectly match during training, a Conv3D block is required to map the conditional prompt knowledge and predict the final mask.

Fig. 5. Unified axial-space mapping of the discrete slice distributions across 6 test cases with 5 lesion categories. The horizontal axis indicates the actual slice index, while the dual-axis aligns the lesion labels and the case identifiers.

Fig. 6. Hierarchical expansion of the medical vocabulary registry for the MSWAL dataset. Semantic relevance to the core concept weakens moving outward: the innermost circle is the baseline VOCAB with 7 core medical categories, while the middle and outermost circles include extended clinical and anatomical variants.

Fig. 4. Segmentation predictions versus the weight of DT-Morph Combined Loss for the identical liver tumor slice. The results reveal the nonlinear morphological evolution of the prediction, demonstrating the transition from over-segmentation to undersegmentation as ω increases.
Table 5. Ablation study results of Many-to-one-CSH.
Table 1. Improvements achieved by GroupPrompt3D.
Table 2. Improvements achieved by Many-to-one-CSH.
Table 3. Ablation study results of DT-MorphLoss.

papers.title: Enhancing Medical Lesion Segmentation via Several Simple Modules
papers.tldr: Three lightweight modules improve medical lesion segmentation topology, cross-domain knowledge reuse, and incremental learning under limited data and compute.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
authors: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi, Yong Deng, Shuheng Shen, Changhua Meng, Xiaofeng Wu, Jie Yang, Wei Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of static supervised fine-tuning data for evolving MCP agents.
Uses rollout feedback to identify capability gaps and learning targets.
Evolves verified seed tasks while preserving aligned verifiers, then recovers or refines teacher trajectories with reusable skills.
Fine-tunes the student on evolved task–trajectory pairs and repeats the process using new feedback.
Reports absolute gains of 16.5% on Toolathlon, 10.2% on MCPMark, and 12.6% on MCP-Atlas over the initial student.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a co-evolution framework for agents and training data, addressing the static data distribution problem in agent fine-tuning. This is a form of test-time adaptation and continual learning for LLM agents.
papers.title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
papers.tldr: EvoMCP co-evolves MCP-agent tasks and training trajectories in a feedback loop, improving agents by continually targeting newly revealed capability gaps.

papers.abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.
authors: Anil Bilgin, Wanda Hou, Pranav Srinivas, Yi-Zhuang You
bullets: Targets quantum LDPC decoding across code families, sizes, physical error rates, and noise models without fine-tuning.
Uses local message passing for scalable predictions and beam search to refine candidate error patterns, trading latency for lower logical error rates.
Introduces a decoder model factory that trains successive models on verified decoding trajectories generated by earlier models.
Repeated experience collection and distillation let decoders improve across generations and adapt to changing noise.
Envisions coupled rapid-decoding and slower learning cycles for continually adapting quantum hardware protection.

figures.caption: Figure 5: BP distillation supplies a transferable starting decoder, while leaving a gap to stronger classical methods. The three shaded code-capacity tasks supply training data; the other nine evaluate the same model without fine-tuning. Logical error rates use 2048 realizations per task. Bars above 0.15 are truncated. Training and comparison settings are in Appendix B.

Figure 11: The final search-enhanced model G+ 3 compared with established decoders on 12 tasks. The three shaded tasks supply training data; the other nine test the same model without further training. Figure 10: Successive models improve single-pass decoding and transfer that improvement to an unseen task. Dashed green curves show single-pass decoding; solid green curves show beam-search decoding. Horizontal lines show reference decoders. Curves are means over five independent model factory runs; bands are the range across those runs. Full generation results are in Appendix E.2.

Figure 1: AI model factories connect a source of training data to new models and their applications. The language-model analogy motivates a corresponding process for quantum computing, with quantum hardware providing experimentally testable outcomes. The return arrows represent model assistance to humans or quantum hardware. In the illustrated approach, data generation supplies training examples, and distillation trains later models on these examples. This paper develops the decoding instance through supervised distillation from search trajectories, with outcome verification supplied by simulation; hardware learning, control, and calibration are prospective applications.

Figure 7: Inference-time search trades computation for accuracy. With the starting GraphMP model fixed, broader and deeper search lowers logical error while increasing decoding time. The surfaces aggregate the three training tasks; measurements and budgets are given in Appendix C.3.

Figure 12: Accuracy and decoding time on a training task and an unseen task. Logical-error curves are fitted to measured data; bands are 90% bootstrap intervals conditional on that model. Times compare GPU GraphMP with single-core CPU reference decoders. They measure time per shot in a stream of syndromes. Fit diagnostics and timing procedures are in Appendices E.5 and E.6.

Figure 13: Adaptation after the noise changes at G3. The same model is evaluated immediately before and after the switch from depolarizing to XZ noise; G4–G6 learn from newly collected trajectories. (a) Mitten150 supplies training data; (b) LP3,5 20 tests adaptation without further training on that task. Dashed green curves show single-pass decoding; solid green curves show beam-search decoding. RelayBP is evaluated with its original and updated noise priors; GraphMP’s beam-search candidate selector retains the original prior. Bands are 90% Wilson intervals. The full experiment is described in Appendix E.7.

Figure 8: Outcome feedback selects search trajectories for training. The collector retains syndromeconsistent, logically correct final predictions together with the intermediate states along their search paths. This work obtains logical feedback in simulation, while dedicated quantum-memory experiments provide a route to device-based verification.

Figure 3: Detector error model. Hidden error events connect to the syndrome bits and logical observables they flip. The decoder sees the syndrome and predicts an error pattern. Highlighted nodes illustrate one realization and its syndrome and logical outcome.

The dashed line marks SNR = 1. Codes sharing a distance are offset horizontally.

Logical error rate is shown for a single pass (top) and for beam search (bottom), on the same 8192 realizations per task under each noise model, averaged over three training seeds. Wilson intervals summarize the pooled shot-level variation; the mean weights the three target tasks equally. Each panel reports ZA→B of Eq. (36) from the depolarizing-data student to the XZ-data student. The unmodified G3 mean is marked for reference. An escape counts as a logical success.

Figure 29: Generation progress after the noise model changes from the depolarizing noise model to the XZ noise model at G3. The nominal error-rate setting and decoding graph remain fixed. Dashed: single-pass decoder GraphMP Gx; solid: search-enhanced decoder GraphMP G+ x ; bands are 90% Wilson intervals on 8192 realizations per task. The BP teacher and Relay-BP step at G3 to their logical error rate under the original prior; the faint lines give their rate under the updated prior. The model factory collects on the first three target tasks only; LP3,5 20 is unseen during adaptation.

The left endpoint is single-pass decoding; the remaining points increase the search depth. Residual-syndrome density of the predicted error pattern is shown above logical error rate, which is decomposed into failures and miscorrections. Shaded bands are 90% confidence intervals; 8192 shots per task, the same shots at every search depth.

The shaded band marks the three code-capacity training tasks. The same model is applied without fine-tuning to the unshaded unseen tasks. The BP teacher, BP+OSD/LSD, and Relay-BP configurations are those of Section A.5.

papers.abstract: Executing an unfamiliar laboratory protocol requires a robot to identify missing capabilities and determine whether each operation remains valid as the experiment progresses. This letter presents BioAgent, an embodied agent that addresses these coupled challenges of capability sufficiency and experimental validity. It matches human-reviewed requirements to validated skills and task packages, selects tool-based implementations for missing behaviors, and requests human teaching when needed during learning. Learned skills undergo sequential task-package validation to check outcomes and compatibility between successive operations. During execution, precondition, outcome, and experimental-state checks govern progression, autonomous recovery, or termination. Execution evidence guides tool selection, while accepted experience supports offline policy updates and task packaging. On the second task, BioAgent reuses 17 skill types unchanged, revises two existing implementations, and acquires five new types. On two dual-arm laboratory tasks with 20 and 31 ordered skill invocations, BioAgent achieves complete-task success rates of 66\% and 58\% with autonomous recovery over 50 runs per task. Across 25 atomic skills evaluated over 50 autonomous trials each with recovery disabled, success rates range from 84\% to 100\%, with 17 skills achieving 50/50.

papers.abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.

papers.abstract: Camera--LiDAR perception on mobile robots and intelligent vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry throughout deployment. Installation variations create uncertainty in the initial extrinsics, while changing observation quality makes frame-wise estimates fluctuate during operation. This paper presents CalibSwitch, an observation-driven framework that separates absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance. A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) combines projection-free bidirectional feature interaction with geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image--point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to determine when a candidate should replace the working geometry consumed by a frozen multimodal detector. On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884$^\circ$. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70\% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Paired geometry--observation uncertainty tests, two real-vehicle platforms, and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution demonstrate the system value of selective geometric-state maintenance for continuous perception.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves $23/36$ successful trials (63.9\%), compared with $19/36$ (52.8\%) with memory alone and $2/36$ (5.6\%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from $7/9$ to $4/9$, while removing retained experience reduces it to $3/9$. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.

The experience module interprets this task-level structure alongside physical evidence and retained lessons, generating contextual feedback while extracting and revising reusable experience. papers.abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.
bullets: Answer-level rewards treat equally correct traces as identical, missing differences in their learning value.
The study compares confidence-based SC with entropy-based UID-Conj., which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness.
Online reward augmentation and offline training are evaluated on AIME-derived problems using Qwen3-1.7B.
UID-Conj. improves online macro-average performance by 2.08 points over unmodified TTRL and exceeds uniform offline weighting by 1.93 points.
Benefits are task-dependent: SC favors judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. often yields stronger training outcomes.

papers.abstract: RGB-thermal (RGB-T) object detectors combine visible and thermal imagery for robust detection, but signal corruption in either stream can substantially degrade accuracy. Restoration-based methods incur significant latency and do not consistently improve downstream accuracy, raising a more direct question: rather than restoring corrupted inputs, can we efficiently adapt the detector to their varying signal quality? Conventional PEFT offers an efficient route, but its input-independent corrections cannot track diverse test-time corruptions. Our controlled corruption sweeps show that corruption types have similar effects near clean conditions but diverge increasingly with severity, motivating corruption-aware, per-input adaptation. We therefore propose PG-FM (Prompt-Guided Feature Modulation), which adapts RGB-T object detectors to the estimated corruption type and severity of each modality. Under controlled RGB-T corruption simulations, PG-FM preserves clean-set performance, improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST, and transfers without retraining to unmodified, naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.
authors: Liuyin Shi, Chengqi Li, Wenbo He
bullets: RGB-T detection can degrade sharply when either the visible or thermal stream is corrupted.
Fixed, input-independent parameter-efficient adaptation cannot handle diverse, severity-dependent corruptions.
PG-FM uses prompts to guide geometric feature modulation based on estimated corruption type and severity for each modality.
Under simulated corruptions, it preserves clean performance and improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST.
The method transfers without retraining to naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.

papers.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
authors: Alexander Detkov, Dashiel Karish, Matthew Oleynikov, Matt Thomson
bullets: Introduces two benchmarks for evaluating deductive reasoning across increasing inference depths.
Uses a controllable formal graph benchmark and a real-world knowledge-composition benchmark.
Compares knowledge supplied in context with knowledge encoded in model weights, without chain-of-thought prompting.
In-context knowledge substantially outperforms deduction over pretrained knowledge, though both degrade with longer compositions.
Findings highlight limitations relevant to prompt-based agent control and continual learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models receive graph adjacency in-context but integrate the information poorly, failing at long-range inferences. DeepSeek, Kimi, Nemotron, and 12 other models answer questions about a random graph of 50–60 nodes given in the prompt as a list of edges, with reasoning off. Each question concerns the nodes exactly k hops from a start node, so k = 1 questions require only direct-neighbor information. a) Verify: is a given node exactly k hops away? Accuracy falls from 93–100% at k = 1 to 49–56% at k = 3, close to chance. b) Count: how many nodes are exactly k hops away? Models count correctly 43–69% of the time at k = 1 and ≤ 16% from k = 2. c) Name one: name a node exactly k hops away. Models name a neighbor at 99–100%, but a node two hops away at only 9–40%. d) Enumerate: list every node exactly k hops away. Models list all neighbors at 71–100%, but no model lists more than 12% of sets correctly from k = 2.

Figure 2: Models compose facts from the prompt far better than from memory. DeepSeek, Kimi, and Nemotron answer k-hop Wikidata questions with reasoning off and information given in context, in memory, or both. a) The chain’s facts are given in the prompt under invented names, among 16 decoy chains with the same relations. All models compose at ≥ 94% up to k = 3, but at k = 6, Kimi composes at 29%, while DeepSeek and Nemotron Ultra fall to chance. b) The facts are recalled from memory without supporting facts in the prompt. Composition reaches only 37–64% at k = 2 and ≤ 12% from k = 4, although every fact is known. c) The facts are given in the prompt under their real names, among 16 real decoy chains, so the model can use both the prompt and memory. Accuracy reaches 36–71% at k = 6.

papers.abstract: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.
authors: Luyao Zhu, Fangfang Zhang, Yi Mei, Ke Chen, Mengjie Zhang
bullets: Addresses poor cross-task generalisation and knowledge loss when scheduling conditions change.
Uses an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance adaptation to new tasks with retention of prior knowledge.
Weights knowledge reuse according to task similarity.
Improves surrogate-model estimation with distance constraints.
Experiments show reduced catastrophic forgetting, strong adaptability, and better performance than compared methods.

papers.abstract: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.
bullets: The study disentangles parent inheritance from per-round feedback breadth under matched evaluation budgets.
Across 1,750 preregistered runs on nine prompt and program-synthesis benchmarks, greedy parent inheritance drives most optimization progress.
Seed-reset search remains weaker even with summaries of all failures or larger proposer models.
Full-set clustering and diverse failure selection help early seed rewrites, but inheritance quickly closes the gap by retaining solved error modes.
In GEPA, validation and minibatch gating consume most compute; proposer reflection is a small cost, suggesting simpler inheritance-based loops can capture most gains.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'Lineage' as a form of memory in LLM-guided optimization, demonstrating that parent inheritance drives optimization progress and effectively captures the benefits of complex reflective loops.
papers.title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization
papers.tldr: In short-budget LLM-guided optimization, preserving and iteratively improving a successful parent matters far more than exposing broader failure feedback.

papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.
bullets: Frames continual world-model learning as a contextual MDP with behavioral and physical context components.
Organizes continual learning into knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition.
Studies direct reuse when behavioral rules stay fixed using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks.
Finds that physical-context changes can substantially degrade zero-shot reuse, depending strongly on observation representation.
Latent diagnostics and ablations indicate that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reliable reuse.

Position + direction contains the agent’s global position and orientation, distance contains local distances from obstacles in the agent’s relative directions, and combined contains both types of information.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies zero-shot generalization bottlenecks in continual world models, directly relevant to world-model reuse and continual RL.
papers.title: Before We Adapt: The Zero-Shot Generalization Bottleneck in Continual World Models
papers.tldr: Zero-shot reuse of learned world models can fail under physical changes, making representation generalization a key bottleneck in continual reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Scientific foundation models (SciFMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of PDEs, including the ability to efficiently adapt to unseen data distributions with additional finetuning. As with all neural architectures, finetuning such models comes with the risk of catastrophic forgetting, whereby adapting to new tasks degrades prior knowledge of the model. We study catastrophic forgetting in Walrus-1.3B, a SciFM for continuum dynamics, over the course of a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation: first finetuning on simulated flow around a cylinder and then adapting to experimental data of the same system. We find that finetuning on the simulations rapidly degrades rollout performance on the original pretraining datasets, with one-step errors increasing up to 35x after just 20 epochs. Subsequent adaptation to real data further erodes performance on the simulated task. We characterize the potential drivers of forgetting, such as dataset dependence and task representation similarity. We then show that replaying as little as 1% simulated data during real-data finetuning recovers most of the lost simulation performance while retaining effective adaptation to the experimental dynamics. Our results identify catastrophic forgetting as a practical obstacle to sim-to-real adaptation of SciFMs and show that lightweight replay strategies significantly improve retention.
authors: Haaris Mian, Miles Cranmer, Alessandro Favero, Payel Mukhopadhyay
bullets: Studies forgetting across two stages: simulated cylinder-flow finetuning followed by experimental-data adaptation.
Simulation finetuning rapidly degrades performance on the model’s original pretraining datasets; one-step errors increase up to 35× after 20 epochs.
Real-data adaptation causes further loss on the simulated task.
Analyzes possible drivers including dataset dependence and task-representation similarity.
Finds that lightweight replay of 1% simulated data recovers most lost simulation performance while retaining effective real-data adaptation.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. papers.abstract: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.
authors: Daniel Levine, David van Dijk, Kenneth Kay
bullets: Targets limitations of existing zero-shot inference and continual-learning models, especially weak inductive biases and externally controlled learning.
Uses internally generated activity and external feedback to create a neuromodulatory signal that gates a local three-factor Hebbian update.
Reports success on zero-shot tasks, emergent zero-shot and continual-learning abilities, and reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms.
The abstract states that AutoHebb outperforms modern learning models on zero-shot and continual-learning tasks.
Comparisons indicate that meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous learning control are all important components.

figures.caption: Figure 16: AutoHebb networks benchmarked in the present study: 1- and 2-neuromodulator AutoHebb (AH-1NM and AH-2NM). For both models, the main network was chosen to be a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with four hidden layers; the models differed by the number of neuromodulators (and corresponding control network; in the 2-neuromodulator network, the control networks were parallel, as diagrammed). AH-2N is loosely inspired by the existernce of multiple neuromodulatory systems in the brain, and was included in benchmarking to evaluate the possibility that parallel neuromodulated plastic architecture would enhance task performance. Note that each set of plastic weights at a given layer in the 2-neuromodulator network were summed (Eq. 18). Top, AH-1N, Bottom, AH-2NM. Note that additional AutoHebb networks were also investigated in this study, and are indicated accordingly were applicable. Implementation details can be found in Appendix E.

Figure 1: AutoHebb architecture. Network weights (W) are either fixed (black) or plastic (red). The architecture consists of a "main" network (here an MLP with hidden layers h) and an auxiliary "control" network (here an MLP with hidden layers c) that receives two inputs: (1) internally generated activity from the main network (here from last hidden layer hlast), and (2) external input reflecting environmental (external) feedback given an output (y) generated by the network. The control network generates a scalar-valued neuromodulatory signal (m, red circle) that gates changes to the plastic weights within network (here Wn∗). See Appendix E for further details; additional network variants in Figure 16.

In contrast, ANML maintains its different group bias and loses its same group accuracy, even on training trials. Figure 2: Meta-learning in AutoHebb. In AutoHebb networks, fixed (non-plastic) network weights were identified through meta-learning optimization, which involves two levels of adaptation: an "inner" and "outer" loop. In the inner loop, corresponding to learning, (3-factor Hebbian) plastic updates to the network occur across an episode, i.e. a sequence of trials (where each trial involves input, output, control, and update steps; see main text). At the start of each episode, fixed weights are frozen and plastic weights are set to 0. In the outer loop, corresponding to metalearning (or meta-training), the network’s fixed weights are updated via optimization based on performance within the episode and/or testing following the episode.

papers.abstract: Continual adaptation requires deciding not only how to update a model, but whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance. CABA provides an auditable retention check for candidate generators exposing comparable policy distributions and a declared update path, while deployment also requires separate evidence of current-task utility.
bullets: Uses frozen historical anchor observations excluded from candidate optimization and compares old versus candidate policies via forward KL divergence.
Provides conditional off-anchor guarantees under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, plus bounds for interpolation, grid resolution, trajectories, and sequential updates.
In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition sensor-policy proxy, mean forgetting fell from 1.01% to 0.00% at ε=0.05, while final average accuracy decreased from 93.04% to 88.48%.
The study demonstrates a retention–plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance.
Deployment still requires separate evidence that the accepted update improves current-task utility.

papers.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
bullets: Supports waypoint, discrete local, pixel-based, and object-directed navigation actions.
Lets agents ask for clarification or assistance when facing ambiguity or difficulty.
Stores observations and dialogue by location to improve future visits.
Evaluated across eight benchmarks spanning four navigation task families and multi-day physical navigation.
Reports strong performance, including 100% first-visit SR across four 100-episode sets and improved R2R revisit SPL from 82.23% to 93.31%.
