papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to solve complex scientific and practical problems via iterative optimization. However, dynamically coordinating diverse search mechanisms as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets evolve remains a critical open challenge. Targeted empirical diagnostics reveal that mechanism effectiveness is highly state-dependent. Motivated by this, we analyze how individual decisions drive final outcomes, decomposing the expected terminal improvement under a shared budget into cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses. Guided by this opportunity-loss theoretical foundation, we propose OptiCom, a unified framework that represents LLM-driven optimizers within a shared configuration space: C=(A,Q,O,E,M,S), corresponding to artifact, query, operator, evaluation, memory, and strategy. Operating within this space, a fast LLM-based Optimization Controller dynamically composes immediate mechanisms through structured Action Packages, while a slower Strategy Adapter refines long-term selection preferences, operator weights, and templates based on accumulated trajectory feedback. Comprehensive evaluations across 32 benchmark groups demonstrate the superiority of framework: OptiCom achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72 among 14 evaluated configurations, securing the top score in 23 groups. Ultimately, these results highlight the broad applicability and high extensibility of OptiCom as a general-purpose paradigm for robust LLM test-time scaling.
bullets: LLM-driven optimization mechanisms vary in effectiveness as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets change.
The framework analyzes terminal improvement as cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses.
OptiCom unifies optimizer components in a shared configuration space covering artifacts, queries, operators, evaluation, memory, and strategy.
A fast controller selects structured Action Packages, while a slower adapter updates preferences, operator weights, and templates from trajectory feedback.
Across 32 benchmark groups and 14 configurations, OptiCom ranked first on average and achieved the top score in 23 groups.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of OptiCom. The Optimization Controller selects and composes Q/O/E/M mechanisms through an Action Package, while the slower Strategy Adapter updates the guidance used by subsequent Controller decisions. Solid arrows show execution and state flow; gray dashed arrows indicate configuration, and purple dashed arrows indicate slower strategy adaptation. Annotations involving ∆t and ℓt highlight how specific architectural components are explicitly designed to expand search opportunities (∆t) and reduce selection losses (ℓt). Composing optimization mechanisms. The analysis in Section 4 identifies two factors governing adaptive optimization: the opportunities provided by available actions, ∆t, and the loss incurred when selecting among them, ℓt. Guided by this decomposition, OptiCom dynamically combines complementary mechanisms within the shared configuration space. To maximize opportunities while mitigating selection loss, the framework operates through a continuous, state-conditioned execution loop driven by two core components: an Optimization Controller for immediate mechanism composition, and a slower Strategy Adapter for long-term guidance revision. Both components operate through LLM API calls with fixed model parameters (see Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.1).

papers.title: OptiCom : A Unified Framework for State-Conditioned Composition in LLM-Driven Optimization

papers.abstract: Retinal fundus images frequently carry more than one disease, and public fundus datasets are heterogeneous and severely long-tailed. Clinical triage suggests a staged design, in which a screening gate, a disease-group router and group-specific classifiers operate in sequence, but it is unclear whether this hierarchy earns its complexity. We present a controlled comparison of three architectures on a unified 39-target label space built from RFMiD 1.0, RFMiD 2.0 and ODIR-5K (12,652 images): (i) a three-stage gated cascade of eight models, (ii) a flat model with 39 independent sigmoid outputs, and (iii) a label-correlation model that replaces the flat linear head with 39 learned label queries and a two-layer transformer decoder. All three share one Swin-V2-B backbone, one preprocessing pipeline and one training protocol, so differences are attributable to the architecture. Staging offers no consistent advantage: tracing every missed disease instance to the stage that lost it shows that the two coarse gates discard 34.2% of true instances while the fine-grained classifiers lose only 6.7%, and the gates' hard zeros depress the cascade's macro-AUC to 0.747. Label-correlation modeling gives the largest single gain, raising the detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682 (0.689 with test-time augmentation). Blending the flat and label-correlation models under four-view test-time augmentation is the best configuration on six of eight metrics (exact match 0.694, micro-F1 0.678, macro-F1 0.456, macro-AUC 0.972). On definition-matched class subsets it matches or exceeds four recent studies on macro- and micro-F1, most clearly on low-support pathologies. We also show that ensembling a gated cascade with continuous-output models is harmful, and that per-source negative sampling is needed to remove a dataset shortcut that otherwise yields a spurious AUC of 1.000.
bullets: The study unifies RFMiD 1.0, RFMiD 2.0, and ODIR-5K into 39 disease targets across 12,652 images.
A three-stage cascade, flat sigmoid model, and transformer-based label-correlation model share the same Swin-V2-B backbone and training setup.
The cascade’s screening gates discard 34.2% of true disease instances, limiting its macro-AUC to 0.747.
Label-correlation modeling improves detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682, or 0.689 with test-time augmentation.
Blending flat and label-correlation models performs best on six of eight metrics and is particularly effective for low-support diseases.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates label-correlation ensembles and test-time augmentation for multi-label classification, relevant to test-time adaptation strategies.
papers.title: Beyond Multi-Stage Pipelines: A Label-Correlation Ensemble for Multi-Label Retinal Fundus Disease Classification
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that a flat ensemble with label-correlation modeling outperforms a complex staged cascade for multi-label retinal disease classification, especially on rare conditions.

papers.abstract: Modern forecasting models are often updated after deployment so they can respond to changing data. These updates can also make predictions worse, so practical systems need a reliable monitor that can detect harmful changes and trigger protection. A natural design is to monitor the same prediction errors that guide the updates. This paper asks whether the statistical guarantee behind such a monitor remains valid when monitoring and adaptation use the same feedback. We study this question in multi-step time-series forecasting. We show that overlapping targets and dependence in forecast errors can break a key assumption required by the guarantee. The monitor may then raise alarms even when no harmful change has occurred, and its response can further damage prediction quality. We also find that adaptation can hide sustained changes from its own monitor, while the original frozen model retains a clearer signal. These results expose a basic failure mode in self-monitored adaptation. They show why reliable deployment requires checking the monitor's assumptions, comparing adaptation with the frozen model under realistic feedback, and limiting the effect of every protective response.
bullets: The paper studies multi-step time-series forecasting systems that adapt after deployment while monitoring the same errors used for adaptation.
Overlapping targets and dependent forecast errors can invalidate exchangeability-based monitoring guarantees.
This may cause false alarms without harmful distribution change, with protective responses further degrading forecasts.
Adaptation can also conceal sustained changes from its own monitor, whereas the frozen model may provide a clearer signal.
Reliable deployment requires validating monitor assumptions, comparing against the frozen model, and limiting protective-response effects.

papers.title: The Premise Is the Problem: Exchangeability Failure in Self-Monitored Test-Time Adaptation

papers.abstract: An agent deployed in a single body cannot learn how fast that body wears, because every trial that would reveal its wear resistance wears the body it would protect. We study this \emph{epoch-one} setting, in which the parameters of a fixed-weight policy are set before the body is drawn and never updated in life. The agent carries a load-gated nociceptive channel and a memory that retains what was felt. We prove that felt cost moves the allocation to the best-\emph{paid} work not yet felt rather than the gentlest, that an agent without retention never sees the felt-cost constraint bind, and that the channel pays only where the threat is individually unpredictable, cheap to avoid and expensive to ignore. We measure per body, setting the agent with channel and memory against the same individual without them, where neither carries a schedule learned across lives. On $2{,}000$ simulated floor-layer knees, with wear anchored to published loss rates, feeling, retaining and substituting extends the working life from age $55.2$ to $59.6$ and raises career output from $33.7$ to $36.1$. $69.3\%$ of bodies gain and \textbf{none lose}. A body that feels but retains nothing past the day gains one of the $+4.4$ years, and retention carries the rest. A population-trained agent gains $+0.65$ years from the same channel at $-0.54$ output. The difference is what a species prior already supplies, and a single body has none. The two are related by an identity, the ablation mean reporting $(1-χ)$ of the per-body value with $χ$ the share a blind schedule already captures, so we report both. Where the regime map predicts value, a care robot sextuples its certified service life and a field-anchored fleet writes off $0.15$ of its machines instead of $0.55$. Where it predicts none, a rover gains little over blind caution, so the map holds in both directions.
bullets: Studies the “epoch-one” setting: policy parameters are fixed before deployment and cannot be updated across life.
Combines a load-gated nociceptive channel with memory of experienced costs to guide work allocation and avoidance.
Across 2,000 simulated floor-layer knees, the full agent extends working life from 55.2 to 59.6 and career output from 33.7 to 36.1; 69.3% of bodies benefit and none lose.
Memory provides most of the benefit: feeling without retaining adds 1 of the 4.4 years gained, while retention supplies the remainder.
A regime map predicts where nociception helps, with reported gains in care robots and field fleets but little benefit for rovers in regimes favoring blind caution.

papers.selection_reason: Studies an embodied agent with nociceptive sensing and memory for wear-aware allocation; fits embodied memory and embodied AI.
papers.title: Nociception as a Control Primitive: Afferent Channels and Nociceptive Memory for Agents Deployed in One Body
papers.tldr: Nociceptive feedback plus memory helps a fixed-policy agent adapt within a single lifetime, extending body life and improving output when threats are unpredictable and costly to ignore.

papers.abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.
authors: Daniel Strau{\ss}, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Motivation: Global retrieval repeatedly searches large stores, while recurrent compression risks discarding information too early.
Method: Separate memory content from address and optimize local neighborhoods using retrieval information value minus accessibility cost.
Key principle: Complementary memories should be co-retrievable when their added value exceeds cost; redundant memories should be excluded despite individual usefulness.
Proof of principle: On MiniGrid Memory, fixed-geometry traversal reached 0.95 mean return after 0.59M steps, versus 0.94M for Gaussian absolute addressing and over 2M for categorical addressing.
Scope: The experiment does not evaluate learned geometry or repeated retrieval, so the full method remains unvalidated.

figures.caption: Table 1: Comparison of retrieval heads on MiniGrid-Memory-S17Random (6 seeds each). Models were pretrained on MiniGrid-Memory-S9 without a retrieval head using a context size of 64. "Steps to 0.95" is the first training step at which the mean (min–max) return reaches 0.95. "> 2.0" indicates that the value was not determined after 2,048,000 steps. The entry No retrieval head (baseline) was tested with only 3 seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes value-indexed memory for stateful long-context agents, tested on MiniGrid Memory; directly relevant to embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
papers.tldr: A value-indexed, persistent local traversal mechanism aims to make stateful retrieval easier by grouping complementary memories while avoiding redundant co-retrieval.

papers.abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.
authors: Nicolas Dufour, Elouan Gard\`es, Amil Dravid, Patrick P\'erez, Loic Landrieu
bullets: Single-block perturbations recover much of the reported improvement, while random output-logit biases often match or exceed full-weight perturbations on reasoning tasks.
The authors propose Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV): generate perturbed predictors, select strong ones on a small validation set, and aggregate their predictions.
A first-order analysis suggests small weight perturbations mainly matter through the logit shifts they induce.
Logit PSV improves vision performance under domain shift, including Earth observation, without modifying model weights.
The approach connects Neural Thickets to sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection, but its scope is limited to the tasks and settings evaluated.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Full-weight PSV versus logit PSV. Both methods share the same selection and voting stages (right), but differ in the perturbation (left). Neural Thickets (top) perturb the full dθdimensional parameter vector, producing N distinct networks. Logit PSV (bottom) keeps one frozen network and adds a V -dimensional bias to the output logits, fixed across decoding steps and inputs.

Figure 4: Logit PSV matches full-weight PSV across tasks and model scales. (a) On OLMo-37B-Instruct, logit PSV matches or exceeds full-weight PSV on all evaluated tasks. (b) Across model scales and tasks, logit PSV closely tracks full-weight PSV.

Figure 5: Temperature-tuned majority voting versus full-weight PSV. (a) On MATH-500 with a strong model, tuned TT-MV matches or exceeds full-weight PSV. (b) On USPTO with a weaker model, TT-MV remains far below PSV, showing the value of validation-based selection; both remain below the majority-class baseline. (c) Across tasks and model scales, TT-MV at T=0.7 closely tracks full-weight PSV, with larger gaps for weaker models and harder tasks.

Figure 7: Single-component perturbations transfer across architectures. Gain over base, in accuracy points, when perturbing one component of the first decoder block of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on GSM8K (K=50; base 44.3%, full-block gain +11.8). Every component improves over base, with the largest gains from the value, up, and output projections. Qwen2.5 uses pre-norm blocks and includes QKV biases, unlike OLMo.

Countdown and USPTO are omitted at 0.5B because the base model cannot perform these tasks.

Figure 12: Peak accuracy of stacked perturbations versus individual methods and a logit-only control. Full-weight PSV stacked on logit PSV is compared against (a) the stronger individual method and (b) the same-mechanism control, which stacks two logit biases. The dashed diagonal indicates equal accuracy. Most points lie on or below it. Above it are 3B and 7B MATH-500 (+1.3, +1.0) and 7B GSM8K (+0.2) in (a), and 7B Countdown (+0.9), 7B MATH-500 (+0.3), and 3B Countdown (+0.2) in (b); only 7B MATH-500 is above it in both.

Peak gain over greedy decoding across ensemble sizes K, comparing full-weight PSV, logit PSV, their combination, and a same-mechanism control that stacks two logit biases with a smaller noise range. The symbol “◦” denotes successive application of two perturbations. Combining weight and logit perturbations rarely improves upon the stronger individual method or the logit-only control, except on 7B MATH-500.
Figure 2: Effect of perturbing individual decoder blocks. Countdown accuracy with OLMo-37B-Instruct (K = 50), perturbing one block at a time while keeping all other weights fixed.

Figure 9: Accuracy as a function of ensemble size K. Plurality-vote accuracy for full-weight PSV, logit PSV, and TT-MV across model scales (rows) and tasks (columns). The dashed line indicates the greedy-base accuracy.

Figure 10: Gain over the greedy base as a function of ensemble size K. Same runs as Figure 9, shown as the accuracy gain ∆ over the greedy base, across model scales (rows) and tasks (columns). The dashed line marks zero gain.

Figure 8: Single-component perturbations remain effective at larger scales. All components improve over base, with the output and value projections among the strongest at both scales.

Table 5: Cross-scale comparison of full-weight and output-space perturbations. Accuracy at K=50 (%) for the greedy base, full-weight PSV, logit PSV, and an input-embedding-bias variant on Qwen2.5 and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct. The input-embedding variant adds a Gaussian bias to token embeddings and is evaluated on Qwen2.5 only. The logit-bias scale is fixed per model rather than chosen per task (σ=0.5 for Qwen2.5-0.5B, 1.0 for 1.5B and 3B, 2.0 for OLMo-3-7B), and fullweight PSV uses σ=0.001. Every method uses N=1000, except full-weight PSV on Countdown (N=2000). Degenerate Qwen2.5-0.5B cells on Countdown and USPTO are omitted. †A constant predictor of the majority reaction class scores 31.9% on USPTO; these cells are at or below it and are not bolded. ‡Above that baseline, but with lower balanced accuracy than full-weight PSV (26.7% against 29.7%).

Table 3: Vision PSV under domain shift. We report improvements relative to linear probing on the frozen DINOv3-7B backbone using worst-region accuracy for FMoW, worst-group accuracy for Waterbirds, and balanced top-1 accuracy for ImageNet. PSV variants use validation-selected ensembles with K = 10; closed-form denotes a single deterministic output recalibration. Weightspace perturbations yield little improvement, whereas output-space methods produce substantial gains on FMow, Waterbirds, which present strong train-to-test shift.

Every component produces nonzero reward variability and improves the final vote, with the largest effects generally obtained from the value and output projections.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), an inference-time method for improving model performance through output diversity and selection, applicable to both language and vision models.
papers.title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
papers.tldr: Neural Thickets gains can largely be explained by output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting rather than nearby weight-space experts.

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.

papers.abstract: Mobile robots must open doors and drawers, yet their scene maps record what each object is and whether it has moved, not how it will respond to a pull. This paper proposes PhysVLMM, a method that maintains a physical belief for every articulated part of a Vision-Language-Motion Map and answers a planner's queries about it, with two algorithms: a map update and a query. Watching a part move provably cannot identify its dynamics, and a measured pull identifies only the pulled part, up to one direction. PhysVLMM therefore (i) keeps that direction as a posterior instead of a point estimate, (ii) passes the evidence of each pull in closed form to the untouched look-alike parts of the map, and (iii) answers whether an action will succeed at a stated risk, or abstains. On real doors and drawers in 18 homes, it identifies the joint type in 86% of held-out pulls (48% for a learned single-view method) and predicts the response to a pull with 41% lower error than differentiable simulation (CRPS 0.323 vs. 0.544), four orders of magnitude faster (13 ms vs. 230 s per case). The posterior lowers the final-position error from 0.460 to 0.270, sharing lowers the force error of untouched parts from 56% to 42%, and at every stated risk from 0.02 to 0.30 the false-safe answers stay within it. Pooling all measured parts of a home does as well as the look-alike groups, and simpler variants predict where a pulled part stops at least as well.
bullets: Addresses the gap between scene maps and the physical response of doors, drawers, and other articulated parts.
Maintains posterior beliefs over motion direction, propagates evidence to untouched look-alike parts, and can answer or abstain based on stated risk.
On real doors and drawers across 18 homes, identified joint types in 86% of held-out pulls.
Reduced pull-response error by 41% versus differentiable simulation and ran four orders of magnitude faster.
Risk-controlled answers remained within the specified false-safe rate from 0.02 to 0.30.

papers.abstract: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.
authors: Juan Belieni, Ana Carolina Erthal, Eliezer de Souza da Silva, Diego Mesquita
bullets: Sequential unlearning can degrade both forgetting and model utility because updates interfere with prior deletions.
COP projects each update onto the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from earlier forget sets.
The method provides a first-order guarantee of non-interference with previous deletions.
It stores only a low-rank basis per layer and does not require past gradients or previous forget data.
On TOFU and RWKU, COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting and outperforms continual-unlearning baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of COP for one linear layer with weights W . The input activations of earlier forget sets are summarized by a compact basis Vk−1, which marks the directions where earlier forgetting lives. At request k, the gradient of the unlearning objective on Fk, optionally combined with a retain term onR, is projected away from these directions, so the update cannot change how the layer responds to earlier forget inputs. After training, the dominant new activation directions of Fk are compressed and added to the basis, giving Vk for the next request.

Utility under COP remains stable as requests accumulate, while base objectives fluctuate or degrade.

Table 1: TOFU results on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (forget05). After each task, forget metrics are computed over all requests seen so far, and model utility (MU) is measured on the retain set and general utility datasets. Bold marks the higher MU within each pair of a base objective and its COP-augmented variant. From the third request onward, every COP variant retains higher utility than its base objective. COP prevents the utility collapse of GA and IDK, whose base versions reach lower EM only as part of that collapse, while forget metrics for NPO and SimNPO remain comparable with and without COP. O3 attains the highest utility but forgets weakly, with EM close to that of the original model. ALKN’s forget metrics fall together with its utility, which collapses as requests accumulate.

Bold marks the higher MU within each pair of a base objective and its COP-augmented variant. papers.abstract: In-context imitation learning (ICIL) adapts robot policies through test-time demonstrations, but long multimodal trajectories constrain how many examples fit in context. We ask what a compressed demonstration should preserve. We propose JEDI, which compresses demonstrations into latent slots trained to predict the query episode's next-stage keyframe in a frozen video-JEPA space. Task and process counterfactuals help the slots preserve execution details, while the predictor selects demonstrations from a bank. Post-training with keypoint tokens enables human-hand conditioning on robots. Experiments on LIBERO and real robots show that JEDI supports many-shot context; LIBERO objective controls show improved success and demonstration following over action-only compression. These findings support query-future prediction as a training objective for preserving execution-relevant information in compressed demonstrations.
authors: Jiazhao Liang, Zhewen He, Shuaihang Yuan, Hao Huang, Yi Fang
bullets: Addresses limited context length when adapting robot policies from long multimodal demonstrations.
Trains latent slots to predict the query episode’s next-stage keyframe in a frozen video-JEPA representation.
Uses task and process counterfactuals to retain task identity and execution information, then selects demonstrations from a bank.
Keypoint-token post-training supports conditioning on human-hand demonstrations for robot control.
Experiments on LIBERO and real robots show many-shot support and improved success and demonstration following over action-only compression in LIBERO controls.

papers.abstract: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.
authors: Jianghan Zhu, Cong Zhang, Ni Zhang, Yifan Yang, Yew Soon Ong, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Targets a limitation of LLM-based automatic operator design: fixed discovery and orchestration processes cannot adapt to changing Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions.
Maintains a persistent harness state and revises modules for experience retrieval, operator improvement, parent selection, and search-step orchestration.
Uses downstream solution quality and runtime as feedback, with discounted UCB scheduling to prioritize promising modules.
A persistent memory filesystem retains candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across successive harness states.
Evaluations on eight MOCO tasks and two evolutionary backbones show strong performance against evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based baselines, plus transfer to related tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving LLM-based optimization harness with persistent memory, relevant to adaptation and LLM agent memory.
papers.title: HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization
papers.tldr: HEMO makes the operator-discovery process itself self-evolving, improving multi-objective combinatorial optimization search through persistent memory and adaptive module updates.

papers.abstract: Continual learning methods for large language models increasingly decide what to learn by surprise, keeping the inputs the model finds least predictable. This rule is unsafe when the stream contains lies. A planted falsehood about something the model knows has low probability under the model's belief, so it is highly surprising by construction, and a surprise-driven learner absorbs nearly every such lie, at a rate similar to random selection with the same budget. We study the problem with LoRA-adapted students (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B) that learn from a stream of true and false claims about invented people and real CounterFact facts. We report four findings. (1) A verifier key, a judge that must approve each claim, removes lies to the extent that its verifier is accurate; real LLM judges are cautious and reject unsourced truths and even source-backed updates. (2) Calibrated regression tests on unrelated knowledge slow learning down without filtering out lies. (3) The original model's own prior flags claims that contradict what it knows, without a judge. It separates lies about known facts from true new facts (AUC 0.78-0.83 across three models) but not from legitimate updates of the same kind of fact (AUC 0.53). It saves 43% of judge calls, but an attacker with access to the model can choose lies that pass it. (4) If trusted sources exist that an attacker cannot plant, routing contradicted claims to evidence recovers legitimate updates and the combined system has the lowest poison rate among learned claims; when an attacker plants matching sources for 30% of the lies, the system ends up worse than the judge alone. The acceptance signals answer different questions, and none of them decides on its own whether a claim is true.
bullets: Surprising false claims about known facts are readily learned, at rates similar to random selection under the same budget.
Verifier approval filters lies according to verifier accuracy, but LLM judges may reject both unsourced truths and source-backed updates.
The model’s prior detects contradictions to known facts (AUC 0.78–0.83) and reduces judge calls by 43%, but misses legitimate same-type updates and can be evaded by attackers.
Routing contradictions to trusted, unplantable sources yields the lowest poison rate; planted matching sources can make the combined system worse than judge-only filtering.
No acceptance signal alone determines whether a claim is true.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots commonly pair a global planner with a local model predictive controller (MPC), but nonconvex obstacle avoidance and a limited horizon can make the robot freeze in complex layouts. Deciding whether to replan, wait, or call for help is a supervisory decision. Recent work queries a large language model (LLM) supervisor on every anomaly, which is slow and costly. We instead distill the LLM online into a decision tree. After each training episode, counterfactual replay labels recoveries as needed, unnecessary, or harmful. These labels retire unhelpful rules. In simulation, on 20 unseen layouts where the MPC alone freezes, the tree handles at least 18 correctly across all seeds, either by reaching the goal or by calling for help when no feasible path exists. The tree matches both an always-query LLM supervisor and expert-designed rules, while issuing no LLM queries at test time. Handwritten rules cannot anticipate the long tail of situations a physical robot will encounter. Online distillation is a promising remedy: the tree handles familiar cases, and the LLM is consulted only for new ones, whose validated recoveries become new rules. Language models can thus also serve as designers of supervisors rather than only as runtime supervisors.
bullets: Targets MPC failures where limited horizons and nonconvex obstacles cause autonomous robots to freeze.

papers.abstract: Molecular discovery requires navigating vast combinatorial search spaces while balancing competing biological objectives. AI agents can automate expert-defined molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MoLRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide subsequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workflows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MoLRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MoLRSI developed a screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design, MoLRSI developed workflows that jointly consider target binding and specificity, producing eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets while Claude Science completely failed. These findings demonstrate how experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives while improving the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.

papers.abstract: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently fail to recognize culture-specific concepts, especially from underrepresented regions. Effectively injecting this long-tail knowledge into existing models remains a challenge. In this work, we investigate knowledge editing as a targeted alternative by introducing CulturalBind, a benchmark comprising 3.2K images of 1K concepts from 6 domains, designed to evaluate culture-aware cross-modal knowledge as well as concept-level knowledge editing in VLMs. Pre-edit evaluation reveals that textual and visual knowledge is decoupled: models often demonstrate text-based knowledge of cultural concepts but fail to identify them from images. We then evaluate editing methods in single and sequential scenarios. Although current methods successfully correct individual visual recognition errors, they exhibit low cross-modal portability, failing to integrate edits into the model's broader parametric knowledge. Furthermore, performance degrades rapidly under sequential editing, highlighting the need for comprehensive adaptation approaches that better consolidate multimodal knowledge over time.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies. Our code is available at https://github.com/jins7/LatentWeave.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.

Experiments across five benchmarks and six model families report up to 32.33% higher task performance than existing methods.

papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study \textit{conditional interaction}, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.
authors: Qi Wang, Yun Qu, Lizhou Cai, Heming Zou, Haoang Chi, Yiqin Lv, Xiang Li, Haiyan Feng, Mengyu Ge, Yize Geng, Yuhang Jiang, Yixiu Mao, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Introduces conditional interaction: predict utility, gate candidates, execute selected actions, and update the predictor.
Applies the framework to training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decisions, and agentic tool use.
Under ideal screening, execution compute can decrease roughly with the inverse density of utility-relevant interactions.
Prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift limit compute savings.
Proposes utility-relevant interaction density as a scaling-efficiency measure beyond total compute.

figures.caption: Figure 7 The generative model, and where System 1 cuts in. The cost is paid in full on generating the sequence 𝑦, while the information lies in the verdict 𝑜 = V(𝑦), often a single bit. System 1 forecasts the belief change that verdict will cause before 𝑦 exists, and the gate generates only if the forecast clears 𝜅𝑡 ; suppressed candidates cost only 𝑐pred. Realized verdicts refit System 1. With information gain as the utility the forecast is the expected Bayesian surprise; for any other declared utility the pipeline forecasts that utility instead.

Figure 1 An Illustrative Roadmap to AGI and its Beyond. As AI development progresses, broad capability resembles a summit that systems approach but may hit diminishing returns due to constraints in data, compute, and parameters. In Era 1 (2012–2020) progress came mainly from scaling model capacity, and in Era 2 (2020–2025) from scaling data and computation. For Era 3 (2026+), this work emphasizes a next-scaling lens: co-designing a cost-effective System-1 that prioritizes interactions by expected utility and a resource-intensive System-2 for complicated tasks. This emphasis becomes increasingly consequential for foundation models and embodied agents as they depend on generation, computation, tool use, and environmental interaction, and thus on the cost of each.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents now do long, multi-step and multi-session software work with little supervision. When a developer comes back to that work, the useful question is not what the model said but what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished. We study this in three parts. First, we verify Agenttrail, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, against its source at commit e4ba2da: nine documented constants and mechanisms hold at file-and-line level, two event pipelines are never unified, and its Map service has an unauthenticated local mutation surface. Second, we run a prototype of our system on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes). With a blind-audited classifier (precision 83.3% and 96.7%) we estimate that 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete after editing had no proof in between. A 10-minute timing heuristic for session hand-offs recovers 6 of the 24 session pairs that content lineage links. 42% of sessions run longer than 24 hours, 48.1% of transcript bytes lie past a 2 MiB replay bound, and 1,326 records in 16 sessions contain credential-like strings. Third, we propose Soei (Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent): an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer that keeps a claim of completion apart from proof. On the same corpus the ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s, detects tampering and replays deterministically. We position the work against concurrent 2026 proposals and define autonomy levels with evidence gates and harness metrics baselined on our data.

On the study corpus, the ledger uses 20% of raw storage, excludes content and credentials, verifies about 126k events/s, and deterministically detects tampering and replays.
Defines autonomy levels, evidence gates, and harness metrics grounded in the observed session data.

papers.abstract: Label-free test-time reinforcement learning adapts vision--language models using rewards derived from their own predictions. However, misinterpreted visual evidence and sensitivity to textual formulation can produce a consistent but incorrect consensus that majority voting reinforces. Cross-view aggregation can expose such errors, but image and text transformations may themselves degrade task-relevant evidence to different extents. We introduce \method, a reliability-aware harmonic consensus framework for multimodal test-time reinforcement learning. \method constructs a $2\times2$ grid combining original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing modes, selects pseudo-labels through weighted harmonic aggregation, and adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a heuristic reliability signal. We formulate consensus as a weighted $\chi^2$-barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized weighted harmonic aggregate, without requiring correct-answer invariance. An exact support--dispersion decomposition characterizes when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings, while a sensitivity analysis establishes how modality reweighting changes pairwise ranking margins, informing interpretation of the heuristic updates. Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, \method outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark--model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances under matched estimation and optimization rollout counts. These results demonstrate improved target-task adaptation and transfer to unseen instances without further updates.
authors: Haotian Lyu, Haoyu Wang, Ru Wang, Feng Ji, Ziwen Li, Jiaxian Guo, Mingming Gong
bullets: Addresses self-reinforcing errors caused by consistent but incorrect prediction consensus and unreliable image/text transformations.
Uses a 2×2 grid of original/perturbed images and direct-solving/reframing prompts.
Selects pseudo-labels with weighted harmonic aggregation and adapts modality weights using smoothed confidence shifts.
Provides a χ²-barycenter formulation, support–dispersion analysis, and ranking-sensitivity analysis for the aggregation method.
Outperforms TTRV in 16/18 adaptation and 17/18 held-out benchmark–model settings across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL scales.

For each instance, rollout rewards are pooled and jointly normalized to compute GRPO advantages.

Curves are smoothed using a time-weighted exponential moving average for visualization. Ground-truth answers are used only for post-hoc evaluation and are unavailable during adaptation. TIMBRE maintains higher pseudo-label accuracy over most later adaptation steps, indicating improved reliability of the generated training signal.

papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems provide critical computation services in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet (MII), and their resilience depends on timely diagnosis of hazards across the data, AI pipeline, and cyber-physical layers. During operation, new hazard types keep emerging with only a few samples each, hazards co-occur, and the diagnosis model runs on memory-constrained computation nodes. Replay-based class-incremental learning (CIL) can learn new hazard classes while revisiting a small memory of past samples, but existing methods assume single-label, balanced streams, store high-dimensional raw samples, and select them independently of the classifier. We propose Class-aware Latent Attention Replay (CLAR), which combines a dual buffer that stores mostly compact latent representations with a few raw samples, an Attention Leverage Score (ALS) that upper-bounds the classifier logit and guides class-balanced reservoir sampling, and an exponential-moving-average teacher that slows latent-space drift. For an idealized buffer model, we prove that the buffer is class-balanced and follows an ALS-weighted class distribution, and that below a critical per-class capacity, ALS-guided replay has a lower replay-gradient error than class-balanced uniform replay. In the case study, On hazard diagnosis data from an MII testbed, CLAR achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 score among the evaluated replay methods with the same buffer size
authors: Avranshu Mahanty, Ran Jin, Yingyan Zeng
bullets: Targets emerging, co-occurring hazards with few samples in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet.
Uses a dual replay buffer containing mostly compact latent features and a small number of raw samples.
Introduces Attention Leverage Scores to guide class-balanced reservoir sampling based on classifier importance.
Uses an exponential-moving-average teacher to reduce latent-space drift during incremental learning.
Theory supports balanced, ALS-weighted replay; an MII testbed study reports the highest mean average weighted F1 among evaluated methods at equal buffer size.

papers.abstract: Discounted regret measures the performance of an online learner by assigning exponentially decaying weights to past losses, reflecting the greater importance of recent losses in non-stationary online learning. While previous work obtains uniform discounted regret bounds over a continuous range of discount factors using a specialized meta-algorithm, its results are limited to convex functions. In this paper, we demonstrate that strongly adaptive regret bounds can directly imply uniform discounted regret guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and exp-concave loss functions. Our key observation is that discounted regret against a fixed comparator admits an exact decomposition into a convex combination of interval regrets. For convex functions, this reduction yields an $O(\sqrt{\log T/(1-\lambda)})$ discounted regret bound for all discount factors $\lambda\in(0,1)$, matching the previous rate over a broader range of discount factors. For strongly convex and exp-concave functions, we provide regret bounds of $O\left(\log T\left(1+\log\frac{1}{1-\lambda}\right)\right)$.
authors: Sifan Yang, Wenhao Yang, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Discounted regret emphasizes recent losses through exponentially decaying weights, making it useful for non-stationary online learning.
The paper shows that discounted regret against a fixed comparator exactly decomposes into a convex combination of interval regrets.
This reduction extends uniform discounted-regret guarantees beyond convex losses to strongly convex and exp-concave losses.
For convex losses, the bound is O(√(log T/(1−λ))) for every λ∈(0,1), while strongly convex and exp-concave losses achieve O(log T(1+log(1/(1−λ)))).

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50\% success on unseen controller modes and 52\% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit \href{https://controller-transfer.github.io}{https://controller-transfer.github.io}.
authors: Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, Dorsa Sadigh
bullets: Addresses conflicting action meanings across robot embodiments, controller types, gains, and compliance settings.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

papers.abstract: Experience can help embodied agents turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring it across tasks remains challenging: previously effective strategies may be inapplicable to the current state or fail to produce their intended outcomes. We present EmbodiExp, a framework for constructing transferable experiences and composing them online during embodied task execution. Our key observation is that tasks often share subgoals whose completion can be assessed independently of overall task success. We therefore introduce an outcome-grounded subgoal experience that specifies a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome. During execution, applicable experiences guide action generation, while verified outcomes can establish the conditions required by subsequent experiences, enabling online composition. Subgoal-level outcome attribution further enables failure utilization: failed trajectories can still contribute verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid. Experiments on multiple embodied benchmarks under a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks demonstrate the effectiveness of EmbodiExp.
authors: Zhifeng Gu, Ying Chen, Rui Jiang, Lei Yi, Bing Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring strategies across tasks when applicability and outcomes vary by state.

Uses subgoal-level outcome attribution to extract local successes and avoidable actions from failed trajectories.
Demonstrates effectiveness across multiple embodied benchmarks with frozen experience banks under a fold-based protocol.

papers.abstract: The central bottleneck in visual generation and editing has migrated from achieving pixel-level fidelity to satisfying densely constrained user specifications through increasingly agentic workflows. Prevailing agentic generation pipelines remain shallow generate-verify-rewrite loops treating VLM judgments as coarse visual feedback, either discarding repair experience or admitting ungated updates that poison skill library. With memorize and govern periods left open, they degrade into ungoverned iterators of repeated trial-and-error rather than continual self-evolving harness. Towards this issue, we present \textbf{VEvo-Harness}, the first causally-guarded continual self-evolving harness system for agentic visual generation. VEvo-Harness introduces four coupled innovations: (1) \textit{a visual traceback} that densifies sparse judgments into root-cause attributions with a hierarchical verification tree; (2) \textit{a visual continual governance} that admits only causally valid skill patches through counterfactual dual-arm image generation replay; (3) \textit{a lifecycle-managed harness state} that hierarchically distills root-cause-anchored episodes across working, experience, and pattern tiers into a persistent skill library of routable and causally verified capabilities; (4) \textit{a heterogeneous sandbox policy} that orchestrates a diverse action space of repair primitives, dynamically routing cost-aware interventions based on root causes to select the most effective strategy. VEvo-Harness surpasses state-of-the-art agentic methods and rivals proprietary generators (\textit{e.g.}, GPT-Image, Nano-Pro) while maintaining the continual harness evolution and generalization.

bullets: Targets the gap between pixel fidelity and satisfying densely constrained visual specifications.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.
authors: Pratik Jawahar, Riccardo Maggioni, Jonas Petersen, Matteo Cozzi, Gian-Alessandro Lombardi, Marek Gajewski, Camilla Mazzoleni, Federico Martelli
bullets: Identifies two access failures: escape failures and reach failures.
Uses a Lorentz squeeze for bounded, re-absorbable energy injection in escape failures.
Uses a gated canonical translation that preserves phase volume exactly for reach failures.
Analytic tests show squeeze cost grows quadratically beyond the access boundary, while matched-channel translation has zero measured potential cost.
Demonstrates compute rationing and non-local routing limits on learned physics-structured memory; benchmark superiority is not the focus.

papers.abstract: Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover. Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it. In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves during data collection to collect more useful data. We propose Data Inoculation (DI), a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make. These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human's continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, "inoculating" the dataset against the learner's future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.
authors: Qiyang Li, Zhiyuan Zhou, Charles Xu, Sergey Levine
bullets: Addresses poor state coverage and compounding errors in demonstration-based robot learning.
Uses shared control: a human teleoperates while an online-trained residual policy perturbs commands toward likely future mistakes.
Continuous human corrections provide recovery demonstrations while perturbations expand the collected state distribution.
Across three real-world tasks, policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL consistently improved or matched performance using DI-collected data.

papers.abstract: We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions, defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done rather than what should have been done, and where data is sparse, a model's predictions may be too uncertain to act on. We provide a framework for addressing this problem using a case study in deceased-donor kidney allocation. Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. One can use AI to flag kidneys at risk of delayed or failed placement for out-of-sequence (OOS) allocation, but this comes at the cost of bypassing candidates higher on the waitlist. Thus, OOS allocation should only be used when the organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence. Using Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network match-run data from 2016-2019 and 2023-2025 (excluding COVID-19-disrupted years), we build the Arbitrator framework, which combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. Our Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data, and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. We show that the Arbitrator correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as OOS candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement and potentially transplanted. We then exploit the interpretability of the Arbitrator to create an agentic audit comparing the learned rules to published clinical literature in order to flag decision-making patterns that are contentious.
authors: Madeleine Pollack, Thomas Daillak, Mehmet Toner, Korkut Uygun, Heidi Yeh, Swati Gupta
bullets: Historical allocation decisions reflect what happened, not necessarily what should have happened, and sparse data can make predictions unreliable.
The framework acts only when model uncertainty cannot change the preferred action; otherwise, it defers to humans or more complex models.
It resolves 93.5% of placement decisions and defers 6.5%.
It identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as candidates for out-of-sequence allocation, with up to 43.9% of discarded kidneys potentially eligible for expedited placement.
An interpretable audit compares learned rules with clinical literature to flag contentious decision patterns.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an 'Arbitrator' framework for decision-making under uncertainty, deferring to humans when predictions are too uncertain. This aligns with test-time learning strategies for handling uncertainty in decision-making.
papers.title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation
papers.tldr: The Arbitrator framework uses interpretable, uncertainty-aware AI to recommend, defer, or audit deceased-donor kidney allocation decisions, potentially reducing discard while limiting unjustified waitlist bypasses.

papers.abstract: Agents deployed at scale repeatedly encounter related problems, and it is natural to let them learn from each other's experience rather than starting over each time. Unfortunately, there is no single way to retain that experience that works well across settings, and no way to know in advance which future problems a given experience will help with. A global history preserves every detail but becomes expensive and mixes together experience that may not belong together; compressing that history into one fixed representation limits the cost but can throw away valuable details. We introduce Routed Continual Learning (Routed CL), an architecture that decides how to partition and retain experience. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, each of which maintains state using one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM-based router either reuses an existing cluster or creates a new one, basing its decision on the problem statement, memory system descriptions, and cluster summaries. We also introduce Context Memory Adapter, which mediates between the memory system and the agentic loop. We evaluate the architecture on a heterogeneous stream that interleaves 301 instances from the six CL-Bench tasks with 97 banking instances from $\tau^3$-Bench. Across four language models and five matched rollouts, Routed Continual Learning raises normalized reward over a single global in-context learning (ICL) history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward, achieves higher mean normalized reward than ICL-only clustering, and reduces estimated API cost by 65-72% relative to Global ICL. These results support approaching continual learning as a routing problem that chooses both a learning mechanism and a state cluster rather than committing to one representation globally.
authors: Michael Philip, Mahesh Balakrishnan, David Geraghty, David Mao, Vidhya Venkat, Ilya Mironov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining shared experience across varied future problems without costly global histories or overly lossy compression.
Clusters past trajectories and uses an LLM router to reuse or create clusters based on the problem, memory-system descriptions, and cluster summaries.
Introduces Context Memory Adapter to connect selected memory systems with the agentic loop.
Evaluated across 398 instances from CL-Bench and τ³-Bench, four language models, and five matched rollouts.
Reported 15–30% gains in normalized reward over global ICL history, higher reward than ICL-only clustering, and 65–72% lower estimated API cost than Global ICL.

papers.abstract: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.
authors: Haotian Zhai, Tianming Sha, Junnan Li
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of one-shot, serial LLM plans for long-horizon interactive tasks.
Builds a hierarchical tree of subgoals and actions, deciding at each step whether to decompose further or issue a grounded low-level action.
Uses symbolic state updates and lightweight memory to inform subsequent planning decisions.
Performs hierarchical backtracking and replanning when an action stalls, regenerating plans from the latest state.
Outperforms prior LLM-based planners in zero-shot evaluation on ALFRED.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of our hierarchical planning framework for embodied instruction following. Given a task instruction and the current visual state, our method recursively decides whether to decompose the current goal into finer-grained subgoals or execute it directly. This process incrementally builds an explicit hierarchical goal tree, shown in the upper-right panel, where higher-level goals are progressively refined into executable actions. In contrast, we compare against two representative paradigms: (1) a fully supervised end-to-end EIF model trained on the full dataset, and (2) an LLM-based method using retrieved few-shot examples. While these baselines may produce incorrect action sequences, our method maintains a structured tree-based plan and performs step-by-step decomposition conditioned on the current state and memory, enabling more accurate long-horizon reasoning and execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of our state-aware decision prompt. The prompt summarizes the role and mission, decision options, input information, available atomic actions, global rules, output format, and a small set of decision-guiding examples. Given the current subgoal together with the current state and memory, the LLM predicts whether to decompose the goal into subtasks or execute it directly.

Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison with and without memory. Without memory, the model predicts an incorrect subgoal after picking up the cleaned lettuce, whereas AtomTree correctly predicts the next subgoal as navigating to the fridge.

Fig. 1: Error analysis on the Valid Seen split of the ALFRED benchmark with respect to ground-truth PDDL plan length, showing that for FLARE, a state-of-the-art few-shot method, incorrect-plan errors dominate overall and become the primary failure mode for long-horizon tasks (PDDL length > 7).
Fig. 5: Comparison between a few-shot baseline and AtomTree on a multi-instance task.

TABLE I: Quantitative comparison on ALFRED [1]. We report SR and GC on four splits: Valid Seen, Valid Unseen, Test Seen, and Test Unseen. We annotate each method by its evaluation setting, publication venue, and whether it is explicitly state- and history-aware. For methods that do not report results on certain splits or metrics, we mark them as “N/A”. Results marked with an asterisk (*) are produced by [13].

TABLE II: Ablation of ATOMTREE on ALFRED validation splits. “Hier.” enables hierarchical planning with Decompose and a subgoal tree. “Memory” adds the state&history memory mt = (St, Ht). “Replan” enables hierarchical backtracking replanning. We report SR on Valid Seen and Valid Unseen.
