papers.selection_reason: Spatial memory for legged robot exploration; fits robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Remember Where You Walk: Learning Spatial Memory for End-to-End Legged Robot Exploration
papers.tldr: LSMM gives legged-robot RL agents spatially grounded memory, enabling them to retain and reconstruct maze layouts over long exploration horizons.

papers.abstract: In replay-free continual learning, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) uses Fisher information matrix (FIM) to protect acquired knowledge by penalizing changes to historically important parameters. However, a local importance estimate at the retained solution does not in general characterize sensitivity after finite parameter displacement. This motivates controlling Fisher sensitivity over a neighborhood of potential future updates. We propose Fisher-Shaped EWC (FS-EWC), which extends the role of FIM from parameter protection to solution formation for future retention. During task learning, FS-EWC minimizes the worst-case empirical FIM trace within a prescribed neighborhood, explicitly favoring solutions that are less sensitive to bounded future displacement. At task completion, trajectory-based model merging constructs the retained solution from multiple optimization states rather than a single terminal iterate, after which FIM is estimated for subsequent consolidation. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that FS-EWC improves performance over EWC, while controlled studies indicate a more favorable stability--plasticity balance and greater tolerance to parameter drift. These results suggest that effective knowledge retention requires both forming solutions with future retention in mind and protecting acquired knowledge.
authors: Liying Wang, Simone Magistri, Joost van de Weijer
bullets: EWC’s local Fisher estimate may not reflect sensitivity after finite parameter changes.
FS-EWC minimizes worst-case empirical Fisher trace within a prescribed update neighborhood during task learning.
Trajectory-based model merging forms the retained solution from multiple optimization states before later consolidation.
Experiments report improved performance over EWC, with better stability–plasticity balance and tolerance to parameter drift.
papers.selection_reason: Enhances EWC for replay-free continual learning by shaping Fisher sensitivity, directly relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: Beyond Parameter Protection: Fisher-Shaped EWC for Replay-Free Continual Learning
papers.tldr: FS-EWC improves replay-free continual learning by shaping solutions to remain stable under future parameter updates, not merely protecting their current important parameters.

papers.abstract: Equilibrium Propagation (EqProp) offers a biologically grounded and hardware-aligned alternative to backpropagation for training Hopfield Networks. However, its behavior in continual learning settings remains largely unexplored. This work confronts catastrophic forgetting in EqProp-trained Hopfield Networks from the inside out, eliminating the need for external data buffers or architectural overhead that standard Experience Replay \textbf{(ER)} and Generative Replay \textbf{(Gen-Replay)} inevitably require. We introduce an Energy-Based Generative Replay strategy \textbf{(EB-Gen)} which exploits the intrinsic generative dynamics of Hopfield Networks, allowing a single model to act as both classifier and replay samples generator. Samples capturing past task knowledge are generated by relaxing a frozen copy of the network, enabling rehearsal solely through internally generated pseudo-data. We evaluate the proposed method in the Class-Incremental setting, using the split versions of the MNIST and CIFAR10 benchmarks and compare it with FineTune, Experience Replay, Generative Replay, Sleep-Like Replay Consolidation (SRC) and Joint training. Our results show that EB-Gen significantly improves stability while preserving plasticity, achieving a 75\% and 64\% average accuracy on Split MNIST and Split CIFAR10 respectively. These findings show that Equilibrium Propagation can be adapted to alleviate catastrophic forgetting without forgoing the traits which made it compelling in the first place.
authors: Victor Cook (LIRMM | ADAC), Gilles Sassatelli (LIRMM | ADAC), Thierry Gil (LIRMM), Mohamed Watfa (LIRMM | ADAC), Marina Reyboz (CEA-LETI)
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting in Equilibrium Propagation–trained Hopfield Networks under class-incremental learning.
Generates pseudo-samples by relaxing a frozen copy of the network, letting one model serve as both classifier and replay generator.
Evaluated on Split MNIST and Split CIFAR10 against FineTune, Experience Replay, Generative Replay, SRC, and Joint training.
Reports average accuracies of 75% on Split MNIST and 64% on Split CIFAR10, with improved stability while retaining plasticity.
Scope is limited to the evaluated class-incremental benchmarks and compared methods.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes generative replay for continual learning in Hopfield networks, directly addressing catastrophic forgetting.
papers.title: Generative Replay for Equilibrium Propagation: Toward Edge-Friendly Continual Learning in Hopfield Networks
papers.tldr: EB-Gen uses Hopfield networks’ own energy-based dynamics to generate replay data, reducing catastrophic forgetting in EqProp-based continual learning without external buffers or extra architectures.

papers.abstract: Every neural-network training run produces not only a model, but also evidence about how models learn. Can these accumulated experiments enable us to predict and compare new training runs before executing them? We study meta-models: models that predict the learning behavior of other models. From this perspective, final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection are different queries to the same training response function. We take a first, humble empirical step toward this goal: treating real language-model training records as native numeric data, we find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Whereas recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, TabPFN requires seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. We argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. Going one step further, augmenting TabPFN with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks. Finally, we pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run, whose ground truth is revealed point by point as training progresses, putting meta-model predictions to the test against training outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting.
bullets: Unifies final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection as queries to one training-response function.
Treats language-model training records as native numeric data rather than text.
TabPFN matched or outperformed a fine-tuned LLM meta-model across multiple evaluated settings without task-specific weight updates.
TabPFN required seconds for fitting and prediction, compared with tens to hundreds of GPU-hours for fine-tuning LLM meta-models.
Adding Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks improved accuracy on selected prediction tasks; a preregistered forecast tests predictions against an ongoing 535B-parameter training run.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Meta Models' to predict learning behavior of other models, comparing TabPFN against LLM meta-models. This advances the field of meta-learning and model selection, relevant to Adaptation and Memory and LLMs.
papers.title: Meta Models: Models that Model Learning
papers.tldr: Meta-models use past training records to predict future model-learning behavior, with tabular learners offering an efficient alternative to LLM-based approaches.

papers.abstract: Field applications in chemical sensing, from portable safety monitors to mobile robots, require models that are lightweight, fast to respond, and can be recalibrated from limited labelled data. Current gas classification pipelines assume controlled sampling cycles and offline feature extraction, and rely on computationally expensive models. With a few thousand neurons and sub-milliwatt power consumption, insects reliably classify odours in open environments. Inspired by the insect olfactory system, we present a neural network architecture that classifies raw sensor array readings using a sparse, high-dimensional binary representation. We evaluate it on random sequences of single gases and binary mixtures, introducing new samples dynamically and classifying gas identity from the transient sensor response. In this setting, the architecture out-performs a linear \gls{svm} on gas mixtures and matches an optimised non-linear \gls{svm}, while maintaining online class-level frequency estimates that distinguish familiar from novel stimuli. It relies exclusively on binary weights and Hebbian-based local learning, remaining computationally lightweight and well suited to ultra-low-power neuromorphic processors. We demonstrated the network on-chip with a hazardous gas detection experiment running on the mixed-signal neuromorphic chip TEXEL. The on-chip classifier yielded an accuracy of 74.6\% while running at 482 $\unit{\nano\joule}$ per inference and 27 \unit{\micro\watt} of static-power.
authors: Ton Juny Pina, Hugh Greatorex, Elisabetta Chicca
bullets: Targets fast, recalibratable gas classification for portable and robotic edge applications using limited labelled data.
Processes raw sensor-array transients with a sparse, high-dimensional binary representation and supports dynamically introduced samples.
Uses binary weights and local Hebbian learning, avoiding offline feature extraction and computationally expensive models.
Outperforms a linear SVM on gas mixtures and matches an optimized nonlinear SVM, while estimating familiar versus novel stimuli.
Demonstrated on the TEXEL neuromorphic chip for hazardous-gas detection at 74.6% accuracy, 482 nJ per inference, and 27 µW static power.
papers.selection_reason: Online gas classification with Hebbian local learning and dynamic sample introduction fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Online gas classification at the edge
papers.tldr: An insect-inspired, binary-weight neural network enables lightweight, online gas classification from raw transient sensor signals on ultra-low-power neuromorphic hardware.

papers.abstract: Continual adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to evolving task distributions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting remains an open problem. Existing strategies often struggle to scale or lack a robust mechanism for zero-shot task-to-expert assignment. We introduce CaLLM, a framework that resolves these tensions by combining metric-based meta-learning with modular parameter isolation via lightweight adapters. First, CaLLM projects each input batch into a task-agnostic embedding space to find its nearest prototype. It then routes the batch to the specific adapter specialized for that data distribution. This formulation provides (i)~controllable cross-task interference by design, (ii)~constant computational complexity regardless of task count, (iii)~seamless integration of novel distributions through prototype expansion, and (iv)~regime agnosticism as the local routing decision enables a unified approach to both online and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that this routing mechanism discovers semantically coherent task groupings while facilitating constructive interference between similar tasks, and keeping overhead at a minimum. Across diverse and fine-grained continual learning benchmarks, CaLLM consistently outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods, establishing prototype-based modular routing as a principled and scalable approach to lifelong adaptation of LLMs.
authors: Bilge Celik, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Addresses continual adaptation under evolving task distributions and catastrophic forgetting.
Embeds each input batch, matches it to the nearest prototype, and selects the corresponding adapter.
Uses modular parameter isolation to control cross-task interference while supporting constructive transfer between similar tasks.
Maintains constant routing complexity as tasks grow and incorporates new distributions by expanding prototypes.
Outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods across diverse continual-learning benchmarks with low overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CaLLM, a framework for continual adaptation of LLMs using non-parametric adapter routing. This directly tackles catastrophic forgetting and task interference, fitting Continual and Online Learning and LLM adaptation.
papers.title: CaLLM: Continual Adaptation of LLMs via Non-Parametric Adapter Routing
papers.tldr: CaLLM continually adapts LLMs by routing inputs to specialized lightweight adapters using nearest task prototypes, reducing forgetting with scalable, zero-shot assignment.

papers.abstract: Streaming multimodal assistants must make response decisions while events are still unfolding. They need to recognize when the available evidence warrants a response, produce an appropriate continuation, and remain silent otherwise. Supervised fine-tuning learns from recorded assistant turns, but does not directly train on the response prefixes produced by the evolving policy itself. We introduce Live-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method that uses privileged hints available only during training to supervise the policy on its own outputs. The policy first generates a continuation from the streaming context alone. The same model then re-evaluates that continuation with a hint describing the relevant evidence, and the resulting distributions guide the unhinted policy. On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, Live-OPSD attains an average score of 59.64 on LiveProBench, 5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline, and stays competitive on OVO-Bench (65.84). These results indicate that guiding the policy on its own outputs with privileged hints improves both when and how a streaming assistant responds.
authors: Kaixuan Du, Xin Wan, Dai Guan, Ming Chen, Xiaoxi Jiang, Guanjun Jiang
bullets: Streaming assistants must decide whether to respond, what to say, or remain silent as events unfold.
The method addresses a gap in supervised fine-tuning, which does not train on prefixes generated by the evolving policy.
It generates a continuation from streaming context, then re-evaluates it with training-only privileged evidence hints.
On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, it scores 59.64 on LiveProBench—5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline—and remains competitive on OVO-Bench at 65.84.
The approach improves both response timing and content, within the evaluated streaming-assistant benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Live-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method for streaming multimodal video models. This directly addresses the need for proactive response decisions in streaming contexts and utilizes privileged hints to guide policy outputs, fitting both Multimodal Foundation Models and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Live-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Proactive Streaming Large Video Models
papers.tldr: Live-OPSD improves proactive streaming video assistants by self-distilling hint-guided judgments onto their own unhinted outputs.

papers.abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.
authors: XinYu Piao, Myunghoon Ryu, Joongheon Kim, Jong-Kook Kim
bullets: Addresses dialogue recall when no external storage or future question knowledge is available.
Generates varied questions for each dialogue turn and writes them with the turn content into model parameters.
Uses matching later user questions to retrieve and answer from parameter-stored content.
Evaluated on five language models, recalling most stored dialogue turns.
Scope: focused on parameter-only recall rather than external-memory systems.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-form in-parameter memorization for dialogue recall, combining test-time parameter updates with LLM memory.
papers.title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
papers.tldr: SKIM stores dialogue turns directly in frozen model parameters using self-generated question keys, enabling later recall without external memory.

papers.abstract: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
authors: Yingkai Yang, Chaoqi Chen, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets open-set test-time adaptation under simultaneous covariate and semantic shifts.
Decomposes normalized features into principal and tail coordinates using the source linear head as an anchor.
Uses soft-routed weighted ridge regression to estimate and subtract principal-space drift conditioned on tail features.
On ImageNet-C with six csOOD datasets, it achieves 2.2% higher H-score than UniEnt and runs 2.5× faster with 12% of its GPU memory.
As a post-correction plug-in, it raises COME to 68.4% H-score with 2% additional memory overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Open-set test-time adaptation via lightweight feature rectification, directly fitting test-time learning.
papers.title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: TALOR is a lightweight, backward-free plug-in that corrects open-set test-time feature drift using the source classifier’s geometry, improving accuracy while reducing adaptation cost.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
authors: Marc Ziegler, Batu \"Ozen, Sami Mentes, Thomas Waschulzik, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses sensor corruption when the robot policy is frozen or inaccessible.
Separates periodic gait dynamics from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair.
On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis improved success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reached 382/640.
Produced no false triggers across 64 held-out fault-free episodes; a matched boosted-tree surrogate showed no repair benefit.
Separate surrogate fits helped Go1 and ANYmal C, while phase-aware gradients performed better.
papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses sensor failure in robot foundation models by proposing a transparent surrogate for online diagnosis and repair of inputs to a frozen locomotion policy. This falls under robot learning (surrogate modeling) and test-time learning (online adaptation).
papers.title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
papers.tldr: A transparent, phase-aware surrogate can diagnose and repair sensor faults around a frozen robot policy, improving simulated locomotion but with limited validation.

papers.abstract: Knowledge improvement in large language models is shifting from predefined knowledge incorporation pipelines toward evaluation-guided updating. Existing methods use evaluation to localize model-specific knowledge weaknesses and guide targeted post-training. However, identifying what to improve does not necessarily provide sufficient information for deciding how to improve it. The same localized weakness can be compatible with distinct operational knowledge states: the relevant knowledge may be unavailable, available but difficult to access reliably, or accessible but ineffective for downstream use. We call this ambiguity knowledge-state aliasing. When compatible states favor different interventions, greater diagnostic resolution alone is insufficient for intervention selection. Moreover, model updates can change the underlying knowledge state before the observed weakness disappears, such that an intervention appropriate in one round may no longer address the bottleneck in the next. To address these challenges, we propose Recursive Knowledge Improvement (RKI), which formulates knowledge improvement as a sequential, state-aware intervention process. RKI organizes knowledge into graph-structured units that provide a shared basis for diagnostic evaluation and targeted intervention across rounds. At each round, RKI localizes knowledge weaknesses, estimates the model's operational knowledge state from diagnostic evidence and intervention history, selects a corresponding intervention, and re-evaluates the updated model before determining the next intervention. On HotpotEval and SafeInternalEval, RKI outperforms existing knowledge incorporation methods by 18.41 points on average. Further analyses show that knowledge states provide additional guidance for intervention selection beyond weakness localization and can change across model updates even when the observed weakness persists.
authors: Runze Jiang, Yan Wang, Boran Jin, Bingyu Zhu, Longtao Huang
bullets: Weakness localization is ambiguous: the same failure may reflect unavailable knowledge, unreliable access, or ineffective downstream use.
RKI treats knowledge improvement as a sequential, state-aware process rather than a one-shot update.
It represents knowledge as graph-structured units shared by diagnosis and targeted intervention.
Each round diagnoses weaknesses, estimates the operational knowledge state using evidence and intervention history, applies a matching intervention, and re-evaluates the model.
On HotpotEval and SafeInternalEval, RKI outperforms existing knowledge incorporation methods by 18.41 points on average; knowledge states may change even when weaknesses persist.
papers.selection_reason: Sequential state-aware knowledge improvement through repeated evaluation and targeted model updates, relevant to continual adaptation.
papers.title: Weakness Localization Is Not Enough: State-Aware Recursive Knowledge Improvement for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Recursive Knowledge Improvement (RKI) uses model-specific knowledge-state diagnosis and iterative intervention selection to improve LLM knowledge more effectively than weakness localization alone.

papers.abstract: Controlling the personality of a language model usually relies on written profiles or named trait categories, so it can only express what an author writes down or what a taxonomy names. We instead propose Personality Latents (PL), which learn a latent for each person from their own writing, with no personality labels and no authored profile, and inject it into a frozen language model as a soft prefix. Following generative latent optimization, each training person receives a free latent that is optimized through the frozen model itself, while an encoder learns to predict these latents so that a new person needs only one forward pass, with optional refinement at test time. We evaluate on held-out people by having the conditioned model answer neutral and interview questions and reading personality from its answers with scorers trained on real human writing. On the MBTI axes PL reaches an AUC of , ahead of persona embedding and prompt-based baselines under identical settings, and the ranking holds when the answers are scored in three different embedding spaces. A latent learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct also transfers personality to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct through a new adapter alone.
bullets: Learns a separate latent for each person directly from their writing, without predefined traits or personality annotations.
Trains an encoder to predict a person’s latent in one forward pass, with optional test-time refinement.
Evaluates personality expression through answers to neutral and interview questions scored by models trained on human writing.
Outperforms persona-embedding and prompt-based baselines on MBTI-axis AUC under matched settings; the ranking holds across three embedding spaces.
Latents learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct transfer to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using only a new adapter.
papers.selection_reason: Learns per-person latent representations for frozen LLMs with optional test-time refinement, fitting deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Personality Latents: Conditioning Frozen Language Models on Individuals from Their Own Writing
papers.tldr: Personality Latents infer an individual’s writing-based personality without labels or profiles and condition frozen language models via a learned soft prefix.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.
authors: Yue Wu, Yang Zhang, Weinan Gan, Chongming Gao, Xinsen Guo, Xiaoyuan Li, Fuli Feng
bullets: In-Place TTT can lose its benefit on realistic web long-context QA because uniform writes let irrelevant content dilute useful information.
Select-TTT conditions each chunk’s write strength on its relevance to the user query.
Relevance is obtained without supervision or added parameters from the frozen output head’s probability mass on query tokens.
A temperature-scaled softmax converts relevance scores into learning-rate multipliers while preserving context-parallel computation.
The method consistently improves long-context QA across two benchmarks and two model backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Query-conditioned selective fast-weight test-time training for LLMs, directly fitting test-time learning.
papers.title: Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Select-TTT improves in-place test-time training for long-context QA by writing query-relevant chunks more strongly into fast-weight memory.

papers.abstract: Multi-view tracking extends visual coverage beyond a single camera, providing complementary observations when targets are occluded or leave the view. This raises a question: how can observations from different views be matched to the correct identities without offline scene-specific training or camera calibration? Progress toward this goal remains limited because many offline formulations assume such deployment-specific knowledge, while online adaptation can amplify association errors. We study this problem as online multi-view identity maintenance (OMIM): targets are initialized once per view, with no further identity labels provided after each initialization. To this end, we introduce OmniGlimpse, an asymmetric propose-verify framework that separates adaptive association from stable identity consolidation. At the representation level, short-term local and cross-view evidence is mapped into target-specific adaptive spaces to propose associations, whereas long-term identity distributions are maintained for verification in a canonical space defined by a frozen encoder. At the update level, short-term evidence may guide current associations, whereas, after bootstrapping, only verified observations may update persistent memory or drive adaptation. Under a unified target-specified evaluation protocol, OmniGlimpse improves over the best evaluated online baseline for each metric by 9.1 IDF1 and 22.1 CVIDF1 points on M3Track. The corresponding gains on MvMHAT are 20.3 and 26.2 points. Despite using no offline scene-specific training, it outperforms offline-trained references in IDF1 and remains competitive in cross-view association. These results support an approach to online identity maintenance that adapts to changing appearances while consolidating reliable evidence into stable identity anchors.
authors: Rangya Zhang, Jiaping Xiao, Yujing Shang, Yuhang Zhang, Mingsheng Li, Mir Feroskhan
bullets: Addresses cross-view identity matching when targets are occluded or leave individual camera views, with identities initialized only once per view.
Uses an asymmetric propose–verify framework: adaptive target-specific spaces propose associations, while frozen-encoder canonical representations verify them.
Updates persistent identity memory and adaptation only with verified observations, limiting error amplification during online adaptation.
Improves substantially over evaluated online baselines on M3Track and MvMHAT, while remaining competitive with offline-trained references for cross-view association.
Scope: relies on a target-specified evaluation protocol and does not provide post-initialization identity labels.
papers.selection_reason: Online multi-view identity maintenance with adaptive association and persistent identity memory; relevant to adaptation and memory.
papers.title: OmniGlimpse: Asymmetric Identity Memory for Online Multi-View Tracking
papers.tldr: OmniGlimpse enables online multi-view identity maintenance without camera calibration or scene-specific training by separating adaptive association from stable identity verification.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.
authors: Jingpu Yang, Tianhao Li, Fengxian Ji, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting incoming examples for supervision and historical examples for replay in continual learning.
Uses compatibility checks and a learned memory gate to choose among general replay, reinforcing compatible examples, or skipping mastered duplicates.
Optimizes an online policy using acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback with bounded replay per arrival.
On WikiBigEdit, reaches 93.66% Original Match after 3K facts and surpasses Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts.
Achieves the highest final scores on four TRACE tasks while maintaining or improving earlier-task performance across diverse domains.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive memory replay for continual learning in LLMs, directly matching the continual/online adaptation subtopic.
papers.title: CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: CAMR adaptively decides what to supervise and replay, improving continual knowledge retention and acquisition under a fixed replay budget.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation updates a deployed model on an unlabeled test stream. In practice this stream often arrives one sample at a time, with the classes in no particular order. A single sample then provides limited information for estimating distribution-level statistics, and selecting samples by confidence can admit predictions that are wrong yet confident. A corruption, however, shifts the features while leaving the decision regions of the frozen classifier unchanged. We therefore propose Origin-recentered Test-Time Adaptation (OriTTA), which constructs fixed geometric targets from the source model and adapts selected features toward them. Seen from the origin of the feature space, the classes lean toward a common direction. We choose a new origin to bring class scores closer together while keeping it near the mean feature of one synthetic prototype per class. From this origin, prototype directions spread more evenly, and each class obtains an axis and an ideal point before any test data arrives. During adaptation, OriTTA aligns selected features with their predicted class axis and penalizes excessive radius, keeps one input per predicted class in memory to limit feature changes for classes absent from the stream, and resets the model when re-classifying this memory reveals collapse. Without tuning for each setting, OriTTA achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C and ImageNet-C in all sixteen combinations of four backbones, two protocols and two stream orders. On ImageNet-C fog, recent methods collapse in up to two thirds of one hundred runs, while OriTTA never does.
authors: Jaeho Hwang, Yujin Oh, Juhyeon Shin, Juhye Lee, Sungroh Yoon, Uiwon Hwang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of adapting to unlabeled streams one sample at a time, where distribution statistics are unreliable and confident predictions may be wrong.
Constructs fixed class-specific geometric targets from the frozen source classifier using synthetic prototypes and a recentered feature-space origin.
Adapts selected features toward predicted class axes, penalizes excessive feature radius, and stores one sample per class to preserve absent-class behavior.
Detects adaptation collapse by reclassifying the stored memory and resets the model when necessary.
Achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 across the reported CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C settings; it avoids collapses observed by recent methods on ImageNet-C fog.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation at batch size 1 from classifier geometry, directly relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: The Batch Size Can Be One: Test-Time Adaptation from Classifier Geometry
papers.tldr: OriTTA enables robust test-time adaptation from single, unordered samples by using classifier geometry rather than batch statistics or confidence selection.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are being applied to Web data streams such as network intrusion detection, where they adapt by updating the labelled rows of their context without retraining. When a past concept returns after leaving the context, a TFM faces a recall-or-relearn decision between restoring stored rows of the concept and relearning it from new labels. We propose MICE (Mixture of In-Context Experts), a training-free learner that cuts the stream into segments at detected changes. It merges a closed segment into a stored context when the TFM's estimated additional error on the segment is within a tolerance, under a capacity limit on stored contexts. A fast level weights the stored contexts and first-in-first-out (FIFO) windows by the log-loss of their predictions on the last labelled batch. We show that, with pure stored contexts and a margin condition, this fast level gains over relearning, in expected accuracy, the normalised positive area between the stored context's accuracy and the TFM's learning curve, up to a first-batch term. A slow level mixes the fast level's prediction with that of the FIFO window of the last labelled rows and bounds the discounted half-Brier regret of MICE against this window at every time. Learning curves measured beforehand predict the ordering of the observed recall gains. MICE outperforms reset, which empties the context at detected drifts, on grid streams with random boundary phases. Merging keeps fewer experts than pools that store every segment, and with fixed segmentation a time-matched snapshot pool matches MICE on the shifted grid. On real streams, MICE has the highest mean accuracy of all policies we compare.
authors: Zhangkai Wu, Xu Zhang, Zhihong Cui, Yiqi Wang, Yi Zhang
bullets: Addresses TFMs’ recall-versus-relearning decision when previously seen concepts return after leaving context.
Segments streams at detected changes and selectively merges segments into a capacity-limited pool of stored contexts.
Uses a fast log-loss weighting level over stored contexts and FIFO windows, plus a slower mixture with the latest labelled rows.
Theory links recall gains to stored-context accuracy and learning curves, and bounds discounted half-Brier regret against a recent-data baseline.
Outperforms context-reset policies on grid streams and achieves the highest mean accuracy among compared policies on real streams; fixed-segmentation snapshots can match it on shifted grids.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free in-context mixture for recurring concept drift, directly relevant to continual/online adaptation of foundation models.
papers.title: Recall or Relearn? A Mixture of In-Context Experts for Recurring Concept Drift
papers.tldr: MICE is a training-free strategy for recurring concept drift that adaptively recalls stored contexts or relearns from recent data, improving recall and accuracy across synthetic and real streams.

papers.abstract: Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Yaxiong Wang, Yujiao Wu, Lianwei Wu, Qi Zhang, Li Zhu, Chaofeng Dong, Le Wu, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Addresses attack-incremental detection, where new forgery mechanisms appear without changing the real/fake interface and prior knowledge must be retained.
Introduces Fable-Bench with joint-modality, text-side, and image-side attack-evolution protocols.
Models authentic replay representations with a real-only Gaussian mixture and uses GRASP for sample-adaptive stability–plasticity control.
Uses VAR to prioritize replay for stages vulnerable to authentic-density degradation, boundary confusion, or mode drift.
Across three protocols and multiple detector architectures, ARISE improves historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual learning for multimodal forgery detection, introducing stability preservation mechanisms to handle evolving attack patterns.
papers.title: ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection
papers.tldr: ARISE improves continual multimodal forgery detection by preserving authentic-content representations while adapting to newly emerging attacks.

papers.abstract: Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. Despite advances in promptable segmentation, autonomously identifying and correcting garment-specific errors without human-provided spatial prompts remains difficult. We propose GarmentSegAgent, an autonomous framework that integrates semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation through iterative textual self-refinement. At its core, we introduce CAST (Constrained Attribution-guided Selective TextGrad), which connects visual error attribution with targeted textual optimization. CAST identifies instruction components responsible for segmentation errors, selectively updates them through textual gradients, and validates the resulting instructions against garment-specific constraints. This enables image-specific error correction at inference time while keeping the underlying foundation models frozen. Experiments on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia demonstrate consistent improvements in region overlap and boundary accuracy, alongside more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad. By enabling visual feedback to guide controlled instruction updates, GarmentSegAgent offers a promising direction for autonomous garment understanding, with potential applications in scalable fashion content analysis, visual retrieval, and consumer-to-shop matching on the Web.
authors: Jia Chen, Chao Huang, Xinrong Hu, Mingdi Huang, Ruyang Zhao, Jun Bai
bullets: Addresses unreliable garment segmentation caused by heterogeneous web fashion imagery and the need for spatial prompts.
Combines semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation in an iterative self-refinement framework.
Introduces CAST, which attributes errors to instruction components, selectively optimizes them, and checks garment-specific constraints.
Evaluations on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia show consistent gains in region overlap and boundary accuracy, with more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad.
Foundation models remain frozen; refinement occurs at inference time through image-specific instruction updates.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes textual self-refinement to autonomously correct segmentation errors at inference time, fitting the test-time learning paradigm.
papers.title: GarmentSegAgent: Autonomous Garment Segmentation for Web Fashion Images via Textual Self-Refinement
papers.tldr: GarmentSegAgent autonomously improves garment segmentation in diverse web fashion images by refining textual instructions from visual error feedback, without human prompts or model fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories couple a learned design surrogate to an instrument, and on every new target domain it must answer four questions: when it can be trusted, how many target measurements it needs, which to make first, and when to stop adapting, switch models or escalate. We state a framework making each measurable (a competence ratio, a budget $k^*(\varepsilon)$, a time-to-target and a priced decision) and instantiate it without wet experiments on six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables as offline laboratories: 107 leave-one-group tiers whose rows are hidden labels. A sealed, pre-registered programme (two sealed negative validations and a pre-registered test on three more tables) and seven frozen closed-loop protocols, each run twice, yield 23 findings. Shift cost is stratified by shift type; no label-free statistic certifies individual candidates; random-split model-family rankings predicted neither the sealed nor the loop rankings. Warm-start residual boosting returns a surrogate to $1.25\times$ its development reference within 20 target rows in 94% of chemistry tiers (27% under a strict noise-floor reading), 90% of laboratory and 40% of device tiers, and a budget planned from the shift type on other tables is not measurably worse on a new one. In the loop, one gain survives drift and shuffled-label controls on all tiers, carried by the sparsely sampled ones: proposing at once and warm-starting on every measurement reaches a 10% target in 2.80 measurements against 3.31 for the reference, and in 5.72 against 11.35 for random proposals on 301 hard units at a 3% tolerance. No label-free acquisition rule survives the shuffled-label control, no interval-aware proposal or other model family does better, and no threshold rule on the tested diagnostics beats always continuing once escalation is priced. No wet-lab validation is claimed.
bullets: Evaluated 107 leave-one-group tiers across six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables using sealed, preregistered offline protocols.
Formalized measurable trust, target-measurement budget, time-to-target, and cost-aware decisions for adapting, switching, or escalating a surrogate.
Warm-start residual boosting recovered near-reference performance within 20 target rows most often in chemistry tiers, less often in laboratory and device tiers.
Propose-then-update reached a 10% target in 2.80 versus 3.31 measurements for the reference, and 5.72 versus 11.35 for random proposals on hard units at 3% tolerance.
Shuffled-label controls invalidated label-free acquisition rules; no tested stopping threshold, interval-aware proposal, or alternative model family consistently improved decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Offline closed-loop framework for adapting learned surrogates on new target domains; relevant to test-time and continual adaptation.
papers.title: When Can a Learned Design Surrogate Be Trusted in a Self-Driving Microfluidics Laboratory? An Offline Closed-Loop Framework Built and Tested on Six Public Tables
papers.tldr: An offline study defines and tests when learned surrogates can be trusted and adapted in self-driving microfluidics, finding that warm-start closed-loop updating helps on sparse, shifted settings but no label-free stopping or acquisition rule is reliable.

papers.abstract: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
authors: Fanqi Yu, Matteo Tiezzi, Cigdem Beyan, Tommaso Apicella, Vittorio Murino
bullets: Targets sequential learning from multimodal demonstrations without storing or revisiting past data.
Uses hierarchical dual attention to separate instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement.
Adds key-level geometric regularization to align representations within tasks and separate them across tasks.
Supports an expandable expert set for continual adaptation and reliable expert selection.
On LIBERO suites, including heterogeneous and paraphrased tasks, it improves AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting; gains are stronger under interference and language variation.
papers.selection_reason: Replay-free lifelong imitation learning for robot manipulation with expert routing and continual adaptation.
papers.title: HIDRA: Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention for Replay-Free Lifelong Imitation Learning
papers.tldr: HIDRA enables replay-free lifelong imitation learning by stabilizing expert routing under continual representation drift.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP). While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified. We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL. We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation $\sigma$ has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques. We observe a significant effect of $\sigma$ on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments. Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
authors: Andrea Vasco Grieco, Evelyn D'Elia, Edoardo Caldarelli, Raffaello Camoriano
bullets: Analyzes loss of plasticity (LoP), where RL agents become less able to learn from new data.
Studies PPO with isotropic Gaussian policies and examines how policy standard deviation σ relates to LoP.
Provides theoretical and experimental evidence that σ substantially affects the extent of LoP.
Connects the findings to why commonly used LoP mitigation techniques may be effective.
Validates the analysis on LoP benchmarks and through deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes loss of plasticity in on-policy RL with robotic-arm deployment; relevant to robot learning and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Bridging Exploration and Loss of Plasticity in On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: The study identifies policy standard deviation in PPO’s isotropic Gaussian policies as a key factor influencing loss of plasticity in continuous-control reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning uses offline pretraining to accelerate subsequent online learning. While many methods assume the offline dataset remains available throughout fine-tuning, there are many settings where this is not the case. Prior work attributes failures in this setting primarily to critic recalibration under distribution shift. We identify a complementary actor-side failure: once the offline data disappears, continued behavioral cloning (BC) no longer preserves the offline behavior distribution and instead refits the behavioral model to the agent's limited, and nonstationary, online experience. We demonstrate that stopping online behavioral fitting while preserving the pretrained expressive prior substantially improves no-retention fine-tuning across implicit flow Q-learning (IFQL), flow Q-learning (FQL), and action-chunked RL (QC) on seven OGBench domains. We trace this failure to a behavioral feedback loop: continuing online behavioral cloning rapidly erases the pretrained prior, inducing representational collapse and action diversity loss that starves the critic of useful exploration. Freezing the prior breaks this cycle, preserving offline coverage while allowing value learning to drive continuous improvement.
authors: Sami Nur Islam, Johan Obando-Ceron, Doina Precup, Aaron Courville, Pablo Samuel Castro
bullets: Identifies an actor-side failure: continued online behavioral cloning refits the policy to limited, nonstationary online data.
This creates a feedback loop that erases the offline prior, reduces action diversity, and limits useful exploration for the critic.
Stopping behavioral fitting preserves offline coverage while allowing value learning to improve the policy.
The approach improves no-retention fine-tuning across IFQL, FQL, and action-chunked RL on seven OGBench domains.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies and mitigates behavioral drift in offline-to-online RL when offline data is unavailable; directly relevant to continual and online learning.
papers.title: Freeze, Don't Clone: Fine-Tuning with Expressive Policies Without Retaining Offline Data
papers.tldr: Freezing the pretrained behavioral prior during online fine-tuning prevents behavioral collapse and improves offline-to-online RL when offline data cannot be retained.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
authors: Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma
bullets: Long-video QA is difficult because sparse frame sampling can miss decisive evidence, while spurious cues can still mislead models.
S-MME benchmarks shortcut-biased behavior from misleading language correlations and salient but irrelevant visual content.
CLEAR estimates bias using question-only and locally salient-clip views, then intervenes on hidden states at inference.
Experiments across five benchmarks show consistent gains in prediction and robustness across different MLLMs.
CLEAR is presented as a complementary test-time scaling approach; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free counterfactual hidden-state intervention to mitigate bias in MLLM long-video QA; relevant to video understanding, multimodal LLMs, and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: The paper diagnoses shortcut biases in MLLMs for long-video QA and introduces training-free CLEAR to reduce misleading linguistic and visual cues during inference.

papers.abstract: Test-time updating lets a language model change persistent state after training---such as model weights, adapter parameters, or a memory module---before or while answering queries. Existing evaluations often compare systems using update count or frequency and performance measured immediately afterward. These summaries omit what is updated, where, when, and in what order. The same total can therefore hide an important difference: one system may answer after one update while another answers after two. We introduce the Control Map, an evaluation framework that records the committed updates preceding each scored answer and separately evaluates behavioral changes, immediate learning (acquisition), later recall (retention), preservation of unrelated behavior (locality), and performance in new settings. We prove when counts alone determine final state and show, under stated assumptions, how differences between pre-answer histories limit differences in average scores. Using ControlMap, our experiments reveal three insights. First, update scheduling matters: at a 760M-parameter checkpoint, 24 schedules with the same update count yield 19.7%--34.2% accuracy. Second, learning an edit does not guarantee that it lasts or remains contained: all six selected CounterFact LoRA settings learn the new information, while ROME retains edits at all 13 operating points but fails locality at each. Third, no editor performs best consistently across models, benchmarks, and tests. Evaluations should therefore report update histories and assess acquisition, retention, and locality separately.
authors: Zehao Zhao, Shangjian Yin, Rui Liu, Chongyang Bai, Mark Ibrahim, Kavosh Asadi, Yuchen Lu, Hang Cui, Hamed Firooz
bullets: Update count alone can hide differences in what is updated, when, and in what order before an answer is scored.
The framework records committed pre-answer updates and evaluates behavioral change, immediate learning, later recall, preservation of unrelated behavior, and new-setting performance.
The authors prove when update counts suffice to determine final state and bound score differences caused by different update histories.
Experiments show scheduling strongly affects accuracy: 24 equal-count schedules at one checkpoint range from 19.7% to 34.2%.
Learning an edit may not imply durability or locality, and no editor is consistently best across models, benchmarks, and tests.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces evaluation framework for test-time model updates, directly relevant to test-time learning and adaptation.
papers.title: Beyond Update Counts: A Control Map for Evaluating Test-Time Model Updates
papers.tldr: The Control Map shows that test-time model-update evaluations must track update histories—not just counts—and separately measure acquisition, retention, locality, and generalization.

papers.abstract: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.
bullets: Frozen latent world models can plan poorly when deployment conditions differ from training.
Prediction-only adaptation fits observed transitions but may remain inaccurate about goal-reaching actions.
OpTTA jointly minimizes observed-transition prediction loss and the planner’s goal-reaching cost on candidate rollouts.
Across manipulation, reaching, and navigation shifts, OpTTA improved final planning success by 13.5 percentage points on average, versus 6.9–7.5 for prediction-only adaptation.
The approach was evaluated with three JEPA world models and both CEM and gradient-based planners, without additional environment interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA) for world models, adding a planning term to prediction loss to improve goal-reaching under distribution shift.
papers.title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
papers.tldr: Optimistic, goal-aware test-time adaptation improves world-model planning under distribution shift more than prediction-only adaptation.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. On a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, RoboDoctor achieves a five-dimension mean score of 57.10, with a native success rate of 49.44%. Recorded interactions illustrate strategy changes, selective correction, and grasp revision. These findings characterize execution-time adaptation in the evaluated system; controlled trials remain necessary to isolate the contribution of cross-episode experience.
authors: Heyang Yu, Haomin Li, Sihang Li, Jixin Yan, Shiyun Peng, Wanqi Zhong, Tianyu Xin, Yuan Yao, Xiaoyu Tian, Yiming Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting robot-policy and language-agent behavior to the consequences of physical interaction.
Uses three revision targets: control allocation between policy and agent, selective intervention, and refinement of physical methods.
Stores linked experience containing decision rationale, attempted method, outcome, and reuse conditions.
On 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, it reports a five-dimension mean score of 57.10 and a native success rate of 49.44%.
The results demonstrate execution-time adaptation, but controlled trials are still needed to isolate the value of cross-episode experience.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes training-free execution-time self-improvement and persistent experience for robot policies, relevant to embodied robot learning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: RoboDoctor: Training-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Robot Policies
papers.tldr: RoboDoctor enables robot policies to improve during execution without changing model weights by using feedback to diagnose, intervene, revise actions, and retain experience.

papers.abstract: Data-enabled predictive control has recently emerged as a promising control paradigm, enabling a transparent optimal-control formulation without the need to learn an explicit dynamics model. This paper presents a number of extensions paving the path towards its use in real-time robotics tasks. Following recent work, we utilize a nonlinear predictor based on Gaussian kernels to represent the relationship between input and output data. We propose a damped Gauss-Newton method that enables real-time control by efficiently exploiting the least-squares structure of the control problem. In addition, we introduce a hybrid buffer management strategy that incorporates informative online data while retaining relevant offline data, allowing the predictor to account for changes in the dynamics. We demonstrate the tracking performance and computational suitability of the proposed method in MuJoCo using a Franka Research 3 arm pushing a block across surface, without prior knowledge of its changing friction values.
authors: Akshun Sharma, Zhongqi Wei, Buqing Ou, Frederike D\"umbgen
bullets: Targets real-time robotic control without learning an explicit dynamics model.
Uses a Gaussian-kernel nonlinear predictor to model input–output relationships.
Introduces a damped Gauss–Newton solver that exploits the control problem’s least-squares structure.
Maintains a hybrid data buffer combining informative online data with relevant offline data to adapt to changing dynamics.
Demonstrates tracking and computational suitability in MuJoCo for a Franka Research 3 pushing task with unknown, changing friction.
papers.selection_reason: Data-enabled predictive control with online buffer adaptation for robotic manipulation; fits robot learning/control and online adaptation.
papers.title: RoKON: Efficient and Adaptive Data-Enabled Predictive Control for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: RoKON makes data-enabled predictive control practical for real-time robotic manipulation by combining nonlinear Gaussian-kernel prediction, efficient optimization, and adaptive data management.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.
authors: Junze Wang, Lei Fan, Dezheng Zhang, Donglin Di, Yang Song, Sidong Liu, Cong Cong
bullets: Addresses two failure modes in test-time prompt tuning: excessive update magnitude and inconsistent directional drift.
Decomposes prompt-update trajectories into magnitude plus persistent, oscillatory, and residual directional components.
Uses Adaptive Koopman Control to shrink expansive updates and Hankel Update Router to preserve persistent directions while suppressing unstable components.
Prompt-agnostic: integrates with existing visual and text TPT methods without changing the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss.
Across 15 datasets, improves 10 baselines, with reported gains of 3–8% for visual prompts and over 2% for text prompts.
papers.selection_reason: Stabilizes test-time prompt tuning via decomposition and control; directly relevant to test-time learning and adaptation.
papers.title: Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition
papers.tldr: TPD stabilizes test-time prompt tuning by controlling update magnitude and direction, improving adaptation across visual and text prompts.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through 3D environments. Maintaining persistent episodic memory remains a challenge for VLM-based streaming agents in long-horizon navigation. We present MEMVLN, a streaming episodic memory framework that maintains a bounded bank of compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, and produces compact memory tokens via cross-attention. We pair the proposed memory with a frozen pretrained geometry encoder. To learn the memory module, we design a masking-based trajectory summarization task with multi-granularity sub-trajectory decomposition, encouraging route reconstruction exclusively from episodic memory. Under navigation training restricted to the official R2R/RxR trajectories, MEMVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics on standard VLN-CE benchmarks. Long-horizon analyses further characterize when episodic memory is useful. For physical evaluation, we collect 30 instruction-conditioned episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, MEMVLN improves success over the VLM baseline from 17% to 40%, and post-training further raises it to 47%.
authors: Yan Wang, Jiangyong Huang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful past observations during long-horizon VLN.
Stores compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, then converts them into memory tokens via cross-attention.
Uses a frozen geometry encoder and a masking-based, multi-granularity trajectory summarization task to train the memory module.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across standard VLN-CE benchmarks under R2R/RxR trajectory restrictions.
In a physical-scene evaluation, success improved from 17% for the VLM baseline to 40%, and to 47% after post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming episodic memory for vision-language navigation; directly relevant to embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: MemVLN: Streaming Episodic Memory for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MEMVLN equips streaming vision-language navigation agents with bounded, pose-aware episodic memory to improve long-horizon navigation in simulated and physical environments.

papers.abstract: In surgical instrument segmentation, the increasing variety of instruments over time poses a significant challenge for existing neural networks, as they are unable to effectively learn such incremental tasks and suffer from catastrophic forgetting. When learning new data, the model experiences a sharp performance drop on previously learned data. Although several continual learning methods have been proposed for incremental understanding tasks in surgical scenarios, the issue of data imbalance often leads to a strong bias in the segmentation head, resulting in poor performance. Data imbalance can occur in two forms: (i) class imbalance between new and old data, and (ii) class imbalance within the same time point of data. Such imbalances often cause the dominant classes to take over the training process of continual semantic segmentation (CSS). To address this issue, we propose SurgCSS, a novel plug-and-play CSS framework for surgical instrument segmentation under data imbalance. Specifically, we generate realistic surgical backgrounds through inpainting and blend instrument foregrounds with the generated backgrounds in a class-aware manner to balance the data distribution in various scenarios. We further propose the Class Desensitization Loss by employing contrastive learning to correct edge biases caused by data imbalance. Moreover, we dynamically fuse the weight parameters of the old and new models to achieve a better trade-off between the biased and unbiased model weights. To investigate the data imbalance problem in surgical scenarios, we construct a new benchmark for surgical instrument CSS by integrating datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving significant performance improvement against existing baselines.
authors: Shifang Zhao, Long Bai, Kun Yuan, Feng Li, Jieming Yu, Wenzhen Dong, Guankun Wang, Mobarakol Islam, Nicolas Padoy, Nassir Navab, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Existing continual segmentation models struggle as new instruments arrive, forgetting previously learned instruments.
It targets both imbalance between old and new classes and imbalance among classes at the same time point.
Synthetic surgical backgrounds and class-aware foreground blending rebalance training scenarios.
Class Desensitization Loss uses contrastive learning to reduce edge bias, while dynamic old/new weight fusion balances model knowledge.
A new integrated benchmark is introduced, and experiments show significant improvements over existing baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Class incremental segmentation with data imbalance and forgetting; fits continual learning.
papers.title: Rethinking Data Imbalance in Class Incremental Surgical Instrument Segmentation
papers.tldr: SurgCSS addresses data imbalance and catastrophic forgetting in class-incremental surgical instrument segmentation through data balancing, bias correction, and model-weight fusion.

papers.abstract: Point cloud models are increasingly deployed through score-only black-box interfaces. Under this access model, test-time rotations outside the training distribution can substantially degrade performance. Although existing mitigations such as equivariant retraining and gradient-based adaptation are effective, they are infeasible without access to model weights or gradients. To address this limitation, we propose CanDO, a test-time canonicalization method that recovers lost performance using only forward queries. Specifically, CanDO searches for an input transformation that maximizes model confidence and uses derivative-free optimization to perform this search without gradients. We further identify three conditions for successful recovery: a training augmentation gap, an accuracy-aligned confidence surrogate, and global search over a multi-modal objective. Across multiple architectures and benchmarks, CanDO recovers 76% of the oracle gap under azimuthal misorientation and 51% under arbitrary SO(3) rotations for object part segmentation.
