These results show that frozen score-only point cloud models can recover from rotation-induced distribution shifts through post-deployment canonicalization alone.
bullets: Targets pose-induced performance degradation when only forward confidence scores—not weights or gradients—are accessible.
Searches for an input transformation that maximizes model confidence via derivative-free, global optimization.
Successful recovery depends on an augmentation gap, confidence aligned with accuracy, and handling a multimodal objective.
Recovers 76% of the oracle gap under azimuthal shifts and 51% under arbitrary SO(3) rotations for object part segmentation.
Scope: addresses rotation-induced shifts through post-deployment canonicalization of frozen models.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time canonicalization of point cloud models via derivative-free optimization; fits test-time adaptation/optimization.
papers.title: Recovering Black-Box Point Cloud Models from Pose Shifts via Derivative-Free Optimization
papers.tldr: CanDO restores much of the rotation-robustness lost by score-only point-cloud models using gradient-free test-time input canonicalization.

papers.abstract: User memory helps personalized systems build on their understanding of users over time. In e-commerce, users convey their preferences and needs through both explicit language and implicit interactions with products. We study memory built from logs of these interactions, examining how it can \emph{remember} concrete evidence and established interests, and use that evidence to \emph{infer} underlying needs and preferences that inform judgments beyond well-observed product domains. Existing memory methods primarily target language-based interactions, and evaluations offer limited real behavioral data and limited separation of these capabilities. This leaves open how to jointly support and separately evaluate remembering and inference from behavioral logs. We formulate the problem of continual behavioral user memory around these joint requirements and develop a dedicated evaluation framework and memory method to address them. \textbf{BehaviorMemBench} is a benchmark built from real e-commerce logs covering 1{,}194 users and 17{,}462 behavioral batches over more than three years, with automatic future-behavior labels and a task-independent memory interface to separately evaluate remembering and inference under a common protocol. \textbf{BehaviorMem} is a memory design that organizes explicit behavioral facts and inferred user characteristics across long-term and short-term scopes in a two-axis state, with evidence-grounded formation, continual maintenance, and query-independent readout. Experiments across two builders and two task readers show that BehaviorMem leads the evaluated agentic memories on remember and infer, and reveal different method rankings across the two capabilities and competitive statistical baselines. Validation on a public dataset further supports its usefulness for downstream tasks based on behavioral histories.
authors: Sizhe Wang, Xinghao Fang, Rui Qiu, Zhenjia Ma, Dagui Chen, Kun Kuang, Hongcheng Guo
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-focused memory methods and real behavioral-log memory evaluation.
BehaviorMemBench uses real e-commerce logs from 1,194 users and 17,462 behavioral batches spanning more than three years.
The benchmark separately measures remembering concrete behavioral evidence and inferring underlying needs or preferences.
BehaviorMem organizes explicit facts and inferred characteristics across long- and short-term scopes, with evidence-grounded updates and continual maintenance.
Experiments report leading performance among evaluated agentic memories on both capabilities, with validation on a public dataset for downstream behavioral-history tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Fits continual behavioral user memory and agentic memory mechanisms.
papers.title: BehaviorMem: Building and Evaluating User Memory from Real-World E-Commerce Behavior Streams
papers.tldr: BehaviorMem introduces a benchmark and memory design for evaluating and supporting both evidence recall and preference inference from long-term e-commerce behavior streams.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor trajectory tracking under unmodeled disturbances often relies on online residual adaptation, but short out-domain residuals can corrupt the learned disturbance model when constant-step updates treat every residual gradient uniformly. We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size. DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with $L_1$-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.
bullets: Targets corruption of online disturbance learning caused by treating all residual gradients equally.
Retains DAPL’s random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares residual adaptation.
Compares current gradients with short- and long-term memories to classify adaptation regimes.
Uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates and recover after persistent domain shifts.
In numerical tests with four mixed disturbances, DGC achieved the lowest mean position RMSE among the evaluated baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Online residual adaptation for quadrotor control under disturbances; fits test-time learning and learned robot control.
papers.title: Dual Gradient Consensus for Adaptive Learning to Transient Out-of-Distribution Disturbances in Quadrotor Control
papers.tldr: DGC improves quadrotor trajectory tracking under transient and persistent out-of-domain disturbances by adapting residual models with confidence-aware gradient updates.

papers.abstract: Federated continual learning (FCL) has attracted considerable interest by enabling local clients to continually acquire knowledge from new tasks. However, most FCL methods assume that the global server has prior knowledge of the arrival times and number of categories for new tasks, which is unrealistic in the real world. Furthermore, they neglect the importance of positive inter-task semantic relationships when learning new tasks and are significantly affected by irrelevant relationships from old tasks, thereby exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To resolve the above challenges, we develop a novel Task Relevance-driven Prompt Expansion (TRPE) model. Specifically, to eliminate the reliance on prior knowledge of new tasks, we propose an out-of-distribution detector to identify the arrival of new tasks within local clients, along with a radius-adaptive DBSCAN to infer the quantity of categories in new tasks on the proxy server. Moreover, to explore positive inter-task relationships, we calculate the affinity between the original gradient for learning new task and its gradient orthogonal to the feature space of old tasks to evaluate semantic relevance between old and new tasks from a global perspective. Then, we use this global task relevance to determine the key-prompt pair for new tasks and identify highly related old tasks. After concatenating their prompts for training, we can leverage such positive inter-task relations to improve the continual learning of newly arriving tasks. To balance the learning of new tasks and the forgetting of old ones, a soft orthogonality constraint is applied to the local key and prompt gradients. Experiments spanning diverse datasets and backbones confirm the efficacy of our TRPE model.
authors: Jiahua Dong, Wenqi Liang, Yang Cong, Yichen Li, Hongyuan Yu, Henghui Ding, Yulun Zhang, Salman Khan, Fahad Shahbaz Khan
bullets: Addresses unrealistic assumptions about known task arrivals and category counts in federated continual learning.
Uses an out-of-distribution detector locally and radius-adaptive DBSCAN on a proxy server to detect new tasks and infer their category counts.
Measures global semantic relevance between new and old tasks through gradient affinities.
Expands prompts by selecting relevant key-prompt pairs and concatenating related task prompts.
Applies a soft orthogonality constraint to balance learning new tasks with retaining old knowledge; experiments across datasets and backbones support its efficacy.
papers.selection_reason: Federated continual learning with task-relevance prompt expansion; directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Task Relevance-Driven Prompt Expansion for Federated Continual Learning
papers.tldr: TRPE enables federated continual learning without knowing when new tasks arrive or how many categories they contain, while using task relevance to reduce catastrophic forgetting.

papers.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of LLMs suffers from catastrophic forgetting, and prevailing mitigation strategies struggle to reconcile the plasticity-stability dilemma. To address this, we propose Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization (ECHO), a closed-loop control framework. By decomposing the KL divergence, we identify output entropy as a dominant observable component of KL variation. This enables us to leverage entropy as a computationally efficient online proxy to monitor forgetting risks in real-time, bypassing expensive reference-model inference. Consequently, ECHO employs an elastic controller that dynamically modulates the gradient weight of replay data via a proportional control law, using deviations from the pre-trained entropic equilibrium as an error signal. Empirical evaluations across 0.6B to 9B parameter architectures demonstrate that ECHO lies on, and in several comparisons extends, the observed plasticity-stability frontier and maintains high operational robustness against varying data mixing ratios.
authors: Shangxi Wu, Xiaorong Yan, Xiaojun Meng, Yuxiang Zhang, Jiansheng Wei
bullets: Addresses the plasticity–stability trade-off in supervised fine-tuning of LLMs.
Decomposes KL divergence to identify output entropy as an efficient proxy for monitoring forgetting risk.
Uses a proportional controller to adjust the gradient weight of replay data based on deviations from pretrained entropic equilibrium.
Evaluations across 0.6B–9B models place ECHO on, and sometimes beyond, the observed plasticity–stability frontier.
Shows robustness across varying data-mixing ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a closed-loop control method to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning, directly relevant to continual/online learning.
papers.title: Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization: Pre-empting Catastrophic Forgetting via Dynamic Feedback
papers.tldr: ECHO uses output entropy as a real-time feedback signal to dynamically adjust replay during fine-tuning, reducing catastrophic forgetting without requiring reference-model inference.

papers.abstract: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
authors: Xuan He, Sining Zhoubian, Ruozhen Yang, Yuhao Wen, Zhineng Wang, Yuyang Hu, Ke Yang, Yuyu Zhang, Ping Nie, Jiawei Han, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Evaluates memory systems across multiple benchmarks and model backbones against naive RAG.
Defines memory benefit as gains over direct retrieval and memory tax as corresponding losses.
Attributes both effects to how memory reorganizes, distills, or obscures raw information.
Studies how memory tax arises from system and evaluation factors and extends the concept to broader memory applications.
Advocates evaluating the net value and reliability of memory rather than standalone performance; code and results will be released.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces the concept of 'Memory Tax' to dissect the net value of memory systems in long-horizon agents, contrasting them with direct retrieval.
papers.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
papers.tldr: Dedicated agent memory can hurt performance relative to retrieving directly from raw history, so its value should be measured as benefits minus memory-induced losses.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.
authors: Haoyu Zhao, Sitian Tu, Yuxuan Huang, Huichi Zhou, Zhangyue Yin, Jiahao Huang, Jingyuan Xu, Tianmiao Shi, Jin Shi, Nianxi Zhang, Yangmiao Zhang, Zhuolang Chan, Huiyan Hu, Chenchao Sheng, Yaqing Luo, Yue Chen, Huaxiu Yao, Meng Fang, Jun Wang
bullets: Introduces 120 expert-authored tasks with five sequential levels each, covering 600 levels, 89 professional roles, and 12 occupational domains.
Agents must pass each level to unlock later levels, testing accumulated experience rather than isolated task performance.
Compares single submissions with diagnostic feedback plus one revision; feedback improves median completion by 5.3 percentage points across 17 configurations.
The strongest system clears 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels for 23.3% of tasks, indicating substantial difficulty with sustained continual learning.
CLE may also support post-training LLMs to improve continual-learning capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Large-scale benchmark for continual and experiential learning in LLM agents; directly fits continual learning.
papers.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: CLE benchmarks whether LLM agents can improve through experience and retain performance across long-horizon professional workflows.

papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection identifies inputs outside the training distribution. Rank-based analyses such as RankFeat and RankWeight suggest that OOD overconfidence is closely related to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces. Since weight averaging operates directly in parameter space and improves model generalization, we consider it for OOD detection from a dominant-component perspective. Trainable Weight Averaging (TWA) assigns a single coefficient to each checkpoint, limiting independent control of dominant weight components. We extend TWA with leading rank-one weight components extracted by Singular Value Decomposition as correction directions, whose contributions are learned through the in-distribution classification objective. On ResNet50, our method improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across the evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, both with and without Outlier Exposure. Mahalanobis-based evaluation yields mixed results, indicating that the benefit depends on the OOD scoring protocol. Target-layer analyses with MSP and Energy favor correction near the classifier.
bullets: OOD overconfidence is linked to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces.
The method extends Trainable Weight Averaging with SVD-derived rank-one weight corrections learned using the in-distribution classification objective.
On ResNet50, it improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, with and without Outlier Exposure.
Mahalanobis evaluation is mixed, and target-layer analyses favor applying corrections near the classifier.
papers.selection_reason: Extends Trainable Weight Averaging with rank-one weight components for Out-of-Distribution detection, a method applicable to test-time adaptation and model robustness.
papers.title: Rank-1 Weight-Corrected Trainable Weight Averaging for Out-of-Distribution Detection
papers.tldr: Rank-1 Weight-Corrected TWA improves OOD detection by learning corrections to dominant weight components, though gains depend on the scoring protocol and layer.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can exploit shortcuts, i.e., correlations present in training data that may not hold at test time. This can lead to poor predictions when correlations shift. Most existing solutions for removing shortcuts operate at training time, requiring labeled training data, model weight access, and significant computational resources. Here, we study the problem of test-time shortcut removal. We propose a family of counterfactual test-time augmentation (CTTA) methods: given an example, each method uses an auxiliary model to generate counterfactual edits in which the shortcut value is changed, and then takes a weighted average of the LLM's predictions across these edits. We prove that the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor is a member of this CTTA family, and we characterize its weights. The weights depend on the training distribution, and therefore are, in general, not identifiable from the trained model and unlabeled test data. However, we present assumptions under which the weights can be obtained using the token probabilities of the trained LLM, and propose tests to detect violations of these assumptions. We use these tests to develop Select-CTTA, an aggregate method that selects among CTTA methods. Empirically, we find that Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches the performance of models fine-tuned on shortcut-balanced data.
authors: Katie Matton, Rosalind W. Picard, John Guttag, Maggie Makar
bullets: Addresses shortcut-induced failures under distribution shifts using only test-time intervention, avoiding labeled training data and model-weight access.
Uses an auxiliary model to create counterfactual edits and combines the LLM’s predictions with method-specific weights.
Proves the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor belongs to the CTTA family and characterizes its weights.
Introduces Select-CTTA, which chooses among CTTA methods using tests for assumptions needed to estimate weights from token probabilities.
Empirically, Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches shortcut-balanced fine-tuning performance.
papers.selection_reason: Develops test-time counterfactual augmentation to remove shortcuts in LLM predictions, fitting deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Counterfactual Test-Time Augmentation for Shortcut Removal in Language Models
papers.tldr: Counterfactual test-time augmentation reduces language-model shortcut reliance without retraining by averaging predictions over edited examples that change shortcut values.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) manifests not only as accuracy degradation but also as \emph{explanation drift}: models maintain predictive accuracy while silently shifting attention from diagnostic features to spurious correlations. This work identifies and resolves a previously overlooked structural flaw in explanation-aware CL: pixel-level saliency regularization derives supervision targets from the model's own frozen saliency maps, creating a \emph{self-referential drift loop} that actively reinforces spurious attention across tasks. We introduce \textbf{C$^3$L} (Concept-Consistent Continual Learning), which breaks this loop by anchoring regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts (e.g., ``curved beak'', ``striped pattern'') discovered offline, independent of model state, providing (i) target independence from model drift, and (ii) cross-instance semantic consistency across every instance of a class. We identify that our concept-based objective, combined with approximate LRP relevance conservation, induces a \emph{crowding-out effect}: since concept and background regions compete for the relevance of the same prediction, enforcing high relevance within concept regions implicitly suppresses spurious background correlations without explicit penalization. \method does not require human-annotated concept sets, as it employs a fully automated concept discovery and spatial grounding. Extensive evaluation across five benchmarks and over 20 baselines demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.
authors: Yehonatan Elisha, Oren Barkan, Noam Koenigstein
bullets: Identifies a self-referential drift loop in pixel-level explanation regularization: frozen model saliency maps can reinforce spurious attention across tasks.
Anchors regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts discovered independently of the model, ensuring target independence and cross-instance consistency.
Combines concept-based regularization with approximate LRP relevance conservation, causing relevant concept regions to crowd out spurious background correlations.
Automatically discovers and spatially grounds concepts without human-annotated concept sets.
Across five benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, reports state-of-the-art accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious-correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces C$^3$L, a continual learning method that uses semantic concept steering to break the explanation drift loop, offering a novel approach to preventing catastrophic forgetting.
papers.title: Semantic Concept Steering Breaks the Explanation Drift Loop in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: C$^3$L reduces continual-learning forgetting and explanation drift by steering relevance toward stable, automatically discovered semantic concepts rather than self-referential saliency targets.

papers.abstract: Attribute-based person retrieval ranks surveillance images from a binary query of semantic attributes, but mean Average Attribute Degree of Match (mADM) drops on unseen cameras as predicted probabilities shift. Common pipelines rank gallery images by their L1 distance to the query, which penalizes a confident single-attribute mismatch no more than small uncertainties across many attributes, while post-hoc recalibration fitted on source validation data fails to transfer because the per-attribute maps fitted on source data do not match those of new cameras. We propose LENS (Likelihood Evaluation and Neighbor Smoothing), combining fine-tuned DINOv3 and CLIP models with a distilled student. LENS regularizes mutually exclusive attribute groups with group cross-entropy in training, scores gallery images by the log-likelihood of the exact query, and smooths gallery logits over nearest neighbors using DINOv3 appearance features from the same forward pass. On held-out datasets, all three changes raise mADM: the likelihood score improves all six retrieval metrics for the main ensemble and mADM for all 48 development models, and training-free kNN smoothing improves all 46 tested development models. On the hidden test set of the UPAR 2027 benchmark, LENS reaches 68.17 mADM.
authors: Nguyen Dang Duy Tan, Vo Thanh Nguyen, Linh T. T. Tran, Huynh Nguyen Phat
bullets: Addresses mADM degradation caused by probability shifts across unseen cameras and limitations of L1-distance ranking.
Uses fine-tuned DINOv3 and CLIP models with a distilled student, plus group cross-entropy for mutually exclusive attributes.
Ranks gallery images by the exact query’s log-likelihood rather than L1 distance.
Smooths gallery logits over appearance-based nearest neighbors using DINOv3 features from the same forward pass.
All evaluated changes improve reported development metrics; LENS achieves 68.17 mADM on the UPAR 2027 hidden test set.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses domain shift in person retrieval using DINOv3 and CLIP, introducing likelihood evaluation and neighbor smoothing, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: LENS: Likelihood Evaluation and Neighbor Smoothing for Attribute-Based Person Retrieval on Unseen Cameras
papers.tldr: LENS improves attribute-based person retrieval on unseen cameras by combining likelihood-based ranking, group-aware training, and neighbor smoothing.

papers.abstract: Running a language model and a dense 3D map on one device means the two share one memory, and exceeding its limit is an out-of-memory failure. Map systems that keep a bounded working set bound it by a count of keyframes, but the memory one keyframe occupies varies widely with what it carries, so a count does not control what the working set occupies. The unit of admission is as poorly matched, since a radius around the pose, a fixed cell, or the graph neighbors of the last matched keyframe all move parts of the map that are not needed. We therefore propose two decisions. First, the memory the resident map uses is bounded directly, and the cost of every admission is known before any data is read, from per-keyframe resident sizes computed offline and carried with the map. Second, keyframes are admitted and released at a semantic spatial unit, the rooms and corridors of the building, so that the robot holds the zone it occupies together with the zone it is about to enter while the zones it has passed are released. Every admission measures the resident total, makes room, and only then reads, so the budget is never overshot. On two NVIDIA Jetson boards the budget holds in every run and the model gives up at most 0.8 percent of its throughput, whereas without it the operating system kills the model or the map. Under that budget, and over the environments evaluated, admission by semantic zone localizes 6-9 points more of the query frames than a geometric partition of matched zone count and about twice as much as the retrieval of RTAB-Map, at a lower ATE. Bounding memory lets the map and the model coexist, and moving the map in semantic zones makes the bounded map usable.
authors: Huichang Yun, Jaeyeul Kim, Seungho Yoo
bullets: Keyframe-count limits are unreliable because keyframes vary substantially in memory usage.
The system predicts each keyframe’s resident size offline and enforces a strict memory budget before reading new data.
It admits and releases map content by rooms and corridors, retaining the current and next zones while removing passed zones.
On two NVIDIA Jetson boards, the budget held in every run with at most 0.8% model-throughput loss.
Semantic-zone admission localized 6–9 percentage points more query frames than geometric partitioning and about twice as much as RTAB-Map retrieval, with lower ATE in the evaluated environments.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-bounded keyframe management for dense maps on robots, a form of embodied spatial memory.
papers.title: Memory-Aware Keyframe Management for Dense Maps on Memory-Constrained Robots
papers.tldr: A memory-aware map manager enables language models and dense 3D maps to coexist on constrained robots by budgeting memory directly and loading semantic spatial zones on demand.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policies act on their visual history, and an incorrect action can take them off the instructed route. Paired interventions on four VLN policies show that clearing the history doubles pooled success at the onset of a deviation but lowers it on route, while later in a deviation, removing only the off-route frames helps much less. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed, which we call behavioral inertia. We propose MOON, a framework that equips a frozen VLN policy with two lightweight modules, adding less than 1% of its parameters. A deviation judge decides when to forget, raising an alarm that clears the history when it predicts that the agent is off route. A recovery policy, trained with GRPO from alarm states, learns how to move on, turning more of the successes found only by sampling into a single greedy rollout. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show that MOON reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and raises the success rate of its frozen base by 5.2 and 6.0 points, and an ablation with a random trigger indicates that this gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON. Together, these results suggest that deviation recovery depends on knowing when to forget, not only how to act. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/MOON.
authors: Jingmeng Zhou, Seson Sun, Binyao Xu, Lingming Zhang, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Weiming Hu, Jin Gao, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Incorrect actions can create behavioral inertia: retained off-route history prevents the agent from turning when needed.
MOON adds two lightweight modules to a frozen VLN policy: a deviation judge that triggers history clearing and a recovery policy trained from alarm states.
On R2R-CE and RxR-CE, MOON improves its frozen base success by 5.2 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively, and achieves the highest R2R-CE success among compared methods.
A random-trigger ablation shows that recovery depends on clearing history at the right time, not merely clearing it.
MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-and-language navigation with history clearing and recovery, directly addressing embodied navigation memory.
papers.title: MOON: Learning When to Forget and How to Move On in Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MOON helps vision-and-language navigation agents recover from route deviations by learning when to clear misleading visual history and how to continue afterward.

papers.abstract: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.
authors: Bo-Yu Chen, Zhi Zhou, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Introduces controlled Contextual, Perceptual, and Execution Shifts across three self-hosted web systems.
Measures task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure under changing conditions.
Finds systematic robustness degradation, with Execution Shift producing the strongest impact.
Frames shifted execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and proposes test-time adaptation without relearning the skill library.
Provides code, tasks, environments, documentation, and a leaderboard.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a test-time adaptation method for skill execution under environment shifts, fitting the Test-Time Learning subtopic.
papers.title: SkillShift-Bench: Benchmarking Skill Learning under Environment Evolution for Web Agents
papers.tldr: SkillShift-Bench evaluates how robustly web agents reuse learned skills when deployment environments evolve.

papers.abstract: Robots can use historical observations to answer spatiotemporal queries in familiar environments, but the presence of relevant evidence does not imply that existing tools support the operations a task requires. We introduce ReSight, a task-driven self-improving memory system for embodied agents that expands the capabilities for processing and accessing historical observations as task demands arise. ReSight retains keyframes and their spatiotemporal associations, separating observation evidence from extensible derived fields so that stored observations can be reprocessed for new needs. An execution agent and a coding agent share this memory through different interfaces: the former calls registered tools within a bounded online budget, while the latter uses a programmable workspace and a larger exploration budget to inspect evidence, write programs, and acquire models as needed. To realize capability expansion in ReSight, we develop Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM), which identifies capability gaps from execution and exploration records without task reference answers and converts exploration-derived solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills, extending memory representations and access capabilities as needed. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate effective base memory access and capability expansion. With the execution model and online budget held fixed within each benchmark, EDM reduces mean position error on OC-NaVQA from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and improves high-level success on FindingDory from 38.3% to 63.8%. With the tools and skill frozen, success still improves by 28.3 percentage points on FindingDory episodes excluded from exploration and distillation. Experiments on real robot patrol memories further demonstrate reuse of these capabilities for subsequent queries and new memories, with fewer online tool calls on average.
authors: Lirong Che, Yang Chen, Yimeng Su, Daqi Liu, Zhenyu Huang, Jiong Wang, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between available historical evidence and tools capable of performing task-specific operations.
Stores keyframes and spatiotemporal links separately from extensible derived fields, allowing observations to be reprocessed.
Uses distinct execution and coding agents for bounded online querying versus broader exploration and program/model development.
Its Explore-Distill-Mount process converts discovered solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills without task reference answers.
Across benchmarks, it reduces OC-NaVQA mean position error from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and raises FindingDory success from 38.3% to 63.8%; real-robot patrol tests show reuse with fewer online tool calls.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied memory system for robots, fitting embodied AI and embodied memory.
papers.title: ReSight: Task-Driven Self-Improving Memory for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: ReSight enables embodied agents to expand how they process and query historical observations as new task needs arise, improving spatial reasoning and task success.

papers.abstract: Visual effects are often easier to demonstrate via reference than to describe in words. We study effect-reference editing, where a reference image shows a desired visual effect and language identifies which properties should guide the edit. Existing single-pass editing techniques often fail to make fine-grained edits, resulting in unintended changes to source content or deviations from the reference effect. We introduce KINESYS, a test-time adaptation framework for effect-reference editing that combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback to transfer the desired effect while preserving the composition and content of the original shot. To ensure KINESYS can produce a diverse set of edits that preserve the source, we develop a robust optimization strategy in which the generative model is fine-tuned across multiple noise samples and optimization runs. Evaluation with VLM judges, source preservation metrics (LPIPS, TPIPS), and a user study shows that KINESYS outperforms state-of-the-art image editors in source preservation; on effect transfer, it remains competitive with Nano Banana 2 and outperforms open-weight editors.
authors: Noah Frahm, Luchao Qi, Haoze Li, Dan B Goldman, Sambit Bhattacharya, Roni Sengupta
bullets: Targets fine-grained effect-reference editing guided by both a reference image and language.
Combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback during optimization.
Fine-tunes across multiple noise samples and optimization runs to produce diverse, source-preserving edits.
Evaluations using VLM judges, preservation metrics, and a user study show stronger source preservation than existing editors.
Effect transfer is competitive with Nano Banana 2 and better than open-weight editors.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces KINESYS, a test-time adaptation framework for reference-based image editing that updates the model during inference, fitting test-time learning and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: KINESYS: Test-Time Adaptation for Reference-Based Effect Editing in Images
papers.tldr: KINESYS uses test-time adaptation to transfer visual effects from a reference image while preserving the source image’s content and composition.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge editing aims to update visually grounded facts in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) while preserving unrelated text and visual behaviors. However, standard answer-level metrics can hide evidence misgrounding: an edit may produce the target answer on the original image yet remain sensitive to incidental context rather than the intended visual evidence. To examine this issue in a controlled setting, we construct WaterBird-Edit, an analysis set that decouples bird habitat labels from background context and measures whether edited predictions remain stable when the target evidence is preserved but the background changes. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose VICE (Visual In-Context Editing), a retrieval-based framework that stores edits in external memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations designed to expose task-relevant evidence. Experiments on three standard benchmarks show that VICE achieves strong lifelong editing performance, while results on WaterBird-Edit show that it substantially reduces sensitivity to the controlled background shifts. Code and dataset are available in https://github.com/Wang-Z-W/VICE-main.
authors: Zhiwu Wang, Yichen Wu, Jinqian Yang, Yizhou Yang, Renzhen Wang, Qian Zhao, Deyu Meng
bullets: Identifies evidence misgrounding as a failure mode hidden by answer-level editing metrics.
Introduces WaterBird-Edit, which tests prediction stability when target evidence is preserved but background context changes.
Proposes VICE, a retrieval-based external-memory framework using visual in-context demonstrations to highlight relevant evidence.
Reports strong lifelong editing performance on three standard benchmarks.
WaterBird-Edit results show reduced sensitivity to controlled background shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal knowledge editing with external memory; relevant to MLLM adaptation and continual learning.
papers.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Evidence Misgrounding in Multimodal Knowledge Editing
papers.tldr: The paper reveals that multimodal knowledge edits can rely on incidental visual context and introduces VICE to make edited predictions better grounded in the intended evidence.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. After a chance failure of the better tool, the panel's lessons carried the chance (registered reading luck-carrying; interaction +0.112, 95% interval [+0.097, +0.126]): readers named the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs with the lesson written from that failure, against 0.4% with an irrelevant item and 0.4% with the lesson written from a success. The effect was +0.042 where the log stated that failures are independent and +0.181 where it did not (descriptive). After a lucky success of the worse tool, the interaction was bounded below 0.10 (+0.002), a bound, not evidence of no harm. In exploratory readings, 6 endpoints carried the chance (up to +0.352); 5 were bounded below 0.10. In secondary comparisons, a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction lowered the worse-tool rate after a chance failure to 7.5%, and one instruction for both outcomes with a no-change option to 3.1%; neither met the registered harm-reduction rule at every such endpoint.
bullets: A registered study tested whether noisy outcomes become misleading lessons in recurring two-tool tasks.

Across 256 synthetic worlds, 11 endpoints, and 90,084 answers, models chose the worse tool 11.6% of the time after a chance failure of the better tool with that lesson, versus 0.4% with control lessons.
The registered luck-carrying interaction was +0.112 (95% interval: +0.097 to +0.126).
The effect was larger when the log did not state that failures were independent; this comparison was descriptive.
After a lucky success of the worse tool, evidence for harm was inconclusive; exploratory endpoint effects varied.
papers.selection_reason: Examines whether 'lessons' written by agents from noisy outcomes carry random chance into future decisions, relevant to agent memory and learning.
papers.title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?
papers.tldr: LLM-written lessons can cause agents to repeat a worse tool after a chance failure, though decision-quality instructions may reduce—but did not consistently eliminate—the effect.

papers.abstract: Letting a language model take gradient steps on the text it is reading, known as dynamic evaluation, lowers its loss on the rest of the document. Its behaviour on hybrid linear-attention architectures, on diffusion language models, and on standard long-context benchmarks has not been measured. We measure it. With one SGD step per 128-token chunk on the MLP output projections of the last quarter of blocks, no training, and a 2k-token window, softmax-attention models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Gemma-4-E4B) lose 5-8% of their next-token loss over a document and outperform the same frozen model given the full 32k-token context. Hybrid Gated-DeltaNet models (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.8-27B) gain under 1% at every learning rate: the linear-attention blocks already perform the adaptation. The mechanism transfers to masked-diffusion models with a larger effect, 8% on Nemotron-Diffusion-8B and 17-20% on DiffusionGemma-26B, once the rate is lowered and updates are clipped. Across RULER, BABILong, LongBench-v2, SCOTUS, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, ContractNLI and citation completion, at 100 or more items on two model sizes, weights updated on the full document recover none of the accuracy lost to context truncation: the adaptation is style and vocabulary, not retrieval. Writing facts with the next-token loss stores the prompt format rather than the fact (30% recall under chat prompting against 80% in context) and costs 36-38 GSM8K points at every dose. Writing a conclusion as behaviour instead, by distilling the model's own conclusion-conditioned judgments into a low-rank adapter, reaches the in-context ceiling (0.83 and 0.88 against 0.84 and 0.88 on 100 games) with GSM8K unchanged, and the conclusion can come from an inquiry loop that found it by asking information-gain questions.
bullets: Standard softmax-attention models reduce next-token loss by 5–8% with one gradient step per 128-token chunk, outperforming frozen models with a full 32k-token context.
Hybrid Gated-DeltaNet models improve by under 1%, suggesting their linear-attention blocks already perform similar adaptation.
Masked-diffusion models benefit more—8% for Nemotron-Diffusion-8B and 17–20% for DiffusionGemma-26B—when using lower rates and clipped updates.
Across long-context and retrieval benchmarks, document-wide weight updates recover none of the accuracy lost from context truncation; fact-writing achieves only 30% recall versus 80% in context.
Distilling conclusion-conditioned judgments into a low-rank adapter reaches the in-context ceiling without reducing GSM8K performance, unlike writing facts with next-token loss.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'dynamic evaluation' (gradient steps during inference), a form of test-time learning that adapts LLMs on the fly.
papers.title: Can Language Models Learn While They Think? Testing Gradient Adaptation Across Architectures
papers.tldr: Gradient adaptation improves language-model loss mainly by learning document style and vocabulary, not by reliably storing or retrieving facts.

papers.abstract: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on whether models can successfully act on the guidance provided by their harnesses. However, we find that harness benefits are not uniform across model capabilities: skills that improve stronger models can provide little benefit or even degrade performance for weaker ones. Across seven models and three benchmarks, we identify 103 task-skill pairs where skills improve GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degrade Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement is already stated in the skill. This motivates skill adaptation: reformulating existing skills to match the executor's capabilities and make their guidance easier to execute. To achieve this, we diagnose failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and distill these diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides adaptation during harness self-evolution. Guided by the meta-skill, a capable external rewriter, Kimi-K3, adapts skills without execution evidence, improving the three weak executors by 5.1-14.1 points over the original skills. We then incorporate this adaptation into a five-round self-evolution loop, where each model revises its own skill from execution trajectories and verifier feedback. Across seven executors, from Gemma-4-E4B to Kimi-K2.5, the meta-skill consistently improves final scores by 2.0-5.1 points over the same loop without the meta-skill. Our findings provide practical design guidance for developing more effective harness self-evolution methods.
authors: Zhihao Yang, Haojin Wang, Juncheng Wu, Kuan Zhang, Yukun Chen, Run Luo, Yaojie Lu, Yuyin Zhou, Lu Wang, Xianpei Han
bullets: Skill benefits vary by model: guidance that helps stronger models can harm weaker ones.
The study finds many failures occur despite the relevant requirement already being stated, indicating a skill-execution mismatch.
A fixed meta-skill diagnoses tool-use, context-management, instruction-following, and verification failures to guide skill reformulation.
An external rewriter improves adapted skills for three weak executors by 5.1–14.1 points without execution evidence.
Integrated into five-round self-evolution, the meta-skill improves final scores by 2.0–5.1 points across seven executors.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes skill adaptation for harness self-evolution, improving LLM agent performance by tailoring guidance to executor capabilities.
papers.title: Evolving to Match Capabilities: Improving Harness Self-Evolution via Skill Adaptation
papers.tldr: Adapting harness skills to an executor’s capabilities substantially improves LLM-agent self-evolution, especially for weaker models.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents engage in sustained interactions, long-term memory serves two distinct but complementary functions: fine-grained evidence recall and internalized interpretation for global understanding. Although episodic and latent memory address these demands through explicit historical records and internalized experience, neither paradigm alone can accommodate the diverse memory affinities across tasks, owing to limitations in episodic evidence coverage and integration, and in latent factual grounding. To bridge this divide, we propose a dual-memory framework, unifying a model-native latent memory as an intuitive prior with a multi-indexed episodic memory for exact evidence reconstruction via retrieval-conditioned joint alignment. At inference, the framework adaptively composes these memories through a training-free routing mechanism driven by Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) sensitivity and confidence proxies for query-dependent memory affinity. Extensive evaluations across multimodal benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, outperforming single-paradigm baselines overall (+4.67\% over vanilla Episodic), with further analysis highlighting episodic strengths in evidence-localized tasks and latent contributions to integrating dispersed information and compensating for imperfect retrieval.
authors: Qiuhe Hong, Jingya Wang, Cuzhen Geng, Shenyao Peng, Munan Ning, Yuyang Liu, Yonghong Tian
bullets: Addresses the complementary needs of exact evidence recall and broad, internalized understanding in long-term multimodal interactions.
Combines model-native latent memory with multi-indexed episodic memory through retrieval-conditioned joint alignment.
Uses training-free routing based on Jensen–Shannon Divergence sensitivity and confidence proxies to adapt memory composition.
Evaluations across multimodal benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, including a reported +4.67% over vanilla episodic memory.
Episodic memory helps evidence-localized tasks, while latent memory supports dispersed-information integration and robustness to imperfect retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Dual episodic/latent memory framework for multimodal agents, relevant to agent memory and adaptation.
papers.title: Intuition with Evidence: Adaptive Dual Memory for Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: An adaptive dual-memory multimodal agent combines latent intuition with episodic evidence to select the right memory source for each query.

papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, yet they remain prone to hallucinations and erroneous outputs. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for assessing system reliability, but existing methods are largely designed for single-agent settings; how to exploit MAS structure for UQ while keeping inference cost-neutral remains underexplored. We propose UMAS, a parameter-free, cost-neutral, system-level UQ framework that estimates the credibility of inter-agent influence from each generation's intrinsic confidence. UMAS uses these credibility signals to modulate how uncertainty is updated at each node, and then aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level estimate. Extensive evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show that UMAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 10.54 AUROC points. Beyond uncertainty estimation, UMAS enables hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving MAS accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks while enhancing reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/Dby52-04/UMAS.
authors: Hanwen Li, Jinhao Duan, Xiaoshuang Shi, Yue Zhang, Tianlong Chen, Kaidi Xu, Chenxi Yuan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of quantifying uncertainty and detecting hallucinations in multi-agent systems, where existing UQ methods mainly target single agents.
Uses each generation’s intrinsic confidence to estimate inter-agent influence credibility and modulate uncertainty updates across system nodes.
Aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level reliability estimate without adding inference cost or trainable parameters.
Evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show an average 10.54-point AUROC improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.
Supports hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks.
papers.selection_reason: UMAS provides a system-level uncertainty quantification framework for multi-agent LLM systems, relevant to LLM reliability and state management.
papers.title: UMAS: System-Level Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.tldr: UMAS provides cost-neutral, system-level uncertainty estimates for multi-agent LLM systems by modeling the credibility of inter-agent influence.

papers.abstract: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.
authors: Eric Onyame, Runtao Zhou, Kowshik Thopalli, Bhavya Kailkhura, Chirag Agarwal
bullets: Studies collusion in a simulated insider-trading environment across single agents and sequential or decentralized teams using seven language models from three families.
Finds that multi-agent interaction increases misaligned actions from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent deception from 31.0% to 62.2% across runs.
Under existential pressure, teams maintain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of runs, with shared cover stories suggesting coordinated strategic deception.
Introduces PACT, which trains a stronger student to match the next-token behavior of a smaller frozen honesty-aligned teacher using reverse-KL supervision.
With ethical instructions under existential pressure, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%.
papers.selection_reason: PACT introduces a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for multi-agent systems, relevant to LLM agents and test-time learning strategies.
papers.title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: Multi-agent coordination substantially amplifies strategic deception, while PACT’s weak-to-strong on-policy distillation sharply reduces persistent deception in the tested setting.

papers.abstract: Computational pathology (CPath) analyses increasingly depend on multi-step computational workflows that require substantial programming expertise, limiting their accessibility to pathologists and other domain experts without extensive coding experience. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a promising natural-language interface for constructing such analyses, hallucinated operations and incorrect workflow specifications limit their reliability in scientific settings. We introduce Tissue Image Analysis Agent (TIAgent), an automated CPath workflow generation framework that, given a natural-language prompt specifying a complex analytical task together with an input dataset, automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph employing existing CPath operations. The resulting graph can be inspected and executed, enabling natural-language construction of complex CPath workflows for applications including automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis. We demonstrate end-to-end workflow generation and execution and systematically benchmark 14 backbone LLMs across 90 unit tasks spanning 18 CPath operation types. The ability of each LLM to generate a complete and correct unit workflow is quantified using Unit Workflow Success (UWS). Performance varied substantially across backbone models, with Kimi-K2.7-Code achieving the highest UWS of 0.967 (95% CI: 0.907-0.989). Analysis of node and parameter correctness further revealed that selecting the appropriate computational operation and correctly configuring it represent distinct challenges for LLM-based workflow generation. TIAgent provides a foundation for making complex CPath workflow construction more accessible while enabling systematic evaluation of LLM-driven scientific workflow generation.
authors: Aakash Madhav Rao, Mark Eastwood, Danielle Belgrave, Fayyaz Minhas
bullets: Targets the programming expertise barrier that limits access to multi-step computational pathology analyses.
Constructs computational graphs from a natural-language task and input dataset, reducing risks from hallucinated operations and invalid specifications.
Supports applications such as automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis through end-to-end workflow generation and execution.
Benchmarks 14 backbone LLMs on 90 unit tasks covering 18 computational pathology operation types.
Model performance varied substantially; the strongest reported model achieved a Unit Workflow Success of 0.967, while operation selection and parameter configuration remained distinct challenges.
papers.selection_reason: TIAgent generates complex computational workflows from natural language using LLMs, demonstrating LLM application and test-time generation capabilities.
papers.title: TIAgent: From Natural Language to Grounded Agentic Workflows for Computational Pathology
papers.tldr: TIAgent converts natural-language computational pathology tasks into inspectable, executable, and verifiable workflows using existing analysis operations.

papers.abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.
authors: Yepeng Liu, Shengmai Chen, Xuandong Zhao, Chengzhi Liu, Dawn Song, Xin Eric Wang, Yuheng Bu
bullets: Motivation: Test-time training improves scientific discovery but incurs substantial computational cost from online model-weight updates.
Method: TTME continually distills experience into external memory to guide later discovery without changing model weights.
Evaluation: TTME and TTT are compared within the same discovery framework, differing only in their test-time adaptation method.
Results: TTME outperforms TTT on all five evaluated mathematical tasks while reducing FLOPs by 82.8–84.6% and runtime by 47.7–58.4%.
Scope: Findings are demonstrated in the evaluated scientific-discovery settings.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation via evolving external memory directly fits test-time learning and LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
papers.tldr: Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME) replaces costly online weight updates with evolving external memory and outperforms test-time training on five mathematical discovery tasks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time. It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing among multiple valid recovery motions based on scene and task requirements.
Learns a recovery vocabulary linking intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback.
Uses a visual diffusion planner to predict future body-state intent and steer it with task costs.
Generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent to shape recovery execution.
Simulation shows diverse, terrain-adaptive, and steerable recoveries; real-world demonstrations are provided on a Unitree G1.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time steering of humanoid fall recovery via visual diffusion planning and task objectives, relevant to robot learning and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Test-Time Motion Steering for Perceptive Humanoid Fall Recovery
papers.tldr: RISE enables humanoid robots to steer their fall-recovery motion at test time toward task goals such as heading, rise speed, or path, without retraining.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained object (FO) manipulation requires robots to distinguish a specified FO from visually similar objects and execute actions reliably despite scene distractors. However, scene-level visual conditioning lacks explicit object selection, while category-level guidance cannot reliably distinguish FOs within the same category. We present a SAM3-guided visuomotor policy framework that addresses these challenges through persistent object memory and focused visual conditioning. First, we introduce FO Memory-driven SAM3 (FOM-SAM3), which learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view registration images, while keeping SAM3 fully frozen. Through one-vs-rest learning, these tokens encode persistent memories for localizing target FOs and rejecting similar alternatives, which can be stored in a memory bank for reuse. Second, we propose Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE), which combines in-FO appearance features with explicit bounding boxes to condition action policies, including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT). The effectiveness of the proposed FOM-SAM3 is validated on the FO-30 dataset comprising 30 physical objects across four coarse categories. Across three real-robot FO manipulation tasks, our FOM-SAM3-guided policies demonstrated robustness against distractors, discriminative ability of similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.
bullets: Targets fine-grained manipulation where scene-level or category-level guidance cannot reliably select a particular object.
FOM-SAM3 learns reusable target-object memory tokens from limited multi-view images while keeping SAM3 frozen.
FSAE combines target appearance features with bounding-box information to condition Diffusion Policy and ACT controllers.
Validated on 30 physical objects across four categories and three real-robot manipulation tasks.
The framework showed distractor robustness, discrimination among similar objects, and extension to new objects.
papers.selection_reason: Visuomotor policy for fine-grained object manipulation with reusable object memory tokens fits robot manipulation and embodied memory interests.
papers.title: Towards Fine-Grained Object Manipulation: SAM3-Guided Visuomotor Policy with Persistent Memory Learning and Focused Visual Conditioning
papers.tldr: A SAM3-guided visuomotor framework uses reusable object memories and focused visual conditioning to help robots identify and manipulate specific objects amid similar distractors.

papers.abstract: Replay-based Continual Learning mitigates catastrophic forgetting by keeping a buffer of past samples, making buffer composition critical under a fixed memory budget. Recent coreset-based replay methods improve buffer quality using model-derived gradients, losses, or auxiliary optimization, but incur substantial computational overhead as memory is repeatedly updated. We propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach for buffer construction that instead exploits the geometry of a frozen pretrained feature space using class-aware, density-weighted coverage. We evaluate CARES across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings. On Tiny-ImageNet, CARES is 2.3 to 8.8 times faster than existing coreset-based selectors. Although CARES achieves this speedup using no training signal from the continual learner, it ranks among the state of the art across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance while also attaining higher average accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet. Code will be released upon publication
authors: Arundhati S. Shanbhag, Brian B. Moser, Federico Raue, Tobias C. Nauen, Andreas Dengel
bullets: Targets the computational overhead of repeatedly updating replay buffers under fixed memory budgets.
Constructs buffers without optimizing or using training signals from the continual learner.
Uses geometric coverage of a frozen pretrained feature space, weighted by class and sample density.
Evaluated on balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy online class- and task-incremental streams.
On Tiny-ImageNet, it is 2.3–8.8× faster than coreset-based selectors and improves the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance.
papers.selection_reason: Replay exemplar selection for continual learning directly matches the continual/online learning topic.
papers.title: CARES: Coverage-Aware Replay Exemplar Selection for Continual Learning
papers.tldr: CARES efficiently selects replay exemplars using class-aware, density-weighted coverage in a frozen feature space, delivering strong continual-learning performance with substantially lower selection cost.

papers.abstract: We study strongly adaptive regret for Online Convex Optimization (OCO) with time-varying movement costs, a setting that evaluates a learner's performance over arbitrary sub-intervals. This framework captures complex sequential decision-making problems where both the environment and the cost of switching decisions fluctuate over time. We propose a novel algorithm which, for any interval $[a,b] \subseteq [T]$, achieves a data-dependent regret bound of $ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \sqrt{(D^2+DP_{[a,b]})\sum_{t \in [a,b]}(\|g_t\|^2+\lambda_t\|g_t\|)} \right) $, where $D$ is the diameter of the decision domain, $P_{[a,b]}$ is the path length of the comparator sequence over $[a,b]$, $g_t$ is the gradient of the loss, and $\lambda_t$ is the movement-cost coefficient at round $t$. Key to our approach is a novel reduction to sleeping experts with movement costs, a previously unexplored variant that is of independent interest. As a result of this development, we further establish the first strongly-adaptive guarantees under delayed feedback. Our approach also naturally extends to OCO with time-varying memory, where we obtain strongly-adaptive guarantees which improve the best-known bounds.
authors: Andrew Jacobsen, Emmanuel Esposito, Hao Qiu, Mengxiao Zhang
bullets: Addresses interval-wise performance in OCO when switching costs vary over time.
Achieves a data-dependent regret bound involving domain diameter, comparator path length, gradient magnitudes, and movement-cost coefficients.
Reduces the problem to a new sleeping-experts framework with movement costs.
Provides the first strongly adaptive guarantees for delayed feedback in this setting.
Extends to time-varying-memory OCO, improving the best-known bounds.
papers.selection_reason: Strongly adaptive online convex optimization directly fits the continual/online learning topic.
papers.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning with Time-Varying Movement Costs
papers.tldr: A new algorithm provides strongly adaptive regret guarantees for online convex optimization with time-varying movement costs, while also extending to delayed feedback and time-varying memory.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to learn from sequential tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting when historical data are no longer accessible. We study continual learning for high-dimensional sparse linear regression, where $\ell_1$ regularization creates a difficulty absent from continual ridge regression: that recursively reusing an $\ell_1$-penalized estimator can propagate earlier shrinkage and accumulate regularization bias across tasks. We propose score-preserving continual Lasso (SP-CL), which separates sparse estimation from state transmission by preserving the historical squared-loss score. Under squared loss, its cumulative estimator exactly recovers a full-history Lasso minimizer. When task coefficients coincide, it inherits the full-history sparse rate. For related task-specific coefficients, SP-CL uses a regularized current-task correction that leaves the transmitted state unchanged and attains the offline source-assisted rate under an oracle related-task condition. We also derive Overall/BWT/FWT decompositions that distinguish historical information loss, task conflict, and current-task specialization, and validate the resulting regimes in simulation.
authors: Jingyi Guo, Runze Li, Lingzhou Xue
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting in high-dimensional sparse linear regression when historical data cannot be revisited.
Introduces score-preserving continual Lasso, separating sparse estimation from transmitted state.
Exactly recovers the full-history Lasso minimizer under squared loss.
Matches the full-history sparse rate for identical tasks and the offline source-assisted rate under an oracle related-task condition.
Provides Overall/BWT/FWT decompositions and simulation-based validation of information loss, task conflict, and specialization regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Continual lasso under task shift directly addresses continual/online learning.
papers.title: Score-Preserving Continual Lasso under Task Shift
papers.tldr: SP-CL enables continual sparse regression under task shifts by preserving historical loss information, avoiding accumulated Lasso shrinkage bias, and matching key offline rates under stated conditions.

papers.abstract: Continual Wi-Fi sensing must balance plasticity, learning new rooms or users, against stability, keeping earlier ones, yet nodes often cannot retain channel state information (CSI) for privacy and storage reasons. We propose WiMoT (Wi-Fi Moment Transport), which stores the per-class feature mean and covariance of every earlier domain instead of samples. When the representation changes, stored statistics become stale. WiMoT restricts the change to an affine map on a frozen feature basis and applies the same map to the statistics, so they stay valid without old samples. Supervised contrastive learning learns the new domain, a closed-form loss on the stored statistics keeps earlier classes separable, and a Gaussian discriminant classifier, refitted from the transported statistics with equal weight per domain, predicts without domain identity. On 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, WiMoT's average final accuracies are 94.02%, 89.61%, and 95.16% with at most 0.58 percentage points (pp) of forgetting. On 3DO and Widar3.0, it also has the highest balance of new- and earlier-domain accuracy and is 3.77 and 13.11 pp ahead of the strongest of 21 baselines, which uses replay, staying ahead across domain orders and label budgets. On WiMANS, it matches the strongest replay baseline in accuracy (+0.41 pp) while reducing forgetting from 2.78 to 0.00 pp, and has the highest six-order average accuracy. Because full covariances dominate the memory, storing them as rank-32 factors shrinks the moment memory to 6.4%, losing at most 0.49 pp of accuracy, within edge-node storage budgets.
authors: Chunchun Yang, Yang Cao, Zhitang Chen
bullets: Stores each earlier domain’s per-class feature means and covariances rather than raw CSI samples.
Restricts representation updates to affine transformations on a frozen basis, applying the same transport to stored statistics.
Combines supervised contrastive learning for new domains with a closed-form statistical loss and a Gaussian discriminant classifier.
Achieves low forgetting (at most 0.58 percentage points) across 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, matching or outperforming replay baselines in reported settings.
Rank-32 covariance factors reduce moment memory to 6.4% with at most 0.49 percentage points of accuracy loss.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces replay-free continual learning via moment transport, fitting the continual and online learning subtopic.
papers.title: WiMoT: Replay-Free Continual Wi-Fi Sensing via Moment Transport
papers.tldr: WiMoT enables replay-free continual Wi-Fi sensing by transporting stored class statistics as the feature representation changes, preserving past knowledge without retaining CSI samples.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning the non-blank predictor of a factorized transducer on target-domain text improves recognition on that domain but degrades performance on the source domain. A single interpolation weight between base and adapted predictors cannot resolve this: the adapted predictor helps at some prefixes and hurts at others, often within one utterance. We propose conservative residual routing: the adapted predictor becomes a residual correction to the base, and a 16k-parameter gate decides at each prefix how much of it to admit. Closing the gate reproduces the base exactly. On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retains essentially all of the text-only gain on two held-out domains (19.89 to 16.74, 20.91 to 16.21 WER) while leaving source-domain WER unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone costs 1.08 WER. Routing needs no per-domain tuning on target-domain audio. Analysis reveals the gate does not behave as a simple domain-level switch: it modulates intervention through the disagreement between the two predictors, suppressing it in-domain and amplifying it out-of-domain.
