authors: Shashi Kumar, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Thibault Ba\~neras-Roux, Sergio Burdisso, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
bullets: Text-only fine-tuning improves target-domain recognition but can harm the source domain, and a single interpolation weight cannot resolve prefix-level conflicts.
The method treats the adapted predictor as a residual correction to the base predictor.
A 16k-parameter gate dynamically controls how much correction to apply at each prefix; closing it exactly recovers the base model.

On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retained target-domain gains while leaving source-domain WER essentially unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone degraded performance by 1.08 WER.
The gate responds to predictor disagreement rather than acting as a simple domain switch, suppressing corrections in-domain and amplifying them out-of-domain.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes residual expert routing for domain adaptation in ASR, allowing the model to dynamically switch between base and adapted predictors based on context.
papers.title: Residual Expert Routing for Text-Only Domain Adaptation of Factorized Transducer ASR
papers.tldr: A small prefix-level gate safely routes text-only domain-adaptation corrections, preserving source-domain ASR while retaining target-domain gains.

papers.abstract: Hybrid forecasting systems combining machine learning and numerical weather prediction offer a promising route toward improved forecast skill while preserving physical consistency. In this study, we investigate online learning of state-dependent model-error corrections within the Integrated Forecasting System using 4D-Var. Building on previous work, we represent model error using a neural network embedded within the forecast model and trained from observations through the data assimilation cycle. First, we introduce a targeted variant of neural-network 4D-Var in which only the neural-network parameters are estimated, while the atmospheric state is provided by a precomputed analysis. We then propose a batched extension that processes assimilation windows in random order and averages parameter increments over multiple windows, drawing inspiration from mini-batch stochastic optimization. Experiments are conducted with the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts at an intermediate resolution. Sequential online learning substantially improves forecasts within the training period, with error reductions exceeding 10%in some cases. However, these improvements fail to generalize to unseen data. In contrast, the proposed batched formulation produces hybrid models that consistently improve forecast skill in out-of-sample experiments. Larger batch sizes accelerate convergence and improve robustness by reducing the noise of parameter updates. Diagnostics further show that the online-trained corrections preserve realistic forecast variability and do not improve skill through artificial smoothing. These results demonstrate that the formulation of the online learning problem is critical for generalisation and establish batched online training as a promising framework for hybrid machine-learning/data-assimilation systems.
authors: Alban Farchi, Marcin Chrust, Massimo Bonavita, Marc Bocquet, Wei Pan, Patrick Laloyaux
bullets: Targets state-dependent model-error corrections in ECMWF’s Integrated Forecasting System using a neural network trained through 4D-Var.
Estimates only neural-network parameters while using a precomputed atmospheric analysis, then extends this with random-order mini-batch assimilation windows.
Sequential online learning improves training-period forecasts but fails to generalize to unseen data.
The batched formulation consistently improves out-of-sample forecast skill; larger batches accelerate convergence and reduce update noise.
Corrections preserve realistic forecast variability rather than gaining skill through artificial smoothing.
papers.selection_reason: Batched online learning of NN model-error corrections in a forecasting system; fits continual and online learning.
papers.title: Batched NN 4D-Var: a performant hybrid model framework for the Integrated Forecasting System
papers.tldr: Batched neural-network 4D-Var improves the generalization and robustness of online model-error correction in hybrid weather forecasting.

papers.abstract: Camera-trap species classification is dominated by large models from well-resourced organisations, which often lack the species-level distinctions regional conservation needs, such as native red versus invasive grey squirrels in the UK. We ask whether open weights let a small team with a modest dataset and a single GPU take a real part in AI development. We fine-tuned the open DeepFaune classifier on 28 UK classes, paired it with the unmodified MegaDetector v6, and compared the resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.2 with DeepFaune v1.5.0 and SpeciesNet on 20,212 hand-verified MammalWeb citizen-science images, after removing sequences sharing any of 1,039 images with our training archive. DeepFaune-UK achieved a strict image-level accuracy of 88.8%, including empty frames, against 56.5% and 59.0% for the baselines, but at DeepFaune's coarser label resolution DeepFaune v1.5.0 was more accurate, though not significantly under contributor resampling (91.4% vs. 88.8%). As DeepFaune v1.5.0 uses a newer DINOv3-based classifier, we applied the identical recipe, without new data, to that classifier. The resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.3 reached 90.6% strict accuracy, narrowed the like-for-like gap to 0.8 points and reduced roe deer misclassified as fallow deer by 69%. On 1,850 images from the 26 contributors with no overlapping images, the three DeepFaune-based models did not differ significantly (90.5%, 90.6%, 89.9% like-for-like). Fine-tuning on 10% of the training crops (about 150 per class) gave out-of-distribution accuracy similar to using all of them, and a DINOv2 run on this subset took about 22 minutes with under 4 GB of GPU memory. Open weights thus make regional model development feasible for small teams, but the largest like-for-like gain came from a newer base model trained by others, so this democratisation depends on large actors continuing to release open weights, under licences that may change.
bullets: A UK-specific model was fine-tuned for 28 classes, including native red and invasive grey squirrels, using an open DeepFaune classifier and unmodified MegaDetector.
DeepFaune-UK v1.2 reached 88.8% strict image-level accuracy, outperforming the reported baselines, but was less accurate at DeepFaune’s coarser label resolution.
Applying the same regional fine-tuning recipe to the newer DINOv3-based classifier produced 90.6% accuracy and reduced roe-deer/fallow-deer confusion by 69%.
Using only 10% of training crops produced similar out-of-distribution accuracy; one subset training run took about 22 minutes and under 4 GB of GPU memory.
The approach supports small-team regional model development, but its largest gain came from a newer model released by a larger organisation, with licensing remaining a limitation.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates efficient fine-tuning of open-weight camera-trap models for regional wildlife classification with modest data. This is a relevant case study in test-time adaptation and continual learning for embodied perception.
papers.title: Standing on Open Shoulders: Regional Fine-Tuning of Open-Weight Camera-Trap Models for UK Wildlife with Modest Data and Compute
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning open-weight camera-trap models with modest UK data and compute can deliver strong regional species classification, though progress still depends on access to newer open base models.

papers.abstract: Adapting ASR to a domain with only untranscribed audio typically relies on pseudo-labeling, a strong teacher transcribes the audio and a student is fine-tuned on it. Because supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats every pseudo-label token as a target, the student inherits the teacher's errors. We show that using the same pseudo-labels as a reward reference for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is more robust to label noise. In the banking domain, GRPO yields 29.3% to 56.2% relative WER improvements over SFT on Whisper-generated labels, and the advantage holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains and four languages. While SFT reproduces almost 100% of teacher errors verbatim, GRPO passes through only 27%. Rollout statistics explain why, erroneous pseudo-label words rarely appear in on-policy rollouts, so group-relative advantages stay aligned with the clean transcript, whereas SFT forces them into the policy's support and collapses the reward variance GRPO relies on.
authors: Shashi Kumar, Yanis Labrak, Sergio Burdisso, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
bullets: SFT makes students inherit nearly all teacher transcription errors, while GRPO passes through far fewer.
GRPO improves relative WER over SFT by 29.3%–56.2% in banking-domain adaptation using Whisper-generated labels.
The benefit holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains, and four languages.
On-policy rollouts rarely contain erroneous pseudo-label words, preserving useful group-relative reward signals.
Scope: results concern semi-supervised ASR adaptation with untranscribed audio and pseudo-label supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Applies Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to semi-supervised ASR, using pseudo-labels as rewards to improve robustness against label noise.
papers.title: Pseudo-Labels as Rewards, Not Targets: Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Semi-Supervised ASR
papers.tldr: Using pseudo-labels as reward references rather than hard targets makes GRPO substantially more robust to noisy ASR supervision than SFT.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
bullets: Uses a coarse-to-fine process: heading scoring followed by symbolic matching of observed objects, room context, and the goal prior.
Fuses phase-dependent graph scores with an LLM direction recommendation for local action selection.
Reports higher success and modestly better path efficiency than WMNav on HM3D v0.1 and MP3D.
On HM3D v0.2, the full model achieves 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL; component ablations lower both metrics.
Evaluation is limited to simulation, and episode-level rerun records are unavailable.
papers.selection_reason: The paper presents HGWM, a hierarchical system for zero-shot object navigation that integrates LLM-generated priors with persistent spatial-semantic memory. It uses a graph-matching approach to combine visual observations with language instructions, directly fitting the Vision-Language Navigation and Robot Navigation subtopics, and utilizes persistent memory for the Embodied Memory subtopic.
papers.title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
papers.tldr: HGWM improves zero-shot object navigation by combining an LLM-derived room prior with persistent graph-based spatial-semantic memory and hierarchical graph matching.

papers.abstract: Single-stage fine-tuning is pervasive, yet catastrophic forgetting persists when the source pre-training data is inaccessible. Data weighting affords a natural lever to modulate sample influence. Yet existing weighting methods lack a principled mechanism to explicitly arbitrate knowledge retention against new-task adaptation, and provide no unified differentiable objective to accommodate auxiliary signals such as sample diversity and sample characteristics. This is because current schemes privilege one goal over the other, and no explicit gradient-compatible encoding exists for such signals. To address this, we propose DRIVE, a principled and efficient weight assignment framework. It derives per-sample weights via a unified differentiable objective where three coupled signals co-evolve: Shapley additivity splits contribution into anti-forgetting and adaptation components, which are reshaped by a covariance-based diversity term and stabilized by a sample-characteristic prior. Far from a mere combination, this yields an end-to-end gradient-based scheme balancing stability against plasticity. Theoretically, we prove that DRIVE enjoys superior stability-plasticity guarantees over existing weighting schemes and enhances parameter estimation robustness. Empirically, it attains superior overall performance, faster convergence, and stronger robustness. Code at https://github.com/luciabcd/DRIVE.
authors: Qing Liu, Xinrui Chen, Yi Du, Ou Wu, Weiyao Zhu
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when source pre-training data is unavailable.
Uses a unified differentiable objective with Shapley-based anti-forgetting and adaptation components.
Incorporates covariance-based sample diversity and sample-characteristic priors into end-to-end gradient-based weighting.
Theoretical analysis establishes stability–plasticity guarantees and improved parameter-estimation robustness.
Experiments report better overall performance, faster convergence, and stronger robustness.
papers.selection_reason: Data weighting for fine-tuning with anti-forgetting and stability-plasticity trade-offs; relevant to continual learning and adaptation.
papers.title: DRIVE: Fine-tuning via Data Contribution- and Diversity-aware Weighting with Prior Regularization
papers.tldr: DRIVE assigns data weights using contribution, diversity, and prior signals to balance knowledge retention with new-task adaptation during fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of agents that mainly retrieve past records without forming causal understanding.
Combines stored causal knowledge with current evidence to build structured Causal Beliefs about factors and action effects.
Uses these beliefs for decisions and continuously updates both task beliefs and longer-term Causal Cognition.
Evaluations show causal knowledge accumulation and transfer across financial, scientific, and everyday tasks.
In financial research, it improves mean rank correlation by 25.4% over a baseline and raises prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic settings.
papers.selection_reason: LLM agent maintains and updates persistent causal knowledge over time, relevant to LLM memory and continual/online adaptation.
papers.title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
papers.tldr: CauProphet equips LLM agents with persistent, updateable causal knowledge to improve decisions and transfer learning across tasks.

papers.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.
authors: Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Introduces a seven-dataset benchmark spanning domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and five independent human labels per instance.
Evaluates annotations against human labeling distributions using Fleiss kappa rather than single-label accuracy alone.
Proposes ANT-OR, which refines prompts by distilling contrastive rules from positive and negative feedback.
Improves agreement@≥2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves near-best distributional alignment, within 2 Fleiss-kappa points of the best result.
Targets complex, evolving guidelines and reasonable annotator disagreement, especially on boundary cases.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark (ANT-A) and a multi-agent optimization framework (ANT-OR) for LLM annotation, focusing on aligning with human distributions and adapting to complex guidelines.
papers.title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
papers.tldr: ANT-A benchmarks LLM annotation against diverse human judgments, while ANT-OR improves multi-agent agreement by learning contrastive decision rules from feedback.

papers.abstract: Multi-task deep learning has been developed to ensure explainability in computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems. These systems simultaneously predict interpretable characteristics of findings in auxiliary tasks to help radiologists assess the reliability of the diagnostic prediction. However, the CAD's opinion would not be referred to when the auxiliary task prediction deviates from the radiologist's expectation. To further leverage CAD's knowledge in the above situation, we proposed a multi-task gradient assist (MGA) method that brings interactivity to multi-task models without additional training. MGA allows radiologists to give feedback to the CAD and ask for additional diagnostic suggestions. Using two datasets of mammography and CT, we show that MGA successfully improves diagnostic accuracy upon feedback on various auxiliary tasks. Compared to an existing method using forward propagation only, MGA performs more robustly and can be combined to further improve accuracy. Our method paves a promising way for integrating artificial intelligence into image diagnosis.
bullets: Addresses cases where CAD auxiliary predictions conflict with a radiologist’s expectations.
Introduces multi-task gradient assist (MGA), enabling interactive feedback without additional training.
Uses radiologist feedback to request updated diagnostic suggestions.
Improves diagnostic accuracy across auxiliary tasks on mammography and CT datasets.
MGA is more robust than a forward-propagation-only method and can be combined with it.
papers.selection_reason: Uses test-time backpropagation from an auxiliary task to incorporate radiologist feedback and improve diagnosis; matches test-time learning.
papers.title: Interactive image diagnosis using test-time backpropagation from the auxiliary task
papers.tldr: A training-free test-time backpropagation method lets radiologists guide multi-task CAD systems through auxiliary-task feedback to improve diagnosis.

papers.abstract: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.
authors: Guoyang Shi, Hongwen Li, Yiding Yu, Zhuang Fu, Siqi Ding, Zhengyuan Chen, JianGuo Chen, Hanyue Zhao, Tianyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses shot-to-shot NBI ion-source tuning when hidden operating conditions evolve and responses are nonstationary.
Combines deterministic extraction of physical and visual features, two-layer trajectory/knowledge memory, MLLM action generation, and independent feasibility checks.
In chronological replay of 455 shots across four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols outperformed waveform images alone for quality classification.
Retrieved context improved agreement with historical action directions, while visual evidence had model-dependent effects.
Demonstrates engineering feasibility for supervised sequential tuning on five ion sources; scope is limited to supervised operation and the evaluated platforms.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal agent for sequential physical instrument control with memory and action constraints; fits VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Adaptive Control of Scientific Instruments with Nonstationary Responses through Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: A physically grounded multimodal agent enables supervised, sequential tuning of nonstationary scientific instruments, achieving an 86.80% beam-extraction rate across 409 executed shots.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.
papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded memory for VLM-based robot planners that selectively retrieves frames, relevant to embodied memory, VLA, and token efficiency.
papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
papers.tldr: LogLook improves robot-planning memory by grounding it in execution logs and letting the model selectively inspect frames and demonstrations, reducing visual context while maintaining or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.
authors: Yanhao Jia, Yi Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu, Pengkun Jiao, Sihan Yang, Ming Ma, Steven Hoi, Erik Cambria
bullets: LongVideo contains about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions spanning visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning.
4DMemoryBench evaluates reasoning across diverse context lengths, targeting persistent memory over long video streams.
The 4DMemory Harness combines four skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and model-specific retrieval-augmented generation.
Across 13 leading models, the harness improves performance by over 50%, while models perform over 10% worse than on a previous benchmark.
The benchmark targets development of agents for complex, long-horizon spatiotemporal tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Long-horizon spatiotemporal memory benchmark and agents; directly relevant to embodied memory and long-video understanding.
papers.title: 4DMemory: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Memory with Harness-Augmented Agents
papers.tldr: 4DMemory introduces a long-horizon video benchmark and tool-augmented harness that substantially improves foundation-model performance on spatiotemporal reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting plays an important role in real-world applications, where probabilistic approaches provide uncertainty estimates for decision-making. Real-world systems are inherently non-stationary, leading to distribution shifts between training and test data. However, existing probabilistic methods mainly focus on modeling data distributions under standard settings, while distribution shift methods often handle such shifts in a coarse manner, failing to characterize shift degree and adapt prediction strategy accordingly. As a result, they often produce miscalibrated and unreliable forecasts. To address this issue, we propose REMIND, a retrieval-guided probabilistic framework for spatiotemporal forecasting under distribution shift. REMIND leverages retrieval to estimate how well current observation are supported by historical patterns, enabling adaptive prediction under different shift regimes. It employs spatiotemporal retrieval to construct a memory bank and introduces a dual branch architecture, combining a memory-calibrated probabilistic branch for mild shifts with a deviation-aware probabilistic branch for severe shifts. A shift-adaptive gate, guided by retrieval similarity and memory dispersion, balances the two branches according to shift degree. We further design a hierarchical Gaussian mixture to capture heterogeneous uncertainty over the dual branch predictions, and introduce a memory perturbation training scheme to improve generalization. Experiments on real-world datasets with distribution shifts demonstrate that REMIND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both forecasting accuracy and probabilistic prediction quality.
authors: Haochen Lv, Jianhao Zhang, Zhichen Lei, Yang Jiang, Xiaowei Mao, Shengnan Guo, Youfang Lin, Huaiyu Wan
bullets: Addresses miscalibrated forecasts caused by non-stationary data and varying shift severity.
Builds a spatiotemporal memory bank to measure support from historical patterns.
Combines mild-shift memory-calibrated and severe-shift deviation-aware probabilistic branches.
Uses a retrieval- and dispersion-guided gate plus hierarchical Gaussian mixtures to model uncertainty.
Experiments on real-world shifted datasets show improved forecasting accuracy and probabilistic quality over existing methods.
papers.selection_reason: Retrieval-guided adaptive forecasting under distribution shift; relevant to test-time adaptation and memory-based prediction.
papers.title: When to Trust Memory: Retrieval-Guided Probabilistic Spatiotemporal Forecasting under Distribution Shift
papers.tldr: REMIND uses retrieval-based memory to detect distribution shifts and adapt probabilistic spatiotemporal forecasts for improved accuracy and reliability.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the engineering implementation methods of the SKG inference framework and provides complete case studies across four domains. Case 1, 2D Dissipative Mechanical System: OOD MSE is 1.69 to 4.12 times lower than the best neural baseline; the state-dependent metric yields a 10^8-order improvement under controlled conditions. Case 2, Target Detection Sim-to-Real: Real-machine mAP increases from 0.2564 to 0.4964 (+24.00 points, single-run experiment, 32 images, point estimate), and AP75 increases from 0.1736 to 0.5765 (+40.29 points), with no real-machine retraining required. Case 3, Sequence Modeling sine to square: OOD MSE is 0.0296 versus Transformer 0.0641 (mean of 5 seeds, p=0.024). Case 4, Molecular Dynamics MD17: ID@100 ADE is 0.0285 versus ESTAG 0.1467; OOD@100 is 0.0316 versus 0.1411 (single seed). For each case, we present the objective, applied SKG theory, parameter settings, baseline comparison protocol, data results, and sources of advantage. Following the cases, we provide the complete methodology: pre-validation, task invariant construction, three-stage training, residual training, and the four theorems and one proposition supporting these methods. This paper not only demonstrates effective configurations of SKG across four domains but also honestly reports the variance of single-run experiments, limitations of single-seed results, negative updates caused by parameterization mismatch, and practical experience of using engineering thresholds as diagnostic signals rather than hard constraints.
authors: Jian An, Chaoshi Wu, Xinpan Luo
bullets: Covers dissipative mechanics, sim-to-real target detection, sine-to-square sequence modeling, and MD17 molecular dynamics.
Methodology includes pre-validation, task-invariant construction, three-stage and residual training, plus supporting theoretical results.
Reported gains include lower OOD error in mechanics and sequence modeling, improved real-machine detection without retraining, and lower MD17 ADE than the cited baseline.
Results include single-run, single-seed, and small-sample experiments, so several findings have limited statistical reliability.
The paper discusses parameterization mismatch, experiment variance, and using engineering thresholds as diagnostics rather than hard constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Presents engineering implementations of the SKG inference framework for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across various domains, focusing on robustness.
papers.title: SKG in Practice: OOD Generalization Cases Across FourDomains
papers.tldr: SKG is implemented and evaluated across four domains, showing promising in- and out-of-distribution performance while documenting practical limitations and diagnostic lessons.

papers.abstract: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task-specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning. We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git
bullets: Addresses the challenge of using expanding interaction histories when context capacity is limited.
Uses a frozen language model with bidirectional memory–skill learning: recurring episodes create or revise skills, while skill-guided interactions generate future memories.
Combines retrieved facts and learned procedures in the agent’s context, adapting retrieval influence based on task outcomes without rewriting stored records.
Evaluated across ten settings covering embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code.
On ALFWorld, joint memory-and-skill serving reached 63.17% success, versus 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving.
papers.selection_reason: Lifelong memory-skill co-adaptation for frozen LLM agents; fits continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: Lifelong Context Adaptation through Bidirectional Memory-Skill Learning
papers.tldr: MemCryst enables lifelong LLM agents to jointly learn and serve memories and reusable skills within bounded context windows.

papers.abstract: Class imbalance and errors near anatomical boundaries remain challenges in medical image segmentation, motivating loss functions that account for these difficulties. Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss adjusts the similarity function during training but requires hyperparameter tuning. We propose Self-Tuned Boundary-Aware t-vMF Dice Loss (STB-tvMF Dice), which adapts the function separately for boundary and interior regions without tuning shape-adaptation parameters. Each region's shape parameter of t-vMF function is determined from its mean prediction-target cosine similarity in the preceding epoch and remains fixed throughout the current epoch. This rule maximizes the slope of the similarity function at the observed mean similarity, providing a principled basis for adaptation without validation-based parameter selection. Experiments on three datasets and architectures demonstrated its effectiveness. On Synapse with U-Net, STB-tvMF Dice achieved a mean DSC of 70.75%, compared with 63.03% for Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss. Our code will be available soon.
bullets: Targets class imbalance and boundary errors in medical image segmentation.
Computes separate t-vMF shape parameters for boundary and interior regions from the preceding epoch’s mean prediction-target cosine similarity.
Keeps parameters fixed within each epoch and selects them to maximize the similarity-function slope at the observed mean similarity.
Evaluated across three datasets and architectures; on Synapse with U-Net, it achieved 70.75% mean DSC versus 63.03% for Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss.
The abstract does not specify the method’s limitations; code is planned for release.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an online adaptation mechanism for loss function parameters (shape parameters of t-vMF) based on data statistics (mean prediction-target cosine similarity) without hyperparameter tuning, fitting the online learning paradigm.
papers.title: Hyperparameter-Free Boundary-Interior t-vMF Dice Loss for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.tldr: STB-tvMF Dice is a hyperparameter-free loss that separately adapts to boundary and interior regions, improving medical image segmentation performance over an adaptive baseline.

papers.abstract: Scientific, engineering, and mathematical reasoning tasks can admit multiple valid solutions, while exhaustive annotation of the full solution set is often prohibitively costly. Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) applies reinforcement learning to unlabeled test instances, offering a label-free approach to multiple-solution reasoning. In this setting, generation frequency serves two opposing objectives: correctness estimation favors frequent outcomes, whereas outcome-level diversity preservation favors less frequent outcomes. We term this tension the \textbf{Frequency Conflict}. To resolve this conflict, we propose MS-TTRL, which obtains frequency-independent correctness estimates through Outcome-Level Self-Verification while reserving generation frequency solely for diversity preservation. Three-State Outcome Cache and the Candidate State support verification reuse across repeated observations and confidence-aware handling of ambiguous outcomes, while Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling selectively strengthens the learning signals of rare, reliably verified outcomes. Experiments across two benchmarks, four multiple-solution tasks, and three backbone models, each evaluated with five random seeds, show that MS-TTRL improves Recovery Rate by 19.13 percentage points on average over the best-performing label-free baseline and approaches the performance of the supervised IPS-GRPO.
authors: Zhixia Zhang, Binqian Xu, Huaiyang Wang, Yikun Ban, Dianbo Liu
bullets: Multiple-solution reasoning lacks exhaustive labels, motivating reinforcement learning directly on unlabeled test instances.
The method uses outcome-level self-verification to estimate correctness independently of generation frequency.
A Three-State Outcome Cache and Candidate State reuse verification and handle ambiguous outcomes with confidence awareness.
Confidence-Gated Inverse Probability Scaling amplifies learning signals for rare outcomes that are reliably verified.
Across two benchmarks, four tasks, and three backbones, MS-TTRL improves Recovery Rate by 19.13 percentage points on average over the strongest label-free baseline and nears supervised IPS-GRPO.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the frequency conflict in test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) for multiple-solution reasoning tasks, proposing a method to balance correctness estimation with diversity preservation.
papers.title: MS-TTRL: Breaking the Frequency Conflict in Multiple-Solution Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MS-TTRL resolves the conflict between correctness estimation and diversity preservation in label-free test-time reinforcement learning for tasks with multiple valid solutions.

papers.abstract: Continual survival analysis on whole-slide images (WSIs) requires models to integrate knowledge from sequentially arriving cancer cohorts while preserving previously learned information. Model merging offers a data-free alternative by combining independently fine-tuned task experts without retaining previous training data. However, the relative behavior of different merging strategies for WSI-based survival prediction remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we establish an end-to-end benchmark for data-free continual model merging, covering task-specific fine-tuning, sequential merging, and inference under both TASK-IL and CLASS-IL settings. We systematically evaluate six representative merging strategies across four TCGA cancer cohorts and three task orders using C-index, IPCW C-index, Forgetting, and Backward Transfer under a controlled protocol. Results show that no merging strategy consistently dominates across all evaluation criteria, while censoring-aware evaluation can substantially alter the relative ranking of the compared methods. This benchmark provides a unified foundation for developing and evaluating more effective continual model merging methods for WSI-based survival analysis.
authors: Vu Minh Tran, Doanh C. Bui, Ma\"i K. Nguyen, Khang Nguyen
bullets: Addresses continual survival prediction as cancer cohorts arrive sequentially without retaining prior training data.
Benchmarks task-specific fine-tuning, sequential merging, and inference under TASK-IL and CLASS-IL settings.
Evaluates six merging strategies across four TCGA cohorts and three task orders using discrimination, forgetting, and backward-transfer metrics.
Finds no strategy consistently dominates across all criteria.
Provides a unified basis for developing and evaluating improved continual model-merging methods for WSI survival analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks data-free continual model merging for sequential medical cohorts, directly within continual learning.
papers.title: Benchmarking Data-Free Continual Model Merging for Whole-Slide Image Survival Analysis
papers.tldr: A controlled benchmark shows that data-free model-merging methods for continual WSI survival analysis have trade-offs, with censoring-aware evaluation changing which strategies appear strongest.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.
authors: Dongki Kim, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Soyeong Jeong, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Addresses the expertise- and effort-intensive bottleneck of translating observations into scientific principles.
Forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships into inductive principles.
Uses the evolving hypotheses and principles to obtain new observations, revise hypotheses, and continually reconstruct principles.
Evaluated on molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction benchmarks.
Outperforms baselines based on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while producing literature-consistent principles.
papers.selection_reason: LLM framework constructs and refines scientific principles from observations at test time; fits test-time learning/optimization.
papers.title: Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery
papers.tldr: Principia is an LLM framework that iteratively turns test-time observations and causal hypotheses into refined scientific principles for discovery.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly prediction (AP) aims to estimate future anomaly risks from current observations, providing early-warning signals for proactive intervention and maintenance in complex systems. Existing unsupervised AP methods follow a perturbation-based paradigm, where predefined or random perturbations are injected into historical windows to simulate abnormal future evolution. However, these methods share perturbations across different variables and contexts, and learn deterministic history-to-future evolution. In reality, anomaly evolution is variable- and context-dependent: the same perturbation may be amplified into abnormal future dynamics in one variable or context, while being absorbed as normal fluctuation in another. In addition, future evolution is not uniquely determined by a historical window, since similar histories may lead to multiple plausible trajectories, such as gradual degradation or abrupt changes. To address these problems, we propose EVOLVE, a unified framework that models unsupervised AP via variable- and context-conditioned perturbations and uncertainty-aware future reasoning. EVOLVE constructs context-specific anomaly perturbations through an adaptive anomaly prototype memory, which can dynamically update and retrieve relevant perturbations at the variable level. EVOLVE models uncertainty by sampling multiple latent historical states and decoding through complementary smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses, and the disagreement among decoded future trajectories is used to estimate future anomaly risk. Extensive experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that EVOLVE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art anomaly prediction baselines.
authors: Jianxin Jin, Kai Zhao, Shiyan Hu, Yang Shu, Peng Chen, Meng Wang, Zhongwen Rao, Yijie Li, Jing Wang, Bin Yang, Chenjuan Guo
bullets: Addresses the limitations of shared perturbations and deterministic history-to-future assumptions in unsupervised anomaly prediction.
Uses an adaptive anomaly prototype memory to retrieve and update variable- and context-specific perturbations.
Samples multiple latent historical states and decodes them with smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses.
Estimates future anomaly risk from disagreement among the resulting possible future trajectories.
Experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets show consistent improvements over existing anomaly-prediction baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a framework for unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly prediction using uncertainty-aware future reasoning and adaptive prototype memories.
papers.title: EVOLVE: Uncertainty-Aware Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Prediction with Adaptive Prototype Memories
papers.tldr: EVOLVE predicts future multivariate time-series anomalies by combining context-specific perturbation memories with uncertainty-aware modeling of multiple possible evolutions.

papers.abstract: Non-stationarity induces test-time distribution shifts in time series forecasting (TSF), resulting in forecast residuals between predictions and the corresponding ground truth. Recent works on test-time adaptation for TSF address this by introducing lightweight calibration modules around frozen forecasters, updated using observations that become incrementally available at test time. Existing approaches typically employ channel-wise adapters, implicitly assuming that forecast residuals are inherently channel-specific. However, we observe that forecast residuals often exhibit substantial shared structure across channels, suggesting that fully independent channel-wise parameterization may be redundant. Motivated by this observation, we propose the Dual-Branch Calibration Module (DBCM), which shares adaptation capacity across channels through a shared adapter while retaining limited channel-specific flexibility through a low-rank channel-wise adapter, further enhanced by channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation. Extensive experiments show that DBCM consistently outperforms prior methods across diverse datasets, horizons, and backbones.
authors: Jaebyeong Jeon, Kunwoo Kang, Sang Yup Lee, Kibok Lee
bullets: Forecast residuals under distribution shift often share structure across channels, making fully independent channel-wise adaptation potentially redundant.
DBCM uses a dual-branch module: a shared adapter plus a low-rank channel-wise adapter.
Channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation further refine the calibration process.
Experiments across diverse datasets, forecasting horizons, and backbones show consistent improvements over prior methods.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Dual-Branch Calibration Module (DBCM) for test-time adaptation in time series forecasting, directly addressing non-stationarity and distribution shifts at inference time.
papers.title: DBCM: Dual-Branch Calibration Module for Test-Time Adaptation in Time Series Forecasting
papers.tldr: DBCM improves test-time adaptation for non-stationary time-series forecasting by combining shared and low-rank channel-specific calibration.

papers.abstract: This paper studies the problem of test-time robustness scaling for large vision-language models (LVLMs), which aims to mitigate language bias during inference. Existing approaches typically adopt test-time scaling techniques such as contrastive decoding to improve inference performance. Despite the progress, the performance of these approaches is far from satisfactory due to intentional evidence removal during perturbations and redundant inference cost. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration (MAGIC). The core of our MAGIC is to evaluate the decision margins of LVLMs to selectively activate textual and visual perturbation branches for efficient debiased inference. In particular, our MAGIC first measures the prediction margins of crucial tokens, and applies a gating function to identify low-confidence responses that are susceptible to language biases. For selected samples, we integrate the token logits from multiple textual and image perturbation branches with the original ones for debiased decision. More importantly, we selectively restore the most informative corrupted views with sharp prediction distributions for ambiguous samples after debiasing, enabling evidence recovery for discriminative decision-making. We further utilize a calibration dataset to actively identify and prune ineffective branches during contrastive debiasing for cost reduction. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed MAGIC in comparison with extensive baselines.
authors: Shunshun Gu, Enze Zhang, Ming Pei, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo
bullets: Targets language bias and inefficient inference in test-time robustness scaling for large vision-language models.
Uses token-level prediction margins to gate textual and visual perturbation branches only for low-confidence responses.
Combines logits from selected perturbations with original predictions to enable debiased decisions.
Restores informative corrupted views with sharp prediction distributions to recover evidence for ambiguous samples.
Uses calibration-based branch pruning to reduce redundant contrastive-debiasing cost; experiments on benchmark datasets support its effectiveness against baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time robustness scaling for LVLMs via contrastive debiasing, fits test-time learning.
papers.title: MAGIC: Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration for VLM Test-time Robustness Scaling
papers.tldr: MAGIC improves LVLM test-time robustness by selectively applying contrastive debiasing and restoring informative visual or textual evidence for ambiguous predictions.

papers.abstract: Regularisation-based class-incremental learning (CIL) methods control the stability-plasticity trade-off through fixed coefficients tuned offline, independently of the continual learning objective and blind to phase-specific variations in data volume, task difficulty, and class similarity. We argue this is a fundamental mismatch and propose REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning, which treats regularisation strength selection as a sequential decision problem. At each incremental phase, a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) agent observes a compact state of current performance metrics and incoming data statistics, and outputs the distillation coefficients for that phase. To respect CIL's constraint on historical data access, the policy is trained entirely on pseudo-CIL tasks constructed from the initial phase, then deployed on the incremental sequence without further adaptation. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that REDAR reduces forgetting and improves forward transfer over fixed and heuristic baselines, and that policies trained on short pseudo-task horizons transfer effectively to longer incremental runs.
authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Peyman Moghadam
bullets: Fixed regularisation coefficients can mismatch changing data volume, task difficulty, and class similarity across phases.
A lightweight RL agent observes performance and incoming-data statistics, then selects phase-specific distillation coefficients.
The policy is trained on pseudo-CIL tasks from the initial phase, avoiding access to historical data during deployment.
Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet show improvements over fixed and heuristic baselines, with transfer from short to longer pseudo-task horizons.
papers.selection_reason: RL-driven adaptive regularization for class-incremental learning; fits continual learning.
papers.title: REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: REDAR uses reinforcement learning to adapt regularisation strengths across class-incremental learning phases, reducing forgetting while improving forward transfer.

papers.abstract: In neural networks, continual learning (CL) is a prominent approach for enabling deployed systems to adapt to dynamic operational environments by effectively learning from new unseen data at runtime. Recently, the neuromorphic continual learning (NCL) concept has emerged as an energy-efficient alternative to CL by leveraging sparse event-based operations. However, NCL performance can be undermined by transient faults in the hardware platforms, which may come from high-energy particle strikes at any time. Currently, NCL reliability under transient faults has not been studied, and hence the corresponding fault-tolerance techniques remain unexplored. To address this, we propose a novel RobustNCL framework to improve NCL reliability in the presence of transient faults in the DRAM-based off-chip memory of hardware platforms through a lightweight detect-and-cure strategy. Specifically, it first monitors the presence of faults during weight data access from off-chip memory, and then cures the accessed weights if anomalous signatures are detected. It provides three curing variants: replacement with zero, min/max value, and most-probable value from the original/clean weight distribution. To support this, the weight curing values are stored in the radiation-hardened memory. Experimental results show that, in the presence of high fault rates (e.g., 5x10^{-4} for memory replay), RobustNCL maintains high accuracy close to the accuracy of fault-free models (i.e., within -0.5% accuracy for the best RobustNCL variant) and significantly improves accuracy from the baseline without fault mitigation across different NCL methods and datasets (i.e., Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100), while incurring negligible latency and energy overheads. These results highlight that our RobustNCL framework is a promising approach for enabling reliable and energy-efficient NCL systems.
authors: Rachmad Vidya Wicaksana Putra, Shuochen Zhou, Muhammad Shafique
bullets: Targets transient faults in off-chip DRAM, a previously unexplored reliability threat for neuromorphic continual learning.
Monitors weight accesses for anomalous signatures and repairs affected weights at runtime.
Supports zero, min/max, or most-probable-value replacement using values stored in radiation-hardened memory.
Across Split MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, it stays within 0.5% of fault-free accuracy in the reported high-fault setting and outperforms mitigation-free NCL.
Scope: evaluates memory-fault mitigation for NCL; effectiveness depends on the tested fault conditions and curing variant.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning methods, specifically neuromorphic continual learning under transient hardware faults.
papers.title: RobustNCL: Robustifying Neuromorphic Continual Learning under Transient Faults with Lightweight Detect-and-Cure Strategy
papers.tldr: RobustNCL improves neuromorphic continual learning reliability under transient DRAM faults using lightweight runtime detection and weight repair with negligible overhead.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) in neural networks is a promising learning approach for updating the knowledge of deployed systems based on new data encountered at run time, that have not been learned during the offline training phase. To enable their power/energy-efficient CL processing, neuromorphic continual learning (NCL) concept with sparse event-based operations have recently been introduced. However, state-of-the-art NCL methods typically employ the memory-hungry data/experience replay, coupled with costly global learning rule (i.e., backpropagation-based surrogate gradient). To address these limitations, we propose ENCL, a novel methodology that enables efficient NCL by employing a lightweight local learning rule and sub-network freezing strategy. ENCL leverages the temporally- and spatially-local learning rule to perform efficient credit assignment for training new tasks, alleviating the expensive cost of global learning rule. ENCL also employs a sub-network freezing strategy based on the given tasks to avoid the needs for network architecture expansion, hence further improving the efficiency and scalability of the NCL training process. To efficiently support this, we train each task with a small number of epochs as well as adjusted learning rate and timestep. Experiment results on task-incremental learning (TIL) scenario show that, our ENCL consistently achieves strong performance across different datasets as compared to state-of-the-art works. Specifically, ENCL achieves competitive accuracy comparable to that of the state-of-the-art data/experience replay, while reducing memory cost by up to 88%, NCL training time by up to 51%, average power consumption by up to 40%, and energy consumption by up to 65% across different benchmarking datasets (i.e., Split MNIST, Split Fashion MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100).
authors: Rachmad Vidya Wicaksana Putra, Shuochen Zhou, Hassan Raza, Muhammad Shafique
bullets: Targets the memory and computational costs of experience replay and global backpropagation-based learning in neuromorphic continual learning.
Uses temporally and spatially local learning for efficient credit assignment when learning new tasks.
Freezes task-associated sub-networks to avoid network expansion and improve scalability.
In task-incremental experiments across Split MNIST, Split Fashion MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100, it achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art replay methods.
Reports reductions of up to 88% in memory, 51% in training time, 40% in average power, and 65% in energy consumption.
papers.selection_reason: Neuromorphic continual learning with local learning rules and network freezing; fits continual learning and efficiency topics.
papers.title: ENCL: Enabling Efficient Neuromorphic Continual Learning with Local Learning Rule and Sub-Network Freezing Strategy
papers.tldr: ENCL enables more efficient neuromorphic continual learning by combining a local learning rule with task-based sub-network freezing, reducing memory, time, power, and energy costs while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
authors: Yuval Kansal, Karen Ullrich, Polina Kirichenko, Ilia Kulikov, Niraj K. Jha, Mohammad Pezeshki, Mark Ibrahim
bullets: Addresses the limits of temporary in-context reflection and costly, interference-prone full fine-tuning.
After failure, the agent reflects, extracts a lesson, distills it into a lightweight adapter, and stores it in a retrievable lesson library.
Uses frozen base weights with adapters adding about 0.02% of the base model’s parameters each.
Across GAIA, Claw-Eval, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, success rates improve by 8.9–17.0 percentage points.
Lessons reduce repeated mistakes, nearly double correction reliability, and transfer to new tasks without additional training.
papers.selection_reason: Self-directed distillation of mistakes into lightweight persistent adapters directly fits test-time and continual learning plus LLM agent-memory topics.
papers.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
papers.tldr: Self-Direction lets agents turn mistakes into persistent, reusable low-rank adapters, improving future task performance without modifying base-model weights.

papers.abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.
authors: Hariharan Devarajan, Neeraj Rajesh, Aniruddha Marathe, Nikoli Dryden, Kin Ng, Michela Taufer
bullets: Addresses the reliance on manually authored skills and curated memory, which causes agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions.
Uses a predictor–validator–corrector loop: tools and skills propose solutions, executions validate them, and outcomes refine a persistent capability store.
Learned capabilities solve recurring tasks on the first attempt in 93–95% of cases across evaluated models.
Each task produces 7.6–30.8 durable capabilities without user instruction; once capabilities exist, creation drops below two per task.
Warm-start execution uses 0.38–0.40 million tokens per task, and Phronix improves correctness and task-solving rates on evaluated workflows and models.
papers.selection_reason: Agent harness that learns, validates, and stores reusable capabilities from executions directly matches continual agent learning and persistent agent-memory topics.
papers.title: Phronix: The Capability-Centric Learning Paradigm for Agents
papers.tldr: Phronix lets agents learn reusable capabilities from their own executions, substantially improving reliability, efficiency, and performance across recurring tasks.

papers.abstract: Federated unlearning (FU) aims to remove a designated target client's influence from a trained model without the prohibitive cost of retraining from scratch. Existing methods largely treat unlearning as a post-hoc, stateless operation, overlooking that client influence is path-dependent: contributions made during training, particularly during critical learning periods (CLPs), can have disproportionate and persistent effects. Moreover, knowledge overlap and intermittent client availability make relying on all retained clients inefficient and impractical. We introduce PDF, a path-dependent client-selection framework based on the insight that retained clients are not equally valuable for unlearning. During training, PDF maintains lightweight, target-agnostic, CLP-weighted histories summarizing each client's accumulated update direction and global-model alignment. Upon an unlearning request, these histories identify and rank retained clients that are globally informative yet weakly coupled to the target, enabling retraining-based unlearning with only the top-$k$ clients over a small number of rounds. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under IID and non-IID settings show that PDF achieves effective forgetting and strong retained utility with substantially fewer retained clients. In particular, PDF achieves $0\%$ forgetting accuracy with retraining-like MIA AUC on non-IID CIFAR-10, improves retained accuracy by up to $6.91$ percentage points over the strongest competing FU baseline on CIFAR-100, and reduces communication by approximately $69\%$ and computation by $57$--$61\%$ relative to Retrain.
bullets: Client influence is path-dependent, especially during critical learning periods, so retained clients are not equally valuable for unlearning.
PDF tracks lightweight, target-agnostic, CLP-weighted histories of each client’s update direction and alignment with the global model.
When unlearning is requested, it ranks clients that are globally informative but weakly coupled to the target and retrains using only the top-k clients.
Across FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 in IID and non-IID settings, PDF preserves retained utility while using substantially fewer clients.
On non-IID CIFAR-10 it reaches 0% forgetting accuracy with retraining-like MIA AUC; relative to Retrain, it cuts communication by about 69% and computation by 57–61%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a path-dependent client selection framework for federated unlearning, which is a transferable technical idea regarding memory management and adaptation in distributed learning systems.
papers.title: Not All Retained Clients Are Equal: Client Selection for Federated Unlearning
papers.tldr: PDF selects the most useful retained clients for federated unlearning, enabling effective forgetting with much lower communication and computation than full retraining.

papers.abstract: Indoor radio map estimation (RME) is essential for wireless applications such as coverage planning, localization, and network deployment. However, most existing methods follow a supervised learning paradigm that requires costly labeled data and task-specific model training. Moreover, indoor environments involve privacy-sensitive information, such as building layouts and structures, that often cannot be centralized. To address these challenges, we make the first attempt to formulate indoor RME as a collaborative in-context learning (ICL) problem. We propose Poly-Ripple, a framework in which multiple clients perform ICL using large autoregressive vision models (LAVMs) without model updates. Each client is prompted by its private demonstrations and predicts the radio map for the same scene query. To capture the causal structure of wireless propagation outward from the transmitter (Tx), we adopt ripple-ordered autoregressive modeling. We further introduce importance-aware aggregation to exploit heterogeneous contextual knowledge distributed across clients under the context length constraint. We provide theoretical analysis and conduct extensive experiments on a public indoor RME benchmark. The experimental results show that Poly-Ripple consistently outperforms representative ICL baselines, while aligning with our theoretical analysis.
bullets: Reframes indoor radio map estimation as a collaborative in-context learning task, reducing reliance on centralized labeled data and task-specific training.
Uses large autoregressive vision models without model updates; each client predicts a shared scene’s radio map from private demonstrations.
Applies ripple-ordered autoregressive modeling to reflect wireless propagation outward from the transmitter.
Introduces importance-aware aggregation to combine heterogeneous client context under limited context length.
Theory and experiments on a public benchmark show consistent improvements over representative in-context learning baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Formulates indoor radio map estimation as a collaborative in-context learning problem, utilizing large autoregressive vision models without model updates, fitting Test-Time Learning.
papers.title: Collaborative In-Context Learning for Indoor Radio Map Estimation
papers.tldr: Poly-Ripple enables privacy-aware, collaborative indoor radio map estimation by combining clients’ private examples with frozen vision-language models.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
bullets: Frozen perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical signals and post cited evidence to a shared board.
An integration agent combines observations with retrieved examples, while a critic may request one revision.
Deterministic verification checks citation validity and whether final emotion claims are entailed by the evidence.
Failures are attributed to components and failure types, then converted into validated targeted prompt patches.
On MER2025, targeted adaptation improves F-score by 0.6–2.2 points across four MLLMs, including 52.3→54.5 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
papers.selection_reason: Applies an agentic framework with prompt-space adaptation to multimodal emotion reasoning using frozen MLLMs, fitting both Multimodal Foundation Models and Test-Time Learning.
papers.title: An Agentic Approach with Evidence-Grounded Verification for Multimodal Emotion Reasoning in Conversation
papers.tldr: An evidence-grounded agentic pipeline diagnoses multimodal emotion-reasoning errors and adapts prompts without updating model weights.

papers.abstract: Continual learning enables vision systems to adapt to ever-changing data distributions. Despite significant advances, existing approaches fail to capture continuous and concurrent shifts in classes and domains, a critical capability for real-world deployment. This work introduces Online VIL (Online Versatile Incremental Learning), a novel scenario where class concepts and visual domains evolve simultaneously online without explicit boundaries. To better adapt to the challenges of such dynamic environments that more closely resemble real-world conditions, we propose a novel framework TopFlow, Topology preservation with Flow matching representation that contains two complementary mechanisms: Domain-agnostic Flow Matching (DFM) and Global Topology Preservation (GTP). DFM guides the model to have domain-agnostic representations by integrating the geodesic flow kernel into contrastive learning. In contrast, GTP maintains the global structure of the feature space without explicitly storing past examples. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that TopFlow effectively addresses the limitations of existing methods within the Online VIL scenario, achieving state-of-the-art performance in challenging Online VIL. The proposed methods suggest potential directions for building continual learning systems in realistic dynamic environments. Our implementation code is available at https://github.com/KU-VGI/Online-VIL.
bullets: Introduces Online Versatile Incremental Learning (Online VIL), where class concepts and domains evolve concurrently without explicit task boundaries.
Combines Domain-agnostic Flow Matching (DFM) with Global Topology Preservation (GTP).
