DFM uses geodesic flow kernels within contrastive learning to learn domain-agnostic representations.
GTP preserves global feature-space structure without storing past examples.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for the challenging Online VIL setting.
papers.selection_reason: Online class- and domain-agnostic incremental learning with flow matching fits continual and online adaptation research.
papers.title: Online Versatile Incremental Learning: Towards Class and Domain-Agnostic Adaptation at Any Time
papers.tldr: TopFlow enables continual vision models to adapt online to simultaneous, boundary-free changes in both classes and visual domains.

papers.abstract: Test-time language models adapt a compact memory while processing the input sequence. This perspective encompasses nonlinear fast-weight learning in LaCT, associative delta-rule updates in DeltaNet, and generalized delta-rule state updates in RWKV-7. Training these models to predict the next token does not explicitly require a fact to remain accessible after many subsequent memory updates. We study delayed supervision for this test-time memory: during post-training, ask a simulator-grounded question only after a long interval of unrelated events, and supervise its answer alongside ordinary next-token prediction. Questions are evaluated on disposable branches, so their answers never enter the continuing event stream. The construction distinguishes retention from revision: a retained fact must remain valid throughout the delay, whereas a revised fact must be answered with its latest value. We evaluate this approach on LaCT-760M and plain DeltaNet-1.3B using TextWorld training trajectories and shared BABILong and RULER evaluation panels, and include a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison. Relative to event-only training, delayed QA improves BABILong by 5.48 percentage points for LaCT and 1.32 points for DeltaNet, and single-needle RULER by 1.45 and 3.27 points, respectively. The RWKV-7 comparison reports gains of 4.60 and 7.00 points on its own panels. These results support delayed semantic supervision as a practical outer training objective for usable test-time memory, while leaving open how much of the benefit derives specifically from delay rather than general question-answering and answer-termination supervision.
bullets: Targets a gap in next-token training: facts need not remain accessible after many memory updates.
Supervises simulator-grounded QA after long delays, using disposable branches so answers do not alter the event stream.
Separately tests retention of unchanged facts and revision to a fact’s latest value.
Improves BABILong and single-needle RULER performance for LaCT and DeltaNet; a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison also shows gains.
The study does not isolate how much improvement comes from delay versus general QA and answer-termination supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Delayed supervision for test-time memory in language models directly addresses inference-time adaptation and persistent LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Delayed Supervision for Test-Time Language Models
papers.tldr: Delayed question-answer supervision improves test-time language models’ ability to retain and revise facts across long sequences of unrelated events.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating Bayesian physiological modeling with optimal control strategies to achieve uncertainty-aware, personalized hemodynamic regulation during fluid resuscitation. An uncertainty-aware variational autoencoder state-space model (UVAE-SSM) was first developed to capture the dynamical relationship between mean arterial pressure (MAP) and fluid infusion using limited data, while explicitly modeling aleatoric uncertainty (i.e., randomness in the measurements, such as sensor noise). Then, a Bayesian nonlinear state-space model (BNSSM) was developed by utilizing Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to capture epistemic uncertainty arising from physiological and patient-specific variability, enabling the creation of a virtual patient generator (VPG). Building on this uncertainty-aware modeling framework, a stochastic radial basis function model predictive control (sRBF-MPC) algorithm was designed to track the MAP target while satisfying physiological constraints. Finally, an online fine-tuning algorithm was developed to adapt the nominal UVAE-SSM using streaming VPG data, enabling progressive personalization during closed-loop therapy. Simulation results across unseen animal subjects and an independent human clinical dataset demonstrated the strong predictive accuracy and cross-population generalizability of the UVAE-SSM and BNSSM models. Closed-loop evaluations confirmed that the proposed sRBF-MPC framework achieved stable MAP regulation while providing better risk-aware control compared to quadratic MPC (Q-MPC) and stochastic quadratic MPC (sQ-MPC). Overall, the proposed framework accounts for inter- and intra-patient variability through online model adaptation, offering a promising step toward uncertainty-aware, personalized hemodynamic modeling and control in critical care.
bullets: Models MAP–fluid infusion dynamics from limited data while representing measurement noise and physiological uncertainty.
Uses Bayesian neural networks to generate virtual patients and support risk-aware control.
Applies stochastic radial basis function model predictive control to track MAP targets under physiological constraints.
Online fine-tuning adapts the model using streaming virtual-patient data for progressive personalization.
Simulations on unseen animal subjects and an independent human dataset showed predictive generalizability and stable closed-loop MAP regulation versus quadratic MPC approaches.
papers.selection_reason: Online Bayesian model fine-tuning from streaming data for personalized control; transferable to test-time and continual learning.
papers.title: Adaptive Uncertainty-Aware Modeling and Stochastic Radial Basis Function Predictive Control for Personalized Fluid Resuscitation
papers.tldr: An uncertainty-aware, adaptive modeling and control framework personalizes fluid resuscitation by regulating mean arterial pressure under physiological and patient-specific variability.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance, AI agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments to tackle complex sequential tasks (e.g., document processing, cross-application collaboration), relying heavily on actions ranging from GUI operations to semantic APIs. However, three core challenges persist: the "scale dilemma" of massive tool ecosystems exceeding LLM context windows, the "non-stationarity" of tool quality due to updates or outages, and the "heterogeneity" of feedback formats (pixels, text, structured data) creating information silos. To address these, we propose AnyAct, a universal action layer that unifies available capabilities into a self-evolving action space, enabling agents to operate efficiently and reliably in large-scale, dynamic tool ecosystems. AnyAct's core design focuses on two objectives: constructing this action space via hierarchical progressive retrieval (filtering task-relevant actions) and test-time reliability evolution (pruning unreliable actions), and enabling reliability-aware action orchestration through a heterogeneous observation grounding module that unifies multi-modal feedback. Additionally, it defines a hybrid action space (primitive + semantic actions) and optimizes for a balance between task success rate and execution cost. Evaluations on LiveMCPBench and OSMCP (a new benchmark we developed for multi-granularity action collaboration) demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. AnyAct delivers substantial performance gains over baseline methods across various LLM base models on LiveMCPBench and improvements are particularly notable for models with constrained native capabilities. On OSMCP, it achieves 77.27% overall success with only 50 steps, which is half the steps required by most competitors.
bullets: Addresses tool-scale limits, changing tool reliability, and incompatible feedback across GUI, API, visual, textual, and structured interfaces.
Builds a self-evolving action space using hierarchical progressive retrieval and test-time pruning of unreliable actions.
Combines primitive and semantic actions with heterogeneous observation grounding for reliability-aware orchestration.
Balances task success with execution cost in dynamic, multi-tool environments.
Reports state-of-the-art results on LiveMCPBench and 77.27% success on OSMCP using 50 steps, notably benefiting models with limited native capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving action space with test-time reliability pruning is transferable to deployment-time adaptation for agents.
papers.title: AnyAct: Universal Action for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.tldr: AnyAct helps LLM agents act reliably in large, changing tool ecosystems by dynamically selecting, evaluating, and coordinating heterogeneous actions.

papers.abstract: We consider online prediction from experts, a fundamental problem in machine learning, under differential privacy constraints. Existing private algorithms achieve near-optimal regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the time horizon. However, this bound becomes suboptimal when $L^\star$, the cumulative loss of the best expert, is significantly less than $T$. In this work, we present the first differentially private algorithm with regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{L^\star})$, offering a substantial improvement in the low-loss regime. Our regret bound matches the non-private lower bound up to poly-logarithmic factors for constant privacy parameters, demonstrating that privacy incurs only a small cost in this setting. Our result assumes that the input sequence is oblivious, i.e., it is fixed in advance and independent of the algorithm's outputs. We also prove that an $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{T})$ regret is inevitable for adaptively generated inputs, even when $L^\star = 0$.
bullets: Addresses the gap between existing private regret bounds of ~O(√T) and easier low-loss cases.
Introduces the first private algorithm with regret ~O(√L⋆) for oblivious input sequences.
For constant privacy parameters, this matches the non-private lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors.
Shows that adaptive inputs necessarily incur ~Ω(√T) regret, even when the best expert has zero loss.
Scope: the improved low-loss guarantee assumes the sequence is fixed in advance and independent of algorithm outputs.
papers.selection_reason: Private online prediction from experts with improved small-loss regret; fits configured online-learning and adaptation interests.
papers.title: Private Online Prediction from Experts with Small Losses
papers.tldr: A differentially private online prediction algorithm achieves near-optimal regret scaling with the best expert’s loss, while adaptive inputs still require horizon-dependent regret.

papers.abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
bullets: Memory gains were highly sensitive to which warmup experiences were sampled: retrieval systems beat No-Memory in only 1 of 10 pools.
A single 15-token caution instruction matched the collision-only benefit of retrieval, and caution-aware metrics removed the rulebook’s apparent lead.
More sophisticated memory representations showed no robust advantage in this evaluation.
Baseline implementation quality and uncontrolled prompts could reverse the reported conclusion about whether memory helps.
The study releases the testbed, audited ports, random seeds, and caches; findings are scoped to this testbed and decisive model setting.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled evaluation of experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents directly connects embodied decision-making with environment-grounded memory.
papers.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
papers.tldr: In one audited HighwayEnv testbed, apparent benefits from experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents largely vanish under resampled warmup pools and token-matched filler controls.

papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.
authors: Ali Najar, Hosein Hasani, Amir Kooshan Fattah, Yasamin Rajabi, Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring unseen tasks from long interaction histories without the quadratic cost of full-trajectory transformer attention.
Uses a causal neural memory for fine-grained, within-episode adaptation and episode-level summaries for long-range task inference.
Supports test-time training and adaptation to unseen tasks and task families.
Achieves over 50% success on held-out Meta-World ML10/45 environments with low training and wall-clock budgets.
Outperforms transformer baselines on long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks through more structured exploration.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning, using neural memory to handle long interaction histories. This fits the Adaptation and Memory topic, specifically test-time learning and embodied memory.
papers.title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: METTA enables efficient long-context meta-reinforcement learning by combining linear-time within-episode memory with compact cross-episode task summaries for test-time adaptation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $\pi_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.
authors: Atiksh Bhardwaj, Edward W. Duan, Junwon Seo, Prithwish Dan, Wei-Chiu Ma, Andrea Bajscy, Preston Culbertson
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable runtime monitoring of VLA policies without continuous human supervision.
Trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate execution progress and flag deviations.
Evaluated with the open-source π₀.₅ VLA on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Competitive with or better than VLM-based monitors and methods trained with failure data for task-failure detection.
Scope: focuses on monitoring execution progress using internal activations rather than preventing failures directly.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Progress Probes P2, a lightweight method for runtime monitoring of VLA models using internal activation probes, enabling inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Progress Probes use lightweight linear probes of a VLA’s internal activations to detect when manipulation tasks are going off-course, avoiding external VLM monitors.

papers.abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.
bullets: Directly estimates a query point’s state, derivatives, and admissible bounds from nearby samples.
Formulates these quantities as latent variables in a constrained local optimisation problem, replacing long global training.
Theoretically provides finite-sample coverage and converges to the true state and derivatives under dense, noiseless sampling.
On six nonlinear benchmark functions, it outperformed Gaussian processes on noiseless data, especially with denser samples.
Prediction after data updates was substantially faster than GP and neural networks, but the advantage applies mainly when few predictions are needed between updates.
papers.selection_reason: On-demand local regression that avoids global training and gives fast first predictions after data updates; relevant to test-time optimization and efficient inference.
papers.title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
papers.tldr: Diona performs local, training-free regression with uncertainty bounds, offering fast updates and strong accuracy under dense sampling.

papers.abstract: Individual preferences often become visible only after deployment, when a user accepts one decision or revokes it in favor of another. Jev-style typed interfaces make this feedback explicit by identifying the selected action and, under revocation, the decision it replaces. We study how these consequences persist across requests as Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback (Jev-DLC). Jev-DLC treats each correction as both evidence about a recurring action identity and a directed relation between the preferred and rejected choices. It preserves these signals in complementary bounded channels above a frozen scorer and combines their scores to shape the next decision. The method retains no raw interaction history, adds no scorer call, and performs no runtime language-model backward pass. We also introduce TCPA-Bench, a chronological suite that credits a correction only through its effect on later decisions. On TCPA-Repeat, Jev-DLC reaches 44.83% user-macro accuracy overall, 2.43 points above Recent-4 history replay. After at least two earlier feedback events, it reaches 56.07%, a 7.54-point margin over the strongest reported comparison at this depth. These results show how explicit typed corrections can become compact causal state for continual personalization.
authors: Yangyang Feng, Jianle Gan, Zhuoyan Feng, Chengwei Qin
bullets: Models each correction as evidence about a recurring action and a directed preferred-versus-rejected relation.
Stores these signals in bounded channels above a frozen scorer and combines them for future decisions.
Requires no additional scorer call or runtime language-model backward pass.
On TCPA-Repeat, achieves 44.83% user-macro accuracy overall, 2.43 points above Recent-4 replay.
After at least two prior feedback events, reaches 56.07%, a 7.54-point margin over the strongest reported comparison at that depth.
papers.selection_reason: Online decision-level continual learning from explicit typed user corrections, directly matching continual and online adaptation.
papers.title: Jev-DLC: Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback
papers.tldr: Jev-DLC turns typed user corrections into compact, persistent causal state for continual personalization without storing raw history or retraining the scorer.

papers.abstract: A conventional embodied agent in an indoor environment builds a map by accumulating noisy real-world measurements and results from heavy inference to guide navigation. While the detailed measurements may differ due to scene changes or sensor settings, the unique topological structure of navigable passages or the connectivity between rooms may provide training-free guidance that complements local observations. We propose a sparse topometric graph as an efficient structural representation for robust indoor navigation, alleviating the need for fine-grained matching, which is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and prone to real-world variations. The map consists of nodes that encode local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges that capture traversable connectivity. A learned graph-matching network finds consistent subgraph structures across sessions by considering both node-level geometric descriptors and neighborhood connectivity. The holistic contextual matching is robust to local ambiguities caused by weak distinctiveness or repetitive structure, and establishes stable correspondences despite local scene changes, different sensor modalities, or limited spatial overlap. We analyze the practicality of the graph through cross-session point-goal navigation, where a goal specified in a prior reference map must be reached from an unknown initial pose in a later session. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest success rates (77.1% on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes), while reducing memory by more than two orders of magnitude compared to point-level representations. The proposed approach further supports cross-session alignment and goal-directed navigation with strong scalability and robust real-world transfer.
authors: Eun Sun Lee, Minkyun Seo, Gwangtak Bae, Junho Kim, Seunggu Kang, Jaesik Park, Young Min Kim
bullets: Represents indoor maps with nodes for local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges for traversable connectivity.
Uses learned graph matching over geometric descriptors and neighborhood structure to establish correspondences across sessions.
Handles local ambiguities, scene changes, different sensor modalities, and limited spatial overlap without training-specific fine-grained matching.
In cross-session point-goal navigation, achieves 77.1% success on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes.
Reduces memory use by more than two orders of magnitude versus point-level representations.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse topometric graph memory and graph-matching for cross-session indoor navigation, fitting robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: A Sparse Topometric Graph for Scalable Cross-Session Indoor Navigation
papers.tldr: A sparse topometric graph enables scalable, robust cross-session indoor navigation by matching room connectivity and local geometry instead of fine-grained measurements.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.
authors: Xun Sun, Thanh Thi Nguyen, Thuy-Trang Vu
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting, loss of plasticity, context limits, and lossy compression in continual learning.
Refines reusable harness skills and stores high-residual examples in bounded memory.
Uses dual-anchor, drift-constrained distillation to internalize experience without excessive parameter drift.

On the 25-stage TRACE+17 stream under fixed memory and compute, matches the strongest parametric baseline for new-task acquisition while achieving the least forgetting and strongest general-capability retention.
papers.selection_reason: Hybrid continual learning with recursive distillation and bounded memory directly addresses continual and online learning under adaptation and memory.
papers.title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning
papers.tldr: HERD combines evolving in-context harnesses with drift-constrained distillation to learn continually while minimizing forgetting and preserving general capabilities.

papers.abstract: GUI agents aim to automate complex user tasks by interacting with mobile interfaces, but ef- fective decision-making in long-horizon set- tings requires reusing prior experience rather than relying solely on the environment ob- servations. Existing memory-based methods typically store experience either at the single- action level or as entire trajectories. Single- step actions are often too fine-grained to carry meaningful semantics, since the success of an individual action does not necessarily imply progress towards the overall goal. In contrast, whole trajectories are often too coarse-grained and difficult to reuse across different tasks. We propose a subgoal-aware memory graph that distils past trajectories into structured, reusable evidence at the level of subgoals. We define a subgoal as consecutive actions shar- ing a single intent, the granularity at which progress toward the task becomes meaning- ful. To reduce redundancy and support cross- task reuse, we organise subgoal experiences as nodes in a graph, where related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved based on the environment observation. On SPA-Bench, our method improves success rate by 11.11% over the baseline.
authors: Dezhao Luo, Daniel Beechey, Derek Yuen, Weilin Luo
bullets: Single-action memories are too fine-grained, while whole-trajectory memories are too coarse and hard to reuse.
The method defines subgoals as consecutive actions sharing one intent.
Past trajectories are distilled into graph nodes representing reusable subgoal experiences.
Related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved using the current environment observation.
Evaluation on SPA-Bench shows an 11.11% success-rate improvement over the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes subgoal-level memory graph for reusing interaction experience in GUI agents.
papers.title: Subgoal-aware Memory Graph for GUI Agent
papers.tldr: A subgoal-aware memory graph helps GUI agents reuse meaningful segments of past experience for long-horizon mobile tasks, improving SPA-Bench success by 11.11% over a baseline.

papers.abstract: Long egocentric videos pose a central challenge for multimodal language models: the visual stream must be compressed into a memory representation that can be searched efficiently while still preserving the evidence needed for question answering. Building on an online textual-memory framework in which first-person videos are converted into temporally grounded captions, this work systematically studies the role of retrieval in episodic-memory video question answering. We evaluate how different retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking strategies affect multiple-choice answering on QAEgo4D-Closed, isolating retrieval as the main variable while keeping the underlying generated memory fixed. Our best configuration, Parent, matches fine-grained caption subchunks, then provides their full parent captions to the reasoner. It achieves 56.4 % accuracy, matching strong full-memory and retrieval baselines while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time. More importantly, our analysis shows that better temporal coverage does not necessarily translate into better answers: increasing the retrieval budget improves temporal Hit@K and Recall@K, but can reduce accuracy by introducing visually plausible distractors and uncertain caption evidence. These findings suggest that retrieval-augmented egocentric memory should not be optimized only for evidence recall, but also for the reliability, specificity, and answer-discriminative value of the retrieved context. The study motivates more structured episodic memories that move beyond raw caption retrieval toward evidence-aware representations for long-form egocentric reasoning.
authors: Raffaele Cali, Giuseppe Lando, Rosario Forte, Antonino Furnari
bullets: Evaluates retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking while keeping the generated textual memory fixed.
The best setup, Parent, retrieves fine-grained caption subchunks but gives their full parent captions to the reasoning model.
Parent reaches 56.4% accuracy while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time.
Larger retrieval budgets improve temporal Hit@K and Recall@K but can hurt accuracy by adding distractors and uncertain evidence.
Results motivate structured, evidence-aware episodic memories beyond raw caption retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Studies retrieval-augmented textual memory for egocentric video QA, directly relevant to embodied memory and learning from egocentric video.
papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Online Textual Memory for Episodic Memory Video Question Answering
papers.tldr: A systematic study shows that effective retrieval for episodic video QA depends on reliable, answer-discriminative evidence—not merely broader temporal coverage.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
authors: Chenyuan Chen, Ran Ding, Lechen Zhang, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
bullets: Addresses non-Markovian manipulation scenes where important visual cues disappear or leave view.
Uses SAM3 to track objects and select key event frames within an adaptive memory budget.
An action expert reads selected frames via cross-attention alongside object tokens encoding appearance, geometry, and time.
Introduces HuMeGo, a benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
Raises success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot; also improves SIMPLE tasks from 70.2% to 86.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLA humanoid manipulation, relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: WholeBodyMem improves humanoid loco-manipulation by selectively remembering task-relevant object events from before the robot acts.

papers.abstract: Our previous analysis found that a model's native hashed N-gram table is where continual updates disturb the base least, but its writes needed backpropagation and changed the pretrained table. We present Delta N-gram, a forward-only write path into that table. The pretrained table T^0 is never modified. Evidence is written into a sparse patch \Delta on the rows it addresses: a 4.1M-parameter writer emits a target and a gate per (position, hash head) event, and a block-averaged delta rule keeps each row a convex combination of its old value and the gated targets. The writer is trained offline on raw text with the pretraining objective; at use time writing takes forward passes only, and clearing \Delta restores the original model. A 0.6B prototype trained to answer questions keeps 16/16 facts after a second write; online gradient writes keep 2--4/16. We study two writers: a plain writer that encodes evidence with the T^0-only model, and a delta writer that reads its current memory while encoding. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the plain writer's memory is document-specific: on 64 held-out news events it lowers continuation NLL by 0.068 nats/token against empty memory and by 0.024 against another document's memory, and 0.063 and 0.013 after 16 intervening articles. The delta writer's memory is more document-specific and keeps more of it under distraction (70% vs 54%). Over 35,000 writes on our previous seven-task chain both writers stay stable and the delta writer drifts less (layer-2 math drift 176% vs 188%); later accuracy changes by -0.26/-0.52pp (-7.29pp for gradient updates) and small-k_i drift is 17.9/17.5% (39.2%). Acquisition is negative, and general-input drift reaches 32.8% (20.75%): format rows read by every example grow to 4--12 times their pretrained norm. Zeroing eight such rows removes over 98% of layer-2 drift on math inputs, together with their NLL gain.
bullets: Writes target and gated values into a sparse patch Δ while leaving the pretrained table unchanged; clearing Δ restores the original model.
A 4.1M-parameter writer is trained offline with the pretraining objective, so inference-time memory updates require only forward passes.
In a 0.6B prototype, it retained all 16/16 facts after a second write, compared with 2–4/16 for online gradient writes.
The learned memory is document-specific and remains more robust under distraction, with the delta writer retaining 70% versus 54% for the plain writer.
Across 35,000 writes, stability was substantially better than gradient updates, but frequent format rows accumulated large drift; zeroing eight rows removed over 98% of layer-2 math drift.
papers.selection_reason: Forward-only continual writing into a language model's native memory; directly relevant to continual learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: Delta N-gram: Forward-Only Continual Writing into a Language Model's Native N-gram Memory
papers.tldr: Delta N-gram enables forward-only continual writing into a frozen language model’s native N-gram memory using a reversible sparse patch.

papers.abstract: Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts face a practical question in unseen regions: can they rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the planner itself adapt? We study this question using a planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none of eight test-time routing schemes improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default, which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an oracle that selects the best expert for each scene reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 m. In contrast, reward-based fine-tuning on just 20 target-region scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean offset of 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 m for the static default. Comparisons under the same target-region training budget show that target-region training drives the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning across training cities also improves open-loop offsets, although closed-loop performance deteriorates. Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate trajectories. These results show the limited headroom for selecting among existing experts and the greater open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
authors: Yun Li, Ehsan Javanmardi, Simon Thompson, Jiachen Gong, Qunli Zhang, Zifan Zeng, Shiming Liu, Peng Wang, Yidu Zhang, Manabu Tsukada
bullets: Across three held-out maps, none of eight routing schemes beats the static default in fleet-mean lateral offset.
Even oracle expert selection improves mean offset by only 0.9 m.
Reward-based fine-tuning on 20 target-region scenes reduces matched offset from 12.4 m to 6.9 m with joint replay.
Target-region training drives the gains, while replay helps limit forgetting on original operating domains.
Some adaptation baselines achieve low offsets through degenerate trajectories; nuPlan results show open-loop gains but closed-loop deterioration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies routing versus adaptation for diffusion planners, with test-time adaptation and target-domain fine-tuning for navigation planning.
papers.title: To Route or to Adapt? Multi-Expert Diffusion Planners in Unseen Regions
papers.tldr: Adapting a diffusion planner with limited target-region training substantially outperforms routing among existing domain experts in unseen regions, though closed-loop performance may worsen.

papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed in high-stakes roles such as therapy, education, and personal assistance, their social cognition must be assessed reliably. Current Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks report aggregate scores that conflate two distinct competencies: explicit ToM (recognizing what someone believes) and applied ToM (using that belief to predict behavior). Building on this distinction, we investigate the gap and its recoverability using four structurally diverse benchmarks. Aggregate reporting obscures uneven competence: on SimpleToM, Llama-3.1-8B scores 51.5 percent overall while recognizing mental states at 99.4 percent and predicting behavior at only 28.9 percent. To assess recovery, we compare structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and our proposed Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters on answered support questions through action reconstruction. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GPT-oss-20B, recovery depends on the model, task, and intervention. On SimpleToM, reminders combined with BSTTT improve Llama's behavior prediction by 40.8 percentage points; reminders account for most of the overall improvement, with BSTTT adding 1.3 to 5.5 points beyond reminders across models. Contextual examples often outperform weight updates, while BSTTT remains stronger in specific model-benchmark settings. Temporal belief tracking remains difficult despite partial recovery. These findings show that aggregate ToM scores can overstate applied competence while hiding performance recoverable through targeted assistance. We recommend decomposed reporting of explicit and applied accuracy alongside intervention comparisons that establish which failures are recoverable and under what conditions.
authors: Prajvi Saxena, Sabine Janzen, Wolfgang Maass
bullets: Aggregate ToM scores can hide a large gap between identifying mental states and applying them to predict behavior.
The study evaluates this gap and its recoverability across four structurally diverse benchmarks.
It compares structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters using action reconstruction.
Recovery varies by model and task: reminders often drive most gains, while BSTTT provides additional improvements in selected settings.
Temporal belief tracking remains difficult, motivating separate reporting of explicit and applied ToM accuracy and intervention effects.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces test-time training for belief-state adaptation in LLMs, fitting test-time learning.
papers.title: Diagnosing the Explicit-to-Applied Theory of Mind Gap in LLMs
papers.tldr: LLMs often recognize others’ beliefs but struggle to use them for behavior prediction, and targeted prompting or lightweight adaptation can partially recover this applied Theory of Mind ability.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can evolve by learning from accumulated experience. Existing approaches extract reusable external knowledge, such as skills and memories, from experience to guide subsequent task solving, with some further internalizing this knowledge through model training. However, different ways of analyzing and transforming the same experience can yield knowledge with substantially different utility, even when the resulting guidance appears reasonable. Inspired by consistency regularization, we identify consistent utility gains across different ways of analyzing the same experience, rather than relying on any single way of analyzing it. We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized knowledge-model co-evolution. It constructs evolution views by perturbing how the same experience is analyzed, producing different knowledge candidates. Knowledge updates are then guided by common gain, which accounts for utility gains and their consistency across views. During model evolution, self-distillation internalizes the evolved knowledge alongside reinforcement learning, using knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation as a contrastive reference. The two processes interleave, with model updates driving further knowledge evolution. Experiments across diverse domains show that SPLICE outperforms knowledge evolution and model training baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points in average accuracy, while its evolved knowledge reduces output tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.
authors: Sirui Chen, Zhining Liu, Chao Zhang, Jingrui He, Zheng Li
bullets: Addresses the unreliability of deriving useful knowledge from a single interpretation of experience.
Perturbs experience analysis to create multiple evolution views and candidate knowledge updates.
Uses common gain to favor utility improvements that are consistent across views.
Interleaves self-distillation and reinforcement learning to internalize evolved knowledge, using consistently harmful knowledge as a contrastive reference.

Across diverse domains, improves average accuracy by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points over knowledge-evolution and model-training baselines, respectively; also reduces tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.
papers.selection_reason: Agent knowledge-model co-evolution from accumulated experience fits continual/online adaptation and learning.
papers.title: Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization
papers.tldr: SPLICE co-evolves external knowledge and LLMs by selecting knowledge improvements that consistently help across multiple analyses of the same experience.

papers.abstract: Domain generalization (DG) aims to improve the generalization of the model to any unseen domains. Targeting this goal, existing DG methods mainly focus on learning domain-invariant features or prompts from the given source domains. However, these methods rely on source-domain data, and collecting and annotating large-scale single- or multi-source datasets is often infeasible, limiting the practical applicability of DG. To tackle this challenge, we propose {\underline{Do}}main \underline{P}rompt Learning (DoP), a method built on a large vision-language model (e.g., CLIP) for zero-shot domain generalization, which recognizes unseen classes in unseen target domains without access to source-domain data. DoP essentially learns the target domain knowledge via prompt both in text and visual modalities to overcome the domain shift in text-visual modalities under the test-time adaptation formulation. Specifically, DoP first takes text domain learning (TDL) to simulate various distribution shifts by learning diverse style tokens implicitly in the text space with inter-style diversity loss and intra-style consistency loss. Subsequently, DoP employs visual domain learning (VDL) to further refine the target-domain-relevant style token generated by TDL by making use of the test visual data with self-supervised learning. Extensive experiments on popular DG benchmark datasets (e.g., PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet) and ImageNet show that our DoP consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art DG approaches. Codes are available at: https://github.com/shiming-chen/DoP.
authors: Shiming Chen, Shuhuang Chen, Salman Khan, Fahad Shahbaz Khan
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of source-data-dependent domain generalization when labeled source datasets are unavailable.
Learns target-domain knowledge through text and visual prompt adaptation under a test-time adaptation setting.
Text Domain Learning simulates diverse style shifts using style tokens with inter-style diversity and intra-style consistency objectives.
Visual Domain Learning refines target-relevant style tokens using unlabeled test images and self-supervised learning.
Experiments on PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, DomainNet, and ImageNet report consistent improvements over existing DG methods.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot domain generalization via test-time prompt learning on CLIP matches test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Zero-Shot Domain Generalization via Domain Prompt Learning
papers.tldr: DoP enables zero-shot domain generalization by adapting CLIP prompts to unseen target domains without using source-domain data.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions and navigate to target locations. However, current VLN agents often suffer severe performance degradation in unseen environments due to distribution shifts. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm to bridge this gap, yet existing methods that rely on unsupervised entropy minimization can propagate errors through the trajectory, causing cascading failures in navigation. Recent methods mitigate this by incorporating human feedback, but they apply trajectory-level supervision uniformly across all steps without localizing the actions is truly informative, leading to inefficient feedback utilization and mismatched optimization granularity. To address these limitations, we propose FETA, a Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation method that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. To reduce unnecessary human interventions, we introduce a hierarchical sample selection strategy to localize informative samples. Specifically, we first filter trajectories whose normalized policy entropy exhibits large fluctuations. Within each selected trajectory, we further select the critical action via an entropy-gradient saliency criterion and query a single binary feedback on its correctness. A discrepancy-aware entropy optimization objective then updates the policy only at the queried step, with adaptive scaling that assigns larger relative weights to samples with greater prediction-feedback discrepancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FETA achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer human interventions, while remaining robust under noisy feedback and continual adaptation settings.
authors: Zixu Wang, Huaquan Zhang, Shoukai Xu, Jinwu Hu, Zhiquan Wen, Mingkui Tan
bullets: Unseen environments can cause severe VLN degradation, while entropy minimization may amplify navigation errors.
FETA hierarchically selects high-value feedback: unstable trajectories first, then critical actions using entropy-gradient saliency.
It queries one binary correctness signal per selected action and updates the policy only at that step.
Discrepancy-aware entropy optimization adaptively emphasizes actions where predictions and feedback disagree.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance with fewer interventions, including robustness to noisy feedback and continual adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Feedback-efficient test-time adaptation for Vision-and-Language Navigation combines embodied instruction following with deployment-time policy update, fitting both configured areas.
papers.title: Asking Less, Adapting Better: Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: FETA improves vision-and-language navigation under distribution shifts by selecting only informative actions for targeted, feedback-efficient test-time adaptation.

papers.abstract: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors -- particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Xinlei Zhang, Chen Chen, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses coarse 3D scene representations, exhaustive exploration, and difficulty handling relocated objects.
Builds a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG) that organizes spaces by functional areas and associated containers.
Uses hierarchical planning to select relevant areas first, then inspect specific containers such as drawers and cabinets.
Continuously integrates perception, memory, and commonsense to relocalize objects as environments change.
Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show higher search success and efficiency than existing baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Functional 3D scene graph and memory-augmented reasoning for object search in dynamic environments fit embodied navigation and memory.
papers.title: CMAR-search: Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning for Object Search in Dynamic Interactive Environments
papers.tldr: CMAR-search combines commonsense, environmental memory, and functional scene understanding to efficiently find objects in dynamic, interactive environments.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Xiaoze Wu, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–semantic richness trade-off in online mapping and the difficulty of relocalizing objects after scene changes.
Represents scenes with sparse anchor nodes that combine semantic, visual, and geometric information for reasoning, verification, and navigation.
Uses on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval to reduce redundant storage while supporting complex queries.
Reuses transient navigation observations to relocalize objects that have moved.
Validated in simulation and real-world settings across retrieval benchmarks and static/dynamic navigation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Anchor-centric multimodal memory for open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation in dynamic scenes; combines spatial understanding with embodied memory.
papers.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: OASIS enables efficient open-vocabulary object retrieval and navigation in dynamic environments using a sparse, multimodal memory built around stable semantic scene anchors.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions. We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch. Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3-18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8-82.6%.
authors: Wei Zhang, Lirong Xiang, Charles Fleming
bullets: Targets the latency of cloud-only agents and the error vulnerability of lightweight local agents in long-horizon embodied tasks.
Uses a lightweight critic to monitor local execution and trigger persistent escalation rather than making stateless per-step routing decisions.
Maintains shared handoff memory so cloud control preserves execution context and task progress without restarting.
Across diverse embodied benchmarks, improves task success by 6.3–18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline.
Approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8–82.6%.
papers.selection_reason: Critic-guided cloud/local escalation with shared handoff memory for embodied agents; improves latency while maintaining task success.
papers.title: Know When to Escalate: Critic-Guided Adaptive Execution for Cloud-Local Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: CARE adaptively escalates embodied-agent control from a fast local model to a stronger cloud model when a critic detects unreliability, improving success while reducing action latency.

papers.abstract: Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide sequential execution over changing GUI states. This raises two challenges: determining HOW each preference should alter execution strategy and WHEN it should take effect along the interaction trajectory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success, offering limited insight into these questions. We introduce PrefDiag-Bench with two components: (1) a categorization of preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect execution; and (2) a stage-wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect and where failures occur. We evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end-to-end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Although existing agents achieve relatively high completion rates on non-personalized tasks, performance is substantially lower on preference-personalized tasks. Even the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves only 47.17% on Process preferences under explicit user profiles. Agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences. Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks: selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end-to-end task success by up to 7.06%. PrefDiag-Bench offers a more systematic evaluation of GUI agents' personalization capabilities beyond overall task success. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zhixin-L/PrefDiag-Bench.
authors: Zhixin Lin, Dongliang Xu, Jungang Li, Shidong Pan, Jun Feng, Yanbin Sun, Jing Li, Liang Liu, Yue Yao
bullets: Categorizes preferences into five types based on how they alter execution.
Uses 1,664 stage-wise probes to identify when preferences should take effect and where failures occur.
Evaluates 11 GUI agent systems using explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs.
Agents struggle most with Ranking and Process preferences; the best reported Process score is 47.17% under explicit profiles.
Providing relevant evidence from user history improves end-to-end success by up to 7.06%.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on behavioral memory logs and personalization in GUI agents, addressing the challenge of retaining and utilizing user history for agent adaptation.
papers.title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents
papers.tldr: PrefDiag-Bench diagnoses how and when mobile GUI agents apply user preferences, revealing major personalization weaknesses despite strong non-personalized task performance.

papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.
authors: Xiaojing Sun, Yuhan Zeng, Xiao Wang
bullets: AI analysts can accumulate false-positive risk as they evolve and adapt to evaluation feedback.
The proposed method validates every candidate version on simulated null-hypothesis data before deployment.
The lifetime probability of ever deploying an invalid version remains bounded, regardless of update strategy or number of proposals.
In bioequivalence and A/B-testing examples, continual validation reduced Type I error rates to at most 0.045 and 0.044 while retaining 82% and 96% of selected valid-update power.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes continual validation for evolving AI analysts with lifetime Type I error control, directly relevant to continual/online learning and safe model deployment.
papers.title: Lifetime-valid decisions by continually evolving AI analysts
papers.tldr: Continual validation lets evolving AI analysts improve over time while controlling the lifetime risk of deploying versions with excessive Type I error.

papers.abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent
authors: Yebo Feng, Jingyang Dai, Liangrui Pan, Nelson Lau, Jiahua Xu, Yang Liu
bullets: Combines nine specialized agents to analyze heterogeneous financial and Web data, set positions, and audit risk.
Uses seven-layer shared memory to provide decisions with market context, calibration, and prior-action history.
Enables reversible, code-graded self-improvement through periodic reflection, deterministic gating, and replay verification.
In a five-month live deployment, it contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; replay tests found no injected-instruction compliance.
A protected invariant core covers order arithmetic, risk rules, and discipline prompts, while backtests indicate reduced maximum drawdown across random-entry policies.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multi-agent system with a shared memory mechanism and self-review process for agents, directly relevant to embodied memory and test-time learning in agent systems.
papers.title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
papers.tldr: Steward is a governed multi-agent LLM investing system that supports self-improvement while protecting core risk and execution safeguards.

papers.abstract: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.
bullets: A pre-registered study compares memory-augmented retrieval, weight-distilled policies, and fixed student policies with the teacher’s retrieval buffer attached.

Distilling memory-augmented behavior into weights improved performance by only 1 percentage point over an action-only control; the test was underpowered, so the claim was withdrawn rather than refuted.
Attaching the frozen retrieval buffer to student weights produced a large gain (+34 percentage points), matching the memory-augmented teacher’s 49.3% reference performance.
Follow-up controls found the buffer substantially improved the base model and other adapters, while adapters added no detectable benefit once retrieval was attached.
On a harder second task, the retrieval advantage was smaller and not significant, with exploratory evidence linking the reduction to limited memory coverage.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies external memory versus policy weights for embodied agents; fits embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
papers.tldr: For this embodied reach task, keeping experience in an external retrieval buffer is more effective than distilling it into policy weights alone.

papers.abstract: Recently, electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have gained traction as portable neural measurement systems. However, the practical deployment of these instruments is often hindered by nonstationarity and cross-subject distribution shifts, which lead to significant intersubject inconsistency. Existing adaptation methods remain impractical for real-time measurement scenarios, as they typically require offline access to source or aggregated target data. To address these challenges, this article proposes memory-augmented online test-time adaptation (OTTA) with perturbation consistency and confidence calibration (MOPC), a source-free framework designed to enhance the reliability of BCI instrumentation. MOPC enables the measurement system to update its decoding parameters on the fly during the inference stage, facilitating single-pass adaptation without accessing sensitive source data. We introduce random-mask perturbations to enforce prediction consistency against inherent EEG signal noise and acquisition artifacts. Furthermore, a confidence-calibrated reweighting loss is designed to integrate feature-space similarity, effectively mitigating unreliable pseudolabels and class imbalance during continuous signal acquisition. To ensure system stability and prevent the catastrophic forgetting of established neural patterns, a lightweight memory module is incorporated to regularize parameter updates within a tight latency budget. Evaluated on the BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI datasets, MOPC achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods by 2.22~\% and 3.67~\%, respectively, while keeping the per-trial adaptation latency to approximately 40--60 ms. This study provides a robust, recalibration-free solution for real-time EEG decoding, marking a significant advancement in the precision and usability of practical BCI measurement instruments.
authors: Kunkun Zhang, Kehao Wu, Zhitao Chen, Haigen Hu, Qianwei Zhou
bullets: Addresses nonstationarity and intersubject distribution shifts that hinder practical EEG-based BCIs.
Uses random-mask perturbations to promote prediction consistency under EEG noise and artifacts.
Applies confidence-calibrated, feature-similarity-based reweighting to reduce unreliable pseudolabel effects and class imbalance.
Adds a lightweight memory module to stabilize updates and limit catastrophic forgetting within a tight latency budget.
On BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI, it reports improvements of 2.22% and 3.67%, respectively, with approximately 40–60 ms per-trial adaptation latency.
papers.selection_reason: Source-free online test-time adaptation with memory for EEG decoding; directly fits test-time and online learning.
papers.title: Memory-Augmented Online Test-Time Adaptation for EEG Motor Imagery via Perturbation Consistency and Confidence Calibration
papers.tldr: MOPC enables source-free, single-pass online adaptation for EEG motor-imagery decoding, improving cross-subject robustness while maintaining low latency.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.
bullets: Addresses costly, hallucination-prone long-horizon planning by constraining LLMs to translate between language and symbolic planning.
Reconstructs the PDDL problem after each observation using parsed facts, hypotheses, and interaction memory.
Positive memory prioritizes plausible missing entities and conditions; negative memory excludes assumptions refuted by feedback.
Evaluated on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille, improving task completion and step efficiency while reducing online token cost versus LLM-planning baselines.
The same offline fine-tuned interface transfers across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-conditioned PDDL planning with interaction and environment memory for partially observable environments fits embodied memory.
papers.title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments
papers.tldr: MemPlan combines memory-conditioned PDDL replanning with a fixed language–symbol interface to improve efficient, reliable planning in partially observable text environments.

papers.abstract: Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite. These results suggest that partial-parameter CPT on a carefully curated corpus is a practical route to efficient MSA adaptation.
authors: Houssam Eddine Boukhalfa, Mourad Bouache, Mourad Dahmane
bullets: Addresses noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the cost of continual pretraining for Arabic LLMs.
Curates MSA data through cleaning, heuristic/model filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication.
