Trains RS-LoRA adapters, the final eight transformer blocks, and embeddings with layer-wise learning rates.
At 5B tokens, reaches 94% of full-parameter CPT’s gain in 52% of the wall-clock time and beats adapter-only baselines.
A 12B model trained on 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples scores 75.3 on OALL v2.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a data-centric continual pretraining framework for Arabic LLMs, relevant to LLM adaptation and continual learning.
papers.title: AQL-Lite: Enabling Efficient Knowledge Acquisition for Arabic LLMs via Data-Centric Continual Pretraining
papers.tldr: AQL-Lite efficiently adapts multilingual LLMs to Modern Standard Arabic by combining high-quality data curation with selective continual pretraining.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning adapts language models to specialized tasks but can disrupt previously acquired behavior. Existing approaches constrain parameters, gradients, or replay objectives, yet the connection between the protected object, the intervening trajectory, and retained outputs remains unclear. We develop a functional-path account that decomposes old-loss changes along realized updates into the controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects. The account yields a conditional refresh budget and identifies the restoring direction supplied by informative replay. Matched QLoRA interventions separate constraint granularity from placement before or after Adam: placement strongly affects retention across the studied code-label audits, whereas the granularity interaction depends on the endpoint. Checkpointed generation separates endpoint recovery from higher sampled-path accuracy, and matched replay schedules reveal loss exposure concealed by final scores. A sequential-task comparison extends this distinction to backward transfer: subspace regularization and projection improve average retention while trading off different old tasks; supervised replay protects both more consistently in this setting. Additional response interfaces distinguish content gains from exact-response retention. These findings connect update-level protection to task-wise behavior and motivate mitigation through explicit functional anchors, trajectory evaluation, and joint old/new auditing.
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
bullets: Existing parameter, gradient, and replay constraints do not fully explain how protected objects translate into retained outputs.

The framework decomposes old-loss changes into controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects, yielding a conditional refresh budget and a replay-based restoring direction.
In matched QLoRA studies, optimizer placement strongly affects retention, while constraint granularity interacts with the endpoint.
Checkpointed generation and matched replay reveal differences between endpoint recovery, sampled-path accuracy, and loss exposure.
Across sequential tasks, subspace methods improve average retention with task-specific trade-offs, whereas supervised replay protects tasks more consistently.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual supervised fine-tuning and forgetting, fitting continual/online learning under adaptation and memory.
papers.title: Why Constrained Updates Still Forget: A Functional-Path Analysis of Continual SFT
papers.tldr: A functional-path analysis shows that preventing forgetting depends not only on what updates constrain, but also on where constraints are applied and how the entire training trajectory affects behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-context continual pre-training (LCCP) is widely used to improve long-context capability, but how its benefits scale with the number of tokens used for LCCP remains unclear. We investigate this question through modeling, monitoring, and validating the benefits of scaling LCCP. First, we establish an empirical additive power law relating long-context performance to model size and the respective token budgets of short-context pre-training and LCCP. Experiments across five model scales and more than one hundred short- and long-context budget configurations show that the fitted law reproduces the observed trends and extrapolates well to held-out model scales. Second, we introduce \textsc{Constant-Last4}, a training and observation protocol that averages the four most recent consecutive checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate run to enable stable monitoring along a single extensible training trajectory. Under this protocol, the same scaling-law form fits well and accurately predicts the LCCP performance trajectory of a 1.22B-parameter model trained on approximately 100B LCCP tokens. Finally, downstream evaluations along this trajectory show continued improvements in long-context performance, with no clear sign of saturation within the evaluated range. These gains persist after both 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, with benefits extending to long-context understanding and agentic tasks. Together, these results argue for continuing to scale LCCP rather than stopping early: its gains are stably observable along an extensible trajectory, quantitatively predictable, and transferable to downstream tasks.
bullets: The study examines how long-context performance scales with model size, short-context pre-training tokens, and LCCP token budgets.
It fits an empirical additive power law that reproduces observed trends and extrapolates to held-out model scales.
The Constant-Last4 protocol stabilizes monitoring by averaging the four latest checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate trajectory.
A 1.22B-parameter model’s performance trajectory is accurately predicted while training on approximately 100B LCCP tokens.
Improvements persist after 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, benefiting long-context understanding and agentic tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical scaling laws for long-context continual pre-training directly advance long-context LLM methods and continual learning.
papers.title: Don't Stop Long-Context Continual Pre-Training Too Early: An Empirical Scaling Law
papers.tldr: Long-context continual pre-training keeps improving long-context and downstream capabilities without clear saturation in the evaluated range, and its gains can be modeled predictably as training tokens increase.

papers.abstract: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.
authors: Ruotong Liao, Meikel Kokowski, Xiaoxiao Sun, Yongqin Xian, Laura Bravo S\'anchez, Shiye Su, Federico Tombari, Serena Yeung-Levy, Volker Tresp
bullets: Evaluates Information Capture, State Tracking, and Location Tracking for ambient memory needs.
Tests two levels of proactiveness: timely notifications and active start-to-stop memory-maintenance interventions.
Includes Daily and Scientific tracks with associated question-answering evaluations.
Finds that even strong proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines struggle to be both timely and accurate.
Supports evaluation of proactive multimodal assistants and video agents operating alongside users.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for proactive memory in streaming egocentric video; directly targets embodied memory and video-language understanding.
papers.title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: ProactEgoMem benchmarks whether video agents can proactively capture, update, and maintain useful memories from streaming egocentric video.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging, as it must preserve fine-grained visual evidence while tracking entity evolution across sessions. Existing abstraction-based memories compress images into text, often discarding visually discriminative details, whereas pixel-preserving memories retain raw observations but struggle to reliably associate diverse observations with persistent entity identities and track their evolving states. To address these limitations, we propose MHG-Mem, a multimodal hypergraph memory that jointly organizes entity identity, state evolution, and provenance to visual evidence. Specifically, MHG-Mem represents distinct entity mentions and their observed facts as individual nodes, grouping identity-consistent mentions and facts through occurrence hyperedges. It then synthesizes aspect-specific evolution states from these grouped observations and links them to supporting entities, facts, and source evidence through evolutionary and evidential hyperedges. To navigate this structured memory, we introduce hypergraph-based agentic search, which adaptively selects an entry layer, traverses typed hyperedges across memory levels, and inspects source observations when fine-grained verification is required. These designs support both detailed visual verification and reasoning over cross-session state changes. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MHG-Mem, improving performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline.
authors: Jielong Tang, Ling-An Zeng, Xujie Yuan, Xiao Dong, Zhiqian Xia, Qingfeng Li, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Rong Yao, Jian Yin
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between text-based memories that lose visual detail and pixel-based memories that struggle with persistent entity tracking.
Represents entity mentions and observed facts as nodes, connecting identity-consistent observations with occurrence hyperedges.
Builds aspect-specific evolution states linked to supporting entities, facts, and source visual evidence.
Uses agentic hypergraph search to navigate memory hierarchies and retrieve fine-grained evidence for verification.
Across three benchmarks, improves performance by 8.20–9.98% over the strongest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multimodal hypergraph memory for agents with provenance and state evolution, directly relevant to memory and adaptation for deployed agents.
papers.title: Remembering Through Change: Provenance-Preserving Hypergraph Memory for Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: MHG-Mem gives multimodal agents provenance-preserving hypergraph memory to retain visual evidence while tracking entity identities and state changes across sessions.

papers.abstract: Adaptive experiments use bandit algorithms to favor interventions with higher expected rewards. However, decision-makers also require reliable inference on current treatment effects: differences between intervention and reference-arm mean rewards at the present time, rather than historical averages. These objectives conflict: reward maximization favors better interventions, whereas current-effect inference requires continued exploration of potentially suboptimal interventions as outcomes change over time. We characterize this tradeoff for $K$-arm bandits with H\"older-smooth mean rewards of exponent $\beta\in(0,1]$ and constant $L$. Requiring high-probability simultaneous coverage of all current effects by confidence intervals of width at most $w$, we establish matching minimax bounds, up to logarithmic factors, on expected dynamic regret. Over horizon $T$, our algorithm TRACE (Tracking Rewards and Current Effects) achieves regret of order $\widetilde{O}_{\beta}\left(\sqrt{KT}+K^{\beta/(2\beta+1)}L^{1/(2\beta+1)}T^{(\beta+1)/(2\beta+1)}+Kw^{-2}(1+L^{1/\beta}w^{-1/\beta})\right)$, where the notation hides logarithms and constants depending only on $\beta$. This regret--precision tradeoff separates reward-learning regret from the cost of refreshing current-effect estimates, which remains unavoidable even when one arm is uniformly optimal. An empirical-Bernstein e-process extension adapts exploration to realized prediction errors while preserving worst-case guarantees. When within-block drift is negligible relative to sampling error, all observations, including reward-learning observations, can be reused for asymptotically normal pointwise inference and stronger local stationarity yields local asymptotic efficiency. Finally, we show that regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness and support our theory with extensive numerical experiments.
bullets: Current-effect inference requires continued exploration of possibly suboptimal arms, conflicting with reward maximization.
For Hölder-smooth mean rewards, the authors derive matching minimax dynamic-regret bounds for simultaneous confidence intervals of width at most $w$.
TRACE separates regret from learning which arms are best from the additional cost of refreshing current-effect estimates.
An empirical-Bernstein e-process extension adapts exploration to observed prediction errors while retaining worst-case guarantees.
Regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness; favorable local-stationarity conditions enable efficient pointwise inference.
papers.selection_reason: Nonstationary bandit algorithm for current-effect inference; directly relevant to online/continual learning.
papers.title: The Price of Current-Effect Inference in Nonstationary Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.tldr: The paper quantifies the unavoidable regret cost of estimating current treatment effects in nonstationary bandits and introduces an algorithm that achieves the optimal regret–precision tradeoff up to logarithmic factors.

papers.abstract: Learning across medical imaging modalities requires making use of images without paired text and accommodating new domains while retaining existing representations. We propose a medical vision-language technique built around an expandable bank of modality experts. Its Multiway Transformer combines shared visual computation with deterministically routed feed-forward experts and a separate text pathway. A modality-aware visual tokenizer supplies targets for masked pretraining on 19.4 million unpaired image rows across seven modalities; contrastive alignment then uses 3.23 million image-text pairs. Additional fundus and optical coherence tomography experts learn from paired data while the original image and text embedding paths remain frozen. With a ViT-Large backbone, the proposed technique achieves the best or tied-best result in 24 of 25 benchmark settings across nine modalities: 10 of 11 zero-shot classification benchmarks, all 10 linear probes, and all four retrieval benchmarks. Mean balanced accuracy is 0.674 for zero-shot classification and 0.856 for linear probing, and mean bidirectional retrieval recall is 20.70%. A separate three-seed sequential experiment with matched adaptation data yields fundus and OCT retrieval gains of 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding fundus or pathology tasks. The preservation argument requires unchanged existing computation paths and inference conditions, and feature-identity checks verify retention on evaluated inputs. The proposed technique provides a modular approach to learning and expanding medical vision-language representations.
authors: DM BAPPY, Eunsu Kim, Hanjoo Lee, Sung Hak Lee, Sangjeong Ahn
bullets: Addresses unpaired multimodal medical images and continual adaptation to new domains without disrupting prior capabilities.
Uses a Multiway Transformer with shared visual computation, deterministically routed modality experts, a separate text pathway, and a modality-aware visual tokenizer.
Pretrains on 19.4M unpaired image rows across seven modalities, then aligns vision and language using 3.23M image-text pairs.
Achieves the best or tied-best performance in 24 of 25 benchmarks across nine modalities, including zero-shot classification, linear probing, and retrieval.
Sequential fundus and OCT adaptation improves retrieval by 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding evaluated tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Expandable multimodal medical vision-language model with modality experts and continual expansion without forgetting.
papers.title: Expandable Modality Experts for Medical Vision-Language Learning
papers.tldr: An expandable bank of modality-specific experts enables medical vision-language models to learn new imaging domains while preserving existing representations.

papers.abstract: Geometric structure is essential for robotic manipulation and understanding the 3D world. Most VLA models rely on 2D representations of current observations, while geometry-aware approaches often require additional 3D information. However, geometry inferred independently from individual observations is often discarded rather than accumulated into a persistent task representation. Our key insight is that action generation needs a compact, task-relevant geometric abstraction that can be continuously updated, rather than a complete, renderable 3D reconstruction at every step. We introduce GeoMem-VLA, a VLA framework that internalizes explicit 3D supervision into dedicated geometric tokens and maintains them as temporal memory for action generation, without directly aligning the VLM's native visual embeddings with the teacher feature space. During training, a frozen geometry foundation model supervises learnable GeoPlan tokens through a geometric flow-matching objective over the current scene point map and future end-effector tracks. These tokens are integrated with the memory of observation representations, where historical information is retrieved, adaptively fused with current observations, and consolidated to retain event frames as the task progresses. At inference, the policy retrieves historical representations and fuses them with the current working representation to predict actions, without invoking the 3D teacher or explicitly reconstructing the scene. After benchmark-specific downstream adaptation, GeoMem-VLA achieves 98.9% average success on LIBERO and 91.10% / 91.24% on RoboTwin's clean/randomized settings. Across five real-world tasks, GeoMem-VLA achieves 78.0% average success. These results suggest that internalizing and remembering 3D scene understanding is a promising approach to robot control.
authors: Qinfan Zhang, Yifan Luo, Haoyuan Shi, Guanlin Liu, Han Dong, Haozhe Shan, Yong Dai, Xiangcong Ren, Xiaozhu Ju
bullets: Addresses the loss of accumulated geometric information in VLA models that primarily use current 2D observations.
Learns dedicated GeoPlan tokens from frozen geometry-model supervision over scene point maps and future end-effector tracks.
Retrieves, fuses, and consolidates geometric and visual memories across time without requiring 3D reconstruction or the teacher model at inference.
Reports 98.9% average success on LIBERO, 91.10%/91.24% on RoboTwin clean/randomized settings, and 78.0% across five real-world tasks.
Scope: performance depends on benchmark-specific downstream adaptation and is evaluated on the reported simulation and real-world tasks.
papers.selection_reason: VLA framework with 3D geometric temporal memory for robot manipulation; directly fits embodied action and memory.
papers.title: GeoMem-VLA: Internalizing 3D Scene Understanding into Temporal Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: GeoMem-VLA equips vision-language-action models with compact, temporally persistent 3D geometric memory for improved robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.
authors: Zhipeng Chen, Yunsen Liang, Yanxi Chen, Hongkang Zhao, Lingyun Feng, Ruiyang Ren, Guoxin Chen, Jia Deng, Feng Chang, Chuan Hao, Ran Tao, Jian Yang, Ji-Rong Wen, Bryan Dai, Wayne Xin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of AI systems with frozen parameters that rely on external updates.
Uses future-event prediction in a living environment that continuously generates verifiable tasks.
Feeds prediction reasoning back into capability through search–prediction decoupling, parameter-level evolution, and reusable skill distillation.
Ranked first on the external FutureX leaderboard for three consecutive weeks, with up to a 195% rating improvement.
Placed among the top three across four base LLMs on synthesized evaluation, exceeding the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley–Terry points.
papers.selection_reason: Agents recursively self-improve from ongoing interaction with a changing environment, fitting continual/online learning.
papers.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
papers.tldr: DeepEvolve is a recursively self-improving forecasting agent that co-evolves with a continuously changing, verifiable environment and achieves strong results on real-world and synthesized evaluations.

papers.abstract: Object detection models for autonomous driving commonly experience substantial performance drops when deployed under adverse weather due to the domain shift between training data and real-world operating conditions. This degradation is especially evident when models trained on clear-weather images encounter foggy environments with reduced visibility and contrast. To address this challenge, we introduce FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework designed to improve the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors in fog. Using RF-DETR as the underlying object detector, FogTTA enables real-time adaptation to the streaming target domain without requiring source data or retraining. The framework follows a teacher-student design, where the deployed model serves as the teacher and generates pseudo labels from weakly augmented target inputs. These predictions are subsequently refined through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering. The student model then learns from strongly augmented target sample using the Varifocal loss to mitigate pseudo-label noise. The teacher is updated via exponential moving averaging to ensure stable and continuous adaptation. Experiments show that FogTTA outperforms prior baselines, delivering improved detection accuracy and stability while maintaining real-time performance.
authors: Ali Abedi, Q. M. Jonathan Wu, Ning Zhang, Shiqi Tian
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by the domain shift from clear to foggy driving environments.
Uses a teacher–student test-time adaptation framework with pseudo-label refinement through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering.
Trains the student on strongly augmented target images with Varifocal loss to reduce pseudo-label noise.
Updates the teacher via exponential moving average for stable, continuous adaptation.
Experiments report improved accuracy and stability over prior baselines while maintaining real-time performance.
papers.selection_reason: Online test-time adaptation for object detection in fog, directly fits test-time learning.
papers.title: FogTTA: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Robust Transformer-based Object Detection in Foggy Weather
papers.tldr: FogTTA enables Transformer-based object detectors to adapt online to foggy conditions without source data or retraining, improving robustness while preserving real-time operation.

papers.abstract: A frozen multi-horizon forecaster can be corrected online from its own residuals. However, under label delay the target of a block arrives only after the whole horizon has passed, and the corrector's retained state grows with the number of channels. Aiming to combine a small retained state with a large error reduction, we propose DRiC (DCT Ridge Corrector), which fits a ridge regression of the leading discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients of the next residual block on those of the frozen forecast and of the latest input block, with sufficient statistics updated recursively. Its local variant, DRiC-L, keeps one such regression per channel; its global variant, DRiC-G, pools all channels into one regression, whose statistics do not depend on the channel count. A guard tracks a running scale of the frozen forecast's residual for each channel; it skips updates on blocks far outside that scale and clips the issued correction. We evaluate on seven datasets (four ETT series, Weather with its missing-value codes filled, Electricity, and Traffic) with DLinear, PatchTST, and iTransformer backbones, against 10 naive, gradient-trained, and closed-form methods. DRiC-L with eight DCT coefficients (DRiC-L8) reduces the mean squared error (MSE) by 14.55% on average over 126 conditions, against 12.98% for ELF, the most accurate comparator, while retaining 15-17 times less state, although ELF is more accurate on Traffic. DRiC-G retains 14.6 kB on the 321-channel Electricity data and 18.9 kB on the 862-channel Traffic data and is the most accurate method at or below its state on both. However, 5 to 7 of the 10 comparators, all with at least 10 times its state, are more accurate there. On the unfilled Weather file, DRiC-L8 without the guard has on average 8.0 times the frozen forecast's MSE, whereas with the guard it reduces the MSE by 7.94%. Code: https://github.com/keiotakmin/dric.
bullets: Addresses label delay and channel-dependent state growth when correcting multi-horizon forecasts online.
Fits recursive ridge regressions on leading DCT coefficients of forecast and recent-input blocks; offers local per-channel (DRiC-L) and pooled (DRiC-G) variants.
A residual-scale guard skips anomalous updates and clips corrections to improve robustness.
Across 126 conditions, DRiC-L8 reduces MSE by 14.55% on average, versus 12.98% for the strongest comparator, while using 15–17× less state.
DRiC-G uses only 14.6–18.9 kB on the largest datasets and performs strongly at comparable state, though higher-state methods can be more accurate and Traffic favors the comparator.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an online residual correction method that updates statistics recursively, fitting the 'Test-Time Learning' category of adapting models during deployment.
papers.title: Local and Global Recursive Ridge Regression for Online Residual Correction of Frozen Multivariate Forecasters under Label Delay
papers.tldr: DRiC provides low-memory online residual correction for frozen multivariate forecasters under delayed labels, achieving substantial average MSE reductions while controlling unstable updates.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.
authors: Tingwen Du, Haoyu Guo, Hanxue Zhang, Xuanxu Wang, Junting Dong, Chao Gao, Mingfei Han, Tao Lu, Mulin Yu, Chunhua Shen, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
bullets: Targets non-Markovian manipulation tasks where progress, past outcomes, partial observability, and errors affect future decisions.
Uses an editable harness around a high-level VLM, paired with a fixed VLA executor for low-level control.
Maintains task context from observations and execution feedback to guide later plans.
Self-evolves by proposing and evaluating harness revisions through environment rollouts before held-out testing.
On RoboMME, autonomous self-evolution improves overall success from 44.38% to 51.38%.
papers.selection_reason: VLA-based robotic manipulation with self-evolving memory harness for history-dependent tasks.
papers.title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
papers.tldr: SERA turns a high-level vision-language model into a self-evolving robotic agent that uses execution history to improve long-horizon manipulation planning.

papers.abstract: We are the first to give a certified rule for whether unseen data belong in a pretrained model's context or its weights, built on an exact law for their information value. That value, the code length saved on held-out queries, equals in expectation the bits stored about the query, plus a prior repair, minus a decoding loss, for any model, architecture, dataset and task. The law's ceilings certify the choice from one measurement, and an anytime-valid test makes it from held-out queries, with error controlled whenever it stops. Every certificate the ceilings issue on a trained transformer, TabPFN, an occupancy network and a stereo network is correct. The test picks TabPFN over XGBoost and a trained surrogate over an in-context learner on airfoil pressure, calls the better of GPT-2's cache and fine-tune in 61,948 of 64,000 query streams over 32 comparisons, and errs in at most 3.3% of null streams. The law also diagnoses when learning in context helps and when it does not. Deleting part of a context is held-out validation of that part in any model, and adding parts one at a time traces the learning curve in context: one patch that sees a shape feature cuts an occupancy network's code length there a hundredfold, while eight that miss it nearly double it, and one camera that sees the surface beats four in a stereo network. Ranked by this label-free valuation, a kriging learner's three best support cars beat four drawn at random, and on a yes-or-no claim the valuation recovers a published evidence adjudicator, with AUROC 0.91.
bullets: Introduces an information-value law equating expected code-length savings with information stored about a query, adjusted for prior repair and decoding loss.
Uses upper bounds and an anytime-valid held-out-query test to certify context-versus-weight choices with controlled error whenever testing stops.
Demonstrates correct certificates across transformers, TabPFN, occupancy, and stereo networks, including 61,948 of 64,000 GPT-2 query streams and at most 3.3% null-stream errors.
Shows the framework can diagnose useful versus unhelpful context: selective patches, cameras, or support examples can substantially improve coding efficiency.
The same label-free valuation recovers a published evidence adjudicator with AUROC 0.91.
papers.selection_reason: Provides an exact information-theoretic rule and certification for choosing between in-context and weight-based adaptation from deployment-time data.
papers.title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: The paper provides certified, anytime-valid rules for deciding whether unseen data should be stored in a model’s context or weights, based on the information they save on held-out queries.

papers.abstract: We propose a novel stochastic cascading bandit setup where probing an ordered shortlist of $K$ out of $L$ arms incurs position-dependent costs, and the learner observes only noisy feedback regarding each arm's true output. We identify a sub-class of noise models for which the optimal shortlist can be found by sorting arms according to a per-arm score: such a score exists for both selection and ordering when the channel has no false positives, and for ordering alone (but not selection) when measurements are costless; however in general neither selection nor ordering is separable once noise and cost are both present. For the case where both selection and ordering scores exist, we provide a UCB-based algorithm with $O((L-K)\log T)$ instance-dependent regret over a time horizon $T$, which matches an algorithm-agnostic lower bound (up to constant factors). For the more challenging scenario where scores don't exist, we develop a new algorithmic template, DP-UCB, that embeds optimism directly inside an exact dynamic program, yielding $O\big(LK\log T\big)$ regret. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through extensive numerical evaluations and simulations over both synthetic and real-world datasets.
bullets: Studies when the optimal shortlist and ordering can be determined by per-arm scores under different noise and cost conditions.
Introduces a UCB algorithm with instance-dependent O((L−K) log T) regret when both selection and ordering are score-separable.
Proposes DP-UCB, which integrates optimism into an exact dynamic program for non-separable settings, achieving O(LK log T) regret.
Provides a matching algorithm-agnostic lower bound up to constants in the score-separable case.
Validates the theoretical results through simulations and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes online cascading bandit algorithms with regret guarantees, fitting continual/online learning.
papers.title: Cascading Bandits with Noisy Observations: Algorithms and Regret Bounds
papers.tldr: This paper develops algorithms and regret guarantees for cascading bandits with position-dependent probing costs and noisy feedback, including a dynamic-programming approach when simple arm rankings fail.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.
authors: Dongfang Li, Zhuoen Chen, Bonian Jia, Zixuan Liu, Zhengxuan Lu, Can Deng, Yukun Shi, Yuhang Meng, Xin Zhang, Jiahe Huang, Fuhao Li, Junmai Wang, Shunyao Wen, Jingjun Sun, Jiaxu Tian, Jiangling Zhang, Zihan Wang, Liangyou Li, Yitong Yao, Shuangyong Song, Beilun Wang, Pengxu Wei, Hanlin Xu, Chang Liu, Yongxiang Li, Baotian Hu, Xiangyang Ji, Min Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Fixed model weights and limited context hinder agents’ long-term learning from experience.
Method: A taxonomy categorizes memory by storage substrate, asset type, and management policy within a two-loop update lifecycle.
Evaluation: The protocol tests retention under interference, adaptation to change, and transfer across tasks.
Framework: A scaling model relates performance to experience, memory capacity, and compute across non-parametric and parametric memory.
Contribution: The paper provides a principled framework for evaluating and designing memory-driven self-improving agents.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), a framework that redefines memory evaluation based on behavioral improvement and future action quality rather than simple retrieval.
papers.title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents
papers.tldr: MCCL reframes agent memory as a mechanism for continual behavioral improvement rather than passive retrieval.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}. A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%. In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%). These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/
authors: Qinghang Liu, Conglin Wang, Zongsheng Li, Boyong He, Han Gao, Pengcheng Wang, Tao Sun, Lige Liu, Chang Liu
bullets: Targets the heavy reasoning burden of retrieving and interpreting history during execution.
Uses hierarchical memory: a short-term visual buffer, semantic-event memory, and executable subtask list.
A high-level VLM converts streaming observations into subtasks, then selects relevant subtasks for a low-level VLA policy.
Trains memory updates with staged supervision expansion and task-grounded self-labeling.
Achieves 56.05% success on RoboMME and 60.83% overall success across four real-world manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical memory with VLM-generated subtask lists for vision-language robot manipulation fits embodied memory and VLA control.
papers.title: Plan First, Act Later: Streaming Reasoning for Executable Memory in Robot Control
papers.tldr: PAL improves long-horizon robot manipulation by planning future-relevant subtasks into executable memory before action time.

papers.abstract: Dynamic local community detection tracks the evolving community of designated seed nodes across graph snapshots. However, it faces two critical challenges: temporal supervision uncertainty, where sparse and outdated labels fail to provide seed-specific guidance under topology changes, and unbounded error cascades, where sequential policy transfer accumulates exploration errors over long horizons. To address these challenges, we propose DISRL, a Dual-scale Incremental Semi-supervised Reinforcement Learning framework. DISRL introduces a supervision construction module that dynamically generates seed-specific guidance from sparse known communities, and a dual-scale community exploration module that stabilizes policy evolution by decoupling short-term adaptation within temporal windows from long-term parameter consolidation across windows. Furthermore, we construct a dynamic graph benchmark with diverse community evolution scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DISRL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under various dynamic settings.
authors: Tianming Zhang, Jinxu Wang, Yixuan Zhang, Zhengyi Yang, Chenyu Hou, Bin Cao, Jing Fan
bullets: Addresses sparse, outdated labels and cascading exploration errors in dynamic community tracking.
Generates seed-specific guidance from known communities through a supervision construction module.
Separates short-term policy adaptation within temporal windows from long-term consolidation across windows.
Introduces a benchmark covering diverse community evolution scenarios.
Experiments show consistent improvement over state-of-the-art baselines across dynamic settings.
papers.selection_reason: Incremental semi-supervised policy learning over dynamic graph snapshots directly fits continual/online adaptation methods.
papers.title: DISRL: Dual-Scale Incremental Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Community Tracking
papers.tldr: DISRL tracks evolving seed-node communities by combining dynamically generated supervision with dual-scale reinforcement learning to reduce adaptation uncertainty and error accumulation.

papers.abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.
authors: Yongqiang Chen, Chenxi Liu, Deyu Zou, Zhenhao Chen, Tongliang Liu, Bo Han, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of low-level, surface-based program mutations without persistent units of control.
Extracts idea-level factors that explain scoring differences between programs and uses them for exploitation and exploration.
Provides theoretical conditions under which idea factors improve sample efficiency.
Improves final performance and sample efficiency by up to 5.0× across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks.
Benefits transfer across 4 other LLMs and 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench.
papers.selection_reason: Idea-level experience extraction and reuse during open-ended evolutionary search is transferable to continual/online adaptation and memory.
papers.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
papers.tldr: ExpEvolve improves evolutionary coding agents by extracting and reusing high-level ideas from program experience to guide future discovery.

papers.abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.
authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Bozhou Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage of offline demonstrations for contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical deployment states.
Uses provenance-conditioned supervised learning to update policies online from human- and policy-generated data.
Evaluated on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, improving task progress and full-task completion over warm-start policies and matched offline demonstrations.
Performs comparably to a fixed-policy data-collection baseline while providing updated checkpoints during deployment.
Each task-specific post-training session completes in under one hour, with learning and checkpoint handling running asynchronously.
papers.selection_reason: Human-in-the-loop online post-training for robot manipulation directly fits embodied manipulation and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: TIDE enables robots to improve manipulation policies during deployment by learning directly from human interventions and policy rollouts without critics, rewards, or action scorers.

papers.abstract: Vision-based insertion requires correcting alignment errors while retaining useful behavior learned from demonstrations. We present ACT--Flow, an online learning framework that couples an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) with a conditional residual flow policy. Following anchor-guided warmup, ACT absorbs successful executed actions through behavioral cloning, while residual targets are recomputed relative to the updated prior. A chunk-level critic learns from successful and failed interactions and evaluates final composed actions. Its estimates weight generated residual candidates for flow matching, complemented by supervision from successful real executions. Candidate scoring is confined to training; deployment uses RGB observations and samples one residual per action chunk. We evaluate the framework on power-plug, USB, and key insertion, together with cable routing and needle threading. Results show a five-task mean success rate of 66% at 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, exceeding the strongest baseline by 18 percentage points at this checkpoint. Evaluations at matched checkpoints with the residual disabled show ACT's mean success increasing from 16% to 76%. Component ablations further support the complementary roles of behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.
authors: Yiqing Yuan, Zhi Li, Jinrong Yang, Mingshan Sun, Mei Yu Zhi, Yong Zhao, Liangliang Ren, Hui Cheng
bullets: Targets alignment correction in insertion and related manipulation tasks while preserving useful demonstration behavior.
Combines an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer with a conditional residual flow policy after anchor-guided warmup.
A chunk-level critic weights residual candidates during training, with additional supervision from successful real executions; deployment uses only RGB observations.
Achieves a 66% mean success rate across five tasks after 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, 18 percentage points above the strongest baseline.
With residuals disabled, ACT's mean success rises from 16% to 76%; ablations support behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Online learning framework that absorbs corrections for vision-based insertion, combining residual flow and critic weighting.
papers.title: Learning to Absorb Corrections: Critic-Weighted Residual Flow for Vision-Based Insertion
papers.tldr: ACT--Flow learns to absorb successful corrections into a vision-based insertion policy while using critic-weighted residual actions to improve performance online.

papers.abstract: A learner's present predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. We study the dynamics of hidden learning structure through two related operations. Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT) describes protected repair of existing function and the learning responses left available after repair. Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT) describes the formation and renewal of trainable structure, distinguishing neutral installation, access to a learning signal, and additional functional directions. The two operations also constrain one another. A repair obligation can force a change in a learning channel, while acquired features can make new protected repairs feasible or reduce the minimum coefficient cost of existing ones. We characterize joint admissibility and response reachability, and give a finite supervised-learning construction in which the two operations together produce a favorable response absent from either operation alone. We implement protected head repair and fixed-capacity LoRA renewal in Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, under replay and output distillation. Across two training trajectories differing in seed and within-task example order, the coordinated policy achieves higher teacher-forced Exact than either separate policy in all four comparisons. It also has the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on the second trajectory. The implementations realize structure-conditioned self-regulation within specified information and action constraints: accessible state readouts and arrived evidence guide repairs and structural renewals, and ordinary learning continues from the modified state.
bullets: Present predictions do not fully determine future learning behavior, motivating analysis of hidden learning structure.
Fiber Regulation Theory models protected repair and the learning responses remaining afterward.
Fiber Acquisition Theory models formation and renewal of trainable structure, including access to learning signals and new functional directions.
The theories jointly characterize admissibility and response reachability, with a finite supervised-learning construction demonstrating a synergistic response.

In Qwen2.5-32B experiments with replay and output distillation, coordinated head repair plus fixed-capacity LoRA renewal achieved higher teacher-forced Exact across four comparisons and the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on one trajectory.
papers.selection_reason: Theory and implementation of learning-structure repair/renewal with LoRA and replay; relevant to continual/online adaptation.
papers.title: Dynamics of Hidden Learning Structure
papers.tldr: A theory and Qwen2.5-32B experiments show that coordinating protected repair with trainable-structure renewal can enable learning responses unavailable to either operation alone.

papers.abstract: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.
authors: Quanling Zhao, Ava Emami, Tsuyoshi Id\'e, Rajiv Joshi, Steven Holmes, Michael Passow, Tajana Rosing
bullets: Addresses the limitations of offline, closed-world wafer defect classifiers in continuously changing manufacturing environments.
Uses hyperdimensional computing with a memory-centric architecture for rapid anomaly detection and compact defect representations.
Models normal spatial patterns, then dynamically groups recurring failures without predefined class counts.
On WM-811K, it improves adjusted Rand index by 13.3 percentage points and normalized mutual information by 10.5 points over the strongest online baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Online open-world defect discovery with dynamically scaling memory; fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing
papers.tldr: WaferHDC enables online discovery and grouping of previously unseen wafer defects without labels, retraining, or storing all raw history.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Haori Lu, Tianyu Gao, Yaoyao Liu, Yingying Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining future-outcome anticipation with accumulated interaction experience in deployed LLM agents.
Uses a world model to imagine outcomes for multiple candidate actions without executing them in the environment.
Applies MPPI-style cost weighting based on predicted task progress and risk to select actions.
Employs dual-branch experience memory to improve both candidate planning and next-observation prediction.
Shows strong overall performance on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three LLM backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes test-time framework combining world-model predictive paths with experience-based adaptation, directly fitting interactive world models and test-time learning.
papers.title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
papers.tldr: A test-time framework helps LLM agents make better decisions by simulating multiple action paths, weighting them by predicted progress and risk, and learning from experience.

papers.abstract: Flow matching learns a generative velocity field by regression, but under distribution drift a field must be deployed before the current data arrive. We study this predictive problem for a fixed, possibly nonconvex, neural class, with dynamic regret against the best represented field of each round. We propose DyProd-FM, which refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and selects among the fits with a sleeping Prod master. Without knowing any drift budget, it attains regret $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\omega+1,1+\sqrt{T\Omega}\})$ in the relative velocity risk variation $\Omega$ and $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\mu+1,1+T^{1/3}V_\mu^{2/3}\})$ in the target-law variation $V_\mu=\sum_t W_2(\mu_{t+1},\mu_t)$, up to approximation and fitting costs. Matching lower bounds for fixed classes show that both rates are optimal in $T$ and in the budgets up to logarithmic factors. Prior optimal dynamic-regret guarantees rely on a convex decision set with strongly convex or exp-concave losses, whereas our class may be nonconvex and no curvature in its parameters is assumed. The target-law rate rests on a second-order link between the two variations, which the base noise of flow matching provides.
bullets: Addresses deployment before current data arrive by minimizing dynamic regret against the best represented flow field at each round.
Refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and uses a sleeping Prod master to select among models without knowing the drift budget.
Achieves near-optimal rates in both relative velocity-risk variation and target-law Wasserstein variation, up to approximation, fitting, and logarithmic costs.
Matching lower bounds establish optimal dependence on time and variation budgets for fixed classes.
The target-law guarantee relies on a second-order relationship between distribution and velocity-risk variation induced by flow-matching noise.
papers.selection_reason: Online learning under distribution drift with dynamic regret for flow matching; fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Minimax-Optimal Predictive Flow Matching under Distribution Drift
papers.tldr: DyProd-FM achieves minimax-optimal predictive flow matching under distribution drift, even for fixed nonconvex neural classes without curvature assumptions.

papers.abstract: Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors. Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations. Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over-specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks. We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline (FLEX), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot's internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features. We evaluate FLEX on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real-world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real-robot demonstrations. Comparisons against single-operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that FLEX achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit-clear-lab.github.io/FLEX/
authors: Audrey Lee, Nathaniel Dennler, Ilia Sucholutsky, Andreea Bobu
bullets: Robot demonstrations show what to do but may not clarify which task features matter, causing misaligned representations.
FLEX iteratively edits representations using three operations: add missing features, generalize overly specific ones, and mask irrelevant ones.
Evaluated on 2D navigation, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation, and real-robot demonstrations with naturalistic language corrections.
All three editing operations are needed for interactive scenarios; FLEX achieves higher normalized reward than compared editing baselines while preserving compact, transferable representations.
papers.selection_reason: Language-guided iterative refinement of robot task representations for adaptive behavior in navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Flexible Language-Guided Representation Editing for Adaptive Robot Behavior
papers.tldr: FLEX lets robots refine task representations through natural-language corrections by adding, generalizing, or masking features, improving adaptive behavior across simulated and real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Adapting language models to new domains during post-training risks degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon commonly known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing mitigation methods largely treat forgetting as a consequence of excessive model drift. They therefore constrain updates by preserving old outputs, replaying old data, or regularizing changes to parameters and representations so that the updated model remains close to its previous state. We take a different view: Rather than pulling the updated model back toward its old state, we translate the new domain into the model's pre-existing knowledge space, making unfamiliar knowledge learnable through familiar procedures. Therefore, we propose Skill Schema Transport (SST), a post-training framework that transports new knowledge into the model's existing skill space. SST abstracts each example type into a skill schema, preserving its essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps while removing domain-specific surface forms. By recasting new examples as instances of reusable procedures, SST turns knowledge update from trajectory memorization into procedural reuse. In continual domain adaptation settings, SST consistently reduces forgetting while improving generalization to related tasks. Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves average final performance on streamed domains by 2.53 to 5.75 points over sequential post-training. It also lowers max-drop forgetting in all evaluated settings, with the largest reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points on the Qwen-3B MATH stream, while substantially recovering the OOD degradation induced by sequential updates.
authors: Zijie Liu, Zhen Tan, Charles Fleming, Tianlong Chen
bullets: Motivation: Continual domain adaptation can degrade previously acquired capabilities.
Method: SST abstracts examples into domain-agnostic skill schemas containing essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps.
Key idea: It promotes procedural reuse instead of memorizing update trajectories or constraining model drift.
Results: Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves final streamed-domain performance by 2.53–5.75 points over sequential post-training.
Scope/result: SST lowers forgetting in all evaluated settings and recovers substantial out-of-domain degradation, including a Qwen-3B MATH-stream max-drop reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes knowledge recasting for continual domain adaptation in language models, directly addressing catastrophic forgetting during sequential adaptation.
papers.title: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Domain Adaptation via Knowledge Recasting
papers.tldr: Skill Schema Transport reduces catastrophic forgetting by recasting new-domain examples as reusable procedures within a language model’s existing skill space.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.
authors: Leann Alhashishi, Christos Margadji, Sebastian William Pattinson
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling long-horizon robotic memory with episode duration.
Fits a neural implicit representation to episode video from a shared meta-learned initialization; the weight delta becomes the memory.
Projects each delta into tokens for language-model question answering and a decoder for joint-command regression.
On RoboMME, the language model performs above chance across question types, while action decoding reaches mean R² = 0.51.
Noise replacement reduces performance by 11.4 points, and random-origin weights are non-decodable, highlighting the importance of meta-learned initialization.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-space episodic memory for robot episodes enables recall and action, directly relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: inr2action: Encoding Robot Episodes as Neural Implicit Representations for Recall and Action
papers.tldr: inr2action stores each robot episode as a fixed-size neural-network weight delta that supports memory-based question answering and action prediction without retrieving frames.

papers.abstract: Comparative Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide critical step-level guidance for autonomous web agents by evaluating state-conditioned preferences between candidate actions. However, existing preference training data synthesized via multi-policy sampling suffers from a severe scarcity of Grounded Minimal Contrastive Pairs (GMCPs)-where competing candidates target genuine on-page elements with identical action types. In representative baselines preference data (namely, WebArbiter), GMCPs account for merely 24.19%, biasing PRMs during training to rely on shallow shortcuts (such as element hallucinations and action type mismatches) rather than acquiring genuine contextual decision semantics. To address these challenges, we propose SURFPRM, a graph-guided process preference synthesis framework for comparative Web PRMs. SURFPRM structures web demonstrations into a persistent Interaction Element Graph that acts as an environment-grounded negative action proposal mechanism, systematically synthesizing contrastive negative actions across spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal confusion axes. This elevates the GMCP proportion from 24.19% to 74.60%, producing the curated SURFPRM-DATA dataset. Across six open-source backbones (3B to 9B parameters), PRMs trained on SURFPRM-DATA outperform baseline-trained models on average on WEBPRMBENCH and rival leading proprietary LLMs. In downstream reward-guided trajectory search on WEBARENA-LITE, SURFPRM provides step-level guidance for both GPT-4o (+14.21%) and GPT-4o-mini (+12.83%) policies, yielding substantial improvements in complex web task success rates.
bullets: Existing preference data contains few Grounded Minimal Contrastive Pairs (GMCPs), encouraging PRMs to use shortcuts instead of contextual decision semantics.
SURFPRM builds a persistent Interaction Element Graph to propose environment-grounded negative actions across spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal confusions.
It raises the GMCP share from 24.19% to 74.60%, producing the SURFPRM-DATA training set.
Across six 3B–9B open-source backbones, SURFPRM-trained PRMs outperform baseline-trained models on average on WEBPRMBENCH.
Reward-guided search improves WEBARENA-LITE success rates for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini by 14.21% and 12.83%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: SURFPRM improves process reward models for web agents by synthesizing grounded preferences via interaction element graphs, enhancing step-level guidance and decision semantics.
papers.title: From Trajectories to Grounded Preferences: Process Preference Synthesis via Interaction Element Graphs for Web PRMs
papers.tldr: SURFPRM improves web-agent process reward models by synthesizing more grounded, minimally contrastive action preferences from interaction graphs.

papers.abstract: Reusable skills help LLM-based agents solve complex tasks, but the agent must receive guidance before it commits to an ineffective approach. Existing skill mechanisms often expose only metadata and load full content on demand, leaving useful guidance unavailable until the agent decides to retrieve it. General memory methods can incur substantial maintenance overhead, while keeping guidance in conversation context risks repeatedly exposing the agent to irrelevant or harmful advice. We propose TipsWarm, a mechanism that complements existing skill mechanisms by maintaining a budgeted pool of skill-derived keypoints, or \textit{warm tips}, for selective injection into the context of every message turn. By separating event-triggered LLM assessment from inexpensive per-turn screening, it makes transferable skill guidance readily available while controlling maintenance costs. In three coding and iterative task-execution benchmarks, TipsWarm achieves the highest task success rate while remaining time-efficient, compared to recent skill and general memory baselines.
bullets: Existing skill systems may reveal guidance only after an agent commits to an ineffective approach.
TipsWarm selectively injects retained “warm tips” into every message turn.
It combines event-triggered LLM assessment with inexpensive per-turn screening.
Across three coding and iterative task-execution benchmarks, it achieves the highest reported task success rate while remaining time-efficient.
The approach is designed to reduce repeated exposure to irrelevant or harmful advice.
papers.selection_reason: TipsWarm addresses agent context management by maintaining a budgeted pool of warm tips, offering a mechanism for timely guidance and efficient memory management during inference.
papers.title: Enabling Timely Guidance before Skill Retrieval: Retaining Helpful Warm Tips in Agent Context
papers.tldr: TipsWarm keeps a budgeted set of useful skill-derived tips available at each turn, improving timely guidance for LLM agents while limiting maintenance overhead.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, perception models often struggle to generalize to new environments due to domain shifts. While unsupervised model adaptation offers a feasible solution without labor-intensive manual labeling, existing methods that rely solely on the ego-vehicle's data often lead to inferior pseudo-labeling performance. To address this critical issue, we propose LDE, Learning from Distributed ``Eyes", a novel framework that transforms collaborative perception (CP) into a source of high-quality supervision for model adaptation. This pseudo-labeling approach is hyperparameter-insensitive and relatively reliable, assuming CP often outperforms single-agent's perception. However, naively implementing this approach encounters (1) the communication bottleneck of sharing rich features under time and bandwidth constraints, (2) the view discrepancy between the CP view and the learner's Field of View (FoV), and (3) the unreliability even in CP-generated labels. To address these issues, we design an adaptation-oriented feature sharing mechanism that selectively transmits the most critical information for adaptation, an FoV filtering method that meticulously eliminates mismatched labels, and a curriculum learning strategy to progressively exploit pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on 3D object detection tasks demonstrate that LDE consistently outperforms both the pre-trained models and state-of-the-art unsupervised adaptation methods.
bullets: Addresses domain-shifted 3D object detection without manual labels, improving on ego-vehicle-only adaptation.
Uses an adaptation-oriented feature-sharing mechanism to reduce communication costs while preserving useful information.
Applies field-of-view filtering to remove collaborative labels that do not match the learner’s view.
Uses curriculum learning to gradually incorporate increasingly reliable pseudo-labels.
Experiments show consistent gains over pretrained models and existing unsupervised adaptation methods, without reported numerical results.
papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised adaptation of driving perception models via collaborative pseudo-labels; fits deployment-time/test-time model adaptation.
papers.title: Learning from Distributed Eyes: Leveraging Collaborative Perception for Automated Model Adaptation
papers.tldr: LDE adapts autonomous-driving perception models to new environments by using collaborative perception from multiple vehicles to generate and progressively learn from more reliable pseudo-labels.

papers.abstract: TS2Vec is one of the strongest self-supervised methods for time series classification, introduced in 2022. It is designed to be trained anew on every dataset: self-supervised pre-training followed by linear probing. Since then, the field has shifted towards foundation models that reuse one encoder across datasets. Yet TS2Vec offers a compact convolutional architecture that operates directly on temporal samples and accepts variable-length inputs without resampling. We ask whether these properties can be retained when the encoder is pre-trained only once, and show that they can: TS2Vec can essentially be turned into a foundation model. Three changes suffice: pre-train on a synthetic corpus, feed the encoder a raw amplitude view and an instance-normalized shape view of the input through two small stems, and distill one specialist encoder per view into a single encoder. The result, TS2Vec-FM, is a 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional network that, kept frozen, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27 under linear probing, within 0.3 pp of MantisV2, the current state of the art, and above TS2Vec trained separately on each target dataset. What we find most interesting is how different TS2Vec-FM is from other foundation models in design: near-parity is reached without attention, without a patch tokenizer, and without intermediate-layer extraction, using an "old-school" convolutional encoder and a two-layer MLP stem.
authors: Vasilii Feofanov, Zhenghan Tai, Andrei Ermakov, Irina Rish
bullets: Retains TS2Vec’s direct temporal processing and support for variable-length inputs without resampling.
Pre-trains once on synthetic data using raw-amplitude and instance-normalized-shape views.
Distills two view-specific specialist encoders into one 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional encoder.
With linear probing, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27, within 0.3 percentage points of MantisV2.
Achieves near-parity without attention, patch tokenization, or intermediate-layer extraction.
papers.selection_reason: Repurposes a time series encoder into a reusable foundation model via distillation, relevant to foundation model reuse and adaptation across datasets.
papers.title: Turning TS2Vec into a Foundation Model for Time Series Classification
papers.tldr: TS2Vec-FM turns TS2Vec into a compact, attention-free time-series foundation model that performs near state-of-the-art classification with a single frozen encoder.
