papers.abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
authors: Xinxin Liu, Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Ming Li, Wentao Bao, Chen Chen, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses reliance on powerful closed-source planners by improving the planner model itself.
Combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning.
Uses harness-specific adapters to unify training across VLA skill invocation and control-code generation while keeping execution components fixed.
On LIBERO-PRO, raises a 9B planner’s success rate from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory.
Framework and trained planner checkpoints are planned for release.
papers.selection_reason: Applies post-training techniques from coding agents to robot planners, significantly improving performance without external memory.
papers.title: AgenticRoboRL: Bringing Coding-Agent Post-Training to Agentic Robotics
papers.tldr: AgenticRoboRL improves robot planners through post-training across diverse robotics harnesses, substantially increasing task success without external memory.

papers.abstract: Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap. We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.
bullets: Problem: Token-level teacher scores can reward safe but delaying actions, creating a rollout–scorer gap that causes students to run out of turns even when the teacher can complete the task.
Method: Mine high-disagreement student states, run teacher takeovers, retain states passing consensus or an LLM-based reward-free check, and fine-tune the teacher on takeover-informed token scores.
Training then uses the repaired teacher as the frozen sole scorer in standard agentic OPD, without task rewards or takeover context.
Across three environments, two teachers, and four students, R2S beats three prior agentic-OPD methods in all 12 evaluated cells.
It gains an average of 12.8 success points over the strongest prior method per cell.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses a specific failure mode in agentic distillation (rollout-scorer gap) and proposes a repair mechanism, relevant to test-time adaptation and agent learning.
papers.title: Capable Teacher, Myopic Scorer: Reward-Free Teacher Repair for Agentic On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: R2S repairs a teacher’s myopic token scorer using reward-free teacher takeovers before on-policy distillation, improving agent success across all tested settings.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image personalization aims to equip pretrained diffusion models with the ability to learn user-specific concepts from only a few reference images. Existing methods, however, typically train each concept independently or assume that all concepts are available simultaneously. In practical applications, concepts often arrive sequentially, requiring models to continually learn new subjects, objects, or styles while minimizing interference with previously acquired concepts. We address this continual concept personalization setting by extending residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models. Our work achieves the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting. Beyond these empirical gains, the learned residual-space dynamics reveal where adaptation capacity is concentrated within the diffusion model. Restricting adaptation to the identified layers by our method preserves nearly the same performance while reducing the number of trainable parameters by up to 72\%, demonstrating that residual-space dynamics can identify the layers that contribute most to continual concept personalization and directly guide more parameter-efficient adaptation.
authors: Yuzhi Liu, Enis Simsar, Giulia Lanzillotta, Thomas Hofmann
bullets: Addresses continual personalization, where user-specific concepts arrive sequentially rather than all at once.
Extends residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models.
Reports the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting.
Uses residual-space dynamics to identify layers most important for adaptation.
Restricting training to those layers preserves nearly the same performance and reduces trainable parameters by up to 72%.
papers.selection_reason: Continual concept personalization in diffusion models directly addresses continual learning with parameter-efficient adaptation.
papers.title: Continual Concept Personalization in Diffusion Models via Residual-Space Adaptation
papers.tldr: A residual-space adaptation approach enables diffusion models to learn concepts sequentially with high fidelity, near-zero forgetting, and up to 72% fewer trainable parameters when focused on key layers.

papers.abstract: Tactile-visual-language models combine vision and touch through a shared language space to recognize objects and materials. In real-world deployment, changes in lighting, contact quality or sensor hardware can shift visual or tactile inputs and degrade recognition performance. When both modalities contribute to a prediction, an unreliable modality can override correct evidence from the other. Since labeled data are generally unavailable during deployment, test-time adaptation offers a way to recover recognition performance from unlabeled observations. In this setting, we find that comparing accumulated observations with the text embeddings of candidate classes reveals modality reliability differences that confidence can miss. Refining features against competing classes also improves recognition beyond geometric alignment alone. These findings motivate SenseAlign, which uses a common semantic reference for test-time modality weighting and feature correction. Alignment Trust weights each modality according to its support for shared predicted classes. Anchor Realignment uses the same class text embeddings to fit a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from alternatives. Both modules use the same unlabeled history while keeping all encoders frozen. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate strong recognition performance under both natural shifts and controlled corruptions.
authors: Chuyang Ye, Qinting Jiang, Jingyan Jiang
bullets: Addresses recognition degradation caused by lighting, contact-quality, and sensor-hardware shifts when labeled deployment data are unavailable.
Alignment Trust weights visual and tactile modalities by their support for shared predicted classes, revealing reliability differences that confidence may miss.
Anchor Realignment learns a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from competing alternatives using class text embeddings.
Both modules reuse unlabeled observation history while keeping all encoders frozen.
Experiments across diverse datasets show strong recognition under natural shifts and controlled corruptions.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time modality weighting and feature correction for tactile-visual-language recognition; fits test-time learning.
papers.title: SenseAlign: Understanding Vision and Touch through Language at Test Time
papers.tldr: SenseAlign adapts frozen vision-touch-language models at test time by using class-text embeddings to reweight unreliable modalities and correct features from unlabeled observations.

papers.abstract: Realistic few-shot adaptation of medical vision-language models (VLMs) can leave low-prevalence classes without any labeled support. The training-free SS- Text+ solver remains operational in this setting, but its zero-support prototypes receive no visual adaptation and fall back to a purely textual class prototype. We in- troduce Gated Knowledge-Guided Prototype Transfer (GProtoT), a pre-repulsion module that transfers supported-class visual residuals to missing classes using VLM similarity and an ontology-based clinical distance. A validation-free evidence gate scales transfer based on semantic relevance and residual agreement, thereby limiting unsupported extrapolation. In 50 paired realistic one-shot trials on MESSIDOR with FLAIR features, severe and proliferative diabetic retinopathy were absent from every support set. Relative to SS-Text+, gated ProtoT improved missing-class recall by 5.23 points, average class accuracy by 1.37 points, and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points. It reduced negative- transfer frequency from 46-48% for ungated transfer to 2%, while at the cost of reductions of 1.20 percentage points in supported-class recall and 0.45 percentage points in top-1 accuracy. These results indicate that evidence-based gating provides a safety mechanism for the knowledge source. GProtoT is based on SS- Text+ and requires no gradients, validation data, or additional model inference, of- fering a low-compute path toward accountable adaptation under incomplete clini- cal supervision. Code is available: https://github.com/sumaiyaafridi/GProtoT
authors: Sumaiya Fazal, Rizwan Qureshi, Laleh Behjat, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou
bullets: Addresses zero-support classes in realistic few-shot medical VLM adaptation, where textual prototypes lack visual adaptation.
Transfers supported-class visual residuals using VLM similarity and ontology-based clinical distance.
Uses a validation-free evidence gate based on semantic relevance and residual agreement to limit unsupported extrapolation.
Across 50 paired one-shot trials on MESSIDOR, missing-class recall improved by 5.23 points and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points.
Reduced negative-transfer frequency to 2%, with modest decreases in supported-class recall and top-1 accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free prototype transfer for zero-support VLM adaptation; fits test-time adaptation under incomplete supervision.
papers.title: Gated Prototype Transfer for Zero-Support Medical Vision Language Model
papers.tldr: GProtoT safely transfers visual knowledge to medical VLM classes with no labeled support, improving missing-class recall while sharply reducing negative transfer without training or validation data.

papers.abstract: Wearable devices increasingly support personalized health and well-being applications, but post-deployment data can differ substantially from those used for training, while purely local adaptation may be limited by the data available on a single device during real-world operation. Conventional federated and decentralized learning rely on recurrent communication and stable connectivity, whereas existing opportunistic approaches often exploit available encounters without adequately considering their utility, compatibility, or communication cost. We propose PULSE, an event-driven framework for personalized opportunistic learning that treats each encounter as an online collaboration decision, selecting either no interaction or a promising nearby peer. Peer gradients are incorporated only when compatible with the local learning direction, while past interactions guide future peer selection. Across human activity recognition, fall detection, and stress recognition under synthetic and real contact traces, PULSE preserves or improves personalized classification performance, while reducing peer-assisted exchanges by 80-94% compared with opportunistic model averaging. On-device experiments further demonstrate its feasibility on wearable hardware: peer-assisted operations require limited energy, while the complete implementation occupies 149.8 KiB of RAM and 561.8 KiB of flash. The obtained results show that selective opportunistic collaboration can provide effective personalization while limiting communication and resource demands on constrained wearable devices.
authors: Mattia Giovanni Campana, Dariush Salami, H\"useyin Yi\u{g}itler, Stephan Sigg
bullets: Addresses distribution shift after deployment and limited data for purely local adaptation.
Uses event-driven peer selection based on encounter utility, compatibility, and past interactions.
Accepts peer gradients only when they align with the device’s local learning direction.
Maintains or improves personalized performance across activity, fall, and stress recognition tasks.
Reduces peer-assisted exchanges by 80–94% versus opportunistic model averaging and fits on constrained wearable hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Online personalized learning with selective peer collaboration for wearables.
papers.title: PULSE: Personalized Opportunistic Learning for Wearable Devices
papers.tldr: PULSE enables wearable devices to personalize models through selective, low-cost collaboration with nearby peers during opportunistic encounters.

papers.abstract: Person re-identification (ReID) ranks an image gallery using either an image query or a textual query. In image-to-image (I2I) ReID, viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, and background changes can make distractors appear more similar than the true match. In text-to-image (T2I) ReID, incomplete or ambiguous descriptions may omit key visual evidence. We study this problem for vision-language model (VLM) based ReID, where attributes such as clothing color and carried objects provide useful fine-grained matching cues. However, directly using attribute-prompt similarities as retrieval scores is unreliable because templated prompts can be biased, correlated, and poorly calibrated. We therefore propose \textbf{PR}ompt-guided \textbf{A}ttribute-based \textbf{I}nference-time \textbf{S}imilarity \textbf{E}nhancement (\texttt{PRAISE}), a query-side test-time adaptation framework for VLM-based ReID. Instead of treating prompts as scores, \texttt{PRAISE} uses a transferable attribute-prompt bank to construct an \emph{Attribute-Conditioned Subspace} (ACS): a query-dependent low-rank subspace induced by the most compatible attribute prompts. ACS provides a controlled attribute-conditioned geometry for reshaping query--gallery affinities and guiding lightweight inference-time updates without identity or attribute labels. Experiments across multiple I2I- and T2I-ReID benchmarks show that \texttt{PRAISE} consistently improves VLM retrieval backbones and outperforms both generic and ReID-specific TTA baselines.
authors: Rajarshi Bhattacharya, Aryan Shukla, Shakeeb Murtaza, Christian Desrosiers, Jose Dolz, Maguelonne Heritier, Eric Granger
bullets: Addresses distractor similarity in image-to-image ReID and incomplete or ambiguous descriptions in text-to-image ReID.
Builds an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace from the most compatible prompts in a transferable attribute-prompt bank.
Uses this subspace to reshape query–gallery affinities and guide lightweight, label-free test-time updates rather than treating prompt similarities as direct scores.
Improves VLM retrieval backbones across multiple I2I- and T2I-ReID benchmarks and outperforms generic and ReID-specific test-time adaptation baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Query-side test-time adaptation for VLM-based person re-identification fits test-time learning research.
papers.title: In PRAISE of Attributes: Grounding Retrieval Geometry with Query-Conditioned Subspaces for Person Re-Identification
papers.tldr: PRAISE improves VLM-based person re-identification by using query-conditioned attribute subspaces to refine retrieval geometry at inference time.

papers.abstract: Automated respiratory sound classification enables continuous, non-invasive respiratory assessment, yet long-term deployment remains challenging due to domain shifts from evolving recording devices and acquisition periods. When privacy and governance regulations prohibit replaying historical data, sequential learning easily overwrites previously acquired knowledge. Preserving dedicated domain experts prevents parameter interference, but selecting the correct expert at inference is difficult under overlapping acoustic distributions and absent domain labels. To resolve this dilemma, we propose APRIL, an exemplar-free domain-incremental framework for RSC. Built on a shared frozen BEATs backbone, APRIL sequentially inherits and isolates low-rank experts to enable new-domain adaptation without altering earlier models. A multi-level prototype router retrieves the top-two candidate experts and dynamically selects the final model by integrating domain-routing posteriors with classification confidence, adaptively weighted by matching ambiguity. We establish standardized device- and temporal-incremental benchmarks on the ICBHI and SPRSound datasets across forward and reversed domain orders. Evaluated over five random seeds, APRIL consistently achieves the highest final-session average Score among compared continual learning approaches, reaching 64.4% and 65.4% on ICBHI, and 83.1% and 82.2% on SPRSound under forward and reversed sequences, respectively. Crucially, average forgetting remains under 1.0% across all protocols, demonstrating robust domain adaptation and long-term knowledge retention without data replay. Overall, APRIL offers a reliable and privacy-preserving paradigm for deploying continuous respiratory sound classification across real-world healthcare settings.
bullets: Addresses domain shifts from evolving recording devices and acquisition periods, where domain labels and historical-data replay may be unavailable.
Uses a shared frozen BEATs backbone with sequentially isolated low-rank experts for exemplar-free domain-incremental adaptation.
A multi-level prototype router selects between two candidate experts using domain posteriors and classification confidence, weighted by ambiguity.
On ICBHI and SPRSound forward/reversed domain sequences, APRIL achieves final-session average Scores of 64.4%/65.4% and 83.1%/82.2%, respectively.
Average forgetting stays below 1.0% across protocols, indicating strong retention without replay.
papers.selection_reason: Domain-incremental continual learning with expert routing for privacy-preserving adaptation.
papers.title: APRIL: Ambiguity-Aware Expert Routing for Respiratory Sound Domain-Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: APRIL enables privacy-preserving respiratory sound classification across changing domains by routing ambiguous inputs to specialized low-rank experts without replaying historical data.

papers.abstract: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under-characterised. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model from an un-fine-tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text-input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non-additively: math-only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip-phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains, so per-phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task-dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.
bullets: Studies an 8.4B-parameter model across vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning.
Math-only distillation erases previously acquired financial knowledge while preserving procedural math ability.
Domain tuning mainly repairs lost capabilities rather than adding entirely new ones.
Skipping a phase maximizes domain knowledge but sacrifices numerical-reasoning gains.
The best checkpoint depends on the task, favoring careful checkpoint retention and phase scheduling over simply adding stages.
papers.selection_reason: Staged post-training of a multimodal foundation model with analysis of phase interactions, forgetting, and capability trade-offs.
papers.title: Staged Continual Adaptation of Multimodal Foundation Models for Japanese Financial Documents
papers.tldr: Staged adaptation of a multimodal model for Japanese financial documents produces task-dependent trade-offs, showing that training phases interact non-additively rather than contributing independently.

papers.abstract: Online Continual Learning (OCL) requires models to learn from non-stationary data streams under a strict single-pass constraint, making them highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. While existing studies have explored various strategies from data, architecture, and optimization perspectives, the optimizer often directly uses generic approaches such as SGD and AdamW. In this work, we reveal a new link between optimization dynamics and OCL needs by recasting Polyak-Ruppert averaging as the engine of "plasticity" and Primal averaging as the anchor of "stability". This inspires our novel optimizer, SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation), which explicitly decouples plasticity and stability by interpolating between a fast-moving "plasticity" sequence and an adaptive "stability" sequence. We theoretically demonstrate that SPIN implicitly employs an inverse Hessian approximation, providing crucial Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy, single-sample Hessian estimates and mitigate forgetting. More importantly, SPIN can be seamlessly integrated into existing OCL methods by taking resulted gradients as input and replacing standard optimizers. Extensive experiments show that using SPIN instead of standard optimizers yields consistent and significant performance gains across multiple OCL approaches, including the challenging rehearsal-free setting and under strict memory constraints.
authors: Yongyi Wu, Zheng Wang, Sen Lin
bullets: OCL must learn from non-stationary streams in a single pass, making generic optimizers vulnerable to forgetting.
SPIN interpolates a fast-moving plasticity sequence with an adaptive stability sequence, inspired by Polyak-Ruppert and Primal averaging.
Its dynamics implicitly approximate the inverse Hessian and apply Tikhonov regularization to suppress noisy single-sample curvature estimates.
SPIN can replace standard optimizers in existing OCL methods without changing their gradient inputs.
Experiments report consistent, significant gains across multiple OCL approaches, including rehearsal-free and strict-memory settings.
papers.selection_reason: Novel optimizer for online continual learning directly targets adaptation and stability-plasticity trade-offs.
papers.title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning
papers.tldr: SPIN is an optimizer for online continual learning that balances rapid adaptation with stability to reduce catastrophic forgetting.

papers.abstract: In object goal navigation (ObjectNav), an embodied agent must find a target object (e.g., "find a bed") in a previously unseen environment, relying on spatial commonsense such as object co-occurrence. Large Language Models (LLMs) encode this commonsense, but deploying them on robots exposes a trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency: cloud-based models incur latency and privacy risks, whereas small on-device LLMs are fast but prone to hallucinated spatial judgments. Hybrid reasoning LLMs offer both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, which raises a key question for embodied agents: when is slow thinking worth its cost? We propose CovNav, a training-free framework that answers this question with Conformal Prediction (CP), turning dual-process (System 1 / System 2) inference into an uncertainty-aware decision. Much like recent decision models such as Jev, CovNav casts each spatial query as a structured binary decision rather than free-form generation: a local LLM in fast mode judges whether the target is likely near an observed object, CP converts its token probabilities into a prediction set, and only ambiguous queries are escalated to slow chain-of-thought reasoning. The object-pair formulation keeps calibration tractable and supports open-set objects through off-the-shelf detectors. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that CovNav surpasses the strongest zero-shot baseline by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points in success rate on HM3D v1 and v2, while invoking slow reasoning for only 12.4% of queries and retaining most of the gain of always-on thinking at a fraction of its latency. Real-robot experiments on a TurtleBot 4 further validate the approach. CovNav shows how calibrated uncertainty can decide when an embodied agent should think slowly, offering a principled form of adaptive test-time reasoning for LLM-based robots.
authors: Pengying Wu, Zhejia Wen, Kang Ding, Kangjie Zhou, Chunxuan Jiao, Wei Pan, Xiangli Nie, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between fast, error-prone on-device reasoning and slower, more capable thinking.
A fast local LLM makes binary object-pair proximity judgments; conformal prediction identifies ambiguous cases for escalation to chain-of-thought reasoning.
The training-free design supports open-set objects detected by off-the-shelf detectors and keeps calibration tractable.
On Gibson and HM3D, CovNav improves HM3D success by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points over the strongest zero-shot baseline while using slow reasoning for 12.4% of queries.
TurtleBot 4 experiments further validate the approach in real-robot navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses Object Goal Navigation (a core robot navigation task) using Conformal Prediction to adaptively switch between fast and slow reasoning, fitting both Robot Navigation and Test-Time Learning.
papers.title: CovNav: Conformal Prediction-Guided Adaptive Inference for Object Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: CovNav uses conformal prediction to trigger slow LLM reasoning only for uncertain spatial queries, improving ObjectNav success while reducing costly inference.

papers.abstract: Medical visual grounding requires models to align clinical descriptions with spatial evidence across heterogeneous imaging domains. However, existing multi-domain post-training strategies typically rely on fixed domain sampling and shared parameter updates, overlooking the need to adapt both which domains receive training and where their updates are applied. To address this issue, we propose PACE-MoE, a policy-guided framework that jointly performs adaptive domain sampling and domain-specific adaptation for medical visual grounding. PACE dynamically assesses the training value of each imaging domain from current-policy feedback and progressively adjusts domain coverage through domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing. Meanwhile, domain-specific LoRA adapters route updates to the corresponding imaging domains while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder. This coordinated design aligns training-data allocation with parameter adaptation without modifying the original reward formulation or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. Experiments across seven medical imaging domains show that PACE-MoE consistently improves grounding performance over fixed-domain training, achieving a 3.64% relative improvement in mean box IoU over the Vanilla baseline. Under matched domain-specific adapter architectures, adaptive sampling alone further improves mean box IoU by 2.07%, demonstrating the benefit of policy-guided domain allocation. These results establish coordinated data-parameter routing as an effective strategy for multi-domain medical visual grounding.
authors: Zhenxuan Wang, Jisheng Dang, Ronghao Lin, Bimei Wang, Jingwen Zhao, Wenjun Ma, Bin Hu, Qi Tian, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses fixed domain sampling and shared updates in heterogeneous medical imaging.
Uses policy feedback to adapt domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing.
Routes domain-specific LoRA updates while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder.
Across seven imaging domains, improves mean box IoU by 3.64% relative to the Vanilla baseline.
Adaptive sampling alone yields a further 2.07% mean box IoU improvement under matched adapters.
papers.selection_reason: Policy-guided domain sampling and domain-specific LoRA for medical visual grounding; relevant to spatial multimodal grounding and continual multi-domain adaptation.
papers.title: PACE-MoE: Adaptive Domain Sampling and Domain-Specific LoRA for Medical Visual Grounding
papers.tldr: PACE-MoE improves multi-domain medical visual grounding by jointly adapting which imaging domains are trained and where parameter updates are applied.

papers.abstract: Online adaptation of the cornering stiffness keeps a model-based sideslip estimator valid as tires change, but competes with learned model correction for the same filter innovation. A corrector with enough parameters can absorb the innovation pattern that a stiffness change produces, and adaptation is suppressed while the fit improves. We propagate the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted measurements through the vehicle states and construct a corrector orthogonal to them. A null-space parameterization enforces the constraint without a penalty coefficient and preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment. In full-vehicle simulation, the stiffness response of the unconstrained corrector declines as its parameter count grows, whereas the orthogonal corrector responds at least as fully as the uncorrected filter at all sizes and lowers sideslip error by 12.7% to 22.0%. In a simulated drive with a stiffness step, the orthogonal corrector adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter and lowers sideslip error during and after the transient. On public real-vehicle data, the 430-parameter unconstrained corrector loses most of its response to deliberate offsets of the filter's nominal stiffness, whereas the orthogonal corrector of the same size retains most of it, with a sideslip error slightly above the uncorrected filter's.
authors: Kyoungtae Ji, Dongyeol Won, Kyoungseok Han
bullets: Problem: Flexible learned corrections can absorb the innovation caused by tire-stiffness changes, suppressing stiffness adaptation.
Method: Propagate stiffness sensitivities through the vehicle model and constrain the corrector to their null space using a penalty-free parameterization.
Contribution: The approach preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment while separating correction from stiffness adaptation.
Results: In simulation, it reduces sideslip error by 12.7%–22.0% and adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter during stiffness transients.
Scope: On public real-vehicle data, it retains most stiffness response for a 430-parameter corrector, though sideslip error is slightly higher than with the uncorrected filter.
papers.selection_reason: Online adaptation of a model-based estimator with sensitivity-orthogonal residual learning; technically transferable to test-time and online adaptation of learned components.
papers.title: Sensitivity-Orthogonal Residual Learning for Adaptive Sideslip and Cornering Stiffness Estimation
papers.tldr: An orthogonality-constrained learned corrector preserves online cornering-stiffness adaptation while improving model-based sideslip estimation.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (PVLMs) achieve strong zero-shot recognition but often suffer performance degradation under target-domain shift. Unsupervised adaptation provides a practical way to improve target-domain performance without labeled data, but it remains challenging because pseudo-labels generated by the model can be unreliable and no labeled validation set is available for model selection or early stopping. We propose a simple framework for unsupervised PVLM adaptation that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. The subset selection strategy constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, enabling adaptation to start from reliable supervision anchors before incorporating broader target-domain data. Cascaded consistency learning further exploits unlabeled samples by using temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering to reduce the influence of uncertain pseudo-labels. To preserve the pretrained embedding structure, the framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts. Experiments across multiple recognition benchmarks with both CLIP and SigLIP backbones show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods. These results suggest that progressive pseudo-label selection and teacher-guided consistency provide an effective and lightweight strategy for adapting PVLM classifiers without labeled target data.
bullets: Addresses unreliable pseudo-labels and the lack of labeled validation data during target-domain adaptation.
Builds a class-balanced pseudo-labeled subset from prediction margins, starting with high-confidence samples and expanding it progressively.
Uses cascaded consistency learning with temporally smoothed teacher predictions, strong/weak augmentations, and confidence filtering.
Updates only visual-encoder normalization parameters and text-initialized class prototypes to preserve pretrained representations.
Across multiple benchmarks with CLIP and SigLIP, consistently improves over zero-shot baselines and remains competitive with recent unsupervised methods.
papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised adaptation of pretrained vision-language models via progressive pseudo-label selection and cascaded consistency.
papers.title: Progressive Subset Selection and Cascaded Consistency for Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation
papers.tldr: A lightweight unsupervised adaptation framework improves vision-language model recognition under domain shift by progressively expanding reliable pseudo-labels and enforcing teacher-guided consistency.

papers.abstract: 4D scene graphs require persistent object identity when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and later reappears as a fresh detection. When appearance and target-centric motion are unavailable, identity recovery must rely on relational history. We formulate cross-visibility-gap identity persistence as historical-node recovery through a remembered target--carrier binding. We introduce CVG-SGM, a perception-frontend-compatible transfer--maintain--read memory. Geometry-weighted cross-node interaction transfers target-specific evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU maintains this information during transport, and a two-time readout combines stored carrier--identity compatibility with current detection--carrier geometry to recover the historical identity. In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, CVG-SGM achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy, compared with 0.570 for both no-memory and parameter-count-matched no-write controls. It also generalizes to scene-disjoint, unseen longer visibility gaps. On real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes, it correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed carrier--identity control. Counterfactual carrier-memory swaps redirect predictions according to the swapped bindings, supporting the role of stored relational information in identity recovery. The current approach remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.
authors: Jiahui Hu, Li Gao, Yu Liu, Pengzhan Zhou
bullets: Addresses identity recovery when objects disappear inside opaque carriers and later reappear as new detections.
Uses geometry-weighted target-to-carrier transfer, per-node GRU memory during transport, and a two-time compatibility readout.
Achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy in the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, versus 0.570 for both no-memory controls.
Correctly re-links 36/36 held-out real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed-binding control.
Generalizes to unseen longer gaps, but remains limited by shared-carrier ambiguity and lacks end-to-end raw-video re-identification.
papers.selection_reason: Memory mechanism for persistent object identity across visibility gaps in 4D scene graphs, combining spatiotemporal memory with 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Cross-Visibility-Gap Identity Persistence for 4D Scene Graphs
papers.tldr: CVG-SGM preserves object identities across visibility gaps by storing target–carrier relational bindings, achieving perfect re-linking in controlled and reported real-feature episodes.

papers.abstract: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.
authors: Laurent Mombaerts, Jonathan Taws, Jacopo Gargano, Dinesh Gaddam, Kevin George, Srijan Tiwari, Shreyas Rajesh
bullets: Prompt evolution uses outcome-driven reflection to update a roughly 900-word forecasting policy.
On a refreshed benchmark of search indices, currencies, commodities, and paired news, the method achieves GM MASE 0.776 versus 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3.
Performance transfers to newer models without measurable loss and updates cost dollars rather than GPU-days.
Untouched monitoring is important: in-loop gains can overstate out-of-loop gains by 2–3×, while error-only objectives suppress the text modality.
Code compilation recovers most gains deterministically; benefits are larger at short horizons, and removing news does not hurt after policy distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free continual adaptation of a frozen LLM forecaster via outcome-driven prompt evolution for multimodal time-series forecasting.
papers.title: Training-Free Continual Learning for Multimodal Forecasting via Prompt Evolution
papers.tldr: Evolving a text guidance block enables a frozen LLM to continually adapt multimodal forecasts without retraining, outperforming tested TSFMs under strict leakage controls.

papers.abstract: Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $\sigma$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off. Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $\tau^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured.
bullets: Verifier strength measures agreement with a trusted reference and bounds how safely a change can improve an agent.
Recoverability depends on whether rollback avoids new verification and restores prior behavior, including effects during deployment.
The proposed rule permits unattended prompt, tool, and skill edits, while requiring human approval for weight updates.
Experiments found an LLM judge could give unchanged scores across inputs without reporting errors, so verifier health must be tested.
Saved-copy rollback restored behavior, but regenerated undo did not; deployed changes also affected 17% of tasks beyond normal variation.
papers.selection_reason: Measures safe unattended agent self-improvement from execution traces, directly relevant to online adaptation and continual agent updates.
papers.title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: Unattended agent self-improvement should require both a measured-strong verifier and a reliably recoverable old version.

papers.abstract: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.
authors: Stella Kombo, Masih Haseli, Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala, Peter I. Renn, Morteza Gharib, Joel W. Burdick
bullets: Addresses model mismatch from unmodeled, spatially varying aerodynamic disturbances during deployment.
Learns an offline nominal Koopman Control Family model, then updates only a lightweight, low-dimensional residual correction online.
Uses causal state-command-state transitions and evaluates disturbance corrections across the MPC prediction horizon.
Hardware tests on a nano-quadrotor in uniform wind and a spatially varying wake show improved multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbances increase.
Designed to satisfy real-time control requirements while preserving the nominal model.
papers.selection_reason: Online learning of disturbance corrections for Koopman MPC during deployment, fitting test-time adaptation for robust robot control.
papers.title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
papers.tldr: A disturbance-aware Koopman MPC framework adapts online to changing wind effects while keeping the nominal model fixed, improving quadrotor prediction and tracking in real time.

papers.abstract: Although deep learning-based point cloud denoising methods have demonstrated impressive results in recent years, their effectiveness usually degrades substantially in real-world scenarios where the noise distribution of test point clouds deviates from that of the training set. To address this challenge, we propose a test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework that enables existing denoising approaches to adapt to unknown noise patterns at test time without relying on additional supervision or retraining from source data. Taking a pre-trained denoising model and a test noisy point cloud as input, TTAD first employs a residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module to estimate the sample-specific noise distribution through analyzing the deviation between the noisy input and its pseudo-clean version denoised by the initial model. Then, a noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module is designed to build sample-specific noisy-noisier test-time training pair from the denoised point cloud, and update the model parameters over a few adaptation steps per sample at test time through contrastive learning. Furthermore, TTAD naturally extends to a continual TTAD (CTTAD) setting, facilitating efficient progressive refinement across sequential test samples with consistent noise distributions, while reducing the computational cost per sample. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the generalization ability of existing denoising models under unseen noise, achieving superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics.
authors: Kun Jiang, Shida Fu, Fanhao Yi, Weiqing Li, Zhiyong Su
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when test-time noise differs from training noise.
Uses residual-driven noise modeling to estimate each input’s sample-specific noise distribution.
Constructs noisy–noisier training pairs for noise-aware contrastive adaptation over a few test-time steps.
Extends to continual TTAD for efficient progressive refinement on sequential samples with consistent noise.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improved generalization across multiple metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation for point cloud denoising under unseen noise; directly fits test-time learning and 3D perception.
papers.title: Test-time Adaptation for Point Cloud Denoising under Unseen Noise
papers.tldr: TTAD adapts pre-trained point cloud denoisers to unseen test-time noise without source data or additional supervision by modeling noise and performing per-sample contrastive updates.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.
authors: Ruhan Wang, Kishan Panaganti, Dongruo Zhou
bullets: LLM agents can self-improve by storing execution experience without changing model parameters.
Stored rules, summaries, and skills enable strategy reuse but may propagate errors through retrieval and reuse.
The paper identifies “error reproduction,” where faulty abstractions influence executions that generate further faulty abstractions.
Anti-Persistence stores trajectories and outcomes but synthesizes task-specific guidance only when needed, discarding it afterward.
Across benchmarks and backbones, it achieves the highest overall held-out success and lowest average LLM-call cost among evaluated memory designs.
papers.selection_reason: Studies external memory design and error propagation in LLM-agent self-improvement, fitting LLM memory and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Persistent abstractions can amplify errors in LLM-agent memory, while reconstructing task guidance on demand improves held-out performance and reduces average LLM-call cost.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.
authors: Lilin Xu, Linyang He, Kaiyuan Hou, Yuang Fan, Minghui Zhao, Xuhai Xu, Xiaofan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the gap between immediate-response agents and delayed everyday intentions that require action hours or days later.
Organizes egocentric video and audio perceptions into context-aware memories with prospective cues linking earlier events to later developments.
Retrieves relevant past events from the current context and performs memory-augmented reasoning to decide whether assistance is needed.
Introduces CPMBench, a benchmark with 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance.
Experiments report the best memory retrieval performance and consistent improvements over all evaluated baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Prospective memory over egocentric sensory contexts directly targets embodied memory for long-horizon proactive assistance.
papers.title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
papers.tldr: ProMemAgent enables long-horizon proactive assistance by using prospective memory over past sensory contexts to anticipate future user needs.

papers.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. This causes parameter updates to entangle primitives and induce drift that degrades performance on earlier compositions. Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL) formalizes this setting by introducing new state-object compositions across tasks. In this paper, we propose Layer-Specific Adaptation with Prototype-Anchored Adapter-Space Transport (LSA-PAST), a parameter-efficient method tailored to composition-IL. LSA integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into a frozen ViT with depth-specialized adapters for states, objects, and compositions. PAST then maps past, anchored prototypes into the current adapter space through a rehearsal-free affine transform fit on current-task data, enabling old prototypes to remain compatible with new adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LSA-PAST achieves state-of-the-art (SOA) accuracy-forgetting trade-off performance for composition-IL.
authors: Kyle Stein, Andrew Arash Mahyari, Guillermo Francia III, Eman El-Sheikh, Jiangpeng He
bullets: Composition-IL introduces new combinations of shared primitives, but standard CIL treats each composition independently and causes representation drift.
LSA applies depth-specific LoRA adapters in a frozen ViT for states, objects, and compositions.
PAST uses a rehearsal-free affine transform to map anchored old prototypes into the current adapter space using current-task data.
Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy–forgetting trade-offs for composition-IL.
papers.selection_reason: Compositional class-incremental learning with LoRA adapters and prototype transport.
papers.title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: LSA-PAST helps models learn new state–object compositions without severely forgetting earlier ones by using specialized adapters and transporting old prototypes between adapter spaces.

papers.abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.
authors: Bo Yan, Qi Zhang, Zhen Tan, Tianlong Chen, Song Wang
bullets: LLM agents must balance deeper reasoning against saving budget for later decisions.
PORA learns the value of longer reasoning by comparing short- and long-reasoning outcomes from the same state.
At inference, a controller combines this value with remaining-budget pressure to select one reasoning length without running both.
It performs strongly across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks.

On BFCL memory, it improves over the strongest existing method by 17.4–32.9 percentage points; on code and mathematics, it matches or exceeds always-long reasoning with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes PORA, a method for LLM agents to dynamically decide when to use short or long reasoning based on outcome-guided comparison, optimizing the reasoning budget during inference.
papers.title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: PORA adaptively chooses short or long reasoning for each agent step, preserving task performance while reducing reasoning costs.

papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.
authors: Akansha Kalra, Ellen R. Novoseller, Vernon J. Lawhern, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses pluralistic alignment when user preferences are heterogeneous and annotators are anonymized.
Jointly learns trajectory embeddings and a shared basis of preference directions using PCA decomposition.
Supports rapid personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization at test time.
Across embodied control tasks, generalizes to out-of-distribution users and supports variable adaptation-query budgets.
Achieves competitive reinforcement-learning and test performance while reducing computational cost.
papers.selection_reason: Personalized policy alignment for embodied control tasks with test-time adaptation to new users; relevant to robot learning and test-time learning.
papers.title: Steerable Pluralistic Policy Alignment from Anonymized Crowd Feedback
papers.tldr: P3L learns steerable, personalized policies from anonymous and conflicting crowd preferences without needing annotator identities.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.
authors: Haonan Zhao, Jiaxuan Chen, Qingyang Liu, Shuochen Chang, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of re-encoding or retrieving video evidence for every question.
Uses causal tracing to identify video-specific model layers for memory adaptation.
Distills the representation changes caused by visual clips into a text-only memory under compact multi-scale supervision.
Evaluated on LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, achieving data-efficient video-free QA with fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods.
Scope: memory is adapted separately for each video, so it is not a universal video memory.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training internalizes long-video memory into parameters for video-free QA.
papers.title: Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training for Long-Video Understanding
papers.tldr: MIT^3 adapts a model per video to store visual knowledge in compact parameters, enabling text-only long-video question answering without repeatedly processing frames.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
authors: Rui Shi, Xunjian Yin, Jiacheng Sang, Zichuan Liu, Shuyan Zhou
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting and the need for different capabilities across long-horizon trajectories.
Trains independent LoRA adapters on a frozen backbone and exposes adapter selection as internal tool-calling actions.
Enables on-demand capability composition instead of fixed parameter configurations or static adapter merging.
On eight deep-research benchmarks, reports 6.2% higher average accuracy than full fine-tuning and 27.5% higher than static LoRA merging.
Supports modular continual adaptation by adding or updating individual adapters without changing the backbone or other capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes WeAct, a method for modular continual adaptation in agents using dynamic weight switching (LoRA adapters) as internal actions, directly addressing catastrophic forgetting in long-horizon agents.
papers.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
papers.tldr: WeAct lets agents dynamically switch among capability-specific LoRA adapters during execution, reducing forgetting and improving deep-research performance.

papers.abstract: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.
bullets: Problem: Human monitoring and corrective interventions do not scale as robot fleets grow.
Method: FERT retrieves relevant successful trajectory segments using failure contexts and fine-tunes the policy with their actions as supervision.
System: FATS asynchronously coordinates experience collection, training, and policy distribution despite robot interruptions.
Results: Across five real-world manipulation tasks, policies reached 93.3–99.2% success on robots excluded from data collection; larger fleets generally improved performance.
Scope: Demonstrated for deployment-time learning in real-world manipulation, including phone packaging, where 96 robots improved success from 79.2% to 98.3%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a collective learning paradigm (CEL) and a specific fine-tuning method (FERT) for robot fleets, directly addressing robot manipulation and learning from deployment experience.
papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots
papers.tldr: Collective experience learning lets robot fleets improve a shared policy from deployment failures and successful trajectories without additional expert corrections, achieving high reliability across manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Federated learning for capacity-heterogeneous clients and federated continual learning are each well studied on their own, but their intersection -- clients holding differently sized models while every client's data stream also drifts over time -- remains underexplored. We study this setting directly, training a ResNet-18 fleet from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, class-incremental), and introduce DROD (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout), which builds on FjORD's Ordered Dropout by using two independent reduction axes to extract sub-models: a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter/FLOP budget ladder, DROD achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model federated learning strategies we compare. Its advantage over the two strongest baseline geometries persists across every replay-buffer size we test and under ER, DER++, and BiC; under EWC, all three geometries collapse alike.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored combination of device capacity heterogeneity and drifting client data.
Extends FjORD’s Ordered Dropout with two independent sub-model reduction axes: shortcut ratio and branch ratio.
Evaluated with ResNet-18 models trained from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 across 10 class-incremental tasks.
Outperforms the two strongest baseline geometries across tested replay-buffer sizes under ER, DER++, and BiC.
Under EWC, DROD and the comparison geometries perform similarly, indicating a scope limitation.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning of models on drifting data streams under federated heterogeneous-device settings.
papers.title: DROD: Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout for Federated Continual Learning on Heterogeneous Devices
papers.tldr: DROD enables federated continual learning with differently sized client models and achieves the best mean accuracy among compared heterogeneous-model strategies in the studied setting.

papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are required to reason over distributed history across modalities and evolving dialogue states. While existing flat cross-modal methods compress visual evidence prematurely and struggle with temporally stale observations, they neglect the necessity to unify multimodal and cross-session evidence. Crucially, raw multimodal memories are inherently entangled and heterogeneous, making fine-grained visual grounding and cross-modal reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present latent multimodal memory reasoning, i.e., LMMR, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term multimodal memory organization into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of converting images to text and relying on static retrieval, LMMR maps both textual hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, establishing sparse activations as common semantic addresses to dynamically construct a turn-level multimodal memory graph. (ii) A graph encoder then aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies across the task-specific latent subgraph, injecting the graph readout as a continuous residual rollout into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens to preserve fine-grained details. Extensive experiments on nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings demonstrate that LMMR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex multimodal dependencies while enabling faithful and grounded responses.
authors: Cai Ke, Xinghao Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Yuni Lai, Keyu Chen, Ruizhi Qiao, Siyu An, Junnan Dong, Ruifeng Xu, Xing Sun
bullets: Addresses distributed, evolving multimodal history, including temporally stale observations and heterogeneous raw memories.
Maps text hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space with sparse semantic addresses.
Builds turn-level multimodal memory graphs and uses a graph encoder to aggregate cross-modal and temporal dependencies.
Injects graph representations into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens for fine-grained grounding.
Experiments across nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in multimodal dependency capture and response faithfulness.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a neuro-symbolic framework for long-term multimodal memory reasoning, mapping visual and textual evidence into a shared latent space to handle spatiotemporal dependencies.
papers.title: Latent Multimodal Memory Reasoning
papers.tldr: LMMR organizes long-term multimodal memories in a shared latent concept space and reasons over their temporal and cross-modal relationships for more faithful responses.

papers.abstract: Real-world intelligent systems increasingly operate under open-world conditions, where user intents are not fixed or exhaustively known a priori and may evolve as new interaction patterns emerge. This paper proposes a unified uncertainty-aware probabilistic framework for continual new intent discovery under an evolving label space. Each utterance is encoded through an adaptive $β$-VAE into a latent mean, used for classification and density modelling and a posterior uncertainty estimate acting as a global reliability signal. Classifier confidence, posterior uncertainty and DP-GMM likelihood are combined through a multi-signal decision mechanism to distinguish known intents from potentially novel samples. Candidate novel instances are clustered through a density-based discovery module and only reliable clusters are promoted to new labels, enabling controlled label-space expansion. Replay and Elastic Weight Consolidation mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve previously acquired knowledge. The paper formalises continual intent discovery as a structured multi-phase open-world problem, introduces adaptive label-space expansion under stability--plasticity constraints and uses posterior uncertainty to regulate trusted-sample selection, pseudo-labelling, novelty admission and replay. Experiments show high novelty precision, stable adaptation across sequential phases and limited forgetting. Near-zero NMI and ARI indicate limited reconstruction of the complete fine-grained intent taxonomy, consistent with the framework's conservative promotion strategy. Qualitative analyses nevertheless reveal dense and locally coherent semantic clusters, showing that reliable novel structures can be discovered without exhaustive recovery of the underlying taxonomy.
bullets: Uses an adaptive β-VAE to model latent representations, classify intents, estimate density, and provide posterior uncertainty.
Combines classifier confidence, uncertainty, and DP-GMM likelihood to detect potentially novel utterances.
Clusters candidate novel samples and promotes only reliable clusters as new labels.
Replay and Elastic Weight Consolidation reduce catastrophic forgetting during sequential adaptation.
Achieves high novelty precision and stable adaptation with limited forgetting, but does not fully reconstruct fine-grained intent taxonomies.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses open-world continual learning with uncertainty-aware mechanisms, relevant to agent adaptation.
papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for Open-World Intent Discovery Under an evolving Label Space
papers.tldr: An uncertainty-aware continual-learning framework discovers and cautiously adds new intents while preserving knowledge under an evolving label space.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
authors: Adrian Remonda, Jiajun Xi, Nicklas Hansen, Marcus Greiff, Thomas Lew, John Talbot, John Subosits, Xiaolong Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost and safety risks of collecting extensive real-world RL data.
Pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulation trajectories.
Uses uncertainty-regularized planning to correct simulation-to-reality mismatch during online adaptation.
