Adapts faster across track and surface changes in simulation, with lower lap times and fewer failures than baselines.
Demonstrates reliable few-shot adaptation on a full-size autonomous race car with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Model-based RL with simulation priors and online adaptation for autonomous racing; fits world models, embodied navigation, and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
papers.tldr: PIA uses biased simulation experience plus limited real-world interaction to rapidly adapt model-based RL controllers for autonomous racing.

papers.abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.
authors: Alessandro Palma, Charles Jones, Tristan Cinquin, Fabian J. Theis, Frederik Wenkel
bullets: Addresses forgetting and replay-distribution degradation in sequential generative-model updates.
Trains a new velocity field to combine frozen historical and incoming-task velocities, weighted by a stability–plasticity coefficient.
Uses mean velocity distillation to access historical trajectories with only a few network evaluations per update.
The method outperforms generative-replay and distillation baselines for class-incremental image generation.
Biological case studies show adaptation across contexts and batches while preserving treatment-effect prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Lifelong generative modeling via trajectory replay; directly addresses continual learning without forgetting.
papers.title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models
papers.tldr: Trajectory replay enables lifelong continuous-time generative modeling without repeatedly simulating historical samples, preserving prior knowledge while adapting to new tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.
authors: Mai Liu, He Sun, Siru Zhong, Kerun Chen, Hao Yan, Xiaohui Lv, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu
bullets: Addresses temporal confusion, incomplete or distorted records, recurring memory errors, and rising storage/retrieval costs.
Uses six linked memory layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural.
Combines contract-constrained memory operations, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with teacher verification, and failure-driven rule repair.
Models storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost–utility allocation under storage and read budgets.
Reports strong results across several benchmarks, including 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, and improved contract compliance from 50.9% to 86.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-layer embodied memory framework directly matches embodied memory subtopic.
papers.title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: BetaMem is a layered, self-improving memory framework that helps embodied agents maintain accurate, traceable long-term memories under changing environments and resource limits.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.
authors: Siwei Cheng, Hao Wu, Zitong Qi, Xinming Zhang, Haoyu Xi, Peiran Yin, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: ReInsBench diagnoses how effectively vision-and-language navigators use historical observations through controlled continuation trials.
Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression removes temporal redundancy while preserving instruction-relevant visual context.
Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders prompt frozen navigators to revisit retained observations on a predefined schedule without extra model calls.
On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN reaches 64.27% and 64.44% success, improving over StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1 by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points.
Visual compression reduces prefill latency and KV-cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%; robot trials support broader sequential instruction-following use.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLN with history compression and reminders, improving navigation while reducing KV cache; fits VLN, embodied memory, and token/cache efficiency.
papers.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: ReInsVLN is a training-free memory framework that compresses and periodically reactivates navigation history, improving VLN performance while reducing inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Latent memory is gaining ground as a lightweight history supplement for GUI agents. It supplies history to a frozen vision-language model via prefix vectors trained with step-wise cross-entropy (CE). While resulting gains are naturally attributed to encoded history, our controlled experiments show they primarily stem from action revision. The prefix learns to alter the model's default actions. However, this revision is unscoped because step-wise CE pushes outputs toward reference actions at every step without explicitly preserving correct decisions. Consequently, it repairs errors but also breaks 8-13% of initially correct answers. Overall accuracy metrics hide these losses. We therefore propose ScopeMem, a latent-memory method for scoped revision. Its encoder conditions prefix generation on the model's initial answer and is trained to correct errors while preserving correct decisions. On the controlled ablation set, ScopeMem reduces the share of broken correct decisions to 5.6% while repairing more errors than any evaluated CE-trained prefix. On AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, and zero-shot AITW, ScopeMem outperforms all evaluated prompting and latent-memory baselines, enabling a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B to match or surpass GUI-specialized agents and Qwen3-VL-32B.
authors: Zhicheng Zheng, Cheng Zhang, Shengping Yu, Tianxiang Zhao
bullets: Latent-memory gains mainly come from changing the agent’s default actions, not merely supplying history.
Standard step-wise cross-entropy revision repairs errors but breaks 8–13% of initially correct decisions.
ScopeMem conditions its prefix memory on the initial answer to enable scoped correction.
It reduces broken correct decisions to 5.6% while repairing more errors than evaluated CE-trained prefixes.
On AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, and zero-shot AITW, it outperforms evaluated prompting and latent-memory baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Latent memory method that scopes revision of frozen GUI agents via memory-conditioned prefixes.
papers.title: ScopeMem: Latent Memory That Learns Where to Revise Frozen GUI Agents
papers.tldr: ScopeMem improves frozen GUI agents by learning to revise incorrect actions while preserving decisions that were already correct.

papers.abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.
authors: Guannan Lai, Zi-Yang Bai, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
bullets: Resource constraints can make existing memory methods ineffective, as irrelevant or ineffective retrieval consumes scarce context and reasoning capacity.
The key challenge is to estimate memory worth—not merely retrieve relevant experiences.
TokenWorth is a lightweight online framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback.
It uses the learned worth signal for both memory retrieval and bounded memory management.
Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and local/API deployments, it achieved the highest task success with the fewest output tokens among evaluated methods.
papers.selection_reason: Learns query-dependent memory worth for lifelong agents under tight memory and token budgets.
papers.title: Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints
papers.tldr: TokenWorth learns which experiences are worth retaining and retrieving, enabling more effective lifelong-agent adaptation under tight resource budgets.

papers.abstract: Multi-label classification is particularly challenging in streaming scenarios, where data arrives sequentially. Online kernel methods offer a promising solution. However, prevailing methods rely on a single preselected kernel, making them prone to suboptimal choices since the global data distribution is unknown in advance in online settings. Although the recent method, Online Kernel Selection for Online Multi-label Classification (OKS-OMC), enables data-driven kernel selection, it fails to fully harness the complementary information from multiple kernels and encounters the curse of kernelization. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel online multi-kernel combination method for large-scale multi-label classification. First, an efficient and robust online single-kernel multi-label method is designed. Second, learning an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers is formalized as a structural risk minimization problem. An improved alternating optimization procedure is developed, in which the combination coefficients are updated by directly minimizing the objective function, while each kernel classifier is updated by minimizing a surrogate upper bound. This procedure decouples the learning of kernel classifiers from combination coefficients, allowing independent classifier updates via our single-kernel method and accelerating convergence to high-quality solutions. Our multi-kernel method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best fixed single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Ablation studies confirm that our method's components outperform their counterparts in OKS-OMC. Comprehensive evaluations across 11 datasets and seven metrics demonstrate our method's overall superiority over existing online multi-label methods.
authors: Tingting Zhai, Wei Liu, Renjian Yu
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of choosing kernels when the data distribution is unknown in advance.
Learns an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers through structural risk minimization.
Uses alternating optimization: combination coefficients directly minimize the objective, while classifiers minimize surrogate upper bounds.
The method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best hindsight-selected single-kernel models.
Ablations and evaluations on 11 datasets using seven metrics show improvements over OKS-OMC and other online multi-label methods.
papers.selection_reason: Online multi-kernel combination for streaming multi-label classification; fits online learning.
papers.title: Optimal Multi-Kernel Combination for Online Multi-Label Classification
papers.tldr: An online multi-kernel method improves streaming multi-label classification by learning complementary kernel combinations rather than relying on a single preselected kernel.

papers.abstract: Once historical clients become unavailable, a federation must serve newcomers through the artifact it leaves behind. How much of its knowledge remains useful in an architecture chosen afterward? We introduce FEDNBO, a seven-dataset benchmark that separates knowledge supply, policy identification, and private-model compilation under disjoint data roles. Controlled studies expose inflated oracle gains, architecture-dependent transfer reversals, and a gap between teacher accuracy and private-model utility. Ordinary public-response distillation provides a competitive reference without public task labels or newcomer samples: gains over strengthened local training are 23.52 and 16.62 percentage points on 300 CelebA identities and 300 FedEMNIST writers, respectively. In a complete-pipeline FedEMNIST comparison, this reference reaches 97.13% accuracy with 12.4 seconds of compilation per architecture, versus 97.03% and 67.5 seconds for a HeteroFedTTA reconstruction at the same epoch budget. Equal-count public-input interventions extend support sensitivity to trainable visual backbones. Together, these results establish an auditable benchmark and a strong reference for evaluating the utility, cost and reliability of post-federation knowledge transfer.
bullets: Separates knowledge supply, policy identification, and private-model compilation using disjoint data roles across seven datasets.
Finds inflated oracle gains, architecture-dependent transfer reversals, and a mismatch between teacher accuracy and private-model utility.

Ordinary public-response distillation is a competitive reference without public labels or newcomer samples, improving over strengthened local training by 23.52 and 16.62 percentage points on CelebA and FedEMNIST, respectively.
On FedEMNIST, it achieves 97.13% accuracy with 12.4 seconds of compilation per architecture, compared with 97.03% and 67.5 seconds for HeteroFedTTA at the same epoch budget.
Equal-count public-input interventions assess support sensitivity for trainable visual backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FEDNBO, a benchmark for knowledge portability to heterogeneous newcomers in federated learning. Relevant to continual and online learning.
papers.title: After the Federation: Benchmarking Knowledge Portability to Heterogeneous Newcomers
papers.tldr: FEDNBO benchmarks how effectively a federation’s remaining knowledge can be transferred to heterogeneous newcomer architectures after historical clients disappear.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.
authors: Rui Wang, Zishen Lai, Jiayu Liu, Cheng Qian, Jeonghwan Kim, Heng Wang, Xuejun Zhang, Jiateng Liu, Bingxuan Li, Shujin Wu, Qing Zong, Tianshi Zheng, Chunyang Li, Qihan Lin, Chen Li, Dadi Guo, Xiusi Chen, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Benchmarks proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments.
Agents must infer hidden rules from evidence and detect implicit rule drift through degraded performance.
Experiments across eight leading LLMs show the task remains challenging; GPT-6 Sol reaches 61.9% calibrated accuracy.
Providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance by nearly 10%.
Agents often reason well with informative evidence but struggle to obtain the right evidence and recognize when prior evidence is outdated.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM agents' proactive exploration and test-time adaptation under rule drift; fits test-time learning.
papers.title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments
papers.tldr: AdaExploreBench tests whether LLM agents can proactively discover hidden environmental rules and adapt when those rules silently change, revealing major weaknesses in evidence acquisition and stale-knowledge detection.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues - such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states - that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window. Project page: https://github.com/FeiyangHong/CondenseVLA
authors: Feiyang Hong, Yujie Wei, Bo Zhao, Xiu Su, Hongxun Yao, Shuo Yang
bullets: Targets short-term cues such as contacts, occlusions, and intermediate object states that single frames cannot resolve.
Uses decoder-side learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention to compress cached per-frame VLM features into a fixed set of history slots.
Regularizes slot attention and embeddings to encourage complementary, non-redundant representations.
Improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8%, reaches 97.2% on LIBERO and 52.8% on real-world tasks.
Achieves 21.6% on memory-dependent RMBench tasks, highlighting limits of a finite recent-history window.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CondenseVLA, a VLA policy that condenses visual history into slot tokens for efficient robot manipulation. This directly addresses robot manipulation and embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: CondenseVLA: Learnable History Condensation for Efficient Multi-Frame VLA
papers.tldr: CondenseVLA efficiently integrates recent visual history into robot actions by learning to condense redundant frame features into complementary slot tokens.

papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.
authors: Yizhou Yang, Jiahong Fu, Zhiwu Wang, Kailong Fan, Haokun Lin, Yichen Wu, Zhenan Sun, Renzhen Wang, Deyu Meng
bullets: Sequential editing can cause cumulative parameter interference and degrade general abilities.
The paper finds that projection-based methods’ robustness mainly comes from update regularization, not null-space projection.
FisherEdit penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while allowing flexibility for new facts.
Its Fisher-geometry formulation has an efficient row-wise closed-form solution.
Experiments across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 show strong performance and improved preservation of downstream accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Fisher information-guided knowledge editing for LLMs, addressing sequential editing and stability, relevant to model adaptation and memory.
papers.title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FisherEdit uses Fisher-information-guided parameter regularization to add knowledge while better preserving LLM stability and general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL) is highly challenging, as it requires (i) learning a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting, and (ii) identifying unknown samples (OOD) without access to known (in-distribution (ID)) data from past tasks, where standard confidence-based OOD scores tend to degrade. Existing methods largely rely on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume closed-world settings, limiting their scalability and reliability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel OOD detection framework for rehearsal-free continual learning, inspired by Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which mitigate catastrophic forgetting via their inherent local neuroplasticity. To better leverage KAN in OOD-CL, we introduce a task-adaptive classifier architecture, TA-KAN, which mitigates recency bias and enhances ID--OOD separability through task-specific control of activation locality. Furthermore, we propose a geometry-guided OOD score that complements TA-KAN classifier confidence without relying on past ID data. Our method significantly improves OOD detection while maintaining strong ID classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD-CL.
authors: Nimeshika Udayangani, Flora D. Salim, Christopher Leckie, Sarah Erfani
bullets: Addresses OOD detection when past task data are unavailable and catastrophic forgetting must be avoided.
Introduces TA-KAN, a task-adaptive classifier designed to reduce recency bias and improve ID–OOD separation.
Adds a geometry-guided OOD score that complements classifier confidence without using past ID data.
Reports significantly improved OOD detection with strong ID classification and state-of-the-art OOD-CL results.
Scope: focuses on rehearsal-free continual-learning settings.
papers.selection_reason: Rehearsal-free continual learning with out-of-distribution detection; directly fits continual and online learning.
papers.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: A rehearsal-free continual-learning framework combines task-adaptive KANs with geometry-guided scoring to detect OOD samples while preserving classification performance.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.
authors: Xiaoyin Chen, Yizheng Huang, Yinglun Xu, Ziyun Zhao, Emmett McQuinn, Julie Liu, Hope Yao
bullets: Studies continual learning for agents facing changing topics, workflows, and domains while keeping model weights frozen.
Evaluates ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness across four drifting task streams built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld.
Self-modification improves aggregate performance but global edits can interfere with unseen tasks and overwrite earlier knowledge.
Memory retrieval localizes updates better, yet can retrieve irrelevant memories and collide when similar queries require different workflows.
Higher plasticity consistently trades off against stability.],
papers.selection_reason: Explicitly studies self-evolving agents as continual learners, focusing on adapting prompts and memory without weight updates. Directly addresses continual learning in agents.
papers.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
papers.tldr: Self-evolving agents improve performance across changing task streams, but their adaptation mechanisms still cause forgetting and interference, making them incomplete continual learners.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can complete a task despite local execution errors that are corrected, bypassed, or carried forward without individually determining its outcome. We call these implicit failures (IFs) and study them as signals for process observability beyond final task outcome. Across 1,828 traces from nine MAS-benchmark configurations, IFs occur in 54.3% of successful and 75.2% of failed traces. We develop taxonomies of error types and subsequent absorption mechanisms, supported by human and cross-model annotation audits. Counterfactual replay further probes how repairing an IF changes the final outcome. To examine the practical value of IFs, we evaluate IF-based best-of-N trace selection against existing process reward models, and introduce a novel RL algorithm, IF-GRPO, that uses IF costs to refine preferences among successful trajectories in GRPO. Experiments show that IF-GRPO exhibits some gains in accuracy and process metrics. Importantly, it exposes trade-offs between task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density. Overall, our results show that IFs provide complementary process observability into how MAS reach their outcomes, including error recovery, propagation, and IF-based process differences that final task success alone does not expose.
authors: Yanwei Huang, Arpit Narechania, Atanu Sinha
bullets: IFs appear in 54.3% of successful traces and 75.2% of failed traces across 1,828 traces from nine benchmark configurations.
The study taxonomizes error types and absorption mechanisms, validated through human and cross-model annotation audits.
Counterfactual replay examines how repairing implicit failures affects final outcomes.
IF-based trace selection and the IF-GRPO reinforcement-learning method use implicit-failure costs to refine process preferences.
Results indicate some gains in accuracy and process metrics, while revealing trade-offs among task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density.
papers.selection_reason: Studies 'implicit failures' in multi-agent systems to provide process observability. This relates to retaining interaction history and error recovery, relevant to embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: MASIF: Implicit Failures for Process Observability in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: Implicit failures—local errors absorbed without changing the final outcome—offer a complementary way to observe and improve multi-agent system processes beyond task success alone.

papers.abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) enables agents to adapt to new tasks without parameter updates, relying on memory to retain what they learn from experience. For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.
authors: Jiawen Wang, Cheng Xue, Peng Zhang, Jochen Renz
bullets: Targets the trade-off between bounded memory and retaining older experience in continual in-context reinforcement learning.
Uses a Transformer policy with a short recent-interaction buffer plus a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience.
Rewrites the summary when the buffer fills, keeping deployment memory and per-decision cost O(1) with task length.
On long partially observable tasks, maintains adapted performance for 8× the training horizon using about 1% of full-history memory, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Summary access is necessary for the benefit; changing or swapping summaries alters adaptation and behavior toward the corresponding task.
papers.selection_reason: Bounded-state in-context RL with recurrent summary memory directly addresses continual adaptation and memory for agents.
papers.title: Remember Less, Adapt Longer: Bounded-State In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Recurrent Summary Memory
papers.tldr: Recurrent Summary Memory lets a fixed-capacity policy retain useful experience and adapt over long-running tasks without growing memory or per-decision costs.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility--diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility--diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility--diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.
authors: Jianhao Zhang, Ou Wu, Yi Du
bullets: Targets noisy, redundant synthetic candidate pools and the difficulty of preserving pretrained capabilities during single-stage fine-tuning.
Builds a navigator by applying the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization, revealing recipe-induced capability drift.
Scores candidates by predictive divergence between the navigator and pretrained model to estimate forgetting-aware utility.
Efficiently selects a utility–diversity constraint set, then distills pretrained behavior on it during new-task fine-tuning.
Experiments report a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation with lower selection overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces NADS for mitigating catastrophic forgetting in LLM fine-tuning using a navigator-guided data selection strategy.
papers.title: NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: NADS selects synthetic data using navigator-model drift to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning without access to pretraining data.

papers.abstract: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. We propose PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning with a compact shared adapter. Specifically, PFedQFT constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using a truncated matrix-exponential approximation followed by QR orthonormalization. Compatible projections reuse these bases, while a globally shared full core preserves the flexibility of each projection. Each client further maintains a lightweight private residual operator, whose directions are learned globally and whose coefficients remain local. Experiments on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones show substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter upload volume, with competitive predictive performance on most tasks.
authors: Qihan Huang, Lingxia Zhang, Guye Zhang, Zizhu Wang, Xiaowei Mao
bullets: Addresses fragmented medical data and the communication and parameter costs of independently learned low-rank adapters.
Builds reusable adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators via truncated matrix exponentials and QR orthonormalization.
Shares a full core across compatible projections while keeping lightweight residual coefficients local to each client.
Evaluated on seven public medical tasks and multiple LLM backbones.
Reports substantial reductions in trainable parameters and per-round adapter uploads, with competitive performance on most tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning of medical LLMs, focusing on efficient adapter sharing and parameter reduction.
papers.title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models
papers.tldr: PFedQFT enables privacy-preserving, personalized federated fine-tuning of medical LLMs using reusable orthonormal adapter bases and lightweight client-specific residuals.

papers.abstract: As deep neural networks are required to continuously adapt to evolving data, class-incremental learning (CIL) has become an active research area. However, most existing works primarily focus on improving accuracy while overlooking confidence calibration, which measures the trustworthiness of the model's predictions. Although temperature scaling (TS) is effective for static calibration, it has rarely been explored in continual settings where data distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Continual Calibration (MT-CC), a novel post-hoc calibration framework that addresses the asymmetric calibration behavior in CIL, where the rate of confidence changes does not align with the rate of accuracy degradation across tasks, leading to different levels of miscalibration. Our key contribution is to design multiple temperature parameters through a lightweight grouping network that separates samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals in CIL. Furthermore, a Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization is incorporated to promote intra-group consistency. Experiments demonstrate that MT-CC significantly improves calibration performance while maintaining accuracy, offering a principled framework for reliable continual learning.
authors: Sungjun Yun, Yonghee Choi, Dong-Jun Han
bullets: Addresses miscalibration in continual learning, where confidence and accuracy change asymmetrically across tasks.
Uses a lightweight grouping network to assign multiple temperature parameters based on confidence statistics and task-aware signals.
Adds Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization to encourage consistency within groups.
Experiments show improved calibration performance while maintaining accuracy.
Scope: a post-hoc calibration framework for evolving class-incremental settings.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses confidence calibration in class-incremental learning, a continual learning setting.
papers.title: MT-CC: Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Asymmetric Calibration Behavior in Class-Incremental Learning
papers.tldr: MT-CC improves confidence calibration in class-incremental learning by applying task-aware, group-specific temperature scaling without sacrificing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised cross-domain person re-identification remains challenging because domain shifts generate noisy pseudo labels that are reinforced during iterative adaptation. Existing clustering-based methods often rely on limited reliability cues or global confidence criteria and may impose hard identity supervision on ambiguous target samples. To address these limitations, we propose CGPLR, a confidence-guided pseudo-label refinement framework for unsupervised domain-adaptive person re-identification. CGPLR estimates sample-level reliability by jointly modeling centroid compatibility, local neighborhood consistency, separation from the strongest competing cluster and temporal assignment stability. The resulting confidence distribution is used to derive cluster-adaptive upper and lower thresholds for a three-way selective decision. Reliable assignments are preserved, recoverable samples are reassigned only when an alternative cluster receives sufficient geometric and neighborhood support and highly ambiguous samples are deferred from hard identity supervision. The learning objective adapts to these decisions through confidence-weighted supervision for preserved samples, cautious corrected-label weighting for reassigned samples and label-free representation consistency for deferred samples. CGPLR achieves 76.4% Rank-1 accuracy and 47.6% mean average precision (mAP) on Market-1501 to MSMT17, and 95.1% Rank-1 accuracy and 87.7% mAP on MSMT17 to Market-1501, demonstrating effective reliability-aware selective adaptation. The code is available at https://github.com/Sundas058/CGPLR.
authors: Sundas Iqbal, Danish Ali, Qing Tian, Yuhui Zheng, Jianping Gou, Weihua Ou
bullets: Addresses noisy pseudo-label reinforcement caused by domain shifts during iterative adaptation.
Combines centroid compatibility, neighborhood consistency, competing-cluster separation, and temporal stability to estimate reliability.
Uses cluster-adaptive thresholds for three-way decisions: preserve reliable labels, cautiously reassign recoverable samples, or defer ambiguous samples.
Applies confidence-weighted supervision to preserved and reassigned samples, plus label-free consistency learning for deferred samples.
Reports 76.4%/47.6% Rank-1/mAP from Market-1501 to MSMT17 and 95.1%/87.7% in the reverse direction.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses unsupervised domain adaptation in person re-identification using confidence-guided pseudo-label refinement, a method applicable to continual learning scenarios.
papers.title: Confidence-Guided Pseudo-Label Refinement for Unsupervised Cross-Domain Person Re-Identification
papers.tldr: CGPLR improves unsupervised cross-domain person re-identification by refining pseudo labels according to sample reliability and deferring ambiguous assignments.

papers.abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $\pi_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang, Maggie Wang, Fangneng Zhan, Manling Li, Qianqian Wang, Mac Schwager, Zhuang Liu, Li Fei-Fei, Mengyu Wang, Paul Pu Liang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving robot policies from limited test-time experience while keeping pretrained weights fixed.
Uses a sparse autoencoder and a shared temporal descriptor of feature activation-order patterns to select a task-specific feature without timestep alignment.
Builds reference banks offline from successful and failed rollouts, then online determines when and how strongly to adjust the feature activation.
With 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, improves success by approximately 10% across simulated and real-world manipulation evaluations.
Scope: requires labeled successful and failed reference rollouts and focuses on steering a selected feature during execution.
papers.selection_reason: Improves pretrained robot action models at test time via few-shot activation steering, fitting learned robot control and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
papers.tldr: SteerAct improves pretrained robot action models at test time by steering one task-relevant feature dynamically, using only a few successful and failed rollouts and without changing model weights.

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. Unlike previous works, we study online tool grounding: binding an already specified tool call to one physical endpoint under service cost and device participation constraints. We propose a framework that learns which physical device should execute each agent-issued call. It formulates selection as a contextual bandit problem and combines adaptive context partitions with hierarchical endpoint trees, so that execution feedback is reused across related requests and devices. Selection balances task success against service cost while respecting device capability, authorization, battery reserves, and availability. Gaussian reward aggregation provides an optional mechanism for protecting individual feedback values. Theoretical results establish a finite-horizon regret bound and differential privacy for released reward statistics under fixed, reward-independent assignments. In a simulated loading-dock workload, the proposed router achieves higher step success and better cost-adjusted service, at lower simulated device energy and latency, than nearest-device, advertised-quality, UCB1, and LinUCB selection.
authors: Yichen Liu, Xiaochong Jiang, Haoran Yu, Lifei Liu
bullets: Addresses tool grounding when multiple physical devices can provide the requested capability.
Uses adaptive context partitions and hierarchical endpoint trees to reuse feedback across related requests and devices.
Selection accounts for service cost, authorization, battery reserves, availability, and device capabilities.
Provides a finite-horizon regret bound and optional differential privacy for aggregated reward statistics.
In a simulated loading-dock workload, it improves step success and cost-adjusted service while reducing simulated energy and latency versus several baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Online contextual-bandit tool grounding for LLM agents selecting physical IoT devices; relevant to online learning and embodied physical interaction.
papers.title: Learning Which Device to Call: Online Tool Grounding for LLM Agents in IoT
papers.tldr: An online contextual-bandit router learns which eligible IoT device should execute each LLM tool call, balancing success, cost, and device constraints.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling of diffusion models with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) has become a promising strategy for sampling under user-specified rewards, such as human preference scores. However, the standard SMC framework typically relies on stochastic proposals and therefore does not directly transfer to flow matching models, in which inference is governed by deterministic ODEs. In this work, we introduce noise-rejuvenated SMC, an inference-time scaling method tailored for text-to-image flow matching models. Our key idea is to perturb each resampled particle by changing its source noise and constructing a new intermediate state using its current endpoint estimate. This moves the particle to another state that remains representable under the flow-matching interpolation form, enabling particle exploration without converting the sampler to an SDE. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism to refine resampled particles before weighting. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image demonstrate consistent improvements in reward-guided generation, while ablation studies validate the contributions of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/shermanlian/NR-SMC.
authors: Wenyi Lian, Zheng Zhao, Thomas B. Sch{\"o}n
bullets: Addresses the challenge of applying standard SMC to flow-matching models, whose ODE-based inference uses deterministic proposals.
Perturbs resampled particles by changing their source noise and reconstructing an intermediate state that remains compatible with flow-matching interpolation.
Adds look-ahead refinement to improve resampled particles before reward weighting.
Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1-dev, and Z-Image show consistent reward-guided generation improvements.
Ablations support the roles of noise rejuvenation and look-ahead refinement.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time SMC scaling for flow-matching text-to-image models; fits test-time optimization and multimodal foundation model sampling.
papers.title: Test-Time Scaling of Text-to-Image Flow Matching Models with Noise-Rejuvenated Sequential Monte Carlo
papers.tldr: Noise-rejuvenated SMC enables reward-guided test-time scaling for deterministic text-to-image flow-matching models without converting them to stochastic samplers.

papers.abstract: Decision models answer typed questions, such as multiple-choice or yes/no questions, with a probability for each option. We add test-time search to frozen decision models, with no training: we show the model a complete proposed answer, read off its probability of saying "Yes" to the proposal's correctness, and search for answers that it rates higher. The search is done either by editing one answer at a time or by joint optimization, which changes several answers at once. Search raises accuracy for every model and test set we tried, and the gains are largest for exact correctness on logic puzzles, where every answer in a task must be right. On 128 such puzzles, it takes Qwen3.8-27B from 2 to 30 exactly correct puzzles ($15\times$) and its per-blank accuracy from 27.8% to 48.5%. On a shared set of 47 puzzles, searching over each model's own Yes/No score raises the per-blank accuracy of StartLux Instant, Perplexity Decider, Clef, and JEV, which we reach only through its public API, by 4.0 to 13.0 percentage points, and raises the number of puzzles they get exactly correct, out of 47 and averaged over three search seeds, from 10 to 35, 9 to 26, 2 to 11, and 9 to 31.7 respectively.
bullets: Targets typed-answer tasks such as multiple-choice and yes/no questions without additional training.
Evaluates complete proposed answers and searches for alternatives rated more likely correct by the model.
Uses either single-answer editing or joint optimization to revise multiple answers simultaneously.
Improves accuracy across all tested models and test sets, with the largest gains on exact logic-puzzle solving.
On 128 puzzles, Qwen3.8-27B’s exactly solved tasks rise from 2 to 30, while per-blank accuracy increases from 27.8% to 48.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time search over frozen decision models is a form of inference-time optimization, matching test-time learning.
papers.title: P(Yes): 15$\times$ Improvements via Test-Time Scaling of Decision Models
papers.tldr: Test-time search over frozen decision models’ Yes/No correctness scores can dramatically improve answer accuracy, including a 15× increase in exactly solved logic puzzles.

papers.abstract: Classical robot control, Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees (BTs), is deterministic and inspectable but fixed at design time: it fails on situations its designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at a cost in latency and non-determinism hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model in the loop permanently and discard what it produces. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime. When a BT node fails, an LLM proposes a minimal, mission-agnostic subtree patch; CMA-ES tunes its parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth its cost; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant-monitored replays, an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library and, once the LLM call rate decays, crystallized into a deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used $11\pm1.4$ LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, 28 and 33 nodes with two patches each, reached $97\pm2\%$ mission success with no learning running, against 12\% for the unpatched tree and 98\% for a hand-coded expert tree, and reproduce decision traces exactly when re-ticked offline. Two negative results: replay admission rejected useful wind recoveries by attributing wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and a static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures.
bullets: Addresses the tension between fixed, safe robot controllers and costly, non-deterministic runtime foundation-model reasoning.
Uses an LLM to propose minimal subtree patches only after node failures; CMA-ES tunes parameters and a contextual bandit selects stored patches versus new LLM calls.
Admits patches through static checks, invariant-monitored replays, and empirical recovery margins, then stores them in a reusable fleet library and crystallizes them into deterministic BTs.
In Project AirSim experiments, crystallized trees achieved 97±2% mission success with no online learning, versus 12% for the unpatched tree and 98% for a hand-coded expert tree.
Replay admission rejected some useful wind-recovery patches, while a static-only variant generalized better to held-out failures.
papers.selection_reason: Uses foundation-model-generated patches and online adaptation to improve autonomous drone control, fitting learned robot control and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees: Amortizing Foundation-Model Reasoning into Deterministic Control for Autonomous Drones
papers.tldr: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees convert foundation-model-generated drone-control patches into deterministic, inspectable BTs, reducing runtime LLM dependence while achieving high mission success in simulation.

papers.abstract: Pedestrians differ in whether they respond to a robot, yet many RL policies assume all are non-reactive to prioritize safety. Policies trained without conditioning on local pedestrians' reactivity may therefore be unnecessarily conservative or rely on cooperation that does not occur. We propose RCRA, an online adaptation framework that modulates a learned residual around a frozen conservative navigation policy according to estimated pedestrian reactivity. A Transformer-based estimator infers latent pedestrian reactivity from motion histories and robot context, providing a more accurate signal for navigation adaptation and improving scenario-averaged simulation accuracy by $12.62$ percentage points over the Bayesian baseline, which assumes known pedestrian goals. These estimates are spatially aggregated into an adaptation scale that gates LoRA modules, enabling cooperative behavior near reactive pedestrians and conservative behavior near non-reactive pedestrians. Among baselines achieving SR above $90\%$ in every scenario, RCRA reduces scenario-averaged path length by $16.7\%$ relative to the conservative backbone and by $7.3\%$ relative to randomized-training baselines. It improves mean SR by $14.88$ percentage points over the reactive-trained policy.
authors: Immanuel R. Santjoko, Benedictus C. G. Cinun, Jing Chen, Bin Hu
bullets: Addresses the conservatism and coordination failures caused by assuming all pedestrians are non-reactive.
Uses a Transformer to infer latent pedestrian reactivity from motion histories and robot context.
Aggregates local reactivity estimates to gate LoRA-based residual adaptations around a frozen conservative policy.
Improves scenario-averaged simulation accuracy by 12.62 percentage points over a Bayesian baseline.
Reduces scenario-averaged path length while maintaining high success rates, and improves mean success rate over a reactive-trained policy.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes RCRA, an online adaptation framework for navigation that conditions on pedestrian reactivity. The use of a Transformer estimator and LoRA gating for dynamic adaptation is a technically meaningful contribution to test-time learning.
papers.title: Learning When to Adapt: Reactivity-Conditioned Residual Adaptation under Human-Robot Distribution Shift
papers.tldr: RCRA adapts robot navigation to pedestrians’ inferred reactivity, enabling cooperation when appropriate while retaining conservative behavior otherwise.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in sequential deep learning arises from a fixed-capacity architectural constraint: parameter updates encoding new tasks perturb weight subspaces supporting prior representations. We introduce the Knowledge Fusion Network (KFN), which mitigates the stability-plasticity trade-off in class-incremental learning through novelty-gated structural expansion rather than parameter negotiation within a shared capacity budget. KFN decouples task acquisition from knowledge consolidation: each incoming task is learned in an isolated lightweight specialist network (2.8M parameters) and integrated into the global model via a Structural Fusion Module that allocates dedicated channel capacity conditioned on a quantitative novelty score. Dual structural isolation--channel-space separation with temporally phased gradient unfreezing--protects consolidated knowledge. On ten-task Split CIFAR-100, KFN achieves 11.94% minimum task accuracy and 71.16% task-10 accuracy, whereas shared-parameter baselines degrade severely: LwF to 9.07% average accuracy (0.00% min), Replay++ to 8.91% (85.08% forgetting), and Replay to 16.21% (73.44% forgetting); KFN's forgetting (57.92%) is 15.5 pp lower than Replay. Furthermore, KFN prevents logit-scale drift, maintaining near-symmetric task performance. Across CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT satellite imagery, KFN's class-incremental retention (72.7% and 42.5%) substantially exceeds the best baselines (29.6% and 0.94%). Crucially, KFN achieves parameter-efficient linear scaling, adding 25% of the base parameter count per step and requiring 25.1% of naive backbone duplication over ten tasks (28.1M vs 112.0M). With a 37.1% peak GPU memory reduction over full retraining, KFN establishes novelty-gated expansion as a practical path beyond fixed-capacity architectures.
authors: Kanishk Bakshi, Amitansu Pattanaik, Kathiravan Srinivasan
bullets: Sequential task updates can disrupt weight subspaces encoding earlier task knowledge under fixed model capacity.
Each task is learned in a lightweight specialist, then integrated through a novelty-conditioned Structural Fusion Module.
Channel separation and phased gradient unfreezing help protect consolidated representations during fusion.
On Split CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT, KFN reports substantially stronger retention than the cited baselines while reducing parameter and peak-memory growth versus naive retraining.
The approach scales linearly by adding 25% of the base parameter count per task, but forgetting is reduced rather than eliminated.
papers.selection_reason: Continual learning with structural expansion and novelty-gated fusion to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
papers.title: Learning without Overwriting: Structural Knowledge Fusion for Continual Learning
papers.tldr: KFN reduces catastrophic forgetting in class-incremental learning by novelty-gated structural expansion that adds isolated capacity instead of overwriting shared parameters.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained rectification of existing generations under a limited additional budget remains a key problem in test-time optimization (TTO) for image generation. As for prior approaches, they could identify residual errors, but could not directly ensure that the model acts on the feedback during reasoning. Such errors stem from multiple sources, such as the initial noise or text prompt, and ultimately induce an execution gap of failing to handle potential deviations along the trajectory generating. However, classic models generally cannot remedy this gap. To narrow it, we propose Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification (RGDR), which turns reflections on completed outputs into corrective interventions on the process of sampling dynamics at the trajectory level. Specifically, RGDR could impact every sampling step by adapting to instantaneous intervention. Moreover, RGDR generates flexible candidates while adjudicating between them and the reference. As experiments show, rectification from RGDR starts from the existing base trajectory and reflection, and RGDR is substantially more effective than former trajectory exploration. Under matched budgets for additional image generation, RGDR's gain in the cross-model average final checklist score over the reference is $1.51\times$ that of TIR prompt refinement and $1.81\times$ that of Dynamic CFG.
authors: Shuo Xu, Hanrui Ying, Debin Liu, Jianjun Li, Zhiyuan Ma
bullets: Addresses test-time optimization when existing generations contain errors from noise, prompts, or trajectory deviations.
Converts output-level reflection into corrective interventions during the image sampling process.
Adapts interventions at each sampling step and evaluates generated candidates against a reference.
Under matched additional-generation budgets, achieves larger checklist-score gains than TIR prompt refinement and Dynamic CFG.
Scope: focuses on fine-grained rectification starting from an existing base trajectory and reflection.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time optimization for image generation with trajectory-level corrective interventions fits test-time learning.
papers.title: Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification for Text-to-Image Generation
papers.tldr: RGDR improves text-to-image generations by using reflections on completed images to dynamically correct the sampling trajectory at every step.

papers.abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free-riding among co-retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill-specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within-group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability-weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence-gated state-transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence-driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.
authors: Xi Zhu, Yuanlin Duan, Changyi Yang, Kai Mei, Riyang Bao, Shichao Zhu, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses redundant, harmful, or internalized skills and unreliable attribution from co-retrieval and task confounding.
Uses randomized skill injection and within-group contrasts in GRPO to estimate each skill’s contribution.
Tracks both skill utility as external scaffolding and model mastery of the corresponding capability.
Applies evidence-gated transitions for skill admission, incubation, retention, retirement, and removal, with a soft library-capacity bound.
Outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluations; analyses show skill values shift during learning.
papers.selection_reason: Skill library lifecycle management with evidence-gated state transitions for agentic RL; relevant to agent memory and continual skill adaptation.
papers.title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: TrackRL uses online causal tracking to manage each skill’s lifecycle as an agentic RL policy evolves.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to accumulate past experiences for continual adaptation. However, effectively reusing memory requires accurately assessing its value, as retrieved experiences may become unreliable when transferred across task contexts. Despite its importance, memory valuation remains largely underexplored, with existing methods relying on historical retrieval success rates that overlook the context dependency of memory usefulness and the varying reliability of estimates under different amounts of evidence. Inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, we propose BEAM (Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory), a framework that reformulates memory value evaluation as a parameterized cognitive inference process, where memory value is represented as a context-conditioned dynamic belief rather than a passive historical statistic. Specifically, BEAM infers memory value beliefs from current task contexts and continuously calibrates them using execution feedback as empirical evidence, transforming memory from passive storage into an adaptive cognitive mechanism for continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments across reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that BEAM consistently improves memory utilization and enables continual self-evolution of LLM agents.
authors: Yiming Xu, Qian Yang, Zihan Chen, Yuefei Wu, Wenhan Zeng, Bin Shi, Bo Dong
bullets: Existing memory valuation based on retrieval success can miss context dependence and uncertainty from limited evidence.
BEAM evaluates each memory through a parameterized cognitive inference process conditioned on the current task.
Execution feedback serves as empirical evidence to continuously calibrate memory-value beliefs.
Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks show improved memory utilization and continual agent self-evolution.
papers.selection_reason: Bayesian memory valuation for self-evolving LLM agents; directly fits agent memory and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Memory as Belief: Bayesian Evolution of Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
papers.tldr: BEAM models memory usefulness as a context-dependent Bayesian belief that updates from task feedback, improving continual self-evolution in LLM agents.

papers.abstract: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
authors: Jiaqi Su, Guibin Zhang, Jie-Jing Shao, Cong Pang, Tiankuo Yao, Ivor Tsang, Haiyan Yin, Shuicheng Yan
bullets: Addresses brain–body mismatch: harnesses may demand unlearned behaviors or constrain existing model capabilities.
Uses a shared evolutionary archive, execution feedback, and a meta-agent to coordinate harness evolution with model checkpoint selection or merging.
Adapts selected models under evolving harnesses using only supervised fine-tuning on self-generated rejection-sampled trajectories.
Reports competitiveness with larger models across multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following.
Exceeds cited baselines on TraceElephant and HomeBench VM, supporting the importance of brain–body alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Model-harness co-evolution with shared evolutionary archive and checkpoint adaptation for recursive self-improvement; relevant to continual adaptation and agent memory.
papers.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?
papers.tldr: CoEvo-RSI aligns evolving agent harnesses with model capabilities through bidirectional historical inheritance, enabling a smaller model to perform competitively across diverse tasks.

papers.abstract: Multiobject tracking (MOT) is a fundamental capability in autonomous navigation, radar and sonar systems, as well as 6G integrated sensing-and-communication (ISAC) networks. In this paper, we propose a neural-enhanced track-before-detect (TkBD) framework that operates directly on complex-valued raw signals and learns a latent representation of unmodeled propagation effects during runtime. We introduce an environment-dependent latent intensity variable that characterizes the signal power of each object in the shared propagation environment. The probability density function of this intensity variable is represented by a normalizing flow and trained online in an unsupervised manner within the sequential Bayesian inference procedure. The learning objective is derived from a variational Bayes formulation by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), thereby accounting for the uncertainties inherent in the Bayesian TkBD problem. To enable scalable inference, we make use of a recently introduced Bayesian TkBD framework that combines belief propagation, which avoids high-dimensional operations, with sequential Monte Carlo methods for efficient low-dimensional updates.
authors: Shaoxiu Wei, Bhaskar Rao, Florian Meyer
bullets: Targets multiobject tracking in autonomous navigation, radar, sonar, and 6G ISAC settings.
Operates directly on complex-valued raw signals while modeling unmodeled propagation effects through a latent representation.
Represents each object’s environment-dependent signal intensity with a normalizing flow trained online and unsupervised.
Optimizes the flow using an ELBO-derived variational Bayes objective to capture inference uncertainty.
Combines belief propagation with sequential Monte Carlo for scalable Bayesian inference.
papers.selection_reason: Online unsupervised training of a normalizing flow within sequential Bayesian inference is a test-time learning/adaptation method.
papers.title: Normalizing Flow for Neural-Enhanced Track-Before-Detect
papers.tldr: A neural-enhanced track-before-detect framework uses online normalizing flows to learn environment-dependent object intensities directly from complex raw signals during Bayesian multiobject tracking.

papers.abstract: We present \'{E}pi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. \'{E}pi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. \'{E}pi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the $n$-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, \'{E}pi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with \'{E}pi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning.
