On 30 FrontierOR tasks, \'{E}pi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. \'{E}pi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.
authors: Yue Huang, Zhangchen Xu, Xiaonan Luo, Zheyuan Liu, Lichi Li, Yiping Wang, Peiyang Song, Eric Gabriel Ramos, Enze Xie, Olexandr Isayev, Paul Liang, Nouha Dziri, Huan Sun, Jianfeng Gao, Ying Liu, Misha Sra, Xiangliang Zhang, Alex Pentland, Zichen Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining continuity and improving methods across autonomous research sessions.
Uses persistent history, hierarchical memory, branching, independent review, and a fixed output verifier.
Reports 120 record-setting mathematical results, including tighter bounds, exact dual certificates, and a computer-assisted partial result related to Tuza’s conjecture.
Its coding variant, Épi-turbo, outperformed Codex by 5.4% on 30 FrontierOR tasks while using 64% of its model cost.
Designed to expose explicit methods and mathematical arguments for human inspection and further development.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Epi, a persistent, self-improving agent for autonomous research. It maintains research history across sessions and evolves methods, which is a strong fit for Embodied Memory and Continual/Online Learning.
papers.title: Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research
papers.tldr: Épi is a persistent, self-improving research agent that carries investigations across sessions, learns from prior experiments, and produces verifiable mathematical and algorithmic results.

papers.abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
authors: Chuan Liu, Tianya Zhao, Xuyu Wang
bullets: Targets overconfident RFF errors when receivers, distances, collection days, or environments change.
Uses a frozen I/Q classifier and requires no target-domain labels.
Combines counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, domain similarity, signal quality, confidence, and prediction margin.
An LLM planner selects diagnostic actions under evidence, trust, cost, and budget constraints.
Evaluations across five datasets and classifier backbones show a 38.7% average source-to-target accuracy drop and frequent high-confidence target errors.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes TrustAgent-RFF, an agentic framework for reliable RF fingerprinting under domain shift. It uses an LLM planner to adapt to new domains, fitting Test-Time Learning and LLM Memory.
papers.title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
papers.tldr: TrustAgent-RFF improves the reliability of RF fingerprinting under domain shift by adaptively gathering diagnostic evidence and deciding whether to accept, reject, or defer predictions.

papers.abstract: Agent networks require reliable ways for requesting agents to verify where data is located, how it can be accessed, and whether the data received matches what the data owner made available. Checksum mismatches can reflect either altered content or serialization differences that preserve data equivalence under specified rules. Data identification mechanisms for agents, such as DataFacts, describe where data can be accessed and provide checksums for checking received data against published references. We propose a serialization-invariant identification method that assigns the same identifier to data representations equivalent under explicit rules. We use DataFacts as a case study, retaining its existing checksum alongside the proposed identifier. In a controlled agent study, we compare the proposed configuration with ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent re-encodings, altered content, and unavailable references. The study includes three model tiers from each of two providers. For equivalent re-encodings, the proposed configuration increased expected-outcome rates by 80.4 percentage points over the ordinary-tool baseline and by 70.2 percentage points over the checksum baseline. The proposed configuration also increased evidence-supported rejection of altered content by 3.5 percentage points over the checksum baseline. We contribute a serialization-invariant identification method with explicit equivalence rules, an integration approach illustrated through DataFacts, and an empirical evaluation against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines.
bullets: Addresses checksum failures caused by harmless serialization differences in agent-published datasets.
Defines explicit equivalence rules and assigns one identifier to equivalent representations.
Integrates the identifier with DataFacts while retaining its existing checksum.
In a controlled study across model tiers and providers, improved expected outcomes for equivalent re-encodings and slightly improved rejection of altered content.
Evaluates against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent, altered, and unavailable-reference cases.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses data integrity and verification in agent networks. While specific to serialization, the concept of ensuring reliable data access and integrity for agents aligns with Embodied Memory and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Same Data, Different Bytes: Serialization-Invariant Integrity Checks for Agent-Published Datasets
papers.tldr: A serialization-invariant identifier helps agents recognize equivalent data representations while still detecting altered content.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.
authors: Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Xinyu Lian, Fan Shu, Sida Li, Feng Yan, Mingjia Zhang, Yuxiong He, Zhewei Yao
bullets: Targets the difficulty of separating algorithmic gains from an under-tuned RL baseline for long-horizon agents.
Uses small-pool overfitting to expose failures hidden by early reward gains and integrates gated rewards, importance-weight control, aligned training/inference engines, and consistent policy state.
Reaches 62.0% pass@1 with Qwen3.5-4B on raw R2E-Gym data, comparable to FrogNano while using about one-sixth as many rollouts.
Filtering and refining multiple datasets improves Qwen3.5-4B to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% and Qwen3.5-9B to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2.
Controlled comparisons find that curation and stronger tests improve held-out performance, while stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for long-horizon agent training (Arctic-SWE) using reinforcement learning. It addresses the challenges of training agents over long horizons and domain shift, fitting both Robot Learning and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design
papers.tldr: Arctic-SWE co-designs asynchronous RL infrastructure and training practices to provide a reproducible long-horizon software-engineering baseline, achieving strong SWE-bench performance without new algorithms.

papers.abstract: Analytic continual learning (ACL) methods such as ACIL and GACL fit a ridge-regression classifier head on frozen features via the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, achieving exemplar-free, exact updates. A separate line of work, Progressive Neural Collapse (ProNC), shows standard continual classifiers benefit from a progressively expanding Simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) target. It is natural to ask whether fusing the two ideas, exact analytic updates and ETF targets, would yield a better closed-form continual learner. We show this is not the case as the fusion turns out to be identical to plain one-hot ACIL. Further, Simplex ETFs are not nested across class counts, so the literal "progressively expand the ETF" construction stops yielding an ETF as new tasks arrive, and it introduces catastrophic forgetting ($4\times$ that of a classic ACIL head). We therefore separate an ETF's two defining properties, equiangularity and equinormality, and apply each on its own to the classifier weights rather than the targets, where the invariance above does not hold. Equinorm post-processing of the fitted weights recovers both tail-class and overall average accuracy across the long-tailed regime from 5:1 to 100:1 imbalance (e.g. +32.0 tail-accuracy points and +16.0 average-accuracy points at 100:1 on CIFAR-100/ViT), transferring in sign across two backbones and two datasets, at a mild cost of 5.4 average-accuracy points on CIFAR-100/ViT on near-balanced streams (below $\approx 3{:}1$). Equiangular geometry, by contrast, is exactly inert on the target side but actively harmful on the weight side, usually losing to plain one-hot. Hence, the generally useful part of Neural Collapse geometry in Analytic Continual Learning is equinorm post-processing of the weights, becoming more useful as class imbalance grows; and equiangularity is at best a no-op and induces catastrophic forgetting at worst.
bullets: Fusing ETF targets with exact ACIL updates is equivalent to plain one-hot ACIL.
Progressively expanding Simplex ETFs are not nested across class counts and can cause substantially more catastrophic forgetting.
Equinorm weight post-processing improves tail and average accuracy under 5:1–100:1 class imbalance, with gains increasing as imbalance grows.
At 100:1 imbalance on CIFAR-100/ViT, it yields +32.0 tail-accuracy points and +16.0 average-accuracy points.
Equinorming costs accuracy on near-balanced streams, while equiangular weight geometry is generally harmful.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses analytic continual learning, class-imbalance, and closed-form updates with a proposed equinorm remedy.
papers.title: An Impossibility Result for ETF Target Geometry, and an Equinorm Remedy for Imbalanced Analytic Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Equinorm post-processing of analytic continual-learning classifier weights improves long-tailed performance, while ETF/equiangular target geometry is ineffective or harmful.

papers.abstract: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.
authors: SeongJun Jeong, Chungwoo Lee, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Addresses adapter and task-selection module growth under fixed onboard storage and compute budgets.
Reuses frozen adapters and adds new adapters only at selected layers, with a penalty discouraging redundant information.
Uses activation-statistic signatures for one-time task identification, then merges the task update into the backbone for control.
Across four LIBERO suites, matches or exceeds adapter baselines while using up to 4.5× less on-disk state per task.
GPU memory and control frequency remain comparable to the backbone as tasks accumulate; retention is also shown on a real UR5 arm.
papers.selection_reason: Lifelong VLA robot learning with sparse adapter reuse and merging; fits robot learning and continual learning.
papers.title: SARAM: Sparse Adapter Allocation with Reuse and Merging for Lifelong Robot Learning
papers.tldr: SARAM enables scalable lifelong robot learning by reusing and sparsely adding adapters while keeping deployment costs nearly independent of the number of tasks.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents in human-centered environments require memory that integrates what they observe with what humans tell them over time. However, existing embodied memories are built primarily from visual experience, leaving open how dialogue with humans can be grounded in the objects encountered throughout that experience. We introduce DialogMem, a two-phase benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). DialogMem provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. We evaluate nine memory representations within a unified framework of memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning for task outputs. In experiments, appending dialogue to visual memory at evaluation time substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains, suggesting that relevant dialogue is present in memory but not grounded to specific objects. Controlled diagnostics show that navigation improves with link quality but falls short of ground-truth object-level memory even under perfect linking. Retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location remain further bottlenecks. These results identify three bottlenecks for dialogue-grounded embodied memory: grounding and organizing dialogue at object-level entries during formation, retrieving the correct entry, and localizing it accurately.
authors: SeongJun Jeong, Junghyun Kim, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Introduces a two-phase benchmark using time-aligned posed RGB-D observations and human dialogue across 27 real-world 3D scenes.
Evaluates nine memory representations through memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning.
Adding dialogue improves QA substantially but provides negligible navigation gains when not grounded to specific objects.
Diagnostics identify bottlenecks in object-level dialogue grounding, correct-entry retrieval, and spatial localization.
Even perfect object linking does not match ground-truth memory performance, indicating additional retrieval and localization challenges.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces benchmark for dialogue-grounded embodied memory in 3D environments, fitting embodied memory subtopic.
papers.title: DialogMem: Evaluating Dialogue-Grounded Embodied Memory in 3D Environments
papers.tldr: DialogMem benchmarks how well embodied agents integrate dialogue with visual experience for object navigation and QA in 3D environments.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric 3D geometry from images is fundamentally ill-posed due to perspective projection ambiguity. Current geometry models incorporate supplied or predicted intrinsics during inference, but do not use them to supervise model adaptation. To refine these predictions, test-time adaptation (TTA) typically relies on external depth measurements. In this paper, we instead use camera intrinsics as an output-side geometric verifier. Comparing the point cloud's viewing rays with those defined by the known intrinsics yields a direct measure of geometric inconsistency. We propose \textit{IntriAdapt}, a TTA framework that minimizes this closed-form geometric residual. By optimizing a lightweight LoRA adapter on a frozen geometry foundation model, our method aligns the prediction with the specific camera model without depth sensors or external priors. We further extend this approach to video sequences, demonstrating that adapting a short sequence generalizes to other sequences captured by the same camera. The adapted model processes held-out images in a feed-forward pass, without repeating optimization for each frame. Experiments on ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks across multiple base models show that \textit{IntriAdapt} consistently outperforms both unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.
authors: Jiaxing Chen, Zizheng Yan, Jingyu Zhuang, Jinwei Chen, Shuguang Cui, Guanying Chen, Qingnan Fan
bullets: Addresses perspective ambiguity in image-based metric 3D geometry estimation.
Minimizes a closed-form residual between predicted point-cloud viewing rays and rays implied by the camera intrinsics.
Optimizes a lightweight LoRA adapter while keeping the geometry foundation model frozen.
Sequence adaptation generalizes across images from the same camera, enabling feed-forward inference on held-out frames.
Across ten single-image and seven sequence benchmarks, it outperforms unadapted and oracle-intrinsics baselines in metric accuracy and relative geometry.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation for metric geometry estimation using camera intrinsics; fits TTA and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: IntriAdapt: Generalizable Intrinsic-Guided Test-Time Adaptation for Metric Geometry Estimation
papers.tldr: IntriAdapt improves metric 3D geometry at test time by using known camera intrinsics as a geometric consistency signal, without depth sensors or external priors.

papers.abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.
authors: Jinming Wang, Ruiheng Zhang, Yong Wang, Zipan Xiong, Keyuan Luo
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen VLA policies to learn from prior failures without updating the model.
Uses an external memory of stress-collected local-depth records to trigger translation-only projection corrections.
Keeps rotation and gripper commands unchanged while intervening on translations.
Primary CALVIN evaluation reduced a depth-based near-collision/stall proxy without changing task-success count, but an independent replication did not reproduce the effect.
Failure analysis highlights endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the absence of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline; physical safety improvement remains unestablished.
papers.selection_reason: External-memory retrieval wrapper for frozen VLA policies with empirical failure analysis; directly relevant to VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Retrieval-triggered Action Projection Adjustment for Frozen VLA Policies: An Empirical Study and Failure Analysis
papers.tldr: RTPC adds retrieval-based translation corrections to frozen VLA actions, but its apparent reduction in near-collision/stall events was not replicated or shown to be retrieval-specific.

papers.abstract: Online scene change detection requires an agent to detect what has changed in a previously mapped environment while it is still on site, observing from unconstrained viewpoints and without access to future observations. This causal setting is strictly harder than its offline counterpart, and online methods have consistently trailed offline accuracy. O-SCD closed that gap by treating change as a persistent property of a 3D Gaussian splatting map of the reference scene, surpassing the strongest offline methods in change detection accuracy while operating at over 10 frames per second. O-SCD optimizes a change field over the Gaussians of the reference map, refitting it to all past cue maps at every frame, a step that consumes more than half of the per-frame budget and forces accuracy to be traded against speed. We present a replay-free formulation that eliminates this trade-off. Because the reference map stays fixed, rendering the change field is a linear operation. Each new observation can therefore be carried onto the map's Gaussians directly, by a single backward pass of the renderer, which reduces multi-view fusion to an exact two-scalar recursion per Gaussian. Past observations are never stored or revisited. The self-supervised objective that O-SCD minimizes by descent also determines the decision threshold exactly, by sorting, yielding a label-free per-frame cutoff whose margin provides a selective-prediction signal. On PASLCD, our method improves mean intersection over union from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 frames per second, even exceeding O-SCD's offline result while remaining strictly causal.
authors: Chamuditha Jayanga Galappaththige, Jason Lai, Lloyd Windrim, Timothy Patten, Donald G. Dansereau, Niko Suenderhauf, Dimity Miller
bullets: Addresses online change detection from unconstrained viewpoints without future observations or stored past observations.
Uses a single backward rendering pass to project each new cue map onto reference-map Gaussians and maintain an exact two-scalar recursion per Gaussian.
Derives a label-free decision threshold by sorting the self-supervised objective, with its margin supporting selective prediction.
On PASLCD, improves mean IoU from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 FPS.
Remains strictly causal while exceeding O-SCD’s reported offline result.
papers.selection_reason: Replay-free online scene-change detection updating a persistent 3D Gaussian map as embodied environment memory.
papers.title: O-SCD++: Replay-Free Online Scene Change Detection via Recursive Evidence Fusion
papers.tldr: O-SCD++ enables faster, replay-free causal scene change detection by recursively fusing evidence directly into a fixed 3D Gaussian map.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
authors: Sizhe Tang, Zuyuan Zhang, Zeyu Fang, Tian Lan
bullets: Addresses the coupled problem of choosing research assignments while learning from the resulting experiences.
Uses a hierarchical framework: a Coordinator organizes search branches and directives, while Scientists generate hypotheses and execution plans.
Alternates GRPO-style updates for both hierarchy levels under a shared best-of-budget objective; execution uses a frozen shared Executor.
Provides theoretical results on objective alignment, coordination gains, private adaptation, and finite-budget regret.
On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD was best on 20 and achieved the highest aggregate normalized MLGym scores; comparisons involve mostly proprietary Scientist baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical test-time training for multi-agent LLM discovery; directly relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
papers.tldr: MELD enables multi-agent scientific discovery to improve recursively by jointly adapting team coordination and individual scientist policies during search.

papers.abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. Preserving its value over time is also difficult: our accumulation baseline without consolidation initially improves but eventually performs below a no-memory baseline. Our key idea is to compare attempts at the same task to identify reusable decisions and refine when they apply. We introduce Hippo, a memory framework inspired by selective hippocampal encoding and replay that learns from these comparisons when shortcomings are diagnosed. It compares the resulting experience with existing memory to merge overlaps and resolve conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. This allows prior guidance to be revised without storing every lesson as a separate entry. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web show performance gains in all three settings and substantially fewer retained experiences than the accumulation baseline. The gains extend across the evaluated base models of varying capabilities, indicating that memory-based adaptation remains useful even for highly capable models.
authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren, Tony Qin, Baoyuan Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of extracting reliable lessons from flawed or mixed-quality attempts.
Uses selective hippocampal-style encoding and replay to diagnose shortcomings and compare attempts on the same task.
Merges overlapping memories and resolves conflicts with explicit applicability conditions instead of storing every lesson separately.
Improves performance on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web while retaining substantially fewer experiences than simple accumulation.
Benefits persist across base models with varying capabilities, including highly capable models.
papers.selection_reason: External-memory agent self-improvement via hippocampal replay; relevant to test-time adaptation and LLM memory.
papers.title: Hippo: Training-Free Agent Self-Evolution via Hippocampal Replay
papers.tldr: Hippo enables LLM agents to self-improve without parameter updates by comparing task attempts and consolidating reusable experience in memory.

papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) beat classifiers lose accuracy on new patients and devices, and source-free adaptation methods that assume class-balanced target batches fail on real recordings, whose label-free prefix is 87.9--98.6% normal beats. We propose Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport (NAGT, GA_NS), which estimates a closed-form symmetric positive-definite congruence map from label-free normal anchors in the first 5 min of each recording and applies it only to the normal and supraventricular prototypes, keeping the ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed. The score offsets and decision rules were set on MIT-BIH only; the rate-invariant RR head (relA) was adopted after the development databases (INCART, SVDB) had been opened; the frozen model was then evaluated once on Icentia11k chest-patch recordings under a pre-registered protocol. In 493 patients (973 recordings, 3,615,388 evaluated beats), NAGT reached an arrhythmia macro-$F_1$ $J = \frac{1}{2}(\text{S-}F_1 + \text{V-}F_1) = 48.7\%$ [95% CI 42.1, 54.7] versus 34.5% without adaptation ($\Delta J = +14.1$ [+8.6, +19.3] pp; 59.8% versus 43.9% in non-AF) and outperformed all five Holm-adjusted comparators, including AdaBN, Tent and T3A. In the 75-patient test subgroup of the historical split (73 analyzed), the gain was not significant (+6.1 [-8.5, +23.4] pp). Adaptation takes a median of 5.8 ms per record without back-propagation.
bullets: Addresses patient/device domain shift when target recordings are heavily dominated by unlabeled normal beats.
Uses a closed-form symmetric positive-definite transport map estimated from normal beats in each recording’s first 5 minutes.
Adapts only normal and supraventricular prototypes while keeping ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed.
On 493 patients and 973 Icentia11k recordings, macro-F1 rose from 34.5% to 48.7%, outperforming five adjusted comparators.
The gain was not significant in a small 73-patient historical test subgroup; median adaptation time was 5.8 ms per record.
papers.selection_reason: Source-free patient adaptation using unlabeled normal anchors at test time; directly fits test-time learning.
papers.title: Transport What Shares the Conduction Pathway: Normal-Anchored SPD Geometric Transport for Source-Free Patient Adaptation of Holter and Patch ECG
papers.tldr: NAGT improves source-free ECG arrhythmia adaptation across patients and devices by transporting normal-anchored prototypes without back-propagation.

papers.abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.
authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang, Hengquan Huang, Shuang Qiu, Min Zhang, Zhongxiang Dai
bullets: Targets query-dependent user preferences when only binary comparisons between candidate responses are available.
Uses a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley–Terry explorer for large discrete persona spaces.
Transfers evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts while retaining query-specific scores.
Evaluated on seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks with reference- and model-based preference simulators.
Achieved the strongest aggregate performance among evaluated baselines under a fixed ten-round comparison budget.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time persona adaptation via dueling bandits, directly relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
papers.tldr: ID-TAP personalizes LLM agents at test time by efficiently selecting informative persona comparisons and transferring preference evidence across related queries.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts pretrained models to distribution shifts encountered during deployment. However, most existing methods rely on the weight representations of the final layer or signals derived from the model's output probability distribution. We study hidden trajectories: the ordered sequence of intermediate representations produced across a deep neural network. We observe that clean and corrupted trajectories become more separable as corruption severity increases. We introduce Drift-TTA, which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and trains them to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those from cleaner inputs. The approach supports two variants: a source-dependent version trained with clean targets, and a source-free setting that learns from corrupted images at different severities. We develop an online TTA approach that freezes the backbone and adapters while updating a scalar gate to control adaptation strength. We further cast trajectory alignment as MAP inference under a Gaussian observation model and derive a KL-based transfer bound characterizing test-time trajectory misalignment in terms of offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and distribution shift between offline and test corruptions. We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C using supervised ViTs and CLIP models. On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, our source-free online approach improves accuracy over no TTA by 13.3 percentage points with ViT-B/16 and 11.6 percentage points with CLIP ViT-B/16, reaching 74.9% and 47.4%, respectively. Under the same setting, prior TTA baselines yield ECEs of 18.00% for ViT and 14.70% for CLIP, while our approach reduces them to 9.53% and 5.77%, respectively. These results demonstrate that hidden trajectory alignment provides an effective signal for both offline correction and lightweight online test-time adaptation.
authors: Amirhossein Sabour, Amir Khasahmadi, Mengliu Zhao
bullets: Existing TTA methods mainly use final-layer weights or output probabilities, while this work exploits ordered intermediate representations.
Drift-TTA adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and learns to reduce hidden-trajectory drift.
It supports source-dependent alignment with clean targets and source-free learning from inputs at varying corruption severities.
An online variant updates only a scalar gate to control adaptation strength, keeping the backbone and adapters frozen.
On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, source-free online Drift-TTA improves accuracy by 13.3 points for ViT-B/16 and 11.6 points for CLIP ViT-B/16, while also reducing calibration error.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces online test-time adaptation via hidden trajectory alignment, directly fitting test-time learning under distribution shift.
papers.title: Hidden Trajectories Don't Lie: Correcting Corruption Drift for Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: Drift-TTA improves test-time adaptation by aligning corrupted models’ hidden representation trajectories with cleaner ones, enabling effective source-free online correction.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly operate in open-ended environments, where they are expected to continually adapt to evolving tasks and distributions, often without access to external supervision. Existing continual learning approaches rely on external supervision, such as labeled data, demonstrations, or reward signals, which can be costly or unavailable in practice. Test-time adaptation removes this dependence by learning from self-generated supervision, but existing methods derive that supervision from the single policy being updated, so once the policy drifts, its own learning signal drifts with it, leading to policy collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Evolution Strategy Reinforcement Learning (ESRL)}, a continual test-time learning framework that draws its self-generated supervision from a population of policies instead of the single policy being trained. ESRL perturbs an anchor policy in parameter space to form a population of nearby policies, samples one trajectory from each, and aggregates their answers into label-free group-relative learning signals for the central student. The anchor is held fixed within each block and refreshed from the student at block boundaries, so the population stays centered on a stable yet current policy and continues to supply diverse and reliable supervision as the student moves. In single-task test-time adaptation across mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, ESRL improves average accuracy by up to 31.7% relative to the base model and 16.6% relative to the strongest test-time adaptation baseline. Notably, ESRL substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting and achieves the strongest final performance in continual learning.
authors: Guangya Hao, Yiting Duan, Longyan Tan, Yunbo Long, Hao Wu, Ge Zheng, Alexandra Brintrup, Zhuokai Zhao
bullets: Addresses policy drift, collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting when external supervision is unavailable.

papers.abstract: Reliable fetal brain biometry on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosing congenital brain anomalies, but artificial intelligence models often lose accuracy under domain shifts. We developed BioTTA, a backbone-agnostic, source-free unsupervised test-time adaptation framework that adapts pretrained models online to individual unlabeled target volumes. This retrospective multicohort study included 394 reconstructed 3D fetal brain MRI volumes at 20-39 gestational weeks, with 11 biometric measurements annotated by radiologists. BioTTA was developed on single-center turbo spin-echo MRI and evaluated on three datasets representing cross-sequence, cross-center, and cross-nation shifts. Biometry accuracy was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE) and the percentage of correct measurements within 4 mm. A web-based reporting platform mapped measurements onto normative growth trajectories and was evaluated against radiologists in four multicenter disease cohorts covering germinal matrix-intraventricular hemorrhage, ventriculomegaly, and cerebellar abnormality. Across all three target datasets, BioTTA outperformed auto-SVRTK, source-only models, and FetalSynthGen, while matching models finetuned with target labels. MAEs ranged from 1.10 to 1.46 mm with a convolutional backbone and from 1.46 to 2.25 mm with a transformer backbone. Diagnostic accuracy ranged from 82.1% to 95.0%, comparable to a senior radiologist. BioTTA supports accurate, generalizable fetal brain biometry and standardized prenatal brain growth assessment across heterogeneous MRI sources.

papers.abstract: LLM agents accumulate valuable task-specific information through their actions, observations, and environmental feedback during multi-turn task execution. When effectively used, this information can help agents refine subsequent decisions and improve task performance. However, the learning value of an interaction depends on its context and subsequent feedback, making it challenging to extract reliable, actionable lessons and revise them as the task unfolds. In this paper, we introduce ReTTT, which enables experience-driven self-adaptation through test-time training on lessons constructed and continually revised within an episode. ReTTT lets the agent reflect on interaction feedback, maintain the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and learn from them by updating an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen. The adapted model then performs both subsequent actions and reflection, coupling policy adaptation with the construction of future learning experience. We evaluate ReTTT on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite using two model families. ReTTT outperforms trajectory-based test-time training across all six model--benchmark settings, improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points. A frozen-reflection comparison further shows a 7.14-point benefit from adapting the reflection policy, while trajectory analysis illustrates how adapted reflection derives more task-specific guidance from failed attempts. These findings suggest that learning to reflect on its own behavior can boost agents' performance on long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models answer questions about images and also generate images with one shared set of weights. This creates a post-training risk that single-purpose models do not have: fine-tuning one capability can damage another that works in a different modality. We measure this cross-modal forgetting for LoRA post-training of Janus-Pro-7B. Every target is chosen by how poorly the base model already handles it, from a poetic register to a language it barely speaks, so that retention is tested against a real intervention; we then evaluate the capabilities we never trained, first after a single run and then after chaining three. A single run looks entirely safe: nothing we did not train degrades on four public benchmarks or in free-form English, even when the adapter cuts held-out Welsh perplexity by 76% with a relative weight change under 2%. That safety belongs to the run, not to the recipe. Chaining three runs destroys the capability learned one run earlier and raises general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude above the never-adapted model, on the very measures that stayed flat before. The cause is in the objective, which constrains only the modality being trained and leaves the other head unconstrained: cutting the learning rate to one fifth does not prevent the collapse, while anchoring the other head removes the damage to the capabilities we never trained, at no cost to what is learned. What is learned also stays inside its own modality, with Welsh acquired from text closing only 3% of the English-Welsh gap in image generation.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have achieved rapid progress by learning unified policies that map sensor observations directly to driving trajectories. However, once deployed, these systems typically remain frozen: they may repeat similar decisions in similar scenes, and failures can only be addressed through costly data collection and retraining. This sharply contrasts with human drivers, who improve lifelong through experience, memory, and reflection. In this work, we ask whether autonomous driving systems can achieve similar post-deployment self-evolution to human drivers. We propose EvoAD, a self-evolving autonomous driving framework via latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. EvoAD stores driving experiences in a bird's-eye-view feature memory pool, retrieves scene-relevant precedents according to geometric and semantic similarity, and uses a latent world model to evaluate the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space. Instead of treating memory as external textual contexts or using world models only for pre-action simulation, EvoAD transforms executed driving outcomes into reusable improvement signals for future decisions. This enables the system to diagnose how prior trajectories could have been improved and to refine behavior in similar future scenarios without retraining the base driving policy. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show consistent improvements across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the potential of world models as reflective mechanisms for post-deployment self-evolution in autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: We develop an index policy for finite-horizon Bernoulli multi-armed bandits from minimax solutions to single-arm bandit (SAB) problems. Each SAB problem involves choosing between an unknown Bernoulli arm and a known reward. We show that minimizing worst-case regret of SAB problems over all non-anticipative policies admits an exact semi-infinite linear programming formulation. The resulting stopping policies offer a natural way to compare arms: the higher the known reward against which a policy continues sampling, the more promising the unknown arm. We turn this intuition into indices based on cumulative continuation probabilities, with a monotone adjustment and a reward-shortfall cap. By relating index errors to the regret of single-arm stopping policies, we establish a distribution-free regret bound of $4.45\sqrt{KT}+10.75K$ for $K$ arms and horizon $T$. This bound matches the minimax-optimal regret order established in the literature. The guarantee extends to rewards supported on $[0,1]$ through Bernoulli randomization. We also provide a finite-grid implementation with quantified approximation loss. In numerical experiments, the SAB-based index policy achieves lower worst-case regret than every tested benchmark policy across all evaluated numbers of arms and horizons, while closely matching the grid-based MAB minimax policy in the two-arm setting.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables language-model agents to personalize future interactions, but a finite memory bank cannot preserve every extracted fact. Existing memory gating policies are typically shared across users and therefore fail to account for user-specific patterns of future reuse. In this paper, we study memory gating at the fact level. We first propose a retrieval-based labeling strategy that labels each fact by whether it is later retrieved and incorporated into responses. We then formulate online memory gating as contextual apple tasting with delayed one-sided feedback, and propose Warm-Start UCB, which combines offline learning from existing data with online adaptation to the current user. Our theoretical analysis establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(T\epsilon \wedge d\sqrt{T})$ when the delay window is at most $O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the total number of rounds, $\epsilon$ is the initialization error, $d$ is the dimension of the feature map, and $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides constant and poly-logarithmic factors. The results of our experiment demonstrate that our method outperforms all baselines under different memory budgets and history lengths, establishing it as a promising personalized memory gating policy.

papers.abstract: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.

papers.abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.

papers.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.
authors: Yong Wang, Boyu Shen, Xinwei Zhang, Yizheng Li, Keyuan Luo
bullets: VLA models struggle with long-horizon tasks because limited temporal context hinders the accumulation and reuse of experience.

papers.tldr: This survey organizes memory mechanisms for long-horizon robotics VLA models and highlights the trade-offs and challenges involved in building lifelong embodied agents.

papers.abstract: Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse, viewpoint-dependent observations. When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering approach or verification actions. We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP). We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states. The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate: rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90--6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.

papers.abstract: Embodied heuristic learning must balance strategic adaptation with the preservation of previously successful behavior. Local repairs may leave structural failures unresolved, whereas broader revisions can introduce regressions that are costly to detect through repeated environment interaction. We introduce SCOPE (Selective Certification Of Program Edits), which uses failed and successful executions as complementary evidence for program revision. Frontier-guided program search annotates a shared diagnostic graph with execution evidence to distinguish supported progress from unresolved checks. Selective behavioral certification uses stateful API replay to restore recorded responses and mutations, checking whether edits preserve selected historical successes. Diagnosis and certification feedback, supplemented by sparse environment diagnostics, guide consecutive repairs across configurations. SCOPE outperforms the strongest baseline in both simulation and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite, it achieves mean success rates of 80.66% and 84.48%, with respective gains of 6.51 and 3.48 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/VDIGPKU/SCOPE.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments. Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration. In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees (BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks. The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation. Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.

papers.abstract: Experience-driven self-evolution offers a promising path for large language model (LLM) agents to continually improve through interaction. Yet existing approaches often rely on successful trajectories or external evaluation signals, leaving unclear whether agents can evolve when such positive anchors are unavailable. We study this question through Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution (CFOE), where agents start without accumulated experience and learn only from failed interactions without privileged guidance. Across three self-evolving paradigms, multiple LLM backbones, and four interactive environments, we uncover a consistent repair-generalization gap: failure-derived experience can help repair previously failed tasks, but rarely yields sustained improvements on unseen tasks. Further analysis shows that agents often misinterpret failures, while even verified-correct experience remains difficult to transfer. Relaxing CFOE reveals that verifier feedback and additional interaction provide limited gains, whereas successful trajectories substantially improve transfer. These findings suggest that current self-evolving agents are better at repairing observed failures than building generalizable capabilities from failure.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them
papers.tldr: Self-evolving LLM agents can repair tasks they previously failed, but failure-only experience rarely transfers into sustained improvement on unseen tasks.

papers.abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.
authors: Junyu Cao, Ruijiang Gao, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky, Mingzhang Yin
bullets: Reframes targeted AI deployment as multiple testing: select individuals whose policy-induced outcomes are unlikely to exceed a user-defined harm threshold.
Uses weighted conformal p-values to address distribution shift between observed behavior and the target policy.
Applies a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure with finite-sample FDR control.
Provides a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee when either the outcome or propensity model is correctly specified.
Synthetic and semi-synthetic studies support the guarantees and demonstrate use as a safety gate for high-risk subgroups.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Conformal Policy Selection, a method for safe AI deployment at inference time using conformal prediction to control false discovery rates for targeted interventions.
papers.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
papers.tldr: Conformal Policy Selection identifies which individuals can safely receive an AI-driven intervention while controlling the false discovery rate of harmful deployments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP retain zero-shot recognition ability, but their open-world use often requires task-agnostic continual learning: tasks arrive sequentially, past data are unavailable, task identity is unknown, and the backbone cannot be retrained. We argue that this setting fails VLMs through three coupled pressures beyond the stability-plasticity tradeoff: (1) modal-consistency drift, (2) representation-space interference, and (3) per-task capacity shortfall. We propose COMET (Collaborative Mixture-of-Expert Transfer) to resolve these three issues respectively as follows. A frozen teacher provides only a feature reference on a shared image-text pool; Tri-Affinity Distillation preserves image-image, text-text, and image-text geometry; and Student-Aware Cross-Expert Distillation aligns new experts with compatible prior experts so routing errors degrade gracefully. We design COMET to keep capacity and inference separate: a contextual bandit keeps or merges full per-task experts using post-training signals, while a reconstruction router selects sparse experts at test time without teacher semantics. On the X-TAIL benchmark, we show that each proposed component improves continual learning performance. COMET shows that continual vision-language adaptation can preserve multimodal geometry, coordinate accumulated experts, and allocate capacity jointly when feature reference, expert shaping, routing, and capacity control are separated by construction.
authors: Seungyoon Woo, Keonhee Park, Gunhee Kim
bullets: Addresses continual learning with sequential tasks, no past data, unknown task identity, and a frozen backbone.
Uses a frozen teacher and Tri-Affinity Distillation to preserve image-image, text-text, and image-text relationships.
Applies Student-Aware Cross-Expert Distillation so new experts align with compatible prior experts and routing mistakes are less harmful.
Separates capacity management from inference: a contextual bandit keeps or merges experts, while a reconstruction router selects sparse experts.
On X-TAIL, the abstract reports that each component improves continual-learning performance.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning for VLMs with expert routing and capacity control.
papers.title: COMET: Decoupled Distillation, Routing, and Capacity Control for Task-Agnostic Continual Vision--Language Learning
papers.tldr: COMET enables task-agnostic continual vision-language learning by separately preserving multimodal geometry, coordinating experts, routing inputs, and controlling model capacity.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents learn from failure, but the value of a failure record can change as execution progresses. We study when retaining, compressing, or removing the same history block improves subsequent execution relative to full-history KEEP. We introduce RECAP, a framework that combines matched context interventions, execution-relational prediction, and independent policy certification. Matched environment states and rollout seeds measure success and continuation prompt-cost differences; prefix-only relations between a failure block and the current execution propose promising edits. Independent task bundles then select a policy subject to harmful-intervention and non-positive-benefit risk constraints under a fixed measurement protocol. A five-seed longitudinal case holds both the failure block and its summary fixed: compression fails at an early state and becomes a cost-saving intervention at a later state. Across five backbones, RECAP produces positive paired-success saving estimates with backbone-specific reliability-efficiency tradeoffs. On Hunyuan-A13B, it edits 43.24% of retained checkpoints while matching KEEP's observed 91.89% continuation success and reducing unconditional mean continuation prompt cost by 4,619.8 tokens (2.13%). The framework provides an execution-level reference for deciding when to forget: retain history by its value to what comes next.
authors: Chenle Chen, Yangbo Wei, Zhijie Zheng, Zhenyu Su, Qifan Wang, Junhong Qian, Chao Yao, Chen Wu, Lei He
bullets: Addresses the changing value of failure records during execution compared with always keeping full history.
Uses matched context interventions, execution-relative prediction, and independent policy certification under risk constraints.
A longitudinal case shows compression can fail early but save cost later, even with the same failure block and summary.
Across five backbones, RECAP finds positive paired-success savings with backbone-specific reliability–efficiency tradeoffs.
On Hunyuan-A13B, it reduced mean continuation prompt cost by 2.13% while matching observed KEEP success of 91.89%.
papers.selection_reason: Risk-controlled context retention and forgetting for long-horizon agents; directly relevant to adaptation and memory during deployment.
papers.title: When to Forget: Risk-Controlled Context Adaptation for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: RECAP selects when to retain, compress, or remove failure history so long-horizon agents can reduce prompt cost without sacrificing continuation success.

papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are trained predominantly on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images but are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for immunohistochemistry (IHC), where cross-hospital differences can impair grading. However, systematic comparisons of correction methods for cross-hospital IHC grading remain limited. To address this gap, we benchmark label-free transformations applied to input images before frozen-FM encoding and to features after frozen-FM encoding using UNI and Virchow2, three IHC markers, and six directed cross-hospital transfers, yielding 12 settings. Among the evaluated input-space methods, our proposed method FIX achieved the largest macro-F1 improvement over no correction, outperforming well-known stain normalization techniques. Among feature-space methods, a simple feature-wise standardization achieved the best improvement over no correction, outperforming CORAL. Under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation, combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.181 and 0.208, respectively, and reduced ordinal error by 0.209 relative to no correction. These results show that input- and feature-space transformations can provide complementary benefits for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology FMs.
authors: Jongwoon Lee, Jhair Gallardo, Christopher Kanan
bullets: Cross-hospital variation can impair IHC grading when H&E-trained foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors.
The study benchmarks input-space corrections and feature-space corrections with UNI and Virchow2 across three IHC markers and six directed hospital transfers.
FIX achieved the strongest improvement among input-space methods, while feature-wise standardization outperformed CORAL in feature space.
Combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and QWK and reduced ordinal error under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes input and feature space corrections for cross-hospital pathology foundation models, relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models and domain adaptation.
papers.title: Input- and Feature-Space Correction for Cross-Hospital IHC Grading
papers.tldr: Label-free corrections applied before and after frozen pathology foundation models improve cross-hospital IHC grading, with complementary gains from combining both.

papers.abstract: Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held-out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. Across three independent design searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra averages 44.23 on the equally weighted five-track score, versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, the strongest evaluated baseline supporting all five tracks, a 50.9% relative improvement. Qualitative analysis relates performance differences to evidence retention and retrieval, while identifying grounding and evidence-use failures. These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task-dependent trade-offs in performance and computational cost. Project page: https://ba-fa-3344.github.io/.
authors: Qianwei Wang, Ce Zhang, Zhanpeng Luo, Pengpeng Su, Shuo Yang, Hao Xu
bullets: Spatial memory must retain and retrieve observations for semantic, metric, and temporal tasks.
A Designer Agent iteratively implements and evaluates memory construction and retrieval with feedback from a fixed Query Agent.
Designs are frozen before evaluation on held-out observation histories and five task tracks, without access to downstream questions.
Across three searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra scores 44.23 versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, a 50.9% relative improvement.
Analysis identifies evidence-retention and retrieval differences, plus grounding and evidence-use failures; performance remains task-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Automated design of spatial memory for robots directly fits embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Spatial Memory by Agents, for Agents
papers.tldr: Coding agents can automatically design spatial memories for robots, substantially improving multi-task performance while exposing trade-offs in grounding, evidence use, and computational cost.

papers.abstract: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present \textbf{MFM}, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. \textbf{Episodic memory} stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and \textbf{spatial memory} associates experiences with locations. \textbf{Semantic and procedural memory} build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and \textbf{working memory} holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes \emph{Mine Diamond from Scratch} and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the \emph{Ender Dragon} task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.
authors: Chloe Su, Jiahan Li, Zhenting Qi, Chaoran Cheng, Haoyu Chen, Sejoon Jun, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of retrieving relevant history while preserving visual and spatial details over long interactions.
Combines episodic, spatial, semantic, procedural, and working memory in a filesystem-based architecture.
Uses searchable textual records to retrieve experiences and inspect their underlying multimodal observations.
Consolidates experiences into reusable knowledge and procedures while retaining links to source episodes.
Improves results across three base models, including stronger performance on long-horizon Minecraft and CUABench-KiCad tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal filesystem memory for long-horizon embodied agents, directly matching embodied memory.
papers.title: Multimodal Filesystem Memory For Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: MFM gives long-horizon embodied agents a searchable multimodal memory that links textual knowledge to original visual-spatial experiences, improving performance on Minecraft and computer-use tasks.

papers.abstract: The web is not static or uniform. Websites that serve the same purpose can look and navigate very differently. Even within a single site, successive redesigns can change how familiar features are presented and accessed. Humans adapt to this by recognizing familiar interaction patterns and reusing what they already know. We give web agents a similar ability with WebMix, a mixture hypernetwork that adapts them to unseen interfaces by composing previously trained low-rank adapters. WebMix begins with a bank of adapters trained on source interfaces. At deployment, a scout agent explores the target interface and summarizes its observations into a compact manual. A lightweight router uses this manual to predict mixing coefficients over the adapter bank, which combine the existing adapters into a new one for inference. Adapting to a new interface takes only a scouting run and a forward pass, without gradient updates on the target. With Qwen and Llama models, we evaluate domain transfer on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2, and version transfer on TimeWarp. In all three settings, WebMix matches or outperforms in-context learning and LoRA baselines, often matching the average success of specialists trained directly on those interfaces. On TimeWarp domain transfer, it gains about 8 percentage points on average over the best baseline with both models. These gains do not come at the cost of seen interfaces, where WebMix keeps its lead, and extend to version transfer. Adapting to a new interface can therefore rely on exploration and composition instead of retraining.
authors: Md Farhan Ishmam, Minh Pham Dinh, Kenneth Marino
bullets: Web interfaces vary across sites and redesigns, motivating reusable adaptation mechanisms.
A scout agent creates a compact manual of the target interface, and a router selects adapter-mixture weights.
The resulting adapter is composed from previously trained adapters and used in a single forward pass without gradient updates.
Evaluated with Qwen and Llama on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2 for domain and version transfer.
WebMix matches or exceeds in-context learning and LoRA baselines, with about an 8-point average gain over the best baseline on TimeWarp domain transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time adaptation by composing pretrained adapters via a hypernetwork router, fitting test-time adaptation interests.
papers.title: Don't Retrain, Remix: Adaptation of Web Agents using Mixture Hypernetworks
papers.tldr: WebMix adapts web agents to unseen website interfaces by composing existing low-rank adapters after a brief scouting run, avoiding target-specific retraining.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a challenge in supervised continual learning, as adapting to new tasks causes representation drift and loss of previously learned information. This raises the question of which representational changes should be constrained while preserving plasticity. We therefore introduce Sparse Autoencoder Geometric Anchoring (SAGA), which converts a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained at each task boundary into local, low-rank constraints on representation drift. Replay examples specify where the constraints apply, while leading right singular directions of the encoder Jacobian specify which changes are penalized. The resulting geometry is input dependent and can be retained without keeping the SAE for subsequent tasks' training. We establish its local relation to latent code matching, define its spectral truncation error, and derive a conditional bound on frozen-readout drift.
