With replay and snapshot history, the method achieves the highest mean Class-IL accuracy and lowest mean forgetting among the evaluated ER, DER++, ER-ACE, and SGD baselines on three pretrained ViT-B/16 benchmarks, with accuracy gains of 12.15, 4.79, and 3.22 percentage points over the strongest conventional baseline on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R, respectively. From scratch results are more mixed, while rank ablations and geometry controls show that SAE-induced low-rank geometry offers useful stability-plasticity trade-offs.
bullets: Addresses representation drift and loss of prior-task knowledge during supervised continual learning.
Converts task-boundary SAEs into input-dependent constraints, using replay examples and leading encoder-Jacobian directions.
Retains the learned geometry without storing the SAE for later-task training.
Provides analyses of latent-code matching, spectral truncation error, and frozen-readout drift bounds.
On three pretrained ViT-B/16 benchmarks, SAGA achieved the best mean Class-IL accuracy and lowest mean forgetting among evaluated baselines; from-scratch results were mixed.
papers.selection_reason: SAE-induced low-rank geometric constraints mitigate catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, directly fitting continual and online learning.
papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Induce Local Geometry for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting
papers.tldr: SAGA uses sparse-autoencoder-induced local, low-rank geometric constraints to reduce catastrophic forgetting while preserving plasticity in continual learning.

papers.abstract: Automated fundus-based diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading can substantially expand screening capacity, but source-trained models degrade sharply across different cameras, clinics, and patient populations. Existing test-time adaptation methods depend on entropy minimization or target information accumulated from image batches and streams. These mechanisms can reinforce confidently incorrect predictions and break down when clinical images arrive independently. We introduce CF-NODE, a novel counterfactual test-time adaptation framework for cross- domain DR grading. Instead of trusting prediction confidence or estimating a target distribution, CF-NODE asks how each prediction responds under a controlled intervention on the evidence supporting it. CF-NODE ranks internal spatial nodes using model-derived attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, progressively attenuates the highest-ranked nodes, and uses the stability of the resulting expected-grade response to apply a bounded calibration of the predicted grade distribution. The framework is fully frozen and adapts every image independently using only geometric views and a fixed source-derived prior, requiring no target-derived information or model updates. We evaluate CF-NODE on five external DR datasets under repeated-seed evaluation against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A. CF-NODE outperforms all four methods with statistically significant improvements over the second-best method, improves AUC on every target domain, and attains the highest average AUC and macro-F1, delivering stronger grade discrimination together with more balanced recognition across DR severity levels. These results demonstrate that counterfactual intervention sensitivity provides consistent and deployment-ready domain robustness for single-image clinical inference.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation across cameras, clinics, and patient populations, where batch- or confidence-based adaptation can reinforce errors.
Ranks internal spatial nodes using attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, then attenuates selected nodes to measure prediction stability.
Calibrates each image’s predicted grade distribution using intervention sensitivity, geometric views, and a fixed source-derived prior.
Evaluated across five external DR datasets against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A; it achieved the highest average AUC and macro-F1 and improved AUC on every target domain.
Supports independent, deployment-oriented inference, but its scope is limited to the evaluated DR cross-domain settings.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a counterfactual test-time adaptation method for single-image clinical inference under domain shift, directly matching test-time learning.
papers.title: CF-NODE: Counterfactual Spatial Node Intervention for Test-Time Adaptation Under Domain Shift, Evaluated Across Five Diabetic Retinopathy Datasets
papers.tldr: CF-NODE improves single-image diabetic retinopathy grading under domain shift by adapting predictions through counterfactual spatial interventions without updating the model or using target-domain data.

papers.abstract: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings
bullets: Tests whether later relearning reflects the specific fact previously learned, rather than familiarity with its components or query format.
Compares matched histories: correct binding (LEARNED), exposure without the binding (CONTROL), and a competing answer in the same slot (WRONG).
In Qwen2.5-1.5B, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL after rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning and partial forgetting.
WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, supporting binding-specific savings, though competitor interference may affect this comparison.
A secondary descriptive analysis estimates roughly 18% fewer optimizer updates for restoration after prior learning, using an unpaired never-seen pool.
papers.selection_reason: Relearning savings in test-time continual learning for language models fits adaptation and memory.
papers.title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Prior learning of a specific fact leaves a measurable relearning advantage even after partial forgetting, indicating that current accuracy can underestimate retained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present \textbf{RingNav}, a \(10.6\)k--parameter visual heading estimator that constrains its memory to the circular manifold \(S^1\). RingNav learns only the turn between consecutive images, while heading is composed directly on the circle. On the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge, RingNav reduces mean absolute turn error by \(27\%\) and accumulated heading error over $4$ sec by \(15\%\) relative to a similarly sized learned-memory model. The structured update also gives exactly zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal. Without fine-tuning, RingNav transfers to real-world drone experiments and continues estimating heading under severe visual degradation. RingNav runs at $27.3$Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and can be deployed on an ultra-low power GAP8 processor at $33.4$Hz.
bullets: Addresses the excessive state maintained by visual navigation systems on computation- and memory-constrained robots.
Uses a 10.6k-parameter model that predicts only the turn between consecutive images and composes heading directly on the circle S¹.
Reduces mean absolute turn error by 27% and 4-second accumulated heading error by 15% versus a similarly sized learned-memory model on the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge.
Provides exact zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal.
Transfers without fine-tuning to real-world drone experiments and runs at 27.3 Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and 33.4 Hz on GAP8.
papers.selection_reason: Learned visual heading estimator for tiny robots with task-shaped circular memory; relevant to robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: RingNav: Task-Shaped Circular Memory for Visual Heading
papers.tldr: RingNav is a tiny visual heading estimator whose memory is constrained to the circular manifold, enabling efficient and robust navigation on resource-limited robots.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video provides a continuous first-person record of everyday activities, making it a natural foundation for wearable AI assistants. Unlike offline video understanding, streaming systems must process observations as they arrive, while queries may refer to experiences from the distant past. Recent work has begun to explore whether information can be recalled across long temporal gaps. Yet remembering how far is only part of the challenge: recurring objects, actions, and locations also require models to remember exactly which detail belongs to which event. We introduce EgoProbe, a benchmark that evaluates streaming egocentric memory along these two complementary dimensions: long-range retention, i.e., how far, and event-specific recall under interference, i.e., how exact. Built on long-form egocentric videos, EgoProbe uses an event-grounded data engine to extend recall intervals, identify related events, and construct event-grounded distractors, followed by human verification. It contains two subsets: EgoProbe-Base, which evaluates long-range recall without intervening related events, and EgoProbe-Echo, which challenges models with similar intervening events and event-grounded distractors. EgoProbe-Echo adopts coarse-to-fine multi-turn probing: the first turn evaluates coarse-grained event recall, while the second tests whether the model can retrieve the target-specific detail associated with the designated event. Extensive evaluation across diverse models reveals substantial limitations in long-range recall, with further challenges in recovering target-event details among related experiences. Even when models correctly answer coarse-grained questions, they often fail to recall the specific details of the designated event. EgoProbe exposes this underexplored failure mode and provides a testbed for advancing long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video understanding.
bullets: Evaluates two dimensions of memory: long-range retention and event-specific recall under interference.
Introduces EgoProbe-Base for unobstructed long-range recall and EgoProbe-Echo for recall amid similar events and distractors.
Uses an event-grounded data engine with human verification to construct extended recall intervals and targeted probes.
EgoProbe-Echo uses coarse-to-fine multi-turn questions to test event identification followed by target-detail retrieval.
Models show substantial weaknesses, often answering coarse event questions correctly while missing details from the designated event.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video.
papers.title: EgoProbe: Benchmarking Long-Range and Exact Memory in Streaming Egocentric Videos
papers.tldr: EgoProbe benchmarks whether streaming video models can both remember distant egocentric events and retrieve the exact details tied to the correct event.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns from rewards has to trust whatever reports those rewards. When the reports suddenly change, either the world changed or the reporter broke. From the reports alone these are indistinguishable, and reinforcement learning theory shows that no amount of further experience separates them. The prescribed escape is richer data about the reporter itself. We ask whether a frozen language model, handed exactly that data, uses it. We build a two-option game in which a payout swap and a lying reporter produce byte-identical histories. Then we add one verified record: an independent check of one round's real result, printed beside what the reporter said about that round. That single line settles the case. We ask three large models, from two families, to answer one question with one letter. Is the reporter honest or lying? They catch a lying reporter almost perfectly. At the 70B class that holds in every condition we tried; the 32B model slips in one wording. They clear an honest reporter far less often, and how often depends on things that should not matter. Averaged over rounds, letters, and wordings, a 72B model calls an honest reporter a liar 38% of the time when nothing has changed at all, and 58% of the time when the payouts moved. A 70B model from a second family calls an honest reporter a liar 26% and 48% of the time. The failure is not one of reading, because in the situation where nothing changed the same models score 0.96 to 1.00 with the answer printed in the prompt. Which surface feature drives it differs by family. For the Qwen models it is which round the record names, and for Llama it is which letter stands for "honest." Adding the record to a prompt that already states the answer makes Llama less likely to give that answer. We had registered a prediction for that 58% before the run: 35%. The failure is larger than we expected.
bullets: A payout change and a lying reporter can generate identical reward histories, making them indistinguishable from reports alone.
The study tests whether one verified comparison between the reporter’s claim and the real outcome resolves this ambiguity for language models.
Models nearly always identify lying reporters, but their accuracy for honest reporters varies substantially with wording and other irrelevant surface features.
False accusations are especially frequent when payouts changed, reaching 58% for one 72B-class model and 48% for another 70B-class model.
Providing the verified record alongside an answer can sometimes reduce, rather than improve, the likelihood of selecting that answer.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a large language model to diagnose corrupted reward channels in reinforcement learning agents, relevant to Test-Time Learning and LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Easy to Catch a Liar, Hard to Clear an Honest One: Language Models Diagnosing a Corrupted Reward Channel from a Verified Record
papers.tldr: Large frozen language models reliably detect lying reward reporters but often falsely accuse honest ones, even when given a verified record that resolves the ambiguity.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-guided Bayesian optimization (BO) uses past observations to guide search, but proposed directions and their revision can remain implicit. We propose Feedback-Guided Search State (FGSS), a structured hypothesis-management interface connecting language-based guidance to observed evidence, executable parameter interventions, and comparative support updates. An LLM reflector proposes and revises hypotheses; a deterministic curator validates them and maintains identities and test records. The evolving state guides candidate construction and priorities. Instantiated on LLAMBO, FGSS-BO retains its surrogate and default expected improvement selection, with a bounded testing policy. On two retrospective protocol/media tasks with nearest-neighbor response oracles, it attains higher sample mean final best and search AUC than the matched LLAMBO baseline and evaluated non-LLM baselines. Prose-reflection and EI-only controls show mixed component effects. Six direct-training hyperparameter-optimization tasks show task-dependent transfer, strongest on diabetes SVM; exact-grid and reaction controls examine other settings. FGSS exposes hypotheses, their execution, and cross-round revisions for inspection while supporting search gains in selected settings.
bullets: Addresses the implicit nature of proposed directions and their revisions in LLM-guided BO.
Uses an LLM reflector to propose/revise hypotheses and a deterministic curator to validate, track, and record tests.
Integrates the evolving hypothesis state into candidate construction and search priorities while retaining LLAMBO’s surrogate and expected-improvement selection.
Outperforms matched LLAMBO and evaluated non-LLM baselines on two retrospective protocol/media tasks, with mixed component effects and task-dependent transfer elsewhere.
Provides inspectable records of hypotheses, executions, and cross-round revisions; gains are strongest only in selected settings.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes FGSS-BO, a hypothesis management interface for LLM-based Bayesian Optimization. It manages hypotheses and updates states during the search process, fitting 'Test-Time Learning' and 'Continual and Online Learning'.
papers.title: FGSS-BO: Feedback-Guided Hypothesis Management for LLM-Based Bayesian Optimization
papers.tldr: FGSS-BO makes LLM-guided Bayesian optimization more explicit and inspectable by managing hypotheses, evidence, interventions, and revisions throughout the search.

papers.abstract: Reliable fault detection is crucial for industrial machinery in large-scale facilities, where unexpected failures can cause costly downtime and production interruptions. Although acoustic monitoring provides a scalable solution for machine condition monitoring, its deployment is often constrained by high false-positive rates. We propose a two-step approach to automatic anomalous sound detection: first, when only normal operating audio samples are available, a regularized unsupervised model is deployed; then, after the first machine fault, a few-shot adaptation strategy exploits the anomalous samples acquired during the fault to improve the system. This adaptation increases the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) from 23.0 to 64.0 and improves detection in the low false-positive-rate region, with the partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (pAUROC) increasing from 39.6 to 72.8. We also show that covariance regularization improves both prediction accuracy and training stability in the unsupervised model. These results provide a practical strategy for acoustic anomaly detection systems, enabling improved accuracy and reduced false alarms.
bullets: Targets costly false alarms in scalable acoustic monitoring of industrial machinery.
Initially trains a regularized unsupervised model using only normal operating sounds.
Adapts the detector with a few anomalous samples collected after the first machine fault.
Adaptation raises AUPR from 23.0 to 64.0 and low-false-positive pAUROC from 39.6 to 72.8.
Covariance regularization improves prediction accuracy and training stability.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a two-step few-shot adaptation strategy for anomalous sound detection, moving from a regularized unsupervised model to a few-shot adaptation using acquired anomalous samples. This fits the 'Test-Time Learning' subtopic as it updates the model during deployment/inference.
papers.title: Few-Shot Adaptation for Anomalous Sound Detection at Low False-Positive Rate
papers.tldr: A two-stage approach uses unsupervised learning followed by few-shot adaptation from the first fault’s audio to improve anomalous sound detection at low false-positive rates.

papers.abstract: Traversability prediction is a critical component of autonomous navigation in unstructured environments, where complex and uncertain robot-terrain interactions pose significant challenges such as traction loss and dynamic instability. Despite recent progress in learning-based traversability prediction, these methods often fail to adapt to novel terrains. Even when adaptation is achieved, retaining experience from previously trained environments remains a challenge, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose a continual learning framework for traversability prediction that incrementally adapts to new terrains using a generative experience recall model. A key virtue of the proposed framework is two folds: i) retain prior experience without storing past data; and ii) incorporate the uncertainty of the generated samples from the recall model, enabling uncertainty-aware adaptation. Real-world experiments with a skid-steering robot validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, demonstrating its ability to adapt across a series of diverse environments while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
bullets: Addresses poor adaptation to novel terrains and catastrophic forgetting in traversability prediction.
Incrementally adapts the model using a generative experience recall model without storing past data.
Uses uncertainty estimates from recalled samples to guide adaptation.
Real-world skid-steering robot experiments show adaptation across diverse environments while mitigating forgetting.
papers.selection_reason: Continual learning with generative experience recall and uncertainty-aware adaptation for traversability prediction in autonomous navigation.
papers.title: Continual Learning for Traversability Prediction with Uncertainty-Aware Adaptation
papers.tldr: A continual-learning framework adapts traversability prediction to new terrains while preserving prior knowledge through uncertainty-aware generative experience recall.

papers.abstract: Real-world post-training of generalist robot policies faces two challenges: partial observability makes action selection ambiguous, while offline post-training methods delay feedback from deployment experience. We present Value as Memory (VaM), a framework that addresses these challenges through value caching and online real-world reinforcement learning (RL). Value caching conditions actions on recent value predictions as task-progress memory, while online updates enable timely policy improvement by combining offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient adaptation. As a result, VaM transitions from offline RL warmup to online autonomous learning with sparse rewards. Across long-horizon tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulation, VaM yields a mean absolute success-rate gain of $29.4\%$ with value caching, while achieving a $32.8\%$ gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training. The evaluated online schedule performs $8\times$ as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than $2\times$ lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.
authors: Wenye Yu, Yijin Chen, Kaiyi Xiong, Wenbo Han, Wendi Chen, Yang Jin, Han Xue, Jun Lv, Cewu Lu, Chuan Wen
bullets: Addresses ambiguous action selection under partial observability and delayed feedback in offline post-training.
Conditions actions on recent value predictions, using them as task-progress memory.
Combines offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for online adaptation with sparse rewards.
On long-horizon deformable-object and contact-rich manipulation tasks, reports 29.4% gain with value caching and 32.8% gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training.
The evaluated schedule performs 8× more policy iterations and records over 2× lower time per gradient step through concurrent data collection and training.
papers.selection_reason: Online value-guided post-training for generalist robot policies with value-based memory; fits robot learning and online adaptation.
papers.title: Value as Memory: Online Value-Guided Post-training for General Robot Policies
papers.tldr: VaM improves general robot policies by using cached value predictions as memory and online RL to adapt efficiently from real-world experience.

papers.abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
authors: Chenyuan Zhou, Yining Hong, Huang Huang, Yunfan Jiang, Wenlong Huang, David Held, Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini, Yue Wang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Leonidas Guibas, Yejin Choi
bullets: Targets hidden environmental factors such as friction, mass, and human-defined rules that affect action outcomes.
Alternates between learning action-conditioned dynamics with fixed latents and optimizing latents with a frozen world model.
At test time, optimizes a newly initialized latent while keeping the world model frozen.
Evaluated across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world tasks, it reduces object prediction error from 15.20 to 7.00 and increases action success from 33.73% to 72.96%.
Ablations indicate that environment latents can be inferred from as little as one test-time interaction trajectory.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes environment latents at test time in action-conditioned robotic world models, fitting interactive world models and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: T2-Z adapts robotic world models to unseen environments by optimizing a compact environment latent from test-time interactions.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation fundamentally requires memory: agents must retain task-relevant information from past observations and interactions and use it to guide future actions. Existing approaches typically preserve raw historical observations, compressed visual tokens, or language summaries, but these representations either expose the action policy to increasingly long histories or risk discarding task-relevant temporal, semantic, and perceptual information. We introduce Mem4Act, a framework for learning effective latent memory as a fixed-size representation explicitly optimized for long-horizon robotic control. Mem4Act addresses three coupled challenges: how to efficiently cover long histories, what information memory should retain, and how to ensure the policy actually relies on memory. To this end, it organizes history via multi-granularity temporal aggregation, preserves complementary semantic and perceptual information through question-answering supervision and key-frame DINO feature reconstruction, and employs memory-first two-stage training to encourage greater use of memory by the action policy. The resulting memory captures both high-level task state and fine-grained perceptual evidence while providing a bounded interface to the action policy. Across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, Mem4Act achieves state-of-the-art performance on memory-dependent control, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%, respectively. Extensive ablations further demonstrate the importance of temporal aggregation, complementary memory supervision, and memory-first training.
authors: Yun Zhang, Zhiyu Huang, Tianhui Cai, Chen Tang, Wei Wang, Jiaqi Ma
bullets: Addresses the limitations of raw histories, visual-token compression, and language summaries in memory-dependent control.
Uses multi-granularity temporal aggregation to efficiently cover long interaction histories.
Combines question-answering supervision with key-frame DINO feature reconstruction to retain complementary semantic and perceptual information.
Applies memory-first two-stage training to encourage the action policy to rely on the learned memory.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Learned fixed-size latent memory for long-horizon robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Mem4Act: Learning Effective Latent Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: Mem4Act learns a fixed-size latent memory that preserves task-relevant temporal, semantic, and perceptual information for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.
authors: Arnav Chavan, Kusha Sareen, Rishabh Tiwari, Abhranil Chandra, Johan Obando-Ceron, Kurt Keutzer, Scott Niekum, Inderjit S Dhillon, Devvrit Khatri
bullets: Addresses capability loss when LLMs are continually fine-tuned, especially with supervised fine-tuning.
Restricts weight updates away from principal singular directions, which are associated with greater forgetting.
Is optimizer-agnostic and compatible with SFT and self-distillation, using dense gradient estimation and subspace refreshing.
Protecting up to 99% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention and can nearly eliminate forgetting for large models.
Produces 2–4× less KL drift than baseline recipes and improves the learning–forgetting tradeoff.
papers.selection_reason: Subspace tuning mitigates catastrophic forgetting in LLM continual learning, directly relevant to continual learning and language foundation models.
papers.title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning
papers.tldr: Subspace Tuning reduces catastrophic forgetting by confining fine-tuning updates to the bottom singular subspace while retaining strong performance on new tasks.

papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.
authors: Zhipeng Ye, Feng Jiang, Qiufeng Wang, Hao Li
bullets: Addresses the underuse of complementary intermediate-layer information and differing feature dimensions in few-shot adaptation.
Uses one forward pass per view to generate descriptors, then combines global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors in class-score space.
Validation labels select the predictor mixture without learned projections; LAMP-F additionally adapts text-anchored class prototypes.
Evaluated on 11 datasets with ViT and ResNet backbones, LAMP and LAMP-F consistently improve over global-feature-only baselines across support budgets.
At 16 shots, LAMP-F reaches 83.57% on ViT-B/16 and 79.10% on ResNet-50; multi-layer integration is identified as the main improvement source.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free few-shot vision-language adaptation via layerwise predictor mixing and cached calibration; aligns with inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation
papers.tldr: LAMP improves training-free few-shot vision-language adaptation by adaptively mixing predictions from multiple encoder layers and global/regional features.

papers.abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
authors: Juliette Marrie, Paul Pacaud, Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Shizhe Chen, Moritz B\"ohle
bullets: Pretrained exclusively on curated public robot, egocentric human, and vision-language data.
Combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert.
Uses register tokens to summarize recent VLM outputs in the action expert’s cache at negligible cost.
Improves simulated and real-robot success, while making pose oscillations about four times rarer.
Outperformed only by roughly twice-as-large models on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand, and RoboCasa365.
papers.selection_reason: VLA with register-token memory, efficient and effective.
papers.title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs
papers.tldr: REKI is a compact 2.4B vision-language-action model with efficient register-token memory that improves robot-control performance and reduces pose oscillations.

papers.abstract: Test-time context optimization adapts frozen language models through textual feedback, but ordinary conditional generation provides no separate control over how strongly to reinforce the distributional changes induced by a context update. We introduce EMO, a training-free framework inspired by expectation--maximization that alternates question-specific context estimation (E-step) and distribution refinement (M-step). The E-step revises a system context using textual gradients from an external judge without access to gold answers. The M-step contrasts next-token distributions under the revised and preceding contexts at a shared prefix to construct a confidence-constrained logit correction. Feedback on the steered response drives the next context update, coupling adaptation across rounds with intervention within each generation. Theoretically, we connect parameter and context optimization through a shared target-KL objective and additive logit representations, and derive the steering vector from context-induced logit displacements. Under context-improvement and faithful-steering assumptions, we prove a one-round decrease in target KL divergence for sufficiently small steering strength. Under greedy decoding across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging $+9.10$ percentage points. With the same judge, it adds $+1.53$ points on average over context-only optimization (TextGrad), with consistent MMLU-Pro gains across models. At matched target-model generation budgets, accuracy advantages over best-of-$N$ are strongest on Llama, while oracle coverage is higher in most comparisons despite fewer candidates. The coverage--selection gap motivates allocating test-time computation jointly to candidate generation and verification.
authors: Wei Xia, Yehui Tang, Zhi-Hong Deng
bullets: Addresses the lack of independent control over how strongly context updates alter a language model’s output distribution.
Uses an expectation–maximization-style loop: an external judge revises question-specific context, then logits are corrected by comparing revised and previous contexts.
Derives steering from context-induced logit changes and theoretically shows reduced target KL divergence under stated assumptions and sufficiently small steering strength.
Across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging +9.10 percentage points.
Outperforms context-only optimization on average and can surpass best-of-N at matched generation budgets, while highlighting a remaining candidate-generation versus verification trade-off.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a closed-loop test-time framework (EMO) for LLM adaptation using alternating context optimization and logit steering, directly relevant to test-time learning and inference-time optimization.
papers.title: EMO: A Closed-Loop Test-Time Computation Framework via Alternating Context Optimization and Logits Steering
papers.tldr: EMO improves test-time adaptation by alternating textual context updates with confidence-constrained logit steering, yielding broad zero-shot gains without training.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet real-world applications often require them to continually acquire new capabilities from sequential tasks, i.e., Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). In typical MLLMs, a projector is employed to align visual representations with the language model. However, existing methods primarily protect the language model from forgetting while continuously updating the projector across tasks. Such asymmetric adaptation can cause substantial representation drift in the projector, increasing the mismatch between the projector and language model and consequently exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To address this issue, we propose Compatible Routing (CART), which explicitly coordinates the adaptation of the projector and language model. Specifically, CART maintains task-specific experts for both modules and combines them through weighted mixtures. CART jointly infers their weights by considering both expert relevance and cross-module compatibility, thereby promoting coordinated adaptation between the two modules. To further control model growth, we introduce relevance-guided expert consolidation, which merges experts exhibiting similar relevance profiles across samples within each module. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CART achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Ling-Xiang Zhang, Tao Hu, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: MCIT requires MLLMs to learn sequential multimodal tasks without losing previously acquired capabilities.
Existing methods mainly protect the language model while continually changing the projector, causing representation drift and cross-module mismatch.
CART maintains task-specific experts for both the projector and language model, then jointly routes them using expert relevance and cross-module compatibility.
Relevance-guided consolidation merges experts with similar sample-level relevance profiles to limit model growth.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no specific datasets or numerical results.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual instruction tuning for multimodal LLMs with coordinated projector and language model adaptation.
papers.title: CART: Compatible Routing for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.tldr: CART reduces catastrophic forgetting in multimodal continual instruction tuning by coordinating projector and language-model adaptation through compatible expert routing.

papers.abstract: Neural networks offer critical adaptability for controlling complex systems where nominal modeling proves intractable. However, when offline-trained neural networks are deployed within closed-loop control systems, their actions fundamentally alter the state distribution upon which they were trained. This paper introduces a unified taxonomy to categorize these sequential failure modes: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Error, the deployment-induced Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error. Through discrete-time sensitivity analysis, this work formalizes how offline-learned parameters locally guarantee a trajectory divergence upon deployment, degrading performance due to local loss geometry. To mitigate this distribution shift, we propose actionable design policies centered on time-scale separated online adaptation. These mechanisms are validated through ablation studies on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator, demonstrating that bounded continuous learning successfully mitigates trajectory divergence whereas static deployments fail, offering concrete guidelines for practitioners deploying machine learning components in safety-critical feedback systems.
bullets: Identifies three sequential failure modes: Closed-Loop Identification Error, deployment-induced Action Error, and continuous Tracking Error.
Uses discrete-time sensitivity analysis to formalize how local loss geometry can cause deployment trajectories to diverge from those seen during training.
Proposes time-scale-separated online adaptation policies to mitigate deployment-induced distribution shift.
Ablations on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator show bounded continuous learning mitigates trajectory divergence, unlike static deployment.
Targets safer deployment of learned control components in safety-critical feedback systems.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes deployment-time distribution shift in closed-loop neural control and proposes online adaptation, fitting test-time and continual learning.
papers.title: Learning Changes the World and Then What Was Learned has Changed: Training and Deploying Neural Networks in the Control Loop
papers.tldr: Offline-trained neural networks can destabilize closed-loop control by changing the data distribution they encounter, while bounded online adaptation helps prevent trajectory divergence.

papers.abstract: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the return to stable following. Moreover, we introduce OccEVT-Bench for closed-loop evaluation of persistent occlusion and collect expert demonstrations for training. On its Risk split, VP-EVT improves success rate by 121.4% relative to a competitive baseline and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%, respectively.
authors: Yanci Wen, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Weixi Situ, Hanjing Ye, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses prolonged target loss caused by pedestrian occlusions in dynamic environments.
Uses language-guided perception to separate target and occluder observations, then combines visual history with ego-motion to estimate relative motion during partial visibility.
Predicts whether continued following will maintain occlusion and selectively triggers viewpoint-adjustment maneuvers through a recurrent controller.
Introduces OccEVT-Bench and expert demonstrations for closed-loop evaluation and training.
On the Risk split, improves success rate by 121.4% and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied visual tracking with proactive visibility preservation, using ego-motion history and recurrent control for target following.
papers.title: VP-EVT: Active Visibility Preservation for Embodied Visual Tracking
papers.tldr: VP-EVT enables embodied visual trackers to proactively avoid persistent occlusions by adjusting the robot’s viewpoint while maintaining target following.

papers.abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.
authors: Xueli Sun, Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Xianzhe Fan, Xi Chen, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses failures caused by committing to a poor action sample during fine-grained manipulation.
Uses two initial samples to detect critical states from within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance.
When triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicted future latent states and task-progress changes.
Improves average real-world completion from 50.8% to 65.5% across pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement, with 326 ms added per triggered decision.
Also reports consistent simulation gains across RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO; verification is applied selectively rather than at every decision.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time verification of flow-based VLA policies using a latent world model to rank action chunks.
papers.title: VeriVLA: Adaptive Test-Time Verification for Flow-Based VLAs with Latent World Models
papers.tldr: VeriVLA improves stochastic flow-based VLA decisions by triggering test-time verification and selecting action chunks with a latent world model.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors safeguard against misinformation, rendering their failures as much a societal as a technical concern. As generators constantly evolve, detectors trained on static datasets miss newly arising threats, while progressive training interferes catastrophically. Yet, mitigating forgetfulness in terms of accuracy, the prevalent focus of continual learning (CL), is insufficient to reflect real-world impact. We therefore scrutinize the effects of CL methods with respect to evolving fairness. To this end, we analyze four dimensions of fairness across diverse demographics for detectors trained progressively on a chronological sequence of 11 real-world deepfake generation methods. Tracking fairness metrics over time, we expose non-trivial interplays between performance and fairness that depend on both the choice of CL algorithm and demographic intersections. We find accuracy degradation to typically exacerbate unfairness and, conversely, fairness improvements to remain scarce over time. Dissecting the CL method families (rehearsal, prompts, regularization), we observe that inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone, but likely entangled with representation learning. We thus issue a call to action for CL methods to take social outcomes into account when balancing the stability-plasticity tradeoff.
authors: Kajaree Das, Oliver B\"ose, Subarnaduti Paul, Gabriel Storch, Martin Mundt
bullets: Studies four fairness dimensions across diverse demographic groups.
Evaluates detectors progressively on 11 chronological, real-world deepfake generation methods.
Finds that accuracy degradation typically worsens unfairness, while fairness improvements are rare over time.
Fairness outcomes vary by continual-learning algorithm and demographic intersection.
Inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone and may involve representation learning.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes fairness of continual learning methods for deepfake detection; fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Time to Fake It: Continual Machine Learning Intensifies Unfairness in Deepfake Detection
papers.tldr: Continual learning can make deepfake detectors increasingly unfair as they adapt to evolving generation methods, so fairness must be treated alongside accuracy.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.
authors: Bruno Arcanjo, Zhaoxing Li, Sebastian Stein
bullets: Addresses preference elicitation when no user choices are yet available.
An LLM describes a new user’s trade-offs, which are mapped to priors over multinomial logit coefficients.
A Bayesian learner updates these priors as user choices accumulate.
Across seven choice datasets, it improves cold-start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5–40 percentage points.
Its benefit is concentrated among early users, with performance comparable to information from roughly 6–40 surveyed users in log-loss terms.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLMs to generate informative priors for test-time preference elicitation, addressing the cold start problem in adaptive systems.
papers.title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
papers.tldr: Agentic-Priors uses LLM-derived, interpretable preference trade-offs to provide informative priors that substantially improve cold-start preference learning.

papers.abstract: Incremental learning (IL) aims to continually acquire new knowledge (plasticity) while retaining previously learned information (stability). However, striking a balance between plasticity and stability remains a significant challenge for intelligent systems. The human brain achieves exceptional balance, owing to various memory units that collaboratively encode and store information. Inspired by human memory mechanisms, this paper introduces an IL framework with knowledge enCoding, Consolidation, and Integration (Co2In). Co2In is designed as a bi-level memory architecture: a working memory for adaptive knowledge acquisition and a long-term memory dedicated to the persistent retention of information. The two memory modules work cooperatively during IL. The working memory first learns from new data to encode knowledge into parameters. Subsequently, Co2In performs a consolidation process to identify underlying patterns in the learned parameters and re-express them into a compact knowledge representation. Next, the knowledge representation and the identified patterns are transformed into separate network layers and integrated into the long-term memory. These designs empower Co2In to accumulate knowledge with high plasticity and stability. We evaluate Co2In on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL settings. Experimental results show that Co2In achieves state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.
authors: Wenju Sun, Qingyong Li, Boyang Li, Wen Wang, Siyu Zhang, Yi Wei, Yangliao Geng
bullets: Addresses the plasticity–stability trade-off in continual learning.
Uses working memory for adaptive learning and long-term memory for persistent retention.
Consolidates learned parameters into compact knowledge representations and integrates them as separate network layers.
Evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL.
Reports state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.
papers.selection_reason: Bi-level memory incremental learning directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Co2In: a Bi-level Memory Incremental Learning Framework with Knowledge Encoding, Consolidation, and Integration
papers.tldr: Co2In uses cooperating working and long-term memories to learn new classes while preserving prior knowledge in exemplar-free incremental learning.

papers.abstract: As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.
bullets: Existing memory systems often retain facts or procedures without assessing claim reliability.
Unreliable entries can harm future performance; the abstract reports this for approximately 12–33% of entries in representative systems.
RIKA hierarchically extracts factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge.
Its Evidence-based Knowledge Admission uses source evidence and later experience to decide which claims are retained, without additional validation tasks.
RIKA achieved the highest aggregate score across six task streams and all four evaluated model backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes reliable knowledge acquisition for continual learning agents, directly fitting continual/online learning and agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Reliable Knowledge Acquisition for Continual Learning Agents
papers.tldr: RIKA improves continual-learning agents by admitting only evidence-supported knowledge into context, achieving the best aggregate performance across evaluated backbones.

papers.abstract: Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy. We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions. Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy. DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space. This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies. Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.
bullets: Expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in a few dimensions, with important directions varying across regions of state space.
DHS learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states replayed through the frozen policy.
It suppresses low-variance coordinates more strongly than high-variance ones, then maps states back while retaining all coordinates.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over unmodified Transformer policies.
Nonlinear coordinates outperform linear alternatives in controlled comparisons; combining DHS with action smoothing helps on some tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time hidden-state steering improves imitation learning policy robustness in manipulation.
papers.title: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering: Improving Imitation Learning Policy Robustness through Expert Hidden-State Geometry
papers.tldr: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering improves imitation-policy robustness to observation noise by reshaping hidden states according to expert-state geometry at test time, without retraining or new demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.
authors: Jing Xia, Changyan Li, Yuduo Wang, Guiyin Tian, Bo Wang, Yifan Liao, Mingjun Li, Shiyan Hu
bullets: Targets service robots entering unmapped buildings without prior on-site traversal or site-specific training.
Uses a floor plan, place clues, and initial topology–odometry alignment instead of a robot-built global SLAM map.
Combines human task constraints and environmental reports with robot-verified physical-state evidence.
Verified node arrivals support translational re-anchoring for visual depth point-goal navigation.
On a Unitree Go2, AVALON completed the reported mission in all 5 runs and avoided timeouts seen with policy-only X-NavDP.
papers.selection_reason: Indoor topological navigation with human-seeded spatial memory and robot navigation, fitting embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: AVALON: Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation with Human-Seeded Topological Memory
papers.tldr: AVALON enables zero-shot indoor robot navigation in human-familiar but robot-unmapped buildings using human-seeded topological memory and evidence-gated memory updates.

papers.abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.
authors: Shuoran Jiang, Wentao Zhu, Yang Xiang, Dongfeng Li, Yunan Zhang, Mengchen Zhao, Yuhui Guo, Kai Chen, Youcheng Pan, Xiangping Wu, Qingcai Chen
bullets: Continual learning in LLMs is challenged by catastrophic forgetting and costly global updates.
Gradient-attribution profiling identifies cognition-associated subnetworks with very low mutual overlap.
CiMEO restricts parameter and optimizer-state updates to the subnetwork selected for each training example.
Across 1.4 million sequential instructions and five generative benchmarks, CiMEO achieved the highest average performance among compared methods while mitigating forgetting.
Subspace and principal-angle analyses suggest localized updates help preserve pretrained representations.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning in LLMs with a method for localized parameter updates to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
papers.title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: CiMEO enables efficient continual learning in LLMs by routing examples to localized functional subnetworks, reducing forgetting while preserving pretrained representations.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents can accumulate interaction feedback, but reliably turning that feedback into reusable experience remains challenging. Existing methods either optimize external experience scaffolds or train experience-related behavior on specific task distributions, leaving open whether experience learning itself can become a transferable model capability. Training such a capability calls for supervision beyond isolated tasks, which mainly support in-episode problem solving rather than revealing what knowledge remains useful across episodes. In this work, we introduce MetaExp, a scalable framework that trains this capability through verifiable task families with controlled cross-task structure. Each family preserves a reusable factor while varying task-specific realizations, enabling transfer without direct solution reuse. We propose two complementary designs: Shared-Tool families keep black-box tools fixed across tasks to elicit operational experience, while Shared-Workflow families preserve latent procedures across changing realizations to elicit procedural experience. We scale environments under both designs, collect and filter sequential interaction trajectories, and fine-tune Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 4,956 trajectories from 1,000 task families. With parameters frozen during downstream evolution, MetaExp improves by +8.5 points on SpreadsheetBench, peaks at +2.3 on APEX-Agents, and improves by +14.8 on AutomationBench. The gains persist under domain-excluded training, supporting experience learning as a transferable capability for continued non-parametric improvement after deployment.
authors: Renhao Li, Xinjie Shen, Yang Su, Jianhong Tu, Derek F. Wong, Dayiheng Liu, Min Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning reusable experience rather than task-specific strategies or external memory scaffolds.
Uses verifiable cross-task families that preserve either shared black-box tools or latent workflows while varying task realizations.
Trains on filtered sequential interaction trajectories from 1,000 task families and evaluates frozen-model downstream evolution.
Reports gains on SpreadsheetBench, APEX-Agents, and AutomationBench, including improvements after excluding training domains.
Supports experience learning as a transferable capability for non-parametric post-deployment improvement.
papers.selection_reason: Trains LLM agents to reuse cross-task experience for continued post-deployment improvement, aligning with continual/online learning.
papers.title: MetaExp: Learning to Self-Improve through Experience via Verifiable Cross-Task Environment Scaling
papers.tldr: MetaExp trains language-model agents to turn interaction feedback into transferable experience, enabling continued improvement across new tasks without updating model parameters.

papers.abstract: We adapt the diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN architecture for longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge. The method combines affine pre-registration, multi-modal deformable registration, and test-time instance optimization. We further introduce PET biomarker preservation losses for metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), including Jacobian-based constraints, and a per-structure rigidity regularization for skeletal structures. The submitted configuration achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with MTV and TLG errors of 3.3% and 3.3%, respectively, on our evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/koegl/psmareg.
authors: Fryderyk K\"ogl, Anna Reithmeir, Daniel M. Lang, Emily Chan, Rickmer Braren, Julia A. Schnabel
bullets: Targets longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration for the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge.
Adapts a diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN pipeline with affine pre-registration, multimodal deformable registration, and test-time optimization.
Adds MTV and TLG biomarker-preservation losses with Jacobian constraints, plus rigidity regularization for skeletal structures.
Achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with 3.3% errors for both MTV and TLG under the reported evaluation protocol.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.
papers.selection_reason: Uses test-time instance optimization in deformable registration, matching test-time learning interests.
papers.title: PET Quantification-Preserving Registration for Longitudinal Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT
papers.tldr: A longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration method preserves PET biomarkers while achieving strong anatomical alignment.

papers.abstract: Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions. Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored. We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM), a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts. MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes. We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry. Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird's-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map. Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 2.60% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory. MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes. The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Hao Ju, Feng Yan, Zhihao Zhong, Heng Yang, Shaofei Huang, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Addresses the limited evaluation of sound-triggered manipulation across diverse, unseen architectural scenes.
Provides 31 scenes, spatial audio and physical interactions, 14.36 million precomputed binaural RIRs, and scene-disjoint single- and multi-event splits.
Augments navigation with pose-aligned depth memory projected into a Bird’s-Eye View occupancy map.
Fuses spatial-memory features with sound context to guide robots toward target regions for physical interaction.
Reports a 2.60% success-rate improvement over existing methods; ablations support the value of spatial memory.
papers.selection_reason: Sound-triggered mobile manipulation with spatial memory and navigation policy; directly relevant to embodied navigation, manipulation, and embodied memory.
papers.title: MuSTMM: Learning Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation across Multiple Scenes
papers.tldr: MuSTMM introduces a multi-scene benchmark and spatial-memory navigation policy for sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: Learning from interaction experience is essential for enabling large language models to continually improve during deployment. Context distillation offers a promising path: privileged information extracted from experience is provided to a teacher, whose behavior is then distilled into a student model that has no access to it. However, both existing forms of context distillation have limitations. Off-policy context distillation trains the student on teacher-generated trajectories and thus suffers from exposure bias; whereas on-policy context distillation trains on the student's own rollouts, whose states are often uninformative and fail to convey behaviors the student cannot yet produce. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Localized Context Distillation (LoCD). LoCD first localizes the critical spans of a student trajectory that require revision. The teacher then regenerates only these spans from the student's own prefix, and the student is trained on the regenerated segments. LoCD thereby concentrates learning on the most informative states while keeping exposure bias low. Extensive experiments across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks demonstrate that LoCD consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves more stable training with smaller and sparser parameter updates.
authors: Zhezheng Hao, Yongkang Yang, Xilin Xia, Jiarui Yu, Yi Liu, Fanjunduo Wei, Peijie Dong, Tianfu Wang, Qiang Lin, Can Wang, Hande Dong, Jiawei Chen
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between off-policy exposure bias and uninformative on-policy rollouts.
Identifies trajectory spans that need revision, then has a teacher regenerate those spans from the student’s prefix.
Trains the student on the regenerated segments, focusing updates on informative states while limiting exposure bias.
Experiments in math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks show consistent gains over strong baselines and more stable training.
Updates are smaller and sparser, though the abstract does not specify detailed quantitative results or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Distills interaction experience into LLMs during deployment; directly fits test-time and continual learning interests.
papers.title: Learning from Interaction Experience via Localized Context Distillation
papers.tldr: Localized Context Distillation improves continual learning from interaction experience by revising only the most critical parts of a student’s own trajectories.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.
authors: Inseok Kong, Geunyoung Jung, Jiyoung Jung
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in 3D point clouds without source data or backpropagation.
Computes token abnormality from attention and geometric relation graphs.
Uses Otsu-based separability to derive each sample’s retained/pruned token partition.
Routes to the pruned prediction only when keep-ratio-penalized entropy favors it.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C.
papers.selection_reason: Source-free 3D test-time adaptation with sample-adaptive token routing; fits test-time learning and token pruning.
papers.title: SATOR: Backpropagation-Free 3D Test-Time Adaptation via Sample-Adaptive Token Routing
