papers.tldr: SATOR enables efficient backpropagation-free 3D test-time adaptation by routing tokens using sample-specific decisions instead of costly purge-size searches.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $\pi_{0.5}$ as LTM-$\pi$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$\pi$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.
authors: Qixin Sun, WenLong Gao, Xiansheng Chen, Zhongyuan Wang, Si Liu, Pengwei Wang
bullets: Stores consecutive-observation transitions in latent form rather than retaining full visual history.
Combines a frozen latent action encoder, lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental, annotation-free inference.
LTM-π reaches 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem without external reasoning models or memory annotations.
Memory scales effectively: RoboMME success rises to 87.50% with tenfold more demonstrations and remains 84.00% under a 200-token budget.
Real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%; a Cup Swap diagnostic underscores the importance of process supervision for temporal composition.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces latent transition memory for vision-language-action robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied memory and VLA policies.
papers.title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LTM gives vision-language-action robots compact latent memories of past state transitions, substantially improving manipulation that depends on hidden history.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.
authors: Wenqiu Tang, Zhen Wan, Yihui Wang, Takahiro Komamizu, Ichiro Ide
bullets: Targets implicit emotional states that must persist across topic shifts from sparse conversational cues.
Uses causal localization on synthetic minimal pairs to find affective attention heads.
Boosts, at the answer position, tokens already attended to by those heads—without externally specified target spans.
Improves prompt-matched baselines by up to 10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and 5.5 on GoEmotions across three LLMs.
Combining SIAB with external supervision yields further gains, while analyses link effects to sparse emotion-enriched heads and layer proximity.
papers.selection_reason: Self-targeted inference-time attention boosting for LLM state reasoning; transferable to test-time internal-state adaptation.
papers.title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
papers.tldr: SIAB improves affective-state reasoning by using an LLM’s own attention patterns to identify and amplify emotion-relevant evidence during inference.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.
authors: Tanush Kalhan, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Sriram Ranga, Amritendu Mukherjee
bullets: Lower LP variance predicts correctness in SFT models, but the relationship weakens with scale and reverses in RL-distilled models.
Training paradigm influences density behavior more strongly than model size, while models show an intrinsic preference for complexity-favoring distributions.
Directly forcing density patterns during inference sharply reduces accuracy, suggesting natural density structure is important for reasoning.
Pre-generation hint injection plus contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points across both density metrics.
Entropy-Gated Density Routing improves accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without external guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time KV-cache steering and entropy-gated adjustments are test-time adaptation of internal states.
papers.title: The Density of Thought: Predicting and Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Information density in chain-of-thought predicts reasoning success in training-dependent ways and can improve accuracy when steered before or during generation with entropy-gated controls.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently been introduced as a promising paradigm for continual learning, where a student policy can be supervised at the token-level. Typically, OPD is performed using a single teacher per prompt rollout (or even per training run). However, this ignores a whole other axis of flexibility that is available due to the on-policy nature - token-level teacher selection during rollouts. Building on this insight, we theoretically explore what makes a teacher and a student compatible for OPD, and leverage our findings to derive several empirical heuristics for teacher selection. In particular, our framework captures several desiderata for OPD: compatible teacher-student reasoning patterns, teacher competence, and induced student diversity. Theoretically, we categorize several types of teacher routing schemes, and we prove that under different scenarios, different routing schemes are likely to be beneficial for optimization and student diversity. We back up our findings with extensive experimental results in domains such as math, coding, kernel generation, and visual reasoning, where we find upwards of 10 percentage points of improvement on pass@$k$ when compared to vanilla OPD and the teacher experts on certain tasks, indicating both capability improvement and diversity over high-quality responses.
authors: Stanley Wei, Jiin Woo, Kaan Ozkara, Youngsuk Park
bullets: Identifies teacher–student compatibility, teacher competence, and induced student diversity as key factors in OPD teacher selection.
Theoretically categorizes teacher-routing schemes and analyzes when different schemes benefit optimization and student diversity.
Derives empirical heuristics for selecting teachers during token-level rollouts.
Experiments across math, coding, kernel generation, and visual reasoning report up to 10 percentage points of pass@$k$ improvement over vanilla OPD and teacher experts on certain tasks.
Results suggest token-level routing can improve both capability and diversity, though benefits vary by scenario and task.
papers.selection_reason: On-policy distillation with token-level teacher selection for continual learning; directly fits continual and online learning.
papers.title: Compatibility Matters: A Framework for Token-Level Teacher Selection in On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: A theory-driven framework selects teachers at the token level in on-policy distillation to improve student–teacher compatibility, capability, and response diversity.

papers.abstract: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all three base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.
authors: Jie Li, Youming Tao, Bowei He, Meng Ding
bullets: Problem: Post-release fine-tuning can recover unlearned knowledge, but defenses must avoid broadly reducing model plasticity.
Method: Apply the same simulated relearning update to both the defended model and an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model.
Model selection uses new-task learning to distinguish selective resistance from general loss of plasticity.
Across TOFU and FaithUn experiments with Llama and Qwen models, UMU reduced harmful and benign relearning and improved new-task accuracy.
A pre-update reference kept relearning low but reduced new-task performance, supporting update-matched evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses selective unlearning and plasticity under continued fine-tuning, directly relevant to continual and online adaptation.
papers.title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Update-Matched Unlearning improves resistance to relearning deleted knowledge while preserving the model’s ability to learn new tasks.

papers.abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.
bullets: Addresses reasoning losses caused by placing LLMs inside software harnesses.
Uses an intelligent coding agent, the “Onboarder,” to iteratively modify the agent’s foundation model, prompt, and harness code.
Operates with only tens of examples and isolates evaluation data in a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage.
Evaluated on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission; results vary substantially across onboarding runs.
Finds that future systems need stronger Onboarder environments, including structured thought interfaces, controlled internet access, and broader model search.
papers.selection_reason: Autonomous agent onboarding adapts an LLM agent to a task during deployment, which is a meaningful adaptation method for deployed agents.
papers.title: AutoOnboarder: Autonomously Onboarding LLM Agents
papers.tldr: AutoOnboarder autonomously adapts an LLM agent’s model, prompt, and harness to improve task performance while reducing cost, matching or exceeding a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29× lower cost in one application.

papers.abstract: Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/
authors: Dohyun Lee, Minho Park, Jeonghoon Park, Dongyoon Hwang, Junha Hyung, Sungwon Hwang, Byungkun Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in proactive assistance, where identical behaviors may indicate different user needs.
Uses a VLM task predictor with Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) to select when and how to assist, and a VLA executor to perform tasks.
Represents routines as a finite-state machine with activity phases, assistance rules, and event-driven transitions.
A reflection VLM updates PAM from daily interaction traces without weight updates or retraining.
In a 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, the system improved with experience, achieved the best reported precision, recall, and F1, and reduced first-fire delay from about 5 seconds to 1 second.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic proactive robot framework with procedural assistance memory and VLA executor; relevant to embodied memory and VLA.
papers.title: An Agentic Framework for Proactive Robots with Procedural Assistance Memory
papers.tldr: A memory-based agentic framework helps robots proactively assist users by learning and updating personalized routine patterns without retraining.

papers.abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.
authors: Miao Su, Yucan Guo, Zixuan Li, Long Bai, Zhongni Hou, Xiaolong Jin, Jiafeng Guo
bullets: Targets the difficulty of locating failures in long-horizon agent executions using only coarse scores or summaries.
A Patch Agent jointly analyzes raw traces, runtime memory state, and architecture code to identify repair targets.
Applies bounded in-place edits while preserving provider identity and memory compatibility.
Improves performance on GAIA, xBench, and unseen ALFWorld tasks, with a median code-change ratio of 4.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Evolving agent memory architectures with execution feedback directly targets LLM/agent memory and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
papers.tldr: MemScope evolves LLM-agent memory systems through evidence-grounded, localized code repairs instead of broad rewrites.

papers.abstract: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.
authors: Sheldon Yu, Tong Yu, Nikki Lijing Kuang, Zhendong Chu, Zhenwei Tang, Sungchul Kim, Lina Yao, Julian McAuley, Junda Wu
bullets: GRPO learns nothing when all attempts for a problem fail because there is no successful exemplar or nonzero group-relative advantage.
RSHD has the policy write a corrective note, re-solve with that note, and admit it only when fresh replay succeeds more often than the original group.
Answer-stating notes are screened out; admitted replays are distilled into the ordinary plain-prompt policy.
The method uses only policy training and outcome verification, with no reference solutions, and requires no notes or extra inference at deployment.
It consistently improves over GRPO across model families, sizes, and two training domains, with gains also transferring out of domain.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method for recovering supervision from failed rollouts during training, which is a form of learning from experience and adaptation.
papers.title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight
papers.tldr: RSHD recovers useful training supervision from entirely failed GRPO rollouts by testing and distilling hindsight-generated corrective notes.

papers.abstract: Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot's geometry and kinematic constraints. On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location. Videos and code are available on the project website: https://mocap-7.github.io/MoCAP-page/.
authors: Yiyang Cai, Tatsuya Kamijo, Ninghao Lu, Zijin Hu, Sherry Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring knowledge from unstructured human videos to robots with different bodies and constraints.
Extracts spatial memory and human approach cues to guide object navigation and selection of manipulation-ready base poses.
Uses a closed-loop code-as-policy agent to coordinate planning and tool-use primitives under robot geometry and kinematic constraints.
On a real mobile manipulator, achieves 80% success on each of two indoor tasks where existing approaches fail.
Video-derived memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, while human approach priors improve reachable-base-pose discovery from 0% to 100% in an unfavorable start setting.
papers.selection_reason: Turns passive human videos into spatial memory and code-as-policy for mobile manipulation; directly relevant to embodied manipulation, human-video learning, robot navigation, and embodied memory.
papers.title: MoCaP: Mobile Code-as-Policies for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation from Passive Human Videos
papers.tldr: MoCaP converts passive human videos into spatial and behavioral guidance for zero-shot mobile manipulation by a robot.

papers.abstract: Safety in agentic systems is inherently sequential: whether an action is safe depends on prior actions, tool outputs, information disclosures, and interactions among agents. Recent work has shifted agent safety guardrails from post-hoc trajectory-level assessment toward step-level action diagnosis and proactive risk prediction, yet existing training objectives provide limited supervision for how step evidence accumulates over time and when it becomes sufficient to justify intervention. We propose \methodlong~(ASPO): a training framework for step-level timely intervention. Pre-fix level stage alignment allows crediting each decision at its own step: it compares each response with the other responses sampled at the same prefix and rewards the action that fits the stage, continuing before the risk is visible, asking while clarification can still avert harm, and stopping before harm is irreversible. Adaptive feedback self-distillation further credits the reasoning behind each decision, with the model itself as a teacher that sees the step annotations on intervention steps and rules mined from its own false alarms on safe steps. Its training data carry a violation taxonomy and an intervention window at every step and are extended through self-evolving multi-agent red-teaming. Finally we present \textsc{StepSafe}, a step-level reasoning guardrail with timely intervention, that achieves the state-of-the-art peformance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks on safety-utility pareto curve with Youden's $J$ of 53.0 (4B) against 46.2.
authors: Siyi Gu, Kunhan Gao, Chao Peter Yang, Sukanta Ganguly, Rex Ying, Arman Cohan
bullets: Targets limited supervision for how step-level safety evidence accumulates and when intervention becomes necessary.
Uses pre-fix level stage alignment to evaluate each action against alternatives from the same interaction prefix.
Applies adaptive feedback self-distillation to teach decision reasoning from intervention annotations and false-alarm rules.
Builds training data with violation taxonomies and per-step intervention windows, expanded through multi-agent red-teaming.
Reports state-of-the-art performance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks, with a Youden’s J score of 53.0 for the 4B model versus 46.2.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training framework for step-level safety intervention, which relates to test-time learning and adaptation for agent safety.
papers.title: StepSafe: Learning Timely Intervention with Context-Aware Safety Reasoning
papers.tldr: StepSafe trains agents to recognize accumulating risk and intervene at the right moment—continuing, clarifying, or stopping—rather than relying on post-hoc safety checks.

papers.abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
authors: Anutam Srinivasan, Siddhant Panse, Glen Chou
bullets: Addresses conservative robust adaptive control that ignores guaranteed future parameter learning and struggles with high-dimensional robots.
Uses system-level synthesis to forecast parameter uncertainty and preserve correlations among disturbances, parameter errors, and estimate updates.
Builds tighter guaranteed reachable sets that incorporate expected information gain during planning.
Demonstrates real-time scalability on nonlinear robots, including whole-body control for a 61-state quadruped.
Validates online dynamics learning and stabilization on a physical Crazyflie drone.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-aware robust adaptive MPC with online parameter learning for robots; fits embodied robot control and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
papers.tldr: A-SLS enables real-time, GPU-accelerated robust adaptive control that plans for future learning to make robot safety guarantees less conservative.

papers.abstract: Skill-policy co-evolution, in which an agent's policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training, is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents. Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank). After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address. In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental. The acceptance rule these methods share (cooperative acceptance) ties a policy's competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation; empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. We therefore introduce the CO-evolution Drift Audit (CODA), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5-13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52-93% of the delivered bank's gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution, from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve, and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited.
authors: Yujie Feng, Xiaobin Wang, Jinluan Yang, Xiaonan Shi, Pengjun Xie, Philip S. Yu, Xiaoming Wu, Jieping Ye
bullets: Existing evaluations test policies only on the skill bank used during co-evolution, overlooking post-deployment drift.
Theoretical and empirical analysis shows cooperative acceptance intrinsically couples policy competence to its co-evolved bank.
CODA simulates skill drift and measures worst-case success, consistency under meaning-preserving edits, and resistance to corrupted skills.
Across four methods and five benchmarks, drift reduced success by 5–13 points and erased 52–93% of gains over no-skill baselines.
The protocol shifts evaluation from peak performance on a fixed bank to robustness as skills evolve.
papers.selection_reason: Audits skill-policy co-evolution under skill drift, directly relevant to continual learning and self-improving agents.
papers.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents
papers.tldr: Skill-policy co-evolution can produce agents that perform well only with their original skill bank, so CODA evaluates robustness to realistic skill drift.

papers.abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-trial gait rankings and long-term gait effectiveness after irreversible leg damage.
Uses persistent outcome profiles and conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot.
Evaluated across 108 MuJoCo tasks involving leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock.
Improved final gait quality and reduced low-quality failures versus an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline; gains appeared across all damage classes.
Ablations most strongly supported conservative uncertainty handling, while aggregate SRQ improvement versus no adaptation was inconclusive.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-guided reset-free gait recovery after leg damage, combining robot learning with online adaptation.
papers.title: Persistent Profile-Guided Reset-Free Recovery Improves Final Gait Selection after Irreversible Leg Damage
papers.tldr: PGRR improves the selection of durable post-damage gaits during reset-free recovery by modeling how repeated execution changes the robot’s physical state.

papers.abstract: A self-improving agent has to decide which new skills to keep, and in practice it keeps whatever earns a high reward, convinces a judge model, or compresses its library, even when the skill is wrong. That is fine until the answers have to be exactly right: over a table of transactions, a total is either right or wrong. We ask a harder question: can an agent grow what it can compute with no reward, no judge, and no answer key, and still be exactly right? A single frozen model runs two nested loops over a small, exact domain-specific language (DSL). The inner loop answers new questions only when two independently written expressions agree on every record. The outer loop discovers its own missing capability and authors an operator for it, admitted only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law, all without ground truth. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, and the outer loop self-extends on disjoint starting sets, inventing operators outside the starting closure; a no-induction control answers none of the new questions. The admission rule is empirically sound: it rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants under an independent reference, even one written by a different model family, where the admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals the field relies on admit most of them. Unmodified, the same mechanism self-extends on two further domains with unrelated schemas, business-ledger and clinical-encounter question answering, growing their answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold. The loop transfers across model families too: run with further proposers, the gate stays sound and independent families self-extend comparably, with only the induction yield tracking each proposer's DSL fluency.
authors: Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Yirou Ge, Yixi Li, Yiming Bian, Zijie Pan, Jenna L. Ballard, Uma Kona, Linsey Pang, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Targets exact answers without rewards, judge models, or answer keys, where incorrect skills cannot be tolerated.
Uses nested loops: agreement between independent expressions answers questions, while agreement between independent operator implementations plus a conservation law admits new operators.
The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set; the outer loop discovers operators beyond the initial DSL closure and fails to expand without induction.
The admission rule rejects all 138 tested buggy operator variants under an independent reference, outperforming simpler admission signals in this evaluation.
The mechanism transfers to business-ledger and clinical-encounter domains, expanding answerable sets by more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Self-improving agent that grows its own DSL through oracle-free operator induction; relevant to continual skill acquisition.
papers.title: A Self-Improving Agent that Grows its Own DSL: Oracle-Free Operator Induction for Exact Question Answering
papers.tldr: An oracle-free agent safely expands its exact-question-answering abilities by admitting only independently verified DSL operators that satisfy conservation laws.

papers.abstract: We study continual linear regression in a high-dimensional regime, where a learner observes a sequence of tasks and updates its parameters sequentially. In this setting, we derive an explicit closed-form expression for the generalization loss of a model trained with gradient descent for a fixed number of steps per task, which holds for arbitrary teachers. We prove that the optimal fixed step size decays nearly inversely with the number of tasks, specifically as $\ln T / T$, for a single teacher and, more generally, i.i.d. teachers. Under this scaling, we show that the resulting generalization loss is asymptotically equivalent to that achieved by optimally tuned L2 (isotropic) regularization. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to generalized ridge regression with diagonal regularization matrices, obtaining a closed-form characterization of the generalization loss and identifying necessary and sufficient conditions under which the optimal regularizer is isotropic. Finally, we identify a regime where the optimal step size remains finite even as the number of tasks tends to infinity, thus revealing a non-trivial tradeoff between task variability and implicit regularization, in contrast to the i.i.d. teacher scaling. Our theoretical predictions are corroborated by experiments on both linear models and neural networks, providing practical guidance for the design of continual learning systems.
bullets: Provides a closed-form generalization-loss expression for fixed-step gradient descent across sequential tasks with arbitrary teachers.
For a single teacher or i.i.d. teachers, the optimal step size decreases nearly as ln(T)/T and matches optimally tuned isotropic L2 regularization asymptotically.
Characterizes generalization loss under diagonal generalized ridge regularization and gives conditions for when the optimal regularizer is isotropic.
Identifies a task-variability regime where the optimal step size remains finite as the number of tasks grows, unlike the i.i.d.-teacher case.
Experiments on linear models and neural networks support the theoretical predictions and offer guidance for continual-learning design.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of continual linear regression and regularization.
papers.title: Optimal Explicit and Implicit Regularization Strengths in High-Dimensional Continual Linear Regression
papers.tldr: The paper derives optimal implicit and explicit regularization strategies for high-dimensional continual linear regression, showing how step size should scale with task count and variability.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.
authors: Runxuan Liu, Jingqi Shi, Baoxin Wang, Honghong Zhao, Haoyuan Xu, Yueqing Sun, Jiafeng Liang, Tao He, Dayong Wu, Qi Gu, Shijin Wang, Ming Liu, Bing Qin
bullets: Addresses the limits of imitation learning and outcome-only reinforcement learning in organizing and exploiting intermediate experience.
Extracts procedural and problematic patterns from trajectories to generate skills through repeated world interactions.
Builds a stratified skill architecture with domain, plan, and action/trap skills for multi-granularity knowledge storage.
Uses structured abstractive memory and state-aware skill fusion to select and combine skills during long-horizon interactions.
Improves open-world task success rates and demonstrates generalization on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive skill system and structured memory for self-evolving agents in open worlds.
papers.title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
papers.tldr: EvolvingBrain enables multimodal agents to self-evolve in open worlds by continually learning structured skills from experience and adapting their use to the current state.

papers.abstract: The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility --- taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer --- and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference-time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a *rich representation*, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairs this.
bullets: Open-world settings involve unknown tasks, few examples, and grouped rather than iid data.
The analysis identifies three requirements: inference-time learning, representations richer than iid generalization needs, and aligned low-dimensional input–output groups.
A consistent inner learner and long contexts spanning related tasks are also predicted to help.
Experiments with language models up to 8B find that models meeting these requirements improve as related-task data accumulates, while others degrade.
Neither model scale nor interleaving different layer types fixes failures to meet the requirements.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses inference-time learning as a core requirement for open-world AI.
papers.title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
papers.tldr: Open-world AI requires inference-time learning, rich representations, and predictive disentanglement to improve across previously unseen related tasks.

papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
bullets: Targets the memory and attention costs of large KV caches during generation.
Initializes compact caches using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity.
Distills attention outputs and log-normalizers from the full cache, then jointly optimizes the cache while freezing model weights.
Uses only generic document prompts, without downstream questions or answers.
Achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32× compression on a RULER task versus 40.0% for KVZip+, with gains across RULER, LongBench, Phonebook Lookup, Qwen3, and MiniCPM5.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training compresses KV caches for long contexts; directly fits KV-cache efficiency and test-time learning.
papers.title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Latent Compaction uses document-specific test-time training to compress KV caches while preserving long-context retrieval accuracy.

papers.abstract: Existing robot policy memories typically evolve with observation sequences, implicitly treating each update as the same amount of physical time. Yet identical observation histories can span different durations and require different actions, exposing physical time as a missing dimension of policy memory. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which learns memory dynamics to retain past events and evolve the memory state over measured time intervals. Observations and prior memory determine the content and time scales of each transition; elapsed time determines how far the state advances. TFP conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies through this memory state and is trained with their native imitation objectives. We evaluate TFP with Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$ through controlled comparisons of memory designs. These experiments show that successful timing depends on both measured intervals and retained history. TFP achieves higher average success than the recurrent and state-space memories we equip with the same intervals and than a variant that feeds the interval to a learned gate. Memory readouts recover the time since an event and motion information after occlusion. Changing the supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions, linking time inputs to behavior. Real-robot tasks requiring timing or memory, together with LIBERO evaluations, demonstrate benefits in physical and general manipulation. These results suggest viewing robot memory not as stored observation history, but as a state that retains past events and evolves with physical time.
authors: Yushen Liang, Yue Peng, Baosheng Jin, Tianluo Zhang, Xinyu Zhang, Shuyi Zhou, Zhuoran Chen, Xinqi Liu, Shenji Wan
bullets: Problem: Standard robot memories treat each update as equal time, so identical observations over different durations can produce inappropriate actions.

Method: TFP learns memory dynamics where observations and prior memory determine transitions, while measured elapsed intervals control state evolution; it conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies.
Results: Controlled comparisons with Diffusion Policy and π₀.₅ show higher average success than matched recurrent, state-space, and interval-gated memories.
Evidence: Memory readouts recover event timing and motion after occlusion, while changing supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions.
Scope: Real-robot timing and memory tasks plus LIBERO evaluations indicate benefits for physical and general manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces physical time into robot policy memory, directly relevant to embodied memory and policy learning.
papers.title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics
papers.tldr: Temporal Flow Policy adds measured physical time to robot policy memory, enabling actions that depend on both what happened and how long ago it occurred.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.
authors: Peidong Wang, Ying Chang, Zhiming Ma, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng, Daqi Liu, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Daling Wang
bullets: Targets failures in pretrained vision-language-action models on unseen long-horizon tasks.
A coding agent first improves skills and the execution harness, then diagnoses persistent sub-step failures by retrying from saved states.
Fine-tunes only unreliable executor sub-steps using self-collected demonstrations and experience reused across tasks.
On 50 RoboCasa365 target tasks, success on unseen composite tasks increases from 4.6% to 13.8% without human demonstrations.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, uses 28% of GPU time and 22% of self-collected demonstrations while achieving slightly higher success.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive self-improvement for embodied VLA agents; fits VLA and adaptation/memory topics.
papers.title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: AdaRSI selectively improves an embodied agent’s skills, harness, or executor weights to recover from persistent failures, substantially improving long-horizon task success with less training cost.

papers.abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.
authors: Siddhant Setia, Junichi Suzuki, Tadashi Nakano
bullets: Addresses incremental performance estimation for bio-nanomachine communication protocols.
Uses a continual-learning model that replays stored simulation samples alongside interpolated and extrapolated synthetic samples.
Regularizes updates to balance adaptation to new settings with retention of earlier knowledge.
Outperforms existing continual-learning methods in overall estimation accuracy across sequential tasks.
Maintains memory stability and learning plasticity at moderate training cost.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a continual learning method with memory replay for sequential task adaptation.
papers.title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication
papers.tldr: Affine Memory Replay enables continual learning for reliable in-sequence molecular communication by adapting to increasingly complex settings while retaining prior knowledge.

papers.abstract: For the fundamental problem of prediction from expert advice, Freund asked whether one could compete with a comparator that switches $k$ times among only $m$ experts. For a discrete set of experts, this problem was resolved by Bousquet and Warmuth (2020), who gave an efficient algorithm with optimal regret matching the information-theoretic limit. We study the analogous problem in online convex optimization, where the action space is continuous. An inefficient algorithm can be derived by discretizing the action space and applying the Bousquet--Warmuth algorithm, giving regret of $\widetilde{O}(md+k)$, while the best known efficient algorithm for this problem has regret $\widetilde{O}(dk)$. We show that this computational inefficiency is inherent, establishing a separation between the information-theoretic and polynomial-time regret achievable for this problem. Specifically, under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, we show that for every polynomial-time algorithm there exist instances for which it incurs at least $(k\sqrt d)^{1-o(1)}$ regret.
authors: Angelos Assos, Anand Brahmbhatt, Elad Hazan
bullets: Studies prediction with expert advice when the action space is continuous and the comparator switches k times among m experts.
An inefficient discretization-based method achieves regret approximately Õ(md+k), matching the information-theoretic scale.
The best known efficient method has regret approximately Õ(dk), revealing a computational gap.
Under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, every polynomial-time algorithm suffers at least (k√d)^(1−o(1)) regret on some instances.
Establishes a separation between achievable regret with unlimited computation and with polynomial-time algorithms.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical online convex optimization with expert tracking, relevant to online/continual learning.
papers.title: Tracking a Small Set of Experts in Online Convex Optimization
papers.tldr: The paper proves that efficiently tracking a comparator switching among a small set of experts in online convex optimization inherently requires substantially more regret than the information-theoretic optimum, assuming the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture.

papers.abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.
authors: Jintian Zhang, Feng He, Xinnian Liang, Ziwen Xu, Haoming Xu, Haojing Huang, Shuangzhi Wu, Ningyu Zhang
bullets: Frames memory consolidation as retaining context-induced gains after the context is removed.
Uses prospective queries and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward updates.
Evaluates consolidation and retention across five task families with single, batch, and sequential updates.
Tested on 4B–120B dense and mixture-of-experts text-only and multimodal models.
After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovered 88.9% of the context-induced gain and retained 99.8% of original non-target performance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory consolidation for LLMs via parametric updates, directly relevant to LLM memory and continual/online learning.
papers.title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
papers.tldr: Cortex consolidates temporary context-driven improvements into compact model updates while preserving non-target capabilities.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints. We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and in a self-supervised manner during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate. Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift. TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic's predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value ("hard") observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions. Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.
authors: Motasem Alfarra, Pietro Mazzaglia, Markus Peschl, Daniel Dijkman, Christos Louizos
bullets: Addresses failures from terrain, payload, and sensing shifts when retraining or manual recalibration is impractical.
Adapts only the actor online using a frozen critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate.
TEMPO regularizes the critic’s predictive distribution to reduce overconfident extrapolation.
A score-based memory prioritizes hard, low-value observations and uses importance sampling under limited compute.
Improves performance across simulated robots and shifts, with gains up to 80%, and transfers to a physical Go2 with added payload.
papers.selection_reason: On-device test-time adaptation of robot policies; core match for test-time learning and embodied robot learning.
papers.title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation For Robot Policies
papers.tldr: TEMPO enables efficient, reward-free online adaptation of robot locomotion policies under deployment shifts using entropy-regularized critic guidance and memory-based sampling.

papers.abstract: An agent can improve its behavior within an unresolved problem by changing how it acts and which experience it retains. We propose MMLA-RSI, a recursive self-improvement scheme with two implementations in Memory-Mediated Learning Architecture: Reasoning-Time Training (RTT) changes the policy state $\Phi$, while Reasoning-Time Memory Adaptation (RTMA) changes authoritative memory $M$. Each route also makes its adaptation method an object of improvement. A current numerical updater trains the policy proposing its successor; a current memory manager chooses the records available to the process proposing its successor. An independently admitted successor takes over the same role in the next generation. We give bounded executable rule languages, shared task/proposal interfaces, and one algorithm for either route or their composition. The RTT instance changes scalar schedules in a clipped-momentum update. The RTMA instance chooses NULL or a complete-row write with possible eviction. A fixed interpreter, trusted committer, and independent evaluator bound what can change. State versions, read closures, and conditional properties describe causal execution, accepted transitions, and finite work. Existing numerical-component studies motivate the construction. In four-candidate program selection, retaining LARC feedback updates reduces expected error by 24.65 and 36.65 percentage points for two trained initializations. In chronological continuous-integration replay, feedback binding is positive while retention increases loss. Completed SQL studies improve substantially over an unadapted substrate but do not establish the required additional online benefit. These results characterize their declared components. The two recursive routes and their joint realization are specified here; their beneficial recursive chains and discovery efficiency remain to be evaluated.
bullets: RTT adapts the policy state, while RTMA adapts authoritative memory and its retention decisions.
Each route recursively improves the mechanism that proposes the next policy or memory-manager successor.
A shared framework uses bounded rule languages, fixed interpreters, trusted commits, independent evaluation, versioned state, and causal execution controls.
Component studies show mixed outcomes: feedback retention helps in program selection, while retention increases loss in continuous-integration replay; SQL studies improve over an unadapted substrate.
The paper does not yet establish the benefit or discovery efficiency of complete recursive chains or their combined realization.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive self-improvement via reasoning-time training and memory adaptation; fits test-time learning.
papers.title: MMLA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through RTT and RTMA
papers.tldr: MMLA-RSI defines two recursive self-improvement routes that adapt an agent’s policy updates or memory management, with preliminary component-level results but no demonstrated beneficial recursive chains yet.

papers.abstract: Nanosatellites (e.g., CubeSats) have the potential to carry out useful science and exploration activities for outer solar system exploration, but their small size leads to tradeoffs between attitude control and science capabilities. Magnetorquers offer a unique compromise as compact actuators that enable three-axis attitude control, but suffer from a loss of control authority and require full knowledge of the planetary magnetic field. In this work, we present a learning-based adaptive model predictive control (MPC) algorithm that plans rotational trajectories for the satellite while accounting for this loss of control authority. Key to our approach is the inclusion of a learned magnetic field model that is trained in simulation using low-fidelity magnetic field data. Using measurements collected online, our proposed algorithm adapts this learned magnetic field model using a simple last-layer update scheme, allowing the MPC controller to quickly adapt to the true planetary magnetic field model and more effectively plan attitude trajectories. We demonstrate the results of our proposed approach for two use cases, (1) Earth-orbit and (2) Uranus-orbit, and show that our learning-based adaptive MPC algorithm improves controller success for these system simulations by 5% and 61%, respectively.
bullets: Magnetorquers enable compact three-axis control but have limited authority and depend on accurate planetary magnetic-field knowledge.
The method combines trajectory-planning MPC with a learned magnetic-field model trained from low-fidelity simulation data.
Online measurements update only the model’s last layer, enabling rapid adaptation to the true magnetic field.
Simulations show controller-success improvements of 5% in Earth orbit and 61% in Uranus orbit.
Evaluation is limited to Earth- and Uranus-orbit system simulations.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based adaptive MPC with online last-layer adaptation of a learned field model; fits test-time/online learning.
papers.title: Learning-Based Adaptive MPC for Magnetorquer-Only Satellite Attitude Control
papers.tldr: A learning-based adaptive MPC improves magnetorquer-only satellite attitude-control success by adapting a simulated magnetic-field model online, especially under Uranus-orbit conditions.

papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads---information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components. We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.
authors: Junlin Chen, Wenhao Wang, Junchao Xu, Qingsong Yao, Fei Xue, Li Sun, Xiao Wang, Ruijie Wang
bullets: Addresses class-incremental GNNs that forget earlier classes and overpredict recently learned ones.
Trains a separate SGC-based expert per session, then freezes it to preserve prior knowledge.
Routes test nodes without task IDs using each expert’s masked-autoencoder reconstruction error.
Bounds capacity by aligning and merging the least-used experts, then distilling them with topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions.
Experiments on four benchmarks show reduced recency bias, stronger performance than continual graph-learning baselines, and bounded capacity without replaying historical graphs.
papers.selection_reason: Class-incremental graph learning with replay-free dynamic MoE; directly addresses continual/online learning.
papers.title: MAEM: Mitigating Recency Bias via a Replay-Free, Capacity-Controlled Dynamic Mixture of Experts for Class-Incremental Graph Learning
papers.tldr: MAEM reduces recency bias and catastrophic forgetting in replay-free class-incremental graph learning using frozen experts, MAE-based routing, and capacity-controlled expert merging.

papers.abstract: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. Unlike language models, where the two stages are naturally aligned, such alignment is less evident in vision based applications. Motivated by this gap, we explore continual pretraining. Specifically, continually pretraining a pretrained ViT encoder using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a prostate segmentation task to enhance task alignment and downstream performance. We further perform layer-wise representational analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to assess representational shifts and their correlation with task outcomes. Our experiments show improved performance in 3 of 6 downstream tasks and comparable results in the others. Our Feature analysis reveals that, for segmentation tasks, continually pretrained encoder features exhibit greater similarity to those of the finetuned encoder than the original pretrained encoder, correlating with observed performance gains.
authors: Bilal A. Sidiqi, Yipei Wang, Shaheer U. Saeed, Shiqi Huang, Daniel C. Alexander, Yipeng Hu
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding of alignment between MRI pretraining and downstream objectives.
Continually pretrains a pretrained ViT encoder on prostate segmentation using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).
Uses layer-wise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to analyze representational shifts and their relationship to task outcomes.
Improves performance on 3 of 6 downstream tasks and achieves comparable results on the remainder.
Continually pretrained features more closely resemble finetuned features for segmentation, aligning with observed gains.
papers.selection_reason: Continual pretraining of a ViT encoder with LoRA for task alignment directly fits continual learning and adaptation.
papers.title: Continual pretraining Prostate MRI ViT Encoder for task alignment
papers.tldr: Continual pretraining a prostate MRI ViT encoder with LoRA improves task alignment, benefiting some downstream tasks while preserving comparable performance on others.

papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables large language models (LLMs) to learn collaboratively from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can compromise global model safety. As federated tasks evolve, changing malicious update patterns challenge the ability of existing defenses to maintain reliable risk detection over time. To address this challenge, we propose Safe-FCL, a framework integrating continual risk awareness with fine-grained safety aggregation for federated continual learning of LLMs. Specifically, the Continual Risk Awareness (CRA) mechanism learns emerging risk patterns across sequential tasks and constrains detector updates using a protective subspace derived from historical features, mitigating forgetting of previously learned malicious patterns while adapting to new risks. To translate risk awareness into aggregation-level safety control, the Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation (FGSA) mechanism combines client-level risk assessments from CRA with module-level deviations from historical update behavior to adaptively regulate aggregation contributions, suppressing potentially malicious updates while minimizing unnecessary restrictions on benign updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Safe-FCL outperforms current SOTA methods, improving global-model Rule and MD-Judge scores in federated continual learning by 0.41% and 0.64%, respectively, while increasing average risk recognition accuracy by 2.01%.
authors: Shuaijie Ma, Yongkang Hu, Yu Cheng, Jiuan Zhou, Yi Xie, Yushuo Zhang, Zhaoxia Yin
bullets: Addresses changing malicious-update patterns that can undermine global LLM safety over sequential federated tasks.
Continual Risk Awareness preserves historical risk knowledge while adapting to emerging threats.
Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation combines client-level risk and module-level update deviations to regulate contributions.
Experiments report gains of 0.41% in Rule, 0.64% in MD-Judge, and 2.01% in average risk-recognition accuracy.],
problem that?
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning of LLMs under evolving federated tasks, fitting the continual/online learning subtopic.
papers.title: Safe-FCL: Continual Risk Awareness and Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation for Federated Continual Learning of LLMs
papers.tldr: Safe-FCL improves safety in federated continual learning of LLMs by continually detecting evolving malicious updates and selectively limiting their aggregation impact.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly improve by distilling experience into reusable skills, but errors in that experience can persist in learned rules and affect later tasks. Existing evaluations largely examine clean learning or perturbations encountered after skills are frozen, leaving robustness during self-evolution insufficiently understood. We introduce RSE-Bench, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluating skill self-evolution under ordinary, non-adversarial noise. It spans four domains and six benchmarks, with controlled perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome--record pairings that preserve the underlying tasks and native scoring rules. The protocol separates noise during learning from input-side noise at evaluation, testing frozen skill stores on held-out tasks. We also introduce \textsc{RSEClaw}, a method-agnostic framework supporting consistent noise injection and process diagnostics of actual exposure and skill updates. Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning retains only $25.5\%$--$42.1\%$ of the aggregate gain achieved by clean self-evolution, depending on the noise type. Perturbations confined to execution records and outcome--record pairings cause average losses comparable to input-side noise, despite leaving the original executions and evaluations intact. Diagnostics further identify differences in candidate skill text that coexist with small changes in mean held-out performance.
authors: Tao Yu, Zhongtian Luo, Yuchen Long, Yiheng Lu, Yuxuan Zhou, Yanpei Gong, Siyi Cao, Yuqing Wu, Haopeng Jin, Zhenghao Zhang, Yujia Yang, Jingmin Zhu, Yunyun Hou, Xinming Wang, Hongzhu Yi, Jiachen Liu, Sirui Wang, Nan Duan, Yan Huang, Liang Wang, Tianjin Huang, Yanyan Zou
bullets: Introduces RSE-Bench, a benchmark spanning four domains and six benchmarks for evaluating robustness to non-adversarial noise during skill learning.
Tests perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome–record pairings while preserving underlying tasks and native scoring.
Separates noise during learning from input-side evaluation noise using frozen skill stores on held-out tasks.
Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning preserves only 25.5%–42.1% of the aggregate gain from clean self-evolution, depending on noise type.
RSEClaw provides method-agnostic noise injection and diagnostics, revealing that execution- and outcome-record noise can hurt comparably to input noise.
papers.selection_reason: Studies skill self-evolution in agents under noise, relating to continual learning from experience and adaptation during deployment.
papers.title: When Non-Adversarial Noise Hurts Learning: Benchmarking Skill Self-Evolution in Agents
