papers.tldr: RSE-Bench shows that ordinary noise during agents’ skill self-evolution can sharply reduce later learning gains, even when tasks and evaluations remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models suffer significant accuracy drops under common corruptions. While test-time adaptation (TTA) successfully mitigates these shifts in CLIP-like contrastive models, its application to generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains underexplored and uniquely challenging due to their sequential token generation. In this work, we demonstrate that representation-based TTA fails to recover performance in MLLMs. Our experiments reveal that even when violating standard TTA assumptions by leveraging target data offline, sample-blind feature alignment recovers only marginal accuracy. We attribute this failure to the nature of corruption shifts: unlike CLIP-like architectures, which benefit from a shared domain-shift direction within a single pooled classification embedding, MLLM visual token sequence shifts are nearly orthogonal and span the full embedding space.These findings bound what any sample-blind, position-shared correction at a single encoder site can achieve, establishing that representation-space interventions alone might be insufficient to ensure corruption robustness in MLLMs.
authors: Miko{\l}aj Pi\'orczy\'nski, Wojciech Masarczyk, Damian S\'ojka, Sebastian Cygert, Bart{\l}omiej Twardowski
bullets: MLLMs experience substantial accuracy drops under common corruptions, and standard TTA strategies do not transfer reliably from CLIP-like models.
Even with offline access to target data, sample-blind feature alignment provides only marginal recovery.
MLLM corruption shifts are nearly orthogonal across visual tokens and span the embedding space, unlike the shared shift direction in pooled CLIP representations.
These results limit the effectiveness of position-shared, single-layer representation corrections for MLLM robustness.
The findings suggest that representation-space interventions alone may be insufficient for corruption robustness in generative MLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time adaptation limits for multimodal LLMs, directly relevant to test-time learning and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: On the Limits of Representation-Based Test-Time Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Representation-based test-time adaptation is fundamentally limited for improving corruption robustness in multimodal LLMs because their visual-token shifts are diverse rather than aligned.

papers.abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.
authors: Fiorenzo Parascandolo, Enver Sangineto, Xiaoyi Yu, Wenhui Tan, Jipei He, Ruihua Song, Rita Cucchiara
bullets: Targets the tendency for longer chain-of-thoughts to be less likely correct.
Models this length-dependent correctness prior with a simple logistic function.
Adapts the prior using unlabeled test data, without fine-tuning the LLM.
Uses the adapted prior to weight votes from independently sampled answers.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over standard MV and other aggregation methods.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptation of majority voting using a length-conditioned prior for LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
papers.tldr: LCMV improves majority voting for LLM reasoning by weighting answers according to a test-time learned prior based on chain-of-thought length.

papers.abstract: Continual learning aims to acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned knowledge. However, updating shared parameters when learning new tasks often overwrites existing knowledge, causing catastrophic forgetting. Memory replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting but rely on previous samples, raising privacy, memory, and scalability concerns. On the other hand, parameter isolation-based methods preserve learned knowledge but may limit knowledge transfer, whereas regularization promotes adaptability but remains susceptible to interference between old and new tasks. To maintain the stability-plasticity trade-off, this paper proposes Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection (SPARS), a replay-free hybrid framework combining global parameter isolation with localized parameter regularization. SPARS estimates parameter importance using either the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) or a novel Confidence Score (CS) estimator that leverages logit sensitivity and achieves comparable performance to FIM without requiring labelled data. Based on parameter importance, SPARS partitions parameters into three importance-aware regions namely, winning, neighboring, and non-important parameter regions. Each region receives a different adaptation strategy: selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning based on its role in the stability-plasticity trade-off. To mitigate classifier bias in class-incremental learning, we employ Quadratic Discriminant Analysis to improve performance on previously learned classes .Experiments on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet demonstrate consistent improvement in average incremental accuracy over existing isolation- and regularization-based methods across task- and class-incremental learning. On TinyImageNet, SPARS achieves the best performance with 6% improvement for class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.
authors: Teif Aldaajani, Huda Hakami, Maha A. Thafar
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting without storing previous samples, avoiding replay-related privacy, memory, and scalability concerns.
Combines global parameter isolation with localized regularization to balance stability and plasticity.
Uses FIM or a label-free Confidence Score estimator to divide parameters into winning, neighboring, and non-important regions.
Applies selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning according to each region’s importance.
Improves average incremental accuracy on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet; on TinyImageNet, it reports a 6% gain in class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a continual learning framework balancing stability and plasticity, directly matching continual and online learning.
papers.title: SPARS: A Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection Framework for Continual Learning
papers.tldr: SPARS is a replay-free continual-learning framework that preserves important knowledge while retaining substantial parameter capacity for future tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.
authors: Seojin Hwang, Youngmin Choi, Hwanhee Lee
bullets: Studies how collaboration, conformity, and competition shape self-evolving multi-agent systems.
Introduces AGORA, which independently varies team composition and interdependence across three evolution mechanisms.
Evaluates the framework on web search, codebase understanding, and document QA.
Finds that evolution alone rarely helps, while suitable scaffolding improves performance by up to 25 points over a strong agent evolved alone.
The strongest member can outperform the same model working alone after developing within the team.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving LLM multi-agent systems; social scaffolding and evolution mechanisms relevant to online adaptation.
papers.title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: Social scaffolding—team composition and interdependence—determines whether self-evolving multi-agent systems improve, often by enabling the strongest member to emerge and lead.

papers.abstract: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.
authors: Ziyang Ling, Shuyu Lu, Ziyi Chen
bullets: Targets prescribing errors caused by fragmented coordination across medical specialties.
Uses a blackboard architecture to structure clinical notes and iteratively refine interpretable drug regimens.
Introduces DSWA for long-term agent trust adjustment based on historical outcomes.
Introduces DFPC for short-term feedback that resolves agent disagreements and prescription conflicts.
On MIMIC-IV records, it reduces drug conflicts and improves prescription coverage and treatment consistency versus LLM baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive multi-agent coordination with online weight adjustment; transferable to continual/online adaptation in agent systems.
papers.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
papers.tldr: PRISMATIC uses adaptive multi-agent collaboration to detect and resolve medication conflicts in complex multimorbid treatment planning.

papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation from fixed-window and non-revisable streaming inference on long video sequences.
Associates spatial context with observations so past geometry can be stored, retrieved, checked against new evidence, and revised.
Evaluated with eight geometry models across five tasks, including pose, depth, point-cloud reconstruction, SLAM, and novel view synthesis.
Consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, with reported reductions of up to 58% in depth error and 43% in Chamfer distance.
Achieves trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM and improves large-scale scene consistency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a revisable external memory (SMORE) for long-horizon 3D geometry, fitting World Models (long-horizon prediction) and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
papers.tldr: SMORE adds revisable external memory to frozen 3D geometry models, enabling long-horizon predictions to retrieve, verify, and correct past estimates for more consistent reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.
bullets: Object-goal navigation requires exploration, object detection, target validation, and reliable mission completion in unfamiliar environments.
A fixed modular study found trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model cost, motivating adaptive coordination.
A rule-based Supervisor dynamically manages navigation, exploration, detection, validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory.
Event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional guidance support adaptive behavior while keeping normal execution lightweight.
Across AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, SR/SPL were 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37; adaptive interventions were more frequent in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive agentic architecture for object-goal navigation with mission memory and recovery.
papers.title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: F2A-ObjectNav adaptively coordinates specialized navigation components to improve object-goal navigation across varied environments.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: A pretrained VLA succeeds on 80% of atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when skills are composed for mobile manipulation.
Failures primarily arise in task planning, navigation/base positioning, and local manipulation.
The proposed system adds demonstration-based planning, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment to a fixed subtask VLA.
Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-guided agentic interventions for long-horizon mobile manipulation with adaptive visual memory.
papers.title: Cracking Mobile Manipulation: From Failure Diagnosis to Agentic Robot System
papers.tldr: Diagnosing bottlenecks across planning, navigation, and manipulation enables targeted agentic interventions that substantially improve long-horizon mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of continual adaptation in conventional pretrained VLA policies.
Adds a reinforcement-learning module that uses past observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.
Refines action generation during deployment without updating the underlying model parameters.
Designed to support diverse history-construction strategies and VLA training pipelines.
Experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate adaptation to unseen scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Deployment-time adaptation of VLA models via in-context RL; directly relevant to VLA and test-time/continual learning.
papers.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: VLRLA enables fixed vision-language-action models to adapt during deployment by learning from accumulated interaction history through in-context reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
authors: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Jointly encodes task, execution stage, and future action continuations in both current-state queries and recorded experiences.
Uses predictive retrieval training and a corpus of 1,695,684 training anchors; introduces a 4,000-query benchmark with an 8,000-entry gallery.
Achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, outperforming the action-free Gemini Embedding 2 baseline in the reported comparisons.
Retrieved experience improves policy success in DROID-Sim and LIBERO, and execution-feedback memory evolution improves performance across five ManiSkill tasks.
Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.
papers.selection_reason: Unified VLA retrieval embeddings for robot in-context learning and task-local memory evolution.
papers.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
papers.tldr: Robota-Embed learns a unified vision-language-action retrieval space that helps robots retrieve useful past experience for in-context learning and task-specific evolution.

papers.abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.
authors: Li Wang, Chen Zhang, Yirong Yang, Xingyu Chen, Jinkun Zhao, Tianhao Peng, Wenjun Wu
bullets: Separates persistent preferences from request-specific corrections to reduce negative transfer.
Decomposes feedback into atomic, independently actionable rules and predicts each rule’s transferability.
Uses rubric-guided rewards and fine-grained credit assignment to evaluate rule content and retention decisions separately.
Jointly optimizes skill induction and skill-conditioned generation with reinforcement learning.
Across five personalized writing tasks and three base models, reports the best overall average performance in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.
papers.selection_reason: Selective retention of reusable skills from user feedback is a continual/online learning problem for LLMs.
papers.title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
papers.tldr: SkillGrain selectively retains feedback rules that are likely to transfer across future requests, improving reusable personalized skill learning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management). Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy. Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.
authors: Minghao Guo, Qingyue Jiao, Xiujin Liu, Jianhong Pang, Ruimeng Yang, Naihao Xu, Liwei Che, Haochen Xue, Ziqi Wang, Xinying Cai, Jiaxuan Luo, Jiaxin Deng, Xuesong Ye, Jintao Qu, Wenyao Gao, Jingwen Gu, Chenyang Zhao, Shichun Liu, Guibin Zhang, Zefang Liu, Siyin Wang, Wujiang Xu, Danrui Li, Zeru Shi, Woongyeong Yeo, Shuang Liu, Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang, Tianyu Yang, Kangsan Kim, Yebowen Hu, Bowen Wen, Bowen Jiang, Haohao Su, Ming Yin, Sheldon Yu, Mian Zhang, Yuyan Chen, Hanrong Zhang, Kai Mei, Zihao Zhang, Mingyu Jin, Xi Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Tianxin Wei, Linyong Nan, Zhenwen Liang, Zhendong Chu, Ziqi Huang, Yongye Su, Sixun Dong, Shujian Liu, Kaiqu Liang, Jiaojiao Han, Zhaoye Fei, Kun Wang, Shihan Dou, Zhichun Guo, Xingjian Diao, Zeqi Gu, Heng Wang, Tao Feng, Cheng Qian, Hamid Palangi, Silei Xu, Xi Yun, Yi Zhu, Shilong Liu, Qingsong Wen, Sung Ju Hwang, Zuxuan Wu, Yu-Gang Jiang, Yiyu Shi, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Jiaxuan You, Julian McAuley, Mengdi Wang, Jiawei Han, Philip S. Yu, Ziyi Ye
bullets: Motivated by the difficulty of continually retaining useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data.
Axis I classifies memory by how information is formed and represented, including embeddings, textual or structured records, and latent or parametric forms.
Axis II categorizes memory management into static, dynamically updated, and self-evolving policies.
The framework synthesizes design patterns and principles for abstraction, temporal validity, provenance, evidence grounding, and policy evolution.
It outlines open challenges and future directions for multimodal agent memory.
papers.selection_reason: Framework for multimodal agent memory, relevant to memory mechanisms for embodied agents and long-horizon adaptation.
papers.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
papers.tldr: This paper presents a two-axis framework for understanding how multimodal agents form, represent, manage, and evolve memory for long-horizon, lifelong interaction.

papers.abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.
authors: Eren Cetin, Julius Erbach, Vukasin Bozic, Hyojun Go, Zixiang Zhao, Nikolai Kalischek, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between bounded memory and recalling observations when the camera revisits a location.
Uses a constant-size slot recurrence with writes keyed by the observing camera and reads queried by the rendering camera.
Avoids explicit 3D reconstruction and growing caches by conditioning recall on inter-view geometry.
Provides confidence estimates to a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, which balances retrieved content with its generative prior.
On Memory Maze and Minecraft trajectories, maintains high-fidelity recall beyond the training horizon with constant memory and per-step cost.
papers.selection_reason: Bounded spatially addressed memory for long-horizon video generation, relevant to video world models and embodied memory.
papers.title: Long-horizon Video Generation with Slot Memory Addressed By Region Tokens
papers.tldr: SMART enables long-horizon video generation with constant memory by retrieving past visual content based on spatial camera regions rather than recency.

papers.abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.
bullets: AIF and Bayes-UCBVI are compared under the same tabular-MDP state abstraction, differing only in exploration bonuses.
Uncalibrated AIF information gain decays too quickly, causing greedy agents to miss optimal actions.
Square-root calibration gives AIF order-$\sqrt{T}$ regret under an exact abstraction.
For fixed rewards, calibrated AIF offers no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI.
For rewards chosen from the agent’s data, calibrated AIF remains effective with a $\sqrt{S}$ factor, while Bayes-UCBVI can be locked out.
papers.selection_reason: Compares Active Inference with standard RL exploration methods, providing theoretical analysis of information-driven exploration and regret bounds, relevant to online learning and adaptation.
papers.title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
papers.tldr: Calibrated information gain makes Active Inference exploration theoretically viable, but its advantage depends on whether rewards are fixed or adaptively chosen.

papers.abstract: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.
bullets: Evaluates nine CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence–structure-based frozen protein encoders.
Uses two enzyme-function datasets at different scales with consistent evaluation settings and varied phase constructions.
Finds no method transfers reliably across encoders, with instability linked to weak gradient stability signals and heterogeneous embedding geometry.
Shows that suitable covariance assumptions and model capacity depend on both dataset scale and encoder.
Concludes that protein CIL must treat the representation as a central design component, not merely a fixed feature extractor.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark of class-incremental learning methods on frozen protein encoders.
papers.title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
papers.tldr: A benchmark shows that vision-based class-incremental learning methods do not reliably transfer to frozen protein encoders, motivating encoder-aware CIL designs.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.
bullets: Addresses failures whose causes occur several steps before the observed error, beyond local reflection or backtracking.
Maintains relational beliefs over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints; execution and diagnostic evidence guide priorities and actions.
Uses an implicit world model to evaluate repair hypotheses, predict progress, and identify relationships among exploration frontiers.
Across three terminal-based benchmarks, it raises aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive exploration-efficiency trends.
A distilled 9B student gains 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline and reduces matched teacher API cost by 54.8%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an implicit world model and persistent belief updates for failure recovery in long-horizon agents, directly relevant to world modeling and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: BELIEFWEAVER improves long-horizon agent failure recovery by combining persistent belief updates with prospective world-model reasoning, achieving higher scores while reducing teacher-inference costs.

papers.abstract: Deep graph learning models deployed in real-world systems often need to cope with non-stationary environments, where the underlying graph distribution drifts continually over time. Prevailing solutions rely on training auxiliary generative modules to synthesize memory graphs for cross-domain adaptation, which incurs substantial computational overhead and scales poorly under prolonged distribution shifts. We argue that a more economical path exists: rather than generating memory, one can crystallize it. To this end, we propose Efficient Memory Crystallization (EMC), a training-free test-time framework that distills each incoming graph domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory through a closed-form solution to a memory-oriented distribution-matching objective, thereby eliminating redundant domain information under continual covariate shifts. To preserve both generalizability and adaptability as the model traverses a long sequence of target domains, EMC further models inter-domain dependencies through state-evolving memories and admits a theoretically grounded, tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of EMC over state-of-the-art baselines on graphs under non-stationary distribution shifts, while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory consumption by 92.4% relative to the recent competitor, making continual graph adaptation practical at scale.
bullets: Addresses the computational and scalability costs of synthesizing memory graphs during prolonged graph distribution shifts.
Uses a training-free, test-time framework with a closed-form distribution-matching objective to distill each incoming domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory.
Models inter-domain dependencies with state-evolving memories to balance generalizability and adaptability across target domains.
Provides a theoretically tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation.
Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory use by 92.4% relative to a recent competitor.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a test-time framework for memory crystallization in graph learning, relevant to test-time adaptation and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Efficient Memory Crystallization for Graph Learning under Non-Stationary Distribution Shifts
papers.tldr: EMC enables efficient continual graph adaptation under non-stationary distribution shifts by crystallizing compact domain memories without training generative modules.

papers.abstract: Evolutionary approaches to LLM-driven discovery often generate new programs from a small set of selected ancestors. This keeps contexts manageable but can omit useful evidence from other experiments, whereas including the full experimental history produces long, redundant contexts. We introduce a simple, single-agent discovery harness built around LabBook, an agent-maintained memory that serves two complementary roles: guiding retrieval of relevant evidence from a complete experimental log and informing the generation of new solutions. At each iteration, the same agent combines its memory with retrieved evidence and jointly produces the next program and an updated LabBook. This separates complete history retention from selective context construction, without requiring an explicit population or branching search structure. On 49 Frontier-CS problems, LabBook improves the observed quality-cost trade-off over the evaluated evolutionary baselines with two backbones, while remaining competitive across nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/BoYuanVisionary/LabBook.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between losing useful past evidence and using overly long experimental contexts.
Maintains an agent-updated LabBook alongside a complete experimental log.
Retrieves relevant evidence and jointly generates the next program and updated memory with a single agent.
Improves the observed quality–cost trade-off over evaluated evolutionary baselines on 49 Frontier-CS problems.
Remains competitive on nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agent-maintained memory system (LabBook) for LLM-driven discovery, relevant to LLM memory and online learning.
papers.title: LabBook: Harnessing Experimental History for Efficient LLM-Driven Discovery
papers.tldr: LabBook helps LLM agents use complete experimental histories without overwhelming context, improving discovery efficiency across diverse tasks.

papers.abstract: Constantly evolving real-world knowledge necessitates models to be updated continuously. Especially in medicine, as clinical evidence changes over time, outdated knowledge can pose safety risks. Existing evaluations of knowledge integration focus on factual recall, offering limited insight into whether newly integrated knowledge is actually usable. Our benchmark MedKIT (Medical Knowledge Integration and Transfer) provides a granular evaluation of how models integrate and apply knowledge under realistic sequences of clinical updates. Each instance corresponds to a factual update derived from clinical evidence, paired with targeted probes that assess transfer across lexical variation, relational transformations, compositional reasoning, and open-ended operationalization, as well as locality tests for knowledge preservation. Using MedKIT, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 knowledge integration strategies across 5 diverse models, including both general-purpose and medical LLMs. Our results reveal a consistent gap between recall and usable knowledge: while most methods achieve strong gains on the original update task and under lexical variation, relational generalization is limited, and no method yields meaningful improvements on compositional or operational tasks. These findings highlight a fundamental challenge in knowledge integration and position MedKIT as a testbed for developing methods that make newly integrated knowledge more consistently usable across tasks and contexts.
bullets: Evaluates knowledge integration under evolving clinical updates rather than factual recall alone.
Tests transfer across lexical variation, relational transformations, compositional reasoning, open-ended operationalization, and knowledge preservation.
Studies 12 integration strategies across 5 general-purpose and medical LLMs.
Most methods improve original-task recall and lexical transfer, but relational generalization remains limited.
No method achieves meaningful gains on compositional or operational tasks, revealing a persistent usability gap.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for knowledge integration and generalization in LLMs under sequential updates, relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: MedKIT: Evaluating Knowledge Integration and Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MedKIT shows that LLMs can recall newly integrated medical facts without reliably applying them across relational, compositional, or operational tasks.

papers.abstract: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce \textbf{LoopWAM}, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other deployed policies. Source-dependent noise sampling unifies behavior learning and action-conditioned world modeling, while quality steering and quality-weighted supervision retain full video supervision across qualities and regulate action imitation. Video and action tokens interact throughout parallel denoising, allowing learned consequences to inform action generation directly. On RoboChallenge Table30-V2, three deployment-and-training rounds raise success from 23.67\% to 43.33\%, a 19.7-percentage-point gain, with a final score of 56.80. LoopWAM also achieves 94.5\% average success on RoboTwin~2.0 and 49.5\% overall success on RoboCasa365 without additional embodied pretraining, obtaining the best overall results among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. On challenging shirt folding task, two rounds of deployment-driven improvement after single-task post-training raise success from 13.20\% to 55.56\%. These results demonstrate closed-loop improvement from mixed-quality experience under both multi-task learning and single-task post-training. \href{https://loop-wam.github.io/}{\textcolor{orange}{Project Page}}
authors: Wenxuan Guo, Yingping Liang, Zhaoguo Wang, Ziyuan Li, Angyuan Ma, Zhenyu Wu, Chengkun Wang, Bingyao Yu, Ze Chen, Borui Zhang, Xiuwei Xu, Meng Zhang, Erjin Zhou, Jiwen Lu
bullets: Addresses the problem that imitating all deployment actions can reinforce failures, while discarding failures loses information about physical interactions and their consequences.
Uses a closed-loop world-action model trained on rollouts from its own and other policies across successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures.
Combines source-dependent noise sampling, quality steering, and quality-weighted supervision to learn from full video data while regulating action imitation.
Video and action tokens interact during parallel denoising, enabling predicted consequences to directly inform action generation.
Across three deployment-and-training rounds, success on RoboChallenge Table30-V2 rose from 23.67% to 43.33%; gains were also reported on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and shirt folding.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop policy improvement from deployment rollouts with action-conditioned world modeling, relevant to robot learning/manipulation, interactive world models, and continual/online learning.
papers.title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
papers.tldr: LoopWAM improves generalist robot policies by learning from mixed-quality deployment rollouts in a closed loop, substantially increasing task success without additional embodied pretraining.

papers.abstract: Bringing general-purpose agents into the physical world calls for an executable representation of physical intelligence. Compared with vision-language-action (VLA) models, which map observations and language instructions directly to actions, code makes control logic explicit and reusable. Code can serve not only as a policy representation but also as the workspace in which the agent solves a task. Rather than following a prescribed workflow of planning, execution, and verification, the agent can autonomously inspect the state, revise and execute code, and use feedback to choose the next step. The success of this SWE-style loop in digital environments motivates its extension to physical tasks. Yet physical execution remains prone to recurring failures. To retain and refine experience for later scenes, we introduce EmbodiedEvo, where a coding agent evolves reusable Skills and Lessons through feedback on a single Playground scene, then freezes the resulting harness for diverse new scenes. On RoboDojo-Sim, EmbodiedEvo achieves an average score of 44.48 and a success rate of 37.82\%, surpassing all officially verified results. Paired tests show the largest gains on memory-dependent tasks and successful reuse of coordinated procedures, while fine contact control remains difficult. Experience from stronger models also improves weaker executors: Astra's experience raises Sol and Luna's success rates by 8.86 and 5.50 percentage points over no experience. Compared with raw interaction history, Skills and Lessons achieve comparable task performance at 53.0\% lower execution cost.
authors: Wenyi Li, Yizhe Chi, Youjie Zheng, Chunyu Liu, Xiaoqiu Wang, Mingju Gao, Zheng Jiang, Deyao Hong, Calvin Xiao, Kaisen Yang, Qinhuai Na
bullets: Targets the challenge of making physical intelligence executable, reusable, and adaptable beyond direct vision-language-action control.
Uses a self-improving code loop in which the agent inspects state, revises and executes code, and incorporates feedback.
Learns Skills and Lessons in a single Playground scene, then freezes the resulting harness for use across diverse scenes.
On RoboDojo-Sim, reports a 44.48 average score and 37.82% success rate, with strongest gains on memory-dependent tasks and coordinated procedures.
Skills and Lessons match raw interaction-history performance at 53.0% lower execution cost; fine contact control remains difficult.
papers.selection_reason: Self-improving coding agents for physical tasks; fits robot learning and continual/test-time adaptation.
papers.title: EmbodiedEvo: Self-improving Coding Agents for Physical Intelligence
papers.tldr: EmbodiedEvo lets coding agents evolve reusable skills and lessons from one physical scene, improving performance and reducing execution cost across new scenes.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than accurate planning at a single frame: it demands reliable closed-loop execution in dynamic environments. Although end-to-end driving policies have advanced rapidly, the accumulated closed-loop errors, especially in unseen scenarios, can push vehicles into states from which the same policy struggles to recover. We address the challenge by treating closed-loop driving safety as a test-time execution problem. We introduce AutoAgent0, an agentic runtime and harness framework that augments existing driving experts with complementary detection skills, rule-based action verification, and feedback-driven recovery. To address inaccurate scene perception, an independent detection module constructs scene context using complementary perception skills, and a rule-based verifier checks proposed trajectories against this context before execution. When the nominal trajectories are unreliable, the orchestrator of the runtime activates Recovery Planning, where an agentic loop constructs alternative action proposals from action primitives and iteratively refines them using verification feedback. This design combines independent scene assessment with feasibility checks and online recovery, addressing both perception errors and the limited recovery capabilities of individual experts. Evaluations on Fail2Drive and NavSafe-$\infty$ demonstrate improved closed-loop robustness over single-expert execution in long-tail and safety-critical scenarios. These results demonstrate that runtime supervision can improve closed-loop robustness across multiple driving experts without retraining the underlying policies.
authors: Jiageng Liu, Seth Z. Zhao, Zewei Zhou, Alejandro Huerta, Aidan Bayer-Calvert, Yuxin Bao, Haotian Lin, Robert Spataru, Zijun Cui, Yining Hong, Bolei Zhou, Jiaqi Ma
bullets: Targets accumulated execution errors and poor recovery in dynamic, unseen, and safety-critical scenarios.
Uses complementary detection to build an independent scene context and verify proposed trajectories before execution.
When nominal actions are unsafe or unreliable, an orchestrator generates and iteratively refines alternatives from action primitives.
Evaluations on Fail2Drive and NavSafe-$\infty$ show greater closed-loop robustness than single-expert execution.
Scope: the framework augments existing driving experts at test time rather than changing or retraining their underlying policies.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic runtime for closed-loop driving safety with test-time recovery; fits robot navigation and test-time learning.
papers.title: AutoAgent0: An Agentic Runtime for Safe Closed-Loop Driving
papers.tldr: AutoAgent0 improves closed-loop autonomous-driving safety by supervising existing policies with independent perception, rule-based verification, and online recovery—without retraining them.

papers.abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.
authors: Xinyi Wang, Bangzheng Li, Hanyu Wang, Lin Zhang, Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Zhenggang Tang, Shyamal Buch, Dejia Xu
bullets: Evaluates three modes: code-as-policy, agent-as-policy, and auto-research fine-tuning of a vision-language-action model.
Introduces controls to distinguish retained learning from more attempts, familiar tasks, privileged state, larger budgets, and chance.
Across seven models, simulated tasks, and physical-robot tasks, longer learning helps mainly when tasks are difficult relative to model capability.
Reusable control code and routines transfer across tasks and simulators, but task-specific solutions transfer poorly; a real-robot gap remains for novel human-designed scenes.
Models differ in their best evolution strategy, and text-only models can match comparable multimodal models when reasoning and tool use compensate for weaker perception.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving agentic robotics framework retains skills and memories across tasks, fitting robot learning and embodied memory.
papers.title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
papers.tldr: SEAR benchmarks whether language-model agents genuinely improve robotic skills and transfer them beyond repeated trial-and-error.

papers.abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC matches or improves control performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.
authors: Haodong Yang, Runhan Huang, Bowen Zhang, Iofai Lei, Zunzhe Zhang, Xiangcheng Zhang, Shaoting Zhu, Linzhan Mou, Yicheng Liu, Hang Zhao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining reliable behavior during long-term autonomous operation.
Uses an explicit conditional energy landscape to refine actions toward equilibrium and assess behavioral consistency.
Introduces Energy-Gated DAgger, triggering expert takeover after persistent energy-consistency violations and aggregating recovery trajectories.
Integrates with Diffusion Transformer and flow-matching vision-language-action policies.
Simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation experiments show maintained or improved robustness, with interventions expanding autonomous capability over time.
papers.selection_reason: Energy-based competence monitoring enables lifelong robot learning with expert intervention and trajectory aggregation, fitting continual learning and manipulation.
papers.title: EqC: Equilibrium Energy Control for Introspective Lifelong Robot Learning
papers.tldr: EqC enables lifelong robot policies to detect when their actions become unreliable, request expert help, and learn from those recoveries.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon
authors: Yuchen Lu, Julian McAuley, Lei Zhang
bullets: Targets redundant processing of histories in persistent, long-horizon tasks.
Builds context from reusable continuation carriers, execution context, and a recent-interaction tail.
Maintains carrier records across context folds, updating only affected records using evidence and environment checks.
Reports gains of 5.8% on OSWorld 2.0 and 7.0% on BrowseComp-Plus.
Reduces total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9% on the respective benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime for long-horizon agents that organizes context around reusable progress to reduce token usage and improve efficiency.
papers.title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: CarryOn organizes long-horizon agent context around reusable task objects instead of repeatedly replaying full interaction histories, improving performance while reducing token usage.

papers.abstract: Language model systems repeatedly make test-time decisions by comparing similarity: they retrieve exemplars, rank candidates, and revise responses. Yet similarity is not unique: lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can point to different candidates, and the task-aligned notion can change across instances. We introduce BASIS (Bayesian Axis Selection via Interactive Signals), a training-free Bayesian method that uses weak test-time feedback to infer which criterion in a supplied, task-specific library governs the current decision. It maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria, updates it from scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs, and selects probes by expected information gain. In a finite noisy model, we characterize when the target-criterion pair is recoverable and show why fixed-criterion and fixed-mixture rules can fail under criterion shift. Across concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement, BASIS improves six-probe concept-recovery Success@1 from 56.0% to 68.1%, reasoning accuracy from 72.3% to 73.1%, and refinement win rate from 61.4% to 63.8% over tuned static mixtures. It also exceeds compute-matched best-of-N selection on reasoning (72.1%) and refinement (61.2%). Gains are largest under criterion mismatch and with larger candidate pools, and matched controls indicate that adaptive criterion weighting explains much of the benefit, with joint target-criterion inference adding further value. BASIS selects only among supplied criteria and does not discover new ones.
bullets: Addresses criterion shift: lexical, semantic, structural, or stylistic similarity may be task-dependent.
Maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria using scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs.
Chooses informative probes via expected information gain without additional training.
Improves concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement over static mixtures; gains are largest under criterion mismatch.
Scope: selects among supplied criteria and cannot discover new similarity dimensions.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free Bayesian method that adapts similarity criteria at test time from weak feedback, fitting test-time learning.
papers.title: Bayesian Test-Time Inference of Task-Aligned Similarity from Weak Interactive Feedback
papers.tldr: BASIS uses weak test-time feedback to Bayesianly infer which supplied similarity criterion matters and adapt decisions accordingly.

papers.abstract: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.
bullets: FloWM stores object information in a spatial feature grid with five built-in velocities; the comparison uses an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as node memory.
Probe design strongly affects FloWM’s apparent recall: single-cell probing finds 66% of hidden blocks versus 89% with FloWM’s own probe.
Without camera frames, FloWM scores 8 points higher in view, attributed to writing back its predictions.
Out of view, the tracker matches FloWM’s range using 14KB versus 5.6MB and handles diagonal motion at 93% recall versus FloWM’s 11%.
Both struggle with faster motion; the tracker reaches 94% when given one additional allowed speed, while FloWM would require 25 grid copies.
papers.selection_reason: Studies object memory in learned robot world models under partial observability, directly relevant to embodied memory and world models.
papers.title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
papers.tldr: In FloWM’s block-world tests, a compact oracle-fed node memory matches or exceeds grid-based object recall while using far less memory and handling unseen motion better, though it is not yet fully learned.

papers.abstract: Recent studies investigate the weight geometry through its spectral structure, which characterizes how the weights transform different input directions. Within this view, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shown to induce dense updates that perturb the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, potentially disrupting the model's prior knowledge. These observations motivate using the geometry of pre-SFT weights as a reference for refining learned SFT updates. We study this perspective as Geometric Calibration and develop SPACE Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement), a lightweight post-hoc method that selectively reverts SFT update components within the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while preserving those in its orthogonal complement. SPACE is a data-free, training-free method that requires only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints. We evaluate SPACE on Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1, and Olmo-3 models ranging from 2B to 14B, across mathematical, coding, and medical SFT, as well as several SFT variants. Overall, SPACE mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) capability regression while further improving in-domain (ID) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints. For math SFT, SPACE yields average ID/OOD gains of 2.85/2.26 points on Qwen2.5-7B, and 2.41/1.52 points on Qwen3-14B-Base, respectively. These results highlight how the geometric relationship between SFT updates and pre-SFT weights shapes the adapted model's capabilities and, more broadly, motivate geometry-aware parameter updates for continual model improvement.
authors: Jianzhu Bao, Jia-Chen Gu, Qingyuan Liu, Haozhen Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Nanyun Peng, Wenya Wang
bullets: SFT can disrupt prior knowledge by perturbing the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along principal directions.
SPACE selectively reverts update components in the pre-SFT principal subspace while preserving updates in the orthogonal complement.
It is a lightweight, data-free, training-free post-hoc method requiring only pre- and post-SFT checkpoints.
Across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo models from 2B–14B and math, coding, and medical tasks, SPACE improves in-domain performance and mitigates out-of-domain degradation.
The approach is evaluated across multiple SFT variants; its scope is limited to checkpoint-based geometric calibration after SFT.
papers.selection_reason: Geometric calibration of SFT to improve OOD performance, offering a novel perspective on model adaptation and parameter updates.
papers.title: Geometric Calibration of Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: SPACE calibrates supervised fine-tuning updates using pre-training weight geometry, improving task performance while reducing out-of-domain regression.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.
authors: St John Grimbly, Nicolas Kuske, Evert A. Boonstra, Charel van Hoof, Rowan Hodson, Benjamin Rosman, Ryan Smith, Mark Solms, Jonathan P. Shock
bullets: Precision increases the reliability of interoceptive information, sharpening posteriors and improving survival.
Preference reweighting prioritises need-relieving outcomes, keeping bodily states farther from lethal boundaries.
Preference reweighting changes which bodily states are experienced and learned, narrowing model coverage while slightly improving accuracy in visited states.
Across 72 additional layouts, both interventions improved average survival and interacted positively, but the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts was not established.
Survival alone does not fully reveal how an agent prioritises needs or learns its body model.
papers.selection_reason: Explores interoceptive prioritization in an embodied agent using active inference, comparing precision and preference reweighting to learn body models and survival strategies.
papers.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
papers.tldr: Precision and preference reweighting are distinct routes to prioritising bodily needs, producing different effects on survival, perception, and learned body models.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning
authors: Jason Ken Adhinarta, Raina Wu, Ashutosh Sharma, Avinash Balakrishnan, Rameswar Panda, Polina Golland, Yoon Kim, Zhang-Wei Hong
bullets: Evaluates SDPO and OPSD across code, science, tool-use, and math reasoning tasks.
Finds reported improvements do not consistently transfer to unseen problems.
Attributes gains largely to overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior.
Shows self-distillation gradients align weakly with reward-optimizing policy gradients.
Concludes that effectively using privileged information for reasoning remains unresolved.
papers.selection_reason: Critical analysis of self-distillation for reasoning in LLMs, relevant to model adaptation and training efficiency.
papers.title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
papers.tldr: Self-distillation methods may improve in-distribution reasoning, but their gains often fail to generalize and do not clearly result from privileged information.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric.
