DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.
authors: Haotian Liu, Yingjian Chen, Xiaohang Xu, Lang Huang, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo, Irene Li
bullets: Targets unresolved intermediate errors that final-answer voting in self-consistency cannot correct.
Builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier.
Applies one focused repair only when verifier-supported refutation connects to the majority answer’s supporting path; otherwise preserves the SC vote.
Across five benchmarks, zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 points for Qwen2.5-7B and 15.83 points for Llama3.1-8B.
Outperforms the evaluated CoT, GoT, GoV, and self-consistency baselines without expanding the initial trace bank.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces DDRG, a framework for fine-grained correction of LLM reasoning using graph alignment on sampled traces, improving upon standard self-consistency voting.
papers.title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
papers.tldr: DDRG improves self-consistent LLM reasoning by aligning sampled reasoning graphs to detect and selectively repair intermediate claim disagreements.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks, allowing each stage to reuse behavioral and value knowledge acquired through prior RL. The inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides current-task actor learning, while prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes. Fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. Across contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware, ACCRUE accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and significantly reduces real-robot training time by 31.0\% to 68.5\%.
authors: Changyeon Kim, Kimin Lee, Yashraj Narang, Yijie Guo
bullets: Addresses the need for task-efficient adaptation without catastrophic forgetting during real-world robot deployment.
Carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks to reuse behavioral and value knowledge.
Adapts the critic using current-task transitions and preserves prior behavior by distilling the actor on a small set of retained episodes.
Uses fixed visual features to maintain compatibility between inherited learners and replay data during base-policy updates.
Across simulated and real contact-rich assembly tasks, it achieves near-zero forgetting and reduces real-robot training time by 31.0%–68.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework for robot foundation models that addresses task retention and sample efficiency, directly fitting 'Robot Learning and Manipulation' and 'Continual and Online Learning'.
papers.title: ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models
papers.tldr: ACCRUE enables robot foundation models to learn new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors through continual off-policy reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based test-time scaling enhances LLM reasoning by aggregating multiple reasoning paths for the same query. Existing methods use answer frequencies or path confidence to compute candidate scores, which do not explicitly characterize comparisons between competing answers. Inspired by the Condorcet principle in social choice theory, we introduce pairwise confidence comparisons between paths supporting different answers to capture answer-level comparative advantage. We combine this comparative evidence with voting support through a KL-regularized objective. Theoretically, we show that this comparative-advantage is equivalent to the adjustment to the traditional voting logits. In this way, our proposed Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA) framework allows comparative evidence to compensate for weaker voting support and correct voting-based ranking errors. Experiments on 10 challenging benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, knowledge reasoning, and code generation with 7 models ranging from 1.7B to 32B parameters speak to the effectiveness of this plug-and-play term. Additional evaluations with external reward scores and online sampling further demonstrate its applicability.
authors: Cong Hua, Qianqian Xu, Zitai Wang, Zhiyong Yang, Shilong Bao, Linchao Zhang, Qingming Huang
bullets: Existing methods rank candidate answers mainly by frequency or path confidence, missing direct comparisons between alternatives.
PGLA adds pairwise confidence evidence for paths supporting different answers, inspired by the Condorcet principle.
A KL-regularized objective combines comparative evidence with voting support and yields an equivalent logit adjustment.
The framework is evaluated across 10 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks with 7 models, plus external-reward and online-sampling settings.
The method is presented as a plug-and-play way to compensate for weaker vote counts and correct ranking errors.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA) to improve LLM reasoning at test time by comparing paths supporting different answers, a novel technique for test-time scaling.
papers.title: Compare to Correct: Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment for LLM Test-Time Scaling
papers.tldr: PGLA improves sampling-based LLM test-time scaling by using pairwise comparisons between competing answers to correct voting-based rankings.

papers.abstract: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, recombination, and joint optimization. We instantiate this paradigm with Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO), comprising an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer that constructs the task-adapted recipe space and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to guide LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. Extensive experiments show that SRO achieves the highest average score in all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations. In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO reaches 41.1 versus 15.4 for the strongest baseline on Qwen3-1.7B with GPT-5.4, and 53.8 versus 40.8 on Qwen3-4B with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuohLiuq/SRO.
authors: Ruohong Liu, Bohan Tang, Lekang Jiang, Jack Umenberger, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of predefined recipe spaces and the implicit, hard-to-reuse edits of open-ended agents.
Introduces task-adapted recipe-space optimization, with explicit choices that support reuse, recombination, and joint optimization.
Uses an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer guided by structured trial evidence and multi-objective Bayesian selection.
Reports the highest average score across all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations.
In joint post-training across three domains and six benchmarks, scores 41.1 vs. 15.4 and 53.8 vs. 40.8 for the strongest baselines in two evaluated settings.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO) for LLM post-training, which involves optimizing a recipe space at deployment time. This fits test-time learning and LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: LLM Agents for Automated Post-Training via Structured Recipe Optimization
papers.tldr: Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO) lets LLM agents adapt and systematically optimize post-training recipes for target tasks, achieving the best reported average scores across evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have shown strong potential for embodied vision-language navigation (VLN), yet their performance degrades on long-horizon trajectories due to context-length limits, redundant historical observations, and unstable spatial alignment across time. These issues make it difficult to both compress long navigation histories and reliably reuse past spatial experience. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MemoryVLN}, a unified memory-driven navigation system built around memory construction and management. During memory construction, \emph{Long Sequence Compression} employs forgetting-curve-inspired temporal sampling to preserve dense recent evidence and sparse yet representative distant observations under a limited token budget. \emph{Ego-Aware Memory Representation} further integrates 2D semantic tokens, 3D geometric tokens, and 6D agent poses, allowing each memory to encode both what was observed and where it was observed. During memory management, \emph{Hierarchical Memory Bank} maintains in-episode and context-level memories through cross-context warm-start and confidence-controlled write-back. \emph{Memory Enhancement} then retrieves the Top-$K$ relevant memories according to the current navigation state and fuses them with the current visual tokens. Together, these mechanisms transform raw navigation history into compact, spatially grounded, selectively retrievable, and reusable navigation experience. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate consistent improvements over the state-of-the-art baselines by a substantial margin (i.e., 2\% and 6.5\% in successful rate).
authors: Xueyao Wei, Yifei Wang, Delun Li, Shaoan Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Addresses context-length limits, redundant observations, and unstable spatial alignment in long trajectories.
Compresses history with temporal sampling that preserves recent evidence and representative distant observations.
Represents memories using 2D semantics, 3D geometry, and 6D agent poses for spatial grounding.
Maintains hierarchical in-episode and cross-context memory, retrieves relevant memories, and fuses them with current visual tokens.
Reports successful-rate gains of 2% on R2R-CE and 6.5% on RxR-CE over state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces MemoryVLN, a memory-driven system for vision-language navigation that constructs ego-aware memory representations and manages hierarchical memory banks, directly fitting Embodied AI and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: MemoryVLN: From Ego-Aware Memory Representation to Cross-Context Memory Reuse in Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MemoryVLN improves long-horizon vision-language navigation by compressing, spatially grounding, and selectively reusing navigation history.

papers.abstract: Automated radar waveform recognition classifies the waveform and modulation type of a received signal. As new waveform variants appear over time, a deployed classifier must learn them without retraining from scratch. Catastrophic Forgetting occurs when learning new waveforms overwrites prior knowledge. Continual Learning (CL) methods tackle this challenge, but prior radar studies only evaluate a few methods on narrow benchmarks. Practitioners lack evidence on which method to deploy or which mechanisms are effective. This work presents the first large-scale benchmark of continual learning for radar waveform recognition. Eighteen CL methods are evaluated on a sequential ten-task problem, drawn from four public datasets spanning 54 waveforms, under task- and class-incremental (TIL, CIL) settings and single- and multi-epoch regimes. Methods that retain data from old tasks lead both TIL and CIL settings. Plain replay alone closes 77-88% of the gap between the lower and upper practical limits under TIL, but only 46-55% under CIL. The internal mechanisms of the leading methods are ablated and statistically tested to identify effective mechanisms. Each ablation is paired against its full method over n=6 training seeds, topped up to n=12 when inconclusive, and p-values are Holm-Bonferroni corrected within each method's family. Ablation results show that several mechanisms confer smaller but statistically significant gains. Combining these mechanisms improves the leading F1 score by 3.4-5.5% and 2.7-4.9% under TIL and CIL, respectively, and the combined models exceed every benchmarked method in both settings for all SNRs. These results give researchers of radar waveform classification systems a mechanism-level basis for design.
authors: Mohamed Rabie, Chinthana J. Panagamuwa, Konstantinos G. Kyriakopoulos
bullets: Evaluates 18 continual-learning methods on 10 sequential tasks covering 54 waveforms from four public datasets.
Assesses task-incremental and class-incremental learning under single- and multi-epoch settings.
Methods retaining data from prior tasks perform best in both settings; plain replay recovers more of the practical performance gap in TIL than CIL.
Ablation studies identify several smaller but statistically significant mechanism-level gains.
Combining effective mechanisms improves the leading F1 score by 3.4–5.5% in TIL and 2.7–4.9% in CIL, outperforming all benchmarked methods across SNRs.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning for radar waveform recognition, providing a large-scale benchmark and mechanism analysis for overcoming catastrophic forgetting.
papers.title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting: Continual Learning for Radar Waveform Classification
papers.tldr: A large benchmark shows that replay-based continual learning best mitigates catastrophic forgetting in radar waveform classification, while combining effective mechanisms further improves performance.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) aims to improve large language model reasoning by exposing agents to alternative solutions and enabling iterative revision. However, standard broadcast-style MAD makes peer answers visible without requiring agents to engage with a particular peer claim. As a result, reliable reasoning may be suppressed by conflicting or majority responses, limiting achievable performance, while erroneous reasoning may persist and degrade final predictions without actionable feedback. We propose TrueMAD, a backbone-agnostic test-time plug-in that introduces one-to-one, free-form peer advice between answer broadcasting and self-revision. Each source agent responds to a target's current reasoning through support, rebuttal, refinement, or further questions, while the target retains control over how to revise. The same mechanism can augment standard MAD and its improved variants without parameter updates. Across AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average, while TrueDMAD improves DMAD by 4.72 and 4.06 points, respectively. Analyses at the utterance, agent-transition, and group levels further show more peer-specific deliberation, more correction-oriented revisions, and more favorable consensus dynamics.
authors: Dezheng Bao, Sihang Du, Renhong Huang, Zhizhang Yuan, Yifei Sun, Yang Yang
bullets: Standard broadcast debate can leave agents disengaged from peer claims, allowing errors or majority influence to persist.
TrueMAD adds one-to-one, free-form peer advice—including support, rebuttal, refinement, or questions—between answer sharing and self-revision.
It is a backbone-agnostic, parameter-free test-time plug-in that can augment standard MAD and improved variants.
On AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA using Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average.
The method produces more peer-specific deliberation, correction-oriented revisions, and favorable consensus dynamics.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes TrueMAD, a test-time plug-in for multi-agent debate that improves LLM reasoning through targeted peer engagement, fitting both LLM agent interaction and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Beyond Answer Sharing: TrueMAD for Targeted Peer Engagement in Multi-Agent Debate
papers.tldr: TrueMAD improves multi-agent debate by directing each agent to give targeted, actionable feedback to a specific peer before revision.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.
authors: Tianyu Huai, Jie Zhou, Bo Mao, Qin Chen, Liang He, Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting execution rewards into generalizable context edits from limited, task-specific evidence.
Uses Groupwise Policy Critique to compare successful and failed rollouts within the same task and context.
Uses Cross-Group Policy Update to refine proposed edits against evidence pooled across tasks, including cases with no proposed edit.
Builds bounded textual patches and adopts candidate contexts based on held-out validation rewards.
Across six benchmarks, improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 points for GPT-5.5 and 15.3 points for Qwen3.8-27B.
papers.selection_reason: Gradient-free test-time adaptation of LLM agent context from rollout feedback fits deployment-time learning.
papers.title: TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management
papers.tldr: TextualRL improves LLM agents by using grouped rollout feedback to create and validate reusable textual context updates without changing model parameters.

papers.abstract: Cross-domain few-shot action recognition (CD-FSAR) aims to recognise unseen action classes in a target domain from a handful of labelled videos. Despite advances in representation learning, CD-FSAR inference still relies on prototypes estimated from extremely limited support examples. To assess this bottleneck, we perform an oracle analysis with the representation fixed. Constructing oracle prototypes and decision boundaries from ground-truth query labels improves 5-way 1-shot accuracy by 7--20 percentage points across five target datasets. This reveals a substantial estimation gap: the representation contains useful discriminative information, but prototypes and boundaries estimated from scarce supports fail to capture each episode's true class structure. Motivated by this, we propose TRACE, a training-free transductive inference framework that improves episode-level estimation without modifying the backbone. TRACE comprises two complementary stages. Confidence-Thresholded Transductive Prototype Refinement (CTPR) refines support-based prototypes using confidently predicted queries. The refined prototypes initialise a lightweight per-episode classifier, which Transductive Classifier Refinement (TCR) further adapts by encouraging confident, class-balanced predictions over all queries. Together, the two stages improve prototype and boundary estimation, enabling better use of information in the unlabelled queries. Across five target datasets (HMDB51, UCF101, SSv2, Diving48, and RareAct) in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong CD-FSAR baseline, including gains of more than six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot, while recovering much of the oracle-estimated gap. These results suggest that improving test-time estimation is a powerful, broadly applicable complement to representation learning for CD-FSAR under extreme support scarcity.
authors: Changyi Li, Zeyu Yang, Yu Xiao
bullets: An oracle analysis shows that scarce-support prototype and decision-boundary estimation is a major bottleneck, despite useful learned representations.
TRACE uses two training-free transductive stages: confidence-based prototype refinement (CTPR) and class-balanced classifier refinement (TCR).
The method leverages confidently predicted unlabelled queries to better estimate each episode’s class structure.
Across five target datasets and both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong baseline, with gains exceeding six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot.
The approach recovers much of the oracle-estimated gap, but its scope is limited to test-time transductive settings with available unlabelled queries.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses few-shot action recognition in video and improves episode-level estimation through training-free transductive test-time refinement.
papers.title: Closing the Estimation Gap: Training-Free Transductive Inference for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition
papers.tldr: TRACE improves cross-domain few-shot action recognition without retraining by refining prototypes and episode-specific classifiers using unlabelled queries.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We propose TRACESTEER, a trace-driven activation steering framework that uses preceding denoising predictions as feedback to jointly adapt steering direction and strength. Specifically, Denoising Feedback Steering (DF-Steering) constructs step-specific steering vectors from preceding predictions and current hidden states. Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate (TS-Gate) regulates their strength using prediction uncertainty and the denoising timestep. With the backbone frozen, factual supervision and magnitude regularization jointly guide the learning of adaptive steering interventions, promoting factual reliability and stability throughout denoising. Experiments on two dLLMs show improved factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalization across five downstream benchmarks.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yili Wang, Yue Tan, Xin He, Rui Miao, Yixin Liu, Yi Chang, Xin Wang
bullets: Targets dLLM-specific challenges: changing denoising states and time-varying hallucination risk.
Uses Denoising Feedback Steering to derive step-specific steering vectors from prior predictions and current hidden states.
Uses a Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate to adjust intervention strength based on uncertainty and denoising timestep.
Learns adaptive interventions with the backbone frozen, combining factual supervision and magnitude regularization.
Improves factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalizes across five downstream benchmarks in experiments on two dLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Activation steering for diffusion LLMs with inference-time adaptation, fitting language foundation models and test-time learning.
papers.title: TRACESTEER: Trace Driven Activation Steering for Hallucination Mitigation in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: TRACESTEER reduces hallucinations in diffusion language models by adapting activation-steering directions and strengths throughout the denoising process.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. However, existing memory benchmarks evaluate only memory writing, retrieval, and organization, so whether agents can forget at the user's explicit request remains under-evaluated. To address this gap, we propose Bemula, the first benchmark dedicated to memory unlearning. It comprises 50 multi-session dialogue instances, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions. Each dialogue has a control version without the requests, so that only systems that have stored the target can earn credit for forgetting. Across the paired versions, five test suites measure storage, removal of the requested information, preservation of unrelated memories, relearning of similar facts, and resistance to extraction attacks. On Bemula, we evaluate six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs, together with the Full Context LLM on two of them. The results are negative. Across all evaluated systems and backbones, no system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end, and most pass none at all. These systems either leave the requested information extractable under simple attacks or delete far more than requested. Memory unlearning therefore remains an open challenge for agent memory design. We release our data and code at https://github.com/Nboxff/bemula-benchmark.
authors: Bofan Xie, Chaokun Wang, Guanchen Ge, Songyao Wang, Fang Niu, Hang Zhang, Wei Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap in evaluating explicit memory deletion in long-term LLM agents.
Introduces 50 multi-session dialogues, 135 forget requests across six types, and 1,742 test questions, with paired control versions.
Evaluates storage, targeted removal, unrelated-memory preservation, relearning, and resistance to extraction attacks.
Tests six memory systems with three backbone LLMs, plus Full Context LLM on two backbones.
No evaluated system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end; failures involve residual extraction or excessive deletion.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Bemula, a benchmark for memory unlearning in LLM agents, and investigates the technical challenges of removing specific information while preserving the rest of the memory state.
papers.title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Bemula benchmarks whether LLM agents can selectively forget user-requested memories while preserving unrelated information, finding that current systems largely fail.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) built on pretrained video generation models adapt quickly to new robotic tasks, but they forget previously learned tasks under sequential fine-tuning. Experience replay (ER) mitigates such forgetting by rehearsing data of previous tasks, yet this data is often unavailable in robotics, where a policy is deployed as weights only and its training data is not shared along with it. In this work, we ask whether a WAM can achieve data-free continual learning by regenerating its own past. Our key observation is that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting. However, replaying such raw rollouts still lags far behind replaying real data, which we attribute to two issues. First, the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done. Second, under open-loop generation, the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations. To address both issues, we present rectified generative replay (R$^2$-WAM), which truncates generated rollouts at task completion with an agentic evaluator and filters out rollouts whose actions are physically inconsistent with the observations. On the four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, R$^2$-WAM reduces forgetting by over 90% relative to sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches ER without accessing any data from previous tasks. Our analysis further reveals that forgetting in WAMs concentrates in inverse dynamics modeling: a forgotten WAM still produces visually plausible observations of previous tasks while its generated actions fail.
authors: Kaipeng Fang, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi, Yunsong Zhou, Hongzi Zhu, Minyi Guo, Jingkuan Song, Lianli Gao
bullets: Problem: Sequentially fine-tuning world action models on new robotic tasks causes forgetting, while prior-task training data may be unavailable.
Method: The model autoregressively regenerates past-task rollouts, truncates them at task completion, and filters action–observation inconsistencies.
Contribution: Rectified generative replay (R²-WAM) supports continual learning without storing or accessing previous data.
Result: Across four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, it reduces forgetting by over 90% versus sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches experience replay.
Finding: Forgetting is concentrated in inverse-dynamics modeling; observations can remain visually plausible while generated actions fail.
papers.selection_reason: Data-free continual learning for world action models via rectified generative replay; directly targets world models and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Data-Free Continual Learning for World Action Model with Rectified Generative Replay
papers.tldr: R²-WAM enables data-free continual learning by replaying self-generated, task-complete, physically consistent rollouts to substantially reduce forgetting in world action models.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.
authors: Francesco Panetta, Federico Di Valerio, Michela Proietti
bullets: Targets continual learning in energy-efficient deep spiking neural networks under low-latency and tight-memory constraints.
Combines Batch Normalization Through Time-stabilized VGG9 SNNs with forward-only Spike Activation Maps.
Aggregates spike-based explanations into spatial attention maps to identify patches for replay.
Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 report improved accuracy–memory trade-offs and competitive performance with substantially lower storage.
Scope is limited to the evaluated datasets, architecture, and memory-constrained replay setting.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a replay-based continual learning method for spiking neural networks to mitigate catastrophic forgetting under memory constraints.
papers.title: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: SAM-guided experience replay helps deep SNNs mitigate catastrophic forgetting while storing only informative image patches instead of full images.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.
authors: Yousef Liang, Ryan Ardalan, Yarden Goraly, Chenhao Zhu, Yue Yin, Jonas Frey, Claire Tomlin, Marco Pavone, Shankar Sastry
bullets: Targets chained-goal navigation under partial observability, where goals may be redirected or newly introduced without explicit transition signals.
Separates latent beliefs into global/local spatial and long/short temporal representations to support exploration and strategic revisitation.
Uses goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation as goals evolve.
Experiments in simulated diverse terrains and on a Spot quadruped show improved chained-goal navigation over baselines.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and real-robot settings; broader scope beyond these settings is not established in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory decomposition framework (GLST) for online chained-goal navigation that separates beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations, directly addressing long-horizon reasoning and memory requirements in embodied agents.
papers.title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: GLST enables mapless robots to navigate long-horizon environments with goals that change online by decomposing memory across spatial and temporal scales.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.
authors: Jin Liu, Ning Xi, Yinbin Miao, Junkang Liu, Ke Cheng, Jianfeng Ma
bullets: Problem: Differential privacy makes it difficult to retain earlier task knowledge while adapting LoRA to new tasks.
Method: Build a stable subspace from privatized past updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights, then privately optimize only one LoRA factor in fixed bases.
The design avoids bilinear noise interactions from jointly perturbing both LoRA factors.
Before merging updates, stable-direction coefficients are rescaled using historical and current update energies.
Across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets, DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting versus evaluated baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Differentially private continual LoRA with stable/plastic subspace construction; directly addresses continual learning under privacy.
papers.title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA
papers.tldr: DP-SPA improves privacy-preserving continual LoRA by separating stable and plastic update subspaces, reducing forgetting while maintaining adaptation across tasks.

papers.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.
authors: Letian Zhu, Han Li, Yifan Yao, Xinping Lei, Xinyu Che, Jiahao Wang, Dianyi Wang, Yucheng Fu, Jiakai Wang, Zhiqi Bai, Wenbo Su, Jiaheng Liu
bullets: Agent Skills need evidence about both procedures and when they apply, which successful task completion alone may not provide.
SSL keeps the Student as the sole environment operator and Skill author, while an Educator guides investigation through questions and advice.
On SkillTransferBench, Fixed-Window SSL achieved 0.801 utility, outperforming no Skill and adapted trajectory/contrastive distillation baselines.
Issue-Guided SSL reached 0.805 utility while using 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL.
The study covers 35 task families and 408 executable cases; results focus on transfer to fresh solver sessions and three model pairs.
papers.selection_reason: Interleaved teaching-and-practice method for acquiring reusable agent skills, fitting adaptation/retention of useful knowledge during continued agent interaction.
papers.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
papers.tldr: Socratic Skill Learning interleaves expert guidance with agent-led practice and revision to produce more transferable reusable skills while reducing teaching cost.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.
authors: Yuqian Fu, Kaiwen Jiang, Zijun Song, Jiawei Wang, Yuanheng Zhu, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between sample-efficient but forgetful SFT and slower, capability-preserving RL.
Uses RL as the main optimizer and selectively activates SFT on state-dependent “hard states” where the policy fails.
Provides a theoretical bound showing that failure-state supervision limits cumulative parameter updates.
Improves performance across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search at 7B and 32B scales.
In continual learning, retains up to 9.6 more capability on prior tasks than SFT→RL baselines while matching or exceeding target-task performance.
papers.selection_reason: Continual learning for LLM agents with selective SFT/RL; fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
papers.tldr: TSRL combines reinforcement learning with targeted expert supervision on failure states to improve continual agent learning while reducing catastrophic forgetting.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.
authors: Ibna Kowsar, Ivan Medri, Fanyu Meng, Xin Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between constraining PEFT weight updates and preserving activation-level knowledge.
Uses a frozen sparse autoencoder to identify task and general-purpose concepts.
Applies two complementary regularization terms: task-concept subspace confinement and general-concept activation anchoring.
Improves retention at comparable accuracy across a CLIP vision panel and in Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning.
Named SAE concepts make the retention constraints inspectable and controllable.
papers.selection_reason: PEFT regularizer that anchors pretrained concepts to prevent forgetting; relevant to adaptation and knowledge retention.
papers.title: Confine to the Task, Anchor the Rest: Concept-Guided Retention Regularizer for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: CGR reduces catastrophic forgetting in PEFT by confining task-related updates and anchoring general concepts in activation space.

papers.abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
authors: Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama, Bo Han
bullets: Long-context inference is costly, motivating test-time encoding of context into model weights.
Weight-encoded information can be confused with the model’s pre-existing knowledge and ignored as context.
The method associates each encoded context with an identifier, enabling the LLM to recite it later.
A prompting framework further guides the model to use the recalled information for subsequent inference.
It outperformed a baseline across controlled tasks and practical benchmarks using off-the-shelf LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Encodes context into LLM weights via test-time updates and distinguishes it from general knowledge, directly fitting test-time learning and LLM memory.
papers.title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
papers.tldr: The paper makes context encoded into temporary LLM weight updates usable by assigning it an identifier and prompting the model to apply the recalled information as context.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.
Uses a shared vision-language model to write structured memories, retrieve past frames, and guide movement or turning.
Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming spatial understanding with embodied memory and active exploration; directly fits embodied memory, spatial intelligence, and vision-language-action.
papers.title: MemAct: Streaming Spatial Understanding with Memory and Active Exploration
papers.tldr: MemAct enables embodied agents to understand spaces over time by combining structured memory, on-demand retrieval, and active exploration in a unified streaming loop.

papers.abstract: Retrospective evaluation of early-warning models may not reflect information available when predictions are issued and outcomes become observable. We developed a time-synchronous prequential framework for online prediction of next-week student disengagement, operationalised as inactivity onset, from Moodle logs. Ordered by calendar time, models were updated only with available outcomes and remained unchanged for all predictions at each prediction cutoff; development, calibration and evaluation were chronologically separate. We compared stochastic gradient descent logistic regression (SGD-LR), online sequential extreme learning machine (OSELM) and echo state network (ESN) across predictive performance, fixed, frozen and rolling threshold policies, calendar-time variation and four behavioural feature sets. Held-out evaluation comprised 49,329 predictions with 37.68% inactivity-onset prevalence. Discrimination was similar (average precision 0.665-0.679; ROC-AUC 0.755-0.774). OSELM had the highest recall, SGD-LR the highest precision and specificity, and ESN the highest Matthews correlation coefficient and balanced accuracy. Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume, whereas rolling adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds. Weekly performance and calibrated-probability distributions varied without sustained deterioration. During model selection, cumulative-and-temporal features achieved the highest individual-set AP, with modest gains from combining all feature groups. These findings indicate that streaming early-warning evaluation should consider calibration, threshold-dependent performance, alert burden and calendar-time variation alongside aggregate discrimination.
authors: David Otoo-Arthur, Terence L. van Zyl
bullets: Addresses leakage and unrealistic retrospective evaluation by using only outcomes available at each prediction cutoff.
Compares SGD-LR, OSELM, and ESN models across threshold policies, calendar-time variation, and behavioural feature sets.
All models showed similar discrimination, while their strengths differed: OSELM in recall, SGD-LR in precision and specificity, and ESN in MCC and balanced accuracy.
Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume; rolling threshold adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds.
Performance varied by week without sustained deterioration, highlighting the importance of calibration, alert burden, and temporal variation.
papers.selection_reason: Prequential online evaluation of streaming prediction models, relevant to online and continual learning methodology.
papers.title: A Time-Synchronous Prequential Evaluation Framework for Next-Week Student Disengagement Prediction from Moodle LMS Logs
papers.tldr: A time-synchronous prequential framework provides a realistic way to evaluate online Moodle-based predictions of next-week student disengagement.

papers.abstract: We propose a continuous learning formulation for $T$ non-forgetting tasks with the spherical parameter space $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ in asymptotic regime $d\rightarrow \infty$. Each task $i$ has an optimum $\bm{\Theta}_i$, minimizing its corresponding loss function $R_i(\bm{w})$ on sphere. We reduce each task $i$ to an acceptable loss region modeled by a geodesic ball $B_{\bm{\Theta}_i}(r_i(d))$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ centered at $\bm{\Theta}_i$ with radius $r_i(d)$. To model task dependencies (similarities), task optima $\bm{\Theta}_i$ are distributed by a Neyman-Scott clustered point process $\Phi$. Cluster centers $\{\bm{Y}_j\}_{j=1}^{N_p}$ form a homogeneous Poisson point process on sphere, while intra-cluster task optima follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution with mean $\bm{Y}_j$ and concentration $\kappa$. Each task $t\in \{1, ..., T\}$ learning algorithm is considered to be a channel $Q_{t}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}_t | \bm{w}_{t-1}, \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\theta}_{1:t-1}), \bm{\theta}_t)$, where $\bm{W}_t$ is the learned parameter of task $t$ and $\mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:t-1})=\bigcap_{i=1}^{t-1}B_{\bm{\Theta}_i}(r_i(d))$. Since in continual learning, the learner does not need to reach $\bm{\Theta}_t$ exactly to successfully learn task $t$, to avoid forgetting as well as reliable learning, it only needs for the learned parameter vector $\bm{W}_{t}$ to enter $B_{\bm{\Theta}_t}(r_t(d)) \cap \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:t-1})$. Using this model, we derive an upper bound on $T$ ensuring $\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{K}_{T}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:T}) \neq \emptyset] \rightarrow 1$ as $d\rightarrow \infty$ and $\kappa/d \rightarrow \alpha$, where $\alpha>0$ is a constant. Finally, for $T$ tasks sampled uniformly from $\Phi$, we derive an upper bound for total information theoretic capacity under the non-forgetting constraint for each task.
bullets: Models each task’s acceptable solutions as a geodesic ball on a spherical parameter space.
Represents task dependencies using a Neyman–Scott clustered process with von Mises–Fisher-distributed optima.
Formulates non-forgetting as the nonempty intersection of all task-specific acceptable-loss regions.
Derives an asymptotic upper bound on the number of tasks whose regions remain jointly feasible.
Derives an upper bound on total information-theoretic capacity for uniformly sampled tasks under non-forgetting constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of non-forgetting task capacity in continual learning, directly relevant to continual and online learning.
papers.title: Effect of Spherical Parameter Space on Number of Non-Forgetting Tasks and Capacity of Continual Learning
papers.tldr: A high-dimensional spherical model quantifies how task similarity affects the number of continually learnable, non-forgetting tasks and their information capacity.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.
authors: Junyi Wu, Zekun Li, Chenhongyi Yang, Chen Guo, Lingchen Yang, Yongan Zhang, Xinyi Zhang, Hongbing Hu, Bartek Rymkowski, Srinath Sridhar, Yan Yan, Xijie Huang
bullets: Addresses spatial memory decay when autoregressive world models generate beyond their active context.
Uses recursive least squares to update fast-weight memory with newly observed visual features keyed by camera pose.
Reads stored scene features with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length.
Distills the autoregressive model into a few-step generator using dual-teacher distribution matching for interactive speed.
Improves revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075, while reaching 20.6 FPS at 1280×704 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU.
papers.selection_reason: Camera-controlled video world model with test-time training as persistent memory, fitting video world models, interactive world models, and test-time learning.
papers.title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models
papers.tldr: World-T3 gives real-time video world models persistent, pose-keyed test-time memory to preserve scene consistency during long-horizon generation.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery with language models requires finding the best valid solution within a finite computational budget. We study how feedback from this search can improve the procedure used to conduct it. We introduce HarnessTTT, a test-time learning framework that trains a harness proposer while keeping the executor frozen. The proposer generates executable harnesses comprising system prompts, reusable skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls. Each harness guides a budgeted discovery rollout, whose outcome provides feedback for updating the proposer. A discovery-oriented policy-gradient objective combines gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages (RLOO), and max-sharpening to favor high-performing proposals. Generated components are validated before execution, and the search retains the best valid solution and selected harnesses across rounds. Across fourteen discovery tasks in mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology, HarnessTTT with a frozen 9B executor improves on OpenEvolve with the same executor on all eleven benchmark tasks (e.g., from 1.17 to 2.64 on circle packing), improves on the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B by up to 92%, holds the best open-weight sub-10B result on nine, and reaches 0.380919 on Erd\H{o}s minimum overlap, better than the best human reference of 0.380927. Scaling the proposer and frozen executor to 27B improves on eleven of fourteen tasks, and transferring the learned harnesses to GPT-5.5 matches or exceeds the strongest reported system of any backbone on nine of fourteen tasks. Together, these results show that harness search can itself be learned at test time: a trained proposer lets a small frozen executor search effectively, and the harnesses it finds carry over to stronger executors.
authors: Yingzi Ma, Yulong Cao, Nanxi Li, Fang Wu, Yizhe Zhang, James Zou, Yejin Choi, Chaowei Xiao
bullets: Addresses how to find high-quality valid solutions under a fixed computational budget for scientific discovery.
Trains a harness proposer while keeping the solution-generating executor frozen; harnesses combine prompts, skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls.
Uses rollout feedback with gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages, and max-sharpening to improve proposed harnesses, while validating components and retaining strong results.
Across 14 tasks, it improves over OpenEvolve on all 11 benchmark tasks and transfers effectively to larger executors, including GPT-5.5.
Scope: results cover mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology; performance gains vary across tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time learning framework that updates a harness proposer from search feedback directly matches test-time learning.
papers.title: HarnessTTT: Learn to Optimize Harness at Test-Time for Scientific Discovery
papers.tldr: HarnessTTT learns better search procedures at test time, enabling a small frozen language model to solve diverse scientific discovery tasks more effectively and transfer its learned harnesses to stronger models.

papers.abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.
authors: Romain Puech, Georgy Salakhutdinov, Dimitris Bertsimas
bullets: Models personalization as contextual dueling bandits over a fixed set of persona prompts, using pairwise choices between two displayed responses.
Introduces a tutoring-focused benchmark with six teaching styles, educational questions, simulated students, hidden preference profiles, and Bradley–Terry reference utilities.
Proposes learning a mixture prior from completed users and updating preferences online for each new user.
On held-out students and topics, the method removes 44–48% of random-pair excess regret and exceeds half the performance of a hindsight per-user linear oracle.
Releases the benchmark, prompts, and code; evaluation relies on LLM-simulated student preferences.
papers.selection_reason: Online LLM personalization from pairwise preferences with cross-user adaptation fits online learning and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
papers.tldr: An online contextual-dueling approach personalizes LLM response styles by learning across users while adapting to each user’s preferences during a session.

papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
authors: Delun Li, Xueyao Wei, Rui Chen, Yifei Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Models navigation where interactions change spatial connectivity, target visibility, or both sequentially.
Introduces MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark covering channel, container, and mixed tasks with interaction-necessity annotations.
Evaluates navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and interaction cost separately.
Proposes MultINav-Agent with interactive perception, expected-change action selection, and post-interaction graph verification.
Reports consistent improvements over adapted baselines across all task types.
papers.selection_reason: Interactive embodied navigation benchmark and agentic framework with persistent state-conditioned interaction graph; fits robot navigation, VLA, and embodied memory.
papers.title: Interactive Navigation Beyond Reachability: Benchmark and Agentic Framework
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and agent framework for navigation tasks requiring interactions such as opening doors and containers to reach or reveal goals.

papers.abstract: Studying event memory requires defining events and their relationships within remembered experience. Autobiographical narratives provide evidence of this organization, but their analytical units must first be established. This study introduces a large language model framework for constructing event representations from narratives and modeling their structure and dynamics with excerpt-level traceability. Explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation guide event construction. In a proof-of-concept application to interviews from five participants, the framework constructed 256 event-states. Multiple correspondence analysis embedded these states in feature-based spaces, with analyses focused on a selected 4-D geometry and 10-D and 13-D reference geometries. Consecutive event-states were significantly closer than expected under randomized narrative order. In the selected 4-D ten-basin solution, similarity between basin-state feature profiles corresponded with similarity between one-step routing profiles; context, mechanism, and theme differentiated full-system pathway engagement. A successor representation modeled expected basin-state occupancy across successive steps. Correlations between basin-centroid distances and complete successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions, with exploratory tests supporting correspondence in at least two solutions across all three geometries. These findings connect feature-based event representations with observed narrative transitions and modeled multistep organization. The framework translates hippocampal principles into source-linked event boundaries and state representations, providing an analytical basis for testing neural accounts of event segmentation and predictive organization during naturalistic recall.
bullets: Defines event boundaries and feature schemas informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation.
Applied to interviews from five participants, producing 256 traceable event-states.
Multidimensional analyses found consecutive event-states were closer than expected under randomized narrative order.
Basin-state similarity aligned with one-step routing profiles, while context, mechanism, and theme differentiated pathway engagement.
Successor-representation analyses linked feature-space distances with modeled multistep occupancy patterns across tested geometries.
papers.selection_reason: LLM framework for event memory and narrative dynamics with hippocampal/navigation-inspired structure, relevant to embodied memory.
papers.title: Event Memory and Narrative Dynamics: A Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional State Spaces
papers.tldr: A source-traceable LLM framework represents autobiographical narratives as multidimensional event states and models their sequential organization, linking narrative transitions to hippocampal-inspired memory principles.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
authors: Ke Gui, Chenghao Shi, Ziyue Wang, Longwen Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Huimin Lu
bullets: Addresses image-goal navigation when targets are outside the current view and persistent spatial memory is required.
Uses learned scene-coordinate localization to anchor current, goal, and history frames in a shared reference frame.
Jointly predicts future states and actions in latent space, avoiding pixel reconstruction and CEM-style planning.
Reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks.
Improves closed-loop success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and SPL from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-grounded world action model for image-goal navigation with latent state-action prediction and persistent spatial memory.
papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: G$^2$WAM enables efficient image-goal navigation by combining geometry-grounded spatial memory with latent world-action modeling, improving trajectory prediction and navigation success without explicit 3D reconstruction or costly planning.

papers.abstract: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%--40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%--2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM's 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
authors: Xin Xu, Ke Cheng, Hao Wang, Yangru Huang, Yanghao Xiao, Zhichao Chen, Zhisheng Zhong, Xun Liu, Yi Li, Qian Li, Haibin Lv, Jun Zhang, Jie Jiang, Zhouchen Lin
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between exploring edit sequences and spending limited budget on evaluating intermediate agents.
Uses Verification-Aware Tree Search to allocate resources between further edits and pending verification based on predicted returns.
Uses Group Verification Optimization to train the improver while keeping the evaluator fixed.
Terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%–40.0%; SpecRSI wins across all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs.
Coding-validation success is 69.4% versus HGM’s 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on improving agent systems through speculative recursive self-improvement, relevant to LLMs and adaptation.
papers.title: Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens: Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Systems
papers.tldr: SpecRSI improves agentic systems by drafting successor agents speculatively while requiring full verification before adoption.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.
authors: Haolin Tian, Yikang Li, Tonghan Wang
bullets: Freezes the pretrained backbone and trains added attention and feed-forward branches at each Transformer layer.
Uses zero-initialized output projections to preserve the original policy at initialization.
Keeps learned pathways explicit, supporting transfer across models and sequential addition of further pathways.
Across five backbones, achieves competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with few trainable parameters.
Transferred pathways provide immediate gains, reaching near-100-update performance after only 10 target-side updates in all tested transfer directions.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for RL adaptation of LLMs using structural pathways, relevant to LLMs and adaptation.
papers.title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: GrowRL makes RL adaptations into compact, transferable Transformer pathways, enabling parameter-efficient reuse across compatible LLMs.

papers.abstract: Humans expand their locomotion capability by wearing appropriate footwear, such as hiking boots for mountains or skates for ice. Footwear changes the ground-contact interface and enables traversal of otherwise difficult terrain. In contrast, locomotion controllers are typically trained for a fixed morphology, and their performance can degrade when shoes alter foot geometry, mass, and friction. We propose SHOES, a sample-efficient framework for adapting locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes. SHOES freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes only lightweight, identity-initialized modulation modules on the robot, preserving the initial behavior while enabling efficient hardware adaptation. We also introduce SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that constrains online adaptation within a user-defined workspace. The simulation results with a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 show that SHOES substantially recovers locomotion performance after footwear-induced morphology changes using limited additional adaptation. Under the same adaptation budget, SHOES outperforms FiLM-only, Linear Adapter-only, and residual-RL baselines. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 fitted with human shoes further evaluate the effectiveness of SHOES for hardware deployment.
authors: Kota Tsuruhara, Tsung-Yuan Chen, Kento Kawaharazuka
