papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical analysis of catastrophic forgetting in online continual learning directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Formalizing Forgetting: Theory of Forgetting for Online Continual Learning
papers.tldr: This work develops a theory explaining how data amount, task similarity, and task order drive forgetting in online continual learning.

papers.abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
authors: Xiaofan Wu, Xi Zeng, Miaoxia Chen, Peishan Chen, Shuyan Li, Chen Wang, Jiyun Yao, Hanyong Zhong, Jiahao Zhu
bullets: The key bottleneck is timing, not visual recognition or semantic reasoning.
Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) describes targets that appear and disappear before processing finishes.
A Perceptual Deadline Contract separates a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline.
The proposed architecture combines an always-on bounded fast path, active durable-memory capture, and deferred multimodal deliberation with tools.
Measured frontier-model latency suggests answers may take 1.2–9.3 seconds or longer, while evidence can disappear sooner.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory architecture and perceptual deadlines for camera-first embodied agents acting on ephemeral visual targets.
papers.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
papers.tldr: Camera-first agents should capture fleeting visual evidence immediately, then reason about it later, because semantic processing may outlast the moment an object is visible.

papers.abstract: Versatile quadruped locomotion depends on a tight coupling between what the robot perceives and what its body can execute. Yet existing visual controllers typically organize depth history using fixed temporal patterns, overlooking that the same temporal span corresponds to different spatial ranges as the robot's speed, posture, and gait phase change. Consequently, the same visual history may be insufficient in one motion state but outdated or misaligned in another. To address this limitation, we propose TempoLoco, a body-aware dynamic visual perception framework that organizes visual memory according to the robot's current locomotion state. TempoLoco learns multiple complementary temporal views from a long depth buffer, encodes them within a shared feature space, and dynamically aggregates them using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. This enables a single policy to align visual anticipation with the robot's current motion capabilities across complex terrains, including stairs, platforms, gaps, discrete obstacles, rough ground, and slopes. From the experiment analysis, TempoLoco achieves a 78.4% success rate, compared with 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion. In separate capability evaluations, it completes 41/45 simulated trials across nine terrain types and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 with a fixed arm, demonstrating robust and deployable locomotion through body-aware dynamic visual perception.
authors: Hao Zhang, Yuping Yan, Yitian Hong, Luying Feng, Tianhong Wang, Fengqi Dai, Wei Chen, Yaochu Jin
bullets: Fixed temporal visual histories can become spatially mismatched as speed, posture, and gait phase change.
TempoLoco learns multiple temporal views from a long depth buffer in a shared feature space.
Proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence dynamically select and fuse the most relevant views.
It achieves a 78.4% success rate versus 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion.
The system completes 41/45 simulated trials and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 across diverse terrains.
papers.selection_reason: Motion-adaptive temporal visual memory for quadruped locomotion; fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Beyond Fixed Visual History: Learning Motion-Adaptive Temporal Receptive Fields for Complex-Terrain Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: TempoLoco dynamically adapts visual-history timescales to a quadruped’s motion state, improving locomotion across complex terrains.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.
authors: Tianle Liu, Gongbo Cheng, Chenggong Ni, Minming Gu, Tao Zhou, Fuyuan Hu, Fan Lyu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing TTD methods discover novel classes only with anonymous labels.
Uses an LLM to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and builds an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space.
At test time, Relational Semantic Grounding compares unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors to propose and rerank candidate concepts.
Applies confidence-guided semantic stabilization to refine discovered concepts over the test stream.
Experiments show improvements over TTD baselines, though the abstract does not report specific numerical results.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time discovery and semantic grounding of novel classes after deployment fits test-time learning.
papers.title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
papers.tldr: SEGA makes test-time discovery more interpretable by assigning semantic concepts to novel classes using attribute-based visual-language grounding.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a route to AI systems that participate in their own continued development. Recent methods allow language agents to retain changes to their parameters, memory, skills, and code for subsequent execution and improvement. We examine how these methods can inform new research ideas through two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy with nine design dimensions organized into four groups: update targets, update organization, update schedule and scope, feedback and selection. This taxonomy places existing methods in a shared design space, where examining individual dimensions and their interactions can inspire new research ideas. Second, we examine how existing RSI methods draw on traditional deep learning, for example through optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning. We develop further ideas by examining more specific learning mechanisms and drawing on evolutionary computation. We also review how existing benchmarks assess self-improvement under online, offline, and offline-to-online settings. Together, these perspectives help researchers develop new RSI research ideas from existing designs and learning mechanisms. RSI papers and resources are available at https://prism-shadow.github.io/awesome-rsi/.
authors: Leijun Zhou, Yanke Yu, Zhihao Liu, Qu Xiang, Tiancheng Hu, Yiru Dong, Yihan Wu, Yangxi Xiang, Xuejun Wu, Xi Chen, Buyue Qian, Yaowei Zheng, Junhao Hu
bullets: Introduces a taxonomy spanning nine RSI design dimensions across update targets, organization, scheduling/scope, and feedback/selection.
Uses the taxonomy to position existing methods in a shared design space and identify promising combinations.
Relates RSI techniques to deep-learning ideas such as optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning.
Draws additional research ideas from specific learning mechanisms and evolutionary computation.
Reviews benchmarks for online, offline, and offline-to-online self-improvement settings.
papers.selection_reason: Taxonomy and analysis of recursive self-improvement spanning continual learning and agent memory; relevant to adaptation and memory.
papers.title: From Existing Methods to New Research Ideas: Two Perspectives on Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: The paper organizes recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods into a unified design framework and connects them to established learning mechanisms to generate new research directions.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones while the model is already deployed, operating directly on a continual unlabeled test-time stream. Existing TTD methods are overly conservative, making known and unknown features collapse together and difficult to separate during test-time adaptation. In this paper, we revisit TTD from an energy perspective and find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable and easily collapses. We therefore propose Energy Ring to stabilize this gap by anchoring the two types of classes on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter enlarges the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, and a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes. During testing, energy-guided confidence weighting improves prediction, and a stability-based rectification mechanism corrects unreliable updates. Experimental results show that Energy Ring significantly improves TTD performance against existing TTD methods.
authors: Tianle Liu, Fan Lyu, Tingliang Feng, Chenggong Ni, Tianqi Wang, Zhang Zhang, Fuyuan Hu, Rui Yao, Tao Zhou
bullets: Targets the collapse of known and unknown feature representations in continual, unlabeled test streams.
Anchors known and unknown classes on separate energy rings to preserve a stable energy gap.
Uses a lightweight adapter to enlarge norm-based separation while retaining known-class directions.
Applies perturbation consistency to compact unknown-class clusters and energy-guided confidence weighting for prediction.
Adds stability-based rectification to correct unreliable test-time updates and reports significant gains over existing TTD methods.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'Energy Ring', a method for stabilizing feature energy during test-time discovery to separate known and unknown classes, directly addressing test-time adaptation challenges.
papers.title: Energy Ring: Stabilizing Feature Energy for Reliable Test-Time Discovery
papers.tldr: Energy Ring improves test-time discovery by stabilizing the energy separation between known and unknown classes during adaptation.

papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.
authors: Yilin Wu, Rutav Shah, Shuaiyi Huang, Sumedh A. Sontakke, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Andrea Bajcsy, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Addresses shortcut learning and deployment latency caused by conditioning on all past observations.
Compresses observations, actions, and proprioception into incrementally updated latent memory for VLA policies.
Uses two-stage training: reconstruct past information and estimate task progress, then jointly fine-tune for action prediction.
Improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26% across simulation and real-world tasks.
Reports the lowest inference latency among evaluated memory-augmented VLAs; ablations support using diverse streams without history curation.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-stream latent memory for VLA robot policies, directly relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
papers.tldr: IMPRINT gives robot policies low-latency, multi-stream latent memory without manually curating history, improving success on memory-intensive tasks.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables time series forecasters to update after deployment as new observations become available. However, adaptation objectives that focus primarily on prediction errors at individual time steps do not fully address the needs of financial time series forecasting. In addition to pointwise return fitting, return direction and the price trajectories reconstructed from sequences of returns are also important. To better account for these properties, we introduce Direction- and Price-Aware Adaptation Loss (DPAL), which combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms. We apply DPAL within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without modifying the source forecaster or the adapter architecture. Across a diverse collection of financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price mean squared error in most evaluated settings.
authors: Wuzhou Lian, Haochun Wang, Yuefan Deng
bullets: Financial TTA objectives based only on pointwise prediction errors may miss directional and price-trajectory quality.
DPAL combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms.
It can be applied within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without changing the forecaster or adapter architecture.
Across diverse financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price MSE in most evaluated settings.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a test-time adaptation loss for financial time-series forecasting, directly matching test-time learning.
papers.title: DPAL: A Test-Time Adaptation Loss for Financial Time Series Forecasting
papers.tldr: DPAL improves test-time adaptation for financial forecasting by jointly optimizing return accuracy, direction, and reconstructed-price calibration.

papers.abstract: Regularization-based continual learning protects each parameter in proportion to an estimate of its importance, yet these estimates come from finite samples and heuristics and are used as if they were exact. We report four studies that start from a biologically inspired mechanism and end with a statistical explanation of it. Motivated by dendritic nanotubes, we let transient lateral links diffuse importance tags between hidden units. Links between co-active units gave no significant gain, but random links with lifetimes of 25 or 200 steps raised final accuracy on 20-task Permuted MNIST by 1.5 to 2.6 points. We show that random diffusion implements linear shrinkage of importance toward the layer mean in expectation. A simulation of the link process alone predicts shrinkage weights of 0.23 and 0.52 for these lifetimes, and graph-free shrinkage at 0.25 and 0.5 reproduces both the accuracy and the dispersion of the consolidated importance, while every activity-dependent rule did worse than random links. A five-seed screen across EWC, SI, and MAS found nominal gains for SI and MAS on Permuted MNIST and losses on task-incremental Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was small and shrinkage cost plasticity. Varying the number of importance samples then separates two mechanisms on Permuted MNIST. For EWC, the gain fell by about ten points per tenfold increase in samples, from 19.6 points with 10 samples to -0.4 with 1000, a variance effect. For MAS, a gain of about one point persisted at 1000 samples, consistent with a bias in the importance measure rather than noise. Shrinkage had no detectable effect for MAS on a domain-incremental CIFAR-100 benchmark. Finally, we show that a standard heteroscedastic empirical Bayes rule shrinks the largest Fisher-type estimates most, which may explain its poor results, and point to a log-scale alternative.
bullets: Activity-dependent dendritic-style links provided no significant benefit; random transient links improved 20-task Permuted MNIST accuracy by 1.5–2.6 points.
The link process is mathematically equivalent in expectation to linear shrinkage, and graph-free shrinkage reproduced both accuracy and importance dispersion.
Benefits varied across methods: SI and MAS gained on Permuted MNIST, while shrinkage hurt Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was already small.
For EWC, gains disappeared as the number of importance samples increased, indicating variance reduction; MAS retained a smaller gain, suggesting estimator bias.
A standard heteroscedastic empirical-Bayes rule over-shrinks large Fisher-type estimates; a log-scale alternative is proposed.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies importance-estimate shrinkage and regularization-based continual learning, fitting the continual and online learning subtopic.
papers.title: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? Two Reasons for Shrinking Importance Estimates in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Random diffusion improves continual learning mainly by statistically shrinking noisy parameter-importance estimates toward the layer mean, with benefits depending on the importance estimator and task setting.

papers.abstract: Image-level MRI harmonization is often evaluated with a frozen site probe, a site classifier trained on raw scans and applied unchanged to harmonized ones: a drop in its accuracy is read as removal of site effects. We audit this practice on ABIDE I (1,112 T1-weighted scans, 17 sites) with ten output sets from seven harmonization methods and controls for chance, head shape, intensity, preprocessing and target alignment. We find that this verdict depends on how the probe is trained, even among probes that classify raw scans well: across random seeds, its balanced accuracy on the same CycleGAN outputs ranges from 0.13 to 0.59 (chance: 0.06). Low frozen-probe accuracy can also arise without harmonization: a Gaussian blur, which increases the intensity distance to the target site, lowers this accuracy to chance. Moreover, where the frozen probe fails, probes trained on the harmonized scans still recover the site, even from intensity histograms alone: on HACA3 outputs, the frozen probe scores 0.25, a probe trained on those outputs 0.75, and one using only their intensity histograms 0.71. Low frozen-probe accuracy therefore does not show that site information has been removed. We recommend reporting several probes trained to convergence, probes trained on harmonized scans, and target alignment.
authors: Muhammad Muqsit Islam, Gloria Garc\'ia Cuenco, Jos\'e M. Mart\'inez, Pierrick Coup\'e
bullets: The audit examines ten harmonized output sets from seven methods on ABIDE I MRI scans, with controls for chance, image properties, preprocessing, and target alignment.
Frozen-probe balanced accuracy varies widely across random seeds on identical outputs, despite strong raw-scan classification performance.
Non-harmonizing changes such as Gaussian blur can reduce frozen-probe accuracy to chance while increasing mismatch with the target site.
Site information can remain recoverable from harmonized scans, including from intensity histograms, even when the frozen probe performs poorly.
The authors recommend multiple converged probes, probes retrained on harmonized outputs, and explicit target-alignment reporting.
papers.selection_reason: Audits evaluation practices for multi-site MRI harmonization, highlighting the limitations of frozen site probes and proposing better metrics for adaptation across sites.
papers.title: Frozen Site-Probe Accuracy Is Not a Standalone Harmonization Score: An Audit of Evaluation Practice for Multi-Site MRI
papers.tldr: Frozen site-probe accuracy is an unreliable standalone measure of MRI harmonization because low scores can reflect probe instability or image degradation rather than removal of site information.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.
authors: Hansi Yang, Linji Hao, Hongyan Hao, An Wang, Han Wu, Qi Gu, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses one-shot, teacher-dependent training pipelines for agents operating in sandbox workspaces with filesystems and shells.
Combines task synthesis, SFT and/or RL training, and diagnosis-driven feedback into an iterative loop.
Uses difficulty growth and agent-free plus agent-based validation to refine generated tasks.
With Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, reports consistent improvements across SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench.
Tasks refined by the loop transfer to smaller Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models, with gains across all reported benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Self-improving agent training loop with iterative task synthesis and feedback; fits continued/online learning and adaptation.
papers.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
papers.tldr: ClawLoop creates a teacher-free, self-improving training cycle for harness-based LLM agents by synthesizing tasks, training the agent, and feeding rollout diagnoses back into future task generation.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. We introduce predictive self-evolution through an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM). Before evaluation, the IDM predicts task-level outcomes of a proposed modification and guides an optional revision. After evaluation, past modifications and their observed outcomes are used to improve the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations. The system can thus improve how it solves tasks, proposes modifications, and predicts their effects. Building on HyperAgents, we evaluate this approach across multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level mathematical grading. Our approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with up to 46% higher average performance over generations. Gains also persist under matched token budgets that include both agent evolution and task evaluation, and extend to held-out tasks. Forecast accuracy improves as the IDM evolves, and the learned predictive knowledge transfers to improve evolution in a new domain.
authors: Zixuan Xie, Chang Xu, Yuhua Jiang, Li Zhao
bullets: Existing self-evolving agents learn from modifications only after evaluation, while aggregate feedback can hide failure-specific repair needs.
The Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM) predicts task-level effects of proposed changes and can guide revisions before evaluation.
Observed modification outcomes update the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations and transfer to new domains.
Evaluated on multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level math grading using HyperAgents as a baseline.
The approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with gains of up to 46% in average performance; forecast accuracy also improves over time.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving agents with an improvement dynamics model that predicts and learns from modifications during deployment; fits test-time and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Predict Before You Modify: Learning Improvement Dynamics for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.tldr: Predictive self-evolution uses an editable model to forecast and refine agent modifications before costly evaluation, improving performance across diverse domains.

papers.abstract: A robot's learned model of its own dynamics is only valid until those dynamics change: actuators wear, payloads shift, and joints stiffen. A model-based agent that keeps training as if nothing happened adapts slowly, dragged back by a replay buffer full of stale experience. We present Changepoint-Aware World Models (CAWM), a DreamerV3 agent that detects an abrupt dynamics shift from its own internal prediction error, using an online CUSUM test against a rolling baseline that fires only on abrupt change rather than on slow learning drift. It then forgets stale replay, keeping the learned representation while flushing obsolete data. On simulated locomotion under two robot-relevant shifts, doubled gravity and halved actuator gain, CAWM recovers substantially faster than passive retraining. It also beats a strong baseline that respawns a fresh dynamics model on detection, the deep-world-model analogue of model-bank methods. With the response triggered at the shift, CAWM gains +95 to +153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds, while matching that respawn at asymptote. Running the detector in closed loop reproduces this gain on the gravity shift. The benefit holds across both shift types, and is largest when the shift is severe enough that old data is genuinely obsolete.
bullets: Targets slow adaptation after actuator wear, payload changes, or joint stiffening make stored experience obsolete.
Uses DreamerV3 with an online CUSUM test on internal prediction error to detect abrupt shifts without reacting to gradual learning drift.
Flushes obsolete replay data instead of retraining from stale experience or replacing the entire dynamics model.
On simulated locomotion with doubled gravity or halved actuator gain, it recovers faster than passive retraining and fresh-model respawning.
With shift-triggered detection, it gains 95–153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds and matches respawning at asymptote; benefits are largest for severe shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Detects dynamics shifts in model-based RL and forgets stale replay, directly relevant to world models, online adaptation, and robot learning.
papers.title: Changepoint-Aware World Models: Detecting Dynamics Shifts and Recovering by Forgetting Stale Replay in Model-Based RL
papers.tldr: CAWM detects abrupt robot-dynamics changes and rapidly adapts by discarding stale replay while preserving its learned representation.

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) in unknown multi-floor environments presents a significant challenge. Recent methods, mostly based on semantic value greedy waypoint selection, spatial topology-enhanced memory, and Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a decision-making framework, have led to improvements. However, these architectures struggle to balance exploration and exploitation for ZSON when encountering unseen environments, especially in multi-floor settings, such as robots getting stuck at narrow intersections, endlessly wandering, or failing to find stair entrances. To overcome these challenges, we propose AERR-Nav, a Zero-Shot Object Navigation framework that dynamically adjusts its state based on the robot's environment. Specifically, AERR-Nav has the following two key advantages: (1) An Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy, enables robots to dynamically transition between three states, facilitating specialized responses to diverse navigation scenarios. (2) An Adaptive Exploration State featuring Fast and Slow-Thinking modes helps robots better balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning based on evolving environmental information. Extensive experiments on the HM3D and MP3D benchmarks demonstrate that our AERR-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the efficacy of our proposed strategy and modules.
authors: Jingzhi Huang, Junkai Huang, Haoyang Yang, Haoang Li, Yi Wang
bullets: Targets common failures such as getting stuck at narrow intersections, wandering indefinitely, and missing stair entrances.
Uses an Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy to select navigation states based on environmental conditions.
Its exploration state combines Fast- and Slow-Thinking modes to balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning.
Experiments on HM3D and MP3D report state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods, with ablations supporting the proposed components.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot object navigation with adaptive exploration-recovery-reminiscing and MLLM-based decision-making; directly fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: AERR-Nav: Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
papers.tldr: AERR-Nav improves zero-shot object navigation in unseen multi-floor environments by adaptively switching among exploration, recovery, and reminiscing behaviors.

papers.abstract: An ideal (language) model must continually update its knowledge. Existing work largely focuses on making these updates efficient after training. We investigate how the organization of time-varying knowledge during pre-training shapes the efficiency of subsequent updates. Models trained on chronologically ordered knowledge specialize in the most recently encountered knowledge; we call them specialists. In contrast, models trained on the same knowledge in randomly shuffled order perform well across all represented time periods; we call them generalists. Surprisingly, specialists require far fewer update steps than generalists to acquire new knowledge. To explain this advantage, we derive a law from first principles that relates update cost to the model's optimization dynamics and that closely predicts empirical results. Guided by these findings, we design a strategy for organizing pre-training data that preserves stable historical knowledge while enabling efficient updates to current knowledge. We also show that the benefits of temporal knowledge organization extend to real-world pre-trained models and existing knowledge update tools, and generalize to other knowledge orderings. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/specialist/
bullets: Chronological training makes models specialize in recently encountered knowledge, whereas shuffled training produces broader generalists.
Specialists need far fewer update steps to learn new knowledge than generalists.
The paper derives a first-principles law linking update cost to optimization dynamics and predicting empirical behavior.
A data-ordering strategy preserves stable historical knowledge while facilitating updates to current knowledge.
The findings extend to real-world pre-trained models, existing knowledge-editing tools, and other knowledge orderings.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how pre-training knowledge organization affects update efficiency, relevant to continual learning and LLM training.
papers.title: Specialists Learn Faster: Knowledge Organization in Pre-training Shapes Knowledge Update Efficiency
papers.tldr: Organizing pre-training knowledge chronologically creates specialists that update substantially more efficiently than generalists while preserving historical knowledge.

papers.abstract: Agent skills provide a lightweight mechanism for self-evolving agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, existing learned skill curators typically optimize curation without explicitly modeling downstream executor behavior. We show that this can cause systematic cross-executor degradation: curators trained with different executors perform best when paired with their own training executor, indicating that effective skill curation is executor-dependent. We formulate behavior-adaptive skill curation and introduce EASE, a framework that learns a single curator that adapts its decisions to different executor behaviors. EASE maintains an online behavioral profile of recent execution patterns and conditions the curator on this profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills to add, modify, or remove skills from an evolving repository. We train the shared curator jointly across multiple frozen executors with reinforcement learning, using retrieval-aware and behavior-aware temporal attribution to focus optimization on curation actions with observable downstream influence. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, with executors ranging from Qwen3-8B/32B and GPT-OSS-120B to unseen Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, EASE outperforms strong skill- and memory-based baselines without per-executor finetuning. EASE also maintains 34.5--41.0% fewer skills, improves skill retrieval by 36.3--38.7% and measured edit utility by 51.8--60.0%, and reduces deployment-time inference tokens by 9.1--14.5%. These results establish behavior-adaptive skill curation as an effective principle for building self-evolving agents.
bullets: Existing curators can degrade performance when paired with executors different from those used in training.
EASE maintains an online profile of executor behavior and conditions curation on that profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills.
A shared curator is jointly trained across frozen executors using retrieval- and behavior-aware reinforcement-learning attribution.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, EASE outperforms skill- and memory-based baselines, including on unseen executors.
EASE uses 34.5–41.0% fewer skills, improves retrieval by 36.3–38.7% and edit utility by 51.8–60.0%, and reduces inference tokens by 9.1–14.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Behavior-adaptive skill curation enables self-evolving agents to continuously adapt; matches online/continual learning focus.
papers.title: EASE: Behavior-Adaptive Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.tldr: EASE enables one skill curator to adapt to different agent executors, improving skill quality and efficiency without per-executor fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: We propose a linearized Physics-Informed Neural Network (lPINN), a reduced-order neural basis method for forward and inverse differential equations. In an offline stage, lPINN learns operator-compatible continuous neural basis functions from an ensemble of numerical solutions. The basis functions are differentiable through automatic differentiation and are pretrained using solution data together with either derivative information or physics residuals. For each new problem instance, the basis functions are frozen and the solution is obtained by minimizing the governing-equation residual together with applicable initial, boundary, regularization, and observational terms. Unlike surrogate and operator-learning methods, the training data define the trial space offline, while the instance-specific solution is computed online by enforcing the governing physics. Relative to vanilla PINNs, lPINN pretrains the nonlinear hidden-layer representation offline and performs online inference only in the final linear layer. We evaluate lPINN on forward and inverse problems for the advection-diffusion equation, Burgers' equation, and the nonlinear pendulum equation. Compared with vanilla PINNs, lPINN achieves lower solution and parameter errors while reducing online inference times by approximately one to more than three orders of magnitude, with the largest gains generally observed for limited residual or measurement data. Cross-resolution experiments show that the learned continuous representation can be evaluated on finer meshes without retraining and with nearly unchanged accuracy.
bullets: Targets faster and more data-efficient solution of forward and inverse differential equations than vanilla PINNs.
Learns differentiable, operator-compatible basis functions from ensembles of numerical solutions, derivative data, or physics residuals.
Freezes the nonlinear representation for each new instance; online optimization enforces governing equations and relevant initial, boundary, observational, and regularization terms.
Evaluated on advection-diffusion, Burgers’, and nonlinear pendulum equations.

Compared with vanilla PINNs, reports lower solution and parameter errors and online speedups of roughly one to over three orders of magnitude, especially with limited residual or measurement data; supports finer meshes without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Instance-specific online residual minimization over frozen pretrained layers is a test-time optimization method with substantial inference-speed gains.
papers.title: Linearized PINN with pretrained nonlinear layers
papers.tldr: lPINN pretrains physics-compatible neural basis functions offline, then solves new forward or inverse differential-equation problems online using only a linear output layer and physics constraints.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in data-driven robot manipulation policies have substantially improved task execution and generalization. However, real-world deployment still relies heavily on humans for failure assessment, correction, and environment reset, while models often fail to continually learn from failures and corrective experience. We present REVOLVE (Robot Evolving via Orchestrated Loops, Verification, and Experience), an automated closed-loop framework for evolving robot manipulation with minimal human intervention. Built on a unified software platform, REVOLVE integrates data collection, policy training and deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning into a single closed-loop workflow. Its Automated Reset and Correction (ARC) architecture automatically resets the environment and intervenes to correct policy failures. Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) continually improves the manipulation policy and agent by feeding real-world interaction and failure--correction data back into policy learning and using an external mismatch memory to refine agent judgments. Experiments across four real-world manipulation tasks show that, after five iterations, REVOLVE improves average policy success rate by 18.5% and agent judgment accuracy by 8.5%, while reducing human effort in data collection and deployment testing by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively. These results demonstrate that REVOLVE transforms real-world deployment into a closed-loop learning process that continually accumulates and uses execution experience, enabling continual evolution of both the policy and supervisory model with substantially less human intervention.
bullets: Addresses the need for humans to assess failures, correct behavior, and reset environments during real-world deployment.
Integrates data collection, policy training/deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning in one workflow.
Uses Automated Reset and Correction (ARC) for recovery and Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) to improve both manipulation policies and agent judgments.
Across four real-world tasks and five iterations, average policy success rose 18.5% and judgment accuracy rose 8.5%.
Human effort in data collection and deployment testing fell by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop continual learning framework for evolving robot manipulation with minimal human intervention.
papers.title: REVOLVE: An Automated Closed-Loop Framework for Evolving Robot Manipulation with Minimal Human Intervention
papers.tldr: REVOLVE creates a closed-loop robot manipulation system that learns from failures and corrections while sharply reducing human involvement.

papers.abstract: Active exploration and semantic navigation require an embodied agent to build memory from partial observations, predict how the evolution of observed spatial memory may support future motion, and convert that prediction into actionable plans. We present GLAM, a goal-conditioned latent world model trained over global spatiotemporal memory, and GLAM NAV, the complete navigation system built around it. Given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and the current robot pose, GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents, allowing future spatial context and navigation intent to be inferred in a shared representation space. The model follows a JEPA-like latent prediction paradigm, operates directly on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstruction, and uses a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are collected by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scene assets and slicing them into multi-timescale prediction samples. On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV improves over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.
bullets: Uses historical map tokens, the navigation goal, and robot pose to jointly predict future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents.
Applies JEPA-like latent prediction directly to map-level tokens instead of reconstructing RGB observations.
GLAM NAV combines the world model with a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to generate actionable navigation plans.
Trained on replayed ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat using HM3D v0.2 scenes and multi-timescale prediction samples.
On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav reproduction subset, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation.
papers.title: GLAM: Training a latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation
papers.tldr: GLAM learns a goal-conditioned latent world model that predicts future spatial memory and navigation waypoints for active exploration and semantic navigation.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.
authors: Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu, Hao Xiao, Shuhan Xue, Qiang Gao, Wanli Ouyang, Pheng Ann Heng, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: Addresses costly feedback and unreliable world-model predictions as policies evolve.
Selects actions and learning data using JEPA-Anything-based predictive world models.
Adapts world models conditionally and retains updated policy–model pairs only after component and compatibility checks.
Reports gains in code repair, GUI task completion, laboratory planning, reaction optimization, and immune-science workflow development.
Scope includes multiple computational and scientific domains; the abstract does not specify broader limitations.],
papers.selection_reason: Uses predictive world models for recursive self-improvement and retains updated policy-model pairs.
papers.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
papers.tldr: RSI-Anything uses predictive world models and validated policy updates to enable recursive self-improvement across diverse tasks with limited external feedback.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source
authors: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou, Jinhao Jing, Zhengwei Xie, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Tests whether interaction history yields reusable skills rather than merely preserved resources or successful actions.
Uses 19 registered evolution chains, task-state graphs, stage verifiers, reset target worlds, matched source conditions, and provenance tracking.
Compares no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled experience under matched step budgets and five seeds using TSR, WGP, and VMP.
Finds a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed agents, while related experience shows no stable transfer.
Stage audits identify early wood-collection and crafting failures that can prevent later capabilities from being observed.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled benchmark for embodied agents' experience-driven self-improvement, capability transfer, and interaction memory.
papers.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
papers.tldr: MC-EvoBench is a controlled Minecraft benchmark showing that agents’ prior experience does not yet reliably produce durable, transferable capabilities.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering module. We propose Dream to Remember (D2R), which continually steers a frozen generalist policy toward new tasks, while retaining its earlier skills. As the steering module learns a new task, a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, anchoring the module to its earlier behavior without a replay buffer or new data. When the world model is faithful enough, D2R learns the new task entirely in imagination. Otherwise, it learns the task in the environment while using the world model only to rehearse prior tasks. On CALVIN, D2R improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, raising average success from 63.7% to 74.8%, while LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence drops it to 11.7%. With a frozen off-the-shelf generalist policy and world model, $\pi_0$ and A2World, D2R learns unseen LIBERO-90 tasks in the environment while keeping $\pi_0$'s performance on the LIBERO suites it was fine-tuned on, even though the world model is not accurate enough for policy optimization. Finally, on a real Franka robot, D2R improves three tasks in sequence entirely in imagination while retaining the earlier improvements.
authors: Bahey Tharwat, Iman Nematollahi, Marvin Alles, Xingyuan Zhang, Akshay L Chandra, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when adapting robot policies to sequentially arriving tasks.
Learns a steering module for a frozen generative policy rather than changing the policy weights.
Uses a frozen pretrained world model to rehearse prior tasks via imagined rollouts, avoiding replay buffers or additional data.
Can learn new tasks entirely in imagination when the world model is sufficiently accurate; otherwise, it combines environment learning with imagined rehearsal.
Demonstrated on CALVIN, LIBERO, and a real Franka robot, retaining prior abilities while improving sequentially added tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Fits robot policy learning/manipulation and continual learning via world-model rehearsal.
papers.title: Dream to Remember: Continual Steering of Generalist Robot Policies with World Models
papers.tldr: D2R continually improves a frozen generalist robot policy on new tasks while preserving earlier skills through world-model rehearsal.

papers.abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is increasingly used to evaluate whether neural networks can infer task-specific transformations from few demonstrations. Recent ARC models differ in architecture, but also in broader training and evaluation protocols, including pretraining data, data augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, making conclusions about architecture benefits debatable. In this work, we study how the performance of the vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM models is affected by pretraining and test-time training (TTT) budgets under a common inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1. We cross five pretraining budgets with four TTT budgets for each test task. Each budget specifies a task-variant count and total sample presentations, defining the controlled training budgets. We observe that increasing TTT sample presentations improves the standard ARC pass@2 metric in all settings for both models. Increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only TRM, whereas VARC often performs better with fewer variants. VARC also remains competitive without pretraining, while TRM benefits much more from it. These results show that pretraining and TTT budgets affect ARC evaluation and motivate reporting at comparable budgets.
bullets: Evaluates vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM under a common protocol.
Crosses five pretraining budgets with four per-task test-time training budgets.
More test-time sample presentations improve pass@2 for both models.
More task variants consistently help TRM but can hurt VARC; TRM benefits more from pretraining.
Findings support reporting ARC results at comparable training and evaluation budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of pretraining and test-time training budgets for ARC models; directly relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: Pretraining and Test-Time Training Budgets Matter for ARC: A Controlled Study of VARC and TRM
papers.tldr: A controlled ARC-AGI-1 study shows that pretraining and test-time training budgets substantially influence VARC and TRM performance, complicating architecture comparisons.

papers.abstract: Earnings call transcription presents a realistic continual learning scenario where Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are updated with new recordings but risk catastrophic forgetting of previously learned financial speech patterns. Adapting Whisper-small from a general-domain speech corpus to the Earnings22 benchmark reveals the opposite: all evaluated methods exhibit improvement on held-out financial speech from the same domain during adaptation rather than forgetting. This task complementarity makes regularization counterproductive. Nevertheless, when regularization is warranted, a layer-wise mini-Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (mini-KFAC) approximation seems to achieve lower word error rates (WERs) and more stable optimization than standard diagonal Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). The results suggest that task complementarity should be assessed before applying continual learning constraints, and prefer mini-KFAC EWC over diagonal EWC when needed.
bullets: Studies continual learning for earnings-call ASR when adapting Whisper-small to financial speech.
All evaluated methods improve held-out speech from the same domain during adaptation, indicating task complementarity.
Regularization is therefore counterproductive for this adaptation scenario.
When regularization is needed, layer-wise mini-KFAC EWC appears to yield lower WER and more stable optimization than diagonal EWC.
The findings recommend checking task complementarity before imposing continual-learning constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates continual learning regularization (EWC and mini-KFAC) for ASR systems, directly addressing the 'Continual and Online Learning' subtopic.
papers.title: Does Financial Speech Need Continual Learning Regularization? A Study of EWC and mini-KFAC on Earnings Call ASR
papers.tldr: Financial ASR adaptation on Earnings22 improves prior financial-speech performance rather than causing forgetting, making continual-learning regularization unnecessary in this setting.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.
authors: Zijun Wang, Yifan Ji, Haidong Xin, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu, Maosong Sun
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retrieving relevant evidence spread across distant sessions.
Stores lightweight episode-level metadata and links to original interactions as retrieval cues.
At test time, progressively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions during reasoning.
Evaluations on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show consistent gains over strong baselines across backbone LLMs.
Deferring construction enables memory organization to adapt dynamically to each query’s information needs.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes test-time memory construction that adaptively builds query-specific memory during inference, directly relevant to LLM memory and test-time learning.
papers.title: Test-Time Memory Construction
papers.tldr: T²Mem builds query-specific memory at inference time, helping LLMs answer questions over long, scattered interaction histories with lower construction overhead.

papers.abstract: The escalating environmental footprint of the Information and Communication Technol- ogy (ICT) sectorwith global Data Center electric- ity usage potentially reaching 3% by 2030 and the imperative for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings demand a foundational shift towards Edge Computing. This article proposes a holis- tic architectural and algorithmic approach for cre- ating autonomous, resilient, and privacy-preserving learning systems within smart buildings, advancing the core concept of the building itself as the data center. Our contributions, demonstrating originality compared to conventional centralized systems, are structured around three main pillars: 1) Validation of resilient data acquisition chains using the af- fordable Arduino ecosystem (Uno R4 WiFi/BME280) and secure persistence solutions including centralized archiving (Node-RED/MySQL) and secure remote transfer (Python/rsync/SSH). 2). The proposal of a lightweight, KOptim orchestration framework, inter- operable with the FIWARE standard, for the dynamic management of Service Level Agreements (SLA). 3) The adaptation and experimental valida- tion of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low- power microcontrollers,We introduce and compare an iterative learning strategy using data buffers, featuring sorting and explicit preservation of extreme samples to maintain diversity. Experimental results on the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data confirm that this novel method, despite introducing a necessary temporal complexity of O(W log W ) due to sorting, achieves convergence and final result quality that is visually equivalent to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states.
bullets: Addresses ICT energy use and the need for real-time smart-building responsiveness by treating the building as a local data center.
Uses Arduino-based sensing with centralized and secure remote data persistence.
Introduces KOptim, a lightweight FIWARE-interoperable framework for dynamic SLA management.
Adapts Generalized Hebbian Algorithm PCA to low-power microcontrollers using buffered, sorted data while preserving extreme samples.
On Tour Perret sensor data, the method identifies two operational states with quality visually equivalent to full-memory processing, at added O(W log W) temporal complexity.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses algorithmic adaptation and memory constraints in edge computing systems for smart buildings, relevant to efficient AI and adaptation strategies.
papers.title: Sustainable Cloud-Fog-Edge Systems for Smart Buildings: Algorithmic Adaptation under Memory Constraints and Dynamic Orchestration Strategies
papers.tldr: A smart-building cloud–fog–edge architecture combines resilient sensing, dynamic SLA orchestration, and memory-efficient PCA learning for autonomous and privacy-preserving operation.

papers.abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.
authors: Yang Wang, Ping Liu, Ruiyu Wang, Xuhua Chen, Lingfeng Zhang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Targets manipulation tasks where execution state must be tracked and previously visible evidence recovered.
Uses a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet temporal compressor with progress prediction and action-conditioned reconstruction.
Adds a task-conditioned frame retriever and encodes selected frames with 16 spatial tokens; the compressor is frozen during joint retrieval-policy training.
On 16 RoboMME tasks, mean success is 49.22% versus 44.51% for FrameSamp+Modul; real-robot mean success is 62.5% versus 37.5%.
Cup-swap failures indicate persistent object-identity tracking remains unresolved.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces memory mechanisms for VLA policies, directly relevant to VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: Dual-stream memory improves vision-language-action manipulation by combining compressed execution history with selective retrieval of relevant past frames.

papers.abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.
authors: Woosung Koh, Hyunsoo Lee, Kyungjae Lee, Haeju Park, Dahyun Lee, Dasol Hwang, Moontae Lee
bullets: Small models struggle with standard self-distillation because they lack strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities.
The authors link poor acquisition and forgetting to distribution shift during post-training, motivating in-distribution learning.
SynthSelf uses a minimally larger, same-family aligner to generate in-distribution rewrites, combined with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling.
Across 4 acquisition datasets, 14 retention benchmarks, and 3 small-model scales, SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 compared methods.
The approach targets low-latency and on-device continual learning, though its scope is evaluated within the reported small-model and benchmark settings.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual post-training and forgetting in small models via synthetic self-distillation, directly relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation
papers.tldr: SynthSelf enables small models to continually learn new capabilities while retaining prior knowledge by using synthetic, in-distribution self-distillation supervision.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.
authors: Chejian Xu, Shujian Zhang, Wenxuan Zhou, John Lambert, Beck Chen, Bo Li, Andrew Hard, Rajiv Mathews
bullets: Addresses the gap between approaches that separately update model weights or agent harnesses.
Uses a dual-role policy as both a Proposer of harness edits and a Reflector that diagnoses outcomes and guides revisions.
Introduces EvoTIDE, which recovers training trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, combining SFT with interleaved GRPO.
Achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, exceeding the reported strongest-baseline results of 62.6% and 41.0%.
Evolved harnesses transfer across tasks; the framework also improves a GPT-5-mini agent from 24.4% to 48.3%.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving agents with weight-harness co-evolution fits adaptation and memory.
papers.title: Evo$^2$: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution
papers.tldr: Evo² jointly evolves language-model weights and agent harnesses, substantially improving self-evolving coding agents and enabling transfer across models and tasks.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.
authors: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He, Rui Huang, Zilong Zheng, Zhenliang Zhang, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Evaluates continual learning through compositional generalization: agents learn basic tasks before tackling unseen advanced tasks.
Experiments span multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinct behaviors.
Experience from basic tasks consistently improves performance on advanced tasks, including as task complexity rises.
Agents struggle in zero-shot settings and fail to gain proportional benefits from increasing amounts of experience.
The benchmark supports research on more effective self-evolving embodied agents.
papers.selection_reason: First benchmark for continual learning in embodied agents, directly combining embodied AI with continual learning evaluation.
papers.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: EmbodiedCLBench introduces the first embodied-simulation benchmark for testing whether agents can continually recombine learned skills to solve increasingly complex tasks.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.
authors: Duy Nguyen, Lesly Miculicich, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Shuo Li, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham, Mohit Bansal, Tomas Pfister, Long T. Le
bullets: Targets safety and security risks when agents access sensitive documents or mutable system states.
Represents guardrails as executable symbolic rules over typed agent events.
Uses an LLM to propose policy patches from deployment feedback, then accepts only structurally valid, conflict-free updates.
An evidence-aware authority layer prevents insufficiently supported rules from affecting decisions.
Outperforms baselines across three benchmarks and under mixed, corrupted-feedback, and longer-horizon conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Lifelong evolution of formal guardrail policies for LLM agents; fits deployment-time adaptation and continual learning.
papers.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
papers.tldr: VEPA enables LLM agent guardrails to adapt to newly observed risks while preserving deterministic, formally verified action decisions.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
authors: Yudong Liu, Yueqian Lin, Zijia Tang, Yuxi Zheng, Yuan Li, Shuai Zhang, Yi Li, Taotao Jing, Shuangjun Liu, Dashan Gao, Ning Bi, Jingwei Sun, Yiran Chen, Hai Helen Li
bullets: Addresses VLA failures on tasks requiring information from events far before the current frame.
Uses SAM-3 for spatial grounding, a VLM writer for concise episodic summaries, and a VLM reasoner to produce grounded subgoals.
Maintains an append-only text memory bank and verifies, corrects, defers, or rejects claims using mechanical visual evidence.
Recovers much of the privileged-oracle performance on a 16-task suite, reaching the oracle ceiling on several tasks.
Transfers to a second benchmark without changing its contracts; performance is scoped to the tested memory-manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Grounded multi-agent memory system with mechanical audit for memory-intensive VLA manipulation.
papers.title: Gamma: Grounded Multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit for Memory-Intensive Manipulation
